cards.q: The three prenatal stages and their durations
cards.a:
The three prenatal stages and their durations
Ovum — 12–14 days
Embryo — 54–56 days
Fetus — 210–214 days

[Ch01 S2–S5]

cards.q: Gestation, expressed three ways (per the slides)
cards.a:
Gestation, expressed three ways (per the slides)
40 weeks = 9 months = 3 trimesters of 3 months each, with 3 stages of development

[Ch01 S2]

cards.q: What defines the END of the embryo stage?
cards.a:
What defines the END of the embryo stage?
A SIZE criterion, not a date — the embryo measures roughly 3 cm head to rump (crown–rump)

[Ch01 S4]

cards.q: Postnatal stages: neonate / infant / child age ranges
cards.a:
Postnatal stages: neonate / infant / child age ranges
Neonate — delivery through the first month of life
Infant — 1 month to 1 year
Child — above 1 year of age

[Ch01 S6]

cards.q: The five pulmonary developmental stages, in order
cards.a:
The five pulmonary developmental stages, in order
Embryonal → Pseudoglandular → Canalicular → Saccular → Alveolar

(S10 spells it "Psuedoglandular"; S12 spells it correctly)

[Ch01 S10–S14]

cards.q: When do the lungs BEGIN to develop?
cards.a:
When do the lungs BEGIN to develop?
At 24 days, during the embryonal stage (first 7 weeks)

[Ch01 S11]

cards.q: When are TRUE alveoli present, and until what age does alveolar number increase?
cards.a:
When are TRUE alveoli present, and until what age does alveolar number increase?
True alveoli present 32–34 weeks
Number of alveoli increases until around age 8

[Ch01 S14]

cards.q: Which is the first major organ to develop, and when is it fully formed?
cards.a:
Which is the first major organ to develop, and when is it fully formed?
The heart — fully formed and functional by the 8th gestational week

[Ch01 S21]

cards.q: When does surfactant production begin?
cards.a:
When does surfactant production begin?
24 weeks gestation

[Ch01 S17]

cards.q: L/S ratio indicating lung maturity — value and gestational age
cards.a:
L/S ratio indicating lung maturity — value and gestational age
L/S ratio 2:1, generally around 35 weeks gestation

[Ch01 S18]

cards.q: Nägele's rule
cards.a:
Nägele's rule
Subtract 3 months from the first day of the last menstrual period, then add 7 days

[Ch02 S11]

cards.q: How is fundal height measured?
cards.a:
How is fundal height measured?
Tape measure on the abdomen — distance from the symphysis pubis to the top of the fundus

[Ch02 S11]

cards.q: Quickening — what is it and when does it occur?
cards.a:
Quickening — what is it and when does it occur?
The first sensation of fetal movement — generally 16–22 weeks

[Ch02 S12]

cards.q: When is the fetal heartbeat heard?
cards.a:
When is the fetal heartbeat heard?
Between week 16 and 20

[Ch02 S12]

cards.q: The two named gestational-age assessment exams
cards.a:
The two named gestational-age assessment exams
Dubowitz and Ballard

(The slides give no point values and no score-to-weeks conversion)

[Ch05 S7]

cards.q: The 7 physical criteria scored by the gestational-age exams
cards.a:
The 7 physical criteria scored by the gestational-age exams
Vernix · skin maturity · lanugo · ear recoil · breast tissue · genitalia · sole creases

[Ch05 S8]

cards.q: The three size-for-gestational-age classifications
cards.a:
The three size-for-gestational-age classifications
AGA — appropriate for gestational age
SGA — small for gestational age
LGA — large for gestational age

(No percentile cut-offs are given on any slide)

[Ch05 S9]

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — percentile cut-offs for SGA / AGA / LGA, and low birth weight
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — percentile cut-offs for SGA / AGA / LGA, and low birth weight
SGA — birth weight < 10th percentile for GA
AGA — 10th–90th percentile
LGA — > 90th percentile
Low birth weight = < 2500 g, regardless of GA (weight-only label)

⚠️ Not on any slide — outside source (WHO / StatPearls)

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — gestational-age week bands (preterm → post-term)
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — gestational-age week bands (preterm → post-term)
Preterm < 37 0/7 wk (late preterm 34 0/7–36 6/7)
Early term 37 0/7–38 6/7
Full term 39 0/7–40 6/7
Late term 41 0/7–41 6/7
Post-term ≥ 42 0/7

The single "term = 37–42 wk" label was retired in 2013 (ACOG CO 579).

⚠️ No slide defines a week band — outside source

cards.q: The extra-fetal ("associated") structures named by the slides
cards.a:
The extra-fetal ("associated") structures named by the slides
Placenta · umbilical cord (three vessels) · amnion · amniotic fluid

[Ch01 S7–S9]

cards.q: The placenta — function, size and weight at term
cards.a:
The placenta — function, size and weight at term
The organ of respiration for the fetus; provides nutrients and oxygen
At term occupies 1/3 of the uterine surface and weighs about 1 pound
There is no exchange of maternal and fetal blood

[Ch01 S7, S21]

cards.q: Amniotic fluid — the four facts the slides give
cards.a:
Amniotic fluid — the four facts the slides give
About 1 liter at term
Constantly absorbed and replenished
Allows fetal movement and provides protection
Aids in thermoregulation

[Ch01 S9]

cards.q: Why fetal pressures allow right-to-left shunting
cards.a:
Why fetal pressures allow right-to-left shunting
Pressures are the reverse of the adult's — pressure in the right is higher than the left, because the developing lungs are highly resistant to blood flow while the placenta is less resistant

[Ch01 S22]

cards.q: The three fetal shunts and where each sends blood
cards.a:
The three fetal shunts and where each sends blood
Ductus venosus → inferior vena cava
Foramen ovale → right to left atrium
Ductus arteriosus → aorta

[Ch01 S24]

cards.q: Fetal lung fluid — composition and function
cards.a:
Fetal lung fluid — composition and function
The lung produces and secretes its own fluid: low pH, low protein and bicarbonate, high sodium and chloride
It maintains patency of the developing airways and shapes the formation, size and shape of potential air spaces

[Ch01 S19]

cards.q: Baroreceptors — type, location, effect
cards.a:
Baroreceptors — type, location, effect
Stretch receptors
Located in the bifurcation of the carotid arteries and in the aortic arch
They stimulate bradycardia and hypotension

[Ch01 S26]

cards.q: Chemoreceptors — sensitivity, role, location
cards.a:
Chemoreceptors — sensitivity, role, location
Sensitive to PaO2, PaCO2 and pH
Provide regulation of ventilation
Located in the carotid arteries and aorta — the carotid and aortic bodies
Aid in initiation of the first breath

[Ch01 S27]

cards.q: What closes the foramen ovale after birth?
cards.a:
What closes the foramen ovale after birth?
After birth systemic blood pressure rises, and that rise causes closing of the foramen ovale

[Ch01 S25]

cards.q: Ductus arteriosus closure — the slide's timeframe
cards.a:
Ductus arteriosus closure — the slide's timeframe
Occurs over 96 hours; if not closed will require surgical intervention

⚠️ The slide reads "Ductus arteriosus occurs over 96 hours" — the missing word is closure

[Ch01 S25]

cards.q: The first breath — what triggers it (biochemical and physical factors)?
cards.a:
The first breath — what triggers it (biochemical and physical factors)?
Biochemical: changes in PaO2 and PaCO2 in the blood, which signal the muscles of ventilation
Physical: compression of the thorax during birth and change in environment

[Ch03 S11]

cards.q: What happens if fetal lung fluid is NOT cleared?
cards.a:
What happens if fetal lung fluid is NOT cleared?
Transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTN), also called RDS type II — "often occurs in babies delivered by Caesarean"

[Ch01 S20]

cards.q: Definition of asphyxia (the slide's three components)
cards.a:
Definition of asphyxia (the slide's three components)
A combination of hypoxia, hypercapnia (hypercarbia), and acidosis
"May lead to irreversible damage to the brain and other vital organs"
Ch07 calls it the result of placental insufficiency

[Ch04 S2] [Ch07 S17]

cards.q: The four causes of fetal asphyxia (maternal / placental / cord / fetal)
cards.a:
The four causes of fetal asphyxia (maternal / placental / cord / fetal)
Maternal — any disorder causing maternal hypoxia or asphyxia
Placental — insufficient placental blood flow, or reduced diffusion of O2/CO2
Cord — occlusion or blockage of umbilical cord flow
Fetal — anemia and drug toxicity

[Ch04 S3–S4]

cards.q: Stated TREATMENT of fetal asphyxia
cards.a:
Stated TREATMENT of fetal asphyxia
"Immediate reversal of hypoxia and acidosis"

Operationally carried out as the Chapter 4 neonatal resuscitation sequence (warmth → airway → PPV → compressions → intubation → epinephrine)

[Ch07 S18]

cards.q: First symptoms of asphyxia (Ch07)
cards.a:
First symptoms of asphyxia (Ch07)
"Symptoms begin with a decreased heart rate and blood pressure"

[Ch07 S17]

cards.q: ⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — primary vs secondary apnea as [Ch04 S5] defines them
cards.a:
⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — primary vs secondary apnea as [Ch04 S5] defines them
ANSWER THE SLIDE:
Primary apnea = "first attempt of fetus to ventilate"; HR and BP drop, PaCO2 rises, pH drops
Secondary apnea = "second attempt of fetus to ventilate"; respirations are weak, gasping, and ineffective

Standard teaching (NOT your slides): rapid breathing → primary apnea → gasping → secondary apnea. Primary responds to stimulation; secondary does not and needs PPV.

[Ch04 S5]

cards.q: Two antenatal signs of fetal asphyxia (Ch02)
cards.a:
Two antenatal signs of fetal asphyxia (Ch02)
Bradycardia — fetal HR less than 100 bpm — "may be caused by asphyxia" [Ch02 S8]
Meconium in amniotic fluid — the dark greenish stool found in the fetal intestine — "may result from a fetal asphyxia episode" [Ch02 S15]

cards.q: Effects of asphyxia on the lungs
cards.a:
Effects of asphyxia on the lungs
The asphyxiated neonate "may not be able to create the necessary negative force to open the alveoli and aid in lung fluid removal"
Persistent fetal circulation is listed as an effect

[Ch04 S6]

cards.q: Consequences of asphyxia listed on [Ch07 S18]
cards.a:
Consequences of asphyxia listed on [Ch07 S18]
Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy · "Preventricular leukomalacia" (slide spelling; standard term is periventricular) · bowel ischemia · necrotizing enterocolitis · disseminated intravascular coagulation

[Ch07 S18]

cards.q: Fetal scalp pH assessment — what it is for
cards.a:
Fetal scalp pH assessment — what it is for
A secondary tool to monitor fetal well-being — "if fetal blood flow is impaired, it can be detected through a drop in pH"

(No value is given on any slide)

[Ch02 S10]

cards.q: The five components of the biophysical profile
cards.a:
The five components of the biophysical profile
Fetal breathing · fetal movement · fetal limb tone · the nonstress test (NST) · amniotic fluid volume

[Ch02 S14]

cards.q: What does the contraction stress test detect?
cards.a:
What does the contraction stress test detect?
Uteroplacental insufficiency

[Ch02 S13]

cards.q: The three INITIAL STEPS of neonatal resuscitation
cards.a:
The three INITIAL STEPS of neonatal resuscitation
Provide warmth · open the airway · clear the airway

[Ch04 S10]

cards.q: The three questions used to decide if resuscitation is needed
cards.a:
The three questions used to decide if resuscitation is needed
Is the neonate term?
Is the neonate crying or breathing?
Is there good muscle tone?

[Ch04 S9]

cards.q: How is heart rate evaluated in neonatal resuscitation?
cards.a:
How is heart rate evaluated in neonatal resuscitation?
Target greater than 100 bpm
Assess at the umbilical stump
Count for six seconds and multiply by 10

[Ch04 S13]

cards.q: How is color / saturation evaluated in neonatal resuscitation?
cards.a:
How is color / saturation evaluated in neonatal resuscitation?
Blue or pink — visually inspect the central trunk
Evaluate oxygen saturation with a pulse oximeter
Supplemental oxygen if necessary

[Ch04 S14]

cards.q: Which medication is the ONLY one indicated during the acute phase of neonatal resuscitation?
cards.a:
Which medication is the ONLY one indicated during the acute phase of neonatal resuscitation?
Epinephrine
Volume expanders for shock or blood loss
Access is through the umbilical vein

(No dose is given on any slide)

[Ch04 S19]

cards.q: Tocolysis — the slide's complete definition
cards.a:
Tocolysis — the slide's complete definition
"Process of stopping labor" — "can be achieved pharmacologically"

⚠️ That one slide is the ENTIRE tocolytic content of the course. No drug or drug class is named anywhere in any deck.

[Ch03 S5]

cards.q: Non-pharmacologic measures against premature labor (the slide's list)
cards.a:
Non-pharmacologic measures against premature labor (the slide's list)
Family planning · assessment for prenatal patients · patient education to identify signs of premature labor and when to seek help

[Ch03 S5]

cards.q: What percentage of pregnancies end in premature labor?
cards.a:
What percentage of pregnancies end in premature labor?
12%

[Ch03 S5]

cards.q: ⚠️ TRAP — where does the word "sympathomimetics" actually appear in this course?
cards.a:
⚠️ TRAP — where does the word "sympathomimetics" actually appear in this course?
Only as an inhaled bronchodilator class — "relaxation of the bronchial smooth muscles leading to bronchodilation" [Ch14 S12] — never as a uterine relaxant.

Beta sympathomimetics as tocolytics are absent from every deck. Magnesium appears only as an electrolyte, never as a tocolytic.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — what are the 48 hours of tocolysis actually FOR?
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — what are the 48 hours of tocolysis actually FOR?
Tocolytics do not stop preterm birth or improve neonatal outcome by themselves. The 48 hours buy:
1. Antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation
2. Maternal transport to a NICU facility
3. MgSO4 for fetal neuroprotection (< 32 wk) + GBS status

⚠️ Not on any slide — ACOG PB No. 171

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — beta sympathomimetics as tocolytics: agents and mechanism
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — beta sympathomimetics as tocolytics: agents and mechanism
Agents: terbutaline; ritodrine (withdrawn US 1998)
Mechanism: β2 stimulation → ↑ cAMP → uterine smooth muscle relaxation
Maternal effects: tachycardia, tremor, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, pulmonary edema
Fetal/neonatal: fetal tachycardia, neonatal hypoglycemia

RT angle: same drug class you give as a bronchodilator — same β2 mechanism on a different smooth muscle.

⚠️ Not on any slide

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the five tocolytic drug classes
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the five tocolytic drug classes
Beta sympathomimetics — terbutaline, ritodrine
Calcium channel blockers — nifedipine
Prostaglandin (COX) inhibitors — indomethacin
Magnesium sulfate
Oxytocin receptor antagonists — atosiban (not available in US)

⚠️ Not on any slide

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — MgSO4: tocolysis vs neuroprotection
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — MgSO4: tocolysis vs neuroprotection
As a tocolytic: weak/ineffective.
As a neuroprotectant: recommended — before anticipated preterm birth < 32 weeks, reduces cerebral palsy.

Exam phrasing: "In preterm labor, magnesium sulfate is given for neonatal neurologic outcome, not for tocolysis."

⚠️ Not on any slide

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — antenatal corticosteroid regimens
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — antenatal corticosteroid regimens
Betamethasone — 12 mg IM × 2 doses, 24 hours apart
Dexamethasone — 6 mg IM × 4 doses, every 12 hours

Recommended 24 0/7 – 33 6/7 weeks if at risk of delivery within 7 days.
They accelerate type II pneumocyte maturation and surfactant production, reducing RDS, IVH, NEC and mortality.

⚠️ Not on any slide

cards.q: The five components of the APGAR score (as the slides list them)
cards.a:
The five components of the APGAR score (as the slides list them)
Respiratory effort · heart rate · muscle tone · reflex irritability · color

[Ch04 S20]

cards.q: ⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — APGAR timing and function per [Ch04 S21]
cards.a:
⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — APGAR timing and function per [Ch04 S21]
ANSWER THE SLIDE: "Assessed every 5 minutes for up to 20 minutes" and the 5-minute Apgar score is predictive of future impairment — that prognostic use is the only "associated function" given.

⚠️ The slide states no 1-minute assessment anywhere.
Standard teaching (NOT your slides): score at 1 and 5 minutes, then every 5 min to 20 min only if the 5-min score is under 7.

[Ch04 S21]

cards.q: Where else in scope is the Apgar score applied to a diagnosis?
cards.a:
Where else in scope is the Apgar score applied to a diagnosis?
Low Apgar scores are listed as a sign of meconium aspiration syndrome, alongside fetal hypoxia, acidosis, and abnormal fetal heart tracings

[Ch07 S19]

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — APGAR 0/1/2 criteria
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — APGAR 0/1/2 criteria
Appearance: blue/pale = 0 · acrocyanosis = 1 · all pink = 2
Pulse: absent = 0 · < 100 = 1 · > 100 = 2
Grimace: none = 0 · grimace/weak cry = 1 · cries/coughs/sneezes = 2
Activity: limp = 0 · some flexion = 1 · active, well flexed = 2
Respirations: absent = 0 · slow/irregular/gasping = 1 · strong cry = 2

⚠️ The 0/1/2 criteria are absent from every deck

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — APGAR total score interpretation bands
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — APGAR total score interpretation bands
5 signs × 0–2 points → range 0–10
7–10 = reassuring / normal
4–6 = moderately abnormal / intermediate
0–3 = low, severely depressed

The 1-min score reflects how the infant tolerated labor/delivery; the 5-min score reflects response to resuscitation.

⚠️ Not on any slide

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — what the Apgar score is NOT used for
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — what the Apgar score is NOT used for
It does not guide resuscitation. Resuscitation is driven by respirations, heart rate and oxygenation, and must begin before the 1-minute score is assigned.

AAP/ACOG: Apgar scores "should not be used to determine the initial need for intervention, what interventions are indicated, or when to initiate them."

⚠️ Not on any slide

cards.q: ⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — the clinical signs of RDS per [Ch07 S3]
cards.a:
⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — the clinical signs of RDS per [Ch07 S3]
ANSWER THE SLIDE: RR above 60 breaths/min · grunting · "Increased FRC" ⚠️ · chest retractions · nasal flaring

⚠️ Standard teaching (NOT your slides): it should be DECREASED FRC — surfactant deficiency raises surface tension → atelectasis → reduced FRC, compliance and lung volumes. That is why RDS is treated with PEEP/CPAP.

[Ch07 S3]

cards.q: Cause of RDS (per the slides)
cards.a:
Cause of RDS (per the slides)
Deficiency of surfactant production by alveolar type II cells
Also called hyaline membrane disease; "scar-like tissue that replaces the normal alveolar tissue"
Immaturity of other organ systems contributes

[Ch07 S2]

cards.q: TTN — cause and signs
cards.a:
TTN — cause and signs
Cause: retention of fetal lung fluid following birth (also called RDS type II; often after Caesarean)
Signs: tachypnea, nasal flaring, retractions, grunting

[Ch07 S31] [Ch01 S20]

cards.q: The newborn observation list — the 7 findings to observe for
cards.a:
The newborn observation list — the 7 findings to observe for
Tachypnea · tachycardia · grunting · retractions · inability to maintain body temperature · reduced vigor · limp appearance

⚠️ The deck gives no thresholds and no severity grading — it is an observation checklist only.

[Ch05 S6]

cards.q: Anatomic predisposition to high work of breathing — [Ch05 S3]
cards.a:
Anatomic predisposition to high work of breathing — [Ch05 S3]
Low pulmonary reserve · thorax lacks stability · large abdominal contents push up on the diaphragm · obligatory nose breathers · heart is large in proportion to the thorax's diameter

[Ch05 S3]

cards.q: Anatomic predisposition to high work of breathing — [Ch05 S2] (airway/chest)
cards.a:
Anatomic predisposition to high work of breathing — [Ch05 S2] (airway/chest)
Diameter of trachea narrow · ribs and sternum mostly cartilage · tongue larger in area than the adult's · large amount of lymphoid tissue in the pharynx · epiglottis larger and less flexible · larynx higher

[Ch05 S2]

cards.q: Infant metabolism vs the adult — and why it matters
cards.a:
Infant metabolism vs the adult — and why it matters
Higher than adults, which increases oxygen requirement and results in challenges to pharmacotherapy

[Ch05 S4]

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — what does GRUNTING tell you?
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — what does GRUNTING tell you?
An expiratory sound from sudden closure of the glottis during expiration, attempting to maintain FRC and prevent alveolar atelectasis — the infant generates its own PEEP.

So grunting points to a low-FRC / low-compliance problem (RDS, pneumonia, atelectasis, TTN) and is the sign that most often earns CPAP.

⚠️ A grunting baby who goes quiet is TIRING, not improving.

No slide states the significance of grunting.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — retraction sites and what each suggests
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — retraction sites and what each suggests
Suprasternal → upper-airway obstruction
Substernal / xiphoid → diaphragm pulling against stiff lungs
Intercostal → lower airway / parenchymal disease
Subcostal → lower airway / parenchymal (more significant than intercostal)

The more sites and the lower/deeper the retraction, the more severe. See-saw (paradoxical) movement is the worst grade.

⚠️ No slide grades or locates retractions

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — nasal flaring and head bobbing
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — nasal flaring and head bobbing
Nasal flaring — compensatory: increases upper airway diameter, reduces resistance and WOB. Neonates are near-obligate nose breathers, so it is an early, cheap sign.
Head bobbing — sternocleidomastoid contraction with each breath = accessory-muscle use. In an infant it means impending respiratory failure.

⚠️ Not on any slide

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — causes of increased WOB organised by mechanism
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — causes of increased WOB organised by mechanism
↑ Airway resistance: choanal atresia, Pierre Robin, laryngomalacia, subglottic stenosis, croup, foreign body, bronchiolitis, asthma
↓ Lung compliance: RDS, TTN, pneumonia/sepsis, meconium aspiration, atelectasis
↓ Chest-wall compliance: pneumothorax, effusion, CDH
Cardiovascular: CHD, PPHN, PDA
Neuromuscular/central: asphyxia, IVH, maternal narcotics, seizures
Systemic: sepsis, hypoglycemia, hypothermia, metabolic acidosis

⚠️ No slide carries a "causes of increased WOB" list

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — frequency order of newborn respiratory distress at term
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — frequency order of newborn respiratory distress at term
TTN → RDS → meconium aspiration → pneumonia/sepsis → pneumothorax, CHD, CDH
(most → least common)

⚠️ Not on any slide — AFP 2026

cards.q: How is neonatal bacterial infection acquired? (the four routes)
cards.a:
How is neonatal bacterial infection acquired? (the four routes)
Through the placenta · traveling through the birth canal · by direct contact with infected maternal tissue · as a hospital-acquired infection

The deck's framework is by route, not by timing.

[Ch08 S2]

cards.q: Source and spread of neonatal bacterial infection
cards.a:
Source and spread of neonatal bacterial infection
"Often caused by organisms found in the maternal intestinal and genital tracts or by poor aseptic technique"
Organisms "may enter the fetal mouth and infect the lungs, intestinal tract, and may even enter the bloodstream"

[Ch08 S4]

cards.q: Diagnosis and treatment of neonatal bacterial infection
cards.a:
Diagnosis and treatment of neonatal bacterial infection
Diagnosis: "by analysis of specimen or blood test"
Treatment: "broad spectrum antibiotics"

(No organism, drug, dose or duration is ever named)

[Ch08 S13]

cards.q: Which class of neonatal infection does the deck say can be prevented by immunization?
cards.a:
Which class of neonatal infection does the deck say can be prevented by immunization?
VIRAL — "viral diseases can be avoided by prevention and immunization"

Immunization is offered for viral, not bacterial, disease.

[Ch08 S13]

cards.q: The five infection-prevention measures
cards.a:
The five infection-prevention measures
Hand hygiene · use of PPE · safe injection practices · safe handling of potentially contaminated materials and equipment · respiratory hygiene / cough etiquette

[Ch08 S14]

cards.q: Neonatal host defense — the five antibodies
cards.a:
Neonatal host defense — the five antibodies
The fetus gets "some protection through maternal factors," then "develops own immunity," with immunity provided through IgA, IgD, IgE, IgG, IgM

[Ch08 S15]

cards.q: ⚠️ NOT IN THE SLIDES — which bacterial organisms cause neonatal infection?
cards.a:
⚠️ NOT IN THE SLIDES — which bacterial organisms cause neonatal infection?
NO bacterial organism is named for neonatal infection anywhere in Ch01–Ch11.
No group B strep, no E. coli, no Listeria, no Staph, no Klebsiella.

Also absent: early-onset vs late-onset distinction, timing windows, and clinical signs of neonatal bacterial infection.

The only bacterial organism names in scope are in the immunization list [Ch11 S5] — none presented as a sepsis pathogen.

cards.q: The neonatal examination sequence (Ch05)
cards.a:
The neonatal examination sequence (Ch05)
Anatomic background → observation survey → history + gestational age → size classification → quiet examination → hands-on examination → neurologic examination

[Ch05 S2–S14]

cards.q: The Quiet Examination — what do you observe?
cards.a:
The Quiet Examination — what do you observe?
Color · lanugo · activity · overall look · respiration

[Ch05 S11]

cards.q: The Hands-on Examination — the deck's order
cards.a:
The Hands-on Examination — the deck's order
Inspect head and mouth → auscultate chest/heart and lungs → evaluate pulses → measure blood pressure → palpate abdomen → auscultate bowel sounds → measure body temperature

⚠️ Percussion is not mentioned anywhere in Chapter 5.

[Ch05 S12–S13]

cards.q: The four neonatal reflexes
cards.a:
The four neonatal reflexes
Rooting · suck · grasp · Moro
The neurologic exam is "dependent upon intrauterine development"

[Ch05 S14]

cards.q: Purpose of the neonatal physical examination (three stated purposes)
cards.a:
Purpose of the neonatal physical examination (three stated purposes)
Discovery of physical defects · determination of successful transition to extrauterine life · maintenance of thermoregulation

[Ch05 S10]

cards.q: Body composition facts that shape the neonatal exam
cards.a:
Body composition facts that shape the neonatal exam
Large skin surface area → prone to heat loss
80% of body weight is water → makes overhydration and dehydration difficult to manage

(The 80% figure is the only numeric value in all of Chapter 5)

[Ch05 S5]

cards.q: Contraindications to neonatal pulmonary function testing
cards.a:
Contraindications to neonatal pulmonary function testing
Active pulmonary bleeding · open chest wound · untreated pneumothorax

[Ch05 S17]

cards.q: Relative contraindications to neonatal PFT (the sedation-risk conditions)
cards.a:
Relative contraindications to neonatal PFT (the sedation-risk conditions)
Risk of interrupted ventilation outweighs benefit; inadequate sedation/paralysis; uncooperative patient; and sedation may cause untoward events in: central hypoventilation, CNS depression, obstructive sleep apnea, severe obesity, esophagitis or gastritis, hepatic or renal dysfunction

[Ch05 S18]

cards.q: What does neonatal pulmonary function testing measure?
cards.a:
What does neonatal pulmonary function testing measure?
Pulmonary compliance and resistance (pneumotachometer, occlusion techniques) · work of breathing · expiratory flow rates · lung volumes · functional residual capacity · crying vital capacity · Pulmonary Function Profile

[Ch05 S19–S20]

cards.q: The pediatric respiratory history questions [Ch10 S6–S7]
cards.a:
The pediatric respiratory history questions [Ch10 S6–S7]
What is the character of the cough? · What is the pattern of breathing? · Is there history/evidence of wheezing? · Is cyanosis present? · Does the patient complain of chest pain? · What is the nature of the sputum?

[Ch10 S6–S7]

cards.q: Standard measurements to begin the pediatric exam
cards.a:
Standard measurements to begin the pediatric exam
Weight · length/height · head circumference · vital signs
Also: provide a safe environment; tailor the exam to the age and response; interact and engage with the child

⚠️ "Vital signs" is listed with no numbers anywhere

[Ch10 S8–S9]

cards.q: Pediatric pulmonary exam — the THREE jobs and the tools for each
cards.a:
Pediatric pulmonary exam — the THREE jobs and the tools for each
1. Evaluate and localize the disease → chest radiograph, auscultate, percussion, palpation [S13]
2. Observe for adequacy of gas exchange → arterial blood gas, pulse oximetry, transcutaneous monitoring [S14]
3. Determine the nature of ventilations → rate · depth · rhythm · ease of breathing [S15]

[Ch10 S13–S15]

cards.q: Pediatric fever — definition and mechanism
cards.a:
Pediatric fever — definition and mechanism
A rectal temperature above 100.4°F or 38°C
A response to endogenous proteins (pyrogens) that raise the temperature setpoint in the hypothalamus

(The only temperature number in scope)

[Ch11 S8]

cards.q: Acute otitis media — cause and the three diagnostic criteria
cards.a:
Acute otitis media — cause and the three diagnostic criteria
Fluid accumulates in the middle ear → inflammation secondary to bacterial infection; Eustachian tube dysfunction is a leading cause

Three criteria: acute onset of symptoms · presence of fluid in the middle ear · signs and symptoms of inflammation

[Ch11 S9]

cards.q: In-scope TREATMENTS attached to distress diagnoses — RDS
cards.a:
In-scope TREATMENTS attached to distress diagnoses — RDS
Prevention is key
Administration of glucocorticoids to the mother before delivery
Provision of artificial surfactant replacement
Provide adequate ventilation without damaging the lungs

[Ch07 S4]

cards.q: In-scope TREATMENTS — epiglottitis, croup, head injury
cards.a:
In-scope TREATMENTS — epiglottitis, croup, head injury
Epiglottitis — apply oxygen, monitor vitals, prepare to intubate if necessary [Ch09 S14]
Croup — humidifiers, adequate hydration, close observation [Ch09 S15]
Head injury — protect airway, provide ventilation and oxygen, be prepared to intubate [Ch09 S25]

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the five Silverman-Andersen parameters
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the five Silverman-Andersen parameters
Upper chest movement (synchrony) · lower chest (intercostal) retraction · xiphoid retraction · nasal flaring · expiratory grunt
Each 0–2, total 0–10. Higher = worse.
0 = none · 1–3 mild · 4–6 moderate · 7–10 severe

⚠️ Direction check: opposite of Apgar — Silverman 0 = comfortable, 10 = severe.

⚠️ No Silverman score anywhere in the slides

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — New Ballard Score structure
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — New Ballard Score structure
12 criteria — 6 neuromuscular (posture, square window, arm recoil, popliteal angle, scarf sign, heel-to-ear) + 6 physical (skin, lanugo, plantar surface, breast, eye/ear, genitals)
Total −10 to +50; best at 12–24 h of age
Every 5 points = 2 weeks (score 40 = 40 weeks)

Dubowitz — older, 21 criteria, 10–15 min; overestimates GA in infants < 33 weeks

⚠️ No point values on any slide

cards.q: Thermoregulation — definition and why it matters
cards.a:
Thermoregulation — definition and why it matters
"The maintenance of equality between heat dissipation and heat production by the body"
"One of the most important aspects in the care of the neonatal patient"

[Ch06 S2]

cards.q: How does the neonate produce heat?
cards.a:
How does the neonate produce heat?
The neonate "relies ENTIRELY on metabolism of BROWN FAT for heat production"
Goal: maintain environmental temperature in the thermal zone

[Ch06 S3]

cards.q: The INTERNAL thermal gradient — definition and the four regulators
cards.a:
The INTERNAL thermal gradient — definition and the four regulators
The temperature difference between the warm body core and the cooler skin
Regulated by: metabolic rate · amount of subcutaneous fat · surface area available for dissipation of heat · distance from body core to skin surface

[Ch06 S4]

cards.q: The EXTERNAL thermal gradient — definition and the four mechanisms
cards.a:
The EXTERNAL thermal gradient — definition and the four mechanisms
The temperature difference between the skin and the environment
Determined by: radiant heat loss · conduction · convection · evaporation

[Ch06 S5]

cards.q: Define the four heat-loss mechanisms [Ch04 S11]
cards.a:
Define the four heat-loss mechanisms [Ch04 S11]
Radiant — transfer of heat from one object to another without their coming in contact
Conductive — loss of heat through direct contact with cooler surfaces
Evaporative — loss of heat through the evaporation of liquids from a surface
Convective — loss of heat due to the movement of air past the skin

[Ch04 S11]

cards.q: Delivery-room thermoregulation — mechanism → method (as the slide pairs them)
cards.a:
Delivery-room thermoregulation — mechanism → method (as the slide pairs them)
Evaporative → immediately dry infant after birth
Radiant → wrap in warm blanket, place on warmer, cover head
Convective and conductive → place on warming mattress or in incubator
Plus: skin-to-skin care (not tied to a mechanism)

[Ch06 S8]

cards.q: Incubator vs open (radiant) warmer
cards.a:
Incubator vs open (radiant) warmer
Incubator — controlled environment, quieter, but limits access
Open warmer — allows access to patient, but difficult to control temperature in the environment

[Ch06 S9]

cards.q: HYPERTHERMIA — the chain [Ch06 S7]
cards.a:
HYPERTHERMIA — the chain [Ch06 S7]
Temperature above normal → peripheral VASODILATION → increased metabolism and oxygen consumption → cerebral blood flow decreases → uncorrected, death

⚠️ "Increased metabolism and O2 consumption" is on the HYPERthermia slide — not the cold-stress slide.

[Ch06 S7]

cards.q: Pediatric hypothermia — what the slides say
cards.a:
Pediatric hypothermia — what the slides say
Usually follows TRAUMA
With a CNS injury the patient may lose the ability to shiver and the body's ability to detect heat loss may be impaired

[Ch11 S10]

cards.q: THE COLD STRESS CHAIN — all five links in causal order
cards.a:
THE COLD STRESS CHAIN — all five links in causal order
1. Hypothermia ("any lowering of the thermoneutral temperature")
↓
2. Peripheral VASOCONSTRICTION
↓
3. Anaerobic metabolism and METABOLIC ACIDOSIS
↓
4. PULMONARY VASOCONSTRICTION and HYPOXEMIA
↓
5. Uncorrected — DEATH

[Ch06 S6]

cards.q: Which link makes cold stress a RESPIRATORY CARE problem?
cards.a:
Which link makes cold stress a RESPIRATORY CARE problem?
Link 4 — pulmonary vasoconstriction and hypoxemia, reached from peripheral vasoconstriction and metabolic acidosis

[Ch06 S6]

cards.q: ⚠️ NOT IN THE SLIDES — what is missing from the cold-stress cascade?
cards.a:
⚠️ NOT IN THE SLIDES — what is missing from the cold-stress cascade?
These are NOT stated anywhere in Ch01–Ch11 — do not cite them to these decks:
• the term "non-shivering thermogenesis"
• depletion of brown fat stores by cold stress
• increased oxygen consumption in cold stress (that's on the HYPERthermia slide)
• glucose consumption / hypoglycemia
• surfactant impairment, apnea, poor weight gain, norepinephrine release

cards.q: ROP — the five etiology statements
cards.a:
ROP — the five etiology statements
Listed under Consequences of Premature Birth:
• "Formation of a scar behind the lens of the eye"
• "Linked to oxygen use"
• "Capillaries aren't fully developed"
• "Vasoconstriction leads to necrosis of the vessels" — the only cause-and-effect statement

[Ch07 S11]

cards.q: ROP — treatment and prevention
cards.a:
ROP — treatment and prevention
Cryotherapy
Laser therapy
Vitrectomy and lensectomy are "under investigation"

[Ch07 S13]

cards.q: ROP stages 1 and 2
cards.a:
ROP stages 1 and 2
Stage 1 — "a thin white demarcation line separating the avascular retina anteriorly from the vascularized retina posteriorly"
Stage 2 — "a ridge is now formed and rises up from the plane of the retina. New vessels may be seen posterior to the ridge"

[Ch07 S12]

cards.q: ROP stages 3, 4 and 5
cards.a:
ROP stages 3, 4 and 5
Stage 3 — "proliferation of extraretinal fibrovascular tissue, often posterior to or connected to the ridge"
Stage 4 — "subtotal detachment of the retina"
Stage 5 — "continued traction and buildup of fluids; the retina becomes completely detached"

[Ch07 S12]

cards.q: NEC — where does it appear in the midterm scope?
cards.a:
NEC — where does it appear in the midterm scope?
Exactly twice, both as an item on someone else's list:
1. As a consequence of intrauterine asphyxia [Ch07 S18]
2. As a complication of neonatal jaundice, alongside kernicterus [Ch06 S28]

⚠️ No definition, pathophysiology, staging, presentation or NEC-specific treatment appears on any in-scope slide.

cards.q: ⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — NEC filed under jaundice
cards.a:
⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — NEC filed under jaundice
ANSWER THE SLIDE: [Ch06 S28] lists necrotizing enterocolitis under Neonatal Jaundice → Complications, with kernicterus.

⚠️ Standard teaching (NOT your slides): NEC is not a complication of jaundice — the placement is wrong. NEC is ischemic-inflammatory bowel necrosis of prematurity; pneumatosis intestinalis on abdominal film is the classic sign.

[Ch06 S28]

cards.q: Pneumothorax — etiology (the "air leak" framing)
cards.a:
Pneumothorax — etiology (the "air leak" framing)
Sits under "Barotraumatic Diseases," also known as air leak syndrome
"Most are caused by mechanical ventilation"
They "develop from rupture of alveoli"
The lesion: "develops when the extraalveolar air ruptures to the external surface of the lung and into the pleural space"
"Can be either spontaneous or tension"

[Ch07 S21–S22]

cards.q: Pneumothorax — signs
cards.a:
Pneumothorax — signs
"Increase in respiratory distress, with retractions and tachypnea; progressing to bradycardic, cyanotic, and may have periods of apnea and hypotension"

[Ch07 S22]

cards.q: ⚠️ Pneumothorax — DIAGNOSIS and TREATMENT per the slides
cards.a:
⚠️ Pneumothorax — DIAGNOSIS and TREATMENT per the slides
Diagnosis: TRANSILLUMINATION — chest x-ray is NOT listed for pneumothorax
Treatment: "depends upon severity" → needle aspiration or placement of chest tube

⚠️ Contrast: pneumomediastinum is "diagnosed by chest x-ray" [Ch07 S24]

[Ch07 S23]

cards.q: The rest of the air-leak family
cards.a:
The rest of the air-leak family
Pneumomediastinum — air dissects through the lung interstitium into the mediastinum; distant, crackly heart sounds; diagnosed by chest x-ray [S24]
Pulmonary air embolism — from high pressures ventilating stiff lungs; "there is no effective treatment" [S27]
Subcutaneous emphysema — secondary to other air leaks; "resolves when air leak is treated" [S27]

[Ch07 S24, S27]

cards.q: Pneumopericardium — signs and diagnosis
cards.a:
Pneumopericardium — signs and diagnosis
Produces severe bradycardia, with muffled or distant heart sounds
Diagnosed with chest x-ray

[Ch07 S25]

cards.q: Neonatal jaundice — definition and how it is measured
cards.a:
Neonatal jaundice — definition and how it is measured
"Yellowish-orange skin color that accompanies increased levels of bilirubin in the blood, called hyperbilirubinemia"
Measured by blood sample

[Ch06 S26]

cards.q: Causes of hyperbilirubinemia (the Ch06 list)
cards.a:
Causes of hyperbilirubinemia (the Ch06 list)
Increased bilirubin in blood · blood disorders · hemorrhage · diabetes · galactosemia · hypothyroidism

[Ch06 S26]

cards.q: PATHOLOGIC JAUNDICE — the five criteria (MEMORIZE)
cards.a:
PATHOLOGIC JAUNDICE — the five criteria (MEMORIZE)
1. Onset — jaundice within the first 24 hours after birth
2. Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin — exceeds 13 mg/dl term, 15 mg/dl premature
3. Rate of rise — more than 5 mg/dl in 24 hours
4. Direct (conjugated) bilirubin — exceeds 1.5 mg/dl
5. Duration — beyond 7 days term, beyond 14 days preemie

[Ch06 S27]

cards.q: Complications of neonatal jaundice
cards.a:
Complications of neonatal jaundice
Kernicterus
Necrotizing enterocolitis ⚠️ (unusual placement — see the slide flag)

[Ch06 S28]

cards.q: ⚠️ What TREATMENT for hyperbilirubinemia is in the midterm scope?
cards.a:
⚠️ What TREATMENT for hyperbilirubinemia is in the midterm scope?
NOTHING. Chapter 6 has no treatment slide for hyperbilirubinemia.

⚠️ The word "phototherapy" does appear — but only as "radiant warmers and phototherapy lights" on the INSENSIBLE WATER LOSS list [Ch06 S17]. No slide prescribes phototherapy for jaundice.

Also absent: exchange transfusion, IVIG, any bilirubin treatment threshold.

cards.q: The three TORCH organisms whose slides list hyperbilirubinemia — and which fraction
cards.a:
The three TORCH organisms whose slides list hyperbilirubinemia — and which fraction
Cytomegalovirus — direct, "secondary to liver damage" (the only mechanism in the course) [Ch08 S8]
Rubella — direct [Ch08 S9]
Toxoplasmosis — direct AND indirect [Ch08 S11]

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — THE TIMING RULE for jaundice
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — THE TIMING RULE for jaundice
Jaundice in the first 24 hours of life is NEVER physiologic. It is pathologic until proven otherwise and demands immediate TSB + hemolysis workup.

Physiologic jaundice: onset after 24 h, peaks day 3–5 (term), resolves by 2–3 weeks, unconjugated, ~75% of cases.

✓ This is the one pathologic criterion where slide and current teaching agree exactly.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — breastfeeding jaundice vs breast-milk jaundice
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — breastfeeding jaundice vs breast-milk jaundice
Breastfeeding jaundice ("breast-NON-feeding") — first week, peaks day 3–5; suboptimal intake → ↑ enterohepatic recirculation; baby dehydrated, losing weight. Fix the feeding (8–12/day).
Breast-milk jaundice — starts late week 1, peaks week 2, lasts 3–12 weeks; substances in milk inhibit conjugation; baby feeding well and thriving.

One-liner: not enough milk, early, baby doing poorly vs the milk itself, later, baby doing fine.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — phototherapy mechanism
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — phototherapy mechanism
Blue-green light at 460–490 nm drives photoisomerization of unconjugated bilirubin in the skin to lumirubin — water-soluble isomers excreted in bile and urine without hepatic conjugation.
Intensive phototherapy = LED blue light, irradiance ≥ 30 µW/cm2/nm, maximal body surface exposed.
Eye shields on; maintain hydration; do NOT give water or dextrose.

⚠️ No slide prescribes phototherapy

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — ABO vs Rh incompatibility
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — ABO vs Rh incompatibility
ABO — mother type O, infant A or B; preformed maternal IgG, no prior sensitization; can affect the FIRSTBORN; usually mild–moderate; DAT often weakly positive
Rh (D) — mother Rh-negative, infant Rh-positive; requires prior sensitization → usually the SECOND pregnancy; severe, hydrops fetalis; DAT strongly positive; prevented with RhoGAM at 28 wk + within 72 h postpartum

⚠️ Not on any slide

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — acute bilirubin encephalopathy → kernicterus
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — acute bilirubin encephalopathy → kernicterus
Free unconjugated bilirubin crosses the BBB and deposits in the basal ganglia, hippocampus and brainstem nuclei.
ABE Phase 1 (days 1–2): poor feeding, lethargy, hypotonia, high-pitched cry
Phase 2: increased extensor tone, opisthotonos, retrocollis, fever
Phase 3: hypertonia/rigidity, stupor/coma, apnea
Chronic kernicterus (>1 yr): choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, sensorineural hearing loss, upward gaze palsy

Kernicterus is permanent and entirely preventable.

cards.q: ⚠️ CONFLICT — pathologic jaundice: three numbers where slide ≠ current teaching
cards.a:
⚠️ CONFLICT — pathologic jaundice: three numbers where slide ≠ current teaching
ANSWER THE SLIDE COLUMN:
Direct bilirubin — slide > 1.5 mg/dL · current: ≥ 5 mg/dL (or >20% of total)
Duration — slide 7 d term / 14 d preterm · current: >2 wk term / >3 wk preterm
Rate of rise — slide >5 mg/dL per 24 h · current: >0.3 mg/dL/h in first 24 h

✓ Onset within 24 h — no conflict

[Ch06 S27]

cards.q: Meconium aspiration syndrome — etiology
cards.a:
Meconium aspiration syndrome — etiology
Filed under "Processes of Intrauterine Origin"
Cause: "Ingestion while in utero" — the whole stated mechanism

Ch02 supplies the missing link: meconium is the "dark greenish stool found in the fetal intestine", and its presence in amniotic fluid "may result from a fetal asphyxia episode" [Ch02 S15]

[Ch07 S19]

cards.q: Meconium aspiration syndrome — SIGNS
cards.a:
Meconium aspiration syndrome — SIGNS
"Low Apgar scores, fetal hypoxia, acidosis, and abnormal fetal heart tracings"
"Green staining of amniotic fluid"

⚠️ Note the slide's framing: hypoxia/acidosis/abnormal tracings are printed under "Signs include," not under causes.

[Ch07 S19]

cards.q: Meconium aspiration syndrome — the four TREATMENTS
cards.a:
Meconium aspiration syndrome — the four TREATMENTS
1. Infusion of warm, sterile saline into the uterus to dilute (amnioinfusion)
2. Intubate and suction if not vigorous
3. Suction mouth and nose with bulb syringe if stable
4. Provide warmed, humidified oxygen

[Ch07 S20]

cards.q: When does the resuscitation deck say to intubate for meconium?
cards.a:
When does the resuscitation deck say to intubate for meconium?
"When thick meconium is present in a nonvigorous infant"

⚠️ Read the trigger as the COMBINATION — thick meconium and a nonvigorous infant. The slide does not direct intubation for meconium in a vigorous infant.

[Ch04 S17]

cards.q: The five indications for INTUBATION [Ch04 S17]
cards.a:
The five indications for INTUBATION [Ch04 S17]
1. Thick meconium in a nonvigorous infant
2. Bag and mask ventilation is difficult or ineffective
3. Prolonged PPV is required due to lung disease
4. Chest compressions have become necessary
5. Extreme prematurity and need for surfactant administration

[Ch04 S17]

cards.q: Intubation difficulties named by the slides
cards.a:
Intubation difficulties named by the slides
Difficulty visualizing the landmarks
Accidental insertion in the esophagus
Advanced too far down the trachea

[Ch04 S18]

cards.q: ⚠️ T16 — what does Chapter 9 actually say about pulseless arrest rhythms?
cards.a:
⚠️ T16 — what does Chapter 9 actually say about pulseless arrest rhythms?
NOTHING. Chapter 9 never splits pulseless arrest into shockable and non-shockable rhythms.

Slide 5 names the PALS algorithm's three branches — "Pulseless arrest / Bradycardia / Tachycardia" — and stops.

The words VF, pulseless VT, shockable, defibrillation, AED, joules, J/kg, asystole, PEA do not appear in ANY deck in the course.

[Ch09 S5]

cards.q: The quantitative PALS parameters the slides DO give
cards.a:
The quantitative PALS parameters the slides DO give
Chest compression rate: 100/min [Ch09 S2]
Ventilation with 100% oxygen [Ch09 S2, S3]
Bag-mask rate: 1 breath every 6 to 8 seconds [Ch09 S3]

⚠️ NOT stated anywhere: compression:ventilation ratio · defibrillation energy · rhythm/pulse-check interval · any drug dose

cards.q: The 11-drug PALS roster [Ch09 S4] — exactly as printed
cards.a:
The 11-drug PALS roster [Ch09 S4] — exactly as printed
adenosine · amiodarone · atropine · calcium · epinephrine · glucose · lidocaine · magnesium · procainamide · sodium bicarbonate · vasopressin

⚠️ One flat alphabetical list — no doses, no rhythm assignment. Any shockable/non-shockable assignment comes from outside the decks.

[Ch09 S4]

cards.q: PALS airway and access points from the slides
cards.a:
PALS airway and access points from the slides
Use oro- or nasopharyngeal airways [S3]
Endotracheal intubation — "reduces risk of gastric inflation and aspiration" [S4]
Vascular access: peripheral or INTRAOSSEOUS [S4]
"Use the monitors to see impacts of treatment" [S2]

[Ch09 S2–S4]

cards.q: NEONATAL chest compressions — the slide's trigger and technique
cards.a:
NEONATAL chest compressions — the slide's trigger and technique
Persistent HR less than 60 bpm, despite tactile stimulation and 30 seconds of adequate PPV
Use thumb or two-finger technique

[Ch04 S16]

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — shockable vs non-shockable rhythms
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — shockable vs non-shockable rhythms
SHOCKABLE (defibrillate): ventricular fibrillation (VF) · pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT)
NON-SHOCKABLE (do NOT shock): asystole · pulseless electrical activity (PEA)

Key contrast: shockable arrests get electricity first; non-shockable arrests get epinephrine first.

⚠️ These words appear in no deck in the course

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — pediatric defibrillation energy
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — pediatric defibrillation energy
First shock: 2 J/kg
Second shock: 4 J/kg
Third and subsequent: ≥ 4 J/kg
Maximum: 10 J/kg or the adult max, whichever is lower

Single shock, then immediately resume compressions.
Do not confuse with cardioversion (pulse present): 0.5–1 J/kg, escalating to 2 J/kg.

⚠️ No joule dose of any kind is in the slides

cards.q: ⚠️ NRP vs PALS — the dividing line
cards.a:
⚠️ NRP vs PALS — the dividing line
The dividing line is the DELIVERY ROOM.

Newborn at birth → NRP: 3:1, 90 compressions + 30 inflations/min, 100% O2, start at HR < 60 after 30 s of effective PPV

Infant/child after the newborn period → PALS: 15:2 (2 rescuers) or 30:2 (1 rescuer), 100–120/min, start CPR at HR < 60 with poor perfusion

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — PALS compression rate, depth and ratios
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — PALS compression rate, depth and ratios
Rate: 100–120/min (all ages)
Depth: ≥ 1/3 AP chest diameter — ~1.5 in (4 cm) infants, ~2 in (5 cm) children
1 rescuer, no advanced airway: 30:2
2 rescuers, infant/child: 15:2
Advanced airway: continuous compressions + 1 breath every 2–3 s (20–30/min)
Rhythm check / compressor change: every 2 minutes; pauses < 10 s

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — pediatric arrest drug doses
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — pediatric arrest drug doses
Epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg IV/IO (0.1 mL/kg of 1:10,000), max single dose 1 mg, repeat q3–5 min
Amiodarone 5 mg/kg bolus (max 300 mg), up to 3 doses — refractory VF/pVT
Lidocaine 1 mg/kg — acceptable alternative to amiodarone

Timing: non-shockable → epinephrine as early as possible; shockable → epinephrine after 2 defibrillation attempts

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the Hs and Ts (reversible causes)
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the Hs and Ts (reversible causes)
H's: Hypovolemia · Hypoxia · Hydrogen ion (acidosis) · Hypoglycemia · Hypo-/hyperkalemia · Hypothermia
T's: Tension pneumothorax · Tamponade (cardiac) · Toxins · Thrombosis (pulmonary) · Thrombosis (coronary)

⚠️ Not on any slide

cards.q: ⚠️ CONFLICT — three resuscitation numbers where slide ≠ current guideline
cards.a:
⚠️ CONFLICT — three resuscitation numbers where slide ≠ current guideline
ANSWER THE SLIDE:
1. Compression rate — slide 100/min [Ch09 S2] · current PALS: 100–120/min
2. Ventilation — slide 1 breath q6–8 s (8–10/min) [Ch09 S3] · current: 1 breath q2–3 s (20–30/min)
3. Infant compression technique — slide says "thumb or two-finger" [Ch04 S16] · 2025 de-recommends the 2-finger technique; the thumb technique the slide names first is the one that survived

cards.q: INSENSIBLE WATER LOSS — all NINE factors
cards.a:
INSENSIBLE WATER LOSS — all NINE factors
[Ch06 S16]: level of maturity · size · respiratory distress · humidity · temperature · skin breakdown
[Ch06 S17]: radiant warmers and phototherapy lights · heat shields · motor activity

⚠️ The slides state NO direction of effect for any of the nine — they are printed as bare nouns. Do not assert that humidity or a heat shield raises or lowers the loss.

cards.q: Why is the PRETERM neonate at risk for insensible water loss?
cards.a:
Why is the PRETERM neonate at risk for insensible water loss?
Premature skin is "very permeable," "thin," and has "diminished adhesion between epidermis and dermis" [Ch06 S13]

This pairs with "skin breakdown" and "level of maturity" on the insensible-loss list [Ch06 S16]

cards.q: ⚠️ NOT IN THE SLIDES — the PEDIATRIC half of insensible water loss
cards.a:
⚠️ NOT IN THE SLIDES — the PEDIATRIC half of insensible water loss
All Chapter 6 fluid/electrolyte content is NEONATAL.
There is no pediatric insensible-loss slide, no age-based maintenance-fluid calculation, and no burn/fever multipliers.

Also absent: any volume (no mL/kg/day figure), any percentage of total body water lost, and any direction of effect.

cards.q: ⚠️ T18 — how many ABG numeric values are in Chapters 1–11?
cards.a:
⚠️ T18 — how many ABG numeric values are in Chapters 1–11?
NOT ONE.

No pH, PaCO2, PaO2, HCO3, base-excess or SpO2 range appears in any in-scope deck, and no chapter states a "classic RDS ABG picture."

Every number lives in Ch15, Ch18 and Chang Ch17 — all out of midterm scope. In-scope, ABG interpretation exists only qualitatively.

cards.q: The ONLY directional acid-base statement in the midterm scope
cards.a:
The ONLY directional acid-base statement in the midterm scope
Primary apnea: "Heart rate and blood pressure drop. PaCO2 rises and the pH drops."

[Ch04 S5]

cards.q: IVH prevention — the slide's rule
cards.a:
IVH prevention — the slide's rule
"Avoid wide fluctuations in blood pressure, oxygenation, and pH"

[Ch07 S16]

cards.q: Complications of RDS [Ch07 S5]
cards.a:
Complications of RDS [Ch07 S5]
Intracranial hemorrhage · barotraumatic injury · disseminated intravascular coagulation · infection · patent ductus arteriosus

[Ch07 S5]

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — normal ABG values: adult vs neonate
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — normal ABG values: adult vs neonate
pH — adult 7.35–7.45 · neonate 7.35–7.45 (>7.30 acceptable in a sick newborn)
PaCO2 — both 35–45 mm Hg
PaO2 — adult 75–100 · neonate 50–70 mm Hg
HCO3 — 22–26 (preterm 20–24) mEq/L
Base excess — neonate −4 to +4
SpO2 — adult 95–100% · neonate 90–95% on O2

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — why is neonatal PaO2 deliberately LOWER than adult?
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — why is neonatal PaO2 deliberately LOWER than adult?
The target sits between two harms:
Too high (hyperoxia) → retinopathy of prematurity, oxygen free-radical lung injury, BPD
Too low (hypoxemia) → pulmonary vasoconstriction, PPHN, lactic acidosis, NEC, death

An adult PaO2 of 60 is "borderline"; in a 27-week preterm it is normal and desirable.

If forced to pick one number: PaO2 50–70 mm Hg.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the 4-step ABG interpretation method
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the 4-step ABG interpretation method
Step 1 — pH. <7.35 acidemia · >7.45 alkalemia
Step 2 — which value moved with the pH? CO2 moving opposite the pH = respiratory. HCO3 moving with the pH = metabolic.
Step 3 — compensation.
Step 4 — oxygenation (PaO2/SaO2), reported separately.

Fully compensated? Decide the primary disorder by which side of 7.40 the pH sits on.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — compensation stages
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — compensation stages
Uncompensated — pH abnormal; only one of PaCO2/HCO3 abnormal
Partially compensated — pH still abnormal; both abnormal, in opposite directions
Fully compensated — pH back inside 7.35–7.45; both abnormal. Primary disorder = whichever side of 7.40 the pH sits on (7.35–7.39 = acidosis primary; 7.41–7.45 = alkalosis primary)

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the ABG picture in RDS, by phase
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the ABG picture in RDS, by phase
Early/mild: pH normal or ↑ (7.45–7.50), PaCO2 ↓ (28–34), PaO2 ↓ — hypoxemia with respiratory ALKALOSIS; hypoxemia is refractory to O2 because it is shunt
Progressing: pH ↓ (7.25–7.32), PaCO2 ↑ (50–60) — respiratory acidosis + hypoxemia
Severe/failing: pH <7.20, PaCO2 >60, PaO2 <40, HCO3 ↓ — COMBINED respiratory + metabolic acidosis (lactic acidosis)

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — permissive hypercapnia in the neonate
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — permissive hypercapnia in the neonate
Accepting a higher PaCO2 to use smaller tidal volumes and lower pressures, reducing volutrauma and BPD.

Mild: 45–54 · Moderate: 55–65 mm Hg
Lower limit — do NOT go below PaCO2 35 mm Hg on mechanical ventilation
pH floor: > 7.22

⚠️ Hypocapnia is NOT safe in a neonate — PaCO2 <30 → severe IVH/PVL; hyperventilating a preterm causes cerebral vasoconstriction.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — targeted PREDUCTAL SpO2 after birth (NRP 9th ed.)
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — targeted PREDUCTAL SpO2 after birth (NRP 9th ed.)
Measured on the right hand/wrist:
2 min — 65–70%
3 min — 70–75%
4 min — 75–80%
5 min — 80–85%
10 min — 85–95%

⚠️ The 8th-edition 1-min = 60–65% row was removed in the 9th edition.

cards.q: TORCH — what does each letter stand for? [Ch08 S3]
cards.a:
TORCH — what does each letter stand for? [Ch08 S3]
T — Toxoplasmosis
O — "Other" ⚠️ never expanded into any organism
R — Rubella
C — Cytomegalovirus
H — Herpes simplex type 2

[Ch08 S3]

cards.q: TORCH — Toxoplasmosis: class, presentation, treatment
cards.a:
TORCH — Toxoplasmosis: class, presentation, treatment
Class: Protozoal and Fungal Infections
Transmission: from mother to fetus through the placenta
Presentation: microcephaly, coma, convulsions, hydrocephalus; hepatosplenomegaly; jaundice with both direct AND indirect hyperbilirubinemia; petechiae; pallor secondary to anemia
Treatment: none stated

[Ch08 S11]

cards.q: TORCH — Rubella: presentation and treatment
cards.a:
TORCH — Rubella: presentation and treatment
Presentation (early-gestation infection): cataracts, cardiac defects, hearing loss, IUGR, chronic encephalitis, direct hyperbilirubinemia, microcephaly
Treatment: none stated — only the general line "viral diseases can be avoided by prevention and immunization"

✓ Cataracts and cardiac defects are UNIQUE to rubella

[Ch08 S9]

cards.q: TORCH — Cytomegalovirus: presentation and treatment
cards.a:
TORCH — Cytomegalovirus: presentation and treatment
"Member of the herpes virus family"
Presentation: IUGR, direct hyperbilirubinemia secondary to LIVER DAMAGE (the only mechanism in the course), hepatosplenomegaly, microcephaly, brain damage, progressive sensorineural hearing loss
Treatment: "nutritional support and general supportive care"

[Ch08 S8]

cards.q: TORCH — Herpes simplex: transmission and treatment
cards.a:
TORCH — Herpes simplex: transmission and treatment
Transmission: "by the ascent of the virus up the birth canal, from infected genitalia, or from direct contact with infected tissues during delivery"
Treatment: "antiviral drugs" (no drug, no dose, no duration)

[Ch08 S10]

cards.q: Which TORCH organisms get a TREATMENT on the slides?
cards.a:
Which TORCH organisms get a TREATMENT on the slides?
Only 2 of 5:
CMV — "nutritional support and general supportive care"
HSV — "antiviral drugs"

⚠️ Rubella and toxoplasmosis get NO treatment at all, and the "O" is never expanded.

cards.q: TORCH — which distinguishing features are UNIQUE, and which do NOT discriminate?
cards.a:
TORCH — which distinguishing features are UNIQUE, and which do NOT discriminate?
Toxoplasmosis only: indirect hyperbilirubinemia, hydrocephalus, coma, convulsions, petechiae, anemia
Rubella only: cataracts, cardiac defects
CMV wording: "progressive sensorineural hearing loss," "brain damage"

⚠️ Microcephaly appears under toxoplasmosis, rubella AND CMV — it does NOT discriminate.

cards.q: ⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — the TORCH "H" inconsistency
cards.a:
⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — the TORCH "H" inconsistency
[Ch08 S3] names only type 2 in the TORCH list, but [Ch08 S10] is headed "Herpes Simplex Types I and II" and then describes only Type I (lips, skin above the waist) — never stating what Type II causes.

Standard teaching (NOT your slides): neonatal disease is most often HSV-2 acquired intrapartum; presents as skin-eye-mouth, CNS, or disseminated; treated with IV acyclovir.

[Ch08 S3, S10]

cards.q: ⚠️ TRAP — does Pneumocystis carinii belong to TORCH?
cards.a:
⚠️ TRAP — does Pneumocystis carinii belong to TORCH?
NO. [Ch08 S12] gives it a treatment — "trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 21 days" — but it sits under "Protozoal and Fungal Infections," and no slide places it inside the TORCH complex.

(That 21 days is the only antimicrobial duration given anywhere in Ch08.)

Standard teaching: the O = "Other", classically syphilis, plus varicella-zoster, parvovirus B19, HIV, hepatitis B, Listeria, enteroviruses.

cards.q: SIDS — everything the course says [Ch09 S26]
cards.a:
SIDS — everything the course says [Ch09 S26]
"Diagnosis is made upon AUTOPSY. Prevention is key. Place infant in PRONE position to sleep ⚠️. SIDS usually hits during WINTER and at NIGHT. Common ages are 2 to 4 months with MALES being affected more frequently than females."

That one slide is the entire SIDS content of the course.

[Ch09 S26]

cards.q: ⚠️⚠️ BIGGEST SLIDE FLAG IN THE COURSE — SIDS sleep position
cards.a:
⚠️⚠️ BIGGEST SLIDE FLAG IN THE COURSE — SIDS sleep position
The slide says: "Place infant in PRONE position to sleep." — answer the slide if the question keys to it.

⚠️ This is backwards and it matters. Standard teaching: infants must be placed SUPINE (on the BACK) to sleep — "Back to Sleep." Prone sleeping is a major modifiable RISK FACTOR for SIDS, not a preventive measure.

Rest of the real guidance: firm flat surface, no soft bedding, room-share without bed-sharing, avoid overheating, no smoke exposure, breastfeed, consider a pacifier.

[Ch09 S26]

cards.q: ⚠️ NOT IN THE SLIDES — what is missing from the SIDS content?
cards.a:
⚠️ NOT IN THE SLIDES — what is missing from the SIDS content?
• No formal definition of SIDS (no "sudden unexplained death of an infant under 1 year")
• The deck does NOT say SIDS is a diagnosis of exclusion — do not add that
• No risk factors beyond age 2–4 months, male sex, winter, nighttime
• No maternal smoking, prematurity, low birth weight, bed-sharing, soft bedding, overheating
• No incidence rate, ethnic distribution, or pathophysiologic theory

cards.q: The EIGHT pediatric anatomic differences [Ch10 S2–S3]
cards.a:
The EIGHT pediatric anatomic differences [Ch10 S2–S3]
Systemic (3): proportionately larger body surface area · skin immature, prone to trauma and chemical absorption · immature blood-brain barrier
Airway (5): tongue proportionally larger in the oropharynx · trachea narrow · epiglottis larger proportionally and U-SHAPED · larynx higher and MORE ANTERIOR · mainstem bronchi have LESS of an angle

[Ch10 S2–S3]

cards.q: ⚠️ Which slides name the ADULT explicitly as the comparator?
cards.a:
⚠️ Which slides name the ADULT explicitly as the comparator?
Only Ch05. "Infant's tongue is larger in area than adult's" [Ch05 S2] and "Metabolism — higher than adults" [Ch05 S4]

⚠️ Chapter 10 NEVER uses the word "adult" — even though its slides are titled "Anatomic and Physiologic Differences." Three Ch10 bullets state no comparator at all.

For an explicit adult comparison in scope, cite Ch05 S2 or S4.

cards.q: ⚠️ The EPIGLOTTIS — the one wording disagreement between Ch05 and Ch10
cards.a:
⚠️ The EPIGLOTTIS — the one wording disagreement between Ch05 and Ch10
Ch05 S2: epiglottis is "larger and LESS FLEXIBLE"
Ch10 S3: epiglottis is "larger proportionally and is U-SHAPED"

Both are in scope; they are not the same descriptor. Quote whichever chapter the question is anchored to.

(Standard teaching says the infant epiglottis is MORE floppy — that floppiness is the whole rationale for the straight blade.)

cards.q: Chapter 9's anatomic contributions in TRAUMA [Ch09 S7]
cards.a:
Chapter 9's anatomic contributions in TRAUMA [Ch09 S7]
"Effects greater body surface area" ⚠️ (garbled — most plausibly "Affects")
"Lesser amounts of soft tissue result in less protection"
"Increased risk of internal injury"
"Large head"

[Ch09 S7]

cards.q: ⚠️ NOT IN THE SLIDES — pediatric airway anatomy gaps
cards.a:
⚠️ NOT IN THE SLIDES — pediatric airway anatomy gaps
Absent from Ch01–Ch11:
• the narrowest point of the pediatric airway — no cricoid ring
• funnel-shaped vs cylindrical airway
• larynx level by vertebra (no C3–C4 vs C4–C5)
• alveolar number, ETT size formula, age-based anatomic table
• the clinical CONSEQUENCES of any of the eight differences — the decks state the anatomy but never say why it matters for intubation

cards.q: The THREE eating disorders of the pediatric patient
cards.a:
The THREE eating disorders of the pediatric patient
Pica · anorexia nervosa · bulimia nervosa

That is the entire content of the slide and of the course. Expect to be asked to name the three.

⚠️ No definitions, criteria, age of onset, prevalence, signs/symptoms or treatment anywhere in scope.

[Ch11 S7]

cards.q: ⚠️ Are eating disorders the same as behavioral problems in this course?
cards.a:
⚠️ Are eating disorders the same as behavioral problems in this course?
NO — do not merge the two lists.

The deck places "Eating Disorders" [Ch11 S7] immediately after "Behavioral Problems" [Ch11 S6] in slide order, but never states that eating disorders ARE behavioral problems.

Pica, anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa are classified separately from behavioral and neurodevelopmental problems.

cards.q: T23 Layer 1 — behavioral development and the domains assessed
cards.a:
T23 Layer 1 — behavioral development and the domains assessed
"Follows a predictable pattern but varies greatly"; "Neurodevelopment is also assessed"

Domains: language development · fine and gross motor skills · personal and social development · cognitive skills

[Ch11 S3]

cards.q: T23 Layer 2 — the FOUR named DEVELOPMENTAL DELAYS
cards.a:
T23 Layer 2 — the FOUR named DEVELOPMENTAL DELAYS
Global developmental delay
Autism spectrum disorder
Attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder
Asperger's syndrome

[Ch11 S4]

cards.q: T23 Layer 3 — the FOUR named BEHAVIORAL PROBLEMS results
cards.a:
T23 Layer 3 — the FOUR named BEHAVIORAL PROBLEMS results
Behavioral problems "may result in":
Sleep problems
Obstructive sleep apnea ⚠️
Oppositional defiant disorder
Conduct disorder

[Ch11 S6]

cards.q: ⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — the OSA–behavior causal DIRECTION
cards.a:
⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — the OSA–behavior causal DIRECTION
ANSWER THE SLIDE: [Ch11 S6] words it as behavioral problems "MAY RESULT IN" obstructive sleep apnea — i.e. OSA as a consequence of behavioral problems.

⚠️ Standard teaching (NOT your slides): the direction is REVERSED. OSA CAUSES the behavioral problems — untreated pediatric OSA produces hyperactivity, inattention and poor school performance, and is frequently mistaken for ADHD. Usual cause: adenotonsillar hypertrophy; treatment: adenotonsillectomy, or CPAP.

[Ch11 S6]

cards.q: The neurological portion of the well-child head-to-toe exam
cards.a:
The neurological portion of the well-child head-to-toe exam
Mental and cognitive status · balance and coordination · cranial nerves

[Ch10 S17]

cards.q: D1 — Alveoli development across the stages
cards.a:
D1 — Alveoli development across the stages
Canalicular (17–26 wk) — "alveoli BEGIN to develop"; bronchioles multiply; lungs vascularize
Saccular (26 to 34–36 wk) — "continued development of the alveoli"
Alveolar — "TRUE alveoli present between 32 and 34 weeks"
After birth — number increases until around age 8

[Ch01 S13–S14]

cards.q: Surface tension and Laplace's law (as the slides state them)
cards.a:
Surface tension and Laplace's law (as the slides state them)
Surface tension "occurs in alveoli"; surface molecules are "pulled inward and together," which "allows surface to shrink"

Laplace's law: "As the RADIUS of the alveoli DECREASES, the surface tension INCREASES"

Surfactant "works in tandem with the change in size of the alveoli"

[Ch01 S15–S16]

cards.q: ⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — the overlapping lung-development week ranges
cards.a:
⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — the overlapping lung-development week ranges
ANSWER AS WRITTEN. [Ch01 S14] puts the saccular stage at "26 to between 34 and 36 weeks," true alveoli at "32 to 34 weeks," and lungs "completely formed" by "24 to 26 weeks" — these ranges overlap and are internally inconsistent as printed.

Standard ranges (NOT your slides): embryonic 0–7 · pseudoglandular 7–17 · canalicular 17–26 · saccular 26–36 · alveolar 36 wk–age 8. "Completely formed by 24–26 wk" should read capable of gas exchange.

[Ch01 S14]

cards.q: D2 — Foramen ovale: definition and closure
cards.a:
D2 — Foramen ovale: definition and closure
Definition: the fetal shunt that "shunts blood from RIGHT to LEFT atrium" [Ch01 S24]
Closure: after birth systemic blood pressure rises, which "causes closing of the foramen ovale" [Ch01 S25]

⚠️ No closure TIME is given for the foramen ovale (only the ductus arteriosus gets one — 96 hours), and no name for the closed remnant.

cards.q: Where does the chest radiograph get used IN SCOPE?
cards.a:
Where does the chest radiograph get used IN SCOPE?
Well-child pulmonary exam — "evaluate and localize the disease" [Ch10 S13]
Bronchopulmonary dysplasia — "diagnosis is difficult"; CXR + lab studies + PFTs [Ch07 S7]
Pneumomediastinum — "diagnosed by chest x-ray" [Ch07 S24]
Pneumopericardium — "diagnosed with chest x-ray" [Ch07 S25]
Foreign body obstruction — "diagnosis by radiograph" [Ch09 S16]

cards.q: ⚠️ NOT IN THE SLIDES — CXR findings vocabulary
cards.a:
⚠️ NOT IN THE SLIDES — CXR findings vocabulary
No radiographic findings vocabulary exists in Ch01–11.
"Ground glass," "reticulogranular," "air bronchograms," "infiltrate," "opacity" appear nowhere in scope.

Also absent: views (PA/AP/lateral/decubitus), ET tube or line position confirmation, exposure/rotation checks, radiation considerations.

(Ch16 is the whole findings-vocabulary chapter — after the midterm.)

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — atelectasis vs consolidation
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — atelectasis vs consolidation
The single distinguishing question is VOLUME. Both are white.

Atelectasis — alveoli COLLAPSED; volume is LOST → shifted fissures, elevated hemidiaphragm, mediastinum pulled TOWARD the opacity. RDS = diffuse atelectasis.
Consolidation — alveoli FILLED with fluid/pus/blood; volume preserved or increased, pulls nothing. Pneumonia = consolidation.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the classic film for RDS, TTN and MAS
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the classic film for RDS, TTN and MAS
RDS — lung volume DECREASED; bilateral symmetric ground-glass opacities, air bronchograms into the periphery
TTN — volume MILDLY INCREASED; perihilar linear/streaky densities, fluid in the fissures, pleural effusions. Clears in 24–72 h — the diagnostic clincher
MAS — HYPERINFLATED from air trapping; coarse, diffuse bilateral patchy opacification; high risk of pneumothorax

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — pneumothorax on a SUPINE neonatal film
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — pneumothorax on a SUPINE neonatal film
Air collects anteromedially → DEEP SULCUS SIGN, hyperlucent hemithorax, unusually sharp heart border
Tension: mediastinal shift away, flattened ipsilateral hemidiaphragm, widened rib spaces

⚠️ In a decompensating infant, transillumination and needle decompression come BEFORE imaging — the same point the slide's pneumothorax flag makes.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — correct radiographic position of ETT, UAC and UVC
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — correct radiographic position of ETT, UAC and UVC
ETT — tip mid-trachea at T2–T3, i.e. 1–2 cm above the carina. Too deep → right mainstem
UAC — HIGH: T6–T9 (preferred) or LOW: L3–L5. Avoid T10–L2 (celiac/SMA/renal). A UAC goes DOWN then loops UP
UVC — tip at the IVC/right-atrium junction, ~T8–T9. A UVC travels straight UP

cards.q: D4 — What do the slides say about the umbilical cord?
cards.a:
D4 — What do the slides say about the umbilical cord?
The "lifeline between mother and fetus" which "consists of THREE vessels" [Ch01 S8]

⚠️ The slides NEVER name all three. The deck never says the cord contains two arteries and one vein — it says only "three vessels." Do not supply the count on an exam keyed to these slides.

cards.q: The umbilical VEIN and ARTERY as the slides use them
cards.a:
The umbilical VEIN and ARTERY as the slides use them
Umbilical VEIN — blood "collects in large vessels until it arrives at umbilical vein"; the "umbilical vein carries blood TO the fetus" [Ch01 S23]. In resuscitation, medication access is through the umbilical vein [Ch04 S19]
Umbilical ARTERY — named only as a catheter/sampling site: "arterial sampling through umbilical stump"; "placement of umbilical artery catheter"; "thrombus formation is the most common complication" [Ch04 S24]

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the three umbilical vessels
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the three umbilical vessels
2 umbilical ARTERIES — fetus → placenta, carrying DEOXYGENATED blood; arise from the fetal internal iliac arteries
1 umbilical VEIN — placenta → fetus, carrying OXYGENATED blood — the most oxygenated blood in the fetus

⚠️ Naming follows the fetus, not the oxygen content — the reverse of the systemic circulation.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — UVC vs UAC clinical use, and preductal sampling
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — UVC vs UAC clinical use, and preductal sampling
Umbilical VEIN → UVC — route for emergency drug and volume administration during resuscitation
Umbilical ARTERY → UAC — sits in the descending aorta below the ductus, so it samples POSTDUCTAL blood only; used for continuous BP and routine gases

⚠️ PREDUCTAL sampling requires the RIGHT RADIAL artery (or right-hand pulse ox). A UAC alone cannot demonstrate the preductal–postductal difference that the PPHN workup looks for.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — postnatal fate of the fetal vessels and shunts
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — postnatal fate of the fetal vessels and shunts
Umbilical vein → ligamentum teres hepatis (round ligament of the liver)
Ductus venosus → ligamentum venosum
Umbilical arteries — distal → medial umbilical ligaments
Umbilical arteries — proximal → remain patent as the superior vesical arteries
Ductus arteriosus → ligamentum arteriosum
Foramen ovale → fossa ovalis

⚠️ No postnatal fate is given for these on any slide

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — two-vessel cord (single umbilical artery)
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — two-vessel cord (single umbilical artery)
One artery + one vein. Incidence ~0.5–1% of pregnancies.
Significance: a marker for congenital anomalies — cardiac, renal/GU, GI, skeletal — and associated with trisomy 18 and 13, fetal growth restriction and preterm birth.
Practical point: count the vessels on the cut cord at delivery and document it.

cards.q: ⚠️ D5 — Is there a normal heart rate table in the midterm scope?
cards.a:
⚠️ D5 — Is there a normal heart rate table in the midterm scope?
NO. There is no "normal heart rate" definition and no normal-HR-by-age table anywhere in Ch01–11.

Every HR number in scope is either a FETAL monitoring value or a NEONATAL RESUSCITATION threshold. Learn them in their own context and do not generalize them into a normal range.

cards.q: FETAL heart rate numbers [Ch02 S6, S8, S9]
cards.a:
FETAL heart rate numbers [Ch02 S6, S8, S9]
Average: 140/min in early gestation, dropping to 120/min near term [S6]
Baseline range: 120–160 bpm [S8]
Variability (healthy, awake fetus): 5–10 bpm [S8]
Accelerations: exceeds 160 bpm for less than 2 minutes [S9]
Decelerations: drops below 120 bpm for less than 2 minutes [S9]

cards.q: How is fetal heart rate obtained?
cards.a:
How is fetal heart rate obtained?
Auscultation · external abdominal transducer · abdominal electrodes · a spiral electrode into the fetal scalp

[Ch02 S6]

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — normal vital signs by age (PALS)
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — normal vital signs by age (PALS)
HR awake / RR / systolic BP
Neonate (<28 d): 100–205 / 30–53† / 67–84
Infant (1 mo–1 y): 100–190 / 30–53 / 72–104
Toddler (1–2 y): 98–140 / 22–37 / 86–106
Preschool (3–5 y): 80–120 / 20–28 / 89–112
School-age (6–11 y): 75–118 / 18–25 / 97–115
Adolescent (12–15 y): 60–100 / 12–20 / 110–131

† For a newborn specifically use RR 30–60, tachypnea >60

cards.q: ⚠️ D6 — the ONLY numeric respiratory rate in the midterm scope
cards.a:
⚠️ D6 — the ONLY numeric respiratory rate in the midterm scope
It is an ABNORMAL one: "a respiratory rate above 60 breaths per minute" as a clinical sign of RDS [Ch07 S3]

No normal respiratory rate is stated anywhere in Ch01–11.

✓ That >60 is the reliable number on the RDS sign slide (unlike "increased FRC").

cards.q: ⚠️⚠️ THE FOUR BREATH RATES — do not mix them
cards.a:
⚠️⚠️ THE FOUR BREATH RATES — do not mix them
30–60/min — NORMAL newborn RR (the patient's own breathing; tachypnea >60)
30–60/min — NRP assisted PPV rate (what YOU deliver to a newborn)
20–30/min (1 breath q2–3 s) — PALS delivered rate
8–10/min (1 breath q6–8 s) — THE SLIDE'S delivered rate [Ch09 S3] — answer this if the question keys to the deck

The first two are numerically identical and mean opposite things. A delivered ventilation rate is never a normal respiratory rate.

cards.q: How is respiration assessed QUALITATIVELY in scope?
cards.a:
How is respiration assessed QUALITATIVELY in scope?
Neonate: "evaluate respirations / good chest rise / regular in depth and pattern" — unlabored and free of grunting, flaring, or retracting [Ch04 S12]
Pediatric: "determine the nature of the patient's ventilations / rate · depth · rhythm · ease of breathing" [Ch10 S15]

cards.q: ⚠️ D7 — Wharton's Jelly: what do the slides say?
cards.a:
⚠️ D7 — Wharton's Jelly: what do the slides say?
NOTHING. Neither "Wharton" nor "jelly" occurs on ANY slide in ANY of the 24 decks — checked against the full course, not just Ch01–11.

The nearest content is the whole of the slides' cord anatomy: "umbilical cord / lifeline between mother and fetus / consists of three vessels" [Ch01 S8].

If this term is on the exam it comes from the Whitaker text or lecture, not the decks.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — Wharton's jelly: what it is and what it's made of
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — Wharton's jelly: what it is and what it's made of
The mucoid (gelatinous) connective tissue of the umbilical cord — a specialized extracellular matrix from extraembryonic mesoderm. Not fat, not muscle.

Composition: glycosaminoglycans — predominantly hyaluronic acid — plus chondroitin sulfate; these are strongly hydrophilic and hold water, making it a gel. Also proteoglycans, collagen (I, III, V), and myofibroblast-like stromal cells.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — Wharton's jelly: FUNCTION (the exam answer)
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — Wharton's jelly: FUNCTION (the exam answer)
1. Mechanical cushion — protects the umbilical vessels from compression, torsion, kinking and bending as the fetus moves, keeping flow uninterrupted. THIS IS THE EXAM-LEVEL ANSWER.
2. Maintains vessel patency — keeps knots and loops from occluding flow
3. Contributes to physiologic cord closure after birth — a natural clamp before the clinical clamp

The amount of jelly is the main determinant of cord diameter.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — Wharton's jelly: clinical relevance
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — Wharton's jelly: clinical relevance
Reduced ("lean") jelly → thin cord; associated with fetal growth restriction, cord stricture, cord accidents, stillbirth
Excessive jelly → thick/edematous cord; associated with gestational diabetes and fetal hydrops
The jelly makes the cord slippery and compressible — which is why the cord is CLAMPED, not tied
Rich source of mesenchymal stromal (stem) cells — basis of cord-blood banking

cards.q: D8 — Amnion: definition
cards.a:
D8 — Amnion: definition
The "sac surrounding the embryo"

Listed under "Development and Function of Intrauterine Structures," on the same slide as the umbilical cord.

[Ch01 S8]

cards.q: The five lung-maturity tests measurable in amniotic fluid
cards.a:
