The five lung-maturity tests measurable in amniotic fluid
L/S ratio (lecithin-to-sphingomyelin) — 2:1, generally around 35 weeks
Shake or foam test
Surfactant-albumin ratio (SAR)
TDx-FLM assay
Fluorescence polarization (FP) assay

[Ch01 S18]

cards.q: D9 — Surfactant: definition and what it does
cards.a:
D9 — Surfactant: definition and what it does
The "substance found on the alveolar wall that LOWERS SURFACE TENSION"
It "reduces muscular effort" and "works in tandem with the change in size of the alveoli"

[Ch01 S16]

cards.q: Surfactant — composition and the two numbers to memorize
cards.a:
Surfactant — composition and the two numbers to memorize
Composition: "phospholipids, neutral lipids, and proteins"

THE TWO NUMBERS:
Production begins at 24 weeks gestation [Ch01 S17]
Mature L/S ratio 2:1 at about 35 weeks [Ch01 S18]

cards.q: ⚠️ NOT IN THE SLIDES — surfactant replacement details
cards.a:
⚠️ NOT IN THE SLIDES — surfactant replacement details
Absent from Ch01–Ch11: no surfactant product or brand name, no mL/kg or mg/kg dose, no number of doses, no dosing interval, no instillation technique, and no prophylactic-versus-rescue timing.

The slides give only: "provision of artificial surfactant replacement" as an RDS treatment [Ch07 S4], and intubation "in cases of extreme prematurity and need for surfactant administration" [Ch04 S17].

cards.q: ⚠️ D10 — the ONLY numeric definition of bradycardia in scope
cards.a:
⚠️ D10 — the ONLY numeric definition of bradycardia in scope
A FETAL heart-pattern value: bradycardia is "less than 100 bpm," and it "may be caused by asphyxia" [Ch02 S8]

⚠️ That is a fetal-monitoring threshold — do NOT present it as a normal or neonatal heart rate.

The word "bradycardia" does not appear in Ch05 at all.

cards.q: ⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — the fetal bradycardia GAP
cards.a:
⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — the fetal bradycardia GAP
ANSWER THE SLIDE. [Ch02 S8] sets the fetal baseline floor at 120 bpm but defines bradycardia as <100 bpm — leaving 100–119 bpm unlabelled.

Standard teaching (NOT your slides): current NICHD closes the gap — normal fetal baseline 110–160, bradycardia below 110, tachycardia above 160. The slide's 120/100/180 figures are an older convention.

[Ch02 S8]

cards.q: Bradycardia elsewhere in scope (always without a number)
cards.a:
Bradycardia elsewhere in scope (always without a number)
Baroreceptors — stretch receptors that "stimulate bradycardia and hypotension" [Ch01 S26]
Apnea — "cessation of breathing for a period sufficient to produce bradycardia and/or cyanosis" [Ch07 S33]
Pneumopericardium — "severe bradycardia, with muffled or distant heart sounds" [Ch07 S25]
PALS — "Bradycardia" named as an algorithm with no value attached [Ch09 S5]

cards.q: ⚠️ "100" is doing TRIPLE DUTY in this course — name the three
cards.a:
⚠️ "100" is doing TRIPLE DUTY in this course — name the three
1. The fetal-monitoring bradycardia cutoff (<100 bpm) [Ch02 S8]
2. The bottom of the PALS awake neonatal HR range
3. The NRP threshold to start PPV (HR <100) [Ch04 S15]

They coincide numerically and are otherwise unrelated. Say which one you mean.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the two NEONATAL heart-rate action numbers
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the two NEONATAL heart-rate action numbers
HR < 100/min (apneic, gasping, or persistently bradycardic) → START PPV
HR < 60/min despite 30 seconds of effective PPV → START CHEST COMPRESSIONS, 3:1 = 90 compressions + 30 inflations/min, 100% O2
HR still < 60 after 60 s of compressions → EPINEPHRINE, preferably IV/UVC

AHA/AAP 2025 Part 5

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the management principle for pediatric bradycardia
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the management principle for pediatric bradycardia
Pediatric bradycardia is a RESPIRATORY problem until proven otherwise — oxygenate and ventilate FIRST, drugs second.

Start CPR if HR <60/min with cardiopulmonary compromise. Epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg; atropine 0.02 mg/kg (min 0.1 mg, max 0.5 mg) for vagal tone/AV block.

Commonest cause in children: HYPOXIA.

cards.q: ⚠️ D11 — the ONLY numeric definition of tachycardia in scope
cards.a:
⚠️ D11 — the ONLY numeric definition of tachycardia in scope
A FETAL heart-pattern value: tachycardia is "consistently above 180 bpm," attributed to "maternal fever or infection"

[Ch02 S9]

⚠️ Neonatally, "tachycardia" is one of the seven newborn observation findings with no number attached [Ch05 S6]; in PALS it is an algorithm name with no value [Ch09 S5].

cards.q: ⚠️ CONFLICT — fetal tachycardia: 180 vs 160
cards.a:
⚠️ CONFLICT — fetal tachycardia: 180 vs 160
ANSWER THE SLIDE: > 180 bpm if the question keys to fetal monitoring [Ch02 S9].

Current NICHD/ACOG threshold is > 160 bpm — which is why the ACOG chorioamnionitis criterion uses >160 for ≥10 min. Answer 160 only if the question explicitly asks the chorioamnionitis criterion.

⚠️ Neither is a NEONATAL number — after birth use the PALS bands.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — sinus tachycardia vs SVT
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — sinus tachycardia vs SVT
Probable SVT if: infants ≥ 220/min · children ≥ 180/min
Sinus tach: P waves present/normal, R-R VARIABLE, compatible cause (fever, pain, volume loss)
SVT: P waves absent/abnormal, R-R NOT variable (monotonous), ABRUPT onset and offset

Do NOT cardiovert sinus tachycardia — it is a symptom, not a rhythm; treat the cause.
Stable SVT: vagal maneuvers → adenosine 0.1 mg/kg (max 6 mg), then 0.2 mg/kg (max 12 mg)

cards.q: D12 — which arterial structures do the slides name?
cards.a:
D12 — which arterial structures do the slides name?
No slide defines "artery" or describes arterial wall structure. The decks give named structures tied to a function or defect:
Ductus arteriosus · aorta · aortic arch · carotid arteries · umbilical artery · pulmonary artery

Plus defects: coarctation of the aorta, overriding aorta (tetralogy), truncus arteriosus

[Ch01 S22–S27; Ch04 S24; Ch08 S24–S30]

cards.q: Pulmonary artery in the congenital defects
cards.a:
Pulmonary artery in the congenital defects
Tetralogy of Fallot — includes "obstruction to flow through the pulmonary artery" and "an overriding aorta" [Ch08 S24]
Transposition — "the pulmonary artery arises from the LEFT ventricle" [Ch08 S25]
Truncus arteriosus — "one large vessel arises from both right and left ventricles" [Ch08 S30]

cards.q: ⚠️ D13 — how many slides mention "obstructive sleep apnea"?
cards.a:
⚠️ D13 — how many slides mention "obstructive sleep apnea"?
Exactly TWO slides in all 24 decks — Ch05 S18 and Ch11 S6 — and on both it is only named in a list, with no definition, pathophysiology or criteria.

OSA is never defined in this course.

cards.q: ⚠️ Neonatal OBSTRUCTIVE APNEA — NOT the same as "obstructive sleep apnea"
cards.a:
⚠️ Neonatal OBSTRUCTIVE APNEA — NOT the same as "obstructive sleep apnea"
[Ch07 S36], under "Other Respiratory Diseases of the Neonate / Apnea / Obstructive":
Cause — "result from anatomic abnormalities"
Workup — "documented by the use of the POLYSOMNOGRAM"
Treatment — "ranges from pharmacologic to surgery"

⚠️ The slide never uses the phrase "obstructive sleep apnea." Cite it as neonatal obstructive apnea, not as the OSA answer.

cards.q: APNEA — the slides' definition and the two types
cards.a:
APNEA — the slides' definition and the two types
"Cessation of breathing for a period sufficient to produce BRADYCARDIA and/or CYANOSIS"

Two types named: Central or nonobstructive, and Obstructive

[Ch07 S33]

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — OSA definition and what separates it from CENTRAL apnea
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — OSA definition and what separates it from CENTRAL apnea
Recurrent partial (hypopnea) or complete (apnea) collapse of the upper airway during sleep, DESPITE CONTINUED RESPIRATORY EFFORT, producing intermittent hypoxemia, hypercapnia, arousals and sleep fragmentation.

⚠️ "Continued effort" is what separates OBSTRUCTIVE from CENTRAL apnea.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — OSA severity by AHI: adults vs children
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — OSA severity by AHI: adults vs children
ADULTS: normal <5 · mild 5–15 · moderate 15–30 · severe >30 · diagnostic cutoff AHI ≥ 5
CHILDREN: normal <1 · mild 1–4.9 · moderate 5–9.9 · severe ≥ 10 · diagnostic cutoff obstructive AHI ≥ 1

Say this out loud: an AHI of 10–15 is only MILD in an adult and SEVERE in a child. The bar is five times lower in children.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — how scored events are defined
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — how scored events are defined
Apnea = ≥ 90% drop in airflow lasting ≥ 10 seconds (adult rule)
Hypopnea = ≥ 30% drop in airflow for ≥ 10 s with ≥ 4% desaturation, OR ≥ 3% desaturation plus an EEG arousal
AHI = (apneas + hypopneas) ÷ hours of sleep

In children, an obstructive apnea is scored by duration of ≥ 2 breath cycles rather than a fixed 10 seconds.

cards.q: D14 — ASD: definition and presentation
cards.a:
D14 — ASD: definition and presentation
Atrial septal defect — "failure of the tissue flap to cover the foramen, allowing the movement of blood between atria"
Presentation: "often symptomless" — those two words are the entire clinical picture the deck gives, and they are the distinguishing point against the other lesions.

⚠️ The slide gives NO shunt direction — only "between atria," never "left-to-right."

[Ch08 S22]

cards.q: ⚠️ ASD — what is conspicuously MISSING versus its neighbours?
cards.a:
⚠️ ASD — what is conspicuously MISSING versus its neighbours?
ASD is the ONE cardiac lesion in the run with NO named diagnostic test and NO treatment, while its neighbours all have one:
VSD — ultrasound · tetralogy — ultrasound + echo · transposition / coarctation / tricuspid atresia — ultrasound + cardiac cath · truncus arteriosus — ECG + cardiac cath

ASD also appears in neither the "reduce blood flow to the lungs" group nor the "increase pulmonary blood flow" group — so no ventilator or oxygen strategy is offered for it.

cards.q: ⚠️ How does Chapter 8 sort congenital heart lesions?
cards.a:
⚠️ How does Chapter 8 sort congenital heart lesions?
By their EFFECT ON PULMONARY BLOOD FLOW — not cyanotic vs acyanotic.

"Reduce blood flow to the lungs" — tricuspid atresia, tetralogy of Fallot [Ch08 S32]
"Increase pulmonary blood flow" — VSD, coarctation of the aorta, subaortic stenosis, PDA, anomalous venous return [Ch08 S33]

⚠️ The words "cyanotic" and "acyanotic" appear NOWHERE in Chapter 8.

cards.q: D15 — the three ways the slides use Body Surface Area
cards.a:
D15 — the three ways the slides use Body Surface Area
1. As a pediatric anatomic difference — "proportionately larger BSA" [Ch10 S2]; neonatal equivalent "large skin surface area / prone to heat loss" [Ch05 S5]
2. In BURNS — "body surface area / follow Rule of Nines" [Ch09 S20]
3. In TRAUMA — "effects greater body surface area" [Ch09 S7]

⚠️ The slides never define BSA and give no formula.

cards.q: Burn degrees as the slides define them
cards.a:
Burn degrees as the slides define them
First degree — "only the epidermis is involved"
Second degree — "extends beyond the epidermis to the superficial dermis"; partial thickness
Third degree — "destroys the dermis and dermal appendages"

[Ch09 S19]

cards.q: Burn management and evaluation per the deck
cards.a:
Burn management and evaluation per the deck
Evaluation: stabilize · assess burn injury · assess hydration status · body surface area by Rule of Nines [Ch09 S20]
Management: maintain tissue perfusion · cover burns with sterile soaked dressings · PREVENT HYPOTHERMIA [Ch09 S21]

cards.q: ⚠️ Rule of Nines — what numbers do the slides give?
cards.a:
⚠️ Rule of Nines — what numbers do the slides give?
NONE. The Rule of Nines is named but none of its percentages are given — no 9% per region, no pediatric head modification, no Lund-Browder chart, no %TBSA thresholds for fluid resuscitation or transfer.

There is also no BSA formula, no m² value, and no body-weight-to-BSA ratio anywhere in the course.

cards.q: D16 — PPHN: definition and other name
cards.a:
D16 — PPHN: definition and other name
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn — also known as PERSISTENT FETAL CIRCULATION

"Severe, persistent pulmonary VASOCONSTRICTION, which causes INCREASED blood pressure in the lungs and DECREASED pulmonary blood flow"

[Ch07 S28]

cards.q: PPHN — presentation and auscultation
cards.a:
PPHN — presentation and auscultation
Presentation: "cyanosis with tachypnea and respiratory distress, usually occurring within a few hours after delivery"
Auscultation: "tricuspid regurgitation can cause a loud single S2 or a harsh systolic murmur"

[Ch07 S29]

cards.q: PPHN — the FIVE diagnostic/evaluation items (learn as a list)
cards.a:
PPHN — the FIVE diagnostic/evaluation items (learn as a list)
1. Hyperoxia test
2. Measurement of PREDUCTAL and POSTDUCTAL PaO2 levels
3. Hyperoxia-hyperventilation test
4. Echocardiogram
5. Lab tests

[Ch07 S29]

cards.q: PPHN — treatment per the slides
cards.a:
PPHN — treatment per the slides
"The maintaining of temperature, fluids and electrolytes, blood sugar, oxygenation, blood pressure and perfusion"
"Minimize handling the patient"
Mechanical ventilation

⚠️ Inhaled nitric oxide, ECMO, alkalinization and sildenafil are NOT on the Ch07 PPHN treatment slide.

[Ch07 S30]

cards.q: ⚠️ The ONE place the in-scope decks connect PPHN to a cause
cards.a:
⚠️ The ONE place the in-scope decks connect PPHN to a cause
"Persistent fetal circulation" — PPHN's other name — is listed in Ch04 as one of the "Effects of asphyxia on lungs" [Ch04 S6]

⚠️ No etiology list for PPHN exists — meconium aspiration, sepsis, CDH and "idiopathic" are never linked to it on the PPHN slides.

cards.q: ⚠️ D17 — Chorioamnionitis: what do the slides say?
cards.a:
⚠️ D17 — Chorioamnionitis: what do the slides say?
The slides NEVER define it. The word appears exactly once in the whole course, as a bare bullet — spelled "Choroamnionitis" ⚠️ — on Chapter 8's Bacterial Infections slide.

The only thing the deck tells you is the category: it is classified as a BACTERIAL infection of the neonate.

[Ch08 S4]

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — chorioamnionitis: definition and current terminology
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — chorioamnionitis: definition and current terminology
Infection with inflammation of any combination of the amniotic fluid, placenta, fetus, fetal membranes or decidua. Usually an ascending polymicrobial infection from the vagina and cervix, most often after membrane rupture.

Terminology: traditional term = chorioamnionitis; ACOG's preferred term since 2017 = "intraamniotic infection"; "Triple I" is the 2015 NICHD research label.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — chorioamnionitis diagnostic criteria
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — chorioamnionitis diagnostic criteria
Fever alone is enough: maternal temp ≥ 39.0°C (102.2°F) on a single reading
Fever + one other: temp 38.0–38.9°C on two readings 30 min apart, PLUS one of:
• fetal tachycardia > 160 bpm for ≥ 10 min
• maternal leukocytosis > 15,000 cells/µL
• purulent fluid from the cervical os

ACOG CO No. 712

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — chorioamnionitis: effects on the NEONATE (the RT list)
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — chorioamnionitis: effects on the NEONATE (the RT list)
Early-onset neonatal sepsis — the classic association; organisms GBS and E. coli
Pneumonia and respiratory distress syndrome
Bronchopulmonary dysplasia
Preterm birth
Neonatal encephalopathy and cerebral palsy
IVH · retinopathy of prematurity · neonatal death

RT cue: notify the neonatal team BEFORE delivery — the infant needs early-onset-sepsis evaluation and a team ready for resuscitation.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — chorioamnionitis management, and the tocolysis link
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — chorioamnionitis management, and the tocolysis link
Intrapartum antibiotics as soon as it is suspected — do not wait for cultures. First line: ampicillin + gentamicin.
Antipyretics; proceed to delivery (but infection alone is rarely an indication for cesarean).

⚠️ It is an ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION TO TOCOLYSIS — the correct response is delivery, not suppression of labor. It is also one of the leading identifiable causes of spontaneous preterm labor.

cards.q: ⚠️ D18 — what do the slides say about the LARYNX?
cards.a:
⚠️ D18 — what do the slides say about the LARYNX?
The slides never define or describe the larynx as a structure. They give only its POSITION:
"Larynx is higher" [Ch05 S2]
"Larynx is higher and more anterior" [Ch10 S3]

⚠️ No cervical vertebral level (no C3/C4 vs C6), no "cricoid is the narrowest point," no funnel-vs-cylinder shape, no blade choice or intubation implication anywhere in Ch01–11.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — infant vs adult larynx: position and epiglottis
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — infant vs adult larynx: position and epiglottis
Laryngeal position: infant C3–C4 at birth vs adult C5–C6 → higher and more anterior, sharper oral–laryngeal axis, harder to line up for a view. Descends mainly between 2–6 years.
Epiglottis: infant is long, narrow, omega (Ω)-shaped, FLOPPY — little elastic cartilage — angled ~45° over the glottis. Adult is broad, flat, firm.

⚠️ Ch10's "U-shaped" and the textbook "omega-shaped" are the SAME description.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — "the cricoid is the narrowest point": know both sides
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — "the cricoid is the narrowest point": know both sides
Classic teaching: below 8–10 years the larynx is funnel-shaped and the CRICOID RING is narrowest; the adult larynx is cylindrical, narrowest at the glottis.
Imaging evidence since 2003: in-vivo studies find the pediatric larynx narrowest at the GLOTTIS, elliptical and cylindrical.

How to answer safely: the glottis is the narrowest measured point, but the cricoid is the functionally limiting point — it is the only complete, non-distensible ring. The classic test answer is still CRICOID.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — why a STRAIGHT (Miller) blade in the young?
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — why a STRAIGHT (Miller) blade in the young?
The straight blade tip goes BENEATH the epiglottis and lifts it DIRECTLY — controlling the long, floppy, omega-shaped epiglottis and displacing the large tongue base.

The curved (Macintosh) blade sits in the vallecula and lifts the epiglottis indirectly via the hyoepiglottic ligament — which only works with a stiffer, more adult-type epiglottis.

Crossover: straight preferred through ~8 years; curved standard from >8 years.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — why 1 mm of edema is catastrophic in an infant (Poiseuille)
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — why 1 mm of edema is catastrophic in an infant (Poiseuille)
Resistance ∝ 1/r⁴ (laminar), worsening toward 1/r⁵ when turbulent — i.e. in a crying child.

Infant (4 mm airway), 1 mm circumferential edema: diameter 4 → 2 mm (50% loss), cross-sectional area ↓75%, resistance ↑16-fold — and ↑32-fold if crying
Adult (8 mm): 8 → 6 mm (25% loss), resistance ↑3-fold

This is why you keep these children CALM.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — airway positioning by age
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — airway positioning by age
Neonate/infant: the large occiput already flexes the head, so a pillow is HARMFUL. Use a neutral position, often with a shoulder roll.
Older child (~≥ 6–8 y) and adult: classic sniffing position — pad under the occiput.

Target at any age: external auditory meatus level with the suprasternal notch. Over-extension worsens the view in infants.

cards.q: D19 — Fetal circulation: the SIX-step pathway
cards.a:
D19 — Fetal circulation: the SIX-step pathway
1. Receives oxygen and nutrients from the placenta
2. Collects in large vessels until it arrives at the umbilical vein
3. Umbilical vein carries blood to the fetus
4. Ductus venosus → inferior vena cava
5. Foramen ovale → right to left atrium
6. Ductus arteriosus → aorta

[Ch01 S23–S24]

cards.q: ⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — do the slides link the fetal shunts to the pressures?
cards.a:
⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — do the slides link the fetal shunts to the pressures?
NO. The deck states the shunts [Ch01 S24] and the pressures/resistances [Ch01 S22] on SEPARATE slides and never states that one causes the other.

⚠️ Do NOT present the causal link ("the shunts exist because right-sided pressure exceeds left") as slide content.

Standard teaching: high PVR and high right-heart pressure drive right-to-left flow. At birth, lung inflation drops PVR, left atrial pressure rises above right, and both shunts close.

cards.q: ⚠️ D20 — Is cyanosis defined anywhere in Ch01–11?
cards.a:
⚠️ D20 — Is cyanosis defined anywhere in Ch01–11?
NO — and no threshold is given.

The closest is an assessment instruction: "evaluate color / blue or pink / VISUALLY INSPECT CENTRAL TRUNK / evaluate oxygen saturation / use a pulse oximeter / provide supplemental oxygen if necessary" [Ch04 S14]

⚠️ "Central cyanosis" and "peripheral cyanosis" are never contrasted as a pair; acrocyanosis never appears. The word "cyanosis" does not occur in Chapter 5 at all.

cards.q: Where cyanosis appears as a SIGN in scope
cards.a:
Where cyanosis appears as a SIGN in scope
Wilson-Mikity — "hyperpnea, transient cyanosis, and retractions" [Ch07 S10]
Pneumothorax — progressing to bradycardic, cyanotic [Ch07 S22]
PPHN — cyanosis with tachypnea, within a few hours of delivery [Ch07 S29]
Apnea — sufficient to produce bradycardia and/or cyanosis [Ch07 S33]
Pediatric history — "is cyanosis present?" [Ch10 S6]
Pediatric skin exam — "cyanosis, pallor, jaundice" [Ch10 S11]

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — central vs peripheral cyanosis
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — central vs peripheral cyanosis
CENTRAL — tongue, lips, oral mucous membranes, trunk; mechanism is arterial HYPOXEMIA; causes: lung disease, cyanotic CHD, hypoventilation, methemoglobinemia. ALWAYS abnormal — needs work-up.
PERIPHERAL — fingertips, toes, hands, feet only; mucous membranes stay PINK; normal SaO2 with sluggish flow and increased O2 extraction; causes: cold, vasoconstriction, low cardiac output, shock. Often benign.

Response to 100% O2: improves with lung disease; does NOT improve with cyanotic CHD (hyperoxia test).

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — acrocyanosis
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — acrocyanosis
Normal in the first 24–48 hours. Peripheral cyanosis around the mouth and extremities in an otherwise pink, well newborn; recurs with cold or crying. Cause: benign vasomotor instability → peripheral vasoconstriction with increased tissue O2 extraction.

The trunk, tongue and mucous membranes are PINK and SpO2 is normal — that is what separates it from central cyanosis. Treatment is warming and reassurance, not oxygen.

⚠️ Central cyanosis persisting beyond the first ~10 minutes of life is NEVER acrocyanosis.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the ~5 g/dL rule and why ANEMIA hides cyanosis
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the ~5 g/dL rule and why ANEMIA hides cyanosis
Cyanosis becomes visible at roughly 5 g/dL of desaturated (reduced) hemoglobin — it depends on the ABSOLUTE AMOUNT, not the percentage.

ANEMIA (Hb 7.5–10): a much greater desaturation is needed before 5 g/dL of reduced Hb exists → cyanosis appears late or never. A severely anemic hypoxemic patient can be pink and dying.
POLYCYTHEMIA (Hb ~21): cyanosis appears early, at a higher SpO2 (~85%), sometimes with adequate oxygen delivery.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — at what SpO2 / PaO2 does cyanosis become visible?
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — at what SpO2 / PaO2 does cyanosis become visible?
SpO2 roughly 80–85% · PaO2 roughly 35–50 mm Hg

Cyanosis is a LATE and UNRELIABLE sign of hypoxemia. By the time you can see it, the patient is already at ~80–85% saturation — roughly 10 saturation points below a preterm's target of 90–95%.

That is precisely why NRP says to use the pulse oximeter instead of colour — which is what [Ch04 S14] tells you to do.

cards.q: D21 — Indications for PPV (memorize as THREE triggers)
cards.a:
D21 — Indications for PPV (memorize as THREE triggers)
PPV is "indicated when the neonate is:
1. APNEIC
2. GASPING
3. or when spontaneous breathing cannot maintain the HEART RATE ABOVE 100 bpm"

That single sentence is the whole indication set.

[Ch04 S15]

cards.q: After starting PPV — the slide's follow-through
cards.a:
After starting PPV — the slide's follow-through
Reevaluate
"If HR is more than 60 but less than 100, continue providing PPV and monitor oxygen saturation"
Evaluate chest rise

[Ch04 S15]

cards.q: ⚠️ NOT IN THE SLIDES — PPV parameters
cards.a:
⚠️ NOT IN THE SLIDES — PPV parameters
Absent: no PPV rate (breaths/min), no PIP or PEEP value, no starting FiO2, no device specification (bag-mask vs T-piece), and no duration for an initial PPV trial.

The only duration in scope is the "30 seconds of adequate PPV" inside the compression criterion [Ch04 S16].

cards.q: D22 — Secondary apnea: the slide's complete definition
cards.a:
D22 — Secondary apnea: the slide's complete definition
The "SECOND attempt of fetus to ventilate," in which "respirations are WEAK, GASPING, and INEFFECTIVE"

That is the complete definition the deck gives.

[Ch04 S5]

cards.q: How do you get from secondary apnea to its treatment using only the slides?
cards.a:
How do you get from secondary apnea to its treatment using only the slides?
Through the word "GASPING."

Secondary apnea's findings include gasping [Ch04 S5], and a gasping neonate is an explicit indication for PPV [Ch04 S15].

⚠️ The slide never names PPV as the treatment OF secondary apnea — you have to make the link yourself.

cards.q: ⚠️ NOT IN THE SLIDES — what is missing from the apnea stages?
cards.a:
⚠️ NOT IN THE SLIDES — what is missing from the apnea stages?
The deck does NOT say secondary apnea is unresponsive to stimulation.
It gives no time course or duration for either stage, no PaO2 values, no numeric pH, and no statement of which stage responds to tactile stimulation.

Standard teaching (NOT your slides): primary apnea responds to stimulation; secondary apnea does not and needs PPV. Because you cannot tell them apart at the bedside, NRP says treat all newborn apnea as secondary and begin PPV.

cards.q: D23 — Lung development: EMBRYONAL and PSEUDOGLANDULAR stages
cards.a:
D23 — Lung development: EMBRYONAL and PSEUDOGLANDULAR stages
Embryonal — "first 7 weeks gestation"; development of anatomical structures of various organ systems; lungs begin to develop at 24 days [Ch01 S11]
Pseudoglandular — "7 to 16 weeks"; further development of respiratory structures; differentiation of nasal cavity, oropharynx, nasopharynx; "lungs begin to look like glands" [Ch01 S12]

cards.q: D23 — Lung development: CANALICULAR, SACCULAR and ALVEOLAR stages
cards.a:
D23 — Lung development: CANALICULAR, SACCULAR and ALVEOLAR stages
Canalicular — "weeks 17 through 26"; terminal and respiratory bronchioles multiply; lungs become vascularized; alveoli begin to develop [S13]
Saccular — "26 to between 34 and 36 weeks"; "by 24 to 26 weeks lungs are completely formed" ⚠️; continued alveolar development [S14]
Alveolar — no gestational start given; true alveoli present 32–34 weeks; alveolar number increases until around age 8 [S14]

cards.q: ⚠️ D24 — how many numeric pH values are in Ch01–11?
cards.a:
⚠️ D24 — how many numeric pH values are in Ch01–11?
NOT ONE. No 7.35, no 7.40, no range — and no mmHg/torr blood-gas number either.

Everything the in-scope decks say about pH is qualitative or directional. Any pH number you have seen in this course comes from a chapter AFTER the midterm.

If an exam question keys to a number, it is drawing on out-of-scope material — flag it with the instructor.

cards.q: Every in-scope mention of pH (all qualitative)
cards.a:
Every in-scope mention of pH (all qualitative)
• Fetal lung fluid has "low pH" [Ch01 S19]
• Chemoreceptors are "sensitive to PaO2, PaCO2, and pH" [Ch01 S27]
• Primary apnea — "PaCO2 rises and the pH drops" [Ch04 S5]
• Fetal scalp pH assessment — named, never given a value [Ch02 S10]
• IVH — "avoid wide fluctuations in blood pressure, oxygenation, and pH" [Ch07 S16]

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — normal pH ranges and thresholds
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — normal pH ranges and thresholds
Normal arterial pH (adult and neonate): 7.35–7.45
Acidemia <7.35 · Alkalemia >7.45
Severe, life-threatening acidemia <7.20
Range compatible with life: 6.80–7.80
Neonatal CAPILLARY pH 7.32–7.42 · VENOUS 7.30–7.40

Because it is a log scale, a fall of 0.3 pH units DOUBLES the H+ concentration.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — neonatal pH targets (what the NICU actually accepts)
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — neonatal pH targets (what the NICU actually accepts)
The neonate is managed to a lower, more permissive pH than an adult — normalizing pH costs ventilator pressure (BPD) and hyperventilation causes brain injury.

> 7.30 generally acceptable in a sick newborn
> 7.25 ABG goal in RDS
> 7.22 floor while tolerating permissive hypercapnia
< 7.20 intervene / re-evaluate

Companion rule: do NOT let PaCO2 fall below 35 mm Hg on the ventilator.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — FETAL SCALP pH decision numbers
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — FETAL SCALP pH decision numbers
≥ 7.25 — NORMAL → continue EFM; repeat in 1 hour if the FHR abnormality persists
7.21–7.24 — pre-acidosis / borderline → repeat within 30 minutes
≤ 7.20 — ACIDOSIS → DELIVER IMMEDIATELY

MEMORIZE: fetal scalp pH ≤ 7.20 triggers immediate delivery.
[Ch02 S10] names the test and gives no value — this is the number that gap needs.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — umbilical cord pH: artery vs vein
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — umbilical cord pH: artery vs vein
ARTERY (reflects the FETUS) — mean pH 7.24–7.27, working range 7.20–7.40
VEIN (reflects placental/maternal supply) — mean pH 7.32–7.34

The arterial pH is ALWAYS the lower of the two — if your two samples are nearly identical, you probably sampled the vein twice.

Thresholds: UA pH < 7.20 = acidemia (obstetric cutoff) · < 7.00 = significant/pathologic fetal acidemia · < 6.70 → ~80% develop neonatal encephalopathy

cards.q: ⚠️ D25 — do the slides ever name an intubation ROUTE?
cards.a:
⚠️ D25 — do the slides ever name an intubation ROUTE?
NEVER. "Orotracheal," "nasotracheal," "oral intubation" and "nasal intubation" return ZERO hits across all 24 decks.

Intubation is always route-unqualified — "intubate," "endotracheal intubation."

⚠️ Learn the distinction the decks DO draw: oro-/nasopharyngeal AIRWAYS are pharyngeal adjuncts, not endotracheal routes [Ch09 S3].

The only routes the decks enumerate are vascular: peripheral or intraosseous, and the umbilical vein.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — orotracheal vs nasotracheal: which for emergencies?
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — orotracheal vs nasotracheal: which for emergencies?
OROTRACHEAL is the route of choice for ALL emergency intubation and resuscitation, neonatal and pediatric — it is fastest, allows a larger tube (lower resistance, easier suctioning), and gives direct visualization.
NASOTRACHEAL — elective/semi-elective; more secure fixation, leaves the mouth free, better tolerated awake. But slower, needs a smaller tube, and EPISTAXIS is the most common complication.

⚠️ Neonates are near-obligate nose-breathers — a nasal tube occupies one nares; orotracheal is preferred in newborns.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — neonatal ETT size by weight / gestational age
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — neonatal ETT size by weight / gestational age
≤ 1200 g (< 28 wk) → 2.5 mm ID
1201–2200 g (28–34 wk) → 3.0 mm ID
> 2200 g (> 34 wk) → 3.5 mm ID

A 3.0 kg term newborn gets a 3.5 mm tube.

⚠️ NRP tops out at 3.5; some RT texts add a 4.0 row for term infants >3000–3800 g — if the professor's table has four rows, use his.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — pediatric ETT size formulas
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — pediatric ETT size formulas
Uncuffed: ID = (age ÷ 4) + 4 — Cole formula
Cuffed, age ≥ 2 yr: ID = (age ÷ 4) + 3.5 — Motoyama
Cuffed, age < 2 yr: ID = (age ÷ 4) + 3.0 — Khine

A cuffed tube is roughly one half-size (0.5 mm) smaller than the uncuffed tube for the same child. Always have the calculated size plus one above and one below at the bedside.

Cuffed ETTs may be used over uncuffed in infants and children; keep cuff pressure < 20–25 cm H2O.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — ETT insertion DEPTH formulas
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — ETT insertion DEPTH formulas
Neonates — the "6 + weight" rule (Tochen's): depth at the upper lip (cm) = 6 + weight in kg. A 3 kg newborn → 9 cm at the lip.

Children < 2 yr: depth (cm) = 3 × ETT internal diameter. A 4.0 tube → 12 cm
Children ≥ 2 yr (APLS): depth (cm) = (age ÷ 2) + 12. An 8-year-old → 16 cm

Cross-check the two — they should agree within about 1 cm.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — confirming ETT placement (know the two "gold standards")
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — confirming ETT placement (know the two "gold standards")
In the trachea, not the esophagus → exhaled CO2 detection / waveform capnography (plus direct visualization of the tube passing the cords)
Correct DEPTH/position → CHEST RADIOGRAPH — a CO2 detector proves the tube is in the trachea, not that it is at the right depth

⚠️ A colorimetric CO2 detector can give a FALSE NEGATIVE in cardiac arrest or very poor pulmonary blood flow.

cards.q: D26 — the FIVE components of parturition
cards.a:
D26 — the FIVE components of parturition
Parturition = "the process of giving birth":
Dilation of the cervix · rupture of the membranes · contraction of the uterus · separation of the placenta · shrinking of the uterus

⚠️ The slides treat cervical dilation as a PROCESS, never as a measurement — no centimeter value appears anywhere in Ch01–11.

[Ch03 S3]

cards.q: The THREE stages of labor as the slides define them
cards.a:
The THREE stages of labor as the slides define them
First Stage — "onset of contractions to full dilatation and effacement of the cervix"
Second Stage — "full dilatation and effacement to delivery of fetus"
Third Stage — "delivery of fetus and placenta"

[Ch03 S4]

cards.q: Dystocia — definition and why it matters
cards.a:
Dystocia — definition and why it matters
"Prolongation of labor secondary to uterine, pelvic, or fetal factors"
"As the length of labor increases, fetal morbidity and mortality increase"

[Ch03 S6]

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the three numbers on every cervical exam
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the three numbers on every cervical exam
Written together as e.g. "5 / 80% / −1":
Dilation — 0 to 10 cm. Width of the internal cervical os. 0 = closed, 10 = complete/fully dilated
Effacement — 0 to 100%. Thinning/shortening; 100% = paper-thin
Station — −5 to +5 cm. Presenting part relative to the maternal ischial spines; 0 = at the spines = ENGAGED; +5 = crowning

⚠️ No cm figure anywhere in Ch01–11

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the active-phase number: 4 cm or 6 cm?
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the active-phase number: 4 cm or 6 cm?
The old Friedman convention put the active phase at 4 cm.
ACOG/SMFM moved it to 6 cm — labor does not accelerate until about 6 cm, and slow progress before 6 cm is normal latent labor, not arrest.

⚠️ Your slides give no cm value at all, so if the professor teaches "active phase begins at 4 cm," answer 4 — but know 6 cm is the current standard.

cards.q: ⚠️ D27 — Placenta previa: what do the slides say?
cards.a:
⚠️ D27 — Placenta previa: what do the slides say?
Named three times, defined ZERO times. No slide says the placenta implants over or near the cervical os, and none gives a classification, bleeding description, or management plan.

The three mentions:
1. As an ultrasound use — "determination of placenta previa" [Ch02 S3]
2. As a high-risk current-obstetric-status factor [Ch02 S21]
3. Under "Abnormal Labor and Delivery", with abruptio placenta [Ch03 S8]

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — placenta previa: definition and classification
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — placenta previa: definition and classification
The placenta implants in the lower uterine segment such that placental tissue overlies the internal cervical os. Vaginal delivery is not possible.

Current terms:
Placenta previa — covers the internal os to any degree
Low-lying placenta — edge within 2 cm of the os but not covering

⚠️ "Partial" and "marginal" were RETIRED — everything is now previa or low-lying, by the 2 cm rule.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — why is digital vaginal exam CONTRAINDICATED in previa?
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — why is digital vaginal exam CONTRAINDICATED in previa?
The examining finger can disrupt the friable placental surface and the low-segment vessels over the os, provoking CATASTROPHIC HEMORRHAGE.

Establish placental location SONOGRAPHICALLY before any vaginal exam in third-trimester bleeding.

Exam-ready phrasing: "Third-trimester PAINLESS bleeding → ULTRASOUND FIRST, hands off the cervix."

cards.q: ⚠️⚠️ OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — PLACENTA PREVIA vs ABRUPTIO PLACENTAE
cards.a:
⚠️⚠️ OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — PLACENTA PREVIA vs ABRUPTIO PLACENTAE
PREVIA — placenta implanted over the internal os; PAINLESS, bright red, recurrent bleeding; uterus soft, non-tender; FHR usually reassuring; ultrasound is DIAGNOSTIC; digital exam CONTRAINDICATED

ABRUPTION — premature separation of a normally implanted placenta; PAINFUL, dark red, may be concealed (~20%); uterus firm, rigid, "board-like," tender; FHR frequently nonreassuring; shock OUT OF PROPORTION to visible loss; leading obstetric cause of DIC; ultrasound poorly sensitive — a clinical diagnosis

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — previa vs abruption: risk factors
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — previa vs abruption: risk factors
PREVIA: prior cesarean (risk rises with number), prior uterine curettage/surgery, prior previa, multiparity, age > 35, multiple gestation, smoking, cocaine, ART
ABRUPTION: maternal hypertension/preeclampsia, TRAUMA, cocaine, smoking, prior abruption, PPROM, rapid uterine decompression, short cord

Delivery for previa: cesarean is mandatory; scheduled at 36 0/7 – 37 6/7 weeks if stable

cards.q: ⚠️ D28 — what indications for cesarean do the slides give?
cards.a:
⚠️ D28 — what indications for cesarean do the slides give?
NONE. The slides define the procedure and give no indications list.

"Cesarean delivery = surgical incision through the maternal abdomen and uterus" [Ch03 S9]

⚠️ No slide in Ch01–11 uses the word "indication" for cesarean. Dystocia, abnormal presentation, cord prolapse, previa and abruption appear in the same chapter section as CONTEXT ONLY — do not present them as indications.

cards.q: The one NEONATAL CONSEQUENCE of cesarean the decks DO state
cards.a:
The one NEONATAL CONSEQUENCE of cesarean the decks DO state
Lung fluid retention "often occurs in babies delivered by Caesarean," producing transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTN) or RDS type II

[Ch01 S20]

(Also: "previous cesarean delivery" is a high-risk obstetric history factor [Ch02 S19])

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the three most common cesarean indications
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — the three most common cesarean indications
1. Labor dystocia / failure to progress — the #1 cause of a PRIMARY cesarean
2. Abnormal or indeterminate fetal heart rate tracing
3. Prior cesarean delivery — the #1 cause of a REPEAT cesarean

Roughly one in three US births is a cesarean.

cards.q: ⚠️⚠️ OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — WHY cesarean babies get TTN (the RT exam question)
cards.a:
⚠️⚠️ OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — WHY cesarean babies get TTN (the RT exam question)
In utero the pulmonary epithelium SECRETES fluid into the airspaces. LABOR triggers a surge of maternal and fetal CATECHOLAMINES and GLUCOCORTICOIDS, which activate epithelial sodium channels (ENaC). ENaC pumps Na+ OUT of the alveolus, and chloride and water follow osmotically — switching the lung from SECRETION to ABSORPTION. Vaginal delivery adds a mechanical thoracic squeeze.

Elective cesarean BEFORE the onset of labor bypasses the catecholamine surge, so ENaC is never fully switched on and fetal lung fluid is RETAINED → reduced compliance → TTN.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — scheduled vs emergency cesarean: the RT implication
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — scheduled vs emergency cesarean: the RT implication
SCHEDULED/ELECTIVE — usually NO labor has occurred → HIGHEST TTN RISK. With no medical indication, do not deliver before 39 0/7 weeks (ACOG CO 765)
EMERGENCY — usually after labor has begun → lower TTN risk, but higher risk of depression/asphyxia requiring full resuscitation

TTN numbers: ~7–10 per 1,000 of all newborns · ~10% at 33–34 wk · ~5% at 35–36 wk · <1% at ≥ 37 wk

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — pediatric OSA: risk factors
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — pediatric OSA: risk factors
Adenotonsillar hypertrophy — THE leading cause, especially ages 2–8 y
Obesity — dominant driver in adolescents; up to 60% prevalence in obese children
Craniofacial anomalies — micrognathia (Pierre Robin), midface hypoplasia, cleft
Down syndrome — midface hypoplasia + macroglossia + hypotonia + obesity
Neuromuscular disease — loss of pharyngeal dilator tone

Prevalence 1.2–5.7%; peak ages 2–8

cards.q: ⚠️⚠️ OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — how do CHILDREN with OSA present? (the key exam point)
cards.a:
⚠️⚠️ OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — how do CHILDREN with OSA present? (the key exam point)
NOT with sleepiness.

Daytime: hyperactivity, inattention, impulsivity, poor school performance, irritability, mood problems. Daytime sleepiness — the adult hallmark — is less common in prepubertal children.
Nighttime: snoring, witnessed pauses, gasping, paradoxical chest movement, hyperextended neck, restless sleep, diaphoresis, mouth breathing, nocturnal enuresis

Children with OSA are frequently misdiagnosed as ADHD. Screening question: ask every child whether they snore.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — pediatric OSA: first-line treatment (and how it differs from adults)
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — pediatric OSA: first-line treatment (and how it differs from adults)
CHILDREN: ADENOTONSILLECTOMY is FIRST-LINE when there is adenotonsillar hypertrophy.
ADULTS: CPAP is first-line.

Then: CPAP if surgery is not indicated or fails · weight loss as an addition · intranasal corticosteroids for mild OSA (AHI <5) · montelukast (FDA boxed warning — neuropsychiatric effects)

Post-op: inpatient monitoring for children < 3 years or with severe OSA.
Reassess 6–8 weeks after starting therapy.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — pediatric OSA: diagnosis
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — pediatric OSA: diagnosis
Overnight, attended, in-laboratory (Level I) polysomnography is the GOLD STANDARD and the only validated test in children. Home sleep apnea testing is NOT adequately validated in children.

⚠️ History and physical CANNOT distinguish primary snoring from OSA — you cannot diagnose it by tonsil size.

PSG before tonsillectomy is recommended in children < 2 years or with obesity, Down syndrome, craniofacial abnormalities, neuromuscular disorders, sickle cell disease or mucopolysaccharidoses.

cards.q: OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — consequences of untreated pediatric OSA
cards.a:
OUTSIDE THE SLIDES — consequences of untreated pediatric OSA
Growth failure / failure to thrive (increased WOB + disrupted nocturnal growth-hormone release)
Pulmonary hypertension → cor pulmonale → right heart failure (chronic nocturnal hypoxemia → hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction)
Systemic hypertension and metabolic/cardiovascular sequelae
Neurocognitive and behavioural impairment
Enuresis, poor quality of life

cards.q: D30 — EPIGLOTTITIS: what it is, hazard, presentation, management
cards.a:
D30 — EPIGLOTTITIS: what it is, hazard, presentation, management
What: "an infection that involves not just the epiglottis but the surrounding tissues"
Hazard: "can cause COMPLETE BLOCKAGE of the airway"
Presentation: "acute onset of sore throat, fever, and dysphagia that progresses to respiratory distress"
Management: "apply oxygen, monitor vitals, prepare to intubate if necessary"

[Ch09 S14]

cards.q: D30 — CROUP: what it is, cause, presentation, management
cards.a:
D30 — CROUP: what it is, cause, presentation, management
What: "a group of inflammatory diseases that affect the SUBGLOTTIC area of the larynx"
Cause: "VIRAL in origin"
Presentation: "onset is that of a common cold, with runny nose, cough, fever, and upper airway congestion"
Management: "humidifiers, adequate hydration, and close observation"

[Ch09 S15]

cards.q: ⭐ EPIGLOTTITIS vs CROUP — the contrast to memorize
cards.a:
⭐ EPIGLOTTITIS vs CROUP — the contrast to memorize
EPIGLOTTITIS — infection of the epiglottis AND surrounding tissues; acute sore throat / fever / dysphagia; can completely block the airway; be ready to INTUBATE

CROUP — VIRAL, inflammatory, SUBGLOTTIC larynx; cold-like onset; humidity, hydration, observation

[Ch09 S14–S15]

cards.q: D30 — FOREIGN BODY OBSTRUCTION
cards.a:
D30 — FOREIGN BODY OBSTRUCTION
Why children: "oral exploration is a major stage during early life"
Why it obstructs: "narrow airways increase risk"
Presentation: "a sudden onset of a dry, hacking cough"
Diagnosis: "diagnosis by radiograph" — Treatment: "treatment to remove object"
Also listed on the slide: "Hydrocarbons" ⚠️ (bare bullet, unexplained)

[Ch09 S16]

cards.q: ⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — how does [Ch09 S17] say CO poisoning is diagnosed?
cards.a:
⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — how does [Ch09 S17] say CO poisoning is diagnosed?
ANSWER THE SLIDE: "smoke inhalation"; "carbon monoxide poisoning"; "diagnosis by monitoring CO2 levels"; "immediately apply oxygen"; "monitor for damage to the airway"

⚠️ Carbon monoxide is CO, not CO2 — wrong test. Standard teaching: CO poisoning is diagnosed by CARBOXYHEMOGLOBIN (COHb) on CO-OXIMETRY. Standard pulse oximetry reads falsely normal. Treat with 100% O2 by non-rebreather; hyperbaric O2 for severe poisoning.

[Ch09 S17]

cards.q: D30 — CHLORINE inhalation: what it is and the FOUR phases
cards.a:
D30 — CHLORINE inhalation: what it is and the FOUR phases
"A greenish-yellow gas that is extremely irritating to the mucous membranes and skin"
Phase 1 — choking and coughing, minimal wheezing, slight oropharyngeal redness
Phase 2 — pharyngeal and pulmonary edema, inflammation, and plugging of the bronchi with mucus
Phase 3 — gradual improvement in pulmonary function
Phase 4 — further improvements in airway function and blood gas status

[Ch09 S18]

cards.q: CHOANAL ATRESIA — definition and management
cards.a:
CHOANAL ATRESIA — definition and management
"The membrane that separates the nasal cavity from the nasopharynx during embryologic development fails to disintegrate and blocks the passage of air"
"Causes severe respiratory distress"
Management: "use of an oral airway or intubation may be required"

[Ch08 S19]

cards.q: PIERRE-ROBIN SEQUENCE — definition and management
cards.a:
PIERRE-ROBIN SEQUENCE — definition and management
"Hypoplasia of the mandible (micrognathia), which forces the tongue to be positioned POSTERIORLY in the pharynx, creating an obstruction to breathing"
Management: "maintain the patient's airway patency until the mandible grows to its appropriate size"

[Ch08 S20]

cards.q: ANAPHYLAXIS — the airway threat and treatment
cards.a:
ANAPHYLAXIS — the airway threat and treatment
"Allergic reaction that is rapid in onset and may cause death"
"Symptoms include hives, skin and eyes itching, swelling of the LIPS, TONGUE, or FACE" — the lip/tongue/face swelling is the airway threat
"Administer EPINEPHRINE" (no dose given)

[Ch09 S29]

cards.q: ⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — "Hydrocarbons" on the foreign-body slide
cards.a:
⚠️ SLIDE FLAG — "Hydrocarbons" on the foreign-body slide
[Ch09 S16] lists "Hydrocarbons" as a bare bullet with no explanatory sentence — the slide does not say whether this means aspirated liquids or ingestion. Ambiguous as printed.

Standard teaching (NOT your slides): the danger is ASPIRATION, not ingestion. Low-viscosity hydrocarbons — gasoline, kerosene, lamp oil, furniture polish — are aspirated easily and cause chemical pneumonitis. Do NOT induce emesis.

cards.q: ⚠️ NOT IN THE SLIDES — upper airway hazard gaps
cards.a:
⚠️ NOT IN THE SLIDES — upper airway hazard gaps
Absent from Ch01–Ch11:
• No thumb-sign / steeple-sign radiographic vocabulary
• No racemic epinephrine or steroids for croup
• No age ranges for either epiglottitis or croup
• No Heimlich / back-blow technique
• No carboxyhemoglobin level for CO poisoning

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Heuer's droplet-size cutoff: droplet vs airborne transmission?
cards.a:
Heuer's droplet-size cutoff: droplet vs airborne transmission?
Droplet = larger than 5 µm — falls out of suspension fast, travels short distances.
Airborne = 5 µm or smaller (droplet nuclei) — stable, travels long distances, even between rooms.
Settling behaviour, not infectivity, separates the two.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Droplet precautions — how close before you mask up?
cards.a:
Droplet precautions — how close before you mask up?
Within 3 feet of the patient. Droplets generally travel 3 feet or less. This is the distance rule to memorize.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Are Transmission-Based Precautions used instead of Standard Precautions?
cards.a:
Are Transmission-Based Precautions used instead of Standard Precautions?
No — always layered ON TOP of Standard Precautions, never instead of them.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Heuer's headline: single best way to prevent transmission?
cards.a:
Heuer's headline: single best way to prevent transmission?
Good hand hygiene. Most hospital-acquired infections come from direct contact between patients and healthcare workers.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Contact precautions — PPE and room?
cards.a:
Contact precautions — PPE and room?
PPE: clean gloves and gown on ENTERING the room; change gloves after contact with infectious material; remove gloves and gown BEFORE leaving, then wash hands.
Room: private room, separate clean and dirty supply areas.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Contact precautions — example diseases?
cards.a:
Contact precautions — example diseases?
GI infections (diarrhea of unknown origin, C. difficile, norovirus), wound and skin infections, multidrug-resistant organisms (MRSA), SARS.
Deck adds: RSV = contact + droplet together.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Droplet precautions — PPE and room?
cards.a:
Droplet precautions — PPE and room?
PPE: surgical mask within 3 feet; eye/face protection for aerosol-generating procedures or contact with secretions; patient wears a mask for transport.
Room: private room, but NO special air handling — the door may stay open.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Droplet precautions — example diseases?
cards.a:
Droplet precautions — example diseases?
Bacterial meningitis, pertussis, influenza, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, group A strep, SARS, epiglottitis (H. influenzae).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Airborne precautions — PPE?
cards.a:
Airborne precautions — PPE?
Fit-tested NIOSH-certified N95 on entering — plus a user-seal check every single time. Eye/face protection for aerosol-generating procedures. For the highest protection or a poor N95 fit: a PAPR. The patient wears a surgical mask if transported.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Airborne precautions — room requirement?
cards.a:
Airborne precautions — room requirement?
Private negative-pressure Airborne Infection Isolation Room (AIIR) with the door CLOSED — air flows into the room so contaminated air can't escape.
If no AIIR available: private room + closed door + mask the patient.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Airborne precautions — example diseases?
cards.a:
Airborne precautions — example diseases?
Tuberculosis, measles (rubeola), chickenpox (varicella-zoster), Aspergillus, smallpox, SARS.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Air changes per hour (ACH) for an isolation room — what does Heuer say?
cards.a:
Air changes per hour (ACH) for an isolation room — what does Heuer say?
Heuer gives NO air-changes-per-hour number anywhere in the book. He specifies only the negative-pressure AIIR and the closed door.
The only ACH figure available is deck-specific: 6 ACH for aerosolized pentamidine. Use 6 if asked — but know it is the pentamidine number, not a Heuer number.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: PPE order — applying (Heuer Table 7-3)
cards.a:
PPE order — applying (Heuer Table 7-3)
1. Hair and foot coverings → 2. Gown → 3. Mask → 4. Goggles/face shield → 5. Gloves.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: PPE order — removing (Heuer Table 7-3)
cards.a:
PPE order — removing (Heuer Table 7-3)
1. Hair and foot coverings → 2. Goggles/face shield → 3. Mask → 4. Gloves (peel down from the wrist, turning inside out) → 5. Gown (inside out).
Note gloves come off 4th, not 1st — a common trap.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Waiting-area rule for respiratory hygiene / cough etiquette?
cards.a:
Waiting-area rule for respiratory hygiene / cough etiquette?
A surgical mask OR spatial separation of more than 3 feet. Plus: cover cough, tissues into a no-touch receptacle, hand hygiene.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Protocol for atypical viral infections (SARS, avian influenza, novel viruses)?
cards.a:
Protocol for atypical viral infections (SARS, avian influenza, novel viruses)?
Combined standard + contact + airborne in an AIIR with the door closed, continued for 14 days after symptom onset or until testing clears the patient.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Aerosol-generating procedures — what goes on the ventilator?
cards.a:
Aerosol-generating procedures — what goes on the ventilator?
HEPA filtration on the EXPIRATORY limb.
Also: PPE covering torso/arms/hands plus eyes/nose/mouth, consider a surgical hood with N95 or a PAPR, doors closed, minimize room entry/exit, consider sedation for intubation and bronchoscopy to minimize coughing.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Which procedures count as aerosol-generating?
cards.a:
Which procedures count as aerosol-generating?

<hr id=answer>

Aerosol drug delivery, sputum induction, bronchoscopy, suctioning, intubation, NIV, HFOV.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: What level of precaution does pneumonia alone get?
cards.a:
What level of precaution does pneumonia alone get?
Standard precautions — 'unless the cause indicates' a higher level (deck).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Does Heuer cover the Spaulding classification?
cards.a:
Does Heuer cover the Spaulding classification?
Yes — but he never uses the name 'Spaulding.' Table 7-5 is that exact three-tier scheme: critical / semicritical / noncritical, sorted by what the device touches.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Spaulding: CRITICAL items — definition, examples, processing?
cards.a:
Spaulding: CRITICAL items — definition, examples, processing?
Introduced into the bloodstream or normally sterile body parts: surgical instruments, intravascular catheters, implants, heart-lung bypass and dialysis components, bronchoscope forceps and brushes.
Processing: STERILIZATION.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Critical items — how do you sterilize heat-tolerant vs heat-sensitive?
cards.a:
Critical items — how do you sterilize heat-tolerant vs heat-sensitive?
Heat-tolerant → steam under pressure (autoclave).
Heat-sensitive → gas or ionized vapor (ethylene oxide, hydrogen peroxide) or immersion in a liquid chemical sterilant (glutaraldehyde, ortho-phthalaldehyde).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Spaulding: SEMICRITICAL items — definition and examples?
cards.a:
Spaulding: SEMICRITICAL items — definition and examples?
Contact intact mucous membranes: endoscopes/bronchoscopes, oral/nasal/tracheal airways, ventilator circuits and humidifiers, PFT mouthpieces and tubing, nondisposable nebulizers, laryngoscope blades, nondisposable resuscitation bags, pressure/gas/temperature probes.
Processing: sterilization OR high-level disinfection — liquid immersion (glutaraldehyde, OPA) or pasteurization.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Heuer's key line about most respiratory care equipment?
cards.a:
Heuer's key line about most respiratory care equipment?
Most respiratory care equipment is SEMICRITICAL — so high-level disinfection is the RT's everyday standard.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Spaulding: NONCRITICAL items — definition, examples, processing?
cards.a:
Spaulding: NONCRITICAL items — definition, examples, processing?
Touch only intact skin or don't touch the patient at all: stethoscopes, the outside of face masks, BP cuffs, the ventilator itself.
Processing: detergent washing or low- to intermediate-level disinfection.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Stethoscope between patients?
cards.a:
Stethoscope between patients?
Wipe the diaphragm with 70% alcohol prep pads, ideally kept visibly wet for at least 10 seconds.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Why must cleaning come BEFORE disinfection?
cards.a:
Why must cleaning come BEFORE disinfection?
Blood, mucus and organic debris shield organisms from the chemical or heat step, so a disinfectant applied over soil never reaches what's underneath.
An item that has not been cleaned cannot be reliably disinfected or sterilized.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Heuer's definition of cleaning vs disinfection?
cards.a:
Heuer's definition of cleaning vs disinfection?
Cleaning = 'the physical removal of foreign material (dirt, organic material), usually with water, detergents, and mechanical action' — it removes rather than kills.
Disinfection = the separate step that inactivates microorganisms.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Bronchoscope — first step at the bedside?
cards.a:
Bronchoscope — first step at the bedside?
Flush water/saline/approved solution through the working channel for 20 seconds, then transport immediately in a sealed contaminated-equipment bag so organic material doesn't dry on.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Bronchoscope reprocessing — enzymatic soak time?
cards.a:
Bronchoscope reprocessing — enzymatic soak time?
5 minutes, after the manufacturer's leak test. Then wipe external surfaces, flush the suction channel, brush all ports until no visible debris comes out, flush again, drain, rinse.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Bronchoscope high-level disinfection — glutaraldehyde immersion time?
cards.a:
Bronchoscope high-level disinfection — glutaraldehyde immersion time?
20 minutes or longer, fully immersing all surfaces. Confirm the disinfectant concentration each time, and fill the working channel by syringe if disinfecting manually.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: After liquid-disinfectant immersion — the rinsing rule?
cards.a:
After liquid-disinfectant immersion — the rinsing rule?
Rinse semicritical equipment with STERILE water.
If that isn't feasible: rinse with filtered or tap water, then rinse with isopropyl alcohol and dry with forced air or in a drying cabinet.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: How is a bronchoscope stored after reprocessing?
cards.a:
How is a bronchoscope stored after reprocessing?
Dry the working channel with 70% alcohol purged with compressed air, remove watertight caps, and hang vertically in a storage cabinet with NO valve attached. Document patient ID, date, bronchoscopist, model, serial number, reprocessing date.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Should you routinely disinfect the internal machinery of a ventilator?
cards.a:
Should you routinely disinfect the internal machinery of a ventilator?
No — do NOT routinely sterilize or disinfect internal ventilator machinery.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: How often do you change in-use circuits, humidifiers, HMEs and closed-suction systems?
cards.a:
How often do you change in-use circuits, humidifiers, HMEs and closed-suction systems?
Do NOT change on a routine schedule. Change only when visibly soiled or malfunctioning.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: What do you fill humidifiers with?
cards.a:
What do you fill humidifiers with?
Sterile water only.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Where does the inspiratory bacterial filter go?
cards.a:
Where does the inspiratory bacterial filter go?
Proximal to the humidifier.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Large-volume nebulizers and infection risk?
cards.a:
Large-volume nebulizers and infection risk?
They are a major infection source. Use prefilled sterile disposables when possible, and replace nondisposable units with a sterile or high-level-disinfected unit every 24 hours.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Small-volume nebulizer between treatments on the same patient?
cards.a:
Small-volume nebulizer between treatments on the same patient?
Clean, rinse with sterile water, air dry.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Open suctioning — catheter rule?
cards.a:
Open suctioning — catheter rule?
A sterile, single-use catheter every time.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: PFT equipment between patients?
cards.a:
PFT equipment between patients?
Change the mouthpiece and HEPA filter between patients — rather than disinfecting the internal workings.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Why does a bronchoscope used on a TB patient get sterilized rather than disinfected?
cards.a:
Why does a bronchoscope used on a TB patient get sterilized rather than disinfected?
M. tuberculosis has a waxy capsule resistant to many disinfectants. TB or hepatitis B exposure escalates a scope to sterilization.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: What do the decks give you on equipment processing?
cards.a:
What do the decks give you on equipment processing?
Only the principle — 'all equipment and supplies must be cleaned, disinfected, or sterilized' before use on another patient.
The decks give NO processing steps, NO agents, and NO times. All of that is Heuer.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Define sterilization.
cards.a:
Define sterilization.
Destroys ALL forms of microbial life — bacteria, viruses, spores, fungi.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Define high-level disinfection.
cards.a:
Define high-level disinfection.
Destroys vegetative bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi and viruses but not necessarily bacterial spores. (Some high-level agents can sterilize given enough contact time.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Define intermediate-level disinfection.
cards.a:
Define intermediate-level disinfection.
Kills vegetative bacteria, mycobacteria, and most viruses and fungi — but not resistant spores.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Define low-level disinfection.
cards.a:
Define low-level disinfection.
Kills most vegetative bacteria, some fungi, and some viruses (hepatitis B and C, HIV) — but NOT mycobacteria and NOT spores. It's for environmental surfaces.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Antiseptic vs germicide vs bacteriostatic?
cards.a:
Antiseptic vs germicide vs bacteriostatic?
Antiseptic — kills organisms on living skin or mucous membranes.
Germicide — any chemical that kills microorganisms.
Bacteriostatic — only inhibits growth.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Pasteurization — temperature, time, and what level does it achieve?
cards.a:
Pasteurization — temperature, time, and what level does it achieve?
Immersion at > 158°F (70°C) for 30 minutes.
High-level DISINFECTION, not sterilization. Used for semicritical heat-sensitive respiratory equipment — ventilator circuits, humidifiers, nondisposable nebulizers.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Glutaraldehyde (Cidex) — high-level disinfection time vs true sterilization time?
cards.a:
Glutaraldehyde (Cidex) — high-level disinfection time vs true sterilization time?
High-level disinfection: 20 minutes at room temperature.
True sterilization: a full 10 HOURS.
Bronchoscope immersion: 20 minutes or longer. Ortho-phthalaldehyde (OPA) is used the same way.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Hydrogen peroxide, liquid — concentration and time?
cards.a:
Hydrogen peroxide, liquid — concentration and time?
3% for 30 minutes — home/CF disinfection of cleaned semicritical items and nebulizer parts.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Isopropyl alcohol — the four numbers to know?
cards.a:
Isopropyl alcohol — the four numbers to know?
70% for 5 minutes (cleaned semicritical items at home).
Stethoscopes: 70% wipes visibly wet ≥ 10 seconds.
Bronchoscope channel dried with 70% alcohol.
Line insertion prep: chlorhexidine 2% in 70% isopropyl alcohol.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Chlorhexidine — what is it, concentration, scrub time?
cards.a:
Chlorhexidine — what is it, concentration, scrub time?
An antiseptic for skin and mucous membranes — NOT a sterilant.
2% (in 70% isopropyl alcohol), scrubbed into the insertion site for 30 seconds.
Uses: CDC central line bundle skin prep, swabbing access ports, daily oral care to prevent VAP.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Sodium hypochlorite (bleach) — the four dilutions?
cards.a:
Sodium hypochlorite (bleach) — the four dilutions?
Routine surfaces during a C. difficile outbreak: 1:10 (dilute 5–6% solution).
Blood/body-fluid spills: 1:100 for small spills (< 10 mL), 1:10 for large spills.
Home semicritical items: 1:50 for 5 minutes.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Bleach and CF nebulizers?
cards.a:
Bleach and CF nebulizers?
Bleach is NOT to be used on CF nebulizers.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: What temperature and cycle time does Heuer give for the steam autoclave and ethylene oxide?
cards.a:
What temperature and cycle time does Heuer give for the steam autoclave and ethylene oxide?
None. Heuer gives no temperature, pressure, or cycle time for the autoclave, and no concentration, cycle time, or aeration time for EtO. Same for ionized hydrogen peroxide vapor.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Heat methods for home equipment (once cleaned)?
cards.a:
Heat methods for home equipment (once cleaned)?
Boil for 5 minutes, microwave submerged in water for 5 minutes, or a dishwasher at ≥ 70°C (158°F) for 30 minutes.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Why shouldn't home patients use ammonia, vinegar, Borax or liquid detergents?
cards.a:
Why shouldn't home patients use ammonia, vinegar, Borax or liquid detergents?
They are ineffective against Staphylococcus aureus. Bleach is the only household product that should be used.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Which method is the best for verifying that sterilization worked?
cards.a:
Which method is the best for verifying that sterilization worked?
Biological indicators — they test whether the cycle killed bacterial spores on impregnated paper strips.
Include them in every cycle containing critical items, and otherwise at least once a week per sterilizer.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Mechanical monitoring of sterilization — what's the catch?
cards.a:
Mechanical monitoring of sterilization — what's the catch?
It checks cycle time, temperature and pressure. Correct readings do NOT guarantee sterility — but incorrect readings flag a problem.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Chemical indicators — what do they tell you?
cards.a:
Chemical indicators — what do they tell you?
They change color when the correct temperature or gas concentration is reached, giving an immediate warning. If the indicator on a package hasn't changed color, get a replacement item.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Mechanical and chemical monitoring look correct, but the biological culture GROWS. What do you recall?
cards.a:
Mechanical and chemical monitoring look correct, but the biological culture GROWS. What do you recall?
Recall critical items only.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: VAP definition — and the source disagreement
cards.a:
VAP definition — and the source disagreement
Heuer: pneumonia in patients ventilated more than 48 hours.
Infectious Pulmonary Disease deck: more than 48 to 72 hours after intubation.
RCP 105 deck slide says 'within 48 hours' — its own notes correct this to '48 hours or more.'
Safest exam answer: 48 hours or more after intubation, in a patient not admitted with pneumonia.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: A patient with severe nosocomial pneumonia needs ventilation after the infection starts. Is that VAP?
cards.a:
A patient with severe nosocomial pneumonia needs ventilation after the infection starts. Is that VAP?
No — that does not meet the VAP definition (Heuer).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: What is the actual risk factor for VAP — the ventilator or the tube?
cards.a:
What is the actual risk factor for VAP — the ventilator or the tube?
The ETT, not the ventilator. It bypasses the filtering defenses of the nose and mouth, and secretions pooling above the cuff leak around it into the lungs.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Primary mechanism of VAP?
cards.a:
Primary mechanism of VAP?
Microaspiration — secretions pooled above the cuff leaking around it into the lungs.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Single greatest risk factor for VAP?
cards.a:
Single greatest risk factor for VAP?
Prolonged mechanical ventilation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: VAP epidemiology — the numbers (decks; Heuer gives no percentages)
cards.a:
VAP epidemiology — the numbers (decks; Heuer gives no percentages)
Affects 10 to 25% of ventilated patients · about 25% of all ICU infections · mortality 33 to 50%.
Trauma, neurosurgical and burn patients have higher rates than respiratory/medical ICU patients.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: VAP incidence over time on the ventilator?
cards.a:
VAP incidence over time on the ventilator?
3% over the first 5 days, then 2% per day for the next 5 days, then 1% per day thereafter.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: How is VAP diagnosed clinically?
cards.a:
How is VAP diagnosed clinically?
No single finding makes the diagnosis. Suspect it with new or progressive infiltrates on CXR/CT plus signs of infection: fever, leukocytosis or leukopenia, and purulent tracheobronchial secretions.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: VAP — the test statistics and CPIS
cards.a:
VAP — the test statistics and CPIS
Infiltrates plus two of the three other criteria: sensitivity 69%, specificity 75%.
A modified CPIS greater than 6 raises suspicion but does not confirm it.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: What CONFIRMS VAP?
cards.a:
What CONFIRMS VAP?
Identifying a pathogen from a lower respiratory tract sample, obtained BEFORE starting or changing antibiotics: bronchoscopic BAL or protected specimen brush (PSB), non-bronchoscopic mini-BAL, or an endotracheal aspirate into a sterile specimen trap.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: VAP — the mechanical clues on the ventilator?
cards.a:
VAP — the mechanical clues on the ventilator?
Falling tidal volume, rising inspiratory and plateau pressures, decreasing compliance.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: VAP organisms shift with time on the vent — the timeline?
cards.a:
VAP organisms shift with time on the vent — the timeline?
First 48 hours = upper-airway flora (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae).
3–7 days = gram-negative bacilli.
More than 7 days = resistant organisms including MRSA.
Start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics, then de-escalate once cultures return.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: VAP bundle — head of bed?
cards.a:
VAP bundle — head of bed?
Elevate 30–45 degrees unless contraindicated. This is the number to memorize.
It prevents gastric reflux aspiration and improves distribution of ventilation and diaphragm efficiency.
Deck contraindications: after neurosurgery, or severe hypotension.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: VAP bundle — sedation and breathing trials?
cards.a:
VAP bundle — sedation and breathing trials?
Daily 'sedation vacations' plus daily spontaneous breathing trials (SBTs) — watch for self-extubation when sedation is stopped.
Deck specifies a 6 to 8 hour daily sedative vacation, paired with a daily spontaneous awakening trial.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: VAP bundle — peptic ulcer prophylaxis agent?
cards.a:
VAP bundle — peptic ulcer prophylaxis agent?
Sucralfate rather than H2 antagonists. (Heuer only; the decks omit this.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: VAP bundle — oral care?
cards.a:
VAP bundle — oral care?
Daily oral care with chlorhexidine, plus assessing the oral cavity, rotating the oral ETT position at least every 24 hours, brushing the teeth, and applying mouth moisturizer/lip balm.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: What is a subglottic (Hi-Lo) ETT and why does it reduce VAP?
cards.a:
What is a subglottic (Hi-Lo) ETT and why does it reduce VAP?
An ETT with a separate dorsal lumen that continuously removes secretions pooled just above the cuff — attacking microaspiration at its source.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Why an in-line / closed-suction catheter system?
cards.a:
Why an in-line / closed-suction catheter system?
The circuit is never broken. The AARC endorses this. Use a T-adapter with a one-way valve for in-line nebulized medications for the same reason.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: VAP prevention — cuff pressure and which technique to avoid?
cards.a:
VAP prevention — cuff pressure and which technique to avoid?
Maintain cuff pressure 20–30 cm H₂O and avoid the minimal leak technique.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Oral or nasal intubation to prevent VAP?
cards.a:
Oral or nasal intubation to prevent VAP?
Oral. Nasal intubation causes sinusitis and more VAP. Better still: avoid intubation entirely — use NIV.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Ventilator circuit changes — the real conflict
cards.a:
Ventilator circuit changes — the real conflict
RCP 105 Wk 5 deck's bundle slide: 'change circuits every 7 days' and 'change inline suction devices and HMEs every 24 hours.'
The same deck's speaker notes, plus Heuer/CDC/AARC: do NOT change circuits on a routine schedule — change only when visibly soiled or malfunctioning, because unnecessary changes increase contamination.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: HME placement and change interval?
cards.a:
HME placement and change interval?
Place vertically above the tracheal tube; change only when visibly soiled.
VAP incidence does NOT differ between heated humidification and HMEs.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: If using a heated humidifier, what do you do with condensate?
cards.a:
If using a heated humidifier, what do you do with condensate?
Drain it away from the patient regularly without breaking the circuit.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: If you remember only four things about VAP prevention?
cards.a:
If you remember only four things about VAP prevention?
Cuff pressure 20–30 cm H₂O · head of bed 30–45° · wash your hands · extubate as early as it is safe.
The deck's clinical pearl: early liberation from mechanical ventilation is the single best way to prevent VAP.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: How much did one hospital cut VAP by, bundling these steps?
cards.a:
How much did one hospital cut VAP by, bundling these steps?
95% in three years.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Mycobacterium tuberculosis — organism characteristics?
cards.a:
Mycobacterium tuberculosis — organism characteristics?
An aerobic, rod-shaped bacillus with a waxy capsule (resistant to many disinfectants) that requires acid-fast staining to be seen.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Why is TB classically UPPER-LOBE disease?
cards.a:
Why is TB classically UPPER-LOBE disease?
It is an obligate aerobe, so it thrives where oxygen tension is highest — the lung apices.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: TB droplet nuclei size — and why it matters?
cards.a:
TB droplet nuclei size — and why it matters?
0.5–1.0 µm — can remain airborne for hours. Well under Heuer's 5 µm airborne cutoff, which makes TB highly contagious in enclosed spaces.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: TB — the PPE asymmetry to remember
cards.a:
TB — the PPE asymmetry to remember
The patient wears a surgical mask; the provider wears an N95 or higher. Limit transport.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Heuer specifically flags which test as requiring airborne precautions when TB exposure is possible?
cards.a:
