Heuer specifically flags which test as requiring airborne precautions when TB exposure is possible?
PFT testing.
Deck's high-risk aerosol-generating list: intubation, sputum induction, bronchoscopy, chest physiotherapy, and aerosolized medication delivery.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Primary TB — what happens and over what timeframe?
cards.a:
Primary TB — what happens and over what timeframe?
Inhaled bacilli implant in alveoli and multiply over 3 to 4 weeks, then get walled off in a tubercle/granuloma with a caseous necrotic core.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Latent TB — is the patient infectious?
cards.a:
Latent TB — is the patient infectious?
No. Bacilli are sealed inside tubercles, dormant for months, years, or life — usually asymptomatic and NOT infectious.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Reactivation (active/postprimary) TB — triggers and presentation?
cards.a:
Reactivation (active/postprimary) TB — triggers and presentation?
Recurrence when immunity falls: malnutrition, crowded/institutional living, HIV/AIDS, steroids, alcohol abuse.
Presents with low-grade fever, extreme fatigue, night sweats, violent cough, greenish or bloody sputum, chest pain, anorexia, weight loss.
The patient is HIGHLY infectious at this stage.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Disseminated (miliary) TB — what and where?
cards.a:
Disseminated (miliary) TB — what and where?
Bacilli spread via blood or lymph, seeding 1–5 mm tubercles in lymph nodes, kidneys, long bones, genital tract, brain and meninges.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Which test for latent TB vs active TB? (Heuer's framing)
cards.a:
Which test for latent TB vs active TB? (Heuer's framing)
Latent infection → tuberculin skin test.
Active infection → serial sputum collection for AFB stain.
Chest x-ray and IGRA are added concurrently to confirm active TB or prior exposure.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Mantoux test — when do you read it?
cards.a:
Mantoux test — when do you read it?
Read the induration at 48–72 hours.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Mantoux induration thresholds — and the source warning
cards.a:
Mantoux induration thresholds — and the source warning
Deck thresholds: < 5 mm = negative · 5–9 mm = suspicious · ≥ 10 mm = positive.
Heuer gives NO induration cut-offs and no read time at all, so these millimetres are the deck's alone.
The CDC's published scheme is risk-stratified (5 / 10 / 15 mm) rather than the single 10 mm line the deck teaches — answer with the deck's numbers for this course.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: A positive PPD means what, exactly?
cards.a:
A positive PPD means what, exactly?
Exposure or latent TB — NOT necessarily active disease.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Sputum collection for AFB — how many, how much, when?
cards.a:
Sputum collection for AFB — how many, how much, when?
3 sputum samples over 8–24 hours, each ≥ 5 mL of deep lung secretions, including an early-morning sample.
Saliva and nasopharyngeal secretions are NOT acceptable.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: AFB stains — what do you see?
cards.a:
AFB stains — what do you see?
Ziehl-Neelsen = red bacilli on a blue background.
Fluorescent stain = yellow-green bacilli, easier to read.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Sputum induction — agent, concentrations, session length?
cards.a:
Sputum induction — agent, concentrations, session length?
Hypertonic saline (3%, 5%, 7%, or 10%) via ultrasonic nebulizer, or a jet nebulizer that can run continuously for the 15- to 20-minute session.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Sputum induction — the safety setup and the stop rule?
cards.a:
Sputum induction — the safety setup and the stop rule?
Negative-pressure room or booth, RT in an N95, using a valved breathing circuit with an expiratory HEPA filter.
Pretreat reactive-airway patients with a fast-acting beta agonist, get a baseline FEV₁ 10–15 minutes after.
STOP if FEV₁ falls ≥ 20%.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Sputum induction — what counts as an adequate sample?
cards.a:
Sputum induction — what counts as an adequate sample?
2 to 5 mL; 4–5 mL is needed for reliable AFB analysis. Space repeat attempts at least 24 hours apart.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: IGRA / QuantiFERON-TB Gold — how does it compare to the Mantoux?
cards.a:
IGRA / QuantiFERON-TB Gold — how does it compare to the Mantoux?
A blood test measuring IFN-γ release after exposure to TB antigens.
Heuer: as sensitive as Mantoux for LATENT TB, and MORE sensitive for ACTIVE TB.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Xpert MTB/RIF & Ultra — speed and what it detects?
cards.a:
Xpert MTB/RIF & Ultra — speed and what it detects?
Rapid molecular test, results in < 2 hours; detects TB and rifampin resistance.
Ultra is more sensitive for smear-negative, pediatric, extrapulmonary, and HIV cases.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Classic TB chest x-ray — early primary disease?
cards.a:
Classic TB chest x-ray — early primary disease?
A Ghon nodule (small area of consolidation), becoming a Ghon complex when the draining lymph nodes are involved. Upper-lobe / apical.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Classic TB chest x-ray — advanced and healed disease?
cards.a:
Classic TB chest x-ray — advanced and healed disease?
Advanced: cavitary lesions, with or without an air-fluid level.
Chronic/healed: calcification, fibrosis, pleural effusion, and retraction of lung segments.
Miliary TB: numerous tiny nodules scattered throughout both lungs.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: What PFT pattern does extensive TB produce?
cards.a:
What PFT pattern does extensive TB produce?
Restrictive: ↓ FVC, ↓ VC / IC / TLC, with a normal or slightly INCREASED FEV₁/FVC ratio.
PFTs are usually normal unless disease is extensive.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Right ventricular enlargement in a TB patient signals what?
cards.a:
Right ventricular enlargement in a TB patient signals what?
Cor pulmonale.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: What TB drug regimen does Heuer give?
cards.a:
What TB drug regimen does Heuer give?
None — Heuer gives no TB drug regimen anywhere in the book. Every drug number is from the Infectious Pulmonary Disease deck: 2–4 drugs for 6–9 months.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: The six-month TB protocol?
cards.a:
The six-month TB protocol?
Induction (first 2 months): INH + RIF + PZA + either EMB or SM.
Continuation (next 4 months): INH + RIF daily or twice weekly.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: The nine-month TB protocol?
cards.a:
The nine-month TB protocol?
INH + RIF daily for 1–2 months, then twice weekly out to 9 months.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Which TB drug is the most effective first-line agent — and what is the prophylaxis regimen?
cards.a:
Which TB drug is the most effective first-line agent — and what is the prophylaxis regimen?
Isoniazid (INH) is the most effective first-line agent; rifampin (RIF) is bactericidal and paired with INH.
Prophylaxis: INH daily for 1 year for exposed individuals or a positive PPD.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: What drives MDR-TB and how is it countered?
cards.a:
What drives MDR-TB and how is it countered?
Noncompliance with the long regimens.
Countered by Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) — a healthcare worker watches each dose — and, once resistance is documented, by adding ≥ 3 additional antibiotics and extending the duration.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Does the deck use the acronym 'RIPE'?
cards.a:
Does the deck use the acronym 'RIPE'?
No. It teaches the induction drugs as INH + RIF + PZA + EMB/SM and never uses the acronym — though those are the same four drugs.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: When do TB patients become non-contagious?
cards.a:
When do TB patients become non-contagious?
Usually after a few weeks — but completing the full course is essential.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Why does Heuer flag biohazardous waste handling for the exam?
cards.a:
Why does Heuer flag biohazardous waste handling for the exam?
It's one of the three stated objectives of Ch 7, and Heuer notes it is an area RTs are typically LEAST familiar with — so expect it.
The decks cover none of it.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Which biohazardous materials matter most to RTs?
cards.a:
Which biohazardous materials matter most to RTs?
Isolation wastes, blood and blood products, and contaminated sharps and needles.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Solid infectious waste — where do you separate and contain it?
cards.a:
Solid infectious waste — where do you separate and contain it?
Separate infectious from noninfectious at the POINT OF GENERATION. Discard and contain all solid infectious waste except sharps at its point of origin, in clearly identifiable, leak-proof, tear- and puncture-resistant containers marked with the biological hazard symbol.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: A biohazard bag is contaminated or punctured — what do you do?
cards.a:
A biohazard bag is contaminated or punctured — what do you do?
Double-bag it. (And keep biohazard bags away from sharp objects in the first place.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: How do you transport waste or sharps containers?
cards.a:
How do you transport waste or sharps containers?
Place them inside a rigid container lined with plastic bags.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Sharps — the three 'nevers'?
cards.a:
Sharps — the three 'nevers'?
Never recap a used needle · never handle it with both hands · never point it toward your body.
If capping is unavoidable: a one-handed 'scoop' technique or a mechanical needle-sheath holder.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Can you remove a used needle from a disposable syringe by hand?
cards.a:
Can you remove a used needle from a disposable syringe by hand?
No — and do not bend, break, or otherwise manipulate needles by hand. All used sharps go into an impervious, rigid, puncture-resistant container made for the purpose.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Sharps are part of a spill — how do you pick them up?
cards.a:
Sharps are part of a spill — how do you pick them up?
With forceps.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Liquid waste (blood, suction fluids) — transport and disposal?
cards.a:
Liquid waste (blood, suction fluids) — transport and disposal?
Transport in capped or tightly stoppered bottles. Then either inactivate using government-approved treatment technologies or carefully pour down a utility sink drain or toilet.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: How is ventilator circuit condensate classified and handled?
cards.a:
How is ventilator circuit condensate classified and handled?
As hazardous liquid waste: wear gloves, drain and discard periodically without letting it flow back toward the patient, then decontaminate hands.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Blood/body-fluid spill — the three-step answer
cards.a:
Blood/body-fluid spill — the three-step answer
(1) Put on protective gloves and whatever other PPE the task requires.
(2) If large amounts, first clean the visible matter with disposable absorbent material and discard in labeled containment.
(3) Disinfect with an EPA-registered tuberculocidal agent, an EPA-registered germicide effective against HIV or hepatitis B, or freshly diluted sodium hypochlorite.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Bleach dilutions for spills?
cards.a:
Bleach dilutions for spills?
1:100 for small spills (< 10 mL) · 1:10 for larger spills.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::01 Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
cards.q: Final disposition of infectious waste?
cards.a:
Final disposition of infectious waste?
Treated by sterilization or incineration. Solid residue → sanitary landfill. Liquid or ground-up waste → sanitary sewer system.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Standard working pressure of piped wall gas?
cards.a:
Standard working pressure of piped wall gas?
50 psi — what ventilators, blenders and flowmeters are built to run on.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: When are high-pressure cylinders used in hospital?
cards.a:
When are high-pressure cylinders used in hospital?
Only where there is no piped gas, during ambulation/transport, or as a home backup.
Specialty gases (He, NO, CO, CO₂) are available only in cylinders.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Cylinder sizes — which are small vs large?
cards.a:
Cylinder sizes — which are small vs large?
Small (portability): A through E, or M.
Large (long runs): G, H, or K.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Home ambulatory cylinder sizes and typical flows?
cards.a:
Home ambulatory cylinder sizes and typical flows?
Small aluminum cylinders: M-6/B, M-9/C, D, or E.
Home flows usually 0.25–4.0 L/min → use a low-flow metering device.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: What is an H cylinder used for in the home?
cards.a:
What is an H cylinder used for in the home?
Backup for concentrator failure or power outage, or for infants on very low flow.
Impractical otherwise — H tanks must be tied together and swapped often.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: What pressure does Heuer's duration table assume for a full cylinder?
cards.a:
What pressure does Heuer's duration table assume for a full cylinder?
2200 psi — with the explicit warning that filling pressures vary; always check the gauge before computing.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: DISS — what is it and where is it used?
cards.a:
DISS — what is it and where is it used?
Diameter Index Safety System — the threaded connection used to take 50 psi directly off a piped source for ventilators/blenders. Also the connector for wall vacuum/suction.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: PISS — what is it and what does a hissing tank mean?
cards.a:
PISS — what is it and what does a hissing tank mean?
Pin Index Safety System — the yoke used on small cylinders.
Heuer's testable troubleshooting line: a hissing tank means a loose connection or a missing/damaged washer on a PISS regulator. (Home version: 'hissing from the regulator → not seated properly, tighten it, or the washer is missing.')

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: ASSS and the 10-year hydrostatic test interval — what does Heuer say?
cards.a:
ASSS and the 10-year hydrostatic test interval — what does Heuer say?
Neither is covered in Heuer or the available decks. (ASSS = American Standard Safety System, the threaded outlet on large cylinders.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Heuer's 7 safe-use steps for cylinders — in order
cards.a:
Heuer's 7 safe-use steps for cylinders — in order
(1) Check the label to confirm the correct gas.
(2) Confirm enough gas for the planned duration.
(3) Transport large cylinders chained to a wheeled cart; small ones in the gurney/wheelchair holder.
(4) Investigate any hissing.
(5) Open the valve slowly all the way, then turn back half a turn to keep it from freezing open.
(6) Record the pressure and compute duration of flow.
(7) Before disconnecting, close the valve and bleed the pressure out of attached devices.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Why open a cylinder valve fully and then turn it back half a turn?
cards.a:
Why open a cylinder valve fully and then turn it back half a turn?
To keep the valve from 'freezing' fully open.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Cylinder storage rules?
cards.a:
Cylinder storage rules?
Secure the cylinders · well-ventilated area · keep FULL cylinders separated from EMPTY ones.
Home: no smoking / no open flame, grounded plugs, a no-smoking sign on the door, attention to tank location, secureness and temperature.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Oxygen cylinders in the MRI suite?
cards.a:
Oxygen cylinders in the MRI suite?
Iron-free equipment only — aluminum cylinders and carts, brass and aluminum regulators.
Deck, more bluntly: the magnet can turn a steel cylinder into a projectile.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: When do you change out a cylinder?
cards.a:
When do you change out a cylinder?
At least 15–30 minutes before the contents are fully exhausted, or when pressure drops below 500 psi.
Transport deck adds: an 'E' cylinder with a wrench must be FULL before transport, and for a possible delay carry at least twice the volume needed for a one-way trip.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: The duration-of-flow formula
cards.a:
The duration-of-flow formula
Duration (min) = (gauge pressure in psig × cylinder factor) ÷ flow (L/min)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Cylinder factors (L/psig) — Heuer Table 6-10
cards.a:
Cylinder factors (L/psig) — Heuer Table 6-10
M-6/B = 0.07 · M-9/C = 0.11 · D = 0.16 · E = 0.28 · G = 2.14 · H/K = 3.14

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Hours of flow at 1 L/min from a full (2200 psi) cylinder
cards.a:
Hours of flow at 1 L/min from a full (2200 psi) cylinder
M-6/B = 2.6 h · M-9/C = 4.0 h · D = 5.9 h · E = 10.3 h · G = 78.5 h · H/K = 115.1 h

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Heliox cylinder factors (Heuer App B Table B-6)
cards.a:
Heliox cylinder factors (Heuer App B Table B-6)
He/O₂: D = 0.14 · E = 0.23 · G = 1.93 · H/K = 2.50
(vs O₂/air: 0.16 · 0.28 · 2.41 · 3.14)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: ⚠ Heuer contradicts himself on which cylinder factor?
cards.a:
⚠ Heuer contradicts himself on which cylinder factor?
The G cylinder.
Table 6-10 (Ch 6, p301) gives G = 2.14; Appendix B Table B-6 (p1048) gives G = 2.41.
Table 6-10 is internally consistent with 2.14 (2.14 × 2200 = 4,708 min = 78.5 h, the printed value; 2.41 would give 88.4 h). The widely published textbook value is 2.41.
Know both and pick whichever matches the answer choices. Every other factor agrees.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Ballpark check: how long does a full E cylinder last at 10 L/min?
cards.a:
Ballpark check: how long does a full E cylinder last at 10 L/min?
About 1 hour. A full H at 10 L/min lasts about 10 times longer — 10 hours.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Worked: E cylinder at 800 psi, set to 5 L/min — how long until empty?
cards.a:
Worked: E cylinder at 800 psi, set to 5 L/min — how long until empty?
Duration = (psig × factor) ÷ flow
= (800 × 0.28) ÷ 5
= 224 ÷ 5
= 44.8 ≈ 45 minutes

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Worked: Full E (2200 psi) at 3 L/min — how long until you must swap it at the 500-psi rule?
cards.a:
Worked: Full E (2200 psi) at 3 L/min — how long until you must swap it at the 500-psi rule?
Usable pressure = 2200 − 500 = 1700 psig
Duration = (1700 × 0.28) ÷ 3 = 476 ÷ 3
= 158.7 min ≈ 2 hours 39 minutes
Sanity check: full E at 10 L/min ≈ 60 min, so at 3 L/min ≈ 200 min to bone-dry. ✔

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Worked: H cylinder at 1800 psi, patient needs 6 L/min — duration?
cards.a:
Worked: H cylinder at 1800 psi, patient needs 6 L/min — duration?
Duration = (1800 × 3.14) ÷ 6 = 5652 ÷ 6
= 942 minutes = 15.7 hours

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: How does a LOX system work, and why bother?
cards.a:
How does a LOX system work, and why bother?
Oxygen stored as a cryogenic liquid in an insulated reservoir, vaporized into gas before it reaches the patient.
The reason: 1 L of liquid O₂ vaporizes into 860 L of gaseous O₂ — an enormously efficient way to store a large supply in a small footprint.
Heuer notes LOX is used less often than in the past now that portable concentrators exist.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: LOX stationary ('base') unit capacity?
cards.a:
LOX stationary ('base') unit capacity?
45 to 100 pounds of LOX, depending on model.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: LOX portable unit — capacity, weight, duration?
cards.a:
LOX portable unit — capacity, weight, duration?
Holds about 1 L of LOX, weighs less than 6 pounds, and — paired with a demand-flow/conserving device — provides 8 hours or more.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: The two LOX conversion factors
cards.a:
The two LOX conversion factors
1 pound of LOX ≈ 344 L of gaseous O₂
1 L of liquid O₂ = 860 L of gaseous O₂
(1 L LOX ≈ 2.5 lb)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: LOX duration formula
cards.a:
LOX duration formula
Gaseous O₂ available (L) = LOX weight (lb) × 344
Duration (min) = total gaseous O₂ (L) ÷ flow (L/min)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Worked: LOX home unit filled to 75 lb, running at 2 L/min continuous — how long?
cards.a:
Worked: LOX home unit filled to 75 lb, running at 2 L/min continuous — how long?
Gas available = 75 × 344 = 25,800 L (Heuer rounds to 'about 26,000 L')
Duration = 25,800 ÷ 2 = 12,900 min
= 215 hours = ≈ 9 days
Heuer: 'enough to last more than a week at 2 L/min (more with a pulse-dose system).'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Intermittent hissing from a stationary LOX tank — what do you do?
cards.a:
Intermittent hissing from a stationary LOX tank — what do you do?
Nothing — intermittent hissing is NORMAL. LOX is stored below its boiling point, so it warms and boils off continuously and the reservoir must vent. Just keep the tank upright.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Loud, constant hissing from a LOX tank with a steady stream of mist — what do you do?
cards.a:
Loud, constant hissing from a LOX tank with a steady stream of mist — what do you do?
This is a PROBLEM. Put the patient on backup O₂ and call the supplier.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Gaseous tank troubleshooting: regulator is on but no O₂ is flowing?
cards.a:
Gaseous tank troubleshooting: regulator is on but no O₂ is flowing?
The tank was never turned on, or it is empty.
If flow still fails with both tank and regulator open → replace the tank.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Do any of the 62 decks cover liquid oxygen?
cards.a:
Do any of the 62 decks cover liquid oxygen?
No — no deck mentions liquid oxygen, LOX, or the 860/344 conversion factors. This item is Heuer-only.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: How does an oxygen concentrator produce O₂?
cards.a:
How does an oxygen concentrator produce O₂?
An electrically powered device that physically separates the O₂ in room air from nitrogen. Most use sodium-aluminum silicate pellets (a molecular sieve) that adsorb nitrogen, CO₂ and water vapor, letting oxygen pass through.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Concentrator purity and maximum flow?
cards.a:
Concentrator purity and maximum flow?
About 90–95% O₂ at flows up to 10 L/min.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: What analyzed concentrator output means the sieve is failing?
cards.a:
What analyzed concentrator output means the sieve is failing?
Less than 85–90% of the manufacturer's spec. → Switch to gaseous backup; replace the concentrator or send for service.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Why does concentrator FiO₂ fall as flow rises — and does Heuer give a curve?
cards.a:
Why does concentrator FiO₂ fall as flow rises — and does Heuer give a curve?
Mechanism: higher flow = less contact time with the sieve = more nitrogen slips through. That's the reason for the 'up to 10 L/min' ceiling.
Heuer does NOT print a purity-vs-flow decay curve — the relationship is not stated numerically in Heuer or the decks.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Which O₂ supply is most cost-efficient for continuous low-flow in alternative settings?
cards.a:
Which O₂ supply is most cost-efficient for continuous low-flow in alternative settings?
The oxygen concentrator.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Portable concentrator (POC) — power sources and battery life?
cards.a:
Portable concentrator (POC) — power sources and battery life?
Household AC, 12-volt DC (cars, RVs), or batteries.
Typical battery life 1–4 hours, optional packs extending to more than 6 hours.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: POC pulse-dose vs continuous-flow — the exam distinction
cards.a:
POC pulse-dose vs continuous-flow — the exam distinction
Most POCs deliver pulse-dose only, enough for patients needing 30% O₂ or less.
Only continuous-flow units can provide more than 30% O₂ — which is what's needed at altitude (airliner cabins).
Continuous-flow POCs are bigger and heavier, so less portable.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: POC start-up sequence — the power-source order?
cards.a:
POC start-up sequence — the power-source order?
AC first, auto-DC next, battery last.
Full sequence: (1) check the air intake filter is clean and positioned; (2) well-ventilated area, inlets/outlets unobstructed; (3) best power source; (4) attach a pulse-dose nasal cannula; (5) power on, confirm self-test, set flow; (6) confirm the unit is sensing inhalation (flashing indicator + pulse sound); (7) expect max output in 1–2 minutes.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Concentrator alarm — most likely cause and fix?
cards.a:
Concentrator alarm — most likely cause and fix?
Intake filters blocked or dirty. → Clean the intake filters; keep them a proper distance from walls and curtains.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Concentrator won't turn on — action?
cards.a:
Concentrator won't turn on — action?
Check power / plug / circuit breaker. If power is fine, put the patient on the gaseous backup and replace the concentrator.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Patient on concentrator cannula at ≥ 4 L/min complains of nasal dryness?
cards.a:
Patient on concentrator cannula at ≥ 4 L/min complains of nasal dryness?
Add a bubble humidifier.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: POC warning indicators — what does 'capacity exceeded' mean and what do you do?
cards.a:
POC warning indicators — what does 'capacity exceeded' mean and what do you do?
The patient's demand has outrun the unit. → Reduce activity, switch to backup.
Other indicators: low battery → AC/DC and charge, else backup O₂. Cannula disconnect → check connections, breathe through the nose; if persistent, backup + call provider. General malfunction / service needed / low O₂ concentration → backup O₂ and call the provider.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Concentrator placement teaching points?
cards.a:
Concentrator placement teaching points?
There is a limit to how much O₂ tubing can be added, so the stationary unit must sit as central as possible in the patient's range of activity. Account for the heat it generates (a closet or small room may not work), don't put intake filters against a wall or curtain, and warn that O₂ tubing is a trip hazard.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Why does a POC work for air travel when a cylinder doesn't?
cards.a:
Why does a POC work for air travel when a cylinder doesn't?
Unlike cylinders, a POC continuously extracts oxygen from the surrounding air rather than being a finite supply.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Airliner cabin altitude — the numbers?
cards.a:
Airliner cabin altitude — the numbers?
Cabins are pressurized to 8,000 ft: PB 564 mm Hg, PaO₂ ≈ 59 mm Hg. A POC reduces high-altitude hypoxia in patients not requiring mechanical ventilation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: How much POC battery should a traveling patient carry?
cards.a:
How much POC battery should a traveling patient carry?
At least 150% of one-way travel time. Battery life is the biggest single consideration because airlines are not required to supply electricity or oxygen for non-emergency use.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Concentrator vs LOX vs cylinder — purity/output?
cards.a:
Concentrator vs LOX vs cylinder — purity/output?
Concentrator: 90–95% O₂, flows up to 10 L/min.
LOX: essentially 100%.
Gaseous cylinders: essentially 100%, compressed at up to 2200 psi, finite volume.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Main advantage and drawback of each home O₂ source?
cards.a:
Main advantage and drawback of each home O₂ source?
Concentrator: most cost-efficient for continuous low-flow, no deliveries — but needs electricity, generates heat, sieve pellets wear out.
LOX: huge supply in a small package — but continuous evaporative loss/venting, needs supplier refills, increasingly uncommon.
Cylinders: simple, no power required — the backup for power failure — but runs out; H tanks must be tied together and replaced frequently.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: What do O₂-conserving devices do to consumption and duration?
cards.a:
What do O₂-conserving devices do to consumption and duration?
They cut O₂ usage by 50–75%, which doubles or triples duration of flow from a bulk source.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: The two types of O₂-conserving device?
cards.a:
The two types of O₂-conserving device?
Simple reservoir cannulas — store O₂ in a small reservoir during exhalation, release it on inhalation. Effective but bulky and not well tolerated.
Pulse-dose/demand-flow systems — a sensor triggers a valve delivering O₂ only during inspiration; systems differ, so flow must be individually adjusted to reach the desired SpO₂.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: A conserving device fails — what flow do you switch to?
cards.a:
A conserving device fails — what flow do you switch to?
A continuous O₂ source at 2–3× the conserving-device flow.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Demand-flow sensor alarm — troubleshooting sequence?
cards.a:
Demand-flow sensor alarm — troubleshooting sequence?
Turn the unit off and back on to reset; check that cannula/tubing connections are tight and not kinked; adjust the cannula for a comfortable fit, then initiate an inspiration.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Heuer's home O₂ prescribing rules — the four NBRC scenarios
cards.a:
Heuer's home O₂ prescribing rules — the four NBRC scenarios
Restricted activity → concentrator plus a gaseous cylinder for backup.
Ambulatory → always recommend a portable source (POC, LOX, or small cylinder).
Especially active / needs extended duration → include an O₂-conserving device.
Sleep-only → a stationary system without portables will suffice.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Appliance of choice at home, and the usual flow ceilings?
cards.a:
Appliance of choice at home, and the usual flow ceilings?
A simple low-flow device (usually nasal cannula) or an O₂-conserving system.
Home cannula flows generally ≤ 4 L/min for adults, ≤ 2 L/min for infants; at those flows supplemental humidification is generally not needed — add it for nasal dryness.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Medicare qualifying criteria for home O₂ — hypoxemia at rest?
cards.a:
Medicare qualifying criteria for home O₂ — hypoxemia at rest?
COPD or other chronic pulmonary disease with SpO₂ ≤ 88% or PaO₂ ≤ 55 torr, at rest, on room air.
For a hospitalized patient, the value must be obtained no sooner than 48 hours before discharge. (Covers stationary AND portable.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Medicare qualifying criteria for sleep-only home O₂?
cards.a:
Medicare qualifying criteria for sleep-only home O₂?
PaO₂ ≤ 55 mm Hg or SaO₂ ≤ 88% during sleep in a patient who is PaO₂ ≥ 56 / SaO₂ ≥ 89% awake, OR a greater-than-normal nocturnal fall (PaO₂ drop > 10 mm Hg).
Covers stationary, NOT portable.
Deck's nocturnal version: a > 5% drop in SpO₂, or SpO₂ < 88%.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: What defines a low-flow device?
cards.a:
What defines a low-flow device?
It delivers gas at a flow less than the patient's inspiratory flow, so delivered O₂ is always diluted with entrained room air and FiO₂ is variable.
That's why low-flow devices are ordered in L/min, not FiO₂ — charted FiO₂ ranges are estimates only.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Nasal cannula rule of thumb — FiO₂ per L/min?
cards.a:
Nasal cannula rule of thumb — FiO₂ per L/min?
Each 1 L/min raises FiO₂ by roughly 4% above room air: 1 ≈ 24%, 2 ≈ 28% … up to 6 L/min ≈ 44–45%.
Heuer's stated adult cannula range: 1–6 L/min, 22–45%.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Heuer Table 6-2 — the four DEVICE factors that raise FiO₂?
cards.a:
Heuer Table 6-2 — the four DEVICE factors that raise FiO₂?
Higher O₂ flow input · reservoir PRESENT · leak ABSENT · valves PRESENT.
(The opposites → more air dilution → lower FiO₂.)
These are the things you control.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Heuer Table 6-2 — the five PATIENT factors that raise FiO₂?
cards.a:
Heuer Table 6-2 — the five PATIENT factors that raise FiO₂?
Lower inspiratory flow · lower tidal volume · slower respiratory rate · lower minute ventilation.
(Higher of any → more dilution → lower FiO₂.)
These you can only observe — which is why with a low-flow system you always evaluate the patient's response to set the flow.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: On a HIGH-flow device, how do you titrate — and why is this the one students get wrong?
cards.a:
On a HIGH-flow device, how do you titrate — and why is this the one students get wrong?
Change the FiO₂, NOT the flow.
Turning flow down on an air-entrainment device does not change FiO₂ — but the reduced total flow may no longer meet inspiratory demand, at which point the patient entrains room air and delivered O₂ becomes variable again.
On a reservoir system, cutting flow can additionally cause CO₂ rebreathing and suffocation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: What happens if an entrainment port is obstructed by bedding, clothing or a hand?
cards.a:
What happens if an entrainment port is obstructed by bedding, clothing or a hand?
Decreased air entrainment → HIGHER delivered O₂ concentration but LOWER total flow, with an unpredictable net effect on the FiO₂ the patient actually inspires.
→ Remove the obstruction and monitor.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: On blenders, how does flow affect FiO₂?
cards.a:
On blenders, how does flow affect FiO₂?
FiO₂ varies with the setting and, to a small degree, with flow: higher flows minimize or eliminate air dilution.
→ Set the desired O₂% on the blender and run the high end of the patient's flow range to guarantee it.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Aerosol tubing entirely blocked by condensate — what's the tell?
cards.a:
Aerosol tubing entirely blocked by condensate — what's the tell?
Tubing filled with water and NO gurgling sound.
→ Drain the condensate and add a water trap.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Delivered O₂% reads HIGHER than set — what does condensate have to do with it?
cards.a:
Delivered O₂% reads HIGHER than set — what does condensate have to do with it?
Condensate creates back pressure in the circuit, acting like a partially obstructed entrainment port.
→ Drain the condensate, add a water trap, check/correct kinking or outlet obstructions.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Intermittent flow or 'bubbling' in a heated-humidifier circuit means what?
cards.a:
Intermittent flow or 'bubbling' in a heated-humidifier circuit means what?
Partial obstruction with condensate.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Why does a circuit rain out, and what are the three fixes?
cards.a:
Why does a circuit rain out, and what are the three fixes?
Gas leaves a heated humidifier saturated and cools as it travels down the tubing, so water vapor condenses and pools.
Fixes: heated-wire circuit, inline water trap, or an HME for temporary use. Water traps go at the LOW POINTS of a circuit.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Why does HFNC avoid rainout by design?
cards.a:
Why does HFNC avoid rainout by design?
It includes a heated delivery system to prevent tubing condensation and gas cooling, and delivers gas at BTPS without condensation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Deck's rule of thumb linking FiO₂ to expected PaO₂?
cards.a:
Deck's rule of thumb linking FiO₂ to expected PaO₂?
PaO₂ should be at least 5 times the O₂%.
So 50% → PaO₂ at least 250 torr; 21% → 80–100 torr; 100% → about 500 torr.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: TDP decision rule: at what FiO₂ do you switch to a high-flow system?
cards.a:
TDP decision rule: at what FiO₂ do you switch to a high-flow system?
FiO₂ greater than 0.40 → select an appropriate high-flow system.
Otherwise start continuous low-flow and adjust per guidelines, titrating on SpO₂ and work of breathing. Use pulse oximetry whenever FiO₂ ≥ 0.44.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Nasal cannula titration increments, high-flow ceiling, discharge goal?
cards.a:
Nasal cannula titration increments, high-flow ceiling, discharge goal?
Standard cannula titrated in 1–2 L/min increments; high-flow systems reach FiO₂ ≥ 0.90; discharge goal SpO₂ ≥ 91% or baseline, watching for oxygen toxicity.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: SpO₂ target in COPD — and why?
cards.a:
SpO₂ target in COPD — and why?
88–92%, because excessive FiO₂ can worsen hypercapnia.
Venturi masks and HFNC are the named devices for precise FiO₂ control.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: HME efficiency per the decks?
cards.a:
HME efficiency per the decks?
70–90% RH at 30–31 °C.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: A weaning checkpoint asks literally: 'Is there water in the ventilator tubing?' Why?
cards.a:
A weaning checkpoint asks literally: 'Is there water in the ventilator tubing?' Why?
A patient failing against a circuit full of condensate is failing on added RESISTANCE, not weak lungs.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Capnography and water — which sampling type is vulnerable?
cards.a:
Capnography and water — which sampling type is vulnerable?
Sidestream — secretions and water get drawn into the sampling tube and occlude it.
Mainstream is unaffected by water condensation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: How do air-entrainment systems set FiO₂ — and what's the inverse relationship?
cards.a:
How do air-entrainment systems set FiO₂ — and what's the inverse relationship?
They mix air and O₂ at ratios set by jet and port size.
Bigger ports / smaller jets → more dilution → LOWER FiO₂ and HIGHER total flow.
Smaller ports / bigger jets → less dilution → HIGHER FiO₂ but LOWER total flow.
That inverse relationship is the whole topic.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Air:O₂ entrainment ratios — the full table (Heuer 6-5)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: The entrainment anchor value to memorize?
cards.a:
The entrainment anchor value to memorize?
60% = 1:1 — the pivot.
Anything below 60% has a ratio GREATER than 1:1 (50% → 1.7:1); anything above 60% has a ratio LESS than 1:1 (70% → 0.6:1).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: At FiO₂ 0.80 and 0.24, how much output does each 1 L/min of flowmeter setting yield?
cards.a:
At FiO₂ 0.80 and 0.24, how much output does each 1 L/min of flowmeter setting yield?
At 0.80: 1.3 L/min of output.
At 0.24: 26 L/min of output.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: The ratio formula ('magic box')
cards.a:
The ratio formula ('magic box')
Air : O₂ ratio = (100 − desired O₂%) ÷ (desired O₂% − 21)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Total flow formula for an entrainment device
cards.a:
Total flow formula for an entrainment device
Total flow = input (O₂) flow × total ratio parts
= input flow × (air parts + O₂ parts)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Heuer's benchmark for a stable FiO₂?
cards.a:
Heuer's benchmark for a stable FiO₂?
'In general, the best way to ensure a stable FiO₂ is to provide a total flow of at least 40 L/min.'
At an input of 10 L/min, only settings at or below 40% O₂ clear that bar.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Why can't you just keep raising the O₂ input flow on an entrainment device?
cards.a:
Why can't you just keep raising the O₂ input flow on an entrainment device?
Input is limited by the back-pressure created at the device jet, typically to 12–15 L/min.
Beyond that: run two air-entrainment nebulizers in parallel to double the flow.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Venturi mask vs air-entrainment nebulizer — input ranges and FiO₂?
cards.a:
Venturi mask vs air-entrainment nebulizer — input ranges and FiO₂?
Venturi mask: 4–12 L/min input, FiO₂ 24–50%.
Air-entrainment nebulizer: 10–15 L/min input, 28–100%, with output that should exceed 60 L/min for a stable FiO₂.
Both become less precise at FiO₂ ≥ 0.35 — because total flow falls as FiO₂ rises.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Worked: 35% air-entrainment mask at 8 L/min input — ratio and total flow?
cards.a:
Worked: 35% air-entrainment mask at 8 L/min input — ratio and total flow?
Air:O₂ = (100 − 35) ÷ (35 − 21) = 65 ÷ 14 = 4.6:1 (Heuer rounds to 5:1)
Total flow = 8 × (5 + 1) = 48 L/min

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Worked decision: adult on a 40% mask, flowmeter at 8 L/min. Does it meet demand?
cards.a:
Worked decision: adult on a 40% mask, flowmeter at 8 L/min. Does it meet demand?
Ratio at 40% = (100−40) ÷ (40−21) = 60 ÷ 19 = 3.16 ≈ 3:1
Parts = 3 + 1 = 4
Total flow = 8 × 4 = 32 L/min
32 < 40 → DOES NOT meet inspiratory demand. The patient entrains extra room air; actual FiO₂ drops below 0.40 and becomes variable.
Fix: raise input to 12 L/min → 12 × 4 = 48 L/min ✔
Note the FiO₂ stays 0.40 — raising input flow changed TOTAL FLOW, not FiO₂.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Worked: why do high-FiO₂ entrainment devices fail? (O₂ input maxed at 15 L/min)
cards.a:
Worked: why do high-FiO₂ entrainment devices fail? (O₂ input maxed at 15 L/min)
50%: parts 2.7 → 15 × 2.7 = 40.5 L/min → barely meets the bar
60%: parts 2 → 15 × 2 = 30 L/min → FAILS
70%: parts 1.6 → 15 × 1.6 = 24 L/min → FAILS badly

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Above FiO₂ 0.60 at flows > 40 L/min, what should you use instead of entrainment?
cards.a:
Above FiO₂ 0.60 at flows > 40 L/min, what should you use instead of entrainment?
A BLENDER-based system — a mechanical/manual blender (requires 50-psi air AND O₂) or a heated high-flow nasal cannula.
Alternative: run two air-entrainment nebulizers in parallel.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Entrainment device, SaO₂ lower than expected — the three branches?
cards.a:
Entrainment device, SaO₂ lower than expected — the three branches?
Inadequate total flow → increase input flow, correct obstructions/leaks.
Inadequate O₂ concentration → increase FiO₂ or switch to a higher-capability device.
Device displaced → reposition.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Nebulizer at high O₂% settings (> 35–40%) — the five fixes?
cards.a:
Nebulizer at high O₂% settings (> 35–40%) — the five fixes?
Maximize input flow · add an open reservoir to the expiratory side of the T-tube · connect multiple nebulizers in parallel · provide an inspiratory reservoir with a one-way expiratory valve · set the nebulizer to a low O₂% and bleed in extra O₂.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Do the decks print an entrainment ratio table?
cards.a:
Do the decks print an entrainment ratio table?
No — searches for 'entrainment,' 'entrain,' and 'air:oxygen' return zero hits across all 62 decks. The table is Heuer-only.
The decks give only the escalation ladder: 2 L nasal cannula → Venturi mask → HFNC or BiPAP → intubation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Non-rebreather — required flow?
cards.a:
Non-rebreather — required flow?
Minimum 10 L/min — and the operative definition of 'enough' is whatever flow keeps the reservoir bag from collapsing.
Heuer's ED scenario for suspected MI: 'nonrebreathing mask, > 10 L/min', or HFNC at ≥ 20 L/min @ 100%.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: NRB — FiO₂ delivered, and what class of device is it?
cards.a:
NRB — FiO₂ delivered, and what class of device is it?
60–80% (Heuer Table 6-1).
It is a low-flow / variable-performance RESERVOIR device, not a true high-flow system — which is exactly why the FiO₂ is a range and not a number.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: NRB valve function — what do the two sets of valves do?
cards.a:
NRB valve function — what do the two sets of valves do?
A one-way valve between bag and mask lets reservoir gas in on inspiration but stops exhaled gas entering the bag.
One-way flaps on the mask ports let exhaled gas out but block room air in.
The NRB is the 'valves present' case in Table 6-2: valves present → less dilution → higher FiO₂.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Hess: what happens if you remove an NRB's valves?
cards.a:
Hess: what happens if you remove an NRB's valves?
'Removing the valves converts the nonrebreathing mask to a partial rebreathing mask.'
Hess: the NRB incorporates valves BOTH between the bag and mask AND on at least one exhalation side port. At the start of inspiration the port valves close and the reservoir valve opens, letting the patient draw 300 to 500 mL of O₂ from the reservoir on top of incoming flow.
Hess is the RCP 202 text — supporting reference, not the book you're graded from.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Why can't an NRB deliver a true 100%?
cards.a:
Why can't an NRB deliver a true 100%?
Hess: 'If the system were perfect, delivery of 100% O₂ would be possible' — but these inexpensive disposable masks cannot provide an airtight fit, and their valves are simple rubber or vinyl.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: NRB: the bag COLLAPSES when the patient inhales — cause and action?
cards.a:
NRB: the bag COLLAPSES when the patient inhales — cause and action?
Inadequate flow, or increased minute ventilation. → INCREASE the flow.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: NRB: the bag fails to remain inflated — cause and action?
cards.a:
NRB: the bag fails to remain inflated — cause and action?
Insufficient input flow; O₂ tubing disconnect or obstruction. → Increase the flowmeter setting; check tubing is connected and unkinked.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: NRB: the bag remains FULLY inflated during inhalation — the three causes in order?
cards.a:
NRB: the bag remains FULLY inflated during inhalation — the three causes in order?
(1) Too much flow → decrease flow until the bag deflates slightly during inspiration.
(2) Flow is right → large mask leak → correct the leak.
(3) Flow and seal are right → inspiratory valve jammed/reversed → repair or replace the mask.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: NRB — the one-line summary of bag behaviour
cards.a:
NRB — the one-line summary of bag behaviour
A collapsing bag means flow is too LOW — turn it up.
A bag that never moves means flow is too high, the mask leaks, or a valve has failed.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: A physician orders an NRB for a 'code blue' patient in respiratory arrest. What do you do?
cards.a:
A physician orders an NRB for a 'code blue' patient in respiratory arrest. What do you do?
An NRB does not provide VENTILATION. Immediately recommend a bag-valve-mask that can give 100% O₂ and actually ventilate.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Switching from a simple mask to an NRB only moves SpO₂ from 83% to 87%. What's going on and what do you recommend?
cards.a:
Switching from a simple mask to an NRB only moves SpO₂ from 83% to 87%. What's going on and what do you recommend?
Cause: inability to meet high inspiratory flow demand at high FiO₂, or alveolar shunting.
→ Recommend an HFNC at 20–40 L/min titrated to SpO₂, or consider mask CPAP with high FiO₂.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: How is heliox delivered to a spontaneously breathing patient?
cards.a:
How is heliox delivered to a spontaneously breathing patient?
Via a tight-fitting nonrebreathing mask or a high-flow cannula.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: House-fire victim with SpO₂ 98% on a cannula — what do you do and why?
cards.a:
House-fire victim with SpO₂ 98% on a cannula — what do you do and why?
Give the highest possible FiO₂ (usually an NRB) plus CO-OXIMETRY, because SpO₂ cannot detect carboxyhemoglobin.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Partial rebreathing mask — flow and FiO₂?
cards.a:
Partial rebreathing mask — flow and FiO₂?
6–10 L/min, 40–70%. (Heuer lists a potential suffocation hazard for both the partial rebreather and the NRB.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Preoxygenation before intubation — the deck's NRB protocol?
cards.a:
Preoxygenation before intubation — the deck's NRB protocol?
100% FiO₂ via a TIGHT-FITTING non-rebreather mask (or BVM with PEEP) for at least 3–5 minutes, or until end-tidal O₂ (ETO₂) > 85–90% if monitored.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: What is the Briggs adaptor?
cards.a:
What is the Briggs adaptor?
The T-piece — a T-shaped connector that is one of the patient interfaces for a large-volume air-entrainment nebulizer (LVN).
Heuer lists the LVN interfaces together: t-piece (Briggs adapter), trach mask, aerosol mask, or face tent.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: The three ports of a T-piece — what connects where?
cards.a:
The three ports of a T-piece — what connects where?
One arm takes the inspiratory limb from the large-volume nebulizer; the stem connects to the patient's artificial airway (ETT or trach).
The third arm is the expiratory limb — and that's the one that matters on the exam.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Why does reservoir tubing on the T-piece expiratory limb matter?
cards.a:
Why does reservoir tubing on the T-piece expiratory limb matter?
Because the LVN's total output is limited, a patient with high inspiratory demand can out-breathe the device and draw room air backward through the open expiratory arm, diluting FiO₂ unpredictably.
A length of corrugated reservoir tubing on the expiratory side acts as a reserve of source gas to pull from instead of room air.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: 'Aerosol mist disappears during inspiration' on a T-tube or mask — what does it mean?
cards.a:
'Aerosol mist disappears during inspiration' on a T-tube or mask — what does it mean?
Heuer's T4 tip, stated as a rule: the FLOW IS INADEQUATE.
Causes: inadequate flow and increased patient inspiratory flow demands.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Prescribing scenario: postoperative patient with an ETT requiring a moderate FiO₂?
cards.a:
Prescribing scenario: postoperative patient with an ETT requiring a moderate FiO₂?
Air-entrainment nebulizer at 40–50% O₂ and a T-tube WITH AN OPEN RESERVOIR. The reservoir is written into the order.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Inadequate mist output from an LVN — the four causes?
cards.a:
Inadequate mist output from an LVN — the four causes?
Inadequate input flow (increase it) · corrugated tube obstruction (drain condensate) · jet orifice misalignment (repair/replace) · low water level (refill).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: The four ways to run an SBT — and do outcomes differ?
cards.a:
The four ways to run an SBT — and do outcomes differ?
T-piece (Briggs adapter) · low-level pressure support (5–8 cm H₂O to offset the ETT) · CPAP (~5 cm H₂O) · automatic tube compensation (ATC).
All of these methods produce similar weaning outcomes.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Why is the T-piece SBT the purest test?
cards.a:
Why is the T-piece SBT the purest test?
It gives NO ventilator assistance at all — the patient performs most or all of the work of breathing, typically for 30 minutes, while being watched for fatigue or distress.
Heuer Ch 11 specifies: T-piece, trach collar, or CPAP ≤ 5 cm H₂O with PS < 5 cm H₂O.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: When do you use a Thorpe tube flowmeter?
cards.a:
When do you use a Thorpe tube flowmeter?
Whenever there is a piped source — 'to deliver a controlled flow of gas to a patient or equipment' → connect a calibrated Thorpe tube to the piped gas at 50 psi. The standard bedside metering device wherever there is wall gas.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: When do you use a Bourdon gauge — and why?
cards.a:
When do you use a Bourdon gauge — and why?
Transport on cylinders: use a flowmeter unaffected by gravity — a Bourdon gauge or an integrated regulator/variable-orifice flow controller (Praxair Grab 'n Go, Western Medica Oxytote).
A Bourdon gauge is NOT gravity-dependent, so it reads the same at any angle.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Why can't a Thorpe tube go on a transport tank?
cards.a:
Why can't a Thorpe tube go on a transport tank?
It is gravity-dependent — it floats a ball or bobbin in a vertical tapered tube, so it must be kept upright and will misread if tipped on a gurney.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: How does each device actually work?
cards.a:
How does each device actually work?
Thorpe tube: MEASURES flow — a float rising in a tapered tube against a variable orifice.
Bourdon gauge: a PRESSURE GAUGE with a scale printed in L/min — it measures pressure upstream of a fixed orifice and infers flow from it.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: The classic Bourdon-gauge exam point — and where it is NOT found
cards.a:
The classic Bourdon-gauge exam point — and where it is NOT found
A Bourdon gauge OVER-READS whenever there is a downstream obstruction (kinked tubing, occluded cannula): back pressure raises the measured pressure while actual flow falls.
This is NOT covered in Heuer or the available decks — Heuer states only which device to use where and why (gravity), never the error behavior.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Hess on the Bourdon gauge — the examinable clause?
cards.a:
Hess on the Bourdon gauge — the examinable clause?
'If the Bourdon gauge outlet became completely obstructed, the gauge continues to show flow even though none is present.'
The gauge is accurate only if outlet flow is unrestricted; add downstream resistance and outlet pressure rises while actual flow decreases.
Practical rule: pneumatic nebulisers present a large downstream resistance and should NOT be used with a Bourdon gauge.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Hess on the pressure-compensated Thorpe tube?
cards.a:
Hess on the pressure-compensated Thorpe tube?
'Unlike flow resistors and Bourdon gauges, a pressure-compensated Thorpe tube flow meter displays the ACTUAL outlet flow regardless of downstream resistance' — provided the inlet pressure remains constant.
Construction: clear tapered glass tube, wider at the top than the bottom, graduated markings, a float, plus a needle valve.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: What is a 'rotameter'?
cards.a:
What is a 'rotameter'?
A flowmeter with a rotating bobbin rather than a spherical float — used where anaesthetic gases need greater accuracy.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: The bench test for a back-pressure-compensated Thorpe tube — where is it documented?
cards.a:
The bench test for a back-pressure-compensated Thorpe tube — where is it documented?
In a compensated tube, the float jumps and returns to zero when the flowmeter is pressurized before the valve is opened.
NOT covered in Heuer or the available decks — look it up in Egan's Fundamentals of Respiratory Care, 'Storage and Delivery of Medical Gases.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Delivering 50-psi unrestricted flow with NO piped source — equipment?
cards.a:
Delivering 50-psi unrestricted flow with NO piped source — equipment?
A large cylinder (H or K) with a preset 50-psi pressure-reducing valve.
For air: a piston air compressor with reservoir.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Delivering controlled flow to a patient with NO piped source — equipment?
cards.a:
Delivering controlled flow to a patient with NO piped source — equipment?
A gas cylinder with a reducing valve and flowmeter, cylinder size chosen by portability need and planned duration.
For air: a portable diaphragm compressor (limited flow/pressure).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Blender setting and measured O₂% disagree substantially — troubleshooting order?
cards.a:
Blender setting and measured O₂% disagree substantially — troubleshooting order?
Check both source pressures (usually ≥ 35 psig) → check for leaks between source and blender → if both check out, replace the blender.
Always verify the prescribed O₂% using an O₂ analyzer, not the dial.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Gold standard for flow calibration, and the accuracy standard?
cards.a:
Gold standard for flow calibration, and the accuracy standard?
A computer-controlled air pump generating standard expiratory waveforms.
Recommended accuracy: ± 5% of the reading or ± 0.2 L/sec, whichever is greater.
General QC principle: two-point calibration before each use.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Heliox through an O₂ flowmeter — the correction factors?
cards.a:
Heliox through an O₂ flowmeter — the correction factors?
1.8 for 80/20 He/O₂ · 1.6 for 70/30 · 1.4 for 60/40.
Worked: 10 L/min indicated on an O₂ flowmeter delivering 80/20 → actual flow = 10 × 1.8 = 18 L/min.
Alternative: use a device calibrated for that He%.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Air compressor output inadequate — troubleshooting order?
cards.a:
Air compressor output inadequate — troubleshooting order?
Check the inlet filter for obstruction → then tubing and connected equipment for obstruction → then tubing and connections for leaks.
Portable compressor won't start: check the outlet for power and the fuse or circuit breaker.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Ventilator pneumatic source pressure alarm — causes?
cards.a:
Ventilator pneumatic source pressure alarm — causes?
Loss of the air or O₂ source below 50 psig triggers electronic or pneumatic reed alarms.
Heuer Ch 11 Table 11-9: gas lines not connected to the high-pressure 50-psi outlets, or gas lines connected to the LOW-pressure outlet (e.g. flowmeters).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::02 Medical Gas, Cylinders & Flow Devices
cards.q: Do 'Bourdon' or 'Thorpe' appear anywhere in the decks?
cards.a:
Do 'Bourdon' or 'Thorpe' appear anywhere in the decks?
No — neither word appears anywhere in the 62 decks. This item is Heuer + Hess only.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: MDI teaching — what do you do before the first puff?
cards.a:
MDI teaching — what do you do before the first puff?
Shake the canister, and PRIME it (waste a dose into the air) if it is new or unused for a few days. Warm a cold canister in the hands or it will not function properly.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: MDI open-mouth technique — the distance?
cards.a:
MDI open-mouth technique — the distance?
Hold the MDI 2 inches (4 cm, about 2 finger widths) from the open mouth with the tongue down — this enhances lung deposition.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: When is closed-mouth MDI technique acceptable?
cards.a:
When is closed-mouth MDI technique acceptable?
Only if ALL three apply: (a) the patient cannot do open-mouth, (b) no spacer is available, and (c) the drug is NOT a steroid.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: MDI — when exactly do you actuate?
cards.a:
MDI — when exactly do you actuate?
At the START of a slow, deep inhalation lasting 3 to 5 seconds — not before it, not after it.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: MDI — breath-hold and interval between puffs?
cards.a:
MDI — breath-hold and interval between puffs?
Hold the breath for 10 seconds for maximum drug deposition, then exhale slowly. Wait about 1 minute between puffs.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Why rinse and spit after an MDI?
cards.a:
Why rinse and spit after an MDI?
Essential with steroids — prevents pharyngitis and oral candidiasis, and reduces the drug swallowed and systemically absorbed.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: How do you close out MDI teaching?
cards.a:
How do you close out MDI teaching?
A return demonstration / teach-back — 'Show me how you're going to use your inhaler at home.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: The classic pMDI failure — what is it, in both directions?
cards.a:
The classic pMDI failure — what is it, in both directions?
TIMING.
Actuating too late, after inspiration has begun → the drug is not inhaled deeply.
Actuating too soon, before inspiration → it dumps in the mouth.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: How does a spacer/VHC fix the MDI problem?
cards.a:
How does a spacer/VHC fix the MDI problem?
It creates space between the MDI and the mouth so the propellant can dry and the larger particles fall out of the stream → less pharyngeal deposition, less coordination required, less thrush with steroids.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Heuer's three rules for who gets a holding chamber?
cards.a:
Heuer's three rules for who gets a holding chamber?
(1) Any adult not acutely ill who cannot coordinate actuation with breathing (a breath-actuated MDI is the alternative).
(2) Most infants and small children → MDI + holding chamber and mask.
(3) Anyone prescribed steroids by MDI.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Technique with a holding chamber attached?
cards.a:
Technique with a holding chamber attached?
Slow deep inhalation (~30 L/min, or 3 to 5 seconds), followed immediately by a 10-second breath-hold.
Actuate only ONCE into the chamber per inhalation — never stack puffs.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Holding chamber with a face mask — how many breaths, and what's the cost?
cards.a:
Holding chamber with a face mask — how many breaths, and what's the cost?
3 to 5 breaths per actuation, with a snug fit.
The mask cuts lung deposition by 50% — wean to a mouthpiece as soon as the child can use one.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: How do you clean a plastic VHC — and why not towel-dry it?
cards.a:
How do you clean a plastic VHC — and why not towel-dry it?
Rinse once a month in water with dilute dishwashing detergent and let it AIR-DRY.
Hand-drying builds an electrostatic charge that pulls the drug onto the chamber walls. Antistatic VHCs avoid the problem.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Plain spacer vs valved holding chamber — the exam distinction
cards.a:
Plain spacer vs valved holding chamber — the exam distinction
Plain spacer: just an open tube — removes big particles and dries propellant, but NO valve, so it still requires coordinated actuation and the patient can blow the dose back out.
VHC: adds a one-way inspiratory valve that holds the aerosol cloud in suspension until the patient inhales and stops exhaling back into the chamber → a bit more deposition.
Heuer's bottom line: VHCs are preferred.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Which three devices must NEVER be used with a spacer or VHC?
cards.a:
Which three devices must NEVER be used with a spacer or VHC?
Breath-actuated MDIs, the Respimat slow-mist inhaler, and DPIs.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Lung deposition: CFC MDI alone vs with a spacer vs HFA?
cards.a:
Lung deposition: CFC MDI alone vs with a spacer vs HFA?
CFC MDI alone: 8.8% · with a spacer: 14.8% · HFA: 53%.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: When is the pMDI the method of choice for children under 5?
cards.a:
When is the pMDI the method of choice for children under 5?
ONLY when used with a reservoir device (spacer or VHC).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: The four ways to raise the lung-to-total-body (L/T) ratio?
cards.a:
The four ways to raise the lung-to-total-body (L/T) ratio?
An efficient device · rinse-and-spit · a reservoir device · proper instruction.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: pMDI — how does it generate aerosol?
cards.a:
pMDI — how does it generate aerosol?
Depressing the canister into the actuator releases drug + propellant through the metering valve; the propellant flashes to vapor and shatters the stream into aerosol.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: pMDI — key cautions?
cards.a:
pMDI — key cautions?
High pharyngeal deposition without a spacer; difficult to deliver high doses; potential for abuse; not all drugs come in MDI form; patients often stop inhaling the instant they actuate.
Propellant is now HFA — CFC banned (deck: one CFC molecule destroys 100,000 ozone molecules).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: DPI — how does it work, and what's the advantage?
cards.a:
DPI — how does it work, and what's the advantage?
Breath-actuated — the patient's own inspiratory flow deagglomerates and carries the powder. No propellant, so no timing or coordination problem. Provides accurate dose counts.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: DPI inspiratory flow requirement — and the three-way source conflict
cards.a:
DPI inspiratory flow requirement — and the three-way source conflict
Heuer Ch 12: rapid, deep inhalation at 60 L/min (or 1–2 sec).
Heuer Ch 6: > 60 L/min.
Chptr 3 deck: 30 to 90 L/min.
Report whichever the question anchors on. Children under 4 usually cannot generate it. Breath-hold encouraged but not required.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: DPI — the four 'nevers'?
cards.a:
DPI — the four 'nevers'?
Never use with a spacer/VHC · never wash or rinse in water (cap and store dry) · never exhale into the device after loading (loses the dose and cakes the powder) · cannot be used during mechanical ventilation.
Rapid inhalation increases large-airway deposition; rinse mouth after.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: SVN / jet nebulizer — input flow and fill volume?
cards.a:
SVN / jet nebulizer — input flow and fill volume?
Compressed O₂ or air at 6 to 8 L/min for optimal particle size.
Fill volume: Heuer Ch 6 says 2.5 to 4 mL; the Chptr 3 deck says a 5 mL fill is the optimal average.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Why is the SVN the fallback device for acutely ill adults?
cards.a:
Why is the SVN the fallback device for acutely ill adults?
It needs the LEAST coordination of any device — slow tidal breathing with occasional deep breaths, any age.
It can give high doses and continuous therapy, and nebulizes both solutions AND suspensions.
As effective as MDI + VHC for bronchodilators in mild-to-moderate asthma exacerbation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: SVN — why is it wasteful?
cards.a:
SVN — why is it wasteful?
Large residual/dead volume — deck: 0.5 to 1.0 mL never aerosolizes, and only 10% to 20% of the emitted dose is inhaled from a reservoir-tube jet neb.
Plus drug prep, long treatment times, contamination risk. Use a mouthpiece — a face mask cuts lung deposition by 50%. Avoid 'blow-by' in infants.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Ultrasonic nebulizer — mechanism and the two cautions?
cards.a:
Ultrasonic nebulizer — mechanism and the two cautions?
A piezoelectric crystal vibrates at ultrasonic frequency to fling aerosol off the solution surface. High-volume, high-density output.
NOT recommended for suspensions, and transducer heat can degrade some drugs.
Needs inspiratory or circuit flow to carry the aerosol — it adds no flow itself.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Vibrating-mesh nebulizer — mechanism and where it's preferred?
cards.a:
Vibrating-mesh nebulizer — mechanism and where it's preferred?
A vibrating plate pushes liquid through a fine mesh of thousands of apertures → uniform fine-particle mist.
Preferred in mechanically ventilated patients; required for some drugs (e.g. aztreonam/Cayston). No propellant, no compressor, no added gas flow.
Caution: the mesh plate clogs with residual drug; nondisposable plates have a limited life span.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: SPAG-2 — what is it and what particle size?
cards.a:
SPAG-2 — what is it and what particle size?
Small Particle Aerosol Generator — a large-volume pneumatic nebulizer with a drying chamber producing an ultrafine aerosol of about 1.3 µm MMD.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Ribavirin via SPAG — the full dosing protocol?
cards.a:
Ribavirin via SPAG — the full dosing protocol?
20 mg/mL, run 12 to 18 hours/day, minimum 3 days, no more than 7 days; 6 g powder reconstituted to 6 g/300 mL. Replace the SPAG reservoir solution every 24 hours.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Ribavirin hazards — and what does Heuer actually say about it?
cards.a:
Ribavirin hazards — and what does Heuer actually say about it?
Hazards: deterioration of pulmonary function, worsening asthma/COPD, pneumothorax, apnea, skin/eye irritation, and healthcare-worker exposure risk.
Heuer's ONLY ribavirin statement is 'Do not recommend ribavirin.' All SPAG detail comes from the Chptr 13 deck.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Define MMAD and GSD.
cards.a:
Define MMAD and GSD.
MMAD (mass median aerodynamic diameter) — the particle diameter above and below which 50% of the aerosol mass lies.
GSD (geometric standard deviation) — the ratio of the size below which 84% of particles fall to the size below which 50% fall; it tells you how tight or scattered the distribution is.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: What size range defines an aerosol, and what is the fine particle fraction?
cards.a:
What size range defines an aerosol, and what is the fine particle fraction?
An aerosol is a suspension of particles from 0.001 to 100 µm in a carrier gas. Real aerosols are heterodisperse.
Fine particle fraction (FPF) — the mass with a high probability of reaching the lower airway — is under 5 to 6 µm.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Heuer's respirable range for an SVN?
cards.a:
Heuer's respirable range for an SVN?
1 to 5 microns — and an input flow of 6 to 8 L/min is what produces it.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Aerosol deposition by particle size — the full ladder
cards.a:
Aerosol deposition by particle size — the full ladder
Over 10 µm — upper airway, nose and mouth.
5 to 10 µm — upper airway and roughly the first six airway generations.
2 to 5 µm — the bronchoactive range, the target for bronchodilators (a typical SVN runs about 2.4 µm).
0.8 to 3 µm — lung parenchyma, terminal airways, alveolar region.
Under 1 µm — largely exhaled again.
Range of clinical interest: 1 to 10 µm.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: What MMAD is recommended for pentamidine, and why?
cards.a:
What MMAD is recommended for pentamidine, and why?
1 to 2 µm — to maximize alveolar deposition and minimize large-airway irritation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Inertial impaction — what drives it and where does it happen?
cards.a:
Inertial impaction — what drives it and where does it happen?
A function of particle MASS and VELOCITY. Happens where flow is fastest and most turbulent and cross-sectional area is smallest — the first 10 airway generations and the oropharynx.
This is exactly what a spacer, a slow inhalation, and holding the MDI 2 inches from the mouth are designed to defeat.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Gravitational settling (sedimentation) — what drives it?
cards.a:
Gravitational settling (sedimentation) — what drives it?
A function of particle SIZE and TIME, with settling rate proportional to the SQUARE of particle size.
This is why the 10-second breath-hold works.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Diffusion (Brownian motion) — when does it dominate?
cards.a:
Diffusion (Brownian motion) — when does it dominate?
For particles under 1 µm — and it usually takes longer than an inspiration lasts, so those particles are breathed back out.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: What does it mean that aerosols are hygroscopic — with the textbook example?
cards.a:
What does it mean that aerosols are hygroscopic — with the textbook example?
They grow when they go from dry ambient air to BTPS at 37 °C.
Example: cromolyn's MMAD grows from 2.31 to 3.02 µm.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Traditional vs newer aerosol devices — what fraction of the dose reaches the airway?
cards.a:
Traditional vs newer aerosol devices — what fraction of the dose reaches the airway?
Traditional: only about 10% to 15%. Newer devices: 30% to 50%.
Particle size is measured by cascade impaction.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: What is the mechanism of incentive spirometry?
cards.a:
What is the mechanism of incentive spirometry?
The sustained maximal inspiration (SMI) — a slow inspiration to near total lung capacity, held long enough to raise transpulmonary pressure, which re-expands collapsed alveoli, recruits low-compliance lung units, and restores FRC.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Indication for incentive spirometry?
