cards.a:
Indication for incentive spirometry?
Prevention and treatment of atelectasis in a patient who is awake, cooperative, and able to breathe deeply — classically after upper abdominal or thoracic surgery, and in prolonged bed rest, restrictive disease and neuromuscular conditions.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: ⚠ Heuer's current-evidence caveat on incentive spirometry?
cards.a:
⚠ Heuer's current-evidence caveat on incentive spirometry?
IS provides little to no benefit after thoracic or upper abdominal surgery and is NO LONGER recommended for routine prophylactic use in postoperative patients — early mobilization and ambulation are now the primary means of preventing postoperative pulmonary complications.
IS remains appropriate for treating documented or suspected atelectasis in a cooperative patient.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Patient selection for IS — the IC threshold, and what do you do if they fail it?
cards.a:
Patient selection for IS — the IC threshold, and what do you do if they fail it?
The patient should generate an inspiratory capacity at least one-third (33%) of predicted.
If they cannot cooperate, or cannot generate an IC > 33% of predicted → recommend IPPB or intermittent CPAP instead.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Why teach incentive spirometry preoperatively?
cards.a:
Why teach incentive spirometry preoperatively?
Because a patient in pain won't learn it — and the pre-op volume also sets the post-op target.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: IS technique — the breath-hold and the three setup steps?
cards.a:
IS technique — the breath-hold and the three setup steps?
Seat the patient upright, splint the incision, and coordinate with pain medication.
Seal the lips, inhale slowly and as fully as possible to full inspiratory capacity, hold 5 to 10 seconds, exhale, and allow adequate recovery time between breaths to avoid hyperventilation and dizziness.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: IS frequency?
cards.a:
IS frequency?
6 to 10 sustained maximal inspirations per hour while awake (Heuer).
Atelectasis deck: approximately 10 breaths per session, hourly while awake.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: IS goal volume — deck target and Heuer's discontinuation criterion?
cards.a:
IS goal volume — deck target and Heuer's discontinuation criterion?
Deck's practical target: at least ONE-HALF of the patient's pre-op inspiratory capacity.
Heuer's discontinuation criterion: volumes greater than 60% to 70% of the predicted IC TOGETHER WITH clinical resolution of atelectasis — improved breath sounds, improved oxygenation, normalized respiratory rate.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: The primary hazard and most common reason IS fails?
cards.a:
The primary hazard and most common reason IS fails?
PAIN. → Medicate and splint.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: The classic incentive spirometry error?
cards.a:
The classic incentive spirometry error?
Blowing INTO the indicator. Make sure the patient INHALES through the device, not exhales into it.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: IS volume target not met — what do you check?
cards.a:
IS volume target not met — what do you check?
All connections and the lip seal for leaks.
If the readout is unreliable or you need a true number: attach a one-way breathing valve and a respirometer to the IS device to measure volume accurately.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Patient gets dizzy or tingly during IS — cause and fix?
cards.a:
Patient gets dizzy or tingly during IS — cause and fix?
The breaths are too frequent (hyperventilation). → Lengthen the recovery pause.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Retained secretions alongside atelectasis — is IS enough?
cards.a:
Retained secretions alongside atelectasis — is IS enough?
No — IS alone is not enough. Add airway clearance therapy.
If the patient simply cannot perform the maneuver, escalate per the Lung Expansion Therapy Protocol to IPPB or CPAP. (Decks note IPPB has been removed from NBRC exams, with IPV and PEP/CPAP as the modern alternatives.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: How does PEP therapy work — the two mechanisms?
cards.a:
How does PEP therapy work — the two mechanisms?
The patient inhales freely and exhales actively but NOT forcibly against resistance at the mouth. That back-pressure:
(1) splints unstable airways open during exhalation, preventing dynamic compression and premature airway closure that traps gas behind mucus plugs;
(2) lets gas move through COLLATERAL CHANNELS (pores of Kohn, canals of Lambert) to get behind retained secretions and push them proximally.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: PEP pressures — device capability vs therapeutic working range?
cards.a:
PEP pressures — device capability vs therapeutic working range?
Device class range: 6 to 25 cm H₂O.
Therapeutic working range: 10 to 20 cm H₂O.
Always START at the LOWEST setting — largest orifice, lowest spring tension or flow — then slowly increase.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Flutter valve — what pressure does it generate?
cards.a:
Flutter valve — what pressure does it generate?
10 to 25 cm H₂O — created by the weight of the steel ball.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: PEP procedure — position, breath count, I:E, and session limit?
cards.a:
PEP procedure — position, breath count, I:E, and session limit?
Upright or semi-Fowler's with the abdomen unrestricted.
Sets of 10 to 20 slow, moderately deep inspirations with a short breath-hold, then active — not forced — exhalation, at an I:E of 1:3 to 1:4.
After each cycle: cough or huff (FET). Repeat the whole cycle 4 to 8 times, not exceeding a 20-minute session.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: What is the forced expiratory technique (huff cough)?
cards.a:
What is the forced expiratory technique (huff cough)?
Two or three huffs with the GLOTTIS OPEN, followed by rest.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: PEP indications?
cards.a:
PEP indications?
Secretion retention and mucus plugging — cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis, COPD exacerbation, asthma with mucus plugging.
Also to prevent or treat atelectasis and to reduce air trapping in asthma and COPD.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Which two PEP devices CANNOT take a nebulizer adaptor?
cards.a:
Which two PEP devices CANNOT take a nebulizer adaptor?
The Flutter valve and the Threshold PEP device. (Several other PEP devices can deliver a bronchodilator simultaneously.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Heuer's honest framing of PEP's effectiveness?
cards.a:
Heuer's honest framing of PEP's effectiveness?
PEP is no more effective than other airway clearance methods — so pick it on patient need and preference.
But if the goal is mobilizing retained secretions, a VIBRATORY PEP device is probably the best choice.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: PEP contraindications?
cards.a:
PEP contraindications?
A patient who cannot tolerate any increased work of breathing, or who is hemodynamically unstable, or who has bullous emphysema, elevated ICP, untreated pneumothorax, sinusitis, epistaxis, or middle-ear problems.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: PEP is NOT PEEP — give the five differences
cards.a:
PEP is NOT PEEP — give the five differences
PEP: patient-generated resistance at the mouth, during EXHALATION only, in a spontaneously breathing patient, via a handheld device, and it RETURNS TO ZERO at end-expiration. Purpose: airway clearance and lung expansion.
PEEP: machine-generated baseline pressure held AT end-expiration in a mechanically ventilated patient, never returns to zero. Purpose: alveolar recruitment and improved oxygenation (raising FRC, reducing shunt).
(CPAP is continuous positive pressure on BOTH inspiration and expiration.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: The three PEP device classes (Heuer's table)?
cards.a:
The three PEP device classes (Heuer's table)?
Flow resistor — exhale against a fixed orifice sized to age and expiratory flow (TheraPEP).
Threshold resistor — exhale against an adjustable counterweight, spring-loaded valve, or reverse Venturi (Threshold PEP; EZPap, which also gives positive pressure on INSPIRATION).
Vibratory PEP — a threshold resistor with an expiratory valve oscillating at 10 to 30 Hz (Flutter, Acapella, Aerobika, Quake).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: How does the Flutter valve work?
cards.a:
How does the Flutter valve work?
A pipe-shaped device with a steel ball resting on a cone-shaped orifice under a perforated cap. Exhaled gas lifts the ball, pressure drops, the ball falls, and the cycle repeats — generating 10 to 25 cm H₂O with oscillation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: The favorite Flutter-vs-Acapella exam discriminator?
cards.a:
The favorite Flutter-vs-Acapella exam discriminator?
The Flutter is GRAVITY-DEPENDENT — its PEP rises when angled above horizontal and with higher expiratory flow, so the patient must hold it correctly.
The Acapella is NOT gravity-dependent, so it works in ANY position — and unlike the Flutter it accepts a nebulizer adaptor.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: How does the Acapella work and how is PEP adjusted?
cards.a:
How does the Acapella work and how is PEP adjusted?
A counterweighted lever and magnet; a plug on the lever intermittently blocks flow to create the oscillations.
PEP is adjusted by turning the knob at the distal end — CLOCKWISE to increase.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Vibratory PEP coaching — what should you feel?
cards.a:
Vibratory PEP coaching — what should you feel?
Vibrations over the central airways during exhalation. If you cannot feel them, the settings are wrong.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: PEP device generates NO pressure — cause?
cards.a:
PEP device generates NO pressure — cause?
Almost always a LEAK — tighten every connection and check the mouth seal.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: PEP device generates unexpectedly HIGH pressure — cause?
cards.a:
PEP device generates unexpectedly HIGH pressure — cause?
The outlet port is obstructed — typically by the patient's hand or the bedding. Keep the port clear.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: What is IPV, in one line?
cards.a:
What is IPV, in one line?
Chest percussion from the INSIDE. High-frequency percussive bursts of gas delivered during the patient's own breath, so the airway is simultaneously hyperinflated AND oscillated.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Why did IPV displace IPPB?
cards.a:
Why did IPV displace IPPB?
It does airway clearance AND lung expansion in one sitting, with aerosol delivery as a bonus.
(Decks note IPPB has been removed from NBRC exams and is no longer recommended in clinical practice.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: IPV percussive frequency — Heuer vs deck?
cards.a:
IPV percussive frequency — Heuer vs deck?
Heuer: 100 to 300 bursts per minute.
Chptr 9 deck: high-flow mini-bursts 'at rates exceeding 200 cycles/min.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: How is IPV percussion titrated?
cards.a:
How is IPV percussion titrated?
Manually activated by a button and titrated by eye and hand — adjust until you can SEE and PALPATE chest wall vibration.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: IPV — what is nebulized during treatment, and what fill volume?
cards.a:
IPV — what is nebulized during treatment, and what fill volume?
Aerosolized saline — normal or hypertonic — routinely nebulized during the treatment. Fill volume 20 mL.
Interface: mouthpiece, mask, or in-line ventilator circuit. Pneumatically powered (e.g. Percussionaire IPV).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Heuer's decision rule: vibratory PEP vs IPV?
cards.a:
Heuer's decision rule: vibratory PEP vs IPV?
If the patient CAN generate adequate inspiratory and expiratory flows → strongly consider a vibratory PEP device (Flutter valve).
If the patient CANNOT generate sufficient flows but would benefit from vibratory PEP → use IPV instead, because IPV supplies the energy the patient cannot.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Who is IPV for?
cards.a:
Who is IPV for?
Cystic fibrosis and COPD patients with thick, tenacious secretions and poor airway clearance, atelectasis, and patients too weak or too obstructed to drive a handheld device.
Deck adds pneumonia, ARDS, and post-surgical patients needing lung expansion, escalated when IS and cough/deep-breathing have not been sufficient.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: The MetaNeb / Volara system — two modes and session length?
cards.a:
The MetaNeb / Volara system — two modes and session length?
Heuer's named alternative to IPV. Combines airway clearance and lung expansion with simultaneous aerosol delivery, in two modes:
CHFO (continuous high-frequency oscillation) — aerosol while oscillating with adjustable pressure pulses.
CPEP (continuous positive expiratory pressure) — continuous positive airway pressure during aerosol delivery.
A typical session is about 10 minutes alternating between the two modes; can run in-line with a ventilator.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: IPV device fails to function — the two causes Heuer gives?
cards.a:
IPV device fails to function — the two causes Heuer gives?
Inadequate source gas pressure, and a leak in the connections.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: IPV contraindications (decks)?
cards.a:
IPV contraindications (decks)?
Untreated pneumothorax, active hemoptysis, recent facial/oral/cranial surgery, hemodynamic instability (hypotension, arrhythmias), and elevated ICP.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Cromolyn sodium — class and brand?
cards.a:
Cromolyn sodium — class and brand?
Mast cell stabilizer — a nonsteroidal anti-asthma (anti-inflammatory) agent, brand name Intal.
The sole member of group 1 in the deck's taxonomy of nonsteroidal anti-asthma drugs (mast cell stabilizers / antileukotrienes / monoclonal antibodies). Its sibling is nedocromil (Tilade).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Cromolyn — mechanism?
cards.a:
Cromolyn — mechanism?
It stabilizes the mast cell membrane and prevents DEGRANULATION, blocking release of histamine, leukotrienes and the other mediators.
It interrupts the allergen → IgE → mast cell → mediator release → bronchoconstriction/edema/mucus cascade before it starts.
It has NO bronchodilator activity whatsoever.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Cromolyn's clinical niche?
cards.a:
Cromolyn's clinical niche?
Prophylaxis in very young children. Heuer's clinical-scenario table pairs 'prophylactic asthma management in patients age 2 years or younger' with montelukast (Singulair) or cromolyn sodium (Intal).
Decks: an alternative to inhaled corticosteroids at step 2 care, chosen for its safety profile. Also used before a known trigger such as exercise or allergen exposure.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Cromolyn dosing — MDI and SVN?
cards.a:
Cromolyn dosing — MDI and SVN?
MDI: 1 mg per puff, 2 to 4 puffs 4 times daily.
SVN: 20 mg per 2 mL ampule (1% solution), 1 ampule 4 times daily.
Compare nedocromil (Tilade): MDI 1.75 mg per puff, 2 to 4 puffs 2 times daily.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: ⚠ The single most testable fact about cromolyn?
cards.a:
⚠ The single most testable fact about cromolyn?
PROPHYLACTIC ONLY — NOT A RESCUE DRUG.
It must NOT be used to treat acute bronchospasm or an asthma attack. It cannot reverse bronchoconstriction that has already happened.
In an acute attack the answer is a SABA (albuterol), never cromolyn.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: How long before cromolyn works?
cards.a:
How long before cromolyn works?
2 to 4 weeks of regular dosing before symptom improvement — so the patient must be told to keep taking it even though nothing seems to be happening.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Cromolyn side effects?
cards.a:
Cromolyn side effects?
Mild, local and annoying rather than dangerous — which is the whole reason it's used in toddlers.
Cough, bronchospasm/wheezing on inhalation, throat irritation and unpleasant taste, nasal congestion, sneezing, nasal itching, nose burning, epistaxis.
Systemic toxicity is minimal because it is poorly absorbed.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: What do the decks say about cromolyn's actual effectiveness?
cards.a:
What do the decks say about cromolyn's actual effectiveness?
Several studies found it NOT effective in the treatment of asthma, and GINA does NOT include cromolyn among its recommended asthma agents — in current practice it is a weak, preventive-only, largely superseded drug.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Two curiosities about cromolyn worth knowing?
cards.a:
Two curiosities about cromolyn worth knowing?
It can suppress the cough associated with ACE inhibitors, and it has anti-sickling effects (hypothesized via blockade of calcium-activated potassium channels).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Inhaled nitric oxide — what is it and what does it do?
cards.a:
Inhaled nitric oxide — what is it and what does it do?
A potent, SELECTIVE pulmonary vasodilator delivered as a gas. It relaxes pulmonary vascular smooth muscle, which reduces intrapulmonary shunting, improves arterial oxygenation, and decreases PVR and pulmonary artery pressure.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Why is INO SELECTIVE?
cards.a:
Why is INO SELECTIVE?
(1) It is inhaled, so it only reaches the vessels around VENTILATED alveoli.
(2) It is inactivated by hemoglobin the instant it crosses into the blood, so it produces no systemic hypotension.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: INO — the molecular mechanism?
cards.a:
INO — the molecular mechanism?
Produced from L-arginine in the vascular endothelium; works by raising cGMP, which lowers intracellular calcium and dilates the vessel.
It does NOT open airways — it opens the blood vessels around ventilated alveoli, which is why it improves V/Q matching.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: INO — the FDA-approved indication?
cards.a:
INO — the FDA-approved indication?
Term and near-term neonates (> 34 weeks' gestation) with hypoxemic respiratory failure associated with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) — used in conjunction with ventilatory support.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: INO in adult ARDS — what does Heuer say?
cards.a:
INO in adult ARDS — what does Heuer say?
It has been used for pulmonary hypertension associated with ARDS, but Heuer is explicit that no significant improvement in long-term clinical outcomes has been shown — it is a rescue/oxygenation maneuver, not a survival therapy.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: INO — supply concentration, initial dose, and working range?
cards.a:
INO — supply concentration, initial dose, and working range?
Supply cylinders: NO at 800 ppm (balance nitrogen).
Recommended INITIAL dose: 20 ppm.
Therapeutic working range: 5 to 20 ppm. After the initial response the dose can often be quickly reduced to 5 to 6 ppm. Treatment may continue up to 14 days.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: INO at 6 ppm with no improvement — what do you do? And at 20 ppm with no improvement?
cards.a:
INO at 6 ppm with no improvement — what do you do? And at 20 ppm with no improvement?
At 6 ppm, no improvement → INCREASE the dose, up to 20 ppm.
At 20 ppm, no improvement → check the equipment setup; if correct, recommend an ALTERNATIVE pharmacologic therapy — do NOT keep climbing.
There is no added benefit above 20 ppm — only added toxicity.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: How is INO delivered into the circuit?
cards.a:
How is INO delivered into the circuit?
Injected into the INSPIRATORY limb near its outlet, with a flow sensor measuring inspiratory flow so the injection rate is automatically adjusted in proportion to gas flow, keeping delivered ppm constant.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Where is the INO sampling line placed, and what is monitored?
cards.a:
Where is the INO sampling line placed, and what is monitored?
NO, NO₂ and O₂ are continuously analyzed through a sampling line near the DISTAL end of the circuit, close to the patient's airway, with alarms for excessive NO, excessive NO₂, and unintended FiO₂ changes.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: How is NO₂ formed, and what raises it?
cards.a:
How is NO₂ formed, and what raises it?
When NO contacts oxygen it is oxidized to NO₂. Delivery equipment is designed to minimize CONTACT TIME between the two gases — and the higher the FiO₂, the more NO₂ is formed.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: NO₂ thresholds — Heuer vs the decks
cards.a:
NO₂ thresholds — Heuer vs the decks
Heuer's alarm/action limit: NO₂ should NOT exceed 2 to 3 ppm.
Decks: NO₂ above 10 ppm causes cell damage, hemorrhage, pulmonary edema and death.
Report both — 2–3 ppm is the action limit, 10 ppm is the cited lethal-injury threshold.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: NO₂ climbs above 2–3 ppm IMMEDIATELY after starting therapy — cause?
cards.a:
NO₂ climbs above 2–3 ppm IMMEDIATELY after starting therapy — cause?
The system was not flushed. → Flush with 100% oxygen before initiating.
If NO₂ exceeds 2–3 ppm later: check/recalibrate the NO₂ analyzer and re-verify the setup for excessive NO-O₂ contact time.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: How does NO cause methemoglobinemia?
cards.a:
How does NO cause methemoglobinemia?
NO binds hemoglobin and oxidizes the iron from ferrous (Fe²⁺) to ferric (Fe³⁺), forming methemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen and shifts the oxyhemoglobin curve LEFT so the remaining normal hemoglobin unloads less O₂.
Monitor by co-oximetry.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Methemoglobin levels — the deck's severity ladder
cards.a:
Methemoglobin levels — the deck's severity ladder
Abnormal above 1% (normal 0–3%) · 3–15% gray/blue skin discoloration · 15–20% cyanosis, often asymptomatic · 25–50% headache, dyspnea, syncope, weakness, confusion, chest pain · 50–70% arrhythmias, delirium, seizures, coma, profound acidosis · over 70% usually fatal.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: The tell for methemoglobinemia — and the treatment?
cards.a:
The tell for methemoglobinemia — and the treatment?
A pulse oximeter stuck near 82–86% despite a high PaO₂, with chocolate-brown blood that does not redden in oxygen.
Confirm with co-oximetry; treat with METHYLENE BLUE (alternatives if contraindicated, e.g. G6PD deficiency: vitamin C, exchange transfusion, hyperbaric O₂).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: INO contraindications?
cards.a:
INO contraindications?
Neonates with certain cardiovascular anomalies — notably coarctation of the aorta and any neonate dependent on a RIGHT-TO-LEFT SHUNT, where dropping PVR removes the shunt the baby is living on.
Also worsening of congestive heart failure. Decks add inhibition of platelet aggregation (bleeding risk) and a negative inotropic effect.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: What happens if you stop INO abruptly?
cards.a:
What happens if you stop INO abruptly?
REBOUND pulmonary hypertension and hypoxemia — the recurrence of the exact problem you were treating, and it can be severe. Wean; never stop abruptly.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: The pre-withdrawal checklist for INO?
cards.a:
The pre-withdrawal checklist for INO?
Reduce to the lowest effective dose, ideally 5 to 6 ppm or less · confirm the patient is hemodynamically stable · verify tolerance of FiO₂ ≤ 40% and PEEP ≤ 5 cm H₂O · monitor closely during withdrawal · be prepared to provide hemodynamic support.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Patient becomes unstable or hypoxemic DURING INO weaning — what do you do?
cards.a:
Patient becomes unstable or hypoxemic DURING INO weaning — what do you do?
Return to the original INO dose.
If INO has already been withdrawn and rebound occurs: increase the FiO₂, give hemodynamic support (vasopressors), consider reinstituting INO, and monitor closely.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Analyzed NO level drops to 0 — cause?
cards.a:
Analyzed NO level drops to 0 — cause?
The NO supply tank is empty — check tank pressure and switch or replace the cylinder.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: NO, NO₂ AND O₂ readings all drop to 0 at once — cause?
cards.a:
NO, NO₂ AND O₂ readings all drop to 0 at once — cause?
The sampling line is obstructed or disconnected — reconnect it and replace the in-line sampling filter.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Why can't you give a bronchodilator by SVN during INO?
cards.a:
Why can't you give a bronchodilator by SVN during INO?
The added nebulizer flow alters the prescribed gas mixture.
→ Deliver the bronchodilator by MDI or MESH nebulizer instead, since neither adds flow (add an MDI adaptor to the circuit).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Why does heliox work?
cards.a:
Why does heliox work?
Its LOW DENSITY. A low-density mixture lowers the driving pressure needed to move gas through the airways — especially the LARGE airways — and converts turbulent flow toward laminar flow through a narrowed segment.
Payoff: it reduces the work of breathing associated with large-airway obstruction.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Is heliox a treatment?
cards.a:
Is heliox a treatment?
No — it is a BRIDGE, not a cure. It buys time while the actual obstruction is treated and does nothing to the underlying pathology.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Heliox indications (Heuer)?
cards.a:
Heliox indications (Heuer)?
Acute upper airway obstruction, reversible obstructive disorders (severe asthma / status asthmaticus), post-extubation stridor, and croup.
Asthma deck lists heliox with magnesium sulfate and subcutaneous epinephrine as adjuncts in refractory cases.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: The rule about mixing heliox?
cards.a:
The rule about mixing heliox?
NEVER mix 100% helium with O₂ yourself. ALWAYS use premixed heliox — and always with at least 20% O₂.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Why does an O₂ flowmeter UNDER-read heliox?
cards.a:
Why does an O₂ flowmeter UNDER-read heliox?
Because helium is far less dense than oxygen, the gas actually moves faster than the float indicates.
→ Either use a flowmeter calibrated for that helium percentage, or multiply the indicated flow by the correction factor.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Heliox correction factors — all three
cards.a:
Heliox correction factors — all three
80% He / 20% O₂ → × 1.8 (10 L/min indicated = 18 L/min actual)
70% He / 30% O₂ → × 1.6 (= 16 L/min)
60% He / 40% O₂ → × 1.4 (= 14 L/min)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: The trade-off that drives every heliox question?
cards.a:
The trade-off that drives every heliox question?
More helium = more therapeutic benefit but LESS oxygen.
So 80/20 gives the most density reduction and the least FiO₂.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Heliox for a spontaneously breathing patient — device and why?
cards.a:
Heliox for a spontaneously breathing patient — device and why?
A TIGHT-FITTING NONREBREATHING MASK, at a flow high enough to meet or exceed the patient's minute ventilation and peak inspiratory flow demand.
The seal is the whole point — any room-air entrainment dilutes the helium away and destroys the density benefit.
Stated alternative: high-flow nasal cannula, now preferred over an oxyhood in infants.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Heliox by oxyhood in infants with bronchiolitis — the problem?
cards.a:
Heliox by oxyhood in infants with bronchiolitis — the problem?
Helium's HIGH THERMAL CONDUCTIVITY causes heat loss and hypothermia, which has limited oxyhood use in favor of high-flow cannula.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Heliox with invasive mechanical ventilation — the requirement?
cards.a:
Heliox with invasive mechanical ventilation — the requirement?
ONLY with a ventilator FDA-APPROVED for heliox delivery, because heliox alters ventilator performance. Even then you may need special modules or conversion factors to adjust settings.
Heliox is NOT recommended with NPPV at this time.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Heliox driving a jet nebulizer — the flow rule?
cards.a:
Heliox driving a jet nebulizer — the flow rule?
Flows must be increased by 50% to 100% when heliox powers a nebulizer.
Because aerosol mass and particle size vary substantially between SVNs, no guideline beyond 'use higher flows' can be given — use only heliox-approved nebulizers and monitor response.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: The non-negotiable heliox monitoring requirement?
cards.a:
The non-negotiable heliox monitoring requirement?
Continuously measure the delivered FiO₂ with an oxygen analyzer that has ACTIVE alarms — whatever the delivery method.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Patient on 80/20 heliox, SpO₂ under 90% — what do you do?
cards.a:
Patient on 80/20 heliox, SpO₂ under 90% — what do you do?
Analyze the FiO₂ to confirm the prescribed concentration is actually being delivered. If it is, recommend a mixture with a higher FiO₂, e.g. 70/30.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Heliox NRB reservoir bag collapses completely on inspiration at 10 L/min — fix?
cards.a:
Heliox NRB reservoir bag collapses completely on inspiration at 10 L/min — fix?
Input flow is insufficient. Use a flow that keeps the bag inflated throughout the breathing cycle, apply the conversion factor if using a standard O₂ flowmeter, and consider a high-flow cannula.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Patient on heliox has a less effective cough — why, and what do you do?
cards.a:
Patient on heliox has a less effective cough — why, and what do you do?
The low-density gas weakens the expulsive phase of a cough.
→ Wash out the heliox with an air-O₂ mixture BEFORE having the patient cough.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::03 Aerosol, Lung Expansion & Specialty Gases
cards.q: Ventilated patient on heliox shows volume loss or a 'beaked' P-V graphic — causes?
cards.a:
Ventilated patient on heliox shows volume loss or a 'beaked' P-V graphic — causes?
Volume loss: excessive loss from an underinflated ETT cuff or failure to apply conversion factors → add air to the cuff; if the seal is fine, confirm the ventilator is heliox-approved and factors are applied.
'Beaked' P-V loop (overdistention): excessive delivered volume because the lower gas density was not accounted for → apply conversion factors, confirm an approved ventilator, monitor closely.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: What is a Levy-Jennings chart?
cards.a:
What is a Levy-Jennings chart?
The standard plotting format for statistical QC — a control chart: 'a record of the measurements of standard samples used for statistical evaluation of analyzer performance.'
Heuer spells it Levy-Jennings; the RCP 103 deck spells it 'Levey-Jennings' — same chart.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: What does a Levy-Jennings chart plot, and how many charts do you keep?
cards.a:
What does a Levy-Jennings chart plot, and how many charts do you keep?
Individual measured values of a control medium over successive runs/days (x-axis = run number or date), against the mean and the standard deviation of the data.
A separate chart for EACH level of control AND for EACH analyte — so a blood gas lab keeps separate charts for pH, PCO₂ and PO₂ at each control level.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Levy-Jennings control limits — where are they set and what do they mean?
cards.a:
Levy-Jennings control limits — where are they set and what do they mean?
±2 SD around the mean.
Inside ±2 SD = 'in control', ready to run patient samples.
Outside ±2 SD = an analytical error.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: How is blood gas analyzer QC actually run?
cards.a:
How is blood gas analyzer QC actually run?
Frequent two-point calibration (usually automated) of pH, PCO₂ and PO₂ using precision gases and buffer solutions.
Plus calibration verification with at least 3 different levels of control media spanning the reportable range, at least daily — and after any maintenance or whenever performance is questioned.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: What is the gold standard for verifying PO₂ and PCO₂?
cards.a:
What is the gold standard for verifying PO₂ and PCO₂?
TONOMETRY — equilibrating a liquid medium to a reference gas of known partial pressures.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: The three control levels the deck describes?
cards.a:
The three control levels the deck describes?
Acidotic, alkalotic, normal — supplied in ampules of about 2–3 mL, judged against ± 2 SD.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: RANDOM error on a Levy-Jennings chart — appearance, meaning, action?
cards.a:
RANDOM error on a Levy-Jennings chart — appearance, meaning, action?
Appearance: ONE isolated point jumps outside the limits, then the next points come back in.
Meaning: normal statistical scatter, or a one-off contamination/handling problem.
Action: if subsequent measures are in control, NO remedial action is needed. Reanalyze the control after a two-point calibration; if the repeat is in control, stop there.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: SYSTEMATIC error (bias) — appearance, meaning, action?
cards.a:
SYSTEMATIC error (bias) — appearance, meaning, action?
Appearance: values move as a group away from the mean and stay there.
Meaning: more serious than random error — incorrect procedure or instrument component failure.
Action: NO patient samples may be analyzed until the problem is corrected. Troubleshoot, repair/replace faulty components, until you get an acceptable two-point calibration and controls within ±2 SD.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: When does RANDOM error become fatal to the instrument?
cards.a:
When does RANDOM error become fatal to the instrument?
When there are FREQUENT random points scattered above and below ±2 SD = poor precision/repeatability → the instrument is 'out of control.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: TREND vs SHIFT — pattern and what each implies
cards.a:
TREND vs SHIFT — pattern and what each implies
TREND: control values drift progressively in one direction over successive runs — a sloping line. Implies gradual deterioration: an aging/failing electrode, a slowly degrading component, reagent or buffer deteriorating over time.
SHIFT: values jump abruptly to a new level and then run flat there. Implies an abrupt change: new reagent/buffer lot, a recalibration, a replaced electrode or membrane, a new gas cylinder.
Both are bias/systematic errors → stop patient testing, troubleshoot, repair/replace, recalibrate, confirm controls within ±2 SD before resuming.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: ⚠ Honest caveat on the word 'shift'
cards.a:
⚠ Honest caveat on the word 'shift'
Heuer describes and illustrates the TREND explicitly ('an upward trend … shifts the mean above the control value, causing a positive measurement bias') but NEVER uses 'shift' as a named QC pattern — and neither do the decks.
Know the shift as the standard companion concept, but expect Heuer-based items to call both of them BIAS ERRORS.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: ⚠ Westgard rules — where do they come from?
cards.a:
⚠ Westgard rules — where do they come from?
The word 'Westgard' does not appear ANYWHERE in Heuer (all chapters checked). It comes only from the RCP 103 lecture deck.
Deck's practical version: one control outside the SD = a warning; two or more consecutive controls outside the acceptable range = an 'out-of-control' situation, requiring the electrode to be recalibrated or replaced.
If a question quotes 'Westgard,' it is coming from the deck.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: What is proficiency testing, and what is at stake?
cards.a:
What is proficiency testing, and what is at stake?
An outside agency sends 'blind'/unknown samples on a schedule; the lab reports results back and the agency compares them to its own and to peer labs using similar instruments.
Discrepancies must be resolved for the lab to keep its certification — which is a prerequisite for Medicare/Medicaid reimbursement.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Define point-of-care testing.
cards.a:
Define point-of-care testing.
'The collection, measurement, and reporting of selected lab tests AT OR NEAR the site of patient care' — at the bedside instead of sending the specimen to the central lab.
Most POCT instruments use disposable cartridges, and calibration occurs with each cartridge test, so minimal user intervention is required.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: The most common RT-performed point-of-care test?
cards.a:
The most common RT-performed point-of-care test?
ABGs — alone or as a combined panel with electrolytes, hemoglobin, glucose, lactate and BUN.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: The I-STAT procedure — the key steps?
cards.a:
The I-STAT procedure — the key steps?
Confirm the power-on-self-test (POST) → select cartridge/panel → scan operator and patient IDs → avoid touching the cartridge contact pads → obtain the sample and analyze within 3 minutes — do NOT place it on ice → mix thoroughly → fill the cartridge to the fill mark → insert → enter sample type, FiO₂ and patient temperature.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: POCT advantages?
cards.a:
POCT advantages?
Speed — I-STAT returns ABG results in about 90 seconds (deck).
Bedside availability in critical care, emergency settings and interfacility transport.
Self-calibrating cartridges — calibration happens automatically with every test.
Heuer calls POCT analyzers 'highly reliable devices.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: POCT — the documentation burden?
cards.a:
POCT — the documentation burden?
Operator competency must be formally documented.
Every result must be auditable/traceable to the patient, the instrument, the operator, the date and time, and the process used — plus complete instrument maintenance records.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: A POCT device fails to calibrate — what do you do?
cards.a:
A POCT device fails to calibrate — what do you do?
Rerun with a NEW cartridge.
If a second attempt fails: remove the device from service and either get a replacement analyzer or send the sample to the central lab.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: What is 'inter-instrumental comparison,' and why does it matter?
cards.a:
What is 'inter-instrumental comparison,' and why does it matter?
Running the same sample on a POCT device and a calibrated bench-top analyzer SIMULTANEOUSLY.
Heuer's T4 tip: this is the BEST way to validate POCT instrument measurements. POCT cannot stand alone.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: A POCT result comes back outside the critical range (e.g. pH < 7.20) — what do you do?
cards.a:
A POCT result comes back outside the critical range (e.g. pH < 7.20) — what do you do?
That is NOT the same as a flagged or out-of-reportable-range result. Treat it as potentially valid data and repeat with a fresh sample and a new cartridge; some protocols require the repeat be done in the central lab.
BUT never wait for a repeat if the findings are life-threatening or match a deteriorating patient — e.g. a POCT PO₂ < 40 torr with signs of severe hypoxemia means raise the FiO₂ NOW and confirm later.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Why is a pulse oximeter not 'calibrated'?
cards.a:
Why is a pulse oximeter not 'calibrated'?
It measures RELATIVE light intensities, not absolute values, so it does not require 'true value' calibration the way a blood gas analyzer does.
Instead you perform an operational verification using a healthy person as a 'biological control.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Pulse oximeter operational verification — Heuer's four steps?
cards.a:
Pulse oximeter operational verification — Heuer's four steps?
(1) Connect the device to a healthy person.
(2) Compare the displayed pulse rate with the pulse measured manually.
(3) Confirm an SpO₂ reading of 97–100%.
(4) Confirm loss-of-signal detection by removing the device.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: When do you take a pulse oximeter OUT OF SERVICE?
cards.a:
When do you take a pulse oximeter OUT OF SERVICE?
An incorrect pulse rate, an SpO₂ below 97% on a healthy subject, or failure to detect loss of signal.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Pulse oximeter stated accuracy — and its blind spot?
cards.a:
Pulse oximeter stated accuracy — and its blind spot?
±2–4% when perfusion is good.
Note: oximeters give few useful data once PaO₂ rises above 100 torr (hyperoxia). SpO₂ is normally > 93–95% on room air.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: HbCO (smoke inhalation / CO poisoning) — which way does SpO₂ err?
cards.a:
HbCO (smoke inhalation / CO poisoning) — which way does SpO₂ err?
Falsely HIGH %HbO₂ — standard 2-wavelength oximeters read CO-saturated Hb as oxygenated.
Do NOT use standard pulse oximetry; use a CO-oximeter.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: High metHb — which way does SpO₂ err?
cards.a:
High metHb — which way does SpO₂ err?
Falsely LOW %HbO₂ if SaO₂ > 85%; falsely HIGH %HbO₂ if SaO₂ < 85%.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Vascular dyes (e.g. methylene blue) — effect on SpO₂?
cards.a:
Vascular dyes (e.g. methylene blue) — effect on SpO₂?
Falsely LOW %HbO₂ — correlate with an ABG SaO₂ before trusting the value.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Dark skin pigmentation and nail polish — effect on SpO₂?
cards.a:
Dark skin pigmentation and nail polish — effect on SpO₂?
Falsely HIGH %HbO₂ (by 3–5%). Remove polish/artificial nails/jewelry, or rotate the probe 90 degrees in an emergency.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Ambient light — effect on SpO₂?
cards.a:
Ambient light — effect on SpO₂?
Varies; falsely HIGH %HbO₂ in sunlight, and may also give a falsely high pulse reading. → Shield the probe.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Poor perfusion / vasoconstriction — effect, and fix?
cards.a:
Poor perfusion / vasoconstriction — effect, and fix?
Inadequate signal, unpredictable results. → Move to a less peripheral site (ear, nose, forehead) or use an ABG.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: The MOST common source of pulse oximeter errors and false alarms?
cards.a:
The MOST common source of pulse oximeter errors and false alarms?
MOTION ARTIFACT. → Relocate the sensor; Masimo SET technology helps.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Probe fitted too tightly — effect on SpO₂?
cards.a:
Probe fitted too tightly — effect on SpO₂?
Venous pooling/pulsation → falsely LOW SpO₂.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: SpO₂ looks wrong — the deck's three bedside checks?
cards.a:
SpO₂ looks wrong — the deck's three bedside checks?
(1) Check the pulse rate against the cardiac monitor.
(2) Confirm the sensor is shielded from bright light.
(3) Confirm the sensor is not fitted too tightly.
'Before you believe the SpO₂, make sure the oximeter is actually seeing the patient's pulse.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: SpO₂ disagrees with the blood gas report — what's the catch?
cards.a:
SpO₂ disagrees with the blood gas report — what's the catch?
The ABG SaO₂ is usually a COMPUTED, not measured, value.
→ Compare the SpO₂ to a HEMOXIMETER's SaO₂ instead, and use the SaO₂ − SpO₂ difference to 'calibrate' the oximeter.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: The two O₂ analyzer technologies — and the power difference?
cards.a:
The two O₂ analyzer technologies — and the power difference?
Clark electrode (polarographic) and galvanic fuel cell.
Polarographic requires external power to maintain the electrode reaction; galvanic does not — but BOTH need external power for ALARM functions.
Both are accurate to ±2% of the actual concentration.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: O₂ analyzer two-point calibration — the points and the four steps?
cards.a:
O₂ analyzer two-point calibration — the points and the four steps?
Points: 100% O₂ and 21% room air.
(1) Expose the sensor to 100% O₂ → (2) after the reading stabilizes, adjust to 100% → (3) remove the sensor → (4) after restabilization, expose to room air and confirm 21% (±2%).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: O₂ analyzer fails a two-point calibration — Heuer's blunt T4 tip?
cards.a:
O₂ analyzer fails a two-point calibration — Heuer's blunt T4 tip?
REPLACE THE PROBE.
Common causes: probe not exposed to room air / to 100% O₂, bad probe, water condensation on the probe membrane (dry the membrane), probe not connected, and for 100% failure specifically a low battery in a polarographic unit.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: O₂ analyzer reads 0% — suspect what?
cards.a:
O₂ analyzer reads 0% — suspect what?
A dead battery, a disconnected probe, or a dead probe.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Do the decks cover O₂ analyzer calibration?
cards.a:
Do the decks cover O₂ analyzer calibration?
No. All 62 decks searched for 'oxygen analyzer,' 'O₂ analyzer,' 'galvanic,' 'polarographic' — the only hit is the RCP 103 deck's mention of the Clark electrode inside a blood gas analyzer.
The 21% / 100% calibration points are Heuer-only.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Spirometry volume calibration — what syringe?
cards.a:
Spirometry volume calibration — what syringe?
A large-volume 3.0-L calibration syringe.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: The ATS volume accuracy standard — and the acceptable range on a 3-L syringe?
cards.a:
The ATS volume accuracy standard — and the acceptable range on a 3-L syringe?
±3% OR ±50 mL, whichever is LARGER.
On a 3.0-L syringe: an acceptable measured volume falls between 2.91 and 3.09 L.
(3% of 3.0 L = 90 mL, larger than 50 mL, so the percentage governs here; the ±50 mL floor protects you at small volumes.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: The full ATS/ERS spirometry QC schedule (Heuer Table 8-5)
cards.a:
The full ATS/ERS spirometry QC schedule (Heuer Table 8-5)
Leaks — DAILY: 3 cm H₂O constant pressure for 1 min; leak must be < 10 mL.
Volume — DAILY: 3-L syringe, ±3% or ±50 mL.
Volume linearity — QUARTERLY: 1-L increments over the entire range.
Flow linearity — WEEKLY: at least three different flow ranges.
Time — QUARTERLY: mechanical recorder vs a stopwatch.
Software — NEW VERSIONS: log the install date, test a known subject ('biological control').

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Spirometer leak check — the procedure and the pass criterion?
cards.a:
Spirometer leak check — the procedure and the pass criterion?
Done daily, BEFORE the volume check and after any cleaning/reassembly.
Inject ~3 L of room air, occlude the circuit at the patient interface, pressurize to 3 cm H₂O, and watch volume change over 1 minute.
The system should lose no more than 10 mL/min. Bigger losses = loose connections, cracked tubing, or missing/damaged seals — fix before testing patients.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: ⚠ Before calibrating a spirometer, what must be turned OFF — and what happens if you forget?
cards.a:
⚠ Before calibrating a spirometer, what must be turned OFF — and what happens if you forget?
BTPS correction must be DEACTIVATED.
Otherwise the calibrating volume will read approximately 10% HIGHER than actual.
(BTPS = body temperature, pressure, saturated — applied to PATIENT volumes, not to the syringe.)
Also enter ambient temperature and altitude/barometric pressure, and zero an electronic flow transducer before calibration.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Volume calibration reads LOW (< 2.91 L) — first action?
cards.a:
Volume calibration reads LOW (< 2.91 L) — first action?
Repeat the LEAK CHECK first.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Volume calibration reads HIGH (> 3.09 L) — the three checks?
cards.a:
Volume calibration reads HIGH (> 3.09 L) — the three checks?
Recheck volume/flow zeroing · confirm BTPS correction is OFF · confirm the syringe and spirometer are at the SAME TEMPERATURE.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Can you test patients after a failed calibration?
cards.a:
Can you test patients after a failed calibration?
No — not until you can both identify the cause AND obtain an accurate calibration on repeat.
If repeated checks are inaccurate with no identifiable mechanical cause, recalibrate the device. Log leak test and volume/flow calibration results daily on a QC log.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Flow calibration — gold standard, accuracy standard, and the acceptable alternative?
cards.a:
Flow calibration — gold standard, accuracy standard, and the acceptable alternative?
Gold standard: a computer-controlled air pump generating standard expiratory waveforms; accuracy ±5% of reading or ±0.2 L/sec, whichever is greater.
Alternative: inject the full 3.0-L syringe at three different time intervals — 0.5 sec (≈6 L/sec), 6 sec (≈0.5 L/sec), and one in between. Volume linearity confirmed if recorded volume deviates by no more than 100 mL from 3.0 L.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: ATS acceptability — how many error-free maneuvers, and free of what five errors?
cards.a:
ATS acceptability — how many error-free maneuvers, and free of what five errors?
At least THREE error-free maneuvers. Free of:
(1) Slow/false start — back-extrapolated volume ≥ 5% of FVC or 150 mL (S-shaped curve).
(2) Coughing during the maneuver.
(3) Breathing during the maneuver (a short plateau; volume may overestimate true FVC).
(4) Variable effort — prematurely ending exhalation (curve ends abruptly in a plateau).
(5) Exhalation time less than 6 seconds.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: The ATS repeatability criterion?
cards.a:
The ATS repeatability criterion?
The two largest values for BOTH the FVC and the FEV₁ must be within 0.150 L (150 mL) of each other.
If either criterion fails, keep testing until both are met or the patient cannot continue.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: The four NLHEP bedside validity prompts (Heuer Table 6-33)?
cards.a:
The four NLHEP bedside validity prompts (Heuer Table 6-33)?
Back-extrapolated volume > 150 mL → 'Don't hesitate.'
Time to peak expiratory flow > 120 ms (> 160 ms for school-age children/adolescents) → 'Blast out faster.'
Forced expiratory time < 6.0 sec with end-of-test volume > 100 mL → 'Blow out longer.'
Repeat FEV₆ values not matching within 150 mL → 'Take a deeper breath.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Do the decks cover any spirometry calibration numbers?
cards.a:
Do the decks cover any spirometry calibration numbers?
No. All 62 searched for 'calibration syringe,' '3-L syringe,' '3.0-L' and ATS standards — nothing. Every calibration number is Heuer's.
What the decks add is technique: new mouthpiece/sensor, remove gum/candy/dentures, keep position consistent and record it, nose clips, coach a full inhalation to TLC, then blast out as fast and long as possible for at least 6 seconds (severe COPD may take up to 15 seconds), repeat for three acceptable maneuvers.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: What do you review before an arterial puncture?
cards.a:
What do you review before an arterial puncture?
The patient's PT, PTT, or INR — to anticipate longer bleeding time. Choose the NONDOMINANT wrist.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Why is the radial artery preferred?
cards.a:
Why is the radial artery preferred?
It is superficial, not adjacent to any large vein, and has ulnar collateral circulation.
Alternatives (brachial, femoral, dorsalis pedis) carry greater risk.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: The modified Allen's test — the full procedure and pass criterion?
cards.a:
The modified Allen's test — the full procedure and pass criterion?
Occlude radial and ulnar arteries with the hand clenched for about 5 seconds → have the patient open the hand (it should look blanched) → release the ULNAR artery → the palm should flush within 5–10 seconds.
A prolonged delay = inadequate ulnar flow → test the other wrist; if both fail, use the brachial artery.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Post-puncture care — how long do you hold, and what do you do after?
cards.a:
Post-puncture care — how long do you hold, and what do you do after?
Compress until bleeding stops — deck: at least 5 minutes, longer for patients on anticoagulants or with prolonged PT/PTT/INR.
Apply a sterile bandage, recheck the site after 20 minutes, and document.
Then: filter cap, expel all air, label with patient identifiers, O₂ settings/FiO₂ and time of draw, and mix thoroughly.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Too much heparin in the collection tube — what happens to each value?
cards.a:
Too much heparin in the collection tube — what happens to each value?
It dilutes the sample:
PaCO₂ falls toward 0 · PaO₂ shifts toward room-air partial pressure (~150 torr) · and because heparin is ACIDIC, pH falls toward 7.0.
Heuer specifies only 'a heparinized syringe' — the error picture is the RCP 103 deck's.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: What must you always document with an ABG?
cards.a:
What must you always document with an ABG?
The FiO₂, the O₂ delivery device, the mode of ventilation and current settings, and the results of any related assessments at the time of sampling.
When reporting, add a brief statement addressing test quality, including any problems with the specimen or its measurement.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: ABG analysis timing — all four windows
cards.a:
ABG analysis timing — all four windows
< 30 minutes at room temperature in a plastic syringe (3 minutes for capillary samples).
< 5 minutes if the sample is for a shunt study.
IMMEDIATELY if the patient has an elevated leukocyte or platelet count.
> 30 minutes → the sample must be in a GLASS syringe chilled to 0–4°C.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: ⚠ ABG timing — the three-way source conflict
cards.a:
⚠ ABG timing — the three-way source conflict
Heuer: < 30 minutes (plastic syringe, room temperature).
RCP 103 deck slide: 'run within 10–30 minutes or place on ice.'
Same deck's speaker notes: 'analyzed within 15 minutes.'
Give 30 minutes on a Heuer/NBRC-style item.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: The three analytical stages — define each
cards.a:
The three analytical stages — define each
PREANALYTICAL: 'result errors due to mistakes in the collection, handling, or storage of samples before analysis.'
ANALYTICAL: 'result errors due to mistakes made during measurement and analysis.'
POSTANALYTICAL: 'result errors due to mistakes in data handling, results reporting, or interpretation.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Heuer's THREE most common preanalytical errors?
cards.a:
Heuer's THREE most common preanalytical errors?
(1) Air contamination (bubbles) · (2) venous admixture · (3) continued blood metabolism.
Also: clots, wrong/excess anticoagulant, failure to ice, mislabeling, not documenting FiO₂/O₂ device/vent settings.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Analytical-stage errors — examples?
cards.a:
Analytical-stage errors — examples?
Uncalibrated or drifting analyzer, failed two-point calibration (low calibration gas, insufficient buffer solution), malfunctioning/degraded electrodes, contaminated buffer solutions, incorrect gas concentrations, poor or ignored QC, improper aspiration/injection of the sample.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Postanalytical errors — examples?
cards.a:
Postanalytical errors — examples?
Transcription errors, wrong patient information, failure to record the FiO₂, reporting without a test-quality statement.
Deck adds: sampling less than 20 minutes after an FiO₂ change.
The RCP 103 deck names a fourth category: interpretation errors — e.g. calling a compensated respiratory acidosis a metabolic acidosis.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: ⚠ AIR BUBBLE in an ABG — effect on each value?
cards.a:
⚠ AIR BUBBLE in an ABG — effect on each value?
PCO₂ DECREASES · pH INCREASES · PO₂ and %HbO₂ VARIABLE.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Air bubble — the mechanism, and why is PO₂ 'variable'?
cards.a:
Air bubble — the mechanism, and why is PO₂ 'variable'?
CO₂ diffuses OUT of the blood into the bubble → measured PaCO₂ falls → pH rises and the sample looks falsely alkalotic.
PaO₂ is pulled toward the room-air partial pressure of ~150 torr — so it reads falsely HIGH if the true PaO₂ was below ~150, and falsely LOW if it was above ~150.
That's why the direction is 'variable,' and why it matters most in hyperoxic patients.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: How do you avoid an air-bubble error?
cards.a:
How do you avoid an air-bubble error?
Expel bubbles immediately · NEVER mix a sample that still contains air bubbles · cap syringes / seal capillary tubes quickly.
Recognition: visible bubbles, and results not consistent with the patient's condition/settings.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: VENOUS ADMIXTURE — effect on each value, and how is it recognized?
cards.a:
VENOUS ADMIXTURE — effect on each value, and how is it recognized?
PCO₂ INCREASES · pH DECREASES · PO₂ and %HbO₂ DECREASE.
Recognized by no pulsations as the syringe fills, darker-looking blood, and results inconsistent with the patient.
Avoid by NOT aspirating the sample, avoiding brachial/femoral sites, and using short-bevel needles.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: ⚠ DELAY WITHOUT ICING — effect on each value, and the mechanism?
cards.a:
⚠ DELAY WITHOUT ICING — effect on each value, and the mechanism?
Blood cells stay alive and metabolically active in the syringe:
They keep producing CO₂ → PaCO₂ INCREASES.
They keep consuming O₂ → PaO₂ DECREASES.
Accumulating CO₂ plus metabolic byproducts lower the pH → falsely ACIDOTIC.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: The favorite exam contrast: air bubble vs delayed analysis
cards.a:
The favorite exam contrast: air bubble vs delayed analysis
They move PCO₂ and pH in OPPOSITE directions.
Air bubble: PCO₂ ↓, pH ↑ (falsely alkalotic).
Delay without icing: PCO₂ ↑, pH ↓ (falsely acidotic).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Why does chilling a sample to 0–4°C work — and what's the POCT exception?
cards.a:
Why does chilling a sample to 0–4°C work — and what's the POCT exception?
Chilling slows cellular metabolism and preserves the values.
Exception: an I-STAT sample is run within 3 minutes and is NOT placed on ice.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: What is a hemoximeter (CO-oximeter)?
cards.a:
What is a hemoximeter (CO-oximeter)?
A multi-wavelength SPECTROPHOTOMETER. Because each hemoglobin species absorbs light at a different set of wavelengths, the device can DIRECTLY MEASURE each species rather than infer it.
Deck vocabulary: hemoximetry = the measurement; hemoximeter = the device.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: What does a hemoximeter directly measure?
cards.a:
What does a hemoximeter directly measure?
Oxyhemoglobin (HbO₂) — a true, MEASURED SaO₂ · Deoxyhemoglobin (HHb) · Carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) · Methemoglobin (MetHb) · Total hemoglobin (tHb).
Heuer's Table 5-4 also lists sulfhemoglobin.
Calibration uses standard solutions with known values for total Hb, HbO₂, COHb and MetHb.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: ⚠ What does a blood gas analyzer actually MEASURE vs CALCULATE?
cards.a:
⚠ What does a blood gas analyzer actually MEASURE vs CALCULATE?
MEASURED — only three things: pH (Sanz electrode), PCO₂ (Severinghaus electrode), PO₂ (Clark electrode).
CALCULATED: HCO₃⁻, base excess, and SaO₂.
The SaO₂ is derived from the PaO₂ via the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve, which assumes normal hemoglobin function.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: What can a blood gas analyzer NOT tell you?
cards.a:
What can a blood gas analyzer NOT tell you?
It cannot distinguish normal hemoglobin from dysfunctional hemoglobins, and does not measure actual Hb content, actual Hb saturation, HbCO, or metHb.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: When is a hemoximeter REQUIRED?
cards.a:
When is a hemoximeter REQUIRED?
Whenever you need accurate measures of ANY hemoglobin parameter.
Smoke inhalation / CO poisoning — Heuer's most common scenario: don't trust the SpO₂ (falsely high) and the PaO₂ can look normal because dissolved oxygen is unaffected.
During inhaled nitric oxide therapy — to monitor metHb.
To 'calibrate' an SpO₂ against actual arterial saturation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Reference COHb levels (deck)?
cards.a:
Reference COHb levels (deck)?
1–3% = normal · 5–10% = smokers · 10–15% = heavy smokers · > 20% = CO poisoning.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Should pulse oximetry ever replace ABG analysis or hemoximetry?
cards.a:
Should pulse oximetry ever replace ABG analysis or hemoximetry?
Never — not when the clinical situation demands accurate oxygenation assessment.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: What does transcutaneous monitoring measure, and how?
cards.a:
What does transcutaneous monitoring measure, and how?
Continuous, noninvasive ESTIMATES of arterial PO₂ and PCO₂ through a skin sensor — reported as PtcO₂ and PtcCO₂.
The sensor holds miniaturized PO₂ and PCO₂ electrodes plus a HEATING ELEMENT. A thin gas-permeable membrane lets O₂ and CO₂ diffuse into the sensor's contact gel, where the electrodes measure their pressures.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Why does the transcutaneous sensor need a heating element?
cards.a:
Why does the transcutaneous sensor need a heating element?
It 'ARTERIALIZES' the blood by dilating the underlying capillary bed and increasing local blood flow — without heat, the gases would not diffuse out fast enough to reflect arterial values.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: ⚠ Transcutaneous electrode temperature — the source conflict
cards.a:
⚠ Transcutaneous electrode temperature — the source conflict
Heuer Ch 3 (classic): 44°C when monitoring both gases; as low as 37°C for PtcCO₂ only.
Heuer Ch 8: newer-generation sensors run at 42°C — less frequent changing/calibration (twice daily), membrane replacement at least every two weeks, arterialization in as little as 3 minutes.
RCP 203 Lssn 2b repeats Ch 3 (44°C / 37°C). Chang (RCP 105): neonatal 40–42°C, maximum 45°C.
Answer 44°C for a standard 'both gases' item.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: How often do you rotate a transcutaneous sensor site, and why?
cards.a:
How often do you rotate a transcutaneous sensor site, and why?
Every 2–6 hours, depending on the sensor temperature, the infant's size, and the manufacturer's recommendation — to avoid burns and skin damage.
(Chang uses every 4 hours to avoid erythema and burns.)
The higher the electrode temperature, the shorter the safe dwell time.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Transcutaneous setup — sites and stabilization time?
cards.a:
Transcutaneous setup — sites and stabilization time?
Choose a site with good superficial circulation: side of the chest, below the clavicles, the abdomen, the inner thigh. Clean with alcohol → adhesive fixation ring → contact gel avoiding air bubbles → apply flat with edges sealed → allow 5–20 minutes to stabilize → set alarms (high PtcO₂ for infants typically 80 torr).
Requires a two-point calibration using precision gas mixtures.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Who is transcutaneous monitoring most accurate in — and what is it best for?
cards.a:
Who is transcutaneous monitoring most accurate in — and what is it best for?
Neonates and infants — less accurate in children and adults.
Infant PtcO₂ monitoring is the best way to assess for HYPEROXEMIA and help prevent Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP).
Keep neonatal PtcO₂ at 50–80 torr, and use PtcO₂ primarily for TREND monitoring.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Which is the more trustworthy transcutaneous value — and why?
cards.a:
Which is the more trustworthy transcutaneous value — and why?
PtcCO₂ — it closely approximates PaCO₂ under most clinical conditions.
Useful in children and adults for continuously assessing ventilation when capnography is unavailable or technically difficult (during NIV or high-frequency ventilation).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: ⚠ PtcO₂ equals PaO₂ only under what two conditions?
cards.a:
⚠ PtcO₂ equals PaO₂ only under what two conditions?
ONLY in well-perfused patients AND only when PaO₂ is less than 100 torr.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: When does PtcO₂ UNDERESTIMATE PaO₂?
cards.a:
When does PtcO₂ UNDERESTIMATE PaO₂?
When PaO₂ is above 100 torr · in vasoconstricted/low-perfusion states (low cardiac output, shock, dehydration) · in children and adults because of thicker skin · when the sensor is underheated · when the sensor sits on a bony surface · when too much pressure or too much contact gel is applied.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: The MOST common transcutaneous problem — and its signature?
cards.a:
The MOST common transcutaneous problem — and its signature?
Air leaking around the adhesive ring.
Air leaks ALWAYS cause a dramatic FALL in PtcCO₂; if the leak is large, both values mimic room air (PO₂ ≈ 150 torr, PCO₂ ≈ 0 torr).
→ Reapply the sensor with a new adhesive ring.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Transcutaneous monitor fails to calibrate — cause and fix?
cards.a:
Transcutaneous monitor fails to calibrate — cause and fix?
Usually a leaking membrane or excessive trapped air under the membrane — both make the calibrating PCO₂ values and the high PO₂ measure read LOWER than expected.
→ Replace the membrane.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Transcutaneous monitoring — contraindications and poor choices?
cards.a:
Transcutaneous monitoring — contraindications and poor choices?
Poor skin integrity or adhesive allergy · shock or poor peripheral circulation · and because of the 5–20 minute setup and stabilization time, it is a poor choice in EMERGENCIES.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: PtcO₂ and a simultaneous PaO₂ disagree — the escalation ladder?
cards.a:
PtcO₂ and a simultaneous PaO₂ disagree — the escalation ladder?
If PaO₂ is substantially higher than PtcO₂ → poor peripheral circulation is the likely cause.
If perfusion is good but they still differ: try another sensor site → then replace the membrane and recalibrate → if they still differ, switch to pulse oximetry or serial ABGs.
For an infant with an anatomic shunt, both must be obtained on the SAME SIDE.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Dual-sensor PtcO₂ screening for CCHD in newborns?
cards.a:
Dual-sensor PtcO₂ screening for CCHD in newborns?
Preductal PtcO₂ (right upper chest) ≥ 15 torr HIGHER than postductal.
Also: wound-tissue PtcO₂ > 30–40 torr indicates perfusion adequate for healing.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: What is ventilator QC called, and how does it differ by machine type?
cards.a:
What is ventilator QC called, and how does it differ by machine type?
OPERATIONAL VERIFICATION.
Noncomputerized ventilators are verified manually per the manufacturer's recommendations; microprocessor-based ventilators use semiautomated self-test programs.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: POST vs EST — what does each test, and when do you run each?
cards.a:
POST vs EST — what does each test, and when do you run each?
POST (power-on-self-test) — tests microprocessor function, zeros the sensors, and does basic patient-function checks such as leak tests. Confirm a successful POST BEFORE applying a ventilator to a patient AND whenever you change the circuit.
EST (extended self-test) — the POST plus more comprehensive function checks. Perform an EST between each application on DIFFERENT patients. Document EST results in writing.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: A ventilator fails self-testing — what do you do?
cards.a:
A ventilator fails self-testing — what do you do?
Take it out of service for repair and replace it with one that has passed operational verification.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Operational verification — apnea alarm test?
cards.a:
Operational verification — apnea alarm test?
Test lung, SIMV rate = 2/min, trigger 8–12 times, then stop triggering and confirm the alarm.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Operational verification — proximal airway pressure display and PEEP control?
cards.a:
Operational verification — proximal airway pressure display and PEEP control?
Pressure display: disconnect the pressure line — must read zero (±1 cm H₂O). At PEEP 10, pressure must return to baseline (±1 cm H₂O) each breath.
PEEP control: set 5 cm H₂O, confirm return to 5 (±1); repeat at 10 and 15.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: The two ventilator leak tests?
cards.a:
The two ventilator leak tests?
Occlusion method: occlude the patient connection, pressure limit at MAXIMUM, peak flow at MINIMUM, deliver a 200–300 mL breath (adults) — the pressure limit should be reached and the high-pressure alarm activate.
Plateau pressure method: set an inspiratory pause ≥ 2 seconds; a drop of 10% or more during the pause indicates a leak.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Operational verification — rate and delivered volume tolerances?
cards.a:
Operational verification — rate and delivered volume tolerances?
Rate: count breaths against a watch — measured rate must be within ONE breath per minute of the set rate and the rate display.
Volume: connect a respirometer to the ventilator outlet — all measurements within ±5% of the set volume.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Why is a capnograph's automatic self-zeroing NOT a full calibration?
cards.a:
Why is a capnograph's automatic self-zeroing NOT a full calibration?
It zeros by aspirating air through a CO₂ scrubber — that is a ONE-POINT calibration. It adjusts only the OFFSET (baseline drift) and does NOT correct instrument GAIN, which is required for accurate CO₂ readings.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Capnograph gain calibration — the standard gas and acceptable range?
cards.a:
Capnograph gain calibration — the standard gas and acceptable range?
A precision mixture of 5% CO₂, equivalent to a PCO₂ of 38 torr at sea level under ATPD, with expected accuracy ±0.3% — an acceptable range of 4.7–5.3% (36–40 torr).
Three-level verification adds a high-precision 10% CO₂ gas (PCO₂ = 76 mm Hg).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Two practical catches when calibrating a capnograph?
cards.a:
Two practical catches when calibrating a capnograph?
(1) Sidestream capnographs must be calibrated using the SAME SETUP used on the patient, because aspiration through the sampling tube creates a pressure difference that changes the measurement.
(2) Capnographs are calibrated under ATPD but measure under BTPS, so the calibration routine must account for that difference.
Mainstream sensors are heated to prevent condensation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::04 Quality Control, Calibration & Blood Gas Sampling
cards.q: Do the decks cover ventilator operational verification?
cards.a:
Do the decks cover ventilator operational verification?
No deck covers POST/EST or the ECRI check numbers.
The only related deck content: RCP 203 Lssn 2b slide 10 — confirm completion of the capnograph's power-on self-test (noting some units do a one-point/low calibration at start-up) — and RCP 105 mentioning a failed self-test as a cause of a ventilator inoperative alarm.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Before you choose BiPAP over intubation, the patient must be what?
cards.a:
Before you choose BiPAP over intubation, the patient must be what?
Spontaneously breathing, alert, cooperative, able to protect the upper airway, and able to manage secretions.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: IPAP vs EPAP — what does each one do?
cards.a:
