IPAP vs EPAP — what does each one do?
IPAP — applied only during INSPIRATION. Think ventilation / VT / CO₂.
EPAP — applied continuously through inspiration AND exhalation; functionally PEEP. Think oxygenation: increases FRC, recruits alveoli, reduces shunt, raises SpO₂.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: What is ΔP in BiPAP, and what is its floor?
cards.a:
What is ΔP in BiPAP, and what is its floor?
ΔP = IPAP − EPAP — the Pressure Support / driving pressure.
Decks: never less than 4 cmH₂O. Heuer: VT is a function of patient effort and ΔP.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ The single most tested BiPAP rule
cards.a:
⚠ The single most tested BiPAP rule
You can ALWAYS raise IPAP without raising EPAP — but you can NEVER raise EPAP without raising IPAP by the same amount (otherwise you eat into ΔP and lose ventilation).
Heuer states it from the other side: 'To avoid changing the PaCO₂, keep ΔP constant.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: BiPAP initial IPAP/EPAP — the three-source conflict
cards.a:
BiPAP initial IPAP/EPAP — the three-source conflict
RCP 105/202 Chang decks: IPAP 8 / EPAP 4.
RCP 105 NIV 2023 deck: IPAP 8–12 / EPAP 4–6.
Heuer: IPAP 10–15 / EPAP 5 (Ch 11 Table 11-7); IPAP 10 in the COPD-exacerbation protocol (Ch 20).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: BiPAP target V<sub>T</sub> and backup rate — deck vs Heuer?
cards.a:
BiPAP target VT and backup rate — deck vs Heuer?
Target VT: decks 8–10 mL/kg IBW; Heuer 6–8 mL/kg.
Backup rate: decks 10–12, or 2–5 breaths below the patient's spontaneous RR; Heuer at least 8/min (Ch 11), 10/min (Ch 20).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ The IPAP ceiling — and why?
cards.a:
⚠ The IPAP ceiling — and why?
Keep IPAP below 20–25 cmH₂O — that is the ESOPHAGEAL OPENING PRESSURE. Above it you insufflate the stomach.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: BiPAP trigger/sensitivity and %I-time (Heuer)?
cards.a:
BiPAP trigger/sensitivity and %I-time (Heuer)?
Trigger: pressure 1–2 cmH₂O below baseline, or flow 1–3 L/min below baseline.
%I-time (timed modes): 20–30%. (Decks: I-time is set off the backup rate only.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: BiPAP Rise, Ramp and Leak settings (decks)?
cards.a:
BiPAP Rise, Ramp and Leak settings (decks)?
Rise: a LOWER number = FASTER.
Ramp: OFF, or 5–45 min.
Total Leak: normal 7–25, never > 60, never '---' or '0'.
Heuer: set rise time to reach the pressure plateau without spiking (a left 'dog-ear').

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's Problem 1: patient on 10/5, improve OXYGENATION only
cards.a:
Heuer's Problem 1: patient on 10/5, improve OXYGENATION only
Raise BOTH equally: 10/5 → 12/7.
ΔP stays 5; the baseline rises.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's Problem 2: patient on 10/5, improve VENTILATION only
cards.a:
Heuer's Problem 2: patient on 10/5, improve VENTILATION only
Raise IPAP only: 10/5 → 15/5 (ΔP 5 → 10; baseline unchanged).
Alternative if oxygenation is stable: LOWER EPAP — 10/5 → 10/3 (ΔP 5 → 7).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's Problem 3: patient on 10/5, improve BOTH
cards.a:
Heuer's Problem 3: patient on 10/5, improve BOTH
Raise both, IPAP more: 10/5 → 15/7.
ΔP 5 → 8 and the baseline rises.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Air trapping / auto-PEEP develops on NPPV with acceptable pH and PaCO₂ — what do you do?
cards.a:
Air trapping / auto-PEEP develops on NPPV with acceptable pH and PaCO₂ — what do you do?
Raise EPAP and IPAP EQUALLY — that counteracts the inspiratory threshold load without changing ventilation.
(Heuer only — the decks lack this rule.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: BiPAP indications (decks)?
cards.a:
BiPAP indications (decks)?
Prevent intubation in end-stage COPD, chronic ventilatory failure, restrictive chest wall disease, neuromuscular disease, nocturnal hypoventilation — plus acute respiratory failure, severe hypoxemia, severe asthma, COPD exacerbation, acute heart failure, post-extubation support, moderate acidemia, moderate hypercarbia, obesity hypoventilation, sleep apnea.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's CPAP-specific indications?
cards.a:
Heuer's CPAP-specific indications?
Obstructive sleep apnea, acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema, postoperative atelectasis — and in neonates RDS and apnea of prematurity.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Acute pulmonary edema — the CPAP numeric conflict, and Heuer's cautions?
cards.a:
Acute pulmonary edema — the CPAP numeric conflict, and Heuer's cautions?
Decks: first-line CPAP 8–12 cmH₂O with 100% O₂.
Heuer: start at 10 cmH₂O and 100% O₂, titrate to SpO₂ > 90%.
Avoid if: systolic BP < 90 mmHg, acute MI, Glasgow ≤ 8, or intubation is needed. Switch to bilevel with a backup rate if hypopnea or hypercapnia appears.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: CPAP for OSA — maximum pressure and the success criterion?
cards.a:
CPAP for OSA — maximum pressure and the success criterion?
Set by prescription or auto-CPAP to a maximum of 15 cmH₂O. Success = AHI < 5/hour.
AHI severity: normal 0–4/h · mild 5–14/h · moderate 15–30/h · severe > 30/h.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: NPPV contraindications — Heuer's RESPIRATORY list?
cards.a:
NPPV contraindications — Heuer's RESPIRATORY list?
Respiratory arrest · upper airway obstruction · unable to protect the airway · unable to clear secretions · high aspiration risk.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: NPPV contraindications — Heuer's NON-RESPIRATORY list?
cards.a:
NPPV contraindications — Heuer's NON-RESPIRATORY list?
Cardiac arrest/hemodynamic instability · mental status changes (obtundation) · active upper GI bleeding · facial surgery or trauma · facial deformity · non-fitting mask with significant leak · nausea or vomiting.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: BiPAP hazards/complications?
cards.a:
BiPAP hazards/complications?
Aerophagia and gastric insufflation, airway dryness, aspiration, claustrophobia, decreased cardiac output, dry mouth, secretion build-up in the mask, eye irritation from leak, pressure sores from the mask/tubing/straps.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ When do you give up on NPPV — decks vs Heuer
cards.a:
⚠ When do you give up on NPPV — decks vs Heuer
Decks: if the patient continues to deteriorate 30 MINUTES after starting NIV, intubate.
Heuer is slower and more specific — NPPV failure = worsening ABGs in the first 1–2 hours, or lack of improvement in ABGs after 4 hours; or severe acidosis (pH < 7.25) with PaCO₂ > 60 torr, severe hypoxemia (P/F < 200), or severe tachypnea (> 35/min).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's NPPV target that the decks lack?
cards.a:
Heuer's NPPV target that the decks lack?
Always aim for a NORMAL pH — not necessarily a normal PCO₂.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: V60 BiPAP alarm settings (decks)?
cards.a:
V60 BiPAP alarm settings (decks)?
Lo Rate: ONE higher than the set backup rate (BUR 12 → Lo Rate 13).
HIP: 5 to 10 ABOVE IPAP. LIP: 2 to 3 BELOW IPAP.
Lo VE: normally 4 or 5 L/min. NIV deck adds high/low pressure ±5 in S/T, Low VE start at 4 then 10–20% below baseline, VT alarms ±150 mL around the desired VT from IBW.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Patient Leak vs Total Leak — which do you monitor?
cards.a:
Patient Leak vs Total Leak — which do you monitor?
Use TOTAL Leak only when a Circuit/Leak Test has been completed with after-market equipment.
Use PATIENT Leak if no circuit test was run.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's minimum alarm requirement for any acute-care NPPV device?
cards.a:
Heuer's minimum alarm requirement for any acute-care NPPV device?
A low-pressure/disconnect alarm and a power-failure alarm — usually plus apnea, and sometimes high/low volume and high pressure.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: BiPAP: high CO₂ → what change? Low CO₂ → what change?
cards.a:
BiPAP: high CO₂ → what change? Low CO₂ → what change?
High CO₂ → INCREASE IPAP (increase ΔP); also raise the mandatory rate if the patient's own rate is low.
Low CO₂ → DECREASE IPAP/ΔP.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: BiPAP: low SpO₂ — Heuer's shunt rule?
cards.a:
BiPAP: low SpO₂ — Heuer's shunt rule?
If PaO₂ ≤ 50 torr on FiO₂ ≥ 0.50 → raise EPAP (keeping ΔP constant).
If it's a simple V/Q problem on FiO₂ < 0.50 → just raise FiO₂.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Weaning off BiPAP — what order?
cards.a:
Weaning off BiPAP — what order?
First drop FiO₂ to ≤ 0.50, THEN lower EPAP.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Deck worked examples: COPD pH 7.28/PaCO₂ 75, and CHF SpO₂ 84% with normal PaCO₂?
cards.a:
Deck worked examples: COPD pH 7.28/PaCO₂ 75, and CHF SpO₂ 84% with normal PaCO₂?
COPD pH 7.28 / PaCO₂ 75 → a VENTILATION problem → raise IPAP.
CHF SpO₂ 84% with normal PaCO₂ → an OXYGENATION problem → raise EPAP.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: AVAPS and C-Flex — what do they do?
cards.a:
AVAPS and C-Flex — what do they do?
AVAPS auto-adjusts pressure support to a user-set target VT.
C-Flex drops pressure at the start of exhalation for comfort.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Weaning off NPPV — Heuer's readiness thresholds
cards.a:
Weaning off NPPV — Heuer's readiness thresholds
Underlying condition mostly resolved · RR < 25/min · HR < 110/min · IPAP < 15 cmH₂O · EPAP < 10 cmH₂O · compensated pH > 7.35 · SpO₂ > 90% on < 50% O₂.
Procedure: wean during daytime hours first, extend time off in increments, use off periods for meals/fluids/airway clearance/skin care, then give at least one more night of support before stopping.
(Heuer only — the decks give no thresholds.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's NPPV interface selection rule?
cards.a:
Heuer's NPPV interface selection rule?
Use an oronasal/full face mask when INITIATING NPPV for ACUTE respiratory failure (lower leakage) — but avoid it if the patient is at high risk of vomiting or aspiration.
For CHRONIC hypercapnic respiratory failure, nasal appliances are preferred because they have less deadspace.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: What must any full oronasal mask have?
cards.a:
What must any full oronasal mask have?
A safety inlet valve. (A nonrebreathing/plateau exhalation valve fixes rebreathing.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Nasal mask — advantages, and its biggest problem?
cards.a:
Nasal mask — advantages, and its biggest problem?
Most common for CPAP/sleep apnea. Less aspiration risk, better secretion clearance, less claustrophobia, easier speech, less deadspace.
Biggest problem: LEAK in mouth-breathers → chin strap.
Fit the smallest mask that does not obstruct the nostrils; treat congestion with humidification.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Nasal pillows — and the one caution?
cards.a:
Nasal pillows — and the one caution?
Smallest, most comfortable; cause nasal congestion, dry mouth, nosebleeds.
Used for CPAP but NOT recommended for BiPAP.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's Table 6-24 interface remedies?
cards.a:
Heuer's Table 6-24 interface remedies?
Mouth leak → chin strap.
Nasal bridge redness → reduce strap tension, forehead spacer, artificial skin/nose pad.
Claustrophobia → clear mask with minimal bulk.
Impeded speech/eating → permit periodic removal.
Vented masks require the vent for exhalation and use only ONE corrugated tube.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The Golden Rule of ventilator modes?
cards.a:
The Golden Rule of ventilator modes?
You can only control ONE of volume or pressure; the other becomes the VARIABLE.
In VC with VT 500 mL, an ARDS patient still gets 500 mL but the PRESSURE rises.
In PC at 20 cmH₂O, that patient still gets 20 cmH₂O but the VT FALLS.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: How does the NBRC classify modes?
cards.a:
How does the NBRC classify modes?
By control variable (volume vs pressure) and by breath sequence (A/C = machine breaths only; SIMV = machine + spontaneous).
→ The four combinations tested: VC A/C, VC SIMV, PC A/C, PC SIMV, with PS and PEEP as add-ons and PRVC and APRV as advanced/dual modes.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The three questions that describe ANY mode?
cards.a:
The three questions that describe ANY mode?
(1) What is controlled?
(2) What TRIGGERS (starts) and CYCLES (ends) the breath? — Trigger = Start, Cycle = Stop.
(3) What is the breath sequence?

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: How do you tell a patient trigger from a time trigger on the waveform?
cards.a:
How do you tell a patient trigger from a time trigger on the waveform?
A PATIENT trigger shows a NEGATIVE DEFLECTION below baseline on the pressure-time waveform.
A TIME trigger shows NO deflection.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Volume Control — how is V<sub>T</sub> achieved, and the up/downside?
cards.a:
Volume Control — how is VT achieved, and the up/downside?
Set VT delivered at a set flow; VT is GUARANTEED, pressure is whatever it takes.
Upside: constant VT despite changes in Crs and Raw; changes in mechanics are easy to detect by watching PIP; predictable PaCO₂.
Downside: pressures rise as compliance falls / resistance rises → barotrauma risk; the fixed square flow pattern can cause asynchrony.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Pressure Control — how is V<sub>T</sub> achieved, and when do you switch VC → PC?
cards.a:
Pressure Control — how is VT achieved, and when do you switch VC → PC?
Set inspiratory pressure is held; VT is whatever the lungs accept and falls if compliance drops or resistance rises.
Upside: variable decelerating flow aids synchrony, less barotrauma risk.
Downside: VT varies and changes in mechanics are HARD to detect — watch VT and VE closely.
Switch VC → PC whenever Pplat exceeds 30 cmH₂O, using a limit ≤ 30.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: CMV (pure Control) — trigger, indications, and the cost?
cards.a:
CMV (pure Control) — trigger, indications, and the cost?
Time-triggered ONLY — no patient triggering allowed. Ventilator does 100% of the work.
Indications: tetanus/seizures, complete rest, crushed chest, paradoxical chest wall movement; also inverse I:E ratio ventilation and permissive hypercapnia.
Cost: needs deep sedation or paralysis; poorly tolerated; patient efforts cause 'fighting the ventilator' and ↑WOB; rapid disuse atrophy.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: A/C — what does every breath get, and what's the classic example?
cards.a:
A/C — what does every breath get, and what's the classic example?
Every breath — assisted or controlled — gets the SAME full preset breath.
Rate set at 12, patient triggers 24 → 24 FULL breaths.
Assist = patient-triggered (negative deflection); Control = time-triggered.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: A/C — benefits and hazards?
cards.a:
A/C — benefits and hazards?
Benefits: full ventilatory support (ARDS, pneumonia, sepsis, post-arrest); minimizes atelectasis, reduces WOB; the patient controls his own rate/PaCO₂ above the set rate and may avoid sedation/paralysis.
Hazards: hyperventilation at high trigger rates from anxiety, fear, pain, brain injury, fever or hypoxemia; trigger/flow/cycle asynchrony raising WOB and O₂ consumption; may worsen auto-PEEP in COPD/asthma.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: SIMV — how do mandatory vs spontaneous breaths differ?
cards.a:
SIMV — how do mandatory vs spontaneous breaths differ?
Mandatory breaths get the preset VT (e.g. 450 mL); spontaneous breaths in between are whatever VT the patient wants (200, 350, 600 mL) — and can be boosted with PS.
Mandatory breaths are time-triggered (rate 10 → one every 60 ÷ 10 = 6 sec) or patient-triggered/synchronized.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: SIMV — benefits, Heuer's specific indication, and the weaning caveat?
cards.a:
SIMV — benefits, Heuer's specific indication, and the weaning caveat?
Benefits: maintains respiratory muscle strength, avoids atrophy, allows graded support, lowers sedation need, lower mean airway pressure than A/C.
Heuer's specific indication: when full support is needed but the patient's rate causes hyperventilation on A/C.
Hazards: hypoventilation at low rates; fatigue without PS.
⚠ NOT recommended as a stand-alone weaning mode — 'being replaced by SBTs on T-tube, CPAP, or BiPAP.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: PSV — the board phrase, and who sets the V<sub>T</sub>?
cards.a:
PSV — the board phrase, and who sets the VT?
'Patient-triggered, pressure-limited, FLOW-cycled' — it ends when flow falls to a preset % of peak flow (commonly ~25%).
The PATIENT sets the VT (effort + compliance + resistance). The same PS 10 gives 700 mL in good lungs and 300 mL in ARDS.
An APNEIC patient cannot be on pure PSV.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: PSV — indications and Heuer's cautions?
cards.a:
PSV — indications and Heuer's cautions?
Indications: low spontaneous VT, high spontaneous rate, increased WOB; overcoming the imposed WOB of the ET tube; boosting spontaneous VT during SIMV/CPAP; weaning and SBTs.
Cautions: hypoventilation without a backup rate, variable VT/VE, and in COPD, flow-cycling to end inspiration may be PROLONGED because of air trapping.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: PRVC (Autoflow, VC+, Volume Guarantee) — how does it work?
cards.a:
PRVC (Autoflow, VC+, Volume Guarantee) — how does it work?
Closed loop: VT is guaranteed while the ventilator finds the LOWEST possible PIP, adjusting the pressure limit breath to breath according to measured mechanics.
Volume-targeted, pressure-controlled ('dual').

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: PRVC — the four disadvantages?
cards.a:
PRVC — the four disadvantages?
(1) Variable patient effort → variable VT and asynchrony.
(2) Severe ↑Raw or ↓Crs can produce unsafe PIP or reduced VT.
(3) ⚠ When patient demand RISES, the pressure level may DROP just when support is most needed — lowering Pmean and causing hypoxemia.
(4) May worsen auto-PEEP; the ventilator cannot tell a patient-caused rise in Raw from a machine-caused one (e.g. a wet filter).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: CPAP as a ventilator mode — what does it NOT do?
cards.a:
CPAP as a ventilator mode — what does it NOT do?
NO mandatory breaths at all — every breath's VT is generated entirely by the patient.
⚠ CPAP improves OXYGENATION but does NOT VENTILATE — the wrong choice for the apneic, oversedated, or severely fatigued patient. Requires adequate drive, VT, and spontaneous PaCO₂.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: APRV — what is it and what are the settings?
cards.a:
APRV — what is it and what are the settings?
CPAP at Phigh with intermittent timed RELEASES to Plow; VT comes from the release plus spontaneous effort. Technically time-triggered, pressure-limited, time-cycled with spontaneous breathing at BOTH levels.
Plow 0–8 cmH₂O · Phigh set for an inflation volume of 4–8 mL/kg PBW but < 30–35 · Thigh 3–5 sec · Tlow 0.2–0.8 sec → ~10–20 cycles/min.
Auto-PEEP is usually present — and DESIRED. Only for patients who can trigger enough spontaneous breaths.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: APRV indications?
cards.a:
APRV indications?
Acute lung injury, especially when Pplat > 30 cmH₂O · refractory hypoxemia from collapsed alveoli · massive atelectasis.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Initial V<sub>T</sub> for full support — Heuer vs the decks
cards.a:
Initial VT for full support — Heuer vs the decks
Heuer: 6–8 mL/kg PBW, keep Pplat ≤ 30–35; 4–6 mL/kg in ARDS.
RCP 105 decks: 5–10 mL/kg IBW; as low as 4 mL/kg in ARDS/severe asthma.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Initial rate and PEEP — Heuer vs the decks
cards.a:
Initial rate and PEEP — Heuer vs the decks
Rate — Heuer: 8–24/min (up to 35/min with a low-VT strategy). Decks: 10 (12) to 20/min.
PEEP — Heuer: 5–10 cmH₂O initially, then to keep SaO₂ ≥ 92% with FiO₂ ≤ 50%. Decks: 5 cmH₂O for refractory hypoxemia (NBRC range 2–6).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Initial FiO₂ and flow/I:E (Heuer)?
cards.a:
Initial FiO₂ and flow/I:E (Heuer)?
FiO₂: 60–100% initially if no SaO₂/PaO₂ data, then to PaO₂ ≥ 60 torr / SaO₂ ≥ 92%.
Flow/I:E: set to achieve I:E ≤ 1:1 (e.g. 1:2, 1:3) and prevent auto-PEEP.
Pressure support in SIMV: 5–10 cmH₂O to overcome tube resistance and keep spontaneous rate < 25/min.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The PBW formulas
cards.a:
The PBW formulas
Males = 50 + 2.3 × (height in inches − 60)
Females = 45.5 + 2.3 × (height in inches − 60)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Worked PBW: a 6-ft (72-in) male — and what if he weighs 120 kg?
cards.a:
Worked PBW: a 6-ft (72-in) male — and what if he weighs 120 kg?
PBW = 50 + 2.3 × (72 − 60) = 50 + 27.6 = ≈ 78 kg
At 8 mL/kg → ≈ 625 mL.
⚠ Even if that man weighs 120 kg (265 lb), you still set 600–800 mL — definitely NOT 1200 mL.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Worked PBW (deck): a 5'10" male
cards.a:
Worked PBW (deck): a 5'10" male
50 + (2.3 × 10) = 73 kg
73 × 8 = 584 mL · 73 × 10 = 730 mL → target ≈ 580–730 mL.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: PSV titration — start, target, and wean-down numbers?
cards.a:
PSV titration — start, target, and wean-down numbers?
Start PS 5–15 cmH₂O (Modes deck) or 5–10 (Heuer).
Titrate to VT 8–10 mL/kg IBW (Modes deck) or 10–15 mL/kg (Weaning deck), with a spontaneous rate < 25/min — all three sources agree on the rate.
Then wean down by 3 to 6 cmH₂O to about 5–6 cmH₂O.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Why do ventilator alarms exist, and what is the most dangerous action in critical care?
cards.a:
Why do ventilator alarms exist, and what is the most dangerous action in critical care?
Alarms exist to activate the clinician to intervene, minimize false alarms and alarm fatigue, and ensure important conditions are not missed.
⚠ The MOST dangerous action in critical care is SILENCING an alarm without determining the cause.
The sequence is always: Alarm → look at the PATIENT → look at the VENTILATOR → determine cause → fix the problem.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: High inspiratory pressure alarm — where is it set?
cards.a:
High inspiratory pressure alarm — where is it set?
Heuer: 50 cmH₂O, or 10–15 cmH₂O ABOVE PIP (use the mandatory-breath PIP during SIMV).
Decks: 10–15 cmH₂O ABOVE observed PIP — and must NOT be raised without justification.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: High inspiratory pressure alarm — causes?
cards.a:
High inspiratory pressure alarm — causes?
Increased resistance or decreased compliance · partial or complete airway obstruction · cough, secretions, mucus plugs · patient–ventilator asynchrony · anxiety, restlessness, pain · alarm accidentally set below the PIP of a pressure-supported breath.
Deck list: water in the circuit, kinked ETT, tension pneumothorax, biting the tube, bronchospasm, blood clot, airway edema, obstructed filter or partially closed HME.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ Low inspiratory pressure alarm — the real Heuer-vs-deck conflict
cards.a:
⚠ Low inspiratory pressure alarm — the real Heuer-vs-deck conflict
Heuer: 8 cmH₂O, or 5–10 cmH₂O BELOW PIP (use the pressure-supported-breath PIP during SIMV).
Decks: 10–15 cmH₂O BELOW observed PIP.
Know both.
Causes: disconnection, airway/circuit leaks, alarm set above the PS-breath PIP, and (Heuer) improved compliance and resistance.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Low exhaled V<sub>T</sub> alarm — settings, causes, and what you see on the loop?
cards.a:
Low exhaled VT alarm — settings, causes, and what you see on the loop?
Heuer: 100 mL or 10–15% below the set VT. Decks: 100 mL below the expired VT.
Causes: disconnection, airway/circuit leaks, pulmonary leak (bronchopleural fistula), shallow spontaneous breathing, coughing, asynchrony.
On the loop: loops do NOT return to zero volume; expiratory volume < inspiratory volume.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Low vs high minute ventilation alarms — settings and causes?
cards.a:
Low vs high minute ventilation alarms — settings and causes?
Low VE — Heuer: 4–5 L/min, or 10–15% below the SIMV/AC minimum. Causes: same as low exhaled VT, plus sedation/anesthesia and low metabolic rate.
High VE — Heuer: 10–15% ABOVE baseline VE. Causes: increased metabolic rate (fever), tachypnea, anxiety/restlessness/pain, patient waking from sedation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Apnea alarm — delay and causes?
cards.a:
Apnea alarm — delay and causes?
Heuer: 20-second delay. Decks: 15–20 seconds.
Causes: sedation/anesthesia, low metabolic rate, set rate < 3/min; decks add circuit disconnection, prolonged neuromuscular block, respiratory center dysfunction, muscle fatigue.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: High frequency alarm — setting and causes?
cards.a:
High frequency alarm — setting and causes?
Decks: 10/min over the observed total rate — must NOT be raised without clear justification.
Causes: genuine need for more minute ventilation (rapid shallow breathing) · insufficient flow or pressure support · excessive sensitivity → AUTOTRIGGERING.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: High PEEP/CPAP alarm — causes?
cards.a:
High PEEP/CPAP alarm — causes?
Auto-PEEP, air trapping, insufficient inspiratory flow (long I-time), insufficient expiratory time, and (Heuer) an obstructed/sticking expiratory or PEEP valve.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: High/Low FiO₂ alarm — setting and causes?
cards.a:
High/Low FiO₂ alarm — setting and causes?
Heuer: preprogrammed, ±5–6% of set FiO₂. Decks: 5–10% above/below the analyzed FiO₂.
Causes: gas source failure (air or O₂), analyzer needs calibration/replacement, a sudden change in delivered FiO₂ (e.g. the 100% suction button).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Temperature alarm (Heuer only) — setting and causes?
cards.a:
Temperature alarm (Heuer only) — setting and causes?
Preprogrammed ±2°C of set temp, not to exceed 41°C.
Causes: dry water chamber, tubing condensation, defective wiring/probe/chamber, heater malfunction, room temperature change, high VE with high flow.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ Heuer's two-alarm pattern-recognition shortcut
cards.a:
⚠ Heuer's two-alarm pattern-recognition shortcut
Low volume + LOW pressure = a LEAK. Check and tighten circuit connections.
Low volume + HIGH pressure = an OBSTRUCTION (inspiratory or expiratory). Find and correct it, drain condensate, replace the HME, suction the patient.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Which is more dangerous — inspiratory or expiratory obstruction?
cards.a:
Which is more dangerous — inspiratory or expiratory obstruction?
EXPIRATORY — it causes rebreathing, asphyxia, or barotrauma.
The most dangerous version is a BLOCKED EXHALATION PORT on a single-limb circuit — a patient grabbing the circuit, or bedding over the port.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Expiratory/PEEP valve — open/leaking vs obstructed/sticking?
cards.a:
Expiratory/PEEP valve — open/leaking vs obstructed/sticking?
Open or leaking → LOW-volume + LOW-PEEP alarms.
Obstructed or sticking → HIGH-pressure + HIGH-PEEP alarms.
Fix: single-limb → check the expiratory valve line or replace the circuit; dual-limb with an INTERNAL valve → replace the VENTILATOR.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ The highest-yield alarm skill: what do PIP and Pplat each include?
cards.a:
⚠ The highest-yield alarm skill: what do PIP and Pplat each include?
PIP = Resistance + Compliance.
Pplat = Compliance ONLY.
PIP − Pplat = Resistance (PTA, transairway pressure).
Heuer: PIP − Pplat ≈ Raw and Pplat − PEEP ≈ Crs.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: High PIP + NORMAL Pplat = which problem, and why doesn't Pplat move?
cards.a:
High PIP + NORMAL Pplat = which problem, and why doesn't Pplat move?
A RESISTANCE problem. PTA widens, Cdyn falls while Crs is unchanged, so Crs − Cdyn widens.
Plateau does not change because flow has STOPPED during the pause, so resistance is not included.
Causes: bronchospasm, excessive secretions, peribronchial/airway edema, partial airway occlusion (mucus plug, kinking, biting); decks add water in the tubing, obstructed filter, partially closed HME.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: High PIP + HIGH Pplat rising in proportion = which problem, and the causes?
cards.a:
High PIP + HIGH Pplat rising in proportion = which problem, and the causes?
A COMPLIANCE problem (PIP − Pplat unchanged).
Causes: atelectasis, pulmonary edema/CHF, ARDS, tension pneumothorax, pleural effusion, overdistention/hyperinflation, ET tube slippage into a mainstem bronchus, bronchial obstruction by a mucus plug, ascites/abdominal distention.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The Weaning deck's split of compliance causes — sudden vs gradual?
cards.a:
The Weaning deck's split of compliance causes — sudden vs gradual?
SUDDEN: tension pneumothorax, pleural effusion, ETT into a mainstem bronchus → SEARCH FOR THE PROBLEM.
GRADUAL: pneumonia, ARDS, atelectasis → TREAT THE DISEASE.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The teacher's one-line phrasing for PIP/Pplat?
cards.a:
The teacher's one-line phrasing for PIP/Pplat?
'When PIP and Plateau move TOGETHER, think LUNGS. When only PIP moves, think AIRWAYS.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The three ventilator circuit families and where each is used?
cards.a:
The three ventilator circuit families and where each is used?
(1) Dual-limb 'wye' — most critical care ventilators; also continuous-flow CPAP circuits.
(2) Single-limb WITH an expiratory ('mushroom') valve — transport and home care ventilators.
(3) Single-limb WITHOUT a valve (leak port) — noninvasive positive-pressure ventilators.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Dual-limb circuit — what does the expiratory limb make possible, and what counts as mechanical deadspace?
cards.a:
Dual-limb circuit — what does the expiratory limb make possible, and what counts as mechanical deadspace?
The expiratory limb returns gas to the ventilator's expiratory/PEEP valve — which is what allows accurate exhaled-volume measurement.
Mechanical deadspace = everything between the WYE and the patient's airway — every HME, MDI adapter, or end-tidal CO₂ adapter you add there increases deadspace.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Single-limb WITH an expiratory valve — how does the valve work?
cards.a:
Single-limb WITH an expiratory valve — how does the valve work?
A separate pneumatic line runs from the ventilator to the valve; pressurized, it blocks outflow during inspiration; at the start of expiration it depressurizes and lets gas out.
Because it holds a set pressure through expiration, this valve can also provide CPAP/PEEP.
Mechanical deadspace = between the built-in expiratory valve and the airway.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ Single-limb leak-port circuit — why must EPAP never fall to near zero?
cards.a:
⚠ Single-limb leak-port circuit — why must EPAP never fall to near zero?
The continuous flow the NPPV device supplies forces expired gas out the exhaust port; combined with normal interface leak this prevents rebreathing.
PEEP/CPAP is created by continuous regulation of pressure and system flow/leak through the demand valve — which is exactly why EPAP must never fall to near zero, or CO₂ is not flushed.
These are the vented masks: one corrugated tube, vent required for exhalation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Why should circuit compliance be as LOW as possible?
cards.a:
Why should circuit compliance be as LOW as possible?
High circuit compliance holds more COMPRESSIBLE VOLUME and reduces the VT actually delivered.
Deck numbers at PIP 40 cmH₂O: a 5 mL/cmH₂O circuit holds 200 mL of the set VT; a 3 mL/cmH₂O circuit holds only 120 mL.
Corrected VT = Expired VT − circuit compressible volume.
A 50 mL loss is huge when VT is 150 mL, trivial when VT is 700 mL.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Why must you never use a 'cheater hose' for the pre-use check?
cards.a:
Why must you never use a 'cheater hose' for the pre-use check?
Use the ACTUAL circuit so it can be leak-tested, measured, and compensated for compressible volume.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's one hard humidification number?
cards.a:
Heuer's one hard humidification number?
Gas reaching the airway must carry at least 30 mg/L of water vapor. All patients ventilated through a tracheal airway need either an active heated humidifier or a passive HME.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heated humidifier — temperature (Heuer vs decks) and probe placement?
cards.a:
Heated humidifier — temperature (Heuer vs decks) and probe placement?
Heuer: 100% relative humidity at 34–41°C.
Decks: as close to 100% RH at body temperature, target 37°C.
Probe: inside the circuit on the INSPIRATORY limb, as close to the patient as possible (at the wye).
Use 34–41°C on a national exam; 37°C if your instructor asks for 'body temperature.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Airway temperature too high or too low — what do you check?
cards.a:
Airway temperature too high or too low — what do you check?
Reset to 34–41°C, then check for: probe not in the circuit, abrupt flow change, low/empty reservoir, a fan or A/C vent blowing on the probe, or unit failure.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: What does an HME actually do — and what does it NOT do?
cards.a:
What does an HME actually do — and what does it NOT do?
It adds NO humidity. It is passive and temporary — it only retains and returns the patient's OWN exhaled heat and moisture (surface impregnated with CaCl₂ or AlCl₂), giving 70–90% RH at 30–31°C.
Placement: between the wye and the airway interface. It always adds deadspace and must be positioned for bidirectional flow.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ When must you NOT use an HME?
cards.a:
⚠ When must you NOT use an HME?
NPPV (one-way flow and large leaks ruin it, and the added deadspace/resistance raises CO₂ and WOB) · ARDS on low VT (< 6 mL/kg) · hypercapnic respiratory failure · dehydration · high minute volume · hypothermia · a large exhalation leak · thick or bloody secretions (which block it and raise circuit resistance).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ MDI through an HME — the source conflict
cards.a:
⚠ MDI through an HME — the source conflict
Decks: the MDI must be placed BETWEEN the HME and the patient's airway.
Heuer: because the HME FILTERS the drug and the aerosol can OBSTRUCT the HME, switch to ACTIVE HEATED HUMIDIFICATION to give aerosolized medication.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Circuit condensation — why is it the most common threat to patency, and what does it cause?
cards.a:
Circuit condensation — why is it the most common threat to patency, and what does it cause?
Gas cools between the humidifier and the patient, water condenses and collects in the tubing, obstructing airflow.
It is a listed cause of the high-pressure alarm, of AUTOCYCLING, and of weaning failure.
Manage with a heated-wire circuit (connectors plug into the low-voltage outlets on the humidifier), inline water traps at low points, or an HME.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Circuit infection control — Heuer's rules?
cards.a:
Circuit infection control — Heuer's rules?
Change circuits ONLY when visibly soiled or malfunctioning · avoid unnecessary disconnections (use in-line/closed suction) · prevent condensate from draining into the airway and avoid contamination disposing of it · use a drainage system that avoids disconnection.
Decks agree: the maximum safe interval is unknown; weekly has been shown optimal; change when visibly soiled.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Define hyperventilation and give the classic ABG.
cards.a:
Define hyperventilation and give the classic ABG.
Increased minute ventilation → decreased PaCO₂ → increased pH = acute respiratory alkalosis.
Deck's classic ABG: pH 7.52, PaCO₂ 30 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 24 mEq/L.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Why does hyperventilation lower ICP — the full chain?
cards.a:
Why does hyperventilation lower ICP — the full chain?
CO₂ is a potent cerebral VASODILATOR, so falling PaCO₂ causes cerebral VASOCONSTRICTION.
CO₂ freely crosses the blood-brain barrier, combines with water to form carbonic acid, dissociating into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻; the lower CSF H⁺ constricts cerebral arterioles.
↑VE → ↓PaCO₂ → ↓cerebral vessel diameter → ↓cerebral blood flow → ↓ICP.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's four causes of a DECREASED ICP?
cards.a:
Heuer's four causes of a DECREASED ICP?
Hyperventilation/hypocapnia · head elevation · decreased CSF volume · severe arterial hypotension.
(Mirror image: avoid hypercapnia, which causes cerebral vasodilation and RAISES ICP.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's ICP numbers?
cards.a:
Heuer's ICP numbers?
Normal 10–15 mmHg supine.
> 20 mmHg for more than 5–10 minutes is abnormally high.
> 25 mmHg for a prolonged period predicts poor outcomes.
Once ICP exceeds 15–20 mmHg, cerebral blood flow can fall to a critical level → secondary ischemia.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ TBI PaCO₂ targets — the deck-vs-Heuer conflict
cards.a:
⚠ TBI PaCO₂ targets — the deck-vs-Heuer conflict
RCP 105 Critical Issues deck: normal PaCO₂ 35–45; temporary hyperventilation to 30–35 for critically elevated ICP or impending herniation; Chang's older allowance of as low as 26 torr in the first 24 hours while insisting you should NOT drive PaCO₂ below 26 (no additional ICP benefit); avoid a prolonged PaCO₂ < 30 unless neurosurgery directs it.
Heuer is tighter: PaCO₂ 35–40 torr, PIP ≤ 30 cmH₂O, SpO₂ > 95%, good synchrony.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's three ONLY situations for hyperventilation in TBI?
cards.a:
Heuer's three ONLY situations for hyperventilation in TBI?
(1) To blunt ICP spikes before procedures such as suctioning.
(2) Confirmed cerebral herniation.
(3) Salvage therapy when high ICP does not respond to standard treatment.
Avoid prophylactic/routine hyperventilation — it lowers ICP but can cause cerebral ISCHEMIA. Also avoid high levels of PEEP (they lower MAP, raise ICP, lower cerebral perfusion pressure).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ The hemoglobin effect of prolonged hyperventilation (decks only)
cards.a:
⚠ The hemoglobin effect of prolonged hyperventilation (decks only)
Respiratory alkalosis lasting more than 24 hours shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the LEFT.
Left = 'Love' — hemoglobin HOLDS ONTO oxygen and will not release it, so despite good saturations the tissues — especially brain tissue — do not get oxygen efficiently.
Result: cerebral tissue hypoxia — dizziness, confusion, altered mental status, decreased cerebral perfusion, worsening neurologic injury.
⚠ This is NOT discussed anywhere in Heuer — it rests on the RCP 105 decks alone.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: What else does prolonged hypocapnia cause?
cards.a:
What else does prolonged hypocapnia cause?
HYPOPHOSPHATEMIA (phosphate shifts into cells) → muscle weakness, DIAPHRAGM weakness, cardiac dysfunction, neurologic dysfunction.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's causes of hyperventilation on A/C — and the three fixes?
cards.a:
Heuer's causes of hyperventilation on A/C — and the three fixes?
Causes: anxiety, fear, pain, brain injury, fever, or hypoxemia driving a high trigger rate.
Fixes: switch to SIMV, add mechanical deadspace, or decrease the set rate (keeping it ≥ 8/min) — or decrease VT if it is above 8 mL/kg.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's NBRC item: VC SIMV, rate 14, VT 6–7 mL/kg, PaCO₂ low with respiratory alkalosis, PaO₂ 115 on FiO₂ 0.40. Action?
cards.a:
Heuer's NBRC item: VC SIMV, rate 14, VT 6–7 mL/kg, PaCO₂ low with respiratory alkalosis, PaO₂ 115 on FiO₂ 0.40. Action?
DECREASE THE RATE.
Because the VT is already appropriate and the problem is ventilation, not oxygenation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ Hyperventilation during weaning — what is the grave mistake?
cards.a:
⚠ Hyperventilation during weaning — what is the grave mistake?
Hyperventilation is a sign of weaning FAILURE. The grave mistake is cutting support to 'normalize' the PaCO₂.
If the ↓PaCO₂ is a response to hypoxia, pain, anxiety, metabolic acidosis, or improper settings, reducing support will worsen the hyperventilation, fatigue the muscles, and cause ventilatory failure.
Find and fix the cause first.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The two framing principles of weaning?
cards.a:
The two framing principles of weaning?
'We don't wean the ventilator — we wean the PATIENT.'
'No single value determines weaning readiness.'
The best predictor of weaning success is IMPROVEMENT OF THE UNDERLYING DISEASE PROCESS.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ Heuer's caution about VC and MIP/NIF that the decks lack?
cards.a:
⚠ Heuer's caution about VC and MIP/NIF that the decks lack?
They are less frequently obtained and are used primarily to track respiratory muscle strength in NEUROMUSCULAR patients — not as the deciding weaning test.
A carefully monitored SBT provides the most valid information.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The Weaning deck's four concept groups?
cards.a:
The Weaning deck's four concept groups?
Clinical Readiness · Ventilatory Readiness (RSBI, RR, VT, VE) · Oxygenation Readiness (P/F, FiO₂, PEEP) · Pulmonary Reserve (VC, MIP/NIF, compliance, VD/VT).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's FIVE formal criteria to even START a weaning assessment
cards.a:
Heuer's FIVE formal criteria to even START a weaning assessment
(1) Evidence of some reversal of the underlying cause of respiratory failure.
(2) Adequate oxygenation — P/F ≥ 150–200, PEEP ≤ 5–8 cmH₂O, FiO₂ ≤ 0.4–0.5.
(3) pH ≥ 7.25.
(4) Hemodynamic stability (no myocardial ischemia, no significant hypotension).
(5) Capability to initiate an inspiratory effort.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: RSBI — formula, how it's measured, and the failure threshold?
cards.a:
RSBI — formula, how it's measured, and the failure threshold?
RSBI = f ÷ VT (in LITERS) — 'Rate ÷ Size.'
Measure OFF the vent for 3 min or until stable. Low = good.
> 105 predicts weaning failure (Heuer). Chang deck: < 100 breaths/min/L; the deck's summary line uses < 105. Heuer's reference range is < 50.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Worked RSBI: patient breathing at 38/min with VT 300 mL
cards.a:
Worked RSBI: patient breathing at 38/min with VT 300 mL
RSBI = 38 ÷ 0.3 = 127 breaths/min/L
ABOVE 105 → predicts WEANING FAILURE.
Companion: from VE instead — VT = VE ÷ f = 11.4 ÷ 38 = 0.30 L = 300 mL.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Why does rapid shallow breathing hurt — and what are the BEST indicators of SBT tolerance?
cards.a:
Why does rapid shallow breathing hurt — and what are the BEST indicators of SBT tolerance?
Rapid shallow breathing increases DEADSPACE ventilation because anatomic VD is FIXED while VT falls.
RR and RSBI are the BEST indicators of tolerance of spontaneous breathing — both sources agree.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: MIP/NIF — normal ranges and critical values?
cards.a:
MIP/NIF — normal ranges and critical values?
Normal — Heuer: −80 to −100 cmH₂O (Table 1-15); −80 to −120 (Table 4-6). Weaning deck: −80 to −100.
Critical: 0 to −20 or −25 cmH₂O (Heuer) — weaker than −20/−25 = cannot sustain spontaneous ventilation.
Weaning deck: < −20 to −30 in 20 sec; Chang's text at least −30; RCP 203 gives a minimum of −20 on vent patients to be extubated.
Effort-dependent; more negative = stronger.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's MIP technique — and why doesn't the patient need to be conscious?
cards.a:
Heuer's MIP technique — and why doesn't the patient need to be conscious?
A manometer on a ONE-WAY VALVE that permits exhalation but NOT inspiration, so the patient 'bucks down' toward residual volume over 15–25 seconds (decks say 20 sec).
Maximum effort is ENSURED by the valve — so the patient need not be conscious.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: MIP disease targets (RCP 203)?
cards.a:
MIP disease targets (RCP 203)?
> −40 for COPD · > −20 for myasthenia gravis.
Studies: MIP averaged −37 in weaned vs −30 in non-weaned.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: MEP — how is it measured, and what is the threshold?
cards.a:
MEP — how is it measured, and what is the threshold?
Measured with a manometer, NO one-way valve, and only on an alert, cooperative patient.
> 60 cmH₂O is Heuer's threshold for adequate secretion clearance before extubation — paired with peak cough flow > 60 L/min.
In neuromuscular disease, danger signs are MEP < 40 cmH₂O (or rapidly declining) and peak cough flow < 270 L/min (4.5 L/sec).
The decks give no MEP threshold.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Vital capacity — normals and critical value?
cards.a:
Vital capacity — normals and critical value?
Heuer: 70 mL/kg PBW (slow VC). Decks: 50 mL/kg IBW (~4.8 L); RCP 203 gives 3–5 L typical adult.
Critical: < 10–15 mL/kg PBW (Heuer); decks say > 10 mL/kg to wean, with RCP 203's critical minimum ~1 L (15 mL/kg).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's slow-VC technique?
cards.a:
Heuer's slow-VC technique?
Inhale as deeply as possible, then exhale SLOWLY and completely until no volume change for at least 2 seconds, repeated at least 3 times, best result recorded.
Decks: Wright respirometer (suction, disconnect, attach, coach, reconnect).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Minute ventilation — normal and critical values?
cards.a:
Minute ventilation — normal and critical values?
Heuer: 5–10 L/min. Decks: 6–10 L/min.
Critical: < 4 L/min or > 10 L/min (Heuer). Decks: excessive WOB is VE > 10 L/min, associated with poor weaning outcomes.
VT = VE ÷ f

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Spontaneous V<sub>T</sub> and RR — normals and critical values?
cards.a:
Spontaneous VT and RR — normals and critical values?
VT — Heuer: 5–7 mL/kg PBW; decks: 5–10 mL/kg. Critical: < 4–5 mL/kg PBW or < 300 mL. Studies: 368 mL in weaned vs 277 mL in non-weaned.
RR — both: 12–20/min. Critical: < 6/min or > 30–35/min; SBT failure if RR > 30–35 or RR changes > 50% from baseline.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: P/F ratio — normals, weaning threshold, and the two severity ladders?
cards.a:
P/F ratio — normals, weaning threshold, and the two severity ladders?
Normal — Heuer: > 500. Decks: > 380.
To START weaning: ≥ 150–200 with PEEP ≤ 5–8 and FiO₂ ≤ 0.4–0.5 (Heuer and RCP 203 agree exactly).
Heuer's ladder: < 300 = acute lung injury · < 200 = severe hypoxemia · < 100 = ARDS.
Decks' ladder: < 300 ALI/mild ARDS · < 200 ARDS · < 150 prone.
Also required: PaO₂ > 60 mmHg (or SaO₂ > 90%) on FiO₂ ≤ 0.40.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ P0.1 (airway occlusion pressure) — where is it documented?
cards.a:
⚠ P0.1 (airway occlusion pressure) — where is it documented?
NOT covered in Heuer OR the available decks.
The entire text was searched for 'P0.1,' 'Pocc,' 'airway occlusion pressure' — the only hit is the definition of MIP, not P0.1 as a drive index. All 62 decks likewise returned nothing.
Look up the threshold (commonly < 4–6 cmH₂O) in Egan's Fundamentals of Respiratory Care, 'Discontinuing Ventilatory Support.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: pH thresholds — to BEGIN weaning vs to PASS the SBT?
cards.a:
pH thresholds — to BEGIN weaning vs to PASS the SBT?
pH ≥ 7.25 to BEGIN weaning (Heuer).
pH ≥ 7.30 and a rise in PaCO₂ ≤ 10 torr to PASS the SBT (Heuer and RCP 203 agree).
Chronic retainers live at 50–60.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Static compliance as a weaning parameter?
cards.a:
Static compliance as a weaning parameter?
> 30 mL/cmH₂O minimum consistent with successful weaning (decks).
Heuer: Crs < 25–30 mL/cmH₂O is associated with increased WOB and weaning difficulty.
Effort-INDEPENDENT. Crs = VT ÷ (Pplat − PEEP)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: V<sub>D</sub>/V<sub>T</sub> — normal and critical, and how is it measured?
cards.a:
VD/VT — normal and critical, and how is it measured?
Normal: 0.25–0.35 (Heuer); decks ~30%.
Critical: > 0.60–0.70 (Heuer); decks say < 60% while intubated.
Effort-INDEPENDENT. Heuer notes it is rarely measured directly via the Bohr equation — usually estimated by volumetric capnography.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Shunt (Qs/Qt) — normal, ladder, and Heuer's shortcut?
cards.a:
Shunt (Qs/Qt) — normal, ladder, and Heuer's shortcut?
Normal ≤ 10%. Threshold < 20%.
10–20% mild · 20–30% significant · > 30% critical.
Heuer's App B shortcut: about 5% shunt per 100 torr of P(A−a)O₂.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: P(A−a)O₂ — normals and thresholds?
cards.a:
P(A−a)O₂ — normals and thresholds?
Heuer: 50–60 torr on 100% O₂ for normal subjects, rising > 600 torr with severe shunt.
Decks: 5–15 mmHg on RA; 25–65 mmHg on 100%. Threshold < 350 mmHg at FiO₂ 1.0.
Decks: 66–300 on RA = V/Q mismatch (FiO₂ up to 60%); > 300 on RA = shunt (vent with PEEP).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: What is the SBT, and what mode should you NOT use for weaning?
cards.a:
What is the SBT, and what mode should you NOT use for weaning?
The SBT is the major diagnostic test and the current standard — 'daily SBTs provide the quickest route to discontinuing mechanical ventilation' (Heuer's exact phrase).
SIMV should be AVOIDED as a stand-alone weaning modality.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The SBT screening period and full duration?
cards.a:
The SBT screening period and full duration?
Screening: 2–5 minutes of monitored spontaneous breathing — watching breathing pattern, vital signs and comfort (RR < 30–35, stable vitals, patient comfortable).
If tolerated: continue at least 30 minutes but no more than 120 minutes.
Chang deck: 'up to 30 minutes'; patients who fail usually do so within the first 20–30 minutes, so a full 120-min trial is often unnecessary.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The four equivalent SBT methods — and Heuer's tiebreakers?
cards.a:
The four equivalent SBT methods — and Heuer's tiebreakers?
Straight T-tube · CPAP (~5 cmH₂O) · pressure support (5–8 cmH₂O to offset the ET tube) · CPAP + PS (decks add automatic tube compensation). No one method is better than another.
Tiebreakers: CPAP helps trigger in patients with auto-PEEP; PS overcomes the imposed WOB of the artificial airway.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: SBT PASS criteria — the full list
cards.a:
SBT PASS criteria — the full list
SpO₂ ≥ 85–90% or PaO₂ ≥ 50–60 torr · pH ≥ 7.30 · rise in PaCO₂ ≤ 10 torr · HR < 120–140/min with a change < 20% from baseline · SBP < 180–200 and > 90 mmHg with a change < 20% · no vasopressors required · RR ≤ 30–35/min with a change < 50% from baseline.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ The SUBJECTIVE SBT failure signs that stop the trial even when the numbers look fine
cards.a:
⚠ The SUBJECTIVE SBT failure signs that stop the trial even when the numbers look fine
Change in mental status (somnolence, coma, agitation, anxiety) · onset or worsening of discomfort · diaphoresis · signs of increased WOB — accessory muscle use and THORACOABDOMINAL PARADOX.
Decks add tachypnea, tachycardia, hypertension, hypotension, hypoxemia, acidosis, arrhythmias.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Patient fails the SBT — what do you do?
cards.a:
Patient fails the SBT — what do you do?
Return to a support level sufficient to maintain oxygenation and ventilation and PREVENT MUSCLE FATIGUE, work with the physician to identify and correct the cause, rest for 24 hours, and repeat the SBT every 24 hours.
Only 13% of patients who pass an SBT and are extubated need reintubation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ Heuer's four EXTUBATION requirements — and why are they separate from weaning?
cards.a:
⚠ Heuer's four EXTUBATION requirements — and why are they separate from weaning?
The decision to extubate is made SEPARATELY from the weaning assessment.
(1) Adequate oxygenation and ventilation without support — demonstrated by the SBT.
(2) Minimal risk of upper airway obstruction — a positive cuff-leak test.
(3) Adequate airway protection — positive gag reflex, a cough reflex, and the ability to raise the head off the bed.
(4) Effective secretion clearance — a deep cough on suctioning and, if alert, MEP > 60 cmH₂O and/or peak cough flow > 60 L/min.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's cuff-leak test — is it quantitative?
cards.a:
Heuer's cuff-leak test — is it quantitative?
No — Heuer's version is QUALITATIVE.
Method: remove secretions above the cuff, fully deflate the cuff, and completely occlude the tube at its outlet. If leakage occurs during spontaneous breathing, that is a 'POSITIVE' test and the airway is likely patent.
⚠ A quantitative threshold (leak volume in mL or % of VT) is NOT covered in Heuer or the available decks.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Hess on the cuff-leak test — does he give a number?
cards.a:
Hess on the cuff-leak test — does he give a number?
No — Hess describes the test but does NOT print a numeric threshold either. Quantitatively 'the leak can be assessed by measuring the volume of the leak or the percentage of the tidal volume that leaks' — the method, but no cut-off.
Hess is sceptical: 'The value of the leak test is controversial because false positives and false negatives are common' — and it increases the risk of ASPIRATION, because secretions on the superior surface of the cuff have a clear path to the lower airway with the cuff down.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Hess: for whom should the cuff-leak test be RESERVED?
cards.a:
Hess: for whom should the cuff-leak test be RESERVED?
Patients at high risk of post-extubation STRIDOR: traumatic intubation · intubation more than 6 days · a large endotracheal tube · female sex · reintubation after unplanned extubation.
Sequencing point: when upper-airway oedema is suspected, prophylactic corticosteroids decrease the risk of post-extubation stridor and reintubation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Extubation — what equipment must be at the bedside?
cards.a:
Extubation — what equipment must be at the bedside?
Suction · BVM · bland-aerosol mask or cannula · an SVN with RACEMIC EPINEPHRINE available · an intubation tray.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's extubation procedure — the steps?
cards.a:
Heuer's extubation procedure — the steps?
Place the patient upright (semi-Fowler's or higher) → suction the tube and the pharynx above the cuff → 100% O₂ by bag for 1–2 minutes → fully deflate the cuff, remove the securing device, insert a new catheter, have the patient COUGH while you apply suction and pull the tube → cool humidified O₂ at a HIGHER FiO₂ than before extubation → assess breath sounds, WOB, vital signs.
If stridor develops: cool humidified O₂ and recommend aerosolized racemic epinephrine.
Then bronchial hygiene/directed coughing; NPO except sips of water for 24 hours.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: What defines weaning failure after extubation, and what causes it?
cards.a:
What defines weaning failure after extubation, and what causes it?
The need for REINTUBATION within 48 hours of extubation.
Caused by hypoventilation and hypercapnia, respiratory acidosis, rapid shallow breathing, excessive secretions, and disuse atrophy.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: After neuromuscular blockade, how do you confirm reversal?
cards.a:
After neuromuscular blockade, how do you confirm reversal?
A 5-second head lift · 5-second tongue protrusion · hand grip · PaO₂ > 80 mmHg · PaCO₂ < 45 mmHg · an adequate MIP and VC.
⚠ But do NOT discontinue support until the DIAPHRAGM can provide adequate ventilation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: A patient is extubated onto NIV/BiPAP — is that weaning failure?
cards.a:
A patient is extubated onto NIV/BiPAP — is that weaning failure?
No — that is 'weaning in progress.'
Heuer agrees, listing 'provide NPPV' as the action to AVOID reintubation in patients who develop mild-to-moderate post-extubation distress.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The organizing rule for ventilator changes from an ABG?
cards.a:
The organizing rule for ventilator changes from an ABG?
CO₂ problem = change VENTILATION (rate and/or VT).
O₂ problem = change OXYGENATION (FiO₂ and/or PEEP).
'Would increasing FiO₂ lower the PaCO₂? No — FiO₂ affects oxygenation, not ventilation.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's pH targets — and when is an abnormal PaCO₂ acceptable?
cards.a:
Heuer's pH targets — and when is an abnormal PaCO₂ acceptable?
pH 7.35–7.45 in most cases, but you may accept as low as 7.25 or as high as 7.50 depending on the underlying problem.
Normalizing the pH may leave the PaCO₂ abnormal — a COPD patient with chronic retention may reach a normal pH at a PaCO₂ of 55 torr or higher, while an uncorrected DKA patient may need a lower-than-normal PaCO₂.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ Rate first or volume first — and why?
cards.a:
⚠ Rate first or volume first — and why?
RATE FIRST. Heuer: adjust the set rate, keeping it between 8 and 24/min (up to 35/min in acute lung injury). Only if rate changes alone will not normalize the pH do you alter VT — and then keep it 4–8 mL/kg PBW with Pplat ≤ 30–35.
Chang deck agrees: increasing frequency is the most common approach; VT is second choice because the adjustable VT range is narrow and excessive VT causes ventilator-induced lung injury.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: pH still below 7.30 with rate, V<sub>T</sub> and Pplat at their limits — what do you do?
cards.a:
pH still below 7.30 with rate, VT and Pplat at their limits — what do you do?
Use PERMISSIVE HYPERCAPNIA — let the PaCO₂ rise as long as the pH stays above 7.20–7.25.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: VC A/C — to ↓PaCO₂ vs to ↑PaCO₂?
cards.a:
VC A/C — to ↓PaCO₂ vs to ↑PaCO₂?
To ↓PaCO₂ / ↑pH: ↑ set rate (keep ≤ 24/min) · ↑ set VT (keep Pplat < 30–35).
To ↑PaCO₂ / ↓pH: ↓ set rate (keep ≥ 8/min) · add mechanical deadspace · ↓ VT if > 8 mL/kg.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: PC A/C and PC SIMV — how do you change PaCO₂?
cards.a:
PC A/C and PC SIMV — how do you change PaCO₂?
PC A/C — to ↓PaCO₂: ↑ set rate (≤ 24/min) · ↑ ΔP (PIP − PEEP). To ↑PaCO₂: ↓ set rate (≥ 6–8/min) · ↓ ΔP.
PC SIMV: same, plus add/increase PS to lower PaCO₂ and ↓ PS to raise it.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: APRV — how do you change PaCO₂?
cards.a:
APRV — how do you change PaCO₂?
To ↓PaCO₂: ↑ release frequency (↓Thigh) · ↑ ΔP (Phigh − Plow).
To ↑PaCO₂: ↓ release frequency (↑Thigh) · ↓ ΔP.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's oxygenation targets?
cards.a:
Heuer's oxygenation targets?
PaO₂ ≥ 65 torr and SaO₂ ≥ 92% for most patients — but as low as PaO₂ 55 torr in COPD or ARDS as long as SaO₂ stays ≥ 88%.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ Heuer's '60-60 rule'
cards.a:
⚠ Heuer's '60-60 rule'
If PaO₂ > 60 torr on FiO₂ < 0.6 → the problem is V/Q imbalance → simply RAISE THE FiO₂.
If PaO₂ < 60 torr on FiO₂ > 0.6 → the problem is SHUNT → PEEP/CPAP must be added or increased.
(A '50-50 rule' works too: if you can hold an acceptable PaO₂/SaO₂ on less than 50% O₂, adjust FiO₂; if not, adjust the baseline pressure.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: When do you recommend the NHLBI ARDS protocol?
cards.a:
When do you recommend the NHLBI ARDS protocol?
If the P/F ratio is ≤ 200, or if 50%+ O₂ with PEEP ≥ 12 cmH₂O still cannot give acceptable values.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Before blaming the lungs for poor oxygenation, what else do you confirm?
cards.a:
Before blaming the lungs for poor oxygenation, what else do you confirm?
Hb ≥ 10 g/dL and adequate circulation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The decks' oxygenation list — and the number-one adjustment?
cards.a:
The decks' oxygenation list — and the number-one adjustment?
Increase FiO₂ · improve ventilation and reduce mechanical deadspace · improve circulation · maintain a normal Hgb · initiate CPAP · initiate PEEP — the NUMBER-ONE ventilator adjustment for improving oxygenation · inverse ratio ventilation · HFOV.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The DESIRED MINUTE VENTILATION formula (Heuer Ch 13)
cards.a:
The DESIRED MINUTE VENTILATION formula (Heuer Ch 13)
New VE = (Known VE × Known PaCO₂) ÷ Desired PaCO₂
Because PaCO₂ is INVERSELY proportional to alveolar ventilation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Worked VE: VT 500 mL at rate 12, PaCO₂ 55, target 40
cards.a:
Worked VE: VT 500 mL at rate 12, PaCO₂ 55, target 40
Known VE = 0.5 × 12 = 6.0 L/min
New VE = (6.0 × 55) ÷ 40 = 330 ÷ 40 = 8.25 L/min
Raise VE from 6.0 to 8.25 L/min (an increase of 2.25 L/min).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Worked RATE: on rate 14, PaCO₂ 60, target 40
cards.a:
Worked RATE: on rate 14, PaCO₂ 60, target 40
New f = (Known f × Known PaCO₂) ÷ Desired PaCO₂
= (14 × 60) ÷ 40 = 840 ÷ 40 = 21
Increase the set rate from 14 to 21/min.
CHECK: 21 is within Heuer's 8–24 ceiling. If it had come out above 24 (or 35 in ALI), you would raise VT instead.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Worked VT: 70-kg PBW, VT 450 at rate 20, PaCO₂ 58, target 45
cards.a:
Worked VT: 70-kg PBW, VT 450 at rate 20, PaCO₂ 58, target 45
New VT = (450 × 58) ÷ 45 = 26,100 ÷ 45 = 580 mL
SAFETY CHECK: 580 ÷ 70 = 8.3 mL/kg PBW — just OVER Heuer's 4–8 mL/kg ceiling. Verify Pplat stays ≤ 30 cmH₂O; if it does not, accept permissive hypercapnia instead (pH may sit at 7.20–7.25).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's App B sanity checks on your math?
cards.a:
Heuer's App B sanity checks on your math?
An adult VE at normal rates should land between 4 and 10 L/min.
If you compute a VT below 200 mL or above 1000 mL for an adult, RECHECK YOUR MATH.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ ABG pH 7.52 / PaCO₂ 30 / HCO₃⁻ 24 — what's the trap?
cards.a:
⚠ ABG pH 7.52 / PaCO₂ 30 / HCO₃⁻ 24 — what's the trap?
Acute respiratory alkalosis.
Only reduce f/VT/PS if the cause is OVER-VENTILATION from an improper setting.
If the ↓PaCO₂ is a RESPONSE to hypoxia, metabolic acidosis, pain or anxiety, do NOT reduce support — further hyperventilation, muscle fatigue, and ventilatory failure are likely. Fix the hypoxia, treat the acidosis, sedate for anxiety.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ ABG pH 7.30 / PaCO₂ 50 / HCO₃⁻ 24 — what's the trap?
cards.a:
⚠ ABG pH 7.30 / PaCO₂ 50 / HCO₃⁻ 24 — what's the trap?
Acute respiratory acidosis. Usual action is ↑f, VT or PS — BUT the same picture occurs with OVERSEDATION or MUSCLE FATIGUE from a premature weaning attempt, in which case increasing the frequency is NOT the right action. Correct the cause and delay weaning.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ COPD patient: pH 7.47 / PaCO₂ 46 / HCO₃⁻ 32 — what is this really?
cards.a:
⚠ COPD patient: pH 7.47 / PaCO₂ 46 / HCO₃⁻ 32 — what is this really?
It reads like 'partially compensated metabolic alkalosis.'
It is really ACUTE RESPIRATORY ALKALOSIS on top of the COPD patient's compensated respiratory acidosis — from acute hypoxia or improper settings.
Fix the cause and the gas returns to his baseline: pH 7.39, PaCO₂ 55, HCO₃⁻ 32.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ A primary METABOLIC acid-base problem — what must you NOT do?
cards.a:
⚠ A primary METABOLIC acid-base problem — what must you NOT do?
Do NOT adjust the ventilator to compensate for metabolic acid-base problems. Do not increase support for metabolic acidosis; do not decrease it for metabolic alkalosis.
Treat the CAUSE: renal failure, DKA, lactic acidosis; for alkalosis, hypokalemia.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Define eucapnic ventilation and permissive hypercapnia.
cards.a:
Define eucapnic ventilation and permissive hypercapnia.
Eucapnic ventilation = PaCO₂ near 40 mmHg, or near 50 mmHg in a CO₂ retainer.
Permissive hypercapnia = deliberate hypoventilation at VT 4–7 mL/kg letting PaCO₂ stay > 50 mmHg. The decks manage the resulting acidosis with bicarbonate or tromethamine (THAM); Heuer simply holds pH > 7.20–7.25.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Why is excessive frequency dangerous, and how do you guard against it?
cards.a:
Why is excessive frequency dangerous, and how do you guard against it?
It shortens E-time and causes AIR TRAPPING — a real risk at RR 30 in COPD: auto-PEEP, hyperinflation, ↑WOB, hypotension.
Heuer's guard: set flow/I-time for an I:E ≤ 1:1, e.g. 1:2 or 1:3.
Deck: VT is decreased by 100–200 mL in COPD to lengthen expiratory time.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The two compliance formulas — and the ONLY difference?
cards.a:
The two compliance formulas — and the ONLY difference?
Cstat (Crs) = VT ÷ (Pplat − PEEP) — lung + chest wall stiffness ONLY (zero flow → no resistance component).
Cdyn = VT ÷ (PIP − PEEP) — total impedance: compliance AND resistance (flow still moving → PTA included).
The only difference is which pressure goes in the denominator: Pplat for static, PIP for dynamic.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The airway resistance formula — and the unit conversion?
cards.a:
The airway resistance formula — and the unit conversion?
Raw = (PIP − Pplat) ÷ Flow in L/sec
Convert: L/min ÷ 60 = L/sec

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's simplified equation of motion — what does the inspiratory pause do?
cards.a:
Heuer's simplified equation of motion — what does the inspiratory pause do?
The driving pressure has two components: the pressure to overcome elastic recoil of lungs and thorax (VT/Crs), and the pressure to overcome airway resistance (flow × Raw).
An end-inspiratory pause during volume control 'PARTITIONS' them apart so you can compute both.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Why is Cdyn ALWAYS less than Crs — and what does the gap mean?
cards.a:
Why is Cdyn ALWAYS less than Crs — and what does the gap mean?
Because (PIP − PEEP) is always greater than (Pplat − PEEP) during volume control.
The gap (Crs − Cdyn) is entirely due to AIRWAY RESISTANCE — the bigger the gap, the bigger resistance's contribution to the driving pressure.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ Static compliance normals — the THREE different answers
cards.a:
⚠ Static compliance normals — the THREE different answers
RCP 105 Principles/Waveform decks: 60–100 mL/cmH₂O, normal around 80.
RCP 203 Lssn 3a: 40–80 mL/cmH₂O for intubated adults.
Heuer Ch 4: 40–80 mL/cmH₂O for intubated adults — matching RCP 203 exactly.
But Heuer's own App B says CLT ranges from 100 (normal) down to 10 (severe, as in ARDS) — an internal inconsistency. Cite 40–80 when the question says 'intubated.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Compliance danger zone and weaning minimum — do the sources agree?
cards.a:
Compliance danger zone and weaning minimum — do the sources agree?
Yes — all three agree.
Danger zone: < 25–30 mL/cmH₂O = increased WOB, weaning difficulty.
Weaning minimum: > 30 mL/cmH₂O.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Airway resistance normals?
cards.a:
Airway resistance normals?
RCP 203 and Heuer Ch 4: 5–12 cmH₂O/L/sec for intubated adults.
Heuer App B: 5–15 cmH₂O/L/sec for orally intubated; expect higher in airway obstruction.
Weaning deck: 0.6–2.4 cmH₂O/L/sec — a NON-intubated normal; it runs higher in ventilated patients because of tube and circuit resistance.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer Problem B.14: VT 700 mL, PEEP 8, PIP 42, Pplat 35 — static compliance?
cards.a:
Heuer Problem B.14: VT 700 mL, PEEP 8, PIP 42, Pplat 35 — static compliance?
CLT = VT ÷ (Pplat − PEEP)
= 700 ÷ (35 − 8) = 700 ÷ 27
= 26 mL/cmH₂O — well under 40: stiff lungs, weaning risk.
⚠ Note the PIP of 42 is a DECOY here.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer Problem B.15: VT 400 mL, flow 75 L/min, PEEP 6, PIP 45, Pplat 30 — Raw?
cards.a:
Heuer Problem B.15: VT 400 mL, flow 75 L/min, PEEP 6, PIP 45, Pplat 30 — Raw?
Convert flow: 75 ÷ 60 = 1.25 L/sec
Raw = (45 − 30) ÷ 1.25 = 15 ÷ 1.25
= 12 cmH₂O/L/sec — top of the 5–12 normal range; borderline high.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: How do you read Pplat off a pressure-time curve?
cards.a:
How do you read Pplat off a pressure-time curve?
Apply an inspiratory pause / end-inspiratory breath hold — 0.5–2.0 seconds during volume-targeted ventilation, using a square inspiratory flow pattern.
Airflow stops, the resistive pressure component disappears, and the trace drops from PIP to a flat shelf — that shelf is the plateau pressure (Pplat, also PALV).
⚠ Bedside mechanics require complete relaxation of the respiratory muscles plus 2–3 seconds of zero flow to equilibrate — sometimes requiring sedation or paralysis.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Two accuracy warnings when reading Pplat?
cards.a:
Two accuracy warnings when reading Pplat?
If the patient EXHALES during the pause → an erratic RISE and a FALSELY HIGH Pplat.
If the patient INHALES during the pause → an erratic DROP and a FALSELY LOW Pplat.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ The special case where PIP = Pplat
cards.a:
⚠ The special case where PIP = Pplat
In a TRUE DESCENDING RAMP flow waveform, flow reaches zero at end-inspiration on its own, so PTA = 0 and PIP = PALV = Pplat.
Under those conditions you may compute static compliance from PIP.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Worked waveform: flow 60 L/min for TI 0.5 sec, true descending ramp, PIP 35
cards.a:
Worked waveform: flow 60 L/min for TI 0.5 sec, true descending ramp, PIP 35
VT = Flow × TI = 1 L/sec × 0.5 sec = 0.5 L = 500 mL
True descending ramp → flow = 0 at end-insp → PIP = PALV = Pplat = 35
Compliance = 500 ÷ 35 = 14.3 mL/cmH₂O
Far below normal — a stiff, non-compliant system.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Both Crs and Cdyn fall proportionately (gap unchanged) — what do you see in VC and PC?
cards.a:
Both Crs and Cdyn fall proportionately (gap unchanged) — what do you see in VC and PC?
A pure COMPLIANCE problem.
In VC: ↑PIP, ↑Pplat, NO change in PIP − Pplat, ↓Cdyn, and a decreased SLOPE of the P-V loop.
In PC: ↓VT and a decreased P-V loop slope.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Cdyn falls while Cstat is unchanged (gap WIDENS) — what do you see in VC and PC?
cards.a:
Cdyn falls while Cstat is unchanged (gap WIDENS) — what do you see in VC and PC?
A pure RESISTANCE problem.
In VC: ↑PIP, ↑(PIP − Pplat), NO change in Pplat, ↓Cdyn, and increased WIDTH of the P-V loop.
In PC: ↓VT — but only if flow continues to the end of the breath (VT is unchanged if flow ceases early) — and a wider P-V loop.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's Box 4-5 trend problem: over 4 h, Pplat − PEEP constant; PIP − Pplat rises 20 → 35
cards.a:
Heuer's Box 4-5 trend problem: over 4 h, Pplat − PEEP constant; PIP − Pplat rises 20 → 35
Crs UNCHANGED at 20 mL/cmH₂O; Raw INCREASING.
DIAGNOSIS: a pure RESISTANCE problem.
LOOK FOR: bronchospasm, excessive secretions, airway edema, partial artificial airway occlusion (mucus plug, kinking, biting).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Which three measurements do NOT depend on patient effort — and why does that matter?
cards.a:
Which three measurements do NOT depend on patient effort — and why does that matter?
Static compliance, airway resistance, and VD/VT — unlike VC and MIP.
