That is exactly why they indicate the PULMONARY WORKLOAD needed to support spontaneous ventilation. Low compliance, high Raw, and a high VD/VT all raise the workload and, past the patient's threshold, hinder weaning.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: When do you measure compliance — the four uses?
cards.a:
When do you measure compliance — the four uses?
(1) As a weaning parameter (> 30 mL/cmH₂O).
(2) Whenever the patient suddenly becomes harder to ventilate — always ask 'has compliance decreased?' and 'has resistance increased?'
(3) To track response to therapy (a more vertical P-V loop after PEEP or surfactant).
(4) Heuer's addition: serial Crs measurement is the ENGINE of the decremental PEEP study.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: PIP vs Pplat vs PIP − Pplat — what does each represent?
cards.a:
PIP vs Pplat vs PIP − Pplat — what does each represent?
PIP = the pressure needed to overcome BOTH airflow resistance AND lung compliance.
Pplat (PALV) = the pressure needed to overcome compliance ONLY.
PIP − Pplat = PTA = RESISTANCE.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: How does PIP behave differently in VC, PC and NPPV?
cards.a:
How does PIP behave differently in VC, PC and NPPV?
In VC, PIP VARIES with mechanics (Crs and Raw) and settings.
In PC, PIP is SET and held constant.
In NPPV, PIP = IPAP.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Driving pressure (ΔP) — definition, and its NPPV equivalent?
cards.a:
Driving pressure (ΔP) — definition, and its NPPV equivalent?
ΔP = PIP − PEEP — the total impedance to inflation (equation of motion).
In NPPV it equals IPAP − EPAP.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ Which is the HONEST driving pressure — PIP − PEEP or Pplat − PEEP?
cards.a:
⚠ Which is the HONEST driving pressure — PIP − PEEP or Pplat − PEEP?
Pplat − PEEP is the TRUE lung driving pressure — the distending pressure across the parenchyma.
PIP − PEEP OVERESTIMATES lung distension in a high-resistance patient (asthma, COPD), because it includes the resistive component.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Mean airway pressure — what determines it and what is it used for?
cards.a:
Mean airway pressure — what determines it and what is it used for?
A function of PIP, I:E ratio and PEEP; it is a key determinant of FRC and oxygenation, and is used in the Oxygenation Index.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Target and limit pressures — decks vs Heuer
cards.a:
Target and limit pressures — decks vs Heuer
Decks: PIP < 50 cmH₂O, Pplat < 35 cmH₂O, with the ARDSNet (2000) recommendation of Pplat < 30 — 'if you remember one ventilator pressure in ARDS, remember this one.'
Heuer, blunter: 'In general, plateau pressures should be kept below 30 cmH₂O to reduce the likelihood of ventilator-induced lung injury,' and patients needing Pplat > 30 during VC should probably be switched to pressure control at a limit of 30 or less.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Barotrauma thresholds (decks)?
cards.a:
Barotrauma thresholds (decks)?
PEEP > 10 cmH₂O, or Pmean > 30 cmH₂O, or PIP > 50 cmH₂O are associated with increased alveolar rupture.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Both PIP and Pplat FALLING — the two possibilities?
cards.a:
Both PIP and Pplat FALLING — the two possibilities?
Compliance improved — OR gas is escaping.
A circuit leak gives a lower-than-expected PIP with a NORMAL return to baseline, whereas air trapping alters the EXPIRATORY phase.
A rising baseline pressure that will not return to zero = AUTO-PEEP.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ Heuer's FIVE definitions of optimal PEEP
cards.a:
⚠ Heuer's FIVE definitions of optimal PEEP
The PEEP level that:
(1) maximizes O₂ delivery to the tissues;
(2) yields the highest static compliance (Crs);
(3) provides the maximum volume change for a given ΔP;
(4) prevents alveolar collapse;
(5) maximizes the average expired tidal %CO₂.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: For optimal-PEEP method 1, what does the NBRC substitute — and what's the rule?
cards.a:
For optimal-PEEP method 1, what does the NBRC substitute — and what's the rule?
It substitutes blood pressure for cardiac output and SpO₂ for ABGs.
Optimum PEEP = the level that maintains SpO₂ ≥ 88–90% WITHOUT lowering the blood pressure.
Heuer's flat rule: whenever cardiac output or BP falls when PEEP is raised, DECREASE PEEP back to its prior setting.
Worked NBRC item: PEEP raised 6 → 10, BP drops → return the PEEP to 6 — not increase FiO₂, give a vasopressor, or draw a gas.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: What does a recruitment maneuver do — and what does the evidence say?
cards.a:
What does a recruitment maneuver do — and what does the evidence say?
It temporarily raises the transpulmonary pressure gradient (Palv − Ppl) to reopen unaerated alveoli, raising end-expiratory lung volume and FRC, improving gas exchange and compliance and reducing spontaneous WOB.
⚠ There is NO evidence that RMs affect morbidity or mortality.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Who is a candidate for a recruitment maneuver?
cards.a:
Who is a candidate for a recruitment maneuver?
Hypoxemia unresponsive to O₂ due to intrapulmonary shunting, P/F < 200–300, and ONLY in hemodynamically stable patients — MAP ≥ 60–65 mmHg with no recent change in vasoactive/inotropic dosing.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The classic '40/40' recruitment maneuver?
cards.a:
The classic '40/40' recruitment maneuver?
CPAP of 40 cmH₂O for up to 40 seconds.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's currently favored recruitment maneuver (Box 11-2)?
cards.a:
Heuer's currently favored recruitment maneuver (Box 11-2)?
Set the high-pressure alarm to 50–55, FiO₂ 1.0, then PEEP 20 / PIP 40 (ΔP 20) for 1–3 minutes; repeat at PEEP 25 / PIP 45 if unsuccessful.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ When do you STOP a recruitment maneuver immediately?
cards.a:
⚠ When do you STOP a recruitment maneuver immediately?
MAP < 60–65 mmHg · SpO₂ drops > 4% · HR > 140 or < 60 · a new chest-tube air leak appears · new arrhythmias develop.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: What counts as a SUCCESSFUL recruitment maneuver?
cards.a:
What counts as a SUCCESSFUL recruitment maneuver?
SaO₂ up ≥ 4–5%, P/F up ≥ 20%, or the same PaO₂/SaO₂ at a LOWER FiO₂ — plus higher Crs (more VT for the same pressure in PC, or the same VT at lower pressure in VC).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The decremental PEEP study (Box 11-3) — the full procedure
cards.a:
The decremental PEEP study (Box 11-3) — the full procedure
Switch to VC at VT 4–6 mL/kg PBW → start from the RM PEEP (20–25) → drop PEEP in 2-cmH₂O steps, 3–5 minutes between steps, measuring Crs = VT ÷ (Pplat − PEEP) each time → continue until you PASS the highest Crs (you must see at least one decrease from the peak) → repeat the recruitment → set PEEP 2 cmH₂O ABOVE the level that gave the highest Crs → check a blood gas after 20–30 minutes.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's Figure 11-16 example: compliance peaks at 39 mL/cmH₂O at a PEEP of 16
cards.a:
Heuer's Figure 11-16 example: compliance peaks at 39 mL/cmH₂O at a PEEP of 16
Optimum PEEP = 16 + 2 = 18 cmH₂O.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ The hemodynamic chain when airway pressures rise
cards.a:
⚠ The hemodynamic chain when airway pressures rise
Positive pressure in the lungs directly increases INTRATHORACIC pressure, and everything follows:
↑intrathoracic pressure → ↓venous return → ↓ventricular filling → ↓stroke volume → ↓cardiac output → ↓oxygen delivery and hypotension. (The garden-hose analogy.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: PPV ALONE vs PPV WITH PEEP — the hemodynamic difference?
cards.a:
PPV ALONE vs PPV WITH PEEP — the hemodynamic difference?
PPV alone: lowers CVP, lowers PAP, decreases pulmonary blood volume and increases systemic blood volume, lowers ventricular filling pressure and output.
PPV WITH PEEP: RAISES pulmonary artery pressure (expanded alveoli compress pulmonary capillaries → ↑PVR), RAISES the measured CVP (blood backs up in the systemic veins even though true venous return is falling), and lowers aortic pressure and cardiac output.
⚠ A high CVP does NOT always mean lots of preload.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Why do ventilated patients drop their urine output?
cards.a:
Why do ventilated patients drop their urine output?
The kidneys receive about 25% of circulating blood volume.
PPV → ↑intrathoracic pressure → ↓venous return → ↓cardiac output → ↓renal blood flow → ↓urine output → renal dysfunction.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ Urine output normals — deck vs Heuer
cards.a:
⚠ Urine output normals — deck vs Heuer
Deck: normal UOP > 400 mL in 24 hours, or > 160 mL in 8 hours.
Heuer: urine averages 1200–1500 mL/day (at least 50 mL/h), and < 25 mL/h is OLIGURIA.
Heuer's 25 mL/h ≈ 600 mL/day — so Heuer's oliguria cutoff is STRICTER than the deck's.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Oliguria plus what other labs signals renal insufficiency?
cards.a:
Oliguria plus what other labs signals renal insufficiency?
BUN above the normal 10–20 mg/dL, creatinine above 0.7–1.5 mg/dL, and rising potassium.
Heuer also lists ↓urine output as a complication of heated humidification during mechanical ventilation. The liver receives about 15% of circulating blood volume, and hepatic perfusion decreases only when PEEP is added to PPV.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Why do we accept the costs — the benefits of PEEP?
cards.a:
Why do we accept the costs — the benefits of PEEP?
It reinflates collapsed alveoli and keeps them inflated during exhalation · decreases the pressure threshold for alveolar inflation · increases FRC · improves ventilation and V/Q · improves oxygenation · decreases WOB.
Indications: intrapulmonary shunting and refractory hypoxemia, decreased FRC and lung compliance, and auto-PEEP not responding to ventilator adjustments.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Auto-PEEP — the four other names, and the definition?
cards.a:
Auto-PEEP — the four other names, and the definition?
Intrinsic PEEP · inadvertent PEEP · occult PEEP · dynamic hyperinflation.
The abnormal, often undetected residual pressure ABOVE baseline remaining in the alveoli at end-exhalation because of AIR TRAPPING.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's auto-PEEP risk profile — and the decks' additions?
cards.a:
Heuer's auto-PEEP risk profile — and the decks' additions?
Heuer: patients with HIGH airway resistance AND HIGH compliance being supported by modes that LIMIT EXPIRATORY TIME.
Decks add: excessive pressure support, significant airway obstruction, high frequency (> 20/min), insufficient inspiratory flow, and a roughly equal (1:1) or inverse I:E ratio — most often in patients with a history of air trapping (COPD, asthma).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The THREE reasons auto-PEEP is dangerous?
cards.a:
The THREE reasons auto-PEEP is dangerous?
(1) It raises the baseline pressure so the patient must work harder to trigger down to the sensitivity level (↑WOB).
(2) It reduces venous return and compromises hemodynamics.
(3) It risks barotrauma.
Deck's warning: distal airway pressure can be as high as 15 cmH₂O while the ventilator's proximal manometer shows nothing.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ How do you DETECT auto-PEEP?
cards.a:
⚠ How do you DETECT auto-PEEP?
It is NOT visible on a normal pressure-time graphic — that's why it's called 'occult.'
Inspect the FLOW-versus-TIME waveform or the FLOW–VOLUME LOOP — the clue is that expiratory flow does NOT return to baseline/zero before the next breath begins.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: How do you MEASURE auto-PEEP — and the formula?
cards.a:
How do you MEASURE auto-PEEP — and the formula?
Apply an end-EXPIRATORY pause (an end-INSPIRATORY pause gives Pplat instead). Once flow ceases, airway pressure equilibrates with the higher alveolar pressure, producing a momentary RISE in the baseline.
Auto-PEEP = end-expiratory pause pressure − set PEEP (deck example: 12 − 5 = 7 cmH₂O).
Total PEEP = set PEEP + auto-PEEP — and this is the PEEP that counts in Crs = VT ÷ (Pplat − TOTAL PEEP).
The patient should be relaxed — often sedated or paralyzed.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Auto-PEEP causes — the EQUIPMENT-related list (Heuer Table 4-17)?
cards.a:
Auto-PEEP causes — the EQUIPMENT-related list (Heuer Table 4-17)?
High ventilator rate · short expiratory time / high I:E ratio · high minute ventilation · partially obstructed ETT or HME · wet expiratory filters · malfunctioning exhalation valve ('sticky valve').

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Auto-PEEP causes — the PATIENT-related list (Heuer Table 4-17)?
cards.a:
Auto-PEEP causes — the PATIENT-related list (Heuer Table 4-17)?
Bronchospasm · small airway collapse · increased secretions · mucus plug ('one-way valve' effect) · patient–ventilator asynchrony · decreased elastic recoil / high compliance.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Auto-PEEP from a high rate / short E-time — the fixes in VC and PC?
cards.a:
Auto-PEEP from a high rate / short E-time — the fixes in VC and PC?
↓ rate (VC or PC) · ↑ inspiratory flow (VC — shortens I-time → lengthens E-time) · ↓ VT (VC; deck says by 100–200 mL in COPD) · ↓ inspiratory time (PC).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Auto-PEEP from high minute ventilation — the fix?
cards.a:
Auto-PEEP from high minute ventilation — the fix?
↓ rate AND ↓ VT, accepting a rise in PaCO₂ as long as pH stays above 7.25 (permissive hypercapnia).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Auto-PEEP from a malfunctioning exhalation valve — the fix?
cards.a:
Auto-PEEP from a malfunctioning exhalation valve — the fix?
Change the ventilator UNIT — many expiratory valves are housed inside the machine.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ Applying external PEEP to offset auto-PEEP — the amount CONFLICTS
cards.a:
⚠ Applying external PEEP to offset auto-PEEP — the amount CONFLICTS
Heuer: up to 50–80% of the measured auto-PEEP.
RCP 203: 80–90%.
Apply it ONLY AFTER ventilator setting changes have been made, and it works best in spontaneously breathing patients — it offsets the inspiratory threshold load so the patient can trigger.
Applies to small airway collapse or decreased elastic recoil / high compliance.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: High spontaneous rate on PS causing auto-PEEP — the deck's fix?
cards.a:
High spontaneous rate on PS causing auto-PEEP — the deck's fix?
Keep PS frequency < 20/min.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The memory hook for the two loops?
cards.a:
The memory hook for the two loops?
'Volume/Pressure Loop = think COMPLIANCE. Flow/Volume Loop = think RESISTANCE.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: What is each SCALAR display for (Heuer Tables 11-10/11-11)?
cards.a:
What is each SCALAR display for (Heuer Tables 11-10/11-11)?
Flow vs time: identify auto-PEEP; assess/adjust PC and PS rise time; assess/adjust PC inspiratory time; identify asynchrony.
Pressure vs time: confirm PIP and PEEP; visually assess mechanics (PIP − Pplat ≈ Raw, Pplat − PEEP ≈ Crs); identify asynchrony.
Volume vs time: identify LEAKS (expired volume does not return to baseline); identify asynchrony.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: What is each LOOP for (Heuer Tables 11-10/11-11)?
cards.a:
What is each LOOP for (Heuer Tables 11-10/11-11)?
Pressure-volume loop: assess overall mechanics; identify overdistention (the 'beak sign'); assess trigger work; adjust PSV levels; identify asynchrony.
Volume-flow loop: assess BRONCHODILATOR RESPONSE; identify auto-PEEP; identify leaks.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Heuer's sweep-speed tip?
cards.a:
Heuer's sweep-speed tip?
A FASTER time scale gives a closer look at individual breaths; a SLOWER sweep speed helps you identify TRENDS.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ The P-V loop — what do the SLOPE and the WIDTH each tell you?
cards.a:
⚠ The P-V loop — what do the SLOPE and the WIDTH each tell you?
The SLOPE is COMPLIANCE — the steeper the slope, the higher the compliance.
The WIDTH is AIRWAY RESISTANCE — the thinner the loop, the lower the Raw; a wider loop means increased Raw.
Volume on the y-axis, pressure on the x-axis; inspiration climbs, exhalation returns.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: What does the dotted line inside a P-V loop represent?
cards.a:
What does the dotted line inside a P-V loop represent?
ALVEOLAR pressure.
The gap between the outer loop (Pao/PIP) and that dotted line is PTA — the pressure being spent on airway resistance rather than inflating the lung.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: How do COMPLIANCE changes move the P-V loop?
cards.a:
How do COMPLIANCE changes move the P-V loop?
DECREASED compliance shifts it toward the PRESSURE axis (to the RIGHT) with NO change in PTA. Deck's numbers: the same 600 mL VT that needed about 30 cmH₂O now needs a little over 40.
INCREASED compliance shifts it toward the VOLUME axis (to the LEFT), also with no change in PTA.
Because PIP and PALV move together, the PTA arrow keeps its width.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ 'On a P-V loop, right is bad and left is good' — and the emphysema trap
cards.a:
⚠ 'On a P-V loop, right is bad and left is good' — and the emphysema trap
RIGHT shift = ARDS, pulmonary edema, atelectasis, pneumonia, fibrosis.
LEFT shift = EMPHYSEMA.
Students wrongly assume emphysema LOWERS compliance — compliance is INCREASED; the lungs stretch easily, the problem is POOR RECOIL.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: How do RESISTANCE changes alter the P-V loop?
cards.a:
How do RESISTANCE changes alter the P-V loop?
They change the WIDTH.
Increased Raw raises PTA, PIP and Pao with NO change in PALV — the loop gets FATTER.
Decreased Raw lowers PTA, PIP and Pao with no change in PALV.
Restated: 'when PIP changes but PALV stays the same, think RESISTANCE.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The static P-V curve is S-shaped — describe the three zones
cards.a:
The static P-V curve is S-shaped — describe the three zones
(1) Low slope at low pressures/volumes — low compliance; high pressure is needed to OPEN collapsed alveoli.
(2) Steep slope at moderate volumes — high compliance; the 'sweet spot' for safe and efficient volume exchange.
(3) Low slope again at high pressures/volumes — the limits of elastic expansion have been reached (overdistention, beak sign).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The Lower Inflection Point — what is it and how much PEEP?
cards.a:
The Lower Inflection Point — what is it and how much PEEP?
On the inspiratory limb the curve rises slowly then suddenly becomes steeper; that change in slope marks the pressure at which a significant number of alveoli begin to OPEN. It appears in lungs with very low compliance.
⚠ Decks: set PEEP 'at or slightly above the LIP.' Heuer is specific: 'PEEP typically is set 2–3 cmH₂O ABOVE the LIP.'
Kettering simply calls the LIP 'best PEEP level.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Why set PEEP above the LIP — and where does it NOT apply well?
cards.a:
Why set PEEP above the LIP — and where does it NOT apply well?
To reduce the opening-pressure requirement, minimize alveolar collapse during expiration, improve recruitment and oxygenation, and reduce repetitive opening and closing (ATELECTRAUMA).
⚠ It applies best to HOMOGENEOUS 'stiff' lungs (non-ARDS). In heterogeneous disease like ARDS, some alveoli recruit while others OVERDISTEND, so PEEP must be individualized — which is exactly why Heuer prefers the decremental PEEP study.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The Upper Inflection Point and the BEAK SIGN?
cards.a:
The Upper Inflection Point and the BEAK SIGN?
At end-inspiration the loop flattens and bends over into a 'duckbill' or 'beak.'
Heuer: beyond the UIP, small changes in VOLUME produce very large increases in PRESSURE — the 'beak sign,' indicating airway OVERDISTENTION from excessive VT.
Overdistended lungs have decreased lung-thorax compliance and risk barotrauma from excessive pressure and volutrauma from excessive volume.
The intervention is to REDUCE THE VT until the beak disappears.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: The LIP/UIP memory line?
cards.a:
The LIP/UIP memory line?
Lower Inflection Point = alveoli OPENING. Upper Inflection Point = alveoli OVERSTRETCHING.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: How does a LEAK appear on the loops?
cards.a:
How does a LEAK appear on the loops?
The loops do NOT return to zero volume and look broken or open, because expiratory volume is less than inspiratory volume — from a leak in the circuit or around the ETT/trach cuff.
The volume-vs-time scalar shows the same thing: expired volume failing to return to baseline.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: ⚠ On the flow-volume loop, why does all the diagnostic information live on the EXPIRATORY limb?
cards.a:
⚠ On the flow-volume loop, why does all the diagnostic information live on the EXPIRATORY limb?
Because peak INSPIRATORY flow is PRESET by the ventilator. The expiratory limb (below the horizontal axis) is the only part the patient's lungs determine.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: What does INCREASED airway resistance do to the expiratory limb of the FVL?
cards.a:
What does INCREASED airway resistance do to the expiratory limb of the FVL?
It LOWERS the peak expiratory flow: the limb becomes flatter, less peaked, does not extend as far downward, and the lungs empty more slowly — the narrow, scooped, blunted limb of bronchospasm, mucus plugging and airway obstruction.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: What does a successful bronchodilator do to the FVL?
cards.a:
What does a successful bronchodilator do to the FVL?
DECREASED resistance RAISES the peak expiratory flow — the limb becomes more peaked and extends farther downward.
Heuer names it exactly: the volume-flow loop is used to assess bronchodilator response — note the improvement in peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) after a treatment.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: Loop shape by breath type (Kettering)?
cards.a:
Loop shape by breath type (Kettering)?
Spontaneous breath: an oval, symmetric P-V loop with no sharp corners and a smooth, less-defined F-V loop.
Assisted breath: begins with a small trigger effort before machine assistance takes over.
Controlled breath: a well-defined P-V loop with SHARP ANGLES and a classic oval F-V loop that returns cleanly to baseline.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: What is patient–ventilator asynchrony, and what does it cost?
cards.a:
What is patient–ventilator asynchrony, and what does it cost?
A lack of coordination between the patient's ventilatory needs and the support provided.
It lengthens BOTH the duration of mechanical ventilation AND the ICU stay.
Three categories: TRIGGER, FLOW, and CYCLE.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: INEFFECTIVE TRIGGER — what do you see and what do you do?
cards.a:
INEFFECTIVE TRIGGER — what do you see and what do you do?
See: pressure and flow scalars show a delayed or absent response to the patient's effort (e.g. the patient must drop the pressure 10 cmH₂O below baseline to trigger).
Do: increase sensitivity · switch to FLOW triggering · reduce/counteract auto-PEEP · reduce sedation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: AUTOCYCLING — what do you see and what do you do?
cards.a:
AUTOCYCLING — what do you see and what do you do?
See: extra breaths triggered WITHOUT patient effort, usually from circuit condensate or leaks.
Do: DECREASE sensitivity · switch to flow triggering · correct leaks · drain condensate and change filters.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: DOUBLE TRIGGERING — what do you see and what do you do?
cards.a:
DOUBLE TRIGGERING — what do you see and what do you do?
See: two consecutive machine breaths with NO interval between them.
Do: ↑ inspiratory flow (VC) · ↑ set VT (VC) · ↑ inspiratory time (PC) · shorten rise time (PC) · ↑ pressure level (PS) · ↓ %cycling criteria (PS).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: FLOW STARVATION (inadequate flow) — what do you see and what do you do?
cards.a:
FLOW STARVATION (inadequate flow) — what do you see and what do you do?
See: 'SCALLOPING' / concavity in the pressure scalar of assisted breaths, or on the flow scalar during volume ventilation.
Do: ↑ flow (VC) · change flow pattern (VC) · switch VC to PC · ↑ set PIP (PC) · shorten rise time (PC) · find and correct the cause of increased ventilatory demand.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::05 Mechanical Ventilation, BiPAP, Weaning & Waveforms
cards.q: EXCESSIVE FLOW — what do you see and what do you do?
cards.a:
EXCESSIVE FLOW — what do you see and what do you do?
See: pressure peak achieved too early (PC), or an upward spike on inspiratory flow (VC).
Do: ↓ inspiratory flow (VC) · ↓ set PIP (PC) · LENGTHEN rise time (PC).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Intubation equipment — the laryngoscope, tube and stylet essentials?
cards.a:
Intubation equipment — the laryngoscope, tube and stylet essentials?
Laryngoscope handle with fresh batteries, Macintosh and Miller blades sizes 00 to 4, ETTs 2 to 10 mm ID — the selected size plus one size larger and one size smaller, a 10-mL syringe, water-soluble lubricant, a stylet (ORAL ONLY — never for nasal; the tip must never extend past the ETT tip), and Magill forceps (required for the nasal route).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Intubation — the rest of the checklist?
cards.a:
Intubation — the rest of the checklist?
Suction with a Yankauer tip · BVM with 100% O₂ · topical anesthetic (2% tetracaine spray, or nebulized 4% lidocaine for elective cases) · colorimetric CO₂ detector or waveform capnography · tape or a commercial holder · a bite block · a stethoscope.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Difficult-airway backup equipment?
cards.a:
Difficult-airway backup equipment?
Bougie (tracheal tube introducer) · lighted stylet/light wand · intubating LMA (Fastrach) · video laryngoscope · fiberoptic bronchoscope · supraglottic airways.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: ⚠ Macintosh vs Miller — the technique difference
cards.a:
⚠ Macintosh vs Miller — the technique difference
Macintosh = CURVED. The tip goes into the VALLECULA (the pocket between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis); lifting the handle lifts the tongue, which raises the epiglottis INDIRECTLY.
Miller = STRAIGHT. It is passed UNDER the epiglottis and lifts it DIRECTLY.
Heuer says only 'Macintosh or Miller depending on preference' — this technique detail comes from the deck. (The deck also lists the Wisconsin as a third straight blade.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: How far past the cords does the ETT go, and to what cuff pressure?
cards.a:
How far past the cords does the ETT go, and to what cuff pressure?
Advance until the CUFF DISAPPEARS 2–3 cm past the cords.
Inflate the cuff to 20–30 cm H₂O.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: How do you auscultate after intubation?
cards.a:
How do you auscultate after intubation?
Auscultate the CHEST for symmetrical breath sounds AND the EPIGASTRIUM for ABSENT gurgling.
Then verify with breath sounds, chest movement, and CO₂ detection/capnography; secure the tube, record the cm mark at the incisors, and confirm position by chest x-ray.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: ⚠ How long may an intubation attempt last — and the source conflict?
cards.a:
⚠ How long may an intubation attempt last — and the source conflict?
Heuer Ch 9: no more than 20 seconds.
Heuer Ch 16 (RT assisting a physician): no more than 30 seconds.
With 1–2 minutes of oxygenation between attempts. Hyperoxygenate 1–2 minutes before the first attempt.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: What does the AHA want for tube confirmation during resuscitation?
cards.a:
What does the AHA want for tube confirmation during resuscitation?
Continuous QUANTITATIVE WAVEFORM CAPNOGRAPHY.
A colorimetric CO₂ detector is the acceptable alternative — confirmed by a purple → yellow/tan color change sustained over SIX OR MORE breaths (2.0–5.0% exhaled CO₂, about 15–38 torr).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: ⚠ The two CO₂-detector traps?
cards.a:
⚠ The two CO₂-detector traps?
FALSE NEGATIVE in cardiac arrest — no pulmonary blood flow.
FALSE POSITIVE with a MAINSTEM intubation — the tube is in the airway, just the wrong one.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Epigastric gurgling after intubation — what do you do?
cards.a:
Epigastric gurgling after intubation — what do you do?
Esophageal intubation. → Deflate, pull the tube, reoxygenate, reintubate.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Decreased breath sounds and chest movement on the LEFT — what and what do you do?
cards.a:
Decreased breath sounds and chest movement on the LEFT — what and what do you do?
Right mainstem intubation. → Withdraw slowly until bilateral.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: ⚠ Heuer is blunt: what are the ONLY two ways to confirm the tube is properly above the carina?
cards.a:
⚠ Heuer is blunt: what are the ONLY two ways to confirm the tube is properly above the carina?
Chest x-ray or fiberoptic laryngoscopy.
Breath sounds and CO₂ prove the tube is in the AIRWAY — not that its DEPTH is right.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Average oral ETT depth at the teeth/incisors?
cards.a:
Average oral ETT depth at the teeth/incisors?
21–23 cm in adult MALES · 19–21 cm in adult FEMALES.
For the NASOtracheal route, ADD 2 cm.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Where should the ETT tip sit on the film — and why does head position matter?
cards.a:
Where should the ETT tip sit on the film — and why does head position matter?
About 4–6 cm above the carina, usually between T2 and T4, with the head NEUTRAL.
The tube travels up and down as the neck flexes and extends — so always read head position with the film.
Too deep → right mainstem. Too shallow → accidental extubation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: M-O-A-N-S — what does it predict and what does it stand for?
cards.a:
M-O-A-N-S — what does it predict and what does it stand for?
Predicts difficult BVM VENTILATION:
Mask seal · Obesity/Obstruction · Aged · No teeth · Stiff lungs.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: L-E-M-O-N — what does it predict and what does it stand for?
cards.a:
L-E-M-O-N — what does it predict and what does it stand for?
Predicts difficult INTUBATION:
Look externally · Evaluate external anatomy · Mallampati · Obesity/Obstruction · Neck mobility.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Mallampati and Cormack-Lehane grades?
cards.a:
Mallampati and Cormack-Lehane grades?
Mallampati: Class I–II = easy · Class III = difficult · Class IV = very difficult (hard palate only).
Cormack-Lehane (direct laryngoscopy): Grade III = epiglottis only · Grade IV = no epiglottis — Grade IV carries over a 90% likelihood of difficult intubation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: OPA — how is it sized and inserted?
cards.a:
OPA — how is it sized and inserted?
Sized by LENGTH: 40 mm (00) premature → 100 mm (5) large adult; 80 mm (3) average adult female · 90 mm (4) average adult male.
Size by measuring the corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw (or to the earlobe).
Insert tip-up (180°) or from the side, then rotate to midline.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: ⚠ OPA — contraindication and the two sizing errors?
cards.a:
⚠ OPA — contraindication and the two sizing errors?
NOT for conscious patients — gagging, vomiting, aspiration. Remove immediately if the patient gags.
Too LARGE occludes the airway (and can cause gastric insufflation); too SMALL pushes the tongue back and obstructs.
Do not tape over the center opening — a suction catheter passes through it.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: NPA — sizing, bevel direction, and where the tip sits?
cards.a:
NPA — sizing, bevel direction, and where the tip sits?
Passed along the floor of the nose (inferior meatus) with the tip behind the tongue above the epiglottis.
#6 (24 Fr) average female · #7 (28 Fr) average male · 32–36 Fr large adult.
Bevel faces the SEPTUM (medially).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: NPA — indications and cautions?
cards.a:
NPA — indications and cautions?
Indications: the alternative to an OPA when the gag reflex is INTACT; seizures/trismus preventing mouth opening; to reduce trauma from repeated nasotracheal suctioning; to guide a bronchoscope.
Cautions: lubricate with water-soluble jelly and pass without force; avoid with nasal trauma, polyps, adenoid hypertrophy; NEVER cut an NPA — the cut edge is sharp. Complications: epistaxis, mucosal trauma, gagging, sinusitis with prolonged use.
If it won't pass: try the other naris, then a smaller size.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: LMA — how is it sized, and to what pressure is it inflated?
cards.a:
LMA — how is it sized, and to what pressure is it inflated?
Sized by WEIGHT: 1 (< 5 kg) → 6 (> 100 kg); size 4 for 50–70 kg (max 30 mL), size 5 for 70–100 kg (max 40 mL).
⚠ Inflate to 60 cm H₂O — NEVER exceed 60 (malposition, tissue damage).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: ⚠ LMA — why is it not a definitive airway, and its cautions?
cards.a:
⚠ LMA — why is it not a definitive airway, and its cautions?
NO aspiration protection; not for long-term PPV.
Contraindicated if aspiration risk is high, and in conscious patients with an intact gag reflex or with trauma/obstructive lesions of the mouth or pharynx.
Keep PPV pressures below 20–30 cm H₂O. Use a BITE BLOCK, not an OPA (an OPA malpositions it).
If a leak occurs, REPOSITION — do not just add air.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Regurgitation occurs with an LMA in place — what do you do?
cards.a:
Regurgitation occurs with an LMA in place — what do you do?
LEAVE THE LMA IN, head-down, disconnect, suction THROUGH it, prepare to intubate.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Why does Heuer discourage NASAL intubation?
cards.a:
Why does Heuer discourage NASAL intubation?
Higher VAP, sinusitis and otitis media · the need for a smaller/longer tube (more airway resistance) · and necrosis of the septum and naris.
The ORAL route is preferred.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: A suction catheter will not pass down the ETT — what does that mean?
cards.a:
A suction catheter will not pass down the ETT — what does that mean?
The tube is KINKED or DISPLACED.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Subglottic (Hi-Lo Evac) ETT — what pressure does the CASS port run at?
cards.a:
Subglottic (Hi-Lo Evac) ETT — what pressure does the CASS port run at?
−20 to −25 mm Hg (Ch 10) / −20 to −30 cm H₂O (Ch 6) / about −25 cm H₂O (Ch 9).
It must be flushed with AIR to stay patent.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Tracheostomy tube — the OD sizing rule and why it matters both ways?
cards.a:
Tracheostomy tube — the OD sizing rule and why it matters both ways?
OD should be no more than two-thirds to three-fourths of the tracheal ID.
Too BIG blocks airflow around a deflated cuff; too SMALL forces unacceptably high cuff pressures to seal.
ISO size 5 and smaller usually cannot hold an inner cannula.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: What is the trach obturator for, and what do you do with it?
cards.a:
What is the trach obturator for, and what do you do with it?
It prevents 'snowplowing' during insertion. Remove it IMMEDIATELY after insertion — and keep it at the bedside.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Advantages of a trach tube over an ETT?
cards.a:
Advantages of a trach tube over an ETT?
Lower resistance · less tube movement · more comfort · easier suctioning · easier reinsertion into a mature stoma.
⚠ Never pull or rock the 15-mm connector. Confirm position by x-ray or fiberoptic scope. Elective tracheotomy is deferred until coagulopathy is corrected.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Tracheostomy BUTTON — what is it for and what does it NOT provide?
cards.a:
Tracheostomy BUTTON — what is it for and what does it NOT provide?
A short cannula flanged at both ends, depth set by spacers, with a plug that forces breathing through the upper airway.
Uses: maintain a patent stoma after the trach tube is removed · facilitate weaning off the trach tube · keep long-term access for lower-airway suctioning.
⚠ Provides NO ventilatory support and NO cuff.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Respiratory distress with an UNCAPPED trach button — what's wrong?
cards.a:
Respiratory distress with an UNCAPPED trach button — what's wrong?
The button is protruding TOO FAR into the trachea. → Reposition by changing the number of spacers; confirm placement with fiberoptic bronchoscopy.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Percutaneous transtracheal jet ventilation — what is it and when?
cards.a:
Percutaneous transtracheal jet ventilation — what is it and when?
A 13- to 14-gauge angiocath through the cricothyroid membrane/trachea, hooked to a 50-psi jet setup for manually triggered 100% O₂.
The 'can't ventilate, can't intubate' rescue. Heuer names it the surgical airway of choice in children UNDER 12 years, whose small tracheal diameter makes cricothyrotomy hazardous.
⚠ A temporizing OXYGENATION route, not a definitive airway — no cuff, no aspiration protection, barotrauma risk.
A percutaneous cricothyrotomy kit (Nu-Trake, QuickTrach, Pertrach) generally requires a patient at least 5 years old.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: The chronic 'transtracheal oxygen catheter' / SCOOP catheter — where is it covered?
cards.a:
The chronic 'transtracheal oxygen catheter' / SCOOP catheter — where is it covered?
NOT covered in Heuer or the available decks — neither source uses that term.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Why does tube SIZE drive cuff PRESSURE?
cards.a:
Why does tube SIZE drive cuff PRESSURE?
Modern cuffs are high-volume, low-pressure so a large floppy cuff seals at low wall pressure.
The causes of HIGH cuff pressure are a tube that is TOO SMALL and incorrect positioning of the ETT.
A tube that is too small requires unacceptably high cuff pressures to achieve a seal.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: ⚠ You can't get a leak-free seal at an acceptable pressure. What's the answer?
cards.a:
⚠ You can't get a leak-free seal at an acceptable pressure. What's the answer?
Keep pressure below 25–30 cm H₂O and recommend EXCHANGING THE TUBE for a larger one (or one with subglottic suction) — NOT adding more air.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Why use the largest appropriate ETT — the physics?
cards.a:
Why use the largest appropriate ETT — the physics?
Poiseuille's law: HALVING the radius requires a 16-FOLD increase in driving pressure / work of breathing.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Cuff pressure — the safe range in both units?
cards.a:
Cuff pressure — the safe range in both units?
20 to 30 cm H₂O is the maintenance range (Heuer Ch 3, Ch 9 and the deck all agree), with 30 cm H₂O the maximum acceptable intracuff pressure and below 20 inviting microaspiration → VAP.
Using 1 mm Hg = 1.36 cm H₂O: 20 cm H₂O ≈ 14.7 mm Hg · 30 cm H₂O ≈ 22 mm Hg.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: ⚠ The internal Heuer wrinkle on cuff pressure?
cards.a:
⚠ The internal Heuer wrinkle on cuff pressure?
Ch 3 says pressures over 25–30 cm H₂O obstruct tissue blood flow, and that most hospitals (including the NBRC 'hospital') set 25 cm H₂O as the high-pressure limit.
Ch 9 (intubation checklist) and the VAP list both say 20–30 cm H₂O.
Take 20–30 as the range and 25 as the conservative NBRC alarm limit.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Tracheal capillary perfusion pressure — and why it sets the range?
cards.a:
Tracheal capillary perfusion pressure — and why it sets the range?
Normally 25 to 35 mm Hg.
Keep the cuff under 25 mm Hg so you stay BELOW capillary perfusion pressure and avoid mucosal ischemia, ulceration and tracheal wall necrosis.
Go LOWER than 25 mm Hg in a HYPOTENSIVE patient, whose perfusion pressure is already reduced.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Rising cuff inflation VOLUME over time suggests what — and should you track it?
cards.a:
Rising cuff inflation VOLUME over time suggests what — and should you track it?
Tracheal dilation / tracheomalacia.
But Heuer does NOT recommend routinely tracking volume, because emptying the cuff to measure it raises aspiration risk.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Minimal Occluding Volume (MOV) — technique and why end-inspiration?
cards.a:
Minimal Occluding Volume (MOV) — technique and why end-inspiration?
Place the stethoscope diaphragm on the trachea and inflate slowly until NO leak is heard at END-INSPIRATION.
End-inspiration is when the trachea is at its WIDEST — so a seal there seals throughout.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: ⚠ Minimal Leak Technique (MLT) — and the conflict about using it
cards.a:
⚠ Minimal Leak Technique (MLT) — and the conflict about using it
Technique: inflate until the leak stops, then slowly withdraw a small amount of air until a SLIGHT leak is heard at end-inspiration.
⚠ The deck presents MOV and MLT as equal options — but Heuer explicitly says to AVOID the minimal leak technique in ventilated patients as part of VAP prevention. Maintain 20–30 cm H₂O instead.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: How do you measure cuff pressure — and why must you always ADJUST it?
cards.a:
How do you measure cuff pressure — and why must you always ADJUST it?
You need a calibrated manometer, a three-way stopcock, and a 10- or 20-mL syringe (or a commercial cuff-pressure bulb). Open all three ports, connect to the pilot valve, add or remove air while watching the manometer.
⚠ Because attaching the manometer itself STEALS VOLUME and lowers the reading, you must always ADJUST the pressure — never just measure it.
Check at least once per shift, and any time the tube is changed or moved, air is added or removed, or a leak appears.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: The two special cuffs?
cards.a:
The two special cuffs?
Lanz valve/reservoir — automatically holds about 30 cm H₂O.
Bivona Fome-Cuf (Kamen-Wilkinson) foam cuff — seals at ATMOSPHERIC pressure; deflate and clamp the pilot line before insertion, then open it to atmosphere once positioned.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Adult ETT sizes — Heuer vs the deck
cards.a:
Adult ETT sizes — Heuer vs the deck
Adult FEMALE — Heuer 7.0–8.0 mm; deck 7–7.5 mm. Insertion 19–21 cm.
Adult MALE — Heuer 8.0–9.0 mm; deck 8–8.5 mm. Insertion 21–23 cm.
Large adult — 8.5 mm and up, insertion 23 cm and up.
Heuer's ranges run a half-size wider at the top in both cases — report both if asked.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: The pediatric ETT formulas
cards.a:
The pediatric ETT formulas
Uncuffed ETT ID (mm) = (age in years ÷ 4) + 4
Cuffed ETT ID (mm) = (age in years ÷ 4) + 3 — cuffed must be slightly smaller.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Worked: ETT size for a 4-year-old and an 8-year-old
cards.a:
Worked: ETT size for a 4-year-old and an 8-year-old
4-year-old: Uncuffed = (4÷4) + 4 = 5.0 mm · Cuffed = (4÷4) + 3 = 4.0 mm
8-year-old: Uncuffed = (8÷4) + 4 = 6.0 mm — exact match to Table 9-8; insertion length 15–17 cm.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Pediatric ETT sizes by age (Heuer Table 9-8)
cards.a:
Pediatric ETT sizes by age (Heuer Table 9-8)
Premature / < 3 kg: 2.5–3.0 uncuffed (9–11 cm) · Newborn–1 yr: 3.0–4.0 (11–12) · 1–3 yr: 4.0 (11–13) · 3 yr: 4.5 (12–14) · 5 yr: 5.0 (13–15) · 6 yr: 5.5 (14–16) · 8 yr: 6.0 (15–17) · 12 yr: 6.5 (17–19) · 16 yr: 7.0 (18–20).
The decks do not give these.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Cuffed or uncuffed in children?
cards.a:
Cuffed or uncuffed in children?
Uncuffed for premature infants and anyone under 3 kg.
Otherwise both are acceptable — and if cuffed, cuff pressure must be held to the manufacturer's spec, usually no more than 20–30 cm H₂O, exactly as in adults.
Hess adds: in a CHILD, keep cuff pressure below 20 cm H₂O (lower than the adult range).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: ⚠ The pediatric airway anatomy point the decks stress?
cards.a:
⚠ The pediatric airway anatomy point the decks stress?
In ADULTS the GLOTTIS is the narrowest point; in CHILDREN it is the CRICOID RING.
1 mm of circumferential edema in an infant cuts airway diameter by MORE THAN 50%.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Hess's weight-based infant ETT depth rule?
cards.a:
Hess's weight-based infant ETT depth rule?
'To estimate the approximate distance to insert the ETT, measured from the LIPS, add 6 cm to the infant's weight in kilograms.'
So a 3 kg neonate ≈ 9 cm at the lip.
Hess also uses length-based tapes for children ≤ 35 kg.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Is there a pediatric DEPTH equation (e.g. 3 × ETT ID) in Heuer?
cards.a:
Is there a pediatric DEPTH equation (e.g. 3 × ETT ID) in Heuer?
No — a pediatric depth equation is NOT covered in Heuer or the available decks. Heuer gives an age-based insertion-length TABLE, not a formula. Use the table's cm ranges.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: When does a chest tube go in, and how is it directed?
cards.a:
When does a chest tube go in, and how is it directed?
When air or fluid in the pleural space stops the lung expanding — pneumothorax, hemothorax, pleural effusion, empyema (pus), or chylothorax — to restore negative intrapleural pressure.
AIR RISES, FLUID FALLS: direct the tube SUPERIORLY toward the apex for AIR and INFERIORLY/posteriorly to a gravity-dependent spot for FLUID.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Chest tube insertion sites — and why over the top of the rib?
cards.a:
Chest tube insertion sites — and why over the top of the rib?
Deck's 'safe triangle': 4th–5th ICS, MIDAXILLARY line for most tubes today (4th–6th ICS midaxillary for blood/fluid; historically 2nd–3rd ICS midclavicular for air).
Heuer: 4th or 5th ICS at the ANTERIOR AXILLARY line — a real wording difference; give both if pressed.
⚠ Always enter OVER THE TOP of the rib, because the intercostal vein, artery and nerve run in the groove UNDER each rib.
Emergency needle decompression: 2nd ICS MIDCLAVICULAR.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Chest tube sizes?
cards.a:
Chest tube sizes?
Heuer's kit: 24–36 Fr.
Deck: 36–40 Fr large adults · 28–32 Fr small adults/teens · 18 Fr children · 12–14 Fr neonates.
16–20 Fr is adequate for AIR; 28–40 Fr (usually 36) for BLOOD or thick fluid.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Chamber 1 — what is it and why does separating it matter?
cards.a:
Chamber 1 — what is it and why does separating it matter?
COLLECTION. Receives blood, pus, chyle or serous fluid by gravity; this is where you read amount, color and consistency.
Because it is separate from the seal, accumulating fluid no longer deepens the water seal or increases the patient's work of breathing — the fatal flaw of the old one-chamber bottle.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Chamber 2 — what is it and to what depth?
cards.a:
Chamber 2 — what is it and to what depth?
WATER SEAL. The long tube is submerged 2 cm below sterile water, making a ONE-WAY VALVE: air escapes the pleural space but atmosphere cannot get back in. A short vent tube prevents pressure buildup.
If the level falls below 2 cm, refill it.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: ⚠ Chamber 3 — what actually determines the suction reaching the patient?
cards.a:
⚠ Chamber 3 — what actually determines the suction reaching the patient?
SUCTION CONTROL. The DEPTH OF WATER in this chamber — NOT the wall vacuum setting — determines the suction delivered to the pleural space.
Fill it to 20 cm of water and the patient gets −20 cm H₂O, whether the wall regulator reads 80 or 150 mm Hg.
Recommended: −10 to −20 cm H₂O (deck); Heuer Ch 6 'usually to obtain −20'; Heuer Ch 16 15–20 cm H₂O after insertion.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: What is tidaling, and what does its absence mean?
cards.a:
What is tidaling, and what does its absence mean?
The water-seal level RISES on spontaneous inspiration and FALLS on expiration (reversed on positive pressure).
Tidaling proves the system is still communicating with the pleural space.
Failure to fluctuate = OBSTRUCTION.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: ⚠ Bubbling — the high-yield distinction between chambers
cards.a:
⚠ Bubbling — the high-yield distinction between chambers
Chamber 3 (suction control): GENTLE CONTINUOUS BUBBLING IS NORMAL and expected. Vigorous bubbling means the wall vacuum is too high — more noise and evaporation, not more suction.
Chamber 2 (water seal): CONTINUOUS BUBBLING MEANS AN AIR LEAK until proven otherwise. (Some leak is expected with a bronchopleural fistula on positive pressure.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: How do you localize a chest-tube air leak?
cards.a:
How do you localize a chest-tube air leak?
Briefly PINCH the chest tube at the insertion site.
If the bubbling STOPS → the leak is at the insertion site or in the PATIENT. → Notify the physician immediately; temporize with a sterile petroleum-jelly gauze pad.
If it CONTINUES → the leak is between the patient and the collection SYSTEM. → Tighten all connections, tape any tear, prepare a new drainage unit.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: No bubbling in the SUCTION CONTROL chamber — what do you check?
cards.a:
No bubbling in the SUCTION CONTROL chamber — what do you check?
That the regulator is ON and set · the suction tubing for leaks/kinks · that the atmospheric vent is open and unobstructed.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: No tidaling in the water seal — the steps?
cards.a:
No tidaling in the water seal — the steps?
Check the collection tubing for kinks and dependent loops, then 'MILK' the tubing toward the collection chamber (do this routinely to prevent clotting).
If milking fails: assess the patient for pneumothorax and notify the physician immediately.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Bubbling stops abruptly — good or bad?
cards.a:
Bubbling stops abruptly — good or bad?
Either: the pneumothorax resolved (good), or the tube is obstructed, kinked or clotted (bad).
Decide with breath sounds, SpO₂, work of breathing and CXR.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: The drainage eyelets become visible — what do you do?
cards.a:
The drainage eyelets become visible — what do you do?
The tube has partially pulled out. → Notify the physician. NEVER push it back in.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: ⚠ Transporting a patient with a chest tube — the two rules?
cards.a:
⚠ Transporting a patient with a chest tube — the two rules?
Keep the unit BELOW CHEST LEVEL.
NEVER CLAMP the chest tube — clamping can convert an air leak into a TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX.
Heuer: 'the one-way seal must be maintained.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Chest tube removal criteria, and what do you watch for after?
cards.a:
Chest tube removal criteria, and what do you watch for after?
Drainage < 100 mL in 24 hours · pneumothorax resolved on CXR · no air leak on a Valsalva or forceful cough — with a follow-up CXR in 4 hours.
After removal: watch 1–2 days for recurrence. CREPITUS at the insertion site always suggests air leaking back into the pleural space.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: HEMOTHORAX on CXR — appearance, tracheal shift, treatment?
cards.a:
HEMOTHORAX on CXR — appearance, tracheal shift, treatment?
Behaves as FLUID: increased radiopacity (white) on the affected side, blunted costophrenic angle, layering fluid level; decreased breath sounds, dullness to percussion, signs of SHOCK.
Confirmed when pleural fluid hematocrit ≥ 50% of blood hematocrit.
Shift AWAY from the affected side.
Treatment: a LARGE-BORE tube (36 Fr typical, 28–40 range) directed INFERIORLY — because blood clots off a small tube.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: PNEUMOTHORAX on CXR — appearance and the supine sign?
cards.a:
PNEUMOTHORAX on CXR — appearance and the supine sign?
Loss of peripheral lung markings · a RADIOLUCENT (black) space between the lung margin and chest wall · possible depression of the hemidiaphragm · DEEP SULCUS SIGN (deepened costophrenic angle) on SUPINE films.
Exam: hyperresonance, decreased fremitus, absent breath sounds, unilateral expansion; tension adds cyanosis, tachycardia, hypotension, pulsus paradoxus.
Shift AWAY — a shift implies a large or tension pneumothorax.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: PLEURISY — what does it look like on CXR?
cards.a:
PLEURISY — what does it look like on CXR?
No distinct CXR appearance of its own in either source.
Recognized clinically by a PLEURAL FRICTION RUB ('the sound of inflamed pleural surfaces rubbing together') plus pleuritic chest pain worse on deep breath or cough.
It shows on film only when an effusion accompanies it. No shift from the inflammation itself.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: INFILTRATES on CXR — appearance, and which one shifts the trachea?
cards.a:
INFILTRATES on CXR — appearance, and which one shifts the trachea?
Increased radiopacity with AIR BRONCHOGRAMS — airway silhouettes surrounded by collapsed/consolidated tissue; patchy or platelike densities. ARDS = bilateral diffuse infiltrates. VAP = a new or progressive infiltrate. Atelectasis adds an ELEVATED hemidiaphragm and crowded vessels/markings.
⚠ Atelectasis/collapse → trachea shifts TOWARD the affected side. Consolidation and ARDS infiltrates alone produce NO shift.
Heuer's rule of thumb: TOWARD areas of collapse, AWAY from space-occupying processes.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: PLEURAL EFFUSION on CXR — the signs and the film to order?
cards.a:
PLEURAL EFFUSION on CXR — the signs and the film to order?
Homogeneous, POSITION-DEPENDENT areas of increased density — confirm with a LATERAL DECUBITUS film.
Loss of sharp costophrenic angles is the EARLIEST sign; a MENISCUS at the fluid–air interface; possible depressed diaphragm and compression atelectasis; massive effusion nearly opacifies the hemithorax.
⚠ Small effusions (< ~300 mL) may be INVISIBLE on an upright film. Recommend lateral views with the AP/PA specifically to assess for effusion.
Shift AWAY.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: ARDS prone positioning — the criteria?
cards.a:
ARDS prone positioning — the criteria?
P/F < 150 on FiO₂ > 0.60 with PEEP ≥ 5, at least 16 hours a day.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: The four questions to ask about any pleural effusion?
cards.a:
The four questions to ask about any pleural effusion?
(1) Should thoracentesis be done? (2) Can the underlying cause be treated? (3) Are antibiotics indicated? (4) Is a chest tube required?
Always treat the CAUSE, not just the fluid. A CHF or cirrhosis effusion often melts away once the systemic problem is managed.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Diagnostic vs therapeutic thoracentesis?
cards.a:
Diagnostic vs therapeutic thoracentesis?
Diagnostic: determines the cause — transudate vs exudate — and obtains cells to assess for malignancy.
Therapeutic: recommended for any effusion large enough to cause respiratory distress or interfere with lung expansion.
There are NO absolute contraindications; relative ones are an uncooperative patient, severe uncorrected bleeding disorder, severe bullous lung disease, insufficient pleural fluid, and skin infection at the site.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Thoracentesis positioning?
cards.a:
Thoracentesis positioning?
If mobile: sitting up and leaning forward on a bedside table.
If not: affected side DOWN at the edge of the bed, slightly rotated, that arm behind the head, mid/posterior axillary line exposed, head of bed up 30°.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: The RT's job during a thoracentesis?
cards.a:
The RT's job during a thoracentesis?
Recommend a COUGH SUPPRESSANT beforehand (coughing during the procedure can cause lung or pleural trauma) · keep the patient still and not coughing · monitor vital signs and SpO₂ · give O₂ to keep SpO₂ ≥ 90% · watch for dyspnea, pallor, coughing · label and route specimens · ensure a post-procedure x-ray or ultrasound to rule out PNEUMOTHORAX.
Call the physician immediately for dyspnea, hypotension, chest pain or hemoptysis.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: ⚠ Empyema — why won't antibiotics alone do?
cards.a:
⚠ Empyema — why won't antibiotics alone do?
Empyema MUST be drained — antibiotics alone do not penetrate thick pus. It may require thoracotomy.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Pleurodesis — mechanism, agents, and the cost?
cards.a:
Pleurodesis — mechanism, agents, and the cost?
A sclerosant (talc, tetracycline, or bleomycin) is instilled into the pleural space to trigger inflammation (pleuritis) that FUSES the visceral and parietal pleura, obliterating the space so fluid or air can no longer accumulate.
The cost is painful pleurisy from that deliberate inflammation.
Used for recurrent malignant effusion and recurrent pneumothorax.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: ⚠ TRANSUDATE vs EXUDATE — the pivot
cards.a:
⚠ TRANSUDATE vs EXUDATE — the pivot
TRANSUDATE: from SYSTEMIC pressure changes — increased hydrostatic or decreased oncotic pressure (CHF, cirrhosis/hepatic hydrothorax, nephrotic syndrome). Thin, watery, low-protein, few cells, normal non-inflamed pleura. → Fix the systemic problem.
EXUDATE: from LOCAL pleural disease — increased capillary permeability from infection (pneumonia, TB), malignancy, or autoimmune disease. High-protein with many cells and debris. → Needs antibiotics, drainage, or a cancer workup.
HIGH PROTEIN = LOCAL PLEURAL DISEASE.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: What LDH level suggests pleural infection — and does Heuer give Light's criteria?
cards.a:
What LDH level suggests pleural infection — and does Heuer give Light's criteria?
LDH more than THREE TIMES the upper limit of normal (often > 1,000 U/L).
⚠ Heuer names the transudate/exudate distinction as the reason to recommend a diagnostic thoracentesis but does NOT reproduce Light's criteria — the protein/LDH detail comes from the pleural-disease deck.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Indwelling tunneled pleural catheter — where is it covered?
cards.a:
Indwelling tunneled pleural catheter — where is it covered?
NOT covered in Heuer or the available decks. The decks offer the pigtail catheter and pleurodesis as the recurrent-effusion options. Look it up separately if your instructor lists it.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Diagnostic vs therapeutic bronchoscopy — the one-liner?
cards.a:
Diagnostic vs therapeutic bronchoscopy — the one-liner?
Diagnostic asks 'what's wrong?' (LOOK); therapeutic asks 'how do we fix it?' (TREAT).
Flexible fiberoptic bronchoscopy is the classic answer when a question wants a procedure that is BOTH.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Diagnostic bronchoscopy indications?
cards.a:
Diagnostic bronchoscopy indications?
Assess a lesion of unknown etiology on CXR · evaluate recurrent atelectasis or pulmonary infiltrates · assess upper airway patency · find the source of HEMOPTYSIS · evaluate unexplained cough, localized/unilateral wheeze, or stridor · follow up suspicious sputum cytology · obtain secretions, washings or biopsies · determine the location and extent of toxic inhalation or aspiration injury · evaluate artificial airway problems.
Add: smoke inhalation or TE fistula · staging of lung cancer · vocal cord paralysis.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Therapeutic bronchoscopy indications?
cards.a:
Therapeutic bronchoscopy indications?
Removal of retained secretions, mucus plugs, obstructing tissue, or FOREIGN BODIES · facilitating intubation of a difficult airway · drainage of an abscess · bronchial toilet · topical thrombin or epinephrine for hemoptysis · stent placement, balloon dilatation of tracheobronchial stenosis, laser/electrosurgical treatment.
BAL itself can be therapeutic — for pulmonary toilet in PULMONARY ALVEOLAR PROTEINOSIS, washing out accumulated surfactant.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Flexible scope — working channel size and routes of entry?
cards.a:
Flexible scope — working channel size and routes of entry?
A steerable insertion tube with a 2- to 2.6-mm working channel for injecting medications, lavage, suctioning and passing instruments.
Routes: the nose, the mouth with a BITE BLOCK, an ETT, or a trach tube.
In a ventilated patient it goes through a special BODAI ADAPTER with a bronchoscopy port, so ventilation, FiO₂ and PEEP are not lost.
Deck: it bends about 180° up and 130° down.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: When do you recommend a RIGID bronchoscope?
cards.a:
When do you recommend a RIGID bronchoscope?
Removing LARGE foreign objects — Heuer specifically says to recommend rigid bronchoscopy under general anesthesia for a foreign body causing MEDIASTINAL SHIFT.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Bronchoscopy ABSOLUTE contraindications?
cards.a:
Bronchoscopy ABSOLUTE contraindications?
No consent (except emergencies) · no experienced clinician available · no resources to manage complications · inability to oxygenate adequately during the procedure · coagulopathy or uncontrolled bleeding · severe obstructive airway disease · severe refractory hypoxemia · hemodynamic instability/dysrhythmias.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Bronchial WASHING vs BAL — what's the difference?
cards.a:
Bronchial WASHING vs BAL — what's the difference?
Washing: pulmonary secretions suctioned into a sterile trap; a small saline flush if secretions are too thick. → microscopic exam, C&S, cytology.
BAL: sterile saline INSTILLED into a lung segment then suctioned back; the return carries cells, bacteria, fungi, viruses. → cytology, chemistry, microbiology.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: BAL — the ATS indications and the one major contraindication?
cards.a:
BAL — the ATS indications and the one major contraindication?
Nonresolving pneumonia · unexplained interstitial or alveolar infiltrates · suspected alveolar hemorrhage · interstitial lung disease. A key tool for diagnosing bacterial VAP and confirming some lung cancers.
The ONLY major contraindication is a predisposition to bleeding.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Bronchial BRUSHING — what does the sheath do?
cards.a:
Bronchial BRUSHING — what does the sheath do?
Loosened surface cells scraped from the mucosa by a shielded/protective-sheathed brush — the sheath prevents contamination on the way IN and OUT. May be done under fluoroscopy if the lesion is not visible.
→ Cytology or microbiology — individual CELLS, not tissue architecture.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: ⚠ Which biopsy technique samples from OUTSIDE the tracheobronchial tree?
cards.a:
⚠ Which biopsy technique samples from OUTSIDE the tracheobronchial tree?
Transbronchial NEEDLE ASPIRATION (TBNA). Heuer: the needle is 'the only technique that allows sampling from outside the tracheobronchial tree, such as from LYMPH NODES.'
Forceps must be inserted with the scope tip in NEUTRAL position to avoid damaging the working channel. Tissue goes in FORMALIN.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: The bronchoscopy memory trick?
cards.a:
The bronchoscopy memory trick?
Forceps = TISSUE. Needle = cells from OUTSIDE the airway. Brush = SURFACE cells.
Biopsy = a Piece (histology); Cytology = Cells.
By location: surface abnormality → brush; visible airway lesion → forceps biopsy; lymph node or mass outside the airway → needle aspiration; lung parenchyma → TBLB.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Foreign-body instruments — which for which object?
cards.a:
Foreign-body instruments — which for which object?
Grasping forceps for irregular SOFT objects.
Basket/snare loop for smooth ROUNDED objects.
Balloon catheter — passed beyond the object, inflated, and slowly withdrawn to bring it up the bronchial tree.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Bronchoscopy anesthesia — the doses?
cards.a:
Bronchoscopy anesthesia — the doses?
Moderate sedation 15–30 minutes before.
Deck: 5 to 10 mL of a 1% to 4% lidocaine solution by aerosol or down the working channel.
Heuer: Xylocaine 2% JELLY on the scope tip and 2% lidocaine LIQUID injected through the channel to anesthetize the cords and lower airway; upper airway prepped as for intubation (2% tetracaine spray or nebulized 4% lidocaine).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: The deck's classic bronchoscopy premedication trio — and the goal?
cards.a:
The deck's classic bronchoscopy premedication trio — and the goal?
Atropine sulfate IM (reduces vagal response, oral secretions, bronchospasm) · morphine sulfate IM (suppresses cough, relieves pain) · a sedative — diazepam (Valium) IV bolus, with modern practice substituting midazolam, propofol or fentanyl.
⚠ The goal is NOT general anesthesia — it is a comfortable, cooperative, SPONTANEOUSLY BREATHING patient.
Keep 1:1000 epinephrine at hand for bleeding.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Which patients are prone to bronchospasm and laryngospasm during bronchoscopy?
cards.a:
Which patients are prone to bronchospasm and laryngospasm during bronchoscopy?
Asthma / hyperreactive airway patients. Watch vital signs, SpO₂ and ECG continuously before, during and after.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Oxygenation during bronchoscopy — the rules?
cards.a:
Oxygenation during bronchoscopy — the rules?
PaO₂ predictably FALLS during bronchoscopy, so ALWAYS give supplemental O₂: nasal cannula for the ORAL route, a modified mask for the NASAL route (deck allows up to 6 L/min in spontaneously breathing patients).
If intubated: raise FiO₂ by 10% or more.
If SpO₂ drops below 90%: immediately raise the FiO₂, or HALT the procedure and give O₂ through the scope's open channel.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: What happens to a VENTILATED patient's mechanics during bronchoscopy?
cards.a:
What happens to a VENTILATED patient's mechanics during bronchoscopy?
Expect INCREASED peak airway pressure and DECREASED delivered VT — the scope is a straw inside a straw.
FiO₂, VT and the high-pressure alarm may all need adjusting.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Bronchoscopy NPO rules and the most common complication?
cards.a:
Bronchoscopy NPO rules and the most common complication?
NPO at least 8 hours BEFORE · NPO at least 2 hours AFTER or until the GAG REFLEX RETURNS · outpatients must not drive until the next day.
HYPOXEMIA is the most common complication; others are bleeding, infection/cross-contamination, and pneumothorax from sharp biopsy instruments.
Expect transient fever and mild hemoptysis for 24 hours, most common after biopsy.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Laser bronchoscopy safety?
cards.a:
Laser bronchoscopy safety?
Keep FiO₂ below 0.40 and NEVER use alcohol to clean the laser tip.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: The governing rule for suction catheter size?
cards.a:
The governing rule for suction catheter size?
Select a catheter that occludes LESS THAN 50% of the ETT internal diameter — less than 70% in infants.
That leaves room for gas to flow around the catheter so you do not evacuate the lung and cause ATELECTASIS.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: ⚠ The two suction-catheter formulas — and which is the default?
cards.a:
⚠ The two suction-catheter formulas — and which is the default?
Heuer Ch 10 (matches Table 10-3): Fr = ETT ID in mm × 2, then step DOWN to the next smallest available French size.
Heuer Appendix B: Fr = 1.5 × ETT ID.
They disagree at 8 mm: App B says 12 Fr; Ch 10's Table 10-3 and Top Tips both say 14 Fr.
The ×2-then-next-smallest rule reproduces Table 10-3 exactly at every size — use it as your default.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Worked: catheter for a 6.0-mm ID tube
cards.a:
Worked: catheter for a 6.0-mm ID tube
6.0 × 2 = 12 → next SMALLEST available French size below 12 → 10 Fr
(Table 10-3 confirms 6.0 → 10 Fr.)
Cross-check with App B: 1.5 × 6.0 = 9 → rounds to 10 Fr — AGREES.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Suction catheter sizes from Table 10-3

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Suction pressure — Heuer Ch 10's recommended ranges and NEVER-EXCEED ceilings?
cards.a:
Suction pressure — Heuer Ch 10's recommended ranges and NEVER-EXCEED ceilings?
Adults: −100 to −120 mm Hg; never exceed −120.
Children: −80 to −100; never exceed −100.
Infants: −60 to −80; never exceed −80.
These ceilings are the safer numbers to quote on an exam.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: ⚠ Why is Heuer Ch 6's wall-regulator range wider?
cards.a:
⚠ Why is Heuer Ch 6's wall-regulator range wider?
Ch 6 Table 6-29: adults −100 to −150 · children −100 to −120 · infants −80 to −100 mm Hg.
Because wall regulators deliver HIGHER FLOW at a given pressure — and it is FLOW that determines performance. That is also why the portable (in. Hg) and wall (mm Hg) numbers are NOT equivalent (portable: adults −12 to −15 in. Hg, children −7 to −12, infants −5 to −7).
The overriding principle: use the LOWEST vacuum that actually removes the secretions.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Three suction numbers not to confuse?
cards.a:
Three suction numbers not to confuse?
Tracheal suctioning: −100 to −120 mm Hg (adults).
CASS through a Hi-Lo ETT: −20 to −25 mm Hg (Ch 10) / −20 to −30 cm H₂O (Ch 6) / ~−25 cm H₂O (Ch 9).
Chest tube drainage: −10 to −20 cm H₂O — an entirely different topic.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: ⚠ Suction duration — the conflict
cards.a:
⚠ Suction duration — the conflict
Heuer: less than 15 seconds — 'applying suction for more than 15 seconds for each attempt should be avoided.'
Chang deck: no more than 10 seconds.
Report both.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: When do you suction — and what are the two indicators?
cards.a:
When do you suction — and what are the two indicators?
Only when INDICATED, never routinely.
Deck's indicators: secretions AUDIBLE on auscultation, or a SAWTOOTH pattern on the expiratory flow waveform.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Pre- and post-oxygenation for suctioning?
cards.a:
Pre- and post-oxygenation for suctioning?
100% O₂ for at least 30–60 seconds before and after.
For NEONATES: 10% above baseline FiO₂.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Why an in-line/closed-suction system on any ventilated patient?
cards.a:
Why an in-line/closed-suction system on any ventilated patient?
It preserves FiO₂ and PEEP and avoids DERECRUITMENT.
Chang deck adds that closed catheters may be changed weekly rather than daily with no significant increase in VAP.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: How far do you insert the suction catheter?
cards.a:
How far do you insert the suction catheter?
SHALLOW suctioning — just beyond the tube tip, about 2 cm in adults.
Do NOT routinely lavage with saline (both sources call it controversial; use it judiciously).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Suctioning hazards?
cards.a:
Suctioning hazards?
Oxygen desaturation/hypoxemia · tissue trauma and bleeding · bronchospasm · cardiac dysrhythmias · hypertension or hypotension · cardiac or respiratory arrest · increased ICP · infection.
Deck adds: pneumothorax from bronchial perforation by a suction catheter has been reported in INFANTS.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Regulator is on at −120 mm Hg with tight connections but NO suction is delivered — what do you check?
cards.a:
Regulator is on at −120 mm Hg with tight connections but NO suction is delivered — what do you check?
That the canister FLOAT VALVE is not blocking the vacuum — or that the canister is not full.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
