cards.q: Nasotracheal suctioning — the ABSOLUTE contraindications?
cards.a:
Nasotracheal suctioning — the ABSOLUTE contraindications?
EPIGLOTTITIS and CROUP.
Others: occluded nasal passages, nasal bleeding, upper respiratory infection, nasal/oral/tracheal injury or surgery, coagulopathy, laryngospasm or bronchospasm.
Use only after other measures fail, in a patient with no artificial airway and an ineffective cough.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::06 Airways, Intubation, Chest Tubes & Bronchoscopy
cards.q: Nasotracheal suctioning technique — and how do you know you're in the trachea?
cards.a:
Nasotracheal suctioning technique — and how do you know you're in the trachea?
Modified sniffing position sitting upright, neck slightly hyperextended, tongue displaced forward, and advance the catheter DURING INSPIRATION so the cords are abducted.
VIGOROUS COUGHING confirms tracheal entry.
⚠ Lubricate with sterile water-soluble jelly — BUT if you are passing through an NPA, lubricate with sterile WATER, not jelly.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ When is a NORMAL breath sound abnormal?
cards.a:
⚠ When is a NORMAL breath sound abnormal?
When it's in the wrong PLACE.
Heuer's example: BRONCHIAL breath sounds heard out over the lung PERIPHERY are abnormal — they replace vesicular sounds when lung tissue gets DENSER, as in atelectasis and pneumonia/consolidation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: When are breath sounds DIMINISHED?
cards.a:
When are breath sounds DIMINISHED?
When breathing is shallow or slow · when airways are obstructed or the lung is hyperinflated (asthma, COPD) · when air or fluid sits in the pleural space · with obesity.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Heuer's four families of adventitious sounds — and the deck's additions?
cards.a:
Heuer's four families of adventitious sounds — and the deck's additions?
Heuer Table 2-16: rhonchi · wheezes · crackles (rales) · stridor — then splits crackles into three types by TIMING.
Deck adds: crackles is the preferred modern term over rales, plus pleural friction rub, diminished breath sounds, and whispering pectoriloquy.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: How do you DOCUMENT an abnormal breath sound — the five attributes?
cards.a:
How do you DOCUMENT an abnormal breath sound — the five attributes?
Pitch · intensity · timing (inspiratory/expiratory, early or late) · location · amount.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: VESICULAR breath sounds — quality and where normal?
cards.a:
VESICULAR breath sounds — quality and where normal?
Low-pitched, soft; heard mostly on INHALATION, with only a minimal exhalation component.
Normal over the PERIPHERY of the lungs.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: BRONCHIAL breath sounds — quality and where normal?
cards.a:
BRONCHIAL breath sounds — quality and where normal?
High-pitched, loud, tubular; expiratory phase EQUAL TO OR LONGER than inspiratory.
Normal ONLY over the trachea. Heard in the periphery → atelectasis or consolidation/pneumonia.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: BRONCHOVESICULAR breath sounds — quality and where normal?
cards.a:
BRONCHOVESICULAR breath sounds — quality and where normal?
Moderate pitch and intensity; EQUAL inspiratory and expiratory phases.
Normal around the UPPER STERNUM (anterior) and BETWEEN THE SCAPULAE (posterior) — abnormal elsewhere.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: RHONCHI — quality, cause, and the key clinical point?
cards.a:
RHONCHI — quality, cause, and the key clinical point?
Coarse, discontinuous. Cause: airflow through MUCUS.
Conditions: pneumonia, bronchitis, inadequate cough.
Often CLEARS with coughing or suctioning.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: WHEEZES — quality, cause, and the classic warning?
cards.a:
WHEEZES — quality, cause, and the classic warning?
High-pitched, usually EXPIRATORY. Cause: rapid airflow through PARTIALLY OBSTRUCTED airways.
⚠ 'All that wheezes is not asthma' — think CHF/pulmonary edema in adults, foreign body in toddlers.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ STRIDOR — quality, cause, and conditions?
cards.a:
⚠ STRIDOR — quality, cause, and conditions?
High-pitched, MONOPHONIC, commonly INSPIRATORY, heard over the NECK.
Cause: rapid airflow through an obstructed UPPER airway.
Conditions: croup, epiglottitis, post-extubation edema, foreign body.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: PLEURAL FRICTION RUB — quality, cause, conditions?
cards.a:
PLEURAL FRICTION RUB — quality, cause, conditions?
Creaking or grating, mainly during INHALATION (can occur in both phases).
Cause: inflamed pleural surfaces rubbing together.
Conditions: pleurisy; deck adds pleural effusion with inflammation, pneumonia, pulmonary infarction from PE.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ Heuer's THREE crackle types — by timing
cards.a:
⚠ Heuer's THREE crackle types — by timing
COARSE (inspiratory AND expiratory): excess airway secretions moving with airflow → bronchitis, respiratory infections. Often clears with coughing.
EARLY INSPIRATORY: scanty, transmitted to the mouth, NOT affected by cough; sudden opening of ATELECTATIC BRONCHI → bronchitis, emphysema, asthma.
LATE INSPIRATORY: diffuse, fine; occur first in the DEPENDENT regions; sudden opening of collapsed PERIPHERAL airways → atelectasis, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, fibrosis.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ The deck teaches crackles as fine vs coarse. What does Heuer teach — and the exam shorthand?
cards.a:
⚠ The deck teaches crackles as fine vs coarse. What does Heuer teach — and the exam shorthand?
Heuer uses THREE categories keyed to TIMING, not a fine/coarse pair.
Learn Heuer's timing version:
EARLY inspiratory = OBSTRUCTIVE disease.
LATE inspiratory = RESTRICTIVE / alveolar-filling disease.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: WHISPERING PECTORILOQUY — what and why?
cards.a:
WHISPERING PECTORILOQUY — what and why?
Whispered words heard LOUD AND CLEAR.
Cause: consolidated tissue transmits sound better → pneumonia/consolidation. (Deck only.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ The CXR–physical exam translation
cards.a:
⚠ The CXR–physical exam translation
On film: radiopacity = WHITE = 'more stuff'; radiolucency = BLACK = 'more air.'
Under your hands: more stuff = DULL percussion + INCREASED fremitus; more air = INCREASED resonance + DECREASED fremitus.
The trachea shifts TOWARD volume loss and AWAY from pressure — exactly the mediastinal shift you see on the film.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Heuer's percussion vocabulary?
cards.a:
Heuer's percussion vocabulary?
Normal resonance = moderately low-pitched, easily heard, over normal air-filled lung.
Increased resonance (tympanic/hyperresonant) = hollow/loud/low-pitched → hyperinflation (acute asthma, COPD) or PNEUMOTHORAX.
Dull/flat = short, muted, high-pitched → increased tissue density (pneumonia, atelectasis, tumors).
Decreased resonance → fluid in the pleural space.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Normal diaphragm excursion by percussion — and when is it reduced?
cards.a:
Normal diaphragm excursion by percussion — and when is it reduced?
5–7 cm in adults. Reduced in neuromuscular disease and severe hyperinflation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: PNEUMOTHORAX — the four-part exam (CXR, percussion, fremitus, breath sounds)?
cards.a:
PNEUMOTHORAX — the four-part exam (CXR, percussion, fremitus, breath sounds)?
CXR: increased radiolucency (blacker); trachea/mediastinum shifted AWAY; hemidiaphragm may look flattened.
Percussion: INCREASED resonance (hyperresonant).
Fremitus: DECREASED — lung separated from the chest wall by air.
Breath sounds: ABSENT; inspection shows unilateral expansion.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: CONSOLIDATION / PNEUMONIA — the four-part exam?
cards.a:
CONSOLIDATION / PNEUMONIA — the four-part exam?
CXR: increased radiopacity (whiter); air bronchograms.
Percussion: DULL.
Fremitus: INCREASED — denser tissue transmits better.
Breath sounds: BRONCHIAL sounds in the periphery + LATE INSPIRATORY crackles; deck adds whispered pectoriloquy.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: PLEURAL EFFUSION — the four-part exam?
cards.a:
PLEURAL EFFUSION — the four-part exam?
CXR: increased radiopacity; blunted costophrenic angle; trachea shifted AWAY if large.
Percussion: DULL (Heuer also calls pleural fluid decreased resonance).
Fremitus: ABSENT.
Breath sounds: ABSENT; unilateral expansion + tracheal shift away.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ATELECTASIS — the four-part exam, and which way does the trachea go?
cards.a:
ATELECTASIS — the four-part exam, and which way does the trachea go?
CXR: increased radiopacity; ELEVATED hemidiaphragm on the affected side; mediastinum/trachea shifted TOWARD.
Percussion: DULL.
Fremitus: ABSENT.
Breath sounds: ABSENT (bronchial sounds and crackles as alveoli reopen).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ Atelectasis fremitus — the contradiction inside Heuer, and the safe answer
cards.a:
⚠ Atelectasis fremitus — the contradiction inside Heuer, and the safe answer
Table 2-18 states flatly 'ABSENT vocal fremitus' for atelectasis — go with this on the exam.
But Heuer's separate Vocal Fremitus list says fremitus is INCREASED with pneumonia AND atelectasis, and DECREASED when a lobe or segment is blocked by a mucus plug or foreign body — so both statements exist in the book.
Safe answer: fremitus is DECREASED/ABSENT when anything SEPARATES or BLOCKS the lung (air, fluid, plug), and INCREASED when SOLID TISSUE conducts (pneumonia).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: COPD — the four-part exam?
cards.a:
COPD — the four-part exam?
CXR: hyperinflation, flattened diaphragm.
Percussion: INCREASED resonance.
Fremitus: DECREASED (hyperinflation).
Breath sounds: diffuse DECREASE + EARLY INSPIRATORY crackles; ↑ AP diameter.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: DIFFUSE INTERSTITIAL FIBROSIS — the four-part exam?
cards.a:
DIFFUSE INTERSTITIAL FIBROSIS — the four-part exam?
CXR: increased radiopacity.
Percussion: slight DECREASE in resonance.
Fremitus: often normal; increased.
Breath sounds: LATE INSPIRATORY crackles; rapid, shallow breathing.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Diaphragm clues on film — the four patterns?
cards.a:
Diaphragm clues on film — the four patterns?
Blunted costophrenic angle → lower-lobe pneumonia or pleural effusion.
Flattened diaphragm → hyperinflation (emphysema/asthma), tension pneumothorax, or large effusion.
Elevated diaphragm → PHRENIC NERVE PARALYSIS, hepatomegaly, or atelectasis.
Air under the diaphragm → perforated GI tract.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Heart failure on CXR — the four findings?
cards.a:
Heart failure on CXR — the four findings?
Cardiomegaly (CT ratio > 50% on a PA film) · prominent upper-lobe vascular markings · Kerley B lines · pleural effusions.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: What is crepitus, and what causes it?
cards.a:
What is crepitus, and what causes it?
The crackling, 'Rice-Krispies' sensation you feel palpating skin with air trapped in the SUBCUTANEOUS tissue.
Especially in patients on POSITIVE-PRESSURE VENTILATION, gas leaks into the tissues around the head, neck and chest forming subcutaneous bubbles — that is subcutaneous emphysema.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ Is subcutaneous emphysema dangerous — and what must you do?
cards.a:
⚠ Is subcutaneous emphysema dangerous — and what must you do?
Heuer says subcutaneous emphysema ITSELF is harmless — but it often occurs together with a PNEUMOTHORAX.
So if you detect crepitus you must (1) assess the patient for pneumothorax and (2) IMMEDIATELY communicate the finding to the physician.
Heuer's T4 tip: neck/upper-chest crepitus in a patient on positive pressure suggests a pneumothorax.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Other causes of crepitus — including the chest-tube one?
cards.a:
Other causes of crepitus — including the chest-tube one?
Thoracic injury or surgery, tracheostomy, post-op air leaks (deck).
Heuer: crepitus at a chest-tube insertion site AFTER the tube is removed always suggests RECURRENCE of air leakage into the pleural space.
Air follows the path of least resistance — extensive crepitus signals a clinically significant leak. Subcutaneous emphysema is itself listed as a cause of increased RADIOLUCENCY on CXR.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: The tracheal-shift memory trick — and the two lists?
cards.a:
The tracheal-shift memory trick — and the two lists?
'TOWARD loss / AWAY from pressure.'
TOWARD the lesion: atelectasis · fibrosis · surgical resection — lost lung volume pulls the mediastinum with it.
AWAY from the lesion: pneumothorax · large pleural effusion · large mass lesions (tumors) — a space-occupying process pushes it across.
Normally the trachea is MIDLINE — palpate just above the sternum, between the clavicles.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: What is the PMI's role in confirming a shift?
cards.a:
What is the PMI's role in confirming a shift?
The PMI (point of maximum impulse) moves with the mediastinum in exactly the same directions — toward atelectasis, away from pneumothorax/effusion — so a displaced PMI is a second confirmation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ Tension pneumothorax — the picture and the immediate action
cards.a:
⚠ Tension pneumothorax — the picture and the immediate action
Suspect when a patient deteriorates RAPIDLY with: unilateral decreased breath sounds and chest expansion · hyperresonance on the affected side · trachea shifted AWAY.
Insert a chest tube immediately, or decompress with a needle thoracostomy — 14-gauge angiocath in adults, 18- or 20-gauge in infants — into the 2nd intercostal space over the top of the 3rd rib, MIDCLAVICULAR line.
⚠ DO NOT delay for a CXR when tension pneumothorax is obvious.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Paradoxical breathing — what is it and what does it mean?
cards.a:
Paradoxical breathing — what is it and what does it mean?
The chest wall or abdominal wall moves IN on inspiration and OUT on exhalation — the opposite of normal.
Heuer calls it abdominal paradox / thoracoabdominal paradox; the deck calls it thoracic-abdominal dyssynchrony or 'see-saw' motion.
Implication: DIAPHRAGMATIC FATIGUE OR PARALYSIS and increased work of breathing.
⚠ It is an EARLY sign of weaning failure that should STOP a spontaneous breathing trial.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Flail chest — definition and clinical findings?
cards.a:
Flail chest — definition and clinical findings?
A flail segment — one or more ribs broken in TWO OR MORE PLACES — leaving that piece of chest wall unattached and unstable.
Findings: fracture-site and inspiratory pain · PARADOXICAL chest motion (segment moves IN with inhalation, OUT with exhalation) · dyspnea · tachypnea.
Diagnosis: CXR. Treatment: EPIDURAL ANALGESIA and SURGICAL FIXATION.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ Flail chest — the key exam point about mechanical ventilation
cards.a:
⚠ Flail chest — the key exam point about mechanical ventilation
Only recommend mechanical ventilation to correct ABNORMAL GAS EXCHANGE (i.e. for the associated pulmonary contusion) — NOT to treat chest-wall instability itself.
⚠ The RCP 105 deck said the ventilator should 'completely take over breathing while the injury heals' — Heuer explicitly CONTRADICTS this.
When ventilation IS needed: intubation + A/C mode (VC, PCV, PRVC or bilevel) with PEEP; try mask CPAP or BiPAP first in an alert, cooperative patient with marginal status.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: What must you watch for after a flail chest — and what must you NOT give?
cards.a:
What must you watch for after a flail chest — and what must you NOT give?
The associated PULMONARY CONTUSION — its full effects may not appear for 24–48 hours, so admit and monitor for worsening hypoxemia and ARDS.
⚠ Do NOT recommend steroids for pulmonary contusion.
Flail chest is also a contraindication to PRONE positioning and a caution for lateral chest compression during CPT.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Define orthopnea — and what does 'always elevated with pillows' imply?
cards.a:
Define orthopnea — and what does 'always elevated with pillows' imply?
A patient's sensation of uncomfortable breathing when LYING DOWN (recumbent), typically relieved by sitting or standing up. Gathered during the INTERVIEW.
On inspection, a patient 'always elevated with pillows' implies orthopnea and CONGESTIVE HEART FAILURE.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: How is breathlessness formally quantified?
cards.a:
How is breathlessness formally quantified?
Bedside shortcut (deck): ask how many PILLOWS the patient sleeps on.
Formally, Heuer uses the BORG SCALE — 0 to 10 (0 = no dyspnea, 10 = maximal), always tied to a predefined level of activity (an exercise-test stage or the end of a 6-minute walk test).
Exercise tolerance: graded cardiopulmonary exercise test = GOLD STANDARD; 6MWT = practical alternative; ATS Breathlessness Scale = simplest.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ BNP — Heuer's numbers vs the deck's
cards.a:
⚠ BNP — Heuer's numbers vs the deck's
Heuer: reference < 20 pg/mL; < 100 RULES OUT CHF; > 500 RULES IN CHF.
Deck: normal < 100 · 100–300 HF may be present · > 300 mild · > 600 moderate · > 900 severe.
Purpose: distinguishes a CARDIAC cause of SOB (CHF) from a PULMONARY one (COPD).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Troponin I and CK-MB — values and timing?
cards.a:
Troponin I and CK-MB — values and timing?
Troponin I — Heuer: < 0.4 µg/L; rises 3–6 hr after insult, peaks at 12 hr, persists 7 DAYS. (⚠ Deck: normal < 0.1 ng/mL.)
CK-MB: < 4–6% of total CK; rises 4–6 hr, peaks at 24 hr, normal in 2–3 days.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: KUSSMAUL breathing — description and cause?
cards.a:
KUSSMAUL breathing — description and cause?
DEEP AND FAST respirations.
Cause: METABOLIC ACIDOSIS, classically diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) — blowing off CO₂. Treat the underlying cause.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: CHEYNE-STOKES breathing — description and cause?
cards.a:
CHEYNE-STOKES breathing — description and cause?
Cycles of progressive RISE AND FALL in VT (waxing and waning), each cycle followed by a period of APNEA.
Cause: CNS disease and CONGESTIVE HEART FAILURE.
Treat the cause; bilevel or adaptive servo-ventilation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: BIOT breathing — description and cause?
cards.a:
BIOT breathing — description and cause?
CLUSTERS of rapid breaths interspersed with periods of apnea (deck: breaths of equal tidal volume, then apnea).
Cause: damage to the MEDULLA by stroke or trauma; brain herniation / ↑ICP. Treat the cause and lower the ICP.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ The clean Cheyne-Stokes vs Biot contrast
cards.a:
⚠ The clean Cheyne-Stokes vs Biot contrast
CHEYNE-STOKES = GRADUAL crescendo-decrescendo in VT → CHF, CNS disease.
BIOT = ABRUPT clusters, NO crescendo → brain damage, ↑ICP.
(The deck and Heuer describe Biot's slightly differently, but both point to the same lesion: medulla / ↑ICP.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: AGONAL and APNEUSTIC breathing?
cards.a:
AGONAL and APNEUSTIC breathing?
AGONAL: gasping, labored, sometimes noisy respirations → cerebral ischemia, cerebral hypoxia/anoxia.
APNEUSTIC: prolonged GASPING INSPIRATION with incomplete expiration → damage to the PONS (trauma, stroke, tumor). Not a named row in Heuer's tables — deck content only.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Tachypnea and bradypnea — numbers and causes?
cards.a:
Tachypnea and bradypnea — numbers and causes?
Tachypnea: RR > 20/min → respiratory distress, restrictive disease, hypoxemia, fever, pain, anxiety, ↑ metabolic rate.
Bradypnea: RR < 12/min → sleep (normal), oversedation, ↓PaCO₂, ↓metabolic rate, hypothermia, respiratory failure/arrest — reverse sedation or support.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Prolonged exhalation vs prolonged inspiration vs rapid-and-shallow?
cards.a:
Prolonged exhalation vs prolonged inspiration vs rapid-and-shallow?
Prolonged EXHALATION → EXPIRATORY obstruction: asthma, COPD.
Prolonged INSPIRATION → UPPER-AIRWAY obstruction: croup, epiglottitis.
Rapid and shallow → LOSS OF LUNG VOLUME: atelectasis, fibrosis, ARDS, pulmonary edema.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: How do you assess level of consciousness quickly — and what is 'oriented × 3'?
cards.a:
How do you assess level of consciousness quickly — and what is 'oriented × 3'?
Ask TIME, PLACE and PERSON. An alert patient is 'oriented × 3' (add situation for × 4). A patient who answers only two is charted × 2, e.g. 'oriented × 2, unaware of time.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Heuer's common causes of disorientation?
cards.a:
Heuer's common causes of disorientation?
Neurologic injury · sedation and analgesics (especially opioids) · severe HYPOXEMIA or HYPERCAPNIA.
Only alert patients can fully cooperate and participate in their care. A depressed sensorium implies poor cerebral oxygenation, degenerative brain disorders, or drug overdose.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: The five levels of consciousness — and which one is the airway red flag?
cards.a:
The five levels of consciousness — and which one is the airway red flag?
ALERT — awake, responsive, oriented × 3.
LETHARGIC — sluggish, slow to respond, but still appropriate.
⚠ OBTUNDED — very drowsy; arousable but REDUCED COUGH/GAG REFLEX → airway-protection concern, aspiration risk ↑.
STUPOROUS — responds only to strong or painful stimuli.
COMATOSE — no response to any stimulus; flaccid; cannot protect the airway.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Deck-only LOC rungs you may still see charted?
cards.a:
Deck-only LOC rungs you may still see charted?
SOMNOLENT — easily aroused but drifts back to sleep (think sleep apnea or excess O₂ in COPD).
CONFUSED — disoriented, inappropriate answers.
SEMI-COMATOSE — minimal response even to pain.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: The AVPU scale?
cards.a:
The AVPU scale?
Alert and oriented (report as oriented × 1, 2 or 3)
Verbal stimulus — note whether the response is appropriate
Pain — firmly pinch the skin; look for moaning or withdrawal
Unresponsive — if no response on one side, try the other; flaccid and silent = unresponsive.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ The Glasgow Coma Scale — range, bands, and the intubation rule
cards.a:
⚠ The Glasgow Coma Scale — range, bands, and the intubation rule
Heuer calls it the most objective assessment of consciousness. Score Eye, Verbal, Motor and sum.
Total: 3 (deep coma) to 15 (fully alert).
Mild 13–15 · Moderate 9–12 · Severe (coma) ≤ 8.
⚠ GCS ≤ 8 = INTUBATE.
Charted as 'E3, V2, M2' = total 7 → severe impairment.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Is the GCS point-by-point component table in Heuer or the decks?
cards.a:
Is the GCS point-by-point component table in Heuer or the decks?
No — Table 2-1 is a FIGURE in the source text and is not reproduced in the available Heuer text or in any deck.
Memorize the 3/15 range, the 13–15 / 9–12 / ≤ 8 bands, and the E-V-M shorthand; get the individual point values from your ACLS/trauma card.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: How much reduced hemoglobin does it take to see cyanosis?
cards.a:
How much reduced hemoglobin does it take to see cyanosis?
At least 5 g/dL of reduced (deoxygenated) hemoglobin.
⚠ The deck supplies this number — Heuer states the physiology without the figure: 'the intensity of cyanosis increases with the amount of Hb in the blood.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: CENTRAL cyanosis — what's wrong, where do you see it, when does it appear?
cards.a:
CENTRAL cyanosis — what's wrong, where do you see it, when does it appear?
An OXYGENATION problem — low SaO₂ from poor oxygenation of blood by the lungs.
Seen in the MUCOUS MEMBRANES of the lips and mouth (deck adds the tongue).
With normal Hb, it generally first appears when SaO₂ drops below 80% (PaO₂ 45–50 torr). Paired with arterial hypoxemia.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: PERIPHERAL cyanosis (acrocyanosis) — what's wrong and where?
cards.a:
PERIPHERAL cyanosis (acrocyanosis) — what's wrong and where?
A PERFUSION / blood-flow problem.
Extremities ONLY — hands, feet, nail beds, fingertips; Heuer also lists mottled/acrocyanotic skin.
⚠ Can occur with a COMPLETELY NORMAL SaO₂. Paired with cool extremities and capillary refill ≥ 3 seconds → circulatory failure.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ Why does ANEMIA mask cyanosis — and what does polycythemia do?
cards.a:
⚠ Why does ANEMIA mask cyanosis — and what does polycythemia do?
The sign depends on an ABSOLUTE AMOUNT of desaturated hemoglobin, not a percentage.
Anemic patients can be SEVERELY HYPOXIC before cyanosis ever appears, because there simply isn't 5 g/dL of reduced Hb to see.
Mirror image: polycythemic patients can LOOK cyanotic yet still have adequate O₂ content.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ How reliable is cyanosis as a sign of hypoxemia?
cards.a:
⚠ How reliable is cyanosis as a sign of hypoxemia?
Late and UNRELIABLE. Visibility is affected by hemoglobin concentration, skin pigmentation, perfusion and lighting.
'Never rely on cyanosis alone to determine oxygenation' — NO cyanosis does NOT mean adequate oxygenation.
Typical NBRC intervention: increase FiO₂ or check ventilation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Define PEA — and what are the four pulseless rhythms?
cards.a:
Define PEA — and what are the four pulseless rhythms?
PEA = the monitor shows ORGANIZED ELECTRICAL ACTIVITY but the patient has NO PULSE.
Heuer's four dysrhythmias producing pulselessness: VF · VT · PEA · ASYSTOLE.
The unifying idea: either NO rhythm, or a rhythm that produces NO PULSE.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ PEA and asystole — shockable?
cards.a:
⚠ PEA and asystole — shockable?
NO. Do NOT defibrillate and NEVER cardiovert.
Management is high-quality CPR + epinephrine 1 mg IV every 3–5 minutes with a flush.
The RT's job is to OXYGENATE, VENTILATE and CORRECT ACIDOSIS — because acidosis and hypoxia BLUNT epinephrine's effect.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Giving epinephrine via the ETT — how?
cards.a:
Giving epinephrine via the ETT — how?
DOUBLE the dose and follow with 10 mL of normal saline — if IV or IO access is not established.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ Capnography during resuscitation — the two thresholds
cards.a:
⚠ Capnography during resuscitation — the two thresholds
If PetCO₂ < 10 mm Hg and intra-arterial diastolic pressure < 20 mm Hg, the QUALITY OF CPR must be improved.
Failure to achieve PetCO₂ > 10 mm Hg after 20 minutes of CPR can be used as an indicator to TERMINATE resuscitation.
Pulse/breathing checks are done generally after five cycles of CPR.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: The 5 H's?
cards.a:
The 5 H's?
Hypovolemia · Hypoxia · Hydrogen ion (acidosis) · Hypo-/hyperkalemia · Hypothermia.
⚠ The H's and T's appear ONLY in Heuer — absent from every deck.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: The 5 T's — and which does the RT own?
cards.a:
The 5 T's — and which does the RT own?
Tension pneumothorax · Tamponade (cardiac) · Toxins (drug overdose, anaphylaxis) · Thrombosis, pulmonary (PE) · Thrombosis, cardiac (MI or ischemia).
The RT owns several directly: HYPOXIA (airway/O₂), HYDROGEN ION (ventilation), and TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX (needle decompression/chest tube).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: IO access and sodium bicarbonate in a code?
cards.a:
IO access and sodium bicarbonate in a code?
IO: if IV access fails, the intraosseous route delivers drugs at IV speed — proximal tibia or humerus, needle out within 3–4 hours.
Sodium bicarbonate 0.5–1 mEq/kg is a LAST RESORT only, to keep pH > 7.15 — and it RAISES CO₂, so you must VENTILATE.
Survival drops 7–10% per minute without CPR, 3–4% per minute with CPR.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ Electrodes vs leads — and why 10 makes 12?
cards.a:
⚠ Electrodes vs leads — and why 10 makes 12?
An ELECTRODE is the sticker on the patient; a LEAD is an electrical VIEW. Electrodes = cameras, leads = pictures.
You place 10 electrodes to produce 12 leads — Heuer: 'there are only 10 actual leads to place, not 12.'
The right leg 'doesn't count' — it is just a GROUND. The difference is made up by the 3 AUGMENTED limb leads (aVR, aVL, aVF), which the machine mathematically derives from RA, LA and LL.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Limb electrode colors and mnemonics?
cards.a:
Limb electrode colors and mnemonics?
RL / GREEN = right leg · LL / RED = left leg · RA / WHITE = right arm · LA / BLACK = left arm.
Mnemonics: 'smoke over fire' (black over red) · 'clouds over grass' (white over green) · 'white on right.'
Apply to MUSCULAR areas of the arms and legs.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Lead I, II and III — which electrodes?
cards.a:
Lead I, II and III — which electrodes?
Lead I = RA(−) → LA(+)
Lead II = RA(−) → LL(+)
Lead III = LA(−) → LL(+)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Chest lead placement V1–V6
cards.a:
Chest lead placement V1–V6
V1: 4th ICS, RIGHT sternal border
V2: 4th ICS, LEFT sternal border
V3: between V2 and V4
V4: 5th ICS, MIDCLAVICULAR line
V5: 5th ICS, ANTERIOR AXILLARY line
V6: 5th ICS, MIDAXILLARY line

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ECG procedure (Heuer Box 3-1)?
cards.a:
ECG procedure (Heuer Box 3-1)?
Turn on and run self-test/calibration → position supine or semi-Fowler's → remove all jewelry and metal, have the patient relax → apply limb electrodes → place chest leads → ensure comfort and privacy → run the tracing, aiming for a stable isoelectric baseline with no noise or electrical interference.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Failure to obtain an ECG signal vs a NOISY signal — causes?
cards.a:
Failure to obtain an ECG signal vs a NOISY signal — causes?
No signal: usually a loose, missing or defective lead, or the patient's HAIR preventing skin contact.
Noisy signal: poor electrical connection · motion artifact · improper filtering; deck adds oily/sweaty skin, shivering/muscle tremor, and 60-Hz interference from nearby equipment.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Heuer's ECG artifact fix list, in order — and the practical RT rule?
cards.a:
Heuer's ECG artifact fix list, in order — and the practical RT rule?
(1) Verify snaps and connectors are clean and corrosion-free → (2) verify electrodes are connected properly → (3) verify the electrode gel is not dry (replace suspect electrodes) → (4) check the main cable for continuity → (5) confirm the patient is motionless, supporting the limbs → (6) verify the filter settings.
⚠ If a tracing suddenly looks bizarre, LOOK AT THE PATIENT before calling it an arrhythmia.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Ischemia/NSTEMI vs acute STEMI on ECG?
cards.a:
Ischemia/NSTEMI vs acute STEMI on ECG?
Ischemia/NSTEMI: ST-segment DEPRESSION (horizontal or downsloping ≥ 0.5 mm) + T-wave flattening or inversion ≥ 1 mm.
Acute STEMI: ST ELEVATION ≥ 2 mm (men) or ≥ 1.5 mm (women) in two contiguous precordial leads, pathologic Q waves, prominent R waves in V1–V2.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ECG electrolyte clues?
cards.a:
ECG electrolyte clues?
TALL T waves = HYPERKALEMIA (also acute MI).
Small/flat/inverted T waves = ISCHEMIA.
Prominent U waves = HYPOKALEMIA or HYPOMAGNESEMIA.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: QRS > 0.12 sec and PR > 0.20 sec — what do they mean?
cards.a:
QRS > 0.12 sec and PR > 0.20 sec — what do they mean?
QRS > 0.12 sec: PVCs, bundle branch block, VT, hyperkalemia.
PR > 0.20 sec: first-degree or Mobitz I AV block.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: The 'rule of 300' for heart rate?
cards.a:
The 'rule of 300' for heart rate?
At 25 mm/sec: each small box = 0.04 sec, each large box = 0.20 sec.
Divide 300 by the number of LARGE BOXES in the R-R interval.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ Can a 12-lead ECG alone diagnose an MI?
cards.a:
⚠ Can a 12-lead ECG alone diagnose an MI?
No — you need presentation PLUS cardiac biomarkers.
And STEMI (thrombolytics/angioplasty) is treated very differently from NSTEMI (antiplatelets/anticoagulants).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: VF and PULSELESS VT — shockable? Energy?
cards.a:
VF and PULSELESS VT — shockable? Energy?
YES — UNSYNCHRONIZED DEFIBRILLATION.
Biphasic: 120–200 J initial (or per manufacturer), same dose for subsequent shocks. Monophasic: 360 J.
Then epinephrine 1 mg IV q3–5 min.
Antiarrhythmics: amiodarone 300 mg rapid infusion, then 150 mg in 3–5 min and every 10 min, up to 2.2 g/day; or lidocaine 1.0–1.5 mg/kg, then 0.5–0.75 mg/kg q5–10 min, up to 3 mg/kg.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ When is CARDIOVERSION never used?
cards.a:
⚠ When is CARDIOVERSION never used?
NEVER for VF, pulseless VT, or POLYMORPHIC/irregular VT — those need UNSYNCHRONIZED DEFIBRILLATION.
Also not used for multifocal atrial or junctional tachycardia.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Synchronized cardioversion energies?
cards.a:
Synchronized cardioversion energies?
A-fib / SVT: 120–200 J biphasic, increase stepwise.
Atrial flutter: 50–100 J biphasic, increase stepwise.
Monomorphic VT WITH a pulse (stable): 100 J biphasic, increase stepwise.
⚠ Immediate cardioversion if the ventricular rate exceeds 150/min despite drugs.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Atrial flutter — the ECG signature?
cards.a:
Atrial flutter — the ECG signature?
'SAWTOOTH' pattern between QRS complexes, NO PR interval.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Adenosine for SVT — the deck's administration points?
cards.a:
Adenosine for SVT — the deck's administration points?
12-second half-life — give central/proximal with the arm RAISED and flush IMMEDIATELY.
Side effects: bronchospasm, dyspnea, cough.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Symptomatic bradycardia — treatment?
cards.a:
Symptomatic bradycardia — treatment?
Atropine 0.5 mg IV q3–5 min, up to a MAXIMUM of 3 mg; positive chronotropes (atropine, epinephrine, dopamine); warm blanket and fluids if hypothermic; evaluate ECG and cardiac enzymes; CPR if needed; pacing.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ PVCs appear during a respiratory procedure — what do you do?
cards.a:
⚠ PVCs appear during a respiratory procedure — what do you do?
STOP what you are doing · give supplemental O₂ to stabilize the patient · notify the physician immediately.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Pediatric defibrillation energies?
cards.a:
Pediatric defibrillation energies?
Initial 2 J/kg; subsequent at least 4 J/kg (higher may be considered). Monophasic 2 J/kg.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: What is a Rapid Response Team, who is on it, and what is its purpose?
cards.a:
What is a Rapid Response Team, who is on it, and what is its purpose?
Heuer calls them medical emergency teams (METs), 'also known as rapid-response teams (RRTs).'
Purpose: intervene and stabilize a patient who is rapidly deteriorating OUTSIDE the ICU — BEFORE cardiopulmonary arrest — to avert a 'code blue.'
Typically an ICU nurse, a physician or PA, and a RESPIRATORY THERAPIST.
⚠ This is NOT in any deck.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ Adult RRT activation criteria — all six
cards.a:
⚠ Adult RRT activation criteria — all six
Mental status: acute change in mental status or overall clinical appearance.
Heart rate: < 40 or > 130 beats/min.
Respiratory rate: < 8/min or > 30/min.
Systolic BP: < 90 mm Hg.
SpO₂: < 90%, especially on supplemental O₂.
Urine output: acute change to less than 50 mL over 4 hours.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: Most common RRT interventions performed or assisted by RTs?
cards.a:
Most common RRT interventions performed or assisted by RTs?
Suctioning · adjusting the FiO₂ · noninvasive ventilation · bronchodilators · arterial blood gas monitoring · intubation.
The RT may also assist with transport to the ICU. Once the MET has responded, details of the event must be recorded in the medical record.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ Do you wait for a physician to arrive before assessing an RRT patient?
cards.a:
⚠ Do you wait for a physician to arrive before assessing an RRT patient?
NO. Assessment should be done IMMEDIATELY by any member of the MET/RRT — RT, nurse, or PA.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: The 'stop therapy and notify' numbers?
cards.a:
The 'stop therapy and notify' numbers?
Marked change in vital signs = 20% above or below baseline, or outside critical limits.
HR increase of more than 20 bpm during a treatment → STOP and notify.
Pain interference score > 4 → report to the physician.
HR normal 60–100; bradycardia < 60; tachycardia > 100. Tachypnea > 20; bradypnea < 12. GCS ≤ 8 → intubate. Capillary refill ≥ 3 sec = poor perfusion.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::07 Clinical Assessment, Breath Sounds, CXR & ECG
cards.q: ⚠ Pulsus paradoxus — the threshold conflict and what it means
cards.a:
⚠ Pulsus paradoxus — the threshold conflict and what it means
Heuer: an abnormal inspiratory systolic drop is more than 6–8 mm Hg.
Deck: > 10 mmHg, and > 25 mmHg in impending respiratory failure.
Signifies SEVERE AIRWAY OBSTRUCTION or CARDIAC TAMPONADE.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: The one rule that runs through the whole volumes/capacities table?
cards.a:
The one rule that runs through the whole volumes/capacities table?
Every 'CAPACITY' is two or more 'VOLUMES' added together.
The four primary volumes (VT, IRV, ERV, RV) never overlap; the four capacities (IC, FRC, VC, TLC) are sums of them.
⚠ RV cannot be measured by spirometry — you can never exhale it — so FRC must be measured indirectly, and everything else falls out of it.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Heuer's volume algebra set (App B Table B-4)
cards.a:
Heuer's volume algebra set (App B Table B-4)
VC = TLC − RV · VC = IRV + VT + ERV
TLC = FRC + IC · TLC = IRV + VT + ERV + RV
RV = FRC − ERV · RV = TLC − VC
FRC = RV + ERV · FRC = TLC − IC

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Worked (Problem B.16): FRC 3800 mL, VT 400 mL, ERV 1300 mL — find RV
cards.a:
Worked (Problem B.16): FRC 3800 mL, VT 400 mL, ERV 1300 mL — find RV
RV = FRC − ERV = 3800 − 1300 = 2500 mL = 2.5 L
(VT is a decoy.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: The four primary volumes — normal adult values?
cards.a:
The four primary volumes — normal adult values?
VT = 0.5 L (500 mL) · IRV = 3.1 L · ERV = 1.2 L · RV = 1.2 L

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: The four capacities — normal adult values and composition?
cards.a:
The four capacities — normal adult values and composition?
IC = 3.6 L = IRV + VT (= TLC 6.0 − FRC 2.4)
FRC = 2.4 L = ERV + RV
VC = 4.8 L = IRV + VT + ERV
TLC = 6.0 L = FRC + IC (all four volumes)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: FVC and FEV₁ — what counts as normal?
cards.a:
FVC and FEV₁ — what counts as normal?
Both: normal ≥ 80% of predicted; abnormal ≤ 80% predicted.
Heuer's ballpark: FEV₁% > 75% and FEV₃% > 95%; normals blow out 80–90% of the FVC in about 3 seconds.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ The FEV₁/FVC ratio — the normal and the obstruction cutoff
cards.a:
⚠ The FEV₁/FVC ratio — the normal and the obstruction cutoff
A normal FEV₁% is 70% or more FOR ALL PATIENTS.
< 70% CONFIRMS OBSTRUCTION (GOLD: post-bronchodilator < 0.70).
Asthma: adults < 0.75–0.80, children < 0.90.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: FEF25–75% vs FEF200–1200 — what does each localize?
cards.a:
FEF25–75% vs FEF200–1200 — what does each localize?
FEF25–75% ≤ 70% of predicted = SMALL airway obstruction (average flow over the middle half of the FVC).
FEF200–1200 ≤ 70% of predicted = LARGE airway obstruction (flow between 200 and 1200 mL of the FVC).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: DLCO — normal and severity bands?
cards.a:
DLCO — normal and severity bands?
Heuer: 25–30 mL/min/mm Hg; deck: 25 ± 5.
< 80% predicted = abnormal. 65–80% mild · 50–65% moderate · < 50% severe.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: The percent-predicted severity bands the NBRC uses?
cards.a:
The percent-predicted severity bands the NBRC uses?
Normal 80–120% · Mild 70–79% · Moderate 50–69% · Severe < 49% of predicted.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: PEFR — Heuer's tip about what it's for?
cards.a:
PEFR — Heuer's tip about what it's for?
Use PEFR to MONITOR obstruction, NOT to DIAGNOSE it.
Monitor airway tone in asthma over time (diary); assess response to bronchodilator — though FEV spirometry is preferred.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: When do you recommend MVV and bronchial provocation?
cards.a:
When do you recommend MVV and bronchial provocation?
MVV: integrated function of airways + lungs + chest cage + muscles; preop evaluation; breathing reserve for exercise testing.
Bronchial provocation: airway hyperreactivity, occupational asthma, risk of developing asthma.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: When do you recommend FRC/TLC and DLCO?
cards.a:
When do you recommend FRC/TLC and DLCO?
FRC and TLC: grade hyperinflation; quantify gas trapped in cysts/bullae by comparing to body-box TGV; assess restriction.
DLCO: follow ILD/fibrosis, emphysema, CF; separate chronic bronchitis vs emphysema vs asthma; amiodarone/bleomycin toxicity.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: What data must be entered before spirometry — and what does a wrong entry cause?
cards.a:
What data must be entered before spirometry — and what does a wrong entry cause?
Age, sex, height, ethnicity — required to compute predicted values.
⚠ Falsely high or low percent-normal computations usually mean INCORRECT PATIENT DATA ENTRY — re-enter and recompute before blaming the patient.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: The ATS acceptability specifics for an FVC maneuver?
cards.a:
The ATS acceptability specifics for an FVC maneuver?
Back-extrapolated volume < 5% of the FVC or 150 mL · trace smooth with a distinct start · minimum 6 seconds with a 1-second plateau · three acceptable maneuvers (max eight attempts) · the two largest FVC and FEV₁ values within 200 mL or 5% of each other.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ If three acceptable maneuvers cannot be obtained — and which is the 'best test'?
cards.a:
⚠ If three acceptable maneuvers cannot be obtained — and which is the 'best test'?
DO NOT REPORT THE RESULTS.
Report the two largest FVC and FEV₁ values even if from DIFFERENT attempts; the best test is the maneuver with the biggest SUM of FVC + FEV₁.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: How long do you wait for peak drug effect in a pre/post study?
cards.a:
How long do you wait for peak drug effect in a pre/post study?
15–30 minutes for spirometry · 10–30 minutes for peak flow.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: The percent-predicted and percent-change formulas?
cards.a:
The percent-predicted and percent-change formulas?
% PREDICTED = (actual ÷ predicted) × 100
% CHANGE = [(post − pre) ÷ pre] × 100

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Worked (B.19): measured FVC 3.25 L, predicted 3.82 L
cards.a:
Worked (B.19): measured FVC 3.25 L, predicted 3.82 L
3.25 ÷ 3.82 × 100 = 85% of normal

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Worked (B.18): pre FEV₁ 2.4 L → post 2.7 L
cards.a:
Worked (B.18): pre FEV₁ 2.4 L → post 2.7 L
(2.7 − 2.4) ÷ 2.4 = 0.3 ÷ 2.4 = 0.125 → 12.5%
MEETS the 12–15% bar — borderline positive.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Worked (Ch 4): pre FEV₁ 3.0 L → post 3.3 L
cards.a:
Worked (Ch 4): pre FEV₁ 3.0 L → post 3.3 L
(3.3 − 3.0) ÷ 3.0 = 0.3 ÷ 3.0 = 0.10 → 10%
NOT a significant response.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ The bronchodilator-response threshold — 'AND' vs 'OR' is a real conflict
cards.a:
⚠ The bronchodilator-response threshold — 'AND' vs 'OR' is a real conflict
Heuer Ch 4 says 'OR': 'FEV₁ improves by at least 12–15% (OR by 200 mL or more in adults) → reversible, as in asthma.'
RCP 203 Lssn 3a and the Asthma deck say 'AND': ≥ 12% AND ≥ 200 mL in adults.
The numbers 12–15% and 200 mL are NOT in dispute — only whether BOTH must be met.
If a question offers only one: pick 12% and 200 mL for a formal PFT lab report, 12–15% for a bedside/PEFR screen.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Asthma deck's other positive-reversibility criteria?
cards.a:
Asthma deck's other positive-reversibility criteria?
≥ 12% of PREDICTED in children; also accepts PEFR day-to-day variability > 10% (adults) / 13% (children).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Which PFT tests are limited by consciousness/cooperation?
cards.a:
Which PFT tests are limited by consciousness/cooperation?
SVC — 'only with alert and cooperative patients.'
MEP — 'can only be measured on an alert and cooperative patient.'
MVV — 'extremely effort dependent, so suboptimal effort could be interpreted as impairment.'
DLCO — 'patients incapable of a breath-hold may not be able to perform the test.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Hazards specific to helium dilution and N₂ washout?
cards.a:
Hazards specific to helium dilution and N₂ washout?
Helium dilution: hypercapnia or hypoxemia may occur if CO₂ is not removed or O₂ not added; leaks from poor mouth seal, perforated eardrums, or tracheostomies invalidate it.
N₂ washout: ventilatory drive may be DEPRESSED in some patients who breathe 100% O₂; wait a minimum of 15 minutes before repeating.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Exercise testing — contraindications and the stop criteria?
cards.a:
Exercise testing — contraindications and the stop criteria?
Contraindications: acute MI, uncontrolled heart failure, unstable angina, significant cardiac dysrhythmias, acute pulmonary disorders, severe hypertension.
Requires direct physician supervision, a fully stocked crash cart with defibrillator, and ACLS-certified staff.
STOP for: wide swings in blood pressure, severe angina, dyspnea, serious arrhythmia, or dizziness/confusion/cyanosis.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: 6MWT contraindications and the O₂ titration stop point?
cards.a:
6MWT contraindications and the O₂ titration stop point?
Not within ONE MONTH of MI or unstable angina.
Relative: resting HR > 120/min · SBP > 180 · DBP > 100 mm Hg.
Terminate O₂ titration with exercise if SaO₂ drops below 85%.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Is the classic AARC hazards list (syncope, pneumothorax, raised ICP…) in Heuer?
cards.a:
Is the classic AARC hazards list (syncope, pneumothorax, raised ICP…) in Heuer?
No — it is NOT printed in Heuer or the decks. It lives in the AARC CPG only.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ Heuer's PFT interpretation algorithm — the strict order and the cutoffs
cards.a:
⚠ Heuer's PFT interpretation algorithm — the strict order and the cutoffs
FEV₁% first → then VC → then TLC → then DLCO.
Cutoffs: < 70% for the FEV₁%, and < 80% predicted for the VC, TLC and DLCO.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: FEV₁% < 70% — then what does DLCO tell you?
cards.a:
FEV₁% < 70% — then what does DLCO tell you?
Obstructive or mixed.
LOW DLCO = EMPHYSEMA.
NORMAL DLCO = ASTHMA or CHRONIC BRONCHITIS — separate those two with a pre/post-bronchodilator study or a methacholine challenge.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: FEV₁% ≥ 70% — how do you finish the tree?
cards.a:
FEV₁% ≥ 70% — how do you finish the tree?
Normal or restrictive. It is RESTRICTIVE if the TLC is LOW.
Then DLCO splits it:
NORMAL or HIGH DLCO = CHEST WALL or NEUROMUSCULAR problem.
LOW DLCO = INTERSTITIAL LUNG DISEASE such as pulmonary fibrosis.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: OBSTRUCTIVE pattern — the full row?
cards.a:
OBSTRUCTIVE pattern — the full row?
FVC: normal or slightly ↓ · FEV₁: ↓↓ (falls MORE than FVC) · FEV₁/FVC: ↓ < 70% · TLC: ↑ (hyperinflation) · RV: ↑ (air trapping; TGV > FRC)
Examples: COPD, emphysema, chronic bronchitis, asthma, bronchiectasis, CF.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: RESTRICTIVE pattern — the full row?
cards.a:
RESTRICTIVE pattern — the full row?
FVC: ↓ < 80% predicted · FEV₁: ↓ · FEV₁/FVC: NORMAL or ↑ (preserved — FEV₁ and FVC fall TOGETHER) · TLC: ↓ < 80% predicted · RV: ↓
Examples: pulmonary fibrosis/ILD, kyphoscoliosis, neuromuscular disease, obesity, large pleural effusion.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: MIXED pattern — and the deck's shorthand?
cards.a:
MIXED pattern — and the deck's shorthand?
FVC ↓ · FEV₁ ↓ · FEV₁/FVC ↓ < 70% · TLC ↓ · RV variable.
Deck rule: 'all three ↓ = COMBINED.' Advanced/overlap disease.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: The flow-volume loop tells — obstructive vs restrictive?
cards.a:
The flow-volume loop tells — obstructive vs restrictive?
Obstructive: a CONCAVE downward expiratory slope = dynamic airway collapse with reduced flows.
Restrictive: HIGH flows with rapid emptying of a markedly REDUCED volume.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ How do you recognize POOR EFFORT?
cards.a:
⚠ How do you recognize POOR EFFORT?
NON-REPRODUCIBILITY. ATS: three acceptable maneuvers, two largest FVC and FEV₁ within 200 mL or 5%. PEFR must be repeated until three values vary by less than 10% — record the HIGHEST.
Also: jerky motion or a slow start (back-extrapolated volume > 5% of FVC or 150 mL is the objective version); exhalation shorter than 6 seconds; no 1-second plateau.
Heuer: 'always consider poor effort or poor technique whenever the PEFR is significantly below normal.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Which tests can ALL be faked low — and the clinical warning?
cards.a:
Which tests can ALL be faked low — and the clinical warning?
PEFR, FVC, FEV₁, MVV, SVC, MIP/NIF, MEP.
Weaning deck: VC and MIP are effort-dependent — poor effort makes a patient look WEAKER than they are.
Neuro deck: 'if a patient is heavily sedated, confused, or unable to follow commands, DON'T assume they have weak respiratory muscles — they may simply be unable to perform the test correctly.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: When do you recommend bronchoprovocation — and what is methacholine?
cards.a:
When do you recommend bronchoprovocation — and what is methacholine?
When spirometry is NONDIAGNOSTIC but asthma is still suspected — the spirometry looks normal or fails to show clear obstruction or reversibility.
Methacholine is a CHOLINERGIC (parasympathomimetic) agent given deliberately to PROVOKE the airways — essentially an induced, controlled attack.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: What makes a methacholine challenge POSITIVE — and where does that number come from?
cards.a:
What makes a methacholine challenge POSITIVE — and where does that number come from?
≥ 20% DECREASE in FEV₁ = airway hyperresponsiveness, consistent with asthma.
⚠ Heuer NEVER prints a numeric % fall for methacholine — the 20% figure comes from the Asthma deck. But Heuer independently uses the same 20% FEV₁ drop for the EXERCISE challenge, so the number is safe to carry over.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Worked: pre-challenge FEV₁ 3.0 L — what value is positive?
cards.a:
Worked: pre-challenge FEV₁ 3.0 L — what value is positive?
20% of 3.0 = 3.0 × 0.20 = 0.6 L
Threshold = 3.0 − 0.6 = 2.4 L
An FEV₁ falling to 2.4 L or below is a POSITIVE test.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: HELIUM DILUTION — how it works and its limitation?
cards.a:
HELIUM DILUTION — how it works and its limitation?
Starting at FRC, the patient rebreathes 5–10% He with soda-lime CO₂ absorption and O₂ added at ~0.25 L/min; the test ends at equilibration (% He constant for 2 min).
Measures ACTUAL FRC — only lung COMMUNICATING with the airways.
⚠ UNDERESTIMATES FRC in air trapping. Easy (tidal breathing only).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: NITROGEN WASHOUT — how it works and its advantage?
cards.a:
NITROGEN WASHOUT — how it works and its advantage?
Starting at FRC, the patient breathes 100% O₂ for 7 minutes or until % N₂ falls below 1.0%; expired N₂ and volume measured continuously.
Measures ACTUAL FRC — again only communicating lung.
Open circuit, no CO₂ absorber needed; DISTRIBUTION OF VENTILATION can be read off the graph. Assumes initial alveolar N₂ of 80% after ≥ 15 min on room air.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: BODY PLETHYSMOGRAPHY — how it works, what it measures, and when is it preferred?
cards.a:
BODY PLETHYSMOGRAPHY — how it works, what it measures, and when is it preferred?
The patient PANTS against a closed shutter in a sealed box; Boyle's law (P₁V₁ = P₂V₂) converts box pressure change to thoracic volume.
Measures TOTAL THORACIC GAS VOLUME (TGV) — ALL intrathoracic gas, communicating or NOT.
⚠ PREFERRED whenever AIR TRAPPING is suspected (bullous emphysema, severe COPD). Needs 3–5 acceptable panting maneuvers at ~1 cycle/sec. Claustrophobic patients may not tolerate it.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ The single tested sentence about FRC vs TGV
cards.a:
⚠ The single tested sentence about FRC vs TGV
'Normally, the FRC and TGV are EQUAL. A TGV that EXCEEDS FRC indicates the presence of TRAPPED GAS that is not in communication with the airways' — as seen in bullous emphysema and air-trapping.
Both dilution methods are repeatable to ±500 mL in adults, and both require starting at FRC with no leaks.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: The single-breath DLCO procedure (the one Heuer details)?
cards.a:
The single-breath DLCO procedure (the one Heuer details)?
Exhale to RV → inhale to TLC a mix of 21% O₂, 10% He, 0.3% CO → 10-second BREATH-HOLD → discard the first (anatomic dead space) portion → collect 0.5–1.0 L of expired gas for % He and % CO.
Repeat after ≥ 4 minutes until results agree within 5% or 3 mL/min/mm Hg.
Helium gives the alveolar volume (VA, an estimate of TLC); CO uptake gives the DLCO.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ The four phases of the single-breath N₂ washout — and where are they documented?
cards.a:
⚠ The four phases of the single-breath N₂ washout — and where are they documented?
Phase I = dead space gas · Phase II = mixed gas (dead space + alveolar) · Phase III = alveolar gas (the plateau) · Phase IV = closing volume.
⚠ NOT covered in Heuer or the available decks — this comes from Hess. The only 'Phase I–IV / alveolar plateau' material in Heuer is the CAPNOGRAM, not the N₂ curve.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: What does the slope of PHASE III tell you?
cards.a:
What does the slope of PHASE III tell you?
Both the slope of phase III and ΔN₂ between 750 and 1250 mL are indices of NON-UNIFORM ventilation.
A FLAT phase III = relatively UNIFORM gas distribution (normal < ~1.5–2% N₂/L).
As distribution becomes more heterogeneous, the slope STEEPENS — poorly ventilated units empty last and are N₂-rich. It steepens in COPD, asthma, bronchiectasis, CF, and with aging.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: What does PHASE IV mark — and what does an early Phase IV mean?
cards.a:
What does PHASE IV mark — and what does an early Phase IV mean?
The onset of AIRWAY CLOSURE in the dependent regions; the volume exhaled during phase IV is the CLOSING VOLUME.
An EARLY phase IV (large closing volume) means small airways are collapsing at a HIGHER-than-normal lung volume — the aging mechanism, and the reason dependent lung traps gas and PaO₂ drifts down.
With obstructive disease, BOTH the closing volume and the phase III slope increase.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ Don't confuse the N₂ curve with the CAPNOGRAM — what are the capnogram's phases?
cards.a:
⚠ Don't confuse the N₂ curve with the CAPNOGRAM — what are the capnogram's phases?
A–B = pure dead space, no CO₂.
B–C = dead space mixing with alveolar gas, CO₂ rising.
C–D = alveolar plateau — PetCO₂ is read at the END of the plateau.
D–E = inhalation of fresh gas, CO₂ falls to zero.
⚠ A clear alveolar plateau may NEVER appear in COPD, CHF, auto-PEEP, V/Q mismatch, and pulmonary emboli.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: What is a shunt — and why is its hypoxemia refractory?
cards.a:
What is a shunt — and why is its hypoxemia refractory?
PERFUSION WITHOUT VENTILATION — 'wasted blood.'
Blood flows past alveoli that get no air and leaves the lung essentially unchanged — which is why shunt produces REFRACTORY hypoxemia that does not respond to more FiO₂.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ Which shunt method is Heuer's — and which is the deck's?
cards.a:
⚠ Which shunt method is Heuer's — and which is the deck's?
Heuer gives ONLY the P(A−a)O₂ SHORTCUT (Box 4-2, App B Table B-2).
The classic CcO₂-based physiologic shunt equation does NOT appear anywhere in Heuer.
Learn both: Heuer's estimate for the NBRC, the classic equation from the deck for the RCP 203/105 exam.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Heuer's estimated-shunt shortcut — the rule and the three steps
cards.a:
Heuer's estimated-shunt shortcut — the rule and the three steps
RULE OF THUMB: breathing 100% O₂, every 100 torr of P(A−a)O₂ ≈ a 5% shunt.
Step 1 — PAO₂ = FiO₂ × (PB − 47) − (1.25 × PaCO₂)
Step 2 — P(A−a)O₂ = PAO₂ − PaO₂
Step 3 — % shunt = [P(A−a)O₂ ÷ 100] × 5
Box 4-2 assumes PaO₂ > 100 torr and C(a−v̄)O₂ = 5 mL/dL.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Worked (Box 4-2): patient on 100% O₂ with a P(A−a)O₂ of 300 torr
cards.a:
Worked (Box 4-2): patient on 100% O₂ with a P(A−a)O₂ of 300 torr
300 ÷ 100 = 3 → 3 × 5 = 15% shunt

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Worked full chain (B.9 + B.10): FiO₂ 1.0, PaO₂ 250, PaCO₂ 60, PB 760
cards.a:
Worked full chain (B.9 + B.10): FiO₂ 1.0, PaO₂ 250, PaCO₂ 60, PB 760
PAO₂ = 1.0 × (760 − 47) − (1.25 × 60) = 713 − 75 = 638 torr
P(A−a)O₂ = 638 − 250 = 388 torr
% shunt = (388 ÷ 100) × 5 = 19.4% → ~20% physiologic shunt

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: The CLASSIC physiologic shunt equation (deck, not Heuer)
cards.a:
The CLASSIC physiologic shunt equation (deck, not Heuer)
Qs/Qt = (CcO₂ − CaO₂) ÷ (CcO₂ − Cv̄O₂)
Where CcO₂ is the ideal END-CAPILLARY content, assumed 100% saturated.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Worked classic shunt: PaO₂ 60/SaO₂ 90%, Pv̄O₂ 40/Sv̄O₂ 75%, Hb 15, FiO₂ 1.0, PaCO₂ 40

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ Normal shunt fraction — the three-way conflict
cards.a:
⚠ Normal shunt fraction — the three-way conflict
RCP 203 Lssn 3a + RCP 105 Wk 1: typically < 5%.
RCP 105 Wk 3 Weaning: 10% or less is normal.
Heuer gives NO explicit 'normal shunt %' — it implies normal by giving P(A−a)O₂ on 100% O₂ = 25–65 torr as normal, which at 5% per 100 torr works out to ≈ 1–3% shunt; and it flags > 300 torr on 100% O₂ as 'severe shunting.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Shunt grading — and the weaning threshold?
cards.a:
Shunt grading — and the weaning threshold?
10–20% mild · 20–30% significant · > 30% critical/severe.
Qs/Qt must be < 20% before a weaning attempt (with P/F ≥ 150).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: The P/F ratio severity ladder (Heuer Table 4-10)?
cards.a:
The P/F ratio severity ladder (Heuer Table 4-10)?
Normal > 350–380
200–300 — V/Q mismatch / mild ARDS
100–200 — some shunting / moderate ARDS
< 100 — refractory hypoxemia, severe shunting / ARDS

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: The a/A ratio ladder?
cards.a:
The a/A ratio ladder?
Normal > 0.75
0.35–0.75 — hypoxemia, likely V/Q mismatch
< 0.35 — hypoxemia due to SHUNTING

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: The Oxygenation Index — formula and thresholds?
cards.a:
The Oxygenation Index — formula and thresholds?
OI = (FiO₂ × mean airway pressure × 100) ÷ PaO₂
Normal < 5–8 · > 8 ≈ P/F < 200 · > 20 severe (consider HFOV) · > 40 high mortality / ECMO indication.
Worked (B.13): OI = (1.0 × 20 × 100) ÷ 50 = 2000 ÷ 50 = 40.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: P(A−a)O₂ — the deck's full reference set?
cards.a:
P(A−a)O₂ — the deck's full reference set?
5–15 mm Hg on room air = normal · 25–65 mm Hg on 100% O₂ = normal.
66–300 mm Hg = V/Q mismatch → FiO₂ up to 60%.
> 300 mm Hg = SHUNTING → ventilate with PEEP.
Weaning criterion: P(A−a)O₂ < 350 mm Hg on FiO₂ 1.0.
Age-adjusted room-air normal = (age ÷ 4) + 4.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: What is CaO₂ — and Heuer's tested caution about PaO₂?
cards.a:
What is CaO₂ — and Heuer's tested caution about PaO₂?
The total oxygen carried in 100 mL (1 dL) of arterial blood — the big part bound to hemoglobin plus the small part dissolved in plasma.
⚠ 'Given that the PaO₂ represents only DISSOLVED oxygen, getting the full picture requires that you also consider both the Hb CONTENT and its SATURATION' — a severely anemic patient can have a normal SpO₂ and still be badly hypoxic.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: The oxygen content formulas — and which constant does Heuer use?
cards.a:
The oxygen content formulas — and which constant does Heuer use?
CaO₂ = (0.003 × PaO₂) + (total Hb × 1.36 × SaO₂)
Cv̄O₂ = (0.003 × Pv̄O₂) + (total Hb × 1.36 × Sv̄O₂)
C(a−v̄)O₂ = CaO₂ − Cv̄O₂
⚠ Heuer uses 1.36 mL O₂/g Hb; the RCP 105 decks use 1.34. Either is accepted — the difference is about 1.5% and will not change a multiple-choice answer.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Worked CaO₂ (B.12): Hb 10 g/dL, PaO₂ 50 torr, SaO₂ 80%
cards.a:
Worked CaO₂ (B.12): Hb 10 g/dL, PaO₂ 50 torr, SaO₂ 80%
Bound = 10 × 1.36 × 0.80 = 10.9 mL/dL
Dissolved = 0.003 × 50 = 0.15 mL/dL
CaO₂ = 11.05 mL/dL
Heuer's ballpark check: with SaO₂ > 75%, CaO₂ in mL/dL is always a bit LARGER than the Hb number but never more than 40% larger. (Hb 10 → expect 10–14. 11.05 passes.)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: The oxygenation normal ranges (Heuer Tables 4-9 and 4-11)
cards.a:
The oxygenation normal ranges (Heuer Tables 4-9 and 4-11)
PaO₂ 80–100 torr · SaO₂ 95–98% · CaO₂ 16–22 mL/dL
Pv̄O₂ 38–42 torr · Sv̄O₂ 68–77% · Cv̄O₂ 14–16 mL/dL
Hb: M 13.5–16.5 g/dL; F 12.0–15 g/dL

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ The normal C(a−v̄)O₂ — how do you say it on the exam?
cards.a:
⚠ The normal C(a−v̄)O₂ — how do you say it on the exam?
'Normally, C(a−v̄)O₂ is LESS THAN 7.0 mL/dL' — and the value assumed in practice (Box 4-2) is about 5 mL/dL.
(The conventionally taught 4–5 mL/dL range sits comfortably inside Heuer's '< 7.0.')

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: What makes C(a−v̄)O₂ widen or narrow?
cards.a:
What makes C(a−v̄)O₂ widen or narrow?
'C(a−v̄)O₂ will INCREASE if O₂ CONSUMPTION increases or CARDIAC OUTPUT decreases. In contrast, it DECREASES when oxygen consumption falls or cardiac output increases.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: A WIDE C(a−v̄)O₂ (> 7 mL/dL) — what does it mean and what causes it?
cards.a:
A WIDE C(a−v̄)O₂ (> 7 mL/dL) — what does it mean and what causes it?
Tissues are stripping MORE O₂ out of each 100 mL because DELIVERY has fallen or DEMAND has risen.
Delivery side: ↓Hb (anemia, hemorrhage) · ↓PaO₂/SaO₂ (hypoxemia, suctioning) · ↓CO (hypovolemia, shock, arrhythmias).
Demand side: hyperthermia, trauma/burns, shivering, seizures.
Travels with a RISING O₂ER and a FALLING Sv̄O₂.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ Cyanide poisoning and sepsis — the Sv̄O₂ trap
cards.a:
⚠ Cyanide poisoning and sepsis — the Sv̄O₂ trap
Sv̄O₂ can be HIGHER than normal even though tissue hypoxia is present — the cells CANNOT USE the oxygen.
For those patients Heuer says MIXED VENOUS LACTATE is the better indicator of tissue oxygenation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: How do you draw a true mixed venous sample?
cards.a:
How do you draw a true mixed venous sample?
Slowly from the DISTAL port of a PULMONARY ARTERY catheter with the BALLOON DEFLATED.
A CVP line sample is an acceptable alternative but typically reads slightly LOWER.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Heuer's tissue-oxygenation thresholds?
cards.a:
Heuer's tissue-oxygenation thresholds?
Sv̄O₂ < 50% or Pv̄O₂ < 27 torr = IMPAIRED TISSUE OXYGENATION.
Sv̄O₂ < 30% (Pv̄O₂ ≈ 20 torr) can cause UNCONSCIOUSNESS and PERMANENT ORGAN DAMAGE.
Deck warning: an ABG that was supposed to be arterial but 'looks mixed venous' usually means the SAMPLE IS BAD.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Define V/Q mismatch, shunt and dead space — and the deck's memory line
cards.a:
Define V/Q mismatch, shunt and dead space — and the deck's memory line
V/Q mismatch: ventilation and perfusion both present but NOT MATCHED. The most common cause of hypoxemia.
Shunt: the extreme low-V/Q end — perfusion with NO ventilation.
Dead space: the mirror image — ventilation with NO perfusion.
'Dead space is wasted AIR. Shunt is wasted BLOOD.'
The four classic causes of hypoxemia: hypoventilation, V/Q mismatch, shunt, diffusion defect.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ Heuer's 60/60 rule — and why 50/50 is equivalent
cards.a:
⚠ Heuer's 60/60 rule — and why 50/50 is equivalent
PaO₂ > 60 torr on FiO₂ < 0.60 → V/Q IMBALANCE. Moderate hypoxemia; 'usually responds well to simple O₂ therapy.' ACTION: O₂ + treat the underlying cause.
PaO₂ < 60 torr on FiO₂ > 0.60 → SEVERE SHUNTING (likely ARDS). Refractory; more FiO₂ 'will do little good and may potentially harm (oxygen toxicity).' ACTION: O₂ PLUS PEEP or CPAP to reopen unventilated alveoli.
Both 60/60 and 50/50 represent a P/F ratio of 100 — so they are equivalent.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: DEAD SPACE — causes, and how does it respond to O₂?
cards.a:
DEAD SPACE — causes, and how does it respond to O₂?
Causes: PE (the board answer), severe hypotension, cardiogenic shock, cardiac arrest, alveoli overdistended by excessive PEEP; mechanical dead space (rising capnogram baseline).
O₂ does NOT fix it — VENTILATION, not oxygenation, is the problem; PaCO₂ RISES.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: What numbers identify dead space?
cards.a:
What numbers identify dead space?
VD/VT normal 0.25–0.35 (Heuer Table 1-15) or 0.30–0.70 (App B ballpark); critical > 0.6–0.7.
PaCO₂ − PECO₂ > 15–20 torr = large dead space.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: The dead space formulas?
cards.a:
The dead space formulas?
Physiologic dead space (Bohr): VD = VT × [(PaCO₂ − PECO₂) ÷ PaCO₂]
Anatomic dead space rule: assume 1 mL per POUND of predicted body weight.
Alveolar ventilation: V̇A = f × (VT − VD)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Worked (B.3): VT 450 mL, PaCO₂ 60, PECO₂ 30
cards.a:
Worked (B.3): VT 450 mL, PaCO₂ 60, PECO₂ 30
VD = 450 × [(60 − 30) ÷ 60] = 450 × 0.5 = 225 mL

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Worked (B.4): 6-ft, 170-lb patient with normal lungs, VT 600 mL
cards.a:
Worked (B.4): 6-ft, 170-lb patient with normal lungs, VT 600 mL
VD = 1 mL/lb × 170 lb = 170 mL
VD/VT = 170 ÷ 600 = 0.28 (normal)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ Why is rapid shallow breathing bad — in one calculation?
cards.a:
⚠ Why is rapid shallow breathing bad — in one calculation?
Same VD, smaller VT:
150 ÷ 500 = 30% but 150 ÷ 300 = 50%
The anatomic dead space is FIXED, so as VT falls, the dead-space FRACTION climbs.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Worked (B.5): alveolar ventilation at f 15, VT 680 mL, VD 200 mL
cards.a:
Worked (B.5): alveolar ventilation at f 15, VT 680 mL, VD 200 mL
V̇A = 15 × (680 − 200) = 15 × 480 = 7.2 L/min

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Which mechanism of hypoxemia is LEAST responsive to oxygen therapy — and why?
cards.a:
Which mechanism of hypoxemia is LEAST responsive to oxygen therapy — and why?
INTRAPULMONARY SHUNT — because oxygen cannot enter alveoli that are not being ventilated.
Needs recruitment: PEEP/CPAP, plus positioning (e.g. proning) to decrease shunting.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: MIP vs MEP — what does each measure?
cards.a:
MIP vs MEP — what does each measure?
MIP (Maximal Inspiratory Pressure), also NIF: INSPIRATORY muscle strength — especially the DIAPHRAGM.
MEP (Maximal Expiratory Pressure): EXPIRATORY muscle strength — the COUGH.
Deck framing: MIP asks 'how STRONG are the breathing muscles?' while VC asks 'how MUCH air can the lungs move?' — successful weaning requires both.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ Does the patient have to be awake for MIP and MEP — the conflict
cards.a:
⚠ Does the patient have to be awake for MIP and MEP — the conflict
Heuer Ch 3: for MIP, the one-way-valve setup ensures maximum effort so 'the patient NEED NOT be conscious.' For MEP, the opposite: 'does NOT require a one-way valve and can ONLY be measured on an alert and cooperative patient.'
RCP 203 Lssn 2b: 'You can only measure MIP and MEP on an alert and cooperative patient.'
Resolution: MEP definitely requires alert and cooperative (both agree). For MIP, go with Heuer — obtainable in an unconscious patient — unless the question is drawn straight off the slide.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Why does a ventilated patient sometimes need time OFF the vent before an MIP?
cards.a:
Why does a ventilated patient sometimes need time OFF the vent before an MIP?
To induce the mild HYPOXIA and HYPERCAPNIA that drive maximal effort.
Because the maneuver can cause anxiety in alert patients, give a careful and reassuring explanation first. The more NEGATIVE the number, the STRONGER the muscles.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ Intubation criteria for Guillain-Barré or myasthenia gravis?
cards.a:
⚠ Intubation criteria for Guillain-Barré or myasthenia gravis?
MIP/NIF less negative than −25 cm H₂O, OR MEP < 40 cm H₂O (or rapidly declining), together with VC < 1.0 L or < 15 mL/kg.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ The MIP normal-value conflict — how do you resolve it?
cards.a:
⚠ The MIP normal-value conflict — how do you resolve it?
Heuer Ch 1 + RCP 105 Weaning deck: normal is −80 to −100 cm H₂O.
RCP 203 Lssn 2b: 'normal NIF is > −60.'
Resolution: −80 to −100 is the TEXTBOOK normal; anything weaker than −60 is abnormal; weaker than −20 to −25 means the patient CANNOT SUSTAIN spontaneous ventilation.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ The MIP wording trap the decks call out?
cards.a:
⚠ The MIP wording trap the decks call out?
Some books write '≥ −20 to −30' because they mean the MAGNITUDE — 'the patient should generate at least 20–30 cm H₂O of negative pressure' — which as a signed measurement is −20, −30, −40, −50 …

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: MIP values that predict weaning — the study numbers?
cards.a:
MIP values that predict weaning — the study numbers?
Weaning likely successful if MIP is at least −30 cm H₂O.
Across 11 studies, MIP averaged −37 cm H₂O in WEANED vs −30 cm H₂O in NON-weaned patients.
Weaning readiness per the deck: −20 to −30 cm H₂O generated in 20 sec.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Heuer's ABG normals?
cards.a:
Heuer's ABG normals?
pH 7.35–7.45 · PaCO₂ 35–45 torr · PaO₂ 80–100 torr · HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mEq/L · BE 0 ± 2 · SaO₂ 95–98%.
Baseline to start from: pH 7.40 / PaCO₂ 40 / HCO₃⁻ 24.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Heuer's four-step ABG method?
cards.a:
Heuer's four-step ABG method?
(1) Categorize the pH. (2) Determine RESPIRATORY involvement (PaCO₂). (3) Determine METABOLIC involvement (HCO₃⁻). (4) Assess for COMPENSATION.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Primary disturbance from pH + PaCO₂ alone?
cards.a:
Primary disturbance from pH + PaCO₂ alone?
pH < 7.35 with PaCO₂ > 45 → RESPIRATORY acidosis
pH < 7.35 with PaCO₂ ≤ 45 → METABOLIC acidosis
pH > 7.45 with PaCO₂ < 35 → RESPIRATORY alkalosis
pH > 7.45 with PaCO₂ ≥ 35 → METABOLIC alkalosis

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ Heuer's compensation rule — it's a BASE-EXCESS method
cards.a:
⚠ Heuer's compensation rule — it's a BASE-EXCESS method
COMPENSATION IS OCCURRING if the PaCO₂ and BE are BOTH abnormally high or BOTH abnormally low.
Then use the pH to name the primary problem:
pH < 7.40 → the primary problem is the one causing ACIDOSIS.
pH > 7.40 → the primary problem is the one causing ALKALOSIS.
FULL vs PARTIAL: pH back inside 7.35–7.45 = FULL; still outside = PARTIAL.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: How do you spot a COMBINED disturbance with the BE method?
cards.a:
How do you spot a COMBINED disturbance with the BE method?
The PaCO₂ and BE DIVERGE in opposite directions:
HIGH PaCO₂ + LOW BE = combined respiratory AND metabolic ACIDOSIS.
LOW PaCO₂ + HIGH BE = combined respiratory AND metabolic ALKALOSIS.
BE > +2 = base gain (metabolic alkalosis); BE < −2 = base deficit (metabolic acidosis).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ Compensation SPEED — and what does a slow lung response mean?
cards.a:
⚠ Compensation SPEED — and what does a slow lung response mean?
Renal/metabolic compensation for a RESPIRATORY problem is SLOW (hours to DAYS) — this is why 'acute' gases have a near-normal HCO₃⁻.
