Respiratory compensation for a METABOLIC problem is FAST (MINUTES).
'A failure of the lungs to QUICKLY compensate for a primary renal/metabolic acid-base disturbance indicates IMPAIRED PULMONARY FUNCTION.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: The deck's numeric rules of thumb for respiratory changes?
cards.a:
The deck's numeric rules of thumb for respiratory changes?
For every 10 mm Hg RISE in PaCO₂: pH falls ~0.06 and HCO₃⁻ rises ~1 mEq/L.
For every 20 mm Hg rise: pH falls ~0.12 and HCO₃⁻ rises ~2 mEq/L.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: The deck's numeric rules of thumb for metabolic changes?
cards.a:
The deck's numeric rules of thumb for metabolic changes?
For every 1 mEq/L FALL in HCO₃⁻, PaCO₂ should fall ~1.2 mm Hg (begins within the first hour, complete by 12–24 hours).
For every 1 mEq/L RISE in HCO₃⁻, PaCO₂ rises ~0.7 mm Hg.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Worked compensation check: PaCO₂ rises acutely from 40 to 60 — what do you expect?
cards.a:
Worked compensation check: PaCO₂ rises acutely from 40 to 60 — what do you expect?
ΔPaCO₂ = 20 → 2 increments
pH: 2 × 0.06 = 0.12 → 7.40 − 0.12 = 7.28 expected
HCO₃⁻: 2 × 1 = 2 → 24 + 2 = 26 expected
⚠ If the measured pH AND HCO₃⁻ are BOTH LOWER than predicted, suspect an added METABOLIC (lactic) acidosis layered on top.
Heuer's version of the same catch: PaCO₂ high + BE low = COMBINED acidosis.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ACUTE (uncompensated) respiratory acidosis — the picture and an example gas?
cards.a:
ACUTE (uncompensated) respiratory acidosis — the picture and an example gas?
pH < 7.35 · PaCO₂ > 45 · HCO₃⁻ NORMAL (the kidneys have not moved yet).
Heuer Box 4-1: pH 7.22 / PCO₂ 65 / HCO₃⁻ 26 / BE −1.
Deck: pH 7.14 / PaCO₂ 105 / HCO₃⁻ 26 / PaO₂ 36 — opioid overdose, RR 6.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: CHRONIC / fully compensated respiratory acidosis — the picture?
cards.a:
CHRONIC / fully compensated respiratory acidosis — the picture?
pH NORMAL but on the ACID side (7.35–7.40) · PaCO₂ increased · HCO₃⁻ MARKEDLY increased (> 26, BE > +2).
Heuer Box 4-1: pH 7.35 / PCO₂ 62 / HCO₃⁻ 33 / BE +7.
Heuer Table 1-5 (COPD): pH 7.36 / PaCO₂ 58 / PaO₂ 62 RA / HCO₃⁻ 34 / BE +7.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ACUTE respiratory alkalosis — the picture and Heuer's key example?
cards.a:
ACUTE respiratory alkalosis — the picture and Heuer's key example?
pH > 7.45 · PaCO₂ < 35 · HCO₃⁻ normal.
Heuer Table 1-5: pH 7.53 / PaCO₂ 27 / PaO₂ 53 on 2 L/min / HCO₃⁻ 22 / BE −7 — pneumonia, asthma, PE: 'the alkalosis is the RESULT of hyperventilation due to the HYPOXEMIA.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ CHRONIC / compensated respiratory alkalosis — why is there no printed example?
cards.a:
⚠ CHRONIC / compensated respiratory alkalosis — why is there no printed example?
No worked example is printed in Heuer or in the RCP 203/103 decks.
Build it from Heuer's own rules: a LOW PaCO₂ with a LOW BE, both abnormal in the same direction = compensation occurring; pH > 7.40 = the primary problem is the alkalosis.
Typical constructed set: pH 7.44 / PaCO₂ 28 / HCO₃⁻ 19 / BE −5 — chronic hyperventilation of high altitude, pregnancy, chronic liver disease, or CNS disease.
Nearest printed confirmation: RCP 105 deck — 'in compensated respiratory alkalosis the pH is on the alkalotic side of normal (7.41 to 7.45).'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: METABOLIC acidosis — the picture and examples?
cards.a:
METABOLIC acidosis — the picture and examples?
pH decreased · PaCO₂ normal or ↓ (compensating FAST) · HCO₃⁻ decreased (< 22, BE < −2).
Heuer Box 4-1 (partially compensated): pH 7.32 / PCO₂ 24 / HCO₃⁻ 12 / BE −13.
Heuer Table 1-5 (DKA): pH 7.32 / PaCO₂ 28 / HCO₃⁻ 14 / BE −10.
Deck severe DKA: pH 6.98 / PaCO₂ 24 / HCO₃⁻ 6 — Kussmaul breathing.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: METABOLIC alkalosis — the picture and Heuer's treatment cue?
cards.a:
METABOLIC alkalosis — the picture and Heuer's treatment cue?
pH increased · PaCO₂ normal or ↑ (compensating) · HCO₃⁻ increased (> 26, BE > +2).
Heuer's treatment cue: HYPOKALEMIA → give potassium; HYPOCHLOREMIA → give chloride.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: COMBINED respiratory + metabolic acidosis — example gases?
cards.a:
COMBINED respiratory + metabolic acidosis — example gases?
pH very low · PaCO₂ high · HCO₃⁻/BE low (they DIVERGE).
Heuer Box 4-1: pH 6.90 / PCO₂ 100 / HCO₃⁻ 19 / BE −12.
Heuer Table 1-5 (cardiopulmonary arrest): pH 7.05 / PaCO₂ 60 / PaO₂ 39 RA / HCO₃⁻ 16 / BE −8.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ Acute-on-chronic ventilatory failure vs acute hyperventilation on chronic — the two deck gases
cards.a:
⚠ Acute-on-chronic ventilatory failure vs acute hyperventilation on chronic — the two deck gases
ACUTE ON CHRONIC ventilatory failure: pH 7.28 / PaCO₂ 99 / HCO₃⁻ 44 / PaO₂ 39 — compare to the patient's baseline 7.36 / 77 / 43 / 61.
ACUTE ALVEOLAR HYPERVENTILATION on chronic ventilatory failure: pH 7.51 / PaCO₂ 52 / HCO₃⁻ 40 / PaO₂ 49 — it LOOKS like partly compensated metabolic alkalosis; the MARKED HYPOXEMIA is the giveaway.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Hypoxemia severity on room air?
cards.a:
Hypoxemia severity on room air?
Mild PaO₂ 60–79 torr · Moderate 40–59 torr · Severe < 40 torr.
⚠ But a PaO₂ < 60 on FiO₂ ≥ 0.60 is SEVERE regardless.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.a:
The 40–50–60 / 70–80–90 rule?
PaO₂ 40 torr ≈ SaO₂ 70%
PaO₂ 50 torr ≈ SaO₂ 80%
PaO₂ 60 torr ≈ SaO₂ 90% ← the clinically critical pair
RCP 203 adds the qualifier '(when SpO₂ is < 90%)' — the rule is a LOWER-END approximation and flattens out above 90%.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: How does Heuer define documented hypoxemia — and the weaning criterion?
cards.a:
How does Heuer define documented hypoxemia — and the weaning criterion?
Adults: PaO₂ < 60 torr or SaO₂ < 90%. Infants: PaO₂ < 50 torr.
An SpO₂ < 90% on ANY FiO₂ indicates the need for supplemental O₂.
Oxygenation weaning criterion: PaO₂ > 60 mmHg / SaO₂ > 90% on FiO₂ ≤ 0.40.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Normal SpO₂ values and what counts as an abnormal decline?
cards.a:
Normal SpO₂ values and what counts as an abnormal decline?
Normal on room air > 93–95% (reference range 95–98%); below 88–90% on any FiO₂ indicates arterial hypoxemia.
Declines of more than 4–5% during exercise or sleep are abnormal.
Oximeters are accurate to ±2–4% with good perfusion.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Normal COHb and metHb — and when must you use hemoximetry?
cards.a:
Normal COHb and metHb — and when must you use hemoximetry?
Normal COHb < 1.5% (3–6% in smokers/city dwellers); normal metHb < 1.5%.
Always use hemoximetry (CO-oximetry) when accurate SaO₂ measurement is essential — SpO₂ OVERestimates true saturation when HbCO is present.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Dual (pre-/postductal) oximetry screening for CCHD?
cards.a:
Dual (pre-/postductal) oximetry screening for CCHD?
Suspect a critical congenital heart defect if BOTH right-hand and foot SpO₂ are < 95%, OR the difference is ≥ 3%.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Normal PaO₂ by age — and where does the decline stop?
cards.a:
Normal PaO₂ by age — and where does the decline stop?
Normal PaO₂ on room air = 100 − (age ÷ 3).
Worked: a 70-year-old → 100 − 23 = 77 torr.
⚠ But the age-related decline LEVELS OFF at 70–75 years, so 75–80 torr is the lower limit of normal for essentially ALL adults at sea level.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: The 5× rule — and its alveolar companion?
cards.a:
The 5× rule — and its alveolar companion?
PaO₂ should be at least 5 × the O₂%. On 50% expect ≈ 250 torr; on 100% expect ≈ 500 torr.
Companion alveolar rule: PAO₂ ≈ 6 × O₂%.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: How much does PaO₂ fall with altitude?
cards.a:
How much does PaO₂ fall with altitude?
About 5 torr per 1,000 ft (up to 10,000 ft).
Worked — Denver at 5,000 ft: 100 − (5 × 5) = 75 torr.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Normal adult inspiratory flow — and Heuer's high-flow benchmark?
cards.a:
Normal adult inspiratory flow — and Heuer's high-flow benchmark?
40–60 L/min. That is the number to compare every calculated answer against.
Heuer: to guarantee a stable FiO₂, a high-flow O₂ system must deliver a total flow of at least 40 L/min — 'because the higher the FiO₂, the higher the input flow required to meet the patient's inspiratory demand.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Heuer's three-step inspiratory flow formula (Box 13-1)?
cards.a:
Heuer's three-step inspiratory flow formula (Box 13-1)?
STEP 1: V̇E = f × VT
STEP 2: %I-time = I part ÷ (I part + E part)
STEP 3: Inspiratory flow (L/min) = V̇E ÷ %I-time (use the DECIMAL)

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Worked (Box 13-1): apneic patient, VC A/C, f 15, VT 600 mL, I:E 1:4 — what flow?
cards.a:
Worked (Box 13-1): apneic patient, VC A/C, f 15, VT 600 mL, I:E 1:4 — what flow?
Step 1: V̇E = 15 × 600 mL = 9,000 mL/min = 9 L/min
Step 2: 1:4 → 1 ÷ (1 + 4) = 0.20 (20% I-time)
Step 3: 9 ÷ 0.20 = 45 L/min
Squarely inside the normal 40–60 L/min range. ✔

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: The quick %I-time conversions?

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Cross-check using time: 45 L/min, VT 0.6 L, f 15
cards.a:
Cross-check using time: 45 L/min, VT 0.6 L, f 15
Flow: 45 ÷ 60 = 0.75 L/sec
Ti = 0.6 ÷ 0.75 = 0.8 sec
Total cycle = 60 ÷ 15 = 4.0 sec → Te = 4.0 − 0.8 = 3.2 sec
I:E = 0.8 : 3.2 = 1:4 ✔

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: ⚠ Why does insufficient inspiratory flow cause auto-PEEP — and what's the fix?
cards.a:
⚠ Why does insufficient inspiratory flow cause auto-PEEP — and what's the fix?
Insufficient flow produces a LONG inspiratory time, which SHORTENS expiratory time and causes air trapping / auto-PEEP.
Heuer: patients with severe expiratory airflow obstruction breathe spontaneously at I:E ratios of 1:4 or 1:5, and if you do not match that, auto-PEEP will occur.
The fix: DECREASE the I:E ratio by increasing E-time and decreasing I-time — that is, by RAISING the inspiratory flow. Normal I:E is 1:2 to 1:4.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: Airway resistance thresholds — deck vs Heuer, and the ETT's own contribution?
cards.a:
Airway resistance thresholds — deck vs Heuer, and the ETT's own contribution?
Normal (deck): 0.6–2.4 cm H₂O/L/sec (≈ 1–3).
Heuer Ch 1: values above 5–9 cm H₂O/L/sec are associated with obstruction.
Deck thresholds: Raw > 5 → airway obstruction; Raw > 10 → severe bronchospasm, mucus plugging, kinked/obstructed ETT.
⚠ Heuer adds: an ETT itself adds at least 4–6 cm H₂O/L/sec to total resistance.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::08 PFTs, Lung Volumes, Shunt & Oxygenation
cards.q: If a patient's inspiratory demand outruns the device — the three options?
cards.a:
If a patient's inspiratory demand outruns the device — the three options?
Recommend a HIGH-FLOW NASAL CANNULA at 20–40 L/min · add a second air-entrainment nebulizer in tandem · bleed in supplemental O₂.
Note also that a DPI requires the patient to generate > 60 L/min of inspiratory flow.

cards.q: Capnometry vs capnography vs capnogram?
cards.a:
Capnometry vs capnography vs capnogram?
Capnometry = the CO₂ NUMBER.
Capnography = number + WAVEFORM.
Capnogram = the actual WAVEFORM.

cards.q: The four phases of the capnogram
cards.a:
The four phases of the capnogram
Phase I (A–B): exhalation of pure anatomic deadspace gas, PCO₂ near 0.
Phase II (B–C): rapid upstroke as deadspace mixes with alveolar gas.
Phase III (C–D): the ALVEOLAR PLATEAU — pure alveolar gas. PETCO₂ is measured at the very END of this plateau.
Phase IV (D–E): inspiratory downstroke, CO₂ falls back to zero.

cards.q: ⚠ What must a good capnogram tracing have — and what does its absence mean?
cards.a:
⚠ What must a good capnogram tracing have — and what does its absence mean?
A ZERO INSPIRATORY BASELINE (PETCO₂ = 0 torr).
If the baseline does NOT return to zero, think CO₂ REBREATHING or a circuit/equipment problem.

cards.q: The abnormal capnogram shapes the decks name?
cards.a:
The abnormal capnogram shapes the decks name?
Bronchospasm/obstructive tracing — a sloping, blunted upstroke and plateau rather than a square wave.
Kinked or obstructed ET tube — PETCO₂ falls in proportion to the obstruction and reads ZERO with complete obstruction.
Sudden loss of waveform AND numbers = circuit DISCONNECTION.
Sudden proportional drop = cardiac arrest from failed lung perfusion.

cards.q: Are 'shark fin' and 'curare cleft' used in your decks?
cards.a:
Are 'shark fin' and 'curare cleft' used in your decks?
No — the decks describe only the bronchospasm tracing. Look up 'curare cleft' (spontaneous effort against a paralytic wearing off) in Chang Fig. 9-13 / Persing Ch 4.

cards.q: MAINSTREAM capnography sensor — advantages and disadvantages?
cards.a:
MAINSTREAM capnography sensor — advantages and disadvantages?
Sits directly in the circuit on an ET-tube adaptor.
Advantages: FAST response time; water condensation does NOT affect it.
Disadvantages: excess WEIGHT on the ET tube · added circuit DEADSPACE · inaccuracy from SECRETIONS on the cell windows · must be manually disconnected to suction.

cards.q: SIDESTREAM (aspirating) sensor — advantages and disadvantages?
cards.a:
SIDESTREAM (aspirating) sensor — advantages and disadvantages?
Analyzer stays inside the monitor; draws a sample through small-bore tubing.
Advantages: easy handling; can attach to a CANNULA or MASK, not just an ET tube.
Disadvantages: secretions/water OCCLUDING the sample line · equipment contamination · a lag time a few tenths of a second longer than mainstream (clinically negligible).

cards.q: Capnography setup and example alarm settings?
cards.a:
Capnography setup and example alarm settings?
Calibrate per manufacturer · complete the power-on self-test · confirm a zero inspiratory baseline · compare the reading against a current PaCO₂ · set alarms.
Example (per protocol): PETCO₂ high 50–55 torr, low 25–30 torr; RR 7–35/min for adults; apnea alarm 20–30 sec.

cards.q: ETCO₂ drops SUDDENLY TO ZERO — the three causes?
cards.a:
ETCO₂ drops SUDDENLY TO ZERO — the three causes?
Ventilator/circuit DISCONNECTION (immediate disappearance of values and waveform) · complete ET tube obstruction/kink · ESOPHAGEAL INTUBATION.
Waveform capnography is the GOLD STANDARD for confirming tracheal placement.

cards.q: ⚠ ETCO₂ decreases suddenly but NOT to zero — causes, and the trap?
cards.a:
⚠ ETCO₂ decreases suddenly but NOT to zero — causes, and the trap?
Cardiac arrest / falling cardiac output — values drop suddenly and proportionally because lung perfusion is inadequate · partial ET tube obstruction or kink · increased alveolar deadspace (e.g. pulmonary embolism).
⚠ This is NOT an improvement in ventilation — so do NOT lower the ventilator rate.

cards.q: ETCO₂ increases GRADUALLY — causes?
cards.a:
ETCO₂ increases GRADUALLY — causes?
Hypoventilation trend (rising PaCO₂ — confirm with ABG) · increased CO₂ production / rising metabolic rate.
A baseline that rises off zero indicates REBREATHING in the circuit.

cards.q: ETCO₂ decreases GRADUALLY — causes, and the CPR numbers?
cards.a:
ETCO₂ decreases GRADUALLY — causes, and the CPR numbers?
Hyperventilation trend (falling PaCO₂) · rising physiologic deadspace / worsening V/Q · falling cardiac output or lung perfusion.
During CPR: PETCO₂ < 10 torr means poor or absent pulmonary blood flow; a RISE in PETCO₂ signals EFFECTIVE COMPRESSIONS or ROSC.

cards.q: Why is PETCO₂ normally LOWER than PaCO₂?
cards.a:
Why is PETCO₂ normally LOWER than PaCO₂?
Because exhaled gas is DILUTED BY DEADSPACE GAS.

cards.q: ⚠ The P(a−et)CO₂ gradient — the two-deck conflict
cards.a:
⚠ The P(a−et)CO₂ gradient — the two-deck conflict
Chang: normal gradient is about 2 mm Hg in normal individuals, with 5 mm Hg considered acceptable in critically ill patients.
RCP 203 (Persing): 1–5 torr.
Normal values: PaCO₂ ≈ 35–45 mm Hg, PETCO₂ ≈ 30–43 mm Hg.

cards.q: What WIDENS the PaCO₂–PETCO₂ gradient?
cards.a:
What WIDENS the PaCO₂–PETCO₂ gradient?
Primarily ALVEOLAR DEADSPACE ventilation — classically PULMONARY EMBOLISM.
Also old age, presence of pulmonary disease, and changes in mechanical tidal volume and ventilator modality.

cards.q: ⚠ Why is PETCO₂ called a 'static measure' — and the clinical consequence?
cards.a:
⚠ Why is PETCO₂ called a 'static measure' — and the clinical consequence?
A fall in PETCO₂ caused by DEADSPACE does NOT mean ventilation improved — so the ventilator frequency must NOT be reduced on that basis.
Once a good PaCO₂-to-PETCO₂ correlation is established for a given patient, the number of routine ABGs can be reduced.

cards.q: Why does invasive hemodynamic monitoring work — the physics?
cards.a:
Why does invasive hemodynamic monitoring work — the physics?
Liquid is NONCOMPRESSIBLE, and pressure applied at one point in a fluid-filled closed system is transmitted EQUALLY to every other point at the SAME LEVEL. A transducer converts that pressure signal into an electronic signal.
Values are reported in mm Hg in the U.S. (kPa under SI).

cards.q: ⚠ Where do you level the transducer, and when do you read CVP and PAWP?
cards.a:
⚠ Where do you level the transducer, and when do you read CVP and PAWP?
Level to the PHLEBOSTATIC AXIS — 4th intercostal space, MIDAXILLARY line.
Read CVP and PAWP at END-EXPIRATION.
⚠ Do NOT remove the patient from PEEP/CPAP to measure.

cards.q: How do you correct a reading for high PEEP?
cards.a:
How do you correct a reading for high PEEP?
If PEEP ≤ 10 cm H₂O: just read at end-expiration.
If PEEP > 10 cm H₂O: Corrected pressure = Measured pressure − [0.5 × (PEEP ÷ 1.36)].

cards.q: ⚠ CVP normal — the deck conflict, and RAP?
cards.a:
⚠ CVP normal — the deck conflict, and RAP?
Chang: CVP (vena cava) 0–6 mm Hg mean.
RCP 103 Clinical Data: 2–6 mm Hg.
Right atrial pressure (RAP): 2–7 mm Hg — slightly higher than the vena cava CVP.

cards.q: RV and PA pressures — normals?
cards.a:
RV and PA pressures — normals?
RV systolic 15–30 · RV diastolic 2–8 mm Hg.
PAP systolic/diastolic 15–25 / 6–12 mm Hg.
Mean PAP 10–20 mm Hg.

cards.q: What defines pulmonary hypertension?
cards.a:
What defines pulmonary hypertension?
Mean PAP > 25 mm Hg at rest (> 30 mm Hg on exertion), or PAP systolic > 35 mm Hg.

cards.q: ⚠ PCWP normal — the deck conflict
cards.a:
⚠ PCWP normal — the deck conflict
Chang slide 23: 8–12 mm Hg.
Slide 21 note: 6–12 mm Hg. Some sources: 4–12 mm Hg.
The decks conflict — know all three.

cards.q: Cardiac output, cardiac index and stroke volume — normals and formulas?
cards.a:
Cardiac output, cardiac index and stroke volume — normals and formulas?
CO: 4–8 L/min (thermodilution).
CI = CO ÷ BSA; normal 2.5–3.5 L/min/m².
SV = CO (mL/min) ÷ HR; normal 60–130 mL/beat.
SVI = SV ÷ BSA — no normal range given in the decks.

cards.q: SVR and PVR — formulas and normals?
cards.a:
SVR and PVR — formulas and normals?
SVR = [(MAP − CVP) ÷ CO] × 80; normal 900–1400 dynes·sec/cm⁵ (15–20 Wood units).
PVR = [(MPAP − PAWP) ÷ CO] × 80; normal 110–250 dynes·sec/cm⁵.

cards.q: Arterial BP, MAP thresholds and pulse pressure?
cards.a:
Arterial BP, MAP thresholds and pulse pressure?
BP: systolic 100–140, diastolic 60–90 mm Hg (RCP 103: systolic 110–140).
MAP ≥ 60 mm Hg needed for TISSUE perfusion; MAP ≥ 70 mm Hg needed to maintain CEREBRAL perfusion pressure.
Pulse pressure 30–40 mm Hg — wide > 40, narrow < 30.

cards.q: ⚠ Why does a rising CVP LOWER cardiac output?
cards.a:
⚠ Why does a rising CVP LOWER cardiac output?
Because venous return = MAP − CVP.
A rising CVP NARROWS that gradient, so venous return falls, ventricular output falls, and cardiac output falls.

cards.q: What raises and lowers the CVP/RAP?
cards.a:
What raises and lowers the CVP/RAP?
CVP/RAP is the right-heart filling pressure — RV PRELOAD.
RISES with: positive pressure ventilation · right ventricular failure (cor pulmonale from chronic pulmonary hypertension, right-sided MI) · fluid overload.
FALLS with: HYPOVOLEMIA.

cards.q: What raises and lowers the PAP?
cards.a:
What raises and lowers the PAP?
RISES with: mechanical ventilation and PEEP · increased PVR · left ventricular dysfunction or failure · mitral valve disease.
FALLS with: hypovolemia.
Ventilator effects are variable and depend on PIP, PEEP, compliance and hemodynamic status.

cards.q: ⚠ PCWP and the cardiogenic vs non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema split
cards.a:
⚠ PCWP and the cardiogenic vs non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema split
PCWP estimates LEFT ATRIAL pressure and LV preload (LVEDP).
PCWP ≥ 18 mm Hg with a near-normal PAP = LEFT VENTRICULAR DYSFUNCTION / left heart failure.
CARDIOGENIC pulmonary edema: PCWP > 18 mm Hg.
NON-CARDIOGENIC (ARDS, increased capillary permeability, acute pulmonary hypertension): PCWP NORMAL or LOW (< 18).
Mitral stenosis or regurgitation also elevate PCWP.

cards.q: The four preload/afterload surrogates?
cards.a:
The four preload/afterload surrogates?
CVP = RV PRELOAD · PCWP = LV PRELOAD · PVR = RV AFTERLOAD · SVR = LV AFTERLOAD.

cards.q: What lowers CO/SV — and what elevates SVR vs PVR?
cards.a:
What lowers CO/SV — and what elevates SVR vs PVR?
CO/SV fall with: low contractility · decreased preload (hypovolemia, shock) · increased afterload (downstream obstruction, hypervolemia).
SVR is elevated in systemic HYPERTENSION.
PVR is elevated in PULMONARY HYPERTENSION and LEFT HEART OBSTRUCTION.

cards.q: SvO₂ — normal, and what makes it FALL?
cards.a:
SvO₂ — normal, and what makes it FALL?
Normal 75% (range 68–77%).
Falls (50–70%) with DECREASED O₂ DELIVERY (low cardiac output, anemia, hypoxic hypoxia) or INCREASED O₂ CONSUMPTION (fever, seizures, increased WOB, stress, pain).
30–50% = onset of lactic acidosis · 25–30% = severe lactic acidosis · < 25% = cellular death.

cards.q: ⚠ What makes SvO₂ RISE — and which are the traps?
cards.a:
⚠ What makes SvO₂ RISE — and which are the traps?
An IMPROPERLY WEDGED PA catheter · reduced O₂ consumption (hypothermia, sedation/analgesia, low metabolic rate) · SEPSIS or CYANIDE POISONING, where tissues CANNOT USE oxygen.

cards.q: The Swan-Ganz catheter — construction?
cards.a:
The Swan-Ganz catheter — construction?
A flow-directed, BALLOON-TIPPED catheter, typically 110 cm long with three lumens, marked in 10-cm segments.
Distal PA port at the tip · proximal injectate port about 30 cm back (sits in the right atrium) · balloon near the tip with a 1.5 mL MAXIMUM inflation volume · thermistor at the tip; a fiberoptic element allows continuous SvO₂.

cards.q: The PA catheter's path — and when is the balloon inflated?
cards.a:
The PA catheter's path — and when is the balloon inflated?
Subclavian or internal jugular vein → SVC → RIGHT ATRIUM (balloon is then INFLATED, and blood flow carries it like wind in a sail) → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → WEDGED in a smaller branch, at which point the balloon is DEFLATED and the catheter secured.

cards.q: ⚠ How do you read PAP vs PCWP?
cards.a:
⚠ How do you read PAP vs PCWP?
PAP is read with the balloon DEFLATED.
PCWP is obtained by MOMENTARILY re-inflating the balloon, reading at END-EXPIRATION, then DEFLATING THE BALLOON IMMEDIATELY.

cards.q: The PCWP/CVP waveform letters?
cards.a:
The PCWP/CVP waveform letters?
a wave = atrial contraction · x descent = fall in pressure after contraction · c wave = AV valve closure · v wave = ventricular contraction with passive atrial filling · y descent = fall in pressure after the AV valve opens.
CVP version: a = atrial systole after the P wave, c = tricuspid closure, v = ventricular systole after the T wave, y = tricuspid opening.

cards.q: How is cardiac output measured by thermodilution?
cards.a:
How is cardiac output measured by thermodilution?
10 mL of iced or room-temperature D5W is injected into the PROXIMAL port, and the temperature change at the THERMISTOR is used to compute flow.

cards.q: Hess on RV pressures — normals and what raises each?
cards.a:
Hess on RV pressures — normals and what raises each?
Normal RV systolic 15 to 30 mm Hg; RV end-diastolic 0 to 8 mm Hg.
Raised RV SYSTOLIC: pulmonary hypertension, pulmonic valve stenosis, acute pulmonary embolism — ⚠ though RV systolic rarely exceeds 40 to 50 mm Hg in the ACUTE setting, a useful discriminator from chronic disease.
Raised RV END-DIASTOLIC: cardiomyopathy, RV ischaemia or infarction, cardiac constriction or tamponade.

cards.q: Hess on the PA tracing — the components and what elevates PA pressures?
cards.a:
Hess on the PA tracing — the components and what elevates PA pressures?
'The main components of the PA tracing are the systolic and diastolic pressures and the DICROTIC NOTCH, which represents closure of the PULMONIC valve.'
Elevated PA pressures occur with VOLUME OVERLOAD or RAISED PVR: left heart failure of any cause, primary lung disease, mitral valve disease, pulmonary embolism, hypoxaemia with pulmonary vasoconstriction, idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension, left-to-right shunts.

cards.q: Arterial catheter complications and measurement problems (the decks' only list)?
cards.a:
Arterial catheter complications and measurement problems (the decks' only list)?
Complications: bleeding, blood clot, infection.
Measurement problems: air bubbles and loose connections (damped signal) · improper transducer leveling (false high/low readings) · inadequate pressure on the flush bag (blood backs up in the tubing) · clotting at the catheter tip or the tip lodging against the vessel wall.
⚠ PA-catheter-specific complications (balloon rupture, pulmonary infarction, arrhythmias, knotting) are NOT covered in the decks — look them up in Chang Table 10-8.

cards.q: MAP vs ICP — conceptually?
cards.a:
MAP vs ICP — conceptually?
MAP is the average pressure in the systemic arteries over the cardiac cycle — a DRIVING pressure for perfusion.
ICP is the pressure inside the skull — the BACK-PRESSURE opposing that flow.

cards.q: The MAP formula — and a worked example?
cards.a:
The MAP formula — and a worked example?
MAP = Diastolic + ⅓ (Systolic − Diastolic)
Worked: 110/70 → 70 + ⅓(40) = 70 + 13.3 ≈ 83 mm Hg

cards.q: The CPP formula — and the two ways to raise it?
cards.a:
The CPP formula — and the two ways to raise it?
CPP = MAP − ICP
CPP is raised EITHER by raising the MAP OR by lowering the ICP.
Normal ICP is < 20 mm Hg.

cards.q: ⚠ The critical CPP threshold and the mortality numbers?
cards.a:
⚠ The critical CPP threshold and the mortality numbers?
CPP ≥ 70 mm Hg (believed to be 70–80 mm Hg).
Mortality increases about 20% for every 10 mm Hg drop in CPP.
In severe head injury, a 35% REDUCTION in mortality was achieved when CPP was kept above 70 mm Hg.

cards.q: What happens to cerebral autoregulation after head trauma?
cards.a:
What happens to cerebral autoregulation after head trauma?
Normally the brain autoregulates its own blood flow regardless of systemic BP — but AUTOREGULATION MAY BE LOST after head trauma, at which point falling CPP produces effects ranging from cerebral ischemia to brain death.
ICP control is generally unnecessary when ICP is already < 20 mm Hg, but IS necessary in closed head injuries.

cards.q: How do ALL diuretics work — and what determines a drug's strength?
cards.a:
How do ALL diuretics work — and what determines a drug's strength?
ALL diuretics work by BLOCKING SODIUM REABSORPTION, and WATER FOLLOWS SALT — NaCl output must exceed NaCl intake.
LOCATION DETERMINES EFFECT: where in the nephron the drug acts determines both its STRENGTH and WHICH ELECTROLYTES (besides Na⁺) are lost.
For respiratory care: less fluid = less pulmonary edema, better oxygenation, decreased work of breathing.

cards.q: OSMOTIC diuretics — example, mechanism, uses, and the caution?
cards.a:
OSMOTIC diuretics — example, mechanism, uses, and the caution?
MANNITOL (preferred, lowest toxicity), glycerin, isosorbide, urea.
Not reabsorbed; impairs proximal tubule and ascending loop NaCl reabsorption; pulls water osmotically.
Main uses: acute renal failure · CEREBRAL EDEMA / ↑ICP in TBI · bronchial provocation.
⚠ Caution: can TRANSIENTLY WORSEN pulmonary edema. Net K⁺ loss in urine.

cards.q: ⚠ CARBONIC ANHYDRASE INHIBITORS — the acid-base effect that is OPPOSITE the other classes?
cards.a:
⚠ CARBONIC ANHYDRASE INHIBITORS — the acid-base effect that is OPPOSITE the other classes?
Acetazolamide (also methazolamide, dichlorphenamide). Acts on the PROXIMAL TUBULE — blocks HCO₃⁻ reabsorption.
⚠ Causes METABOLIC ACIDOSIS — the expected effect, OPPOSITE of the other classes. Also hypokalemia.
Very WEAK diuretics; used to TREAT metabolic alkalosis, altitude sickness, glaucoma.

cards.q: LOOP diuretics — site, and the five adverse effects?
cards.a:
LOOP diuretics — site, and the five adverse effects?
Furosemide (Lasix), bumetanide, torsemide, ethacrynic acid. ASCENDING LOOP OF HENLE — inhibits Na⁺/K⁺/Cl⁻ reabsorption; blocks up to ~20% of NaCl and H₂O.
HYPOKALEMIA (most important — can cause ARRHYTHMIAS) · hypochloremia · METABOLIC ALKALOSIS · hypovolemia/hypotension · CALCIUM LOSS · dose-related OTOTOXICITY (tinnitus, usually reversible hearing loss).

cards.q: THIAZIDES — site, and the two distinguishing effects?
cards.a:
THIAZIDES — site, and the two distinguishing effects?
Hydrochlorothiazide class. DISTAL TUBULE — inhibits NaCl reabsorption.
⚠ HYPERGLYCEMIA — thiazides have the STRONGEST DIABETOGENIC activity (DKA reported).
⚠ They RETAIN CALCIUM — the OPPOSITE of loops.
Also milder hypokalemia, mild volume depletion. Narrow therapeutic margin.

cards.q: The two POTASSIUM-SPARING classes — and the shared danger?
cards.a:
The two POTASSIUM-SPARING classes — and the shared danger?
Aldosterone blockers — spironolactone (Aldactone), eplerenone: distal convoluted tubule, competitively blocks ALDOSTERONE. Mainly cirrhosis/ascites, hyperaldosteronism.
Na⁺ channel blockers — triamterene, amiloride: collecting duct, directly blocks Na⁺ channels. Triamterene needs LIVER activation — avoid in liver disease.
⚠ BOTH cause HYPERKALEMIA — MORE LIFE-THREATENING than K⁺ depletion.

cards.q: ⚠ 'Loops for Lungs' — and the five-minute effect
cards.a:
⚠ 'Loops for Lungs' — and the five-minute effect
LOOP diuretics are the first-line, most powerful agents for ACUTE PULMONARY EDEMA and CHF.
Beyond diuresis, IV furosemide produces ACUTE VASODILATION WITHIN FIVE MINUTES — seen as a decrease in PCWP, BP and SVR.
The patient feels better BEFORE urine output even increases (↓preload, ↓pulmonary congestion).

cards.q: Which diuretic class is first-line for mild HYPERTENSION — and which is supportive?
cards.a:
Which diuretic class is first-line for mild HYPERTENSION — and which is supportive?
THIAZIDES are first-line for mild hypertension and chronic management — NOT for acute pulmonary edema.
Potassium-sparing agents are SUPPORTIVE — added to protect K⁺.
The most common and most powerful combination is a LOOP + a THIAZIDE (different nephron sites → additive/synergistic) — at the cost of MORE electrolyte loss.

cards.q: ⚠ The hypokalemia → metabolic alkalosis link
cards.a:
⚠ The hypokalemia → metabolic alkalosis link
When Cl⁻ is low (hypochloremia) or K⁺ is low (hypokalemia), the kidney is FORCED TO EXCHANGE Na⁺ FOR H⁺ instead; that loss of H⁺ in the urine produces METABOLIC ALKALOSIS.
So the classic loop-diuretic patient shows HYPOKALEMIA + HYPOCHLOREMIA + METABOLIC ALKALOSIS — and low K⁺ carries a real arrhythmia risk.
⚠ Exception: CAIs cause metabolic ACIDOSIS — which is exactly why acetazolamide is used to TREAT a diuretic-induced metabolic alkalosis in a ventilated patient.

cards.q: Diuretics in pregnancy and children?
cards.a:
Diuretics in pregnancy and children?
NOT recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding (infant dehydration risk).
In children doses are smaller, and FUROSEMIDE is the most effective and least toxic pediatric diuretic — though loops may cause nephrocalcinosis and decreased bone mass density.

cards.q: The PtcO₂ electrode — construction?
cards.a:
The PtcO₂ electrode — construction?
A combined PLATINUM and SILVER electrode under an oxygen-permeable, HYDROPHOBIC (water-repelling) membrane with a reservoir of phosphate buffer and potassium chloride.
The membrane lets O₂ and CO₂ through but BLOCKS moisture and electrolytes.

cards.q: ⚠ Transcutaneous electrode temperature — all the numbers
cards.a:
⚠ Transcutaneous electrode temperature — all the numbers
44°C is the usual setting when monitoring BOTH PtcO₂ and PtcCO₂.
As low as 37°C is adequate if only PtcCO₂ is monitored.
Chang: 44°C for PtcCO₂, with 40–42°C in NEONATES, maximum 45°C.

cards.q: Transcutaneous placement sites and setup sequence?
cards.a:
Transcutaneous placement sites and setup sequence?
Sites with good superficial circulation — the side of the chest, the abdomen, or the inner thigh.
Clean with alcohol → apply the adhesive fixation ring → apply contact gel AVOIDING AIR BUBBLES → seat the sensor FLAT with the edges sealed → allow 5–20 minutes to stabilize.

cards.q: ⚠ Site rotation interval — the deck conflict
cards.a:
⚠ Site rotation interval — the deck conflict
Chang: change the site every 4 HOURS to avoid erythema and burns.
RCP 203 procedure deck: every 2–6 HOURS, depending on sensor temperature, infant size, and manufacturer recommendation.

cards.q: Transcutaneous targets in neonates — and why it matters?
cards.a:
Transcutaneous targets in neonates — and why it matters?
In neonates PtcO₂ closely approximates PaO₂. Keep PtcO₂ in the 50–80 torr trend range (Chang: optimal 50–70 mm Hg); set the high PtcO₂ infant alarm around 80 torr.
Infant PtcO₂ is the BEST way to screen for HYPEROXEMIA and help prevent RETINOPATHY OF PREMATURITY (ROP).

cards.q: Transcutaneous monitoring in ADULTS — which value is useful?
cards.a:
Transcutaneous monitoring in ADULTS — which value is useful?
PtcO₂ reads LOW in adults because of THICKER SKIN — so pulse oximetry is preferred.
PtcCO₂, however, is RELIABLE in hemodynamically stable adults and is a good choice when capnography is difficult, e.g. during NPPV.

cards.q: ⚠ Why does PtcCO₂ normally read HIGHER than PaCO₂?
cards.a:
⚠ Why does PtcCO₂ normally read HIGHER than PaCO₂?
Because HEATING THE TISSUE INCREASES LOCAL CO₂ PRODUCTION.
In poor perfusion/shock, PtcO₂ falls disproportionately and PtcCO₂ reads FALSELY HIGH from tissue CO₂ accumulation.

cards.q: What makes transcutaneous monitoring inaccurate — the full list?
cards.a:
What makes transcutaneous monitoring inaccurate — the full list?
Poor perfusion / shock / low cardiac output / dehydration · skin edema · hypothermia · a PaO₂ or operating range above 80–100 mm Hg · an underheated sensor · placement on a BONY surface · too much pressure or too much contact gel · poor skin integrity or adhesive allergy · and the 5–20 minute setup time that rules it out in EMERGENCIES.

cards.q: After setup or a site change, how do you validate a transcutaneous monitor?
cards.a:
After setup or a site change, how do you validate a transcutaneous monitor?
Correlate against a SIMULTANEOUS arterial or capillary sample, and RECORD THE MONITOR VALUE AT THE MOMENT THE SAMPLE IS DRAWN.
If the PaO₂ is substantially HIGHER than the PtcO₂, suspect POOR PERIPHERAL CIRCULATION.

cards.q: Home apnea monitoring — the three indications?
cards.a:
Home apnea monitoring — the three indications?
Neonates being treated for recurrent apnea accompanied by bradycardia or O₂ desaturation · at-risk babies discharged with a prescription for home apnea monitoring · some older children and adults with conditions affecting the CONTROL OF BREATHING.

cards.q: How do apnea monitors work, where do the sensors go, and typical settings?
cards.a:
How do apnea monitors work, where do the sensors go, and typical settings?
Two chest-wall sensors detect respiratory movement by changes in ELECTRICAL IMPEDANCE, placed on the right and left sides of the chest, MIDWAY between the nipple line and the midaxillary line, where chest motion is greatest.
Typical settings: heart-rate alarm 80–210/min for neonates (lower limits for older babies) and an apnea time alarm of 15–20 seconds.

cards.q: ⚠ The key limitation of impedance apnea monitoring?
cards.a:
⚠ The key limitation of impedance apnea monitoring?
Because impedance measures CHEST WALL MOVEMENT and NOT AIRFLOW, simple apnea monitoring CANNOT DETECT OBSTRUCTIVE SLEEP APNEA.
Patients suspected of OSA need POLYSOMNOGRAPHY — and caregivers must always confirm status by VISUAL INSPECTION.

cards.q: Apnea vs PATHOLOGIC apnea vs periodic breathing?
cards.a:
Apnea vs PATHOLOGIC apnea vs periodic breathing?
Apnea = cessation of respiratory effort (short central pauses < 10 sec can be NORMAL at any age).
PATHOLOGIC apnea = apnea longer than 20 seconds, OR associated with cyanosis, abrupt marked pallor, hypotonia, or bradycardia (< 80–100 bpm in neonates).
Periodic breathing = three or more pauses of > 3 seconds with < 20 seconds of breathing between them — NOT associated with cyanosis or heart-rate change, and CAN BE NORMAL.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: APGAR — when is it scored, what do the letters stand for, and what's the range?
cards.a:
APGAR — when is it scored, what do the letters stand for, and what's the range?
At 1 minute and again at 5 minutes after birth.
Appearance (color) · Pulse (heart rate) · Grimace (reflex irritability) · Activity (muscle tone) · Respirations (respiratory effort).
Each scored 0–2; total 0–10. Created in 1952 by Dr. Virginia Apgar, an anesthesiologist.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: ⚠ The single most important APGAR rule?
cards.a:
⚠ The single most important APGAR rule?
NEEDED INTERVENTIONS MUST NEVER BE DELAYED TO OBTAIN THE APGAR SCORE.
Apgar does NOT decide whether resuscitation begins — resuscitation decisions are made from the baby's condition immediately after birth. You do not wait for the 1-minute score.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: APGAR score interpretation bands?
cards.a:
APGAR score interpretation bands?
7–10 = NORMAL.
4–6 = MODERATELY DEPRESSED — typically needs more intensive support.
0–3 = SEVERELY DEPRESSED — usually undergoes resuscitation; requires immediate assessment/support.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: APGAR — the full scoring table (Hess Table 22-1)
cards.a:
APGAR — the full scoring table (Hess Table 22-1)
Heart rate: 0 = none · 1 = < 100/min · 2 = > 100/min
Respiratory effort: 0 = none · 1 = weak, irregular · 2 = strong cry
Color: 0 = pale blue · 1 = body pink, extremities blue · 2 = completely pink
Reflex (irritability to suction): 0 = no response · 1 = grimace · 2 = cry, cough, or sneeze
Muscle tone: 0 = limp · 1 = some flexion · 2 = well flexed

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: When is a 10-minute APGAR assigned — and what does a persistent 0 mean?
cards.a:
When is a 10-minute APGAR assigned — and what does a persistent 0 mean?
When the score is less than 7 at 5 minutes, an additional score is usually assigned at 10 minutes.
⚠ If the Apgar score remains 0 after 10 minutes of resuscitation, the infant is unlikely to survive.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: ⚠ Why is the APGAR less useful in premature infants?
cards.a:
⚠ Why is the APGAR less useful in premature infants?
Because THREE of the five criteria — muscle tone, respiratory effort, and reflex irritability — depend on NEUROLOGICAL MATURITY.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: APGAR vs GLASGOW vs BALLARD vs SILVERMAN — what question does each answer?
cards.a:
APGAR vs GLASGOW vs BALLARD vs SILVERMAN — what question does each answer?
APGAR: 'How is this newborn doing RIGHT NOW?'
BALLARD: 'How many WEEKS OLD is this newborn?'
GLASGOW: 'How CONSCIOUS is this patient?'
SILVERMAN: 'How much RESPIRATORY DISTRESS is this neonate in?'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: The Ballard score — what does it assess and what does it produce?
cards.a:
The Ballard score — what does it assess and what does it produce?
Gestational age via NEUROMUSCULAR + PHYSICAL maturity characteristics. Performed after birth, once the infant can be examined — especially useful in premature infants.
The total converts to an ESTIMATED GESTATIONAL AGE IN WEEKS (normal full term 38–42 wks; term ≈ 37–42 wks).
RTs normally do not perform the Ballard — but you must recognize what it evaluates.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: The Silverman-Anderson Index — the five features and the interpretation bands?
cards.a:
The Silverman-Anderson Index — the five features and the interpretation bands?
Chest/abdominal movement · intercostal retractions · xiphoid retractions · nasal flaring · expiratory grunting — each scored 0/1/2, max 10.
0 = no distress · 1–6 = mild to moderate · ≥ 7 = IMPENDING RESPIRATORY FAILURE.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: Silverman-Anderson — the full scoring table (Heuer Table 20-30)
cards.a:
Silverman-Anderson — the full scoring table (Heuer Table 20-30)
Chest/abdominal movement: 0 = synchronized · 1 = lag on inspiration · 2 = SEESAW movement
Intercostal retractions: 0 = none · 1 = just visible · 2 = marked
Xiphoid retractions: 0 = none · 1 = just visible · 2 = marked
Nasal flaring: 0 = none · 1 = minimal · 2 = marked
Expiratory grunting: 0 = none · 1 = STETHOSCOPE ONLY · 2 = NAKED EAR

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: How does LATE hypoxemia show in a neonate?
cards.a:
How does LATE hypoxemia show in a neonate?
Central cyanosis in room air, or a PREDUCTAL SpO₂ that will not normalize or falls back below 90%.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: ⚠ The L/S ratio — the number, and the course caveat
cards.a:
⚠ The L/S ratio — the number, and the course caveat
Lecithin/sphingomyelin (L/S) ratio > 2:1 indicates FETAL LUNG MATURITY.
⚠ Your instructor explicitly EXCLUDED this ('Do not study … L/S ratio, PG, L/A ratio') — but Heuer states it plainly and it is standard NBRC content.
Mechanism: lecithin rises sharply near term while sphingomyelin stays roughly flat, so the ratio rising past 2 is the maturity signal.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: The other two fetal lung maturity markers?
cards.a:
The other two fetal lung maturity markers?
Lecithin/albumin (L/A) ratio ≥ 40.0 — the parallel maturity threshold.
Phosphatidylglycerol (PG) PRESENT — a confirmatory marker, particularly useful in DIABETIC MOTHERS where the L/S ratio can mislead.
An immature ratio predicts IRDS from surfactant deficiency — the reason for antenatal steroids and postnatal surfactant replacement.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: What is lecithin, in pharmacology terms?
cards.a:
What is lecithin, in pharmacology terms?
Lecithin = DPPC (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) — the surfactant component predominantly responsible for REDUCING ALVEOLAR SURFACE TENSION.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: Surfactant composition, where it's made, and what triggers secretion?
cards.a:
Surfactant composition, where it's made, and what triggers secretion?
85–90% LIPID by weight, mostly phosphatidylcholine (75–80%), plus proteins SP-A, SP-B, SP-C, SP-D.
Synthesized in TYPE II ALVEOLAR CELLS, stored in vesicles called LAMELLAR BODIES.
LUNG INFLATION is the major stimulus for secretion.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: ⚠ Why are one or two doses of exogenous surfactant usually enough?
cards.a:
⚠ Why are one or two doses of exogenous surfactant usually enough?
Because 90–95% of surfactant is TAKEN BACK UP by the Type II cell, REPROCESSED, and RE-SECRETED.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: Surfactant prophylaxis thresholds for RDS?
cards.a:
Surfactant prophylaxis thresholds for RDS?
Premature infants < 29 WEEKS gestational age at high risk, or weighing < 1250 GRAMS at birth.
The basic problem in RDS: lack of surfactant from lung immaturity → HIGH SURFACE TENSION → higher ventilating pressures needed.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: ⚠ Why do pediatric airways decompensate so fast?
cards.a:
⚠ Why do pediatric airways decompensate so fast?
In CHILDREN the narrowest point is the CRICOID RING (in adults it's the glottis), and the airway is FUNNEL-SHAPED, getting narrower as you go down.
1 mm of circumferential edema cuts the airway diameter by MORE THAN 50% in an infant — the same 1 mm in an adult is merely 'noticeable.'
That's why croup, epiglottitis, post-extubation edema, and airway trauma make pediatric patients deteriorate rapidly.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: ⚠ The two board-level radiographic pearls?
cards.a:
⚠ The two board-level radiographic pearls?
CROUP → STEEPLE SIGN → AP view (subglottic narrowing/edema BELOW the vocal cords).
EPIGLOTTITIS → THUMB SIGN → LATERAL NECK view (the swollen epiglottis).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: ⚠ The most important safety rule with suspected epiglottitis?
cards.a:
⚠ The most important safety rule with suspected epiglottitis?
AIRWAY MANAGEMENT TAKES PRIORITY OVER OBTAINING AN X-RAY if the child is unstable or has significant airway compromise.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: CROUP vs EPIGLOTTITIS — organism and location of swelling?
cards.a:
CROUP vs EPIGLOTTITIS — organism and location of swelling?
CROUP (laryngotracheobronchitis): VIRAL — human parainfluenza viruses (HPIV), infecting larynx, trachea, bronchi. SUBGLOTTIC swelling — below the vocal cords. Symptoms appear 2 to 7 days after infection.
EPIGLOTTITIS: BACTERIAL — Haemophilus influenzae. SUPRAGLOTTIC — swollen epiglottis. Much less common in children following Hib vaccination.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: Racemic epinephrine — concentration, dose, and the three uses named?
cards.a:
Racemic epinephrine — concentration, dose, and the three uses named?
2.25% solution, 0.25–0.5 mL (= 5.63–11.25 mg), QID. A strong α-adrenergic that reduces airway swelling.
Used for: CROUP · EPIGLOTTITIS · POST-EXTUBATION STRIDOR.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: ⚠ The 'do not examine the throat' rule — is it in your decks?
cards.a:
⚠ The 'do not examine the throat' rule — is it in your decks?
NOT covered in any available slide deck.
The decks give only the closest principle — with suspected epiglottitis, secure the airway before obtaining imaging if the child is unstable.
The classic rule — 'never depress the tongue or inspect the pharynx in suspected epiglottitis, because it can trigger complete laryngospasm/obstruction; examine only in the OR with intubation capability' — is not written in any deck. Look it up in a pediatric emergency reference.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: ⚠ The single distinguishing question between OSA and CSA?
cards.a:
⚠ The single distinguishing question between OSA and CSA?
IS THERE VENTILATORY EFFORT?
OSA: the brain sends the signal and the chest works, but the upper airway COLLAPSES — airflow absent while ventilatory effort PERSISTS.
CSA: the airway is open but the brain does not send the signal — BOTH airflow AND ventilatory effort stop. On PSG: no nasal/oral airflow AND no thoracoabdominal movement.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: What is MIXED apnea — and how is it treated?
cards.a:
What is MIXED apnea — and how is it treated?
It starts as a CENTRAL event and then becomes OBSTRUCTIVE.
It is an EVENT, not a separate condition — and patients with predominantly mixed apnea are classified and treated as OSA.
OSA affects roughly 25% of U.S. adults and is a major cause of excessive daytime sleepiness.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: OSA mechanism at the muscle level — and the three cardinal features?
cards.a:
OSA mechanism at the muscle level — and the three cardinal features?
The GENIOGLOSSUS fails to oppose collapsing forces, and the tongue falls into the oropharynx.
Cardinal features: obstructive APNEAS · HYPOPNEAS · RERAs. Episodes often end with fricative breathing (snorting).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: OSA risk factors?
cards.a:
OSA risk factors?
OBESITY (strongest predictor) · large neck size · male sex · age > 65 · hypertension, diabetes, chronic nasal congestion, family history, alcohol, sedatives, smoking · ethnicity (higher in Black, Hispanic, Pacific Islander populations under age 35).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: CSA — the two subtypes and their causes?
cards.a:
CSA — the two subtypes and their causes?
HYPERVENTILATION-related (most common): primary CSA, CHEYNE-STOKES, high altitude.
HYPOVENTILATION-related: CNS depressants, neuromuscular disease, severe COPD.
Causes: heart failure with Cheyne-Stokes breathing · CNS/brain stem lesions or injury · drugs (opioids, alcohol, benzodiazepines) · high altitude · neuromuscular disease (Guillain-Barré, myasthenia gravis). Atrial fibrillation often associated.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: Define HYPOPNEA and RERA.
cards.a:
Define HYPOPNEA and RERA.
HYPOPNEA = airflow ↓ ≥ 30% for ≥ 10 sec with a ≥ 3% SpO₂ drop or arousal.
RERA = increased effort / flattened nasal pressure ≥ 10 sec ending in AROUSAL, NOT meeting apnea/hypopnea criteria.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: The gold standard for diagnosing OSA — and the two alternatives?
cards.a:
The gold standard for diagnosing OSA — and the two alternatives?
Full-night ATTENDED IN-LAB POLYSOMNOGRAPHY (PSG).
Split-night: first half diagnostic, second half CPAP/BiPAP titration.
⚠ Home sleep test uses TOTAL RECORDING TIME and reports RDI instead of AHI — because there's NO EEG, it can't measure total SLEEP time.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: The diagnostic AHI thresholds — and the formula?
cards.a:
The diagnostic AHI thresholds — and the formula?
Confirmed when AHI ≥ 15/hr in an ASYMPTOMATIC patient, OR AHI ≥ 5/hr WITH symptoms (sleepiness, fatigue, snoring, pauses). 75% of events must be obstructive.
AHI = (apneas + hypopneas) ÷ total SLEEP time in hours — e.g. 100 events ÷ 8 hr = 12.5/hr.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: OSA severity bands?
cards.a:
OSA severity bands?
Mild 5–15/hr — occasional daytime sleepiness.
Moderate 15–30/hr — frequent naps, decreased performance.
Severe > 30/hr, or SpO₂ < 90% for > 20% of sleep time — high accident risk, pulmonary hypertension, arrhythmias, cor pulmonale.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: OSA treatment — first-line and the alternatives?
cards.a:
OSA treatment — first-line and the alternatives?
Behavior modification (WEIGHT LOSS most effective, exercise, avoid alcohol/sedatives, avoid supine position) + PAP = FIRST-LINE: CPAP most common, also BiPAP, APAP.
Oral appliances (MAD or tongue-retaining) for mild/moderate or CPAP intolerance · surgery for correctable obstruction · implantable upper-airway stimulator (Inspire) if CPAP fails.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: ⚠ CSA treatment — what comes first?
cards.a:
⚠ CSA treatment — what comes first?
TREAT THE UNDERLYING CAUSE FIRST (CHF, stroke, encephalitis).
Then CPAP/BiPAP or ADAPTIVE SERVO-VENTILATION (ASV) — initial CPAP range +5 to +10 cmH₂O.
Respiratory stimulants (acetazolamide, theophylline) if CSA persists.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: How do you GROUP these four diseases?
cards.a:
How do you GROUP these four diseases?
Bacterial pneumonia and pulmonary fibrosis both produce a RESTRICTIVE picture — dull percussion, bronchial breath sounds, crackles, whispered pectoriloquy.
EMPHYSEMA is the only OBSTRUCTIVE one.
PE is the odd one out — the CXR is often NORMAL.
Three of the four (PNA, PE, fibrosis) share the same ABG trajectory: acute alveolar hyperventilation with hypoxemia early → acute ventilatory failure when severe.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: BACTERIAL PNEUMONIA — presentation and the fever discriminator?
cards.a:
BACTERIAL PNEUMONIA — presentation and the fever discriminator?
Diaphoretic, cyanotic, tachypnea; crackles, bronchial breath sounds, whispered pectoriloquy; dull percussion; cough starts dry → productive yellow/green, RUST-COLORED sputum or hemoptysis.
⚠ Fever > 101°F (bacterial) vs < 101°F (viral). ↑HR, ↑RR, ↑BP.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: BACTERIAL PNEUMONIA — CXR, labs, and the key distinguishing feature?
cards.a:
BACTERIAL PNEUMONIA — CXR, labs, and the key distinguishing feature?
CXR: ↑ density from consolidation/atelectasis; AIR BRONCHOGRAMS (classic); possible abscess with air-fluid level or pleural effusion/empyema.
Labs: ↑ WBC (bacterial) vs ↓/normal WBC (viral); sputum C&S.
Key: AIR BRONCHOGRAMS + ↑WBC + fever > 101°F. ⚠ Hypoxemia is from CAPILLARY SHUNTING and is REFRACTORY to O₂ therapy.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: EMPHYSEMA ('Pink Puffer') — presentation?
cards.a:
EMPHYSEMA ('Pink Puffer') — presentation?
Thin, CACHECTIC · BARREL CHEST · PURSED-LIP breathing · heavy accessory muscle use · tachypnea · minimal cough, little/no sputum · PINK skin tone · HYPERRESONANT percussion · decreased breath sounds — a QUIET CHEST.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: EMPHYSEMA — CXR, ABG, labs, and the key distinguishing feature?
cards.a:
EMPHYSEMA — CXR, ABG, labs, and the key distinguishing feature?
CXR: HYPERLUCENCY, hyperinflation, ↑A-P diameter, FLATTENED/DEPRESSED DIAPHRAGMS, blebs/bullae.
ABG: COMPENSATED respiratory acidosis with hypoxemia; during exacerbation, acute-on-chronic.
Labs: Hct/Hgb normal in mild–moderate; α₁-antitrypsin < 15–20% of normal is highly suggestive of AATD emphysema.
Key: ↓ DLCO (alveolar-capillary membrane destroyed) + obstructive PFT. ⚠ Pulmonary HTN/cor pulmonale is UNCOMMON in emphysema — vs COMMON in chronic bronchitis.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: PULMONARY EMBOLISM — presentation and the classic triad?
cards.a:
PULMONARY EMBOLISM — presentation and the classic triad?
Sudden dyspnea, PLEURITIC chest pain, cough ± hemoptysis, wheezing; tachycardia, arrhythmias, right heart strain, ↑S₂, weak pulse, hypotension; anxiety, diaphoresis, syncope, cyanosis; LEG SWELLING (DVT clue).
Classic triad: SUDDEN DYSPNEA + TACHYCARDIA + CHEST PAIN.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: ⚠ PE — what is the CXR FOR, and what makes the diagnosis?
cards.a:
⚠ PE — what is the CXR FOR, and what makes the diagnosis?
The CXR is often NORMAL — its role is to RULE OUT pneumonia/pneumothorax.
D-dimer: a NORMAL result RULES OUT PE; elevated > 500 ng/mL only SUGGESTS a clot and is NOT specific.
CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) = GOLD STANDARD (V/Q scan if CT contraindicated); venous ultrasound for DVT.
DEAD-SPACE VENTILATION is the hallmark physiology.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: ⚠ PE ABG — and the twist in severe cases?
cards.a:
⚠ PE ABG — and the twist in severe cases?
Mild–moderate: acute alveolar hyperventilation with hypoxemia (↓PaCO₂, ↑pH).
Severe: acute ventilatory failure with hypoxemia (↑PaCO₂, ↓pH).
⚠ Severe hypoxia → LACTIC ACIDOSIS drops the pH LOWER than the PaCO₂ predicts.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: PULMONARY FIBROSIS / ILD — presentation?
cards.a:
PULMONARY FIBROSIS / ILD — presentation?
Tachypnea, ↑HR, ↑BP · cyanosis, DIGITAL CLUBBING · cor pulmonale signs — distended neck veins, pitting edema, enlarged tender liver · NONPRODUCTIVE cough · ↑ TACTILE & VOCAL FREMITUS, dull percussion, bronchial breath sounds, FINE CRACKLES, pleural friction rub, whispered pectoriloquy.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: PULMONARY FIBROSIS — CXR, ABG, labs, and the DLCO exception?
cards.a:
PULMONARY FIBROSIS — CXR, ABG, labs, and the DLCO exception?
CXR: BILATERAL RETICULONODULAR pattern, granulomas, cavity formation, HONEYCOMBING, pleural thickening.
ABG severe: CHRONIC ventilatory failure — ↑PaCO₂ with significantly ↑HCO₃⁻ and a NORMAL pH (fully compensated).
Labs: ↑ Hct and ↑ Hgb (POLYCYTHEMIA) from chronic hypoxemia.
Key: HONEYCOMBING + ↑ FREMITUS (fibrosis transmits vibration) + restrictive PFT.
⚠ ↓DLCO in most ILDs — EXCEPT Goodpasture's and idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis, where ALVEOLAR BLOOD FALSELY RAISES the DLCO.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: The two ways pneumonia is classified?
cards.a:
The two ways pneumonia is classified?
By PATHOGEN (bacterial, viral, fungal) — the ideal method, because it allows targeted treatment.
By CLINICAL SETTING — used when the organism can't be identified quickly, which is how most pneumonia is labeled at the bedside.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: ⚠ What does 'ATYPICAL' pneumonia actually mean?
cards.a:
⚠ What does 'ATYPICAL' pneumonia actually mean?
It's about LAB/IMAGING BEHAVIOR, not severity.
The organism escapes identification by standard bacteriologic tests, there is only moderate sputum, NO alveolar consolidation, NO alveolar exudate, and only a moderate WBC elevation.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the most common cause — 'walking pneumonia.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: CAP — definition and the leading organisms?
cards.a:
CAP — definition and the leading organisms?
Acquired through NORMAL SOCIAL CONTACT, outside a hospital or healthcare setting.
Streptococcus pneumoniae — the leading cause, > 80% of bacterial cases; Staphylococcus; Haemophilus influenzae (6 types); Legionella pneumophila; Klebsiella (lobar pneumonia); Moraxella catarrhalis; Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: Legionella pneumophila — what is it known for?
cards.a:
Legionella pneumophila — what is it known for?
Listed as a common cause of COMMUNITY-ACQUIRED TYPICAL pneumonia, and 'known for causing LEGIONNAIRES' DISEASE.'

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: Atypical CAP organisms?
cards.a:
Atypical CAP organisms?
Mycoplasma pneumoniae — most common; NO CELL WALL; children/young adults; 'walking pneumonia.'
Coxiella burnetii — Q fever, livestock aerosols.
Viruses ≈ 50% of ALL pneumonias — RSV, parainfluenza, human metapneumovirus in children; influenza A & B in adults; adenovirus in both.
Presentation: subacute onset over days–weeks; pulmonary PLUS extrapulmonary findings (cough + headache, fatigue, diarrhea).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: HAP vs HCAP vs VAP — the definitions?
cards.a:
HAP vs HCAP vs VAP — the definitions?
HAP: occurs ≥ 48 hours after hospital admission and not present on admission. Organisms: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, MSSA, MRSA.
HCAP: not currently hospitalized but hospitalized within 90 days, resides in a nursing home/LTC facility, or received parenteral antimicrobials, chemotherapy, or wound care within 30 days. Risk for MDR organisms.
VAP: develops > 48 to 72 hours after endotracheal intubation; considered PREVENTABLE → reimbursement penalties.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: ASPIRATION pneumonia — the three forms, organisms, and the pH numbers?
cards.a:
ASPIRATION pneumonia — the three forms, organisms, and the pH numbers?
Three forms: TOXIC INJURY (gastric acid) · OBSTRUCTION (foreign body/fluid) · INFECTION.
The presumed cause of nearly ALL anaerobic pulmonary infections.
Organisms: anaerobic oral flora — Peptostreptococcus, Bacteroides, Prevotella, Fusobacterium, plus Klebsiella, S. aureus, M. tuberculosis.
⚠ Aspirate pH ≤ 2.5 is often FATAL; pH > 5.9 is usually reversible.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: The four accessory muscles of INSPIRATION — and the red-letter takeaway?
cards.a:
The four accessory muscles of INSPIRATION — and the red-letter takeaway?
Sternocleidomastoid · scalenes · upper trapezius · pectoralis major.
⚠ ACCESSORY MUSCLE USE AT REST = INCREASED WORK OF BREATHING. Commonly seen in emphysema.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: What cluster travels with accessory muscle use — and what does it mean during weaning?
cards.a:
What cluster travels with accessory muscle use — and what does it mean during weaning?
Tachypnea · thoracic-abdominal dyssynchrony ('see-saw') · retractions · nasal flaring · pursed-lip breathing · tripod position/inability to lie flat · diaphoresis.
⚠ In a ventilated or weaning patient, new accessory muscle use + tachycardia + diaphoresis + paradoxical abdominal movement are the EARLIEST signs of WEANING FAILURE — stop the trial. DON'T WAIT FOR THE ABG.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: ⚠ How does hypoxia appear in an infant — and what's unique to infants?
cards.a:
⚠ How does hypoxia appear in an infant — and what's unique to infants?
Infants show hypoxia through VISIBLE WORK OF BREATHING before they show it through numbers.
The classic cluster: tachypnea, retractions, nasal flaring, wheezing/crackles, hypoxemia — and, UNIQUELY IN INFANTS, APNEA (e.g. RSV/bronchiolitis). Adults do not typically do this.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: Why are RETRACTIONS more pronounced in children?
cards.a:
Why are RETRACTIONS more pronounced in children?
Because of INCREASED CHEST WALL COMPLIANCE. Retractions occur when the chest wall moves inward during inspiration, and signal significant airway obstruction.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: Tachypnea in an infant — what is the mechanism?
cards.a:
Tachypnea in an infant — what is the mechanism?
The earliest compensation — hypoxemia stimulates PERIPHERAL CHEMORECEPTORS; stiff/low-compliance lungs force rapid, shallow breathing.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: ⚠ Why can a severely ANEMIC infant be badly hypoxemic without looking cyanotic?
cards.a:
⚠ Why can a severely ANEMIC infant be badly hypoxemic without looking cyanotic?
Because cyanosis only becomes visible when the blood holds at least 5 g/dL of REDUCED HEMOGLOBIN.
Check lips, mucosa, tongue (central) and nail beds/fingertips (peripheral).

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: EXPIRATORY GRUNTING — what is it mechanically, and how is it scored?
cards.a:
EXPIRATORY GRUNTING — what is it mechanically, and how is it scored?
Mechanically it is EXHALATION AGAINST A PARTIALLY CLOSED GLOTTIS, generating AUTO-PEEP to hold alveoli open.
Scored on Silverman-Anderson Row 5: 0 = none · 1 = audible by STETHOSCOPE only · 2 = audible to the NAKED EAR.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::10 Neonatal, Pediatric Airway, Sleep Apnea & Disease Comparison
cards.q: A high-risk infant with retractions, tachypnea, cyanosis, hypotension AND asymmetrical chest motion — what do you think of?
cards.a:
A high-risk infant with retractions, tachypnea, cyanosis, hypotension AND asymmetrical chest motion — what do you think of?
PNEUMOTHORAX — and consider TRANSILLUMINATION at the bedside.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::11 Conflicting Numbers — Book vs Deck
cards.q: ⚠ CONFLICT — G cylinder factor
cards.a:
⚠ CONFLICT — G cylinder factor
Heuer Ch 6 Table 6-10 says 2.14. Heuer Appendix B Table B-6 says 2.41.
Heuer contradicts ITSELF. Table 6-10's own duration column (78.5 h) is internally consistent with 2.14; 2.41 is the more commonly published value.
→ Ask your instructor.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::11 Conflicting Numbers — Book vs Deck
cards.q: ⚠ CONFLICT — suction catheter size for an 8.0 mm ETT
cards.a:
⚠ CONFLICT — suction catheter size for an 8.0 mm ETT
Heuer App B (Fr = 1.5 × ID) → 12 Fr.
Heuer Ch 10 Table 10-3 (Fr = ID × 2, step down) → 14 Fr.
Two different rules in ONE book. The Ch 10 table is the one in the airway chapter — prefer it, but know both.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::11 Conflicting Numbers — Book vs Deck
cards.q: ⚠ CONFLICT — suction duration
cards.a:
⚠ CONFLICT — suction duration
Chang deck: ≤ 10 sec. Heuer Ch 10: < 15 sec per attempt.
The deck is stricter. → Answer the DECK's number in this course.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::11 Conflicting Numbers — Book vs Deck
cards.q: ⚠ CONFLICT — adult suction vacuum
cards.a:
⚠ CONFLICT — adult suction vacuum
Heuer Ch 10: −100 to −120 mm Hg (never > −120).
Heuer Ch 6 Table 6-29: −100 to −150 mm Hg.
Heuer internal conflict. Ch 10 is the CLINICAL chapter — prefer −100 to −120.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::11 Conflicting Numbers — Book vs Deck
cards.q: ⚠ CONFLICT — adult ETT size
cards.a:
⚠ CONFLICT — adult ETT size
Heuer: 7.0–8.0 (F) / 8.0–9.0 (M).
Deck: 7–7.5 (F) / 8–8.5 (M).
Ranges OVERLAP — either is defensible.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::11 Conflicting Numbers — Book vs Deck
cards.q: ⚠ CONFLICT — cuff pressure ceiling
cards.a:
⚠ CONFLICT — cuff pressure ceiling
Most sources: 20–30 cm H₂O.
Heuer Ch 3: 25 cm H₂O is the NBRC high limit.
→ Know 20–30 as the RANGE and 25 as the NBRC ALARM THRESHOLD.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::11 Conflicting Numbers — Book vs Deck
cards.q: ⚠ CONFLICT — minimal leak technique
cards.a:
⚠ CONFLICT — minimal leak technique
The deck TEACHES MLT. Heuer says AVOID MLT and use MOV.
This is a GENUINE PRACTICE CHANGE, not a typo. → Answer to your instructor.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::11 Conflicting Numbers — Book vs Deck
cards.q: ⚠ CONFLICT — chest tube insertion site and suction
cards.a:
⚠ CONFLICT — chest tube insertion site and suction
Site: Heuer says ANTERIOR AXILLARY; the deck says MIDAXILLARY. Both are used clinically.
Suction: deck says −10 to −20 cm H₂O; Heuer Ch 16 says 15–20 cm H₂O. Same magnitude — the SIGN CONVENTION differs.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::11 Conflicting Numbers — Book vs Deck
cards.q: ⚠ CONFLICT — static compliance and airway resistance normals
cards.a:
⚠ CONFLICT — static compliance and airway resistance normals
Static compliance: Chang decks 60–100 mL/cm H₂O vs RCP 203 40–80 for INTUBATED adults.
Raw: Weaning deck 0.6–2.4 vs RCP 203 5–12 cm H₂O/L/sec.
⚠ Neither is truly a contradiction — it's INTUBATED vs NON-INTUBATED populations. Intubated patients read lower compliance and higher resistance.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::11 Conflicting Numbers — Book vs Deck
cards.q: ⚠ CONFLICT — RSBI threshold
cards.a:
⚠ CONFLICT — RSBI threshold
Chang: < 100. NBRC/protocols: < 105.
Both are printed on the SAME SLIDE. NBRC exams use 105.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::11 Conflicting Numbers — Book vs Deck
cards.q: ⚠ CONFLICT — NIF/MIP normal and weaning threshold
cards.a:
⚠ CONFLICT — NIF/MIP normal and weaning threshold
Normal: Weaning deck −80 to −100 vs RCP 203 Lssn 2b '> −60.'
The weaning threshold ALSO varies: −20, −20 to −30, and −30 all appear.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::11 Conflicting Numbers — Book vs Deck
cards.q: ⚠ CONFLICT — plateau pressure ceiling
cards.a:
⚠ CONFLICT — plateau pressure ceiling
Chang: < 35 cm H₂O. ARDSNet: < 30 cm H₂O.
MODERN PRACTICE IS < 30.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::11 Conflicting Numbers — Book vs Deck
cards.q: ⚠ CONFLICT — bronchodilator response
cards.a:
⚠ CONFLICT — bronchodilator response
ATS/Hess: 12% AND 200 mL.
Heuer: 12–15%, OR ≥ 200 mL.
Heuer is the LOOSER rule — and it is your course's book.

cards.d: RCP 203::Tier 3::11 Conflicting Numbers — Book vs Deck
cards.q: ⚠ CONFLICT — normal shunt fraction
cards.a:
⚠ CONFLICT — normal shunt fraction
Lssn 3a and RCP 105: < 5%. Weaning deck: ≤ 10%.
Resolution: < 5% is NORMAL; 5–10% is a clinically TOLERABLE range.

cards.q: The three exam-strategy rules?
cards.a:
The three exam-strategy rules?
'Know what you know; and know you know it!!'
'NBRC WORLD ONLY — forget about everything else!!'
⚠ 'TRUST YOUR FIRST INSTINCT WHEN YOU CHOOSE AN ANSWER!!' — too many students, after reviewing the exam, wish they had stayed with their first choice.

cards.q: Word play — Bronchoprovocation test = ?
cards.a:
Word play — Bronchoprovocation test = ?
Methacholine Challenge

cards.q: Word play — Cardio-Respiratory arrest = ? · Chronic Hypercarbia = ?
cards.a:
Word play — Cardio-Respiratory arrest = ? · Chronic Hypercarbia = ?
Cardio-Respiratory arrest = Full Arrest
Chronic Hypercarbia = CO₂ Retainer

cards.q: Word play — Controlled O₂ concentration = ?
cards.a:
Word play — Controlled O₂ concentration = ?
Specific FiO₂

cards.q: ⚠ Word play — Heart Failure = ?
cards.a:
⚠ Word play — Heart Failure = ?
Heart Failure = Cardiac Arrest = Cardiac Failure
⚠ O₂ does NOT help!

cards.q: ⚠ Word play — HFNC = ? (and the trap)
cards.a:
⚠ Word play — HFNC = ? (and the trap)
HFNC = VapoTherm or Optiflow (Fisher & Paykel)
⚠ NOT 'HFNC' up to 15 L — that is not high-flow.

cards.q: Word play — Induction Agents = ? · Imbalance = ? · Inclusion Criteria = ?
cards.a:
Word play — Induction Agents = ? · Imbalance = ? · Inclusion Criteria = ?
Induction Agents = Anesthetic Meds
Imbalance = Mismatch
Inclusion Criteria = Indication

cards.q: Word play — Liberation Parameters = ? · Long-standing = ?
cards.a:
Word play — Liberation Parameters = ? · Long-standing = ?
Liberation Parameters = Weaning
Long-standing = Chronic

cards.q: Word play — Mainstay = ?
cards.a:
Word play — Mainstay = ?
Best suited for / Therapy of choice (1st choice)

cards.q: Word play — the NIV family = ?
cards.a:
Word play — the NIV family = ?
NIPPV = NPPV = NIV = BiPAP

cards.q: Word play — No purposeful movement to command = ? · Oxygen-induced Hypoventilation = ?
cards.a:
Word play — No purposeful movement to command = ? · Oxygen-induced Hypoventilation = ?
No purposeful movement to command = UNCONSCIOUS
Oxygen-induced Hypoventilation = Knocked out the HYPOXIC DRIVE

cards.q: Word play — PBW = ? · RRT = ? · SIMV = ?
cards.a:
Word play — PBW = ? · RRT = ? · SIMV = ?
PBW (predicted body weight) = IBW (ideal body weight)
Rapid Response Team (RRT) = Medical Emergency Team (MET)
SIMV = IMV

cards.q: ⚠ The special precaution words — the full list
cards.a:
⚠ The special precaution words — the full list
Adequate · At least · Blunted · Except · First · Most commonly used · Most likely · Next · Nonpulmonary · Not · Observation · Obliterated · Precedence (importance) · Recommend at this time (first step) · Routinely · Severe · Significance · Warrants · Laryngotracheal (injury).

cards.q: ⚠ Three trick-word traps spelled out?
cards.a:
⚠ Three trick-word traps spelled out?
'Aggressive pain control' does NOT mean too much meds.
'Changes to treatment plan' and 'ACTUAL ORDERS' are NOT the same.
'Eliminate' does NOT mean 'Filter' — lungs vs kidneys.
'Mechanical Ventilation' = vent OR BiPAP, not vents only.

cards.q: ⚠ Which two words are NOT the same?
cards.a:
⚠ Which two words are NOT the same?
SEVERE and SIGNIFICANT are NOT THE SAME.

cards.q: What does a CLOSED-ended question give you, and when should you use one?
cards.a:
What does a CLOSED-ended question give you, and when should you use one?
A short, specific answer — usually yes/no or a single piece of data. The slides say they 'give limited insight' but deliver specific information FAST.
Use when you need an answer quickly — especially with a patient in respiratory distress.
'Are you short of breath right now?' · 'Do you use oxygen at home?'

cards.q: What does an OPEN-ended question give you?
cards.a:
What does an OPEN-ended question give you?
Thought-provoking, BROADER information — it lets the patient tell their story and often uncovers things you never would have thought to ask.
'Tell me what happens when you become short of breath.'

cards.q: Which question type is correct — closed or open?
cards.a:
Which question type is correct — closed or open?
Both are appropriate. The RT's skill is knowing WHEN to use each.

cards.q: What is the interview strategy for questioning a patient?
cards.a:
What is the interview strategy for questioning a patient?
Start BROAD → then NARROW DOWN.
'Tell me about your cough' → 'When did it start?' → 'Is it productive?' → 'What color is the sputum?'

cards.q: Which TWO question types must you avoid, and why?
cards.a:
Which TWO question types must you avoid, and why?
LEADING questions — 'You're feeling better after that treatment, aren't you?' nudges the patient toward the answer you want and produces false or slanted information.
COMPOUND questions — asking several things at once, so a 'yes' tells you nothing.

cards.q: Name the summary sequence for a patient interview.
cards.a:
Name the summary sequence for a patient interview.
Open-ended → Closed-ended → Clarify → Silence/Facilitation → Summarize/Confirm.

cards.q: Name the nine questioning techniques.
cards.a:
Name the nine questioning techniques.
Closed-ended · open-ended · clarification · leading (AVOID) · compound · facilitation · respectfully identify inconsistencies · silence/pause · support and reassurance.

cards.q: In the 5 Levels of Communication, which number is the most SUPERFICIAL?
cards.a:
In the 5 Levels of Communication, which number is the most SUPERFICIAL?
Level 5. The levels count DOWN — 5 is most superficial, 1 is deepest.

cards.q: What is Level 5 communication?
cards.a:
What is Level 5 communication?
Cliché conversation — basic social interaction, little meaningful information ('How are you today?' 'Fine').
Not useless — it is often how rapport BEGINS.

cards.q: What is Level 4 communication, and why does it matter?
cards.a:
What is Level 4 communication, and why does it matter?
Reporting facts — exchanging objective information ('I've been coughing for three days,' 'I'm on 2 liters at home').
This is where MOST routine healthcare communication happens.

cards.q: What is Level 3 communication, and how should you respond to it?
cards.a:
What is Level 3 communication, and how should you respond to it?
Personal ideas or judgments — the patient shares what they think or believe ('I don't think these treatments are helping').
EXPLORE it instead of CORRECTING it.

cards.q: What is Level 2 communication?
cards.a:
What is Level 2 communication?
Feelings and emotions — the patient trusts you enough to say how they actually feel.
'I'm scared I'll end up on the ventilator again.'

cards.q: What is Level 1 communication, and does it belong in the RT–patient relationship?
cards.a:
What is Level 1 communication, and does it belong in the RT–patient relationship?
Peak communication — the highest, intimate level, reserved for a select few: close personal relationships.
NO — it is not the RT–patient relationship.

cards.q: Which levels are the therapeutic 'sweet spot' the RT must reach?
cards.a:
Which levels are the therapeutic 'sweet spot' the RT must reach?
Levels 2–3. The RT must move BEYOND superficial communication (Levels 4–5) and build enough trust to reach meaningful therapeutic communication.

cards.q: A patient communicates at Level 2. Should the RT reciprocate at Level 2?
cards.a:
A patient communicates at Level 2. Should the RT reciprocate at Level 2?
NO — this is the professional boundary.
Patient self-disclosure gets a THERAPEUTIC RESPONSE — not the RT's own personal fears.

cards.q: Name the three-step chain for building a therapeutic relationship.
cards.a:
Name the three-step chain for building a therapeutic relationship.
Rapport → Trust → Cooperation.
The overall goal is relationships built on honesty, trust and respect.

cards.q: Give the three percentages of the 3 V's of Communication.
cards.a:
Give the three percentages of the 3 V's of Communication.
Verbal = 7% (the words)
Vocal = 38% (tone, volume, pitch, rate)
Visual = 55% (facial expressions, gestures, posture, body language)
→ 93% of communication is NONVERBAL.

cards.q: When verbal and nonverbal messages CONFLICT, which does the listener trust?
cards.a:
When verbal and nonverbal messages CONFLICT, which does the listener trust?
The VOCAL and VISUAL channels — especially when interpreting feelings and attitudes.
So verbal + vocal + visual must be CONGRUENT.

cards.q: Give the classic RT failure example of incongruent communication.
cards.a:
Give the classic RT failure example of incongruent communication.
Telling an anxious patient 'Take your time, I'm here with you' while looking at your watch, standing by the door, and sighing.
The words say one thing; the vocal and visual say HURRY UP.

cards.q: What is the caveat about the 7 / 38 / 55 percentages?
cards.a:
What is the caveat about the 7 / 38 / 55 percentages?
They come from Albert Mehrabian's 1960s research on communicating FEELINGS AND ATTITUDES when verbal and nonverbal signals are INCONSISTENT.
Mehrabian himself said the formula does NOT apply to communication generally — you cannot get 93% of 'Change the PEEP to 10 cmH₂O' from a face and tone.
Memorize 7/38/55 for the exam, but know it is an overgeneralization.

cards.q: Define proxemics.
cards.a:
Define proxemics.
