cards.q: Name the causes of hypoventilation.
cards.a:
Name the causes of hypoventilation.
Respiratory-center depression · neuromuscular weakness · obesity-hypoventilation syndrome (Pickwickian) · chronic hypoventilation syndromes · O₂-induced hypoventilation in the COPD patient given too much oxygen.

cards.q: How do you avoid O₂-induced hypoventilation in COPD?
cards.a:
How do you avoid O₂-induced hypoventilation in COPD?
Hold PaO₂ around 55–60 torr and use a 28% AIR-ENTRAINMENT DEVICE.
⚠ CPAP alone does NOT overcome hypoventilation — you need BILEVEL support.

cards.q: Contrast what hypocapnia and hypercapnia do to ICP in a TBI patient.
cards.a:
Contrast what hypocapnia and hypercapnia do to ICP in a TBI patient.
HYPOCAPNIA → cerebral VASOCONSTRICTION → LOWER ICP, but RISK OF ISCHEMIA (so it is not recommended routinely).
HYPERCAPNIA → cerebral VASODILATION → INCREASED ICP.

cards.q: Give the quick exam contrast between the five breathing patterns.
cards.a:
Give the quick exam contrast between the five breathing patterns.
DIAPHRAGMATIC and PURSED-LIP are TAUGHT TECHNIQUES (inspiratory and expiratory respectively).
THORACIC is the BAD PATTERN you are training away.
HYPER- and HYPOVENTILATION are ACID-BASE STATES defined by the PaCO₂ — not by how fast the patient looks like they are breathing.

cards.q: What is glossopharyngeal ('frog') breathing, and who is it for?
cards.a:
What is glossopharyngeal ('frog') breathing, and who is it for?
It uses the GLOSSOPHARYNGEAL MUSCLES to CAPTURE AND SWALLOW AIR, which improves spontaneous ventilation in patients with NEUROMUSCULAR DISEASE.

cards.q: What does inspiratory muscle training accomplish?
cards.a:
What does inspiratory muscle training accomplish?
It helps COPD patients manage their DYSPNEA, increase EXERCISE TOLERANCE, and improve health-related QUALITY OF LIFE.
It may also improve diaphragm function in certain neuromuscular disorders and may aid in WEANING ventilator-dependent patients.

cards.q: What are the two IMT device types — and which is preferred, and why?
cards.a:
What are the two IMT device types — and which is preferred, and why?
Flow resistors and THRESHOLD resistors (similar to PEP resistors, except the patient INHALES against the resistor).
SPRING-LOADED THRESHOLD resistors are PREFERRED, because they can be set to a SPECIFIC NEGATIVE PRESSURE — giving a CONSTANT MUSCLE LOAD INDEPENDENT OF FLOW.
If you must use a flow resistor, attach a manometer to the monitoring port.

cards.q: Give the steps for starting IMT.
cards.a:
Give the steps for starting IMT.
(1) Train the patient in proper DIAPHRAGMATIC BREATHING first.
(2) Measure MIP/PImax with a CALIBRATED MANOMETER.
(3) Start with SLOW breathing — fewer than 10–12 breaths/min — with MINIMAL initial resistance.
(4) Slowly increase resistance until inspiratory pressure is 30% OR MORE of MIP/PImax.
(5) Then 10- to 15-minute sessions, ONCE OR TWICE per day.
(6) Keep a detailed TREATMENT LOG.

cards.q: Give the IMT intensity recommendation and weekly progression.
cards.a:
Give the IMT intensity recommendation and weekly progression.
Minimum of 30% of PImax (lower initial intensity may be needed in COPD patients), increased by 5% of PImax PER WEEK as tolerated.

cards.q: Give the IMT session length, frequency per day, and days per week.
cards.a:
Give the IMT session length, frequency per day, and days per week.
Total of 30 MINUTES PER DAY, divided over 1–2 sessions (initial sessions may need to be limited to 3–5 minutes).
1–2 sessions per day · 4–6 days per week according to patient tolerance.

cards.q: How long before IMT produces functional improvement — and how long should it continue?
cards.a:
How long before IMT produces functional improvement — and how long should it continue?
Functional improvement usually requires AT LEAST 5 WEEKS of training.
Continue INDEFINITELY to maintain the benefit.

cards.q: ⚠ What happens if a patient STOPS inspiratory muscle training?
cards.a:
⚠ What happens if a patient STOPS inspiratory muscle training?
Patients progressively LOSE ANY HEALTH-RELATED BENEFIT if they cease training.
That is the argument for continuing indefinitely.

cards.q: The MIP does not improve after IMT. What do you do?
cards.a:
The MIP does not improve after IMT. What do you do?
INTERVIEW THE PATIENT and INSPECT THE TREATMENT LOG to find out why — usually NONCOMPLIANCE.

cards.q: What do you do if an adverse reaction occurs during breathing exercises or IMT?
cards.a:
What do you do if an adverse reaction occurs during breathing exercises or IMT?
STOP THE THERAPY.

cards.q: Which branch is acetylcholine the neurotransmitter of, and what inactivates it?
cards.a:
Which branch is acetylcholine the neurotransmitter of, and what inactivates it?
The PARASYMPATHETIC ('rest-and-digest') branch — and one of the two PNS neurotransmitters, the other being norepinephrine.
Inactivated by CHOLINESTERASE (acetylcholinesterase, AchE) enzymes.

cards.q: Name the two acetylcholine receptor families.
cards.a:
Name the two acetylcholine receptor families.
MUSCARINIC and NICOTINIC.

cards.q: Which muscarinic subtypes sit on the heart and on airway smooth muscle?
cards.a:
Which muscarinic subtypes sit on the heart and on airway smooth muscle?
M2 = HEART · M3 = AIRWAY SMOOTH MUSCLE (M3 is also on blood vessels).
The full family is M1–M5.

cards.q: What happens when Ach acts on a parasympathetic effector organ?
cards.a:
What happens when Ach acts on a parasympathetic effector organ?
↓ HR, BP, RR · ↓ atrial force · BRONCHOCONSTRICTION · ↑ salivary secretions · MIOSIS · ↑ GI motility · ↑ insulin secretion.

cards.q: Which receptor type carries the impulse across the autonomic GANGLION?
cards.a:
Which receptor type carries the impulse across the autonomic GANGLION?
NICOTINIC. Ach carries the impulse across the ganglion — the second of the two parasympathetic sites.

cards.q: What happens at the neuromuscular junction, and which receptor is involved?
cards.a:
What happens at the neuromuscular junction, and which receptor is involved?
NICOTINIC receptors on the muscle END PLATE.
Ach released → binds the end-plate receptor → DEPOLARIZATION → muscle CONTRACTION.
This is the SOMATIC (voluntary) system — NOT autonomic.

cards.q: Which sympathetic fibres release acetylcholine instead of norepinephrine?
cards.a:
Which sympathetic fibres release acetylcholine instead of norepinephrine?
Sympathetic cholinergic fibres to the SWEAT GLANDS — the one anatomical exception.
⚠ NOT covered in Heuer or the available decks — look up 'sympathetic cholinergic sudomotor fibres' in a general pharmacology/A&P text.

cards.q: Distinguish DIRECT-acting from INDIRECT-acting cholinergic drugs, with an example of each.
cards.a:
Distinguish DIRECT-acting from INDIRECT-acting cholinergic drugs, with an example of each.
DIRECT-acting = MIMICS Ach — methacholine, used for the asthma methacholine challenge test.
INDIRECT-acting = INHIBITS CHOLINESTERASE so more Ach piles up — neostigmine, which treats Myasthenia Gravis and reverses nondepolarizing paralytics.

cards.q: What is a cholinesterase REACTIVATOR, and what is it for?
cards.a:
What is a cholinesterase REACTIVATOR, and what is it for?
PRALIDOXIME — for ORGANOPHOSPHATE TOXICITY.

cards.q: Name the prototype anticholinergic and its effects.
cards.a:
Name the prototype anticholinergic and its effects.
ATROPINE, a competitive antagonist.
Effects: BRONCHODILATION · DRYING OF SECRETIONS · antidiarrheal. Treats bradycardia, organophosphate poisoning, and mushroom ingestion.
Scopolamine is used for motion sickness.

cards.q: How do NONDEPOLARIZING neuromuscular blockers work, and what are three examples?
cards.a:
How do NONDEPOLARIZING neuromuscular blockers work, and what are three examples?
They INHIBIT/BLOCK Ach at the receptor → prolonged paralysis for controlled ventilation.
Vecuronium · cisatracurium · pancuronium.

cards.q: How does succinylcholine work, and what is it used for?
cards.a:
How does succinylcholine work, and what is it used for?
A DEPOLARIZING agent — it BINDS AND ACTIVATES, causing sustained depolarization so the end plate goes REFRACTORY/UNEXCITABLE → FLACCID PARALYSIS.
Short-acting — used for INTUBATION.

cards.q: What is the underlying defect in Myasthenia Gravis?
cards.a:
What is the underlying defect in Myasthenia Gravis?
An anti-acetylcholine receptor (anti-AchR) ANTIBODY blocks Ach receptors at the myoneural junction → FATIGABILITY.

cards.q: How does the tensilon test distinguish myasthenic from cholinergic crisis?
cards.a:
How does the tensilon test distinguish myasthenic from cholinergic crisis?
Patient IMPROVES = MYASTHENIC crisis.
Patient WORSENS = CHOLINERGIC crisis — too much Ach at the myoneural junction: diaphoresis, bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, miosis. ATROPINE is the treatment.

cards.q: Define intracranial pressure and name what it is measured with.
cards.a:
Define intracranial pressure and name what it is measured with.
The pressure inside the skull — brain tissue + blood + cerebrospinal fluid.
Measured by an INTRAVENTRICULAR CATHETER or INTRAPARENCHYMAL PROBE.
Monitored in TBI, intracranial hemorrhage, and cerebral edema.

cards.q: Give the four ICP threshold numbers.
cards.a:
Give the four ICP threshold numbers.
10–15 mm Hg = normal in a supine healthy adult.
> 20 mm Hg for more than 5–10 minutes = abnormally high / unsafe.
> 25 mm Hg for a prolonged period = critical, poor outcomes.
> 15–20 mm Hg = cerebral blood flow can fall to a critical level → secondary ischemia.

cards.q: Give the TBI management goals for ICP, CPP and MAP.
cards.a:
Give the TBI management goals for ICP, CPP and MAP.
Keep ICP < 20 mm Hg · CPP ≥ 60 mm Hg (CPP = MAP − ICP) · MAP > 75 mm Hg.

cards.q: Name the four causes of DECREASED ICP.
cards.a:
Name the four causes of DECREASED ICP.
Head elevation · decrease in CSF volume · severe arterial hypotension · hyperventilation/hypocapnia.

cards.q: Name the therapeutic ways to lower ICP.
cards.a:
Name the therapeutic ways to lower ICP.
Osmotic diuresis with MANNITOL or HYPERTONIC SALINE · ventricular drainage · sedation · head of bed up 30–40 degrees.

cards.q: ⚠ Why does Heuer say to AVOID routine prophylactic hyperventilation?
cards.a:
⚠ Why does Heuer say to AVOID routine prophylactic hyperventilation?
Because it can cause CEREBRAL ISCHEMIA.
Use it ONLY before suctioning, in confirmed herniation, or as salvage therapy.

cards.q: Name the causes of INCREASED ICP.
cards.a:
Name the causes of INCREASED ICP.
Increased brain volume (edema or tumor) · increased blood volume inside the skull (hemorrhage/hematoma) · restricted venous outflow (CVP > ICP) · right heart failure / cor pulmonale · high intrathoracic pressure (high PEEP, recruitment maneuvers) · severe arterial hypertension · hypoventilation/hypercapnia · hypoxia · hydrocephalus.

cards.q: Why does hypercapnia raise ICP?
cards.a:
Why does hypercapnia raise ICP?
Because CO₂ causes CEREBRAL VASODILATION.

cards.q: Which RT procedures raise ICP?
cards.a:
Which RT procedures raise ICP?
Moving/positioning (especially TRENDELENBURG) · flexion or hyperextension of the NECK · intubation · suctioning/coughing · ventilator asynchrony · high PEEP / high mean airway pressure · recruitment maneuvers.

cards.q: What does Biot breathing point to, and what is the treatment?
cards.a:
What does Biot breathing point to, and what is the treatment?
Clusters of rapid breaths with apnea → MEDULLA damage or ↑ICP.
Treat the cause and LOWER THE ICP.

cards.q: Why is mannitol called 'a brain drug, not a lung drug' — and what is the caution?
cards.a:
Why is mannitol called 'a brain drug, not a lung drug' — and what is the caution?
It is NOT REABSORBED in the tubule, so it pulls water OSMOTICALLY and reduces brain swelling.
⚠ CAUTION: mannitol FIRST PULLS FLUID INTO THE BLOODSTREAM, so it can TRANSIENTLY WORSEN pulmonary edema and CHF.

cards.q: Name the body's two major control systems, and the two divisions of the nervous system.
cards.a:
Name the body's two major control systems, and the two divisions of the nervous system.
Control systems: the NERVOUS system and the ENDOCRINE system.
CNS = brain + spinal cord — 'the command center,' SENDS the signal.
PNS = all nerves outside the CNS — 'the wiring system,' CARRIES the signal.

cards.q: Name the three classes of neurons in the PNS.
cards.a:
Name the three classes of neurons in the PNS.
SENSORY · SOMATIC · AUTONOMIC.

cards.q: Distinguish the somatic motor system from the ANS — and which do NMBAs affect?
cards.a:
Distinguish the somatic motor system from the ANS — and which do NMBAs affect?
SOMATIC MOTOR → skeletal muscle, VOLUNTARY — this is where NMBAs work.
ANS → organs, INVOLUNTARY — NMBAs do NOT affect it.
The ANS is the motor-neuron arm of the PNS and is generally considered an EFFERENT system.

cards.q: Describe how a nerve impulse becomes a chemical signal.
cards.a:
Describe how a nerve impulse becomes a chemical signal.
Nerve impulses are ELECTROCHEMICAL: an electrical ACTION POTENTIAL travels the fibre, then converts to CHEMICAL transmission at the SYNAPSE, releasing a neurotransmitter onto the neuroeffector site.

cards.q: Name the three catecholamines, where they come from, and how norepinephrine's action ends.
cards.a:
Name the three catecholamines, where they come from, and how norepinephrine's action ends.
Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine — released from the ADRENAL MEDULLA.
Norepinephrine's action is terminated by REUPTAKE, COMT, and MAO.

cards.q: Give the four adrenergic receptors and what each does.
cards.a:
Give the four adrenergic receptors and what each does.
α1 = EXCITATORY (vasoconstriction)
α2 = INHIBITORY (presynaptic — shuts off further neurotransmitter release)
β1 = EXCITATORY in the HEART
β2 = in the LUNGS (smooth-muscle relaxation = BRONCHODILATION)
Plus dopaminergic.

cards.q: What are NANC nerves, and what does each type do?
cards.a:
What are NANC nerves, and what does each type do?
NonAdrenergic NonCholinergic — they use neither transmitter.
INHIBITORY NANC relaxes airway smooth muscle (BRONCHODILATION) via VIP or NITRIC OXIDE.
EXCITATORY NANC causes BRONCHOCONSTRICTION via SUBSTANCE P on afferent sensory fibres.

cards.q: Give the fibre ORIGIN for parasympathetic vs sympathetic.
cards.a:
Give the fibre ORIGIN for parasympathetic vs sympathetic.
Parasympathetic = CRANIOSACRAL (cranial + sacral cord).
Sympathetic = THORACOLUMBAR (thoracic + lumbar cord).

cards.q: Give the fibre LENGTHS for parasympathetic vs sympathetic.
cards.a:
Give the fibre LENGTHS for parasympathetic vs sympathetic.
Parasympathetic: LONG preganglionic, SHORT postganglionic.
Sympathetic: SHORT preganglionic, LONG postganglionic.

cards.q: Contrast the parasympathetic and sympathetic effects on the eye and GI motility.
cards.a:
Contrast the parasympathetic and sympathetic effects on the eye and GI motility.
EYE — Parasympathetic: MIOSIS (constriction). Sympathetic: MYDRIASIS (dilation).
GI MOTILITY — Parasympathetic: INCREASED. Sympathetic: DECREASED.

cards.q: Contrast the parasympathetic and sympathetic RESPONSE PATTERNS.
cards.a:
Contrast the parasympathetic and sympathetic RESPONSE PATTERNS.
Parasympathetic: LOCALIZED, calming, day-to-day (digestion, bladder, basal bronchial mucus).
Sympathetic: WIDESPREAD, rapid — a general ALARM system. Not essential to life, but allows coping with violent stress.

cards.q: What does SLUD stand for, and when do you see it?
cards.a:
What does SLUD stand for, and when do you see it?
Salivation · Lacrimation · Urination · Defecation.
Seen with PARASYMPATHETIC OVERSTIMULATION.

cards.q: Give the four drug terms for the two autonomic branches.
cards.a:
Give the four drug terms for the two autonomic branches.
PARASYMPATHOMIMETIC = CHOLINERGIC · PARASYMPATHOLYTIC = ANTICHOLINERGIC
SYMPATHOMIMETIC = ADRENERGIC · SYMPATHOLYTIC = ANTIADRENERGIC

cards.q: Name the three parts of a neuron, and what bridges the axon to skeletal muscle.
cards.a:
Name the three parts of a neuron, and what bridges the axon to skeletal muscle.
Cell body · axons · dendrites.
The gap between the axon and the skeletal muscle fibre is the NEUROMUSCULAR JUNCTION, and transmission across it is chemically mediated by ACETYLCHOLINE.

cards.q: Distinguish depolarization from repolarization.
cards.a:
Distinguish depolarization from repolarization.
DEPOLARIZATION = the shift of the cell's normally NEGATIVE internal charge toward POSITIVE — a brief event that lets the impulse travel along the cell and jump to the next.
REPOLARIZATION = the return to the NEGATIVE resting membrane potential.

cards.q: Distinguish AFFERENT from EFFERENT, with the memory hooks.
cards.a:
Distinguish AFFERENT from EFFERENT, with the memory hooks.
AFFERENT = periphery → spinal cord (SENSORY, 'A-rrives').
EFFERENT = brain/spinal cord → neuroeffector site (MOTOR, 'E-xits').
Deck hook: 'The Action Affects the situation, leading to an End result, the Effect.'

cards.q: Describe the two-neuron chain of the autonomic system.
cards.a:
Describe the two-neuron chain of the autonomic system.
A PREGANGLIONIC fibre to the GANGLION, then a POSTGANGLIONIC fibre to the EFFECTOR — with the relative lengths flipped between the two branches.

cards.q: What happens in Guillain-Barré syndrome?
cards.a:
What happens in Guillain-Barré syndrome?
Inflammation destroys the MYELIN SHEATHS surrounding spinal-root and peripheral nerves → severe MUSCLE WEAKNESS and DIMINISHED REFLEXES.

cards.q: Where is the dorsal respiratory group, and what is it the primary controller of?
cards.a:
Where is the dorsal respiratory group, and what is it the primary controller of?
Along the LATERAL WALLS within the MEDULLA, in the NUCLEUS TRACTUS SOLITARIUS (NTS).
Hess's summary line: the DRG is the PRIMARY CONTROLLER OF THE DEPTH AND RATE OF INSPIRATION.

cards.q: What does the DRG receive, and where does it send efferents?
cards.a:
What does the DRG receive, and where does it send efferents?
RECEIVES: afferent impulses from the VAGUS (X) and GLOSSOPHARYNGEAL (IX) nerves, which modify the basic breathing pattern by STIMULATING INSPIRATION.
SENDS: efferents to the PHRENIC NERVE (driving the diaphragm) and to the EXTERNAL INTERCOSTAL motor nerves.

cards.q: Describe the normal inspiratory ramp, with its timings.
cards.a:
Describe the normal inspiratory ramp, with its timings.
A ramp signal that increases in force gradually for about 2 SECONDS, followed by cessation of inspiration for about 3 SECONDS — giving progressively stronger inspiratory-muscle contraction and a gradual rise in lung inflation.
In stressed breathing or exercise, peripheral receptors make the ramp STEEPER, so inflation is more rapid.

cards.q: Where is the ventral respiratory group, and what does it contain?
cards.a:
Where is the ventral respiratory group, and what does it contain?
In the MEDULLA, in two separate nuclei ANTERIOR AND LATERAL to each DRG. It contains BOTH inspiratory and expiratory neurons:
NUCLEUS AMBIGUUS — inspiratory neurons innervating the LARYNGEAL and PHARYNGEAL muscles.
NUCLEUS RETROAMBIGUALIS — both inspiratory and expiratory neurons.

cards.q: Where is the pneumotaxic centre, and what does it control?
cards.a:
Where is the pneumotaxic centre, and what does it control?
The UPPER PONS. It receives vagal afferents that fine-tune rhythm and BLOCKS stimulation of the DRG and VRG from the apneustic centre — it controls the STOPPING POINT of the inspiratory ramp.

cards.q: What does a STRONG vs WEAK pneumotaxic signal do?
cards.a:
What does a STRONG vs WEAK pneumotaxic signal do?
STRONG: SHORTENS inspiratory time, RAISES the rate → LOWER tidal volumes.
WEAK: LENGTHENS inspiration, LOWERS the rate → HIGHER tidal volumes.

cards.q: Where is the apneustic centre, and what happens if the pneumotaxic centre is destroyed?
cards.a:
Where is the apneustic centre, and what happens if the pneumotaxic centre is destroyed?
The LOWER PONS — it STIMULATES the inspiratory neurons of the DRG and VRG; normally the pneumotaxic centre inhibits it.
If the pneumotaxic centre is destroyed, the apneustic centre TAKES OVER and PREVENTS THE INSPIRATORY RAMP FROM SHUTTING OFF → PROLONGED INSPIRATION with a shortened expiratory time (apneustic breathing).

cards.q: Give the one-line way to keep the four respiratory centres straight.
cards.a:
Give the one-line way to keep the four respiratory centres straight.
DRG = depth and rate of inspiration (medulla, NTS)
VRG = inspiratory AND expiratory neurons, including the airway muscles (medulla)
PNEUMOTAXIC = upper pons, the OFF switch that ENDS inspiration
APNEUSTIC = lower pons, the ON switch the pneumotaxic centre keeps in check

cards.q: What does apneustic breathing indicate, and Cheyne-Stokes?
cards.a:
What does apneustic breathing indicate, and Cheyne-Stokes?
APNEUSTIC (prolonged gasping inspiration with incomplete expiration) → damage to the PONS from trauma, stroke or tumor.
CHEYNE-STOKES (waxing/waning tidal volumes with apneic periods) → CNS disease or severe CHF, and is common in TBI.

cards.q: ⚠ Which two 'medullas' in these decks are NOT the brainstem?
cards.a:
⚠ Which two 'medullas' in these decks are NOT the brainstem?
The RENAL medulla — inner kidney, contains the RENAL PYRAMIDS, where the Loop of Henle dips down.
The ADRENAL medulla — source of circulating CATECHOLAMINES.
Do not confuse them on the exam.

cards.q: Give the spinal cord injury levels and their effect on breathing.
cards.a:
Give the spinal cord injury levels and their effect on breathing.
ABOVE C3: damages the nerves innervating the respiratory muscles — typically requires artificial ventilatory support.
C3–C5: some nerves may remain intact — may breathe without support, at least some of the time.
BELOW C5: may breathe on their own, but expect REDUCED VITAL CAPACITY and an INABILITY TO COUGH/clear secretions.

cards.q: Distinguish tetraplegia from paraplegia by injury level.
cards.a:
Distinguish tetraplegia from paraplegia by injury level.
C1–C7 = TETRAPLEGIA — partial or complete loss of muscle function in ALL FOUR extremities.
Thoracic, lumbar or sacral = PARAPLEGIA — loss of motor + sensory function in the LOWER LIMBS AND TRUNK.

cards.q: Distinguish neurogenic from hemorrhagic shock in a spinal cord injury.
cards.a:
Distinguish neurogenic from hemorrhagic shock in a spinal cord injury.
NEUROGENIC — above T6 with BRADYCARDIA + HYPOTHERMIA: skin FLUSHED, WARM, DRY from vasodilation.
HEMORRHAGIC — at or below T6 with TACHYCARDIA + NORMAL core temperature: extremities COLD, CLAMMY, PALE.

cards.q: What does Heuer say about the phrenic nerve on a chest x-ray?
cards.a:
What does Heuer say about the phrenic nerve on a chest x-ray?
A condition affecting the phrenic nerve, such as QUADRIPLEGIA, often shows an ELEVATED DIAPHRAGM on chest x-ray.
Unilateral phrenic nerve paralysis produces a UNILATERAL REDUCTION IN CHEST MOVEMENT on the affected side.

cards.q: Give the spinal cord injury management pearls.
cards.a:
Give the spinal cord injury management pearls.
IMMOBILIZE head, neck and spine in a NEUTRAL position · continuous pulse oximetry and end-tidal CO₂ for all severe SCI · if APNEA is present, assume a COMPLETE HIGH CERVICAL injury and start manual ventilation IMMEDIATELY · ~1 in 4 SCI patients also has head trauma · measure VC and MIP/NIF once conscious · expect severe BRADYCARDIA from vagal stimulation during intubation (preoxygenate, IV atropine or topical lidocaine).

cards.q: Distinguish a COMPLETE from an INCOMPLETE spinal cord injury — and can it change?
cards.a:
Distinguish a COMPLETE from an INCOMPLETE spinal cord injury — and can it change?
COMPLETE = no sensory/motor function below the injury. INCOMPLETE = some function remains.
⚠ YES — an injury can PROGRESS from incomplete to complete as edema/bleeding/ischemia evolve.

cards.q: Give the one-line division of labour between lungs and kidneys in acid-base.
cards.a:
Give the one-line division of labour between lungs and kidneys in acid-base.
LUNGS → regulate CO₂ (VOLATILE acid).
KIDNEYS → regulate H⁺ and HCO₃⁻ (FIXED/NONVOLATILE acid).

cards.q: Name the fixed acids, and why only the kidney can clear them.
cards.a:
Name the fixed acids, and why only the kidney can clear them.
PHOSPHORIC, URIC, LACTIC and KETONE acids.
The respiratory system regulates carbonic acid by eliminating CO₂ — but it CANNOT EXCRETE the other acids produced by cellular metabolism.

cards.q: Describe GLOMERULAR FILTRATION and give the normal GFR.
cards.a:
Describe GLOMERULAR FILTRATION and give the normal GFR.
Blood → Tubule. PASSIVE.
HYDROSTATIC pressure PUSHES OUT (favors filtration); ONCOTIC/OSMOTIC pressure PULLS IN (opposes it).
Normal GFR ≈ 120–125 mL/min; young healthy adults ~90–120 mL/min/1.73 m².
It is NONSPECIFIC — it dumps everything in.

cards.q: Describe TUBULAR REABSORPTION.
cards.a:
Describe TUBULAR REABSORPTION.
Tubule → Blood. 'RECLAIMING PLASMA.'
Begins in the PROXIMAL TUBULE and is HIGHLY SELECTIVE.
Water reabsorption FOLLOWS Na⁺ reabsorption — 'water follows sodium.'
The proximal tubule is the primary site of HCO₃⁻ reabsorption.

cards.q: Describe TUBULAR SECRETION and name what gets secreted.
cards.a:
Describe TUBULAR SECRETION and name what gets secreted.
Blood → Tubule. 'CLEARING WASTE.'
H⁺, K⁺, NH₄⁺, creatinine, organic acids, drugs, urea, uric acid.

cards.q: Give the excretion equation, and distinguish secretion from excretion.
cards.a:
Give the excretion equation, and distinguish secretion from excretion.
Amount excreted = FILTERED − REABSORBED + SECRETED.
⚠ Secretion ≠ excretion: the kidney SECRETES H⁺ INTO THE TUBULE so it can be EXCRETED in urine.

cards.q: How does the kidney respond to ACIDOSIS, and to ALKALOSIS?
cards.a:
How does the kidney respond to ACIDOSIS, and to ALKALOSIS?
ACIDOSIS (pH < 7.35) → ↑ H⁺ SECRETION into the urine and ↑ HCO₃⁻ RETENTION → pH rises.
ALKALOSIS (pH > 7.45) → ↑ HCO₃⁻ EXCRETION in the urine → pH falls.

cards.q: Name the four renal mechanisms for handling an acid load.
cards.a:
Name the four renal mechanisms for handling an acid load.
(1) ↑ HCO₃⁻ REABSORPTION, mostly in the PROXIMAL tubules
(2) ↑ H⁺ SECRETION into the tubular lumen, particularly at the DISTAL CONVOLUTED TUBULES and COLLECTING DUCTS
(3) AMMONIA (NH₃) made from GLUTAMINE in the proximal tubule, binding H⁺ as AMMONIUM (NH₄⁺)
(4) PHOSPHATE BUFFERING — HPO₄²⁻ + H⁺ → H₂PO₄⁻

cards.q: Why does the ammonia mechanism matter?
cards.a:
Why does the ammonia mechanism matter?
It lets you DUMP ACID WITHOUT MAKING THE URINE DANGEROUSLY ACIDIC.

cards.q: ⚠ How fast is renal compensation compared with respiratory?
cards.a:
⚠ How fast is renal compensation compared with respiratory?
Renal compensation is SLOW — HOURS TO DAYS. The lungs work in MINUTES.
That timing difference is a classic exam point.

cards.q: Explain why low chloride or low potassium causes metabolic ALKALOSIS.
cards.a:
Explain why low chloride or low potassium causes metabolic ALKALOSIS.
Na⁺ reabsorbed with Cl⁻ is electrically and pH NEUTRAL. But Na⁺ EXCHANGED for H⁺ or K⁺ shifts pH.
So LOW Cl⁻ or LOW K⁺ FORCES Na⁺ to trade for H⁺ → you LOSE H⁺ → METABOLIC ALKALOSIS (↑pH, ↑HCO₃⁻).
Memory hook: LOSE H⁺ = ALKALOSIS; LOSE HCO₃⁻ = ACIDOSIS.

cards.q: How much fluid do the kidneys filter per day versus how much urine is made?
cards.a:
How much fluid do the kidneys filter per day versus how much urine is made?
They filter nearly 200 L per day, yet normal urine output is only 1 to 2 L/day — because the vast majority of the filtrate is REABSORBED.

cards.q: What share of oxygen and cardiac output do the kidneys take — and why so much oxygen?
cards.a:
What share of oxygen and cardiac output do the kidneys take — and why so much oxygen?
20–25% of all the oxygen the body uses at rest, and ~22% of cardiac output (≈ 1.1 L/min).
Because renal tubular cells do enormous amounts of ACTIVE TRANSPORT during reabsorption.
About 20% of blood flowing through the nephron (≈130 mL/min) is filtered, and 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed.

cards.q: ⚠ Give the urine output normals and oliguria thresholds — from BOTH sources.
cards.a:
⚠ Give the urine output normals and oliguria thresholds — from BOTH sources.
DIURETICS DECK: normal 30–60 mL/hr (1–2 L/day) · OLIGURIA < 30 mL/hr · ANURIA < 50 mL/day · POLYURIA > 60 mL/hr.
HEUER: normal 1200–1500 mL/day, i.e. at least 50 mL/hr · OLIGURIA < 25 mL/hr.
Know both.

cards.q: What urine output change activates the medical emergency team?
cards.a:
What urine output change activates the medical emergency team?
An acute change to LESS THAN 50 mL OVER 4 HOURS.

cards.q: Which is the more severe emergency — oliguria or anuria — and what does it signal?
cards.a:
Which is the more severe emergency — oliguria or anuria — and what does it signal?
ANURIA — near-complete kidney failure (AKI), dehydration, or total obstruction.
Falling UOP is an EARLY RED FLAG in shock, hypotension and poor cardiac output (CHF).

cards.q: Distinguish AZOTEMIA from UREMIA.
cards.a:
Distinguish AZOTEMIA from UREMIA.
AZOTEMIA = abnormal LABS ONLY — ↑ nitrogenous wastes (↑BUN/creatinine) in the blood.
UREMIA = abnormal LABS + SYMPTOMS — the clinical syndrome of severe renal dysfunction.

cards.q: Define Acute Kidney Injury and give its oliguria threshold.
cards.a:
Define Acute Kidney Injury and give its oliguria threshold.
An ABRUPT ↓ in renal function; ↑ BUN and creatinine. (Replaces the term 'acute renal failure.')
May cause oliguria < 400 mL/day; can result from severe hypotension / renal ischemia.

cards.q: Define Chronic Kidney Disease and name its three consequences.
cards.a:
Define Chronic Kidney Disease and name its three consequences.
PROGRESSIVE, long-term ↓ in function/GFR; ↑ BUN and creatinine.
Fluid/Na⁺ retention → PULMONARY EDEMA · ↑K⁺ → HYPERKALEMIA · ↓H⁺ excretion → METABOLIC ACIDOSIS.

cards.q: Give the BUN and creatinine normals and their ratio.
cards.a:
Give the BUN and creatinine normals and their ratio.
BUN 7–20 mg/dL · creatinine 0.7–1.3 mg/dL (men) / 0.6–1.1 mg/dL (women) · BUN:creatinine ratio ~10:1 to 20:1.
Urine is ~95% water.

cards.q: Trace the path of urine, and name the act of urinating.
cards.a:
Trace the path of urine, and name the act of urinating.
Kidney → ureter → urinary bladder → urethra.
The act of urinating is MICTURITION.

cards.q: Give the cardiopulmonary consequences of uremia.
cards.a:
Give the cardiopulmonary consequences of uremia.
HYPERTENSION (fluid/Na⁺ retention) → PULMONARY EDEMA (fluid overload) → PERICARDITIS (severe uremia) → KUSSMAUL RESPIRATIONS (respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis).

cards.q: What are the RT's responsibilities in renal dysfunction?
cards.a:
What are the RT's responsibilities in renal dysfunction?
Assess oxygenation and ventilation · monitor ABGs for metabolic acidosis and respiratory compensation · recognize KUSSMAUL respirations · assess/treat pulmonary edema and hypoxemia · provide O₂ or ventilatory support · watch for HYPERKALEMIA and ECG CHANGES.

cards.q: Where does the weight-based urine output rule come from?
cards.a:
Where does the weight-based urine output rule come from?
⚠ Weight-based UOP (0.5–1 mL/kg/hr normal, oliguria < 0.5 mL/kg/hr) is NOT in these decks.
The only mL/kg/hr number Heuer gives is the 1.0 mL/kg/hr BURN RESUSCITATION goal.

cards.q: Why does DKA belong in the renal section?
cards.a:
Why does DKA belong in the renal section?
Because the RENAL system is what clears KETONE ACIDS — the respiratory system can only eliminate carbonic acid as CO₂.

cards.q: Interpret the classic DKA ABG: pH 7.32, PaCO₂ 28, PaO₂ 108 RA, HCO₃⁻ 14, BE −10.
cards.a:
Interpret the classic DKA ABG: pH 7.32, PaCO₂ 28, PaO₂ 108 RA, HCO₃⁻ 14, BE −10.
PARTIALLY COMPENSATED METABOLIC ACIDOSIS WITH NORMAL OXYGENATION.
pH 7.32 acidemic · PaCO₂ 28 low = the respiratory compensation · PaO₂ 108 normal — DKA is a ventilation/acid-base problem, not an oxygenation one · HCO₃⁻ 14 low = the primary problem · BE −10 confirms metabolic origin.

cards.q: ⚠ In severe DKA on the ventilator, what must you NOT 'fix'?
cards.a:
⚠ In severe DKA on the ventilator, what must you NOT 'fix'?
A normal pH may be achievable ONLY via hyperventilation — i.e. with a LOWER-THAN-NORMAL PaCO₂.
Do NOT 'fix' that PaCO₂ down to 40 and drive the pH into the floor.

cards.q: Describe Kussmaul respirations — and what distinguishes them from Cheyne-Stokes and Biot?
cards.a:
Describe Kussmaul respirations — and what distinguishes them from Cheyne-Stokes and Biot?
DEEP and FAST/labored breathing; the patient looks 'AIR HUNGRY,' taking large volumes with each breath.
⚠ REGULAR rhythm with NO APNEIC PAUSES — that is what separates it from Cheyne-Stokes and Biot. Often noisy because the breaths are so deep.

cards.q: Why is Kussmaul breathing compensatory, and what is the treatment?
cards.a:
Why is Kussmaul breathing compensatory, and what is the treatment?
The patient BLOWS OFF CO₂ (an acid in solution) to RAISE THE pH.
Treatment: treat the UNDERLYING CAUSE.

cards.q: Give the pathway from renal failure to Kussmaul breathing.
cards.a:
Give the pathway from renal failure to Kussmaul breathing.
↓ renal H⁺ excretion → METABOLIC ACIDOSIS → ↓ pH → ↑ VENTILATION → KUSSMAUL RESPIRATIONS.
Kussmaul is seen in ANY severe metabolic acidosis, including severe renal failure — not just DKA.

cards.q: Which diuretic class can precipitate DKA?
cards.a:
Which diuretic class can precipitate DKA?
THIAZIDES — they have the strongest diabetogenic activity, raising serum glucose, and some cases of DKA have been reported.

cards.q: What DKA details are still missing from your sources?
cards.a:
What DKA details are still missing from your sources?
⚠ DKA's diagnostic GLUCOSE, ANION GAP, and serum/urine KETONE numbers, plus its INSULIN/FLUID treatment, are NOT covered.
Look them up in an endocrine or acid-base chapter.

cards.q: Give the one concept that runs the entire diuretics chapter.
cards.a:
Give the one concept that runs the entire diuretics chapter.
WATER FOLLOWS SODIUM.
Diuretics do NOT increase filtration and do NOT chase water; they BLOCK Na⁺ from re-entering the tubule cell, so Na⁺ stays in the tubule, water stays with it, and urine output rises.
LOCATION DETERMINES EFFECT.

cards.q: Give the normal distribution of sodium reabsorption along the nephron.
cards.a:
Give the normal distribution of sodium reabsorption along the nephron.
70% proximal tubule · 20% Loop of Henle · 10% distal tubule.
ALDOSTERONE increases Na⁺ and H₂O reabsorption in the DISTAL tubule while DUMPING K⁺.

cards.q: Why do diuretics matter to an RT?
cards.a:
Why do diuretics matter to an RT?
Less fluid = DRIER LUNGS = ↓ pulmonary edema, ↑ oxygenation, ↓ work of breathing.

cards.q: Give the loop diuretic's site, mechanism and potency.
cards.a:
Give the loop diuretic's site, mechanism and potency.
Furosemide (Lasix), bumetanide, torsemide, ethacrynic acid.
ASCENDING LOOP OF HENLE — blocks Na⁺/K⁺/Cl⁻ reabsorption → up to 20% of NaCl and H₂O excreted = MOST POTENT.

cards.q: Why does IV furosemide help before any urine appears?
cards.a:
Why does IV furosemide help before any urine appears?
IV VASODILATION WITHIN 5 MINUTES — ↓ PCWP, BP and SVR — so work of breathing and oxygenation improve BEFORE urine appears.
It is #1 for pulmonary edema/CHF.

cards.q: Name the loop diuretic's adverse effects.
cards.a:
Name the loop diuretic's adverse effects.
HYPOKALEMIA · METABOLIC ALKALOSIS · HYPOVOLEMIA · OTOTOXICITY (usually reversible) · LOSES Ca²⁺.

cards.q: Give the thiazide's site, first-line use, and two distinguishing effects.
cards.a:
Give the thiazide's site, first-line use, and two distinguishing effects.
DISTAL TUBULE — blocks NaCl reabsorption; moderate strength; also ↓ peripheral vascular resistance.
FIRST-LINE for mild HYPERTENSION — NOT for acute pulmonary edema.
⚠ KEEPS CALCIUM (opposite of loops) · ↑ BLOOD GLUCOSE / reported DKA. Narrow therapeutic margin.

cards.q: Give the two potassium-sparing classes, their sites, and the shared danger.
cards.a:
Give the two potassium-sparing classes, their sites, and the shared danger.
ALDOSTERONE ANTAGONISTS — spironolactone (Aldactone), eplerenone (Inspra): DISTAL CONVOLUTED TUBULE, competitively blocks aldosterone. For cirrhosis/ascites, hyperaldosteronism.
Na⁺ CHANNEL BLOCKERS — triamterene, amiloride (Midamor): COLLECTING DUCTS, directly block Na⁺ channels.
⚠ BOTH cause HYPERKALEMIA — MORE LIFE-THREATENING than K⁺ depletion.

cards.q: For CHF pulmonary edema with a serum K⁺ below 3.5, what does Heuer recommend?
cards.a:
For CHF pulmonary edema with a serum K⁺ below 3.5, what does Heuer recommend?
A K⁺-SPARING agent such as AMILORIDE — instead of furosemide.

cards.q: Which diuretic combination is most common, and what is the trade-off?
cards.a:
Which diuretic combination is most common, and what is the trade-off?
LOOP + THIAZIDE — agents at different nephron sites give an additive/synergistic response.
Trade-off: stronger diuresis but higher risk of HYPOKALEMIA, DEHYDRATION and HYPOTENSION.

cards.q: Name the most common adverse effects of diuretics overall.
cards.a:
Name the most common adverse effects of diuretics overall.
HYPOVOLEMIA · ELECTROLYTE ABNORMALITIES (hypokalemia is #1) · ACID-BASE DISORDERS.
Hypokalemia + hypochloremia → METABOLIC ALKALOSIS.

cards.q: What is the role of diuretics in ARDS?
cards.a:
What is the role of diuretics in ARDS?
SUPPORTIVE ONLY — ARDS is noncardiogenic pulmonary edema from LEAKY CAPILLARIES.
Though reduced PCWP is associated with increased survival.

cards.q: Give the diuretic cautions for preterm infants.
cards.a:
Give the diuretic cautions for preterm infants.
Routine SUSTAINED use in preterm infants with chronic lung disease is NOT recommended, and aerosolized furosemide helps only SHORT-TERM.
In children generally: smaller doses, with FUROSEMIDE the most effective and least toxic — but risk of nephrocalcinosis and ↓ bone density.

cards.q: What three questions describe ANY ventilator mode?
cards.a:
What three questions describe ANY ventilator mode?
(1) What is the CONTROL VARIABLE — volume or pressure?
(2) What STARTS and ENDS the breath (trigger/cycle)?
(3) What BREATH SEQUENCE is allowed — CMV, IMV, or CSV?
'Don't memorize ventilator names. Learn how to DESCRIBE ventilator modes.'

cards.q: In Volume Control, what is preset and what varies?
cards.a:
In Volume Control, what is preset and what varies?
VOLUME AND FLOW are both preset before inspiration. V_T is GUARANTEED; PRESSURE varies.
If compliance ↓ or Raw ↑, PIP/Pplat RISE but V_T stays the same.

cards.q: Give the VC trigger, limit and cycle.
cards.a:
Give the VC trigger, limit and cycle.
Trigger: patient or time · Limit: volume/flow · Cycle: VOLUME — the breath ends when the preset V_T is delivered.

cards.q: What do the VC waveforms look like?
cards.a:
What do the VC waveforms look like?
Flow waveform = SQUARE/CONSTANT.
Pressure waveform 'CLIMBS LIKE A MOUNTAIN.'

cards.q: In Pressure Control, what is preset and what varies?
cards.a:
In Pressure Control, what is preset and what varies?
A preset PRESSURE PLATEAU held for a preset I-TIME. V_T VARIES with compliance and Raw.
Flow waveform = DECELERATING; pressure waveform is a flat 'TABLE.'

cards.q: Calculate the PIP in pressure control with PC 20 and PEEP 10.
cards.a:
Calculate the PIP in pressure control with PC 20 and PEEP 10.
PIP = PC setting + PEEP = 20 + 10 = 30 cmH₂O.

cards.q: Give the PC trigger, limit and cycle — and when do you choose PC?
cards.a:
Give the PC trigger, limit and cycle — and when do you choose PC?
TIME-triggered, PRESSURE-limited, TIME-cycled (may also be patient-triggered for extra breaths).
2nd choice. Use for severe ARDS / low compliance, and any time limiting airway pressure matters more than guaranteeing V_T — VC pressures ≥ 50 cmH₂O cause barotrauma.

cards.q: In Chang's Control mode (CMV), what can the patient do?
cards.a:
In Chang's Control mode (CMV), what can the patient do?
NOTHING — patient triggering and spontaneous breathing are NOT possible.
The ventilator does 100% of the work: preset V_T, preset rate. TIME-triggered only.

cards.q: When is Chang's Control mode used, and what does it require?
cards.a:
When is Chang's Control mode used, and what does it require?
Tetanus/seizures · complete rest · crushed chest injury/flail chest · paradoxical chest wall movement.
Requires DEEP SEDATION ± PARALYSIS.

cards.q: ⚠ How fast does diaphragm atrophy set in during controlled ventilation?
cards.a:
⚠ How fast does diaphragm atrophy set in during controlled ventilation?
18–69 HOURS of inactivity causes marked MYOFIBER ATROPHY.

cards.q: ⚠ In control mode, which two alarms matter most, and why?
cards.a:
⚠ In control mode, which two alarms matter most, and why?
LOW EXHALED VOLUME and LOW INSPIRATORY PRESSURE — because the patient is 100% ventilator-dependent.

cards.q: In Hess's terminology, what is CMV?
cards.a:
In Hess's terminology, what is CMV?
Continuous Mandatory Ventilation = A/C. A BREATH SEQUENCE, not a knob: EVERY breath is MANDATORY, whether the patient triggered it or the timer did.
The control variable can be VC or PC → VC-CMV or PC-CMV.

cards.q: Name the complication of A/C in an anxious patient.
cards.a:
Name the complication of A/C in an anxious patient.
ALVEOLAR HYPERVENTILATION → RESPIRATORY ALKALOSIS, if an anxious or injured-drive patient triggers 25–35 fully supported breaths/min.

cards.q: What is the major problem with unsynchronized IMV?
cards.a:
What is the major problem with unsynchronized IMV?
BREATH STACKING / AIR TRAPPING → auto-PEEP, hyperinflation, ↑ airway pressures, ↑ WOB, barotrauma risk.
Because mandatory breaths land on a RIGID CLOCK — the ventilator does not wait for the patient.

cards.q: What does the 'S' in SIMV actually do?
cards.a:
What does the 'S' in SIMV actually do?
The mandatory breath is SYNCHRONIZED to the patient's effort inside a small SYNCHRONIZATION WINDOW, so mandatory and spontaneous breaths don't collide — the mandatory breath is delivered WITH the effort instead of on top of a half-finished exhalation.

cards.q: In SIMV, what volume do spontaneous breaths get?
cards.a:
In SIMV, what volume do spontaneous breaths get?
Whatever V_T the patient generates — 200, 350, 600 mL. The ventilator does NOT force them to the set volume.
Only the mandatory breaths get the preset V_T.

cards.q: ⚠ Set rate 10, patient triggers 20 — how many mandatory breaths in A/C vs SIMV?
cards.a:
⚠ Set rate 10, patient triggers 20 — how many mandatory breaths in A/C vs SIMV?
A/C gives 20 MANDATORY breaths.
SIMV gives 10 mandatory + 10 SPONTANEOUS.
The single highest-yield mode contrast.

cards.q: ⚠ Can the mandatory rate exceed the set rate in SIMV? In CMV?
cards.a:
⚠ Can the mandatory rate exceed the set rate in SIMV? In CMV?
In IMV/SIMV the mandatory rate can NEVER EXCEED the set rate — but it CAN be lower.
In CMV it CAN exceed it.

cards.q: What is the complication of SIMV without pressure support?
cards.a:
What is the complication of SIMV without pressure support?
MUSCLE FATIGUE and WEANING FAILURE — which is why you see SIMV + PS (e.g. SIMV 10, V_T 450, FiO₂ 30%, PS 8, PEEP +5).

cards.q: Give the typical SIMV weaning sequence.
cards.a:
Give the typical SIMV weaning sequence.
SIMV 12 → 8 → 4 → CPAP/PS.

cards.q: What is MMV, and when does it deliver a breath?
cards.a:
What is MMV, and when does it deliver a breath?
Mandatory Minute Ventilation — a closed-loop IMV-type mode.
Mandatory breaths are delivered ONLY when the measured minute ventilation drops BELOW a preset threshold — a backup/weaning safety net.

cards.q: What do you set in PRVC, and what does the ventilator do?
cards.a:
What do you set in PRVC, and what does the ventilator do?
You set RR, V_T, FiO₂, PEEP.
The ventilator automatically adjusts INSPIRATORY PRESSURE to deliver the target V_T at the LOWEST POSSIBLE PIP — by lowering flow (↓flow = ↓resistance = ↓pressure) and lengthening I-time.
Compliance worsens → it RAISES pressure; compliance improves → it LOWERS pressure.

cards.q: Name the other trade names for PRVC.
cards.a:
Name the other trade names for PRVC.
Autoflow (Dräger) · Volume Control Plus (PB) · Adaptive Pressure Control/Ventilation (Servo-i) · Volume-Targeted Pressure Control · Pressure Controlled Volume Guarantee.
Targeting scheme = ADAPTIVE.

cards.q: Compare plain VC with PRVC.
cards.a:
Compare plain VC with PRVC.
Plain VC is OPEN-LOOP, set-point — it delivers what you set and NEVER ADAPTS, so a stiffening lung means a rising pressure you have to NOTICE.
PRVC is CLOSED-LOOP and ADAPTIVE — it watches delivered volume and re-adjusts the pressure EVERY BREATH. Like cruise control: hill gets steeper, car adds gas by itself.
Both guarantee volume; only PRVC also protects the pressure.

cards.q: What does VC+ do that traditional VC does not?
cards.a:
What does VC+ do that traditional VC does not?
It gives VARIABLE FLOW to meet patient demand.
Traditional VC says 'sorry, you're getting 60 L/min'; VC+ gives the flow the patient asks for — better synchrony at the same target V_T and lowest airway pressure.
It uses a test breath to estimate compliance, and excess pressure from coughing is vented through the ACTIVE EXHALATION VALVE.

cards.q: In Volume Support, what does the ventilator vary — and who sets the rate?
cards.a:
In Volume Support, what does the ventilator vary — and who sets the rate?
It varies the PRESSURE SUPPORT LEVEL breath to breath to hit a target V_T.
Less patient effort → MORE PS; more patient effort → LESS PS.
The PATIENT sets rate, minute ventilation and I-time.

cards.q: Give the three-part classification of PSV.
cards.a:
Give the three-part classification of PSV.
Patient-triggered · Pressure-limited · FLOW-CYCLED — inspiration ends when inspiratory flow falls to ~25% of peak flow.

cards.q: What determines V_T in PSV — and who can't use it?
cards.a:
What determines V_T in PSV — and who can't use it?
The PATIENT — effort + compliance + resistance. PS = HELP, not a breath. Only active during SPONTANEOUS breaths.
⚠ CANNOT be used on an APNEIC patient.

cards.q: How do you titrate pressure support?
cards.a:
How do you titrate pressure support?
Titrate to V_T 8–10 mL/kg IBW and spontaneous f < 25/min.

cards.q: Distinguish PSV from Volume Support.
cards.a:
Distinguish PSV from Volume Support.
PSV guarantees PRESSURE and lets VOLUME vary.
Volume Support guarantees VOLUME and lets PRESSURE vary.
BOTH are patient-triggered, pressure-limited, flow-cycled.

cards.q: What is the decks' bottom-line test for a closed-loop mode?
cards.a:
What is the decks' bottom-line test for a closed-loop mode?
'Is the ventilator simply DELIVERING WHAT I SET, or is it automatically MAKING ADJUSTMENTS? If it's automatically adjusting, you're dealing with a CLOSED-LOOP system.'

cards.q: Name the closed-loop family of modes.
cards.a:
Name the closed-loop family of modes.
PSV · PAV · MMV · ASV (Adaptive Support Ventilation) · volume-assured pressure support · PRVC · NAVA.
PSV is the model closed-loop example — the clinician sets the pressure plateau (constant input) and the ventilator uses variable flow that changes with the patient's lung characteristics.

cards.q: Give the one-line discriminator between PAV and PSV.
cards.a:
Give the one-line discriminator between PAV and PSV.
PSV delivers the SAME SET PRESSURE every breath.
PAV delivers a pressure that is RECALCULATED CONTINUOUSLY to stay PROPORTIONAL TO THE PATIENT'S OWN EFFORT.
⚠ No deck states this mechanistically — it comes from Hess Ch 19.

cards.q: Give the two APRV pressure levels, and what sets the tidal volume.
cards.a:
Give the two APRV pressure levels, and what sets the tidal volume.
A HIGHER airway pressure (e.g. 10 cm H₂O) and a LOWER RELEASE pressure (usually 0 cm H₂O).
V_T is determined by the PRESSURE GRADIENT between the two levels.

cards.q: ⚠ How is the APRV breath cycle INVERTED?
cards.a:
⚠ How is the APRV breath cycle INVERTED?
EXHALATION occurs during the PRESSURE RELEASE, and INHALATION occurs when pressure RETURNS to the higher airway pressure.

cards.q: How do you wean APRV — and what happens at a release frequency of zero?
cards.a:
How do you wean APRV — and what happens at a release frequency of zero?
Wean by DECREASING THE FREQUENCY OF PRESSURE RELEASE.
When the release frequency reaches ZERO, the patient is essentially on CPAP.

cards.q: What APRV details are missing from the vault?
cards.a:
What APRV details are missing from the vault?
⚠ No deck uses the terms P-high, P-low, T-high or T-low, and no deck gives numeric T-high/T-low settings or an ARDS-specific APRV indication.
Look them up in Chang Chapter 4 (Operating Modes) — the Weaning deck explicitly defers to it.

cards.q: Give the HFOV frequency range in Hz and breaths/min, and the V_T.
cards.a:
Give the HFOV frequency range in Hz and breaths/min, and the V_T.
3–15 Hz = 180–900 breaths/min, delivering a V_T often SMALLER THAN ANATOMIC DEAD SPACE.
A piston/diaphragm oscillates gas back and forth around a constant MEAN AIRWAY PRESSURE.

cards.q: On HFOV, what controls oxygenation and what controls ventilation?
cards.a:
On HFOV, what controls oxygenation and what controls ventilation?
OXYGENATION = P̄aw + FiO₂.
VENTILATION (CO₂) = AMPLITUDE (ΔP/power) + FREQUENCY.

cards.q: ⚠ On HFOV, how do you fix hypoventilation?
cards.a:
⚠ On HFOV, how do you fix hypoventilation?
HIGHER AMPLITUDE or LOWER FREQUENCY.
(Hyperventilation: lower amplitude or higher frequency.)
⚠ Note the frequency relationship is the OPPOSITE of conventional ventilation.

cards.q: Give the adult HFOV weaning sequence.
cards.a:
Give the adult HFOV weaning sequence.
Meet weaning criteria → wean FiO₂ to 40% → reduce P̄aw by 2–3 cmH₂O every 4–6 hrs to a 22–24 cmH₂O range.

cards.q: What must a patient have to be on CPAP?
cards.a:
What must a patient have to be on CPAP?
Adequate DRIVE, adequate V_T, and sustainable SPONTANEOUS VENTILATION — watch the PaCO₂.
Good for OSA, CHF, post-extubation; BAD for the apneic, over-sedated or fatigued patient.
CPAP helps OXYGENATION; it does NOT breathe for the patient.

cards.q: Give the BiPAP starting pressures and adjustment increment.
cards.a:
Give the BiPAP starting pressures and adjustment increment.
Start IPAP 8 cmH₂O / EPAP 4 cmH₂O (commonly IPAP 8–10, EPAP 4–5), adjusted in 2 cmH₂O increments.
IPAP = ventilation = CO₂. EPAP = PEEP = oxygenation.

cards.q: A COPD patient has a PaCO₂ of 75. BiPAP or CPAP?
cards.a:
A COPD patient has a PaCO₂ of 75. BiPAP or CPAP?
BiPAP — not CPAP. A CO₂ problem needs the IPAP/EPAP gradient to ventilate; CPAP provides one continuous pressure and does not ventilate.

cards.q: ⚠ State the rule about controlling volume versus pressure.
cards.a:
⚠ State the rule about controlling volume versus pressure.
'If you control the VOLUME, the PRESSURES go up and down; if you control the PRESSURE, the VOLUMES go up and down. You CANNOT guarantee BOTH simultaneously.'
Volume Control = Set Volume → Watch Pressure.
Pressure Control = Set Pressure → Watch Volume.

cards.q: Work it: V_T 500 mL set in VC, patient develops ARDS. What changes?
cards.a:
Work it: V_T 500 mL set in VC, patient develops ARDS. What changes?
V_T is STILL 500 mL — but PIP RISES from 20 to 35 cmH₂O.

cards.q: Work it: PC 20 cmH₂O set, patient develops ARDS. What changes?
cards.a:
Work it: PC 20 cmH₂O set, patient develops ARDS. What changes?
Pressure is STILL 20 — but V_T FALLS from 500 to 300 mL.

cards.q: ⚠ Is a patient-triggered A/C breath spontaneous?
cards.a:
⚠ Is a patient-triggered A/C breath spontaneous?
NO — it is still MANDATORY, because the VENTILATOR CYCLES IT OFF.
Patient-triggered ≠ spontaneous. A classic NBRC trap.

cards.q: How does Automode switch between modes?
cards.a:
How does Automode switch between modes?
No spontaneous trigger for 12 sec (adult) → PRVC (time-triggered, preset V_T, variable PIP).
Two consecutive patient-triggered breaths → VOLUME SUPPORT (patient-triggered, pressure-limited, flow-cycled).
Sleeping patient → PRVC; awake patient → Volume Support.

cards.q: Define a phase variable, and define a breath.
cards.a:
Define a phase variable, and define a breath.
A phase variable is the thing the ventilator MEASURES and uses to START, SUSTAIN and END each phase.
A breath = one cycle of POSITIVE flow (inspiration) plus NEGATIVE flow (expiration) on the flow–time curve.

cards.q: What is the TRIGGER, and what are the options?
cards.a:
What is the TRIGGER, and what are the options?
What STARTS inspiration — 'Who started the breath?'
PATIENT (pressure trigger or flow trigger) or TIME (the set rate/backup timer).

cards.q: How do you tell a patient trigger from a time trigger on the waveform?
cards.a:
How do you tell a patient trigger from a time trigger on the waveform?
A PATIENT trigger shows a small NEGATIVE DEFLECTION below baseline BEFORE the breath.
A TIME trigger has NO negative deflection.

cards.q: What goes wrong if sensitivity is set too insensitive, or too sensitive?
cards.a:
What goes wrong if sensitivity is set too insensitive, or too sensitive?
TOO INSENSITIVE (e.g. −5 cmH₂O) → the patient CAN'T TRIGGER and FATIGUES.
TOO SENSITIVE (e.g. −0.5 cmH₂O or a 0.5 L/min flow trigger) → AUTO-TRIGGERING.

cards.q: What is the LIMIT, and what is it in each mode?
cards.a:
What is the LIMIT, and what is it in each mode?
What is held CONSTANT DURING inspiration — the value the breath will not exceed while gas is flowing.
In VC the limit is VOLUME/FLOW. In PC and PSV the limit is PRESSURE.

cards.q: What is the CYCLE, and what cycles VC, PCV and PSV?
cards.a:
What is the CYCLE, and what cycles VC, PCV and PSV?
What ENDS inspiration and starts exhalation.
VC = VOLUME-cycled · PCV = TIME-cycled · PSV = FLOW-cycled (ends when flow falls to ~25% of peak) — not by time, not by volume, not by pressure.

cards.q: Define BASELINE, and what raises it?
cards.a:
Define BASELINE, and what raises it?
The pressure the ventilator RETURNS TO at end-expiration — the reference point everything else is measured from.
Normally 0 cmH₂O; PEEP raises the baseline (5, 8, 10 cmH₂O).

cards.q: With PEEP 5 and PIP 25, what pressure actually causes inspiration?
cards.a:
With PEEP 5 and PIP 25, what pressure actually causes inspiration?
25 − 5 = 20 cmH₂O — the DRIVING PRESSURE / pressure above PEEP.

cards.q: ⚠ Why does auto-PEEP hurt triggering?
cards.a:
⚠ Why does auto-PEEP hurt triggering?
It RAISES THE BASELINE the patient must drag the airway pressure BELOW to reach the sensitivity threshold.

cards.q: How do trigger and cycle together classify a breath?
cards.a:
How do trigger and cycle together classify a breath?
If the PATIENT controls BOTH the start and the end → SPONTANEOUS (CPAP, PSV).
If the VENTILATOR controls EITHER one → MANDATORY (A/C, VC/AC, PC/AC, SIMV mandatory breaths).

cards.q: Give the three-part label for PSV and for PCV.
cards.a:
Give the three-part label for PSV and for PCV.
PSV = patient-triggered, pressure-limited, FLOW-cycled.
PCV = time-triggered, pressure-limited, TIME-cycled.

cards.q: Distinguish the independent from the dependent variable.
cards.a:
Distinguish the independent from the dependent variable.
The variable the ventilator GUARANTEES is the INDEPENDENT (control) variable; the one left to FLOAT is the DEPENDENT variable.
VC: volume independent → pressure dependent.
PC: pressure independent → volume dependent.

cards.q: Name the three control variables — and which is used in the ICU?
cards.a:
Name the three control variables — and which is used in the ICU?
VOLUME, PRESSURE and TIME (time control = HFOV/jet, where flow, volume and pressure are ALL dependent on lung mechanics).
In the ICU it is essentially always VC or PC.

cards.q: Give the full three-part classification of any mode.
cards.a:
Give the full three-part classification of any mode.
CONTROL VARIABLE (VC/PC) + BREATH SEQUENCE (CMV/IMV/CSV) + TARGETING SCHEME (set-point, dual, bio-variable, servo, adaptive, optimal, intelligent).

cards.q: Name the five ventilatory patterns — and why is there no sixth?
cards.a:
Name the five ventilatory patterns — and why is there no sixth?
VC-CMV · VC-IMV · PC-CMV · PC-IMV · PC-CSV.
There is NO VC-CSV, because a truly SPONTANEOUS breath can't have an IMPOSED volume and flow pattern.
Targeting: A/C and SIMV = set-point; PRVC/Autoflow = adaptive; ASV = intelligent.

cards.q: Define PEEP, and is it a mode?
cards.a:
Define PEEP, and is it a mode?
Positive End-Expiratory Pressure — it increases the END-EXPIRATORY / BASELINE airway pressure. Normally airway pressure returns to 0; with PEEP it stays elevated.
⚠ It is NOT a stand-alone mode — it is applied ALONG WITH another mode. CPAP is the same pressure applied to a fully spontaneous patient.

cards.q: Give the PEEP benefit chain.
cards.a:
Give the PEEP benefit chain.
↓ the pressure threshold for alveolar inflation → ↑ FRC → improves ventilation → ↑ V/Q → improves oxygenation → ↓ WOB.
It recruits collapsed alveoli and reduces shunt. PEEP is the #1 ventilator adjustment for improving oxygenation.

cards.q: Why does FRC matter?
cards.a:
Why does FRC matter?
FRC is the gas remaining after a NORMAL exhalation (diaphragm at rest).
It maintains continuous gas exchange BETWEEN breaths, prevents alveolar collapse, buffers against hypoxemia, stabilizes lung volume, and supports V/Q matching.

cards.q: Name the three indications for PEEP, and the P/F threshold.
cards.a:
Name the three indications for PEEP, and the P/F threshold.
Intrapulmonary SHUNTING and REFRACTORY HYPOXEMIA — consider PEEP when PaO₂/FiO₂ < 200 mmHg.
Decreased FRC and decreased lung compliance.
AUTO-PEEP not responding to ventilator setting adjustments.

cards.q: What FiO₂ ceiling are you trying to stay under by adding PEEP?
cards.a:
What FiO₂ ceiling are you trying to stay under by adding PEEP?
Keep FiO₂ < 60% / PaO₂ < 80 mmHg — < 60 mmHg in COPD — to prevent O₂ TOXICITY.

cards.q: Define OPTIMAL PEEP, and how is it titrated?
cards.a:
Define OPTIMAL PEEP, and how is it titrated?
The LOWEST pressure level that offers the MOST benefits with the LEAST side effects.
Titrated using PaO₂, compliance, O₂ saturation, and ventilator waveforms.
In the deck's worked example, 10 cmH₂O is optimal because the next step up (12) DECREASED both PaO₂ and compliance.

cards.q: ⚠ At what PEEP does barotrauma risk begin?
cards.a:
⚠ At what PEEP does barotrauma risk begin?
PEEP > 10 cmH₂O — 'PEEP > 10 (or P̄aw > 30, or PIP > 50 cmH₂O) is associated with an increased incidence of ALVEOLAR RUPTURE or BAROTRAUMA.'
Second threshold: PEEP > 15 combined with intra-abdominal pressure > 20 cmH₂O adversely affects the cardiovascular, renal and pulmonary systems — the lungs get squeezed from both directions.

cards.q: Explain how PEEP decreases venous return.
cards.a:
Explain how PEEP decreases venous return.
PLEURAL PRESSURE BECOMES LESS NEGATIVE, so the pressure gradient to the RIGHT ATRIUM FALLS → ↓ PRELOAD → ↓ CARDIAC OUTPUT → HYPOTENSION.
'The major downside of too much PEEP is hypotension from decreased venous return.' Garden-hose analogy: positive pressure squeezes the great veins.

cards.q: ⚠ In which patients may PEEP raise ICP, and how?
cards.a:
⚠ In which patients may PEEP raise ICP, and how?
In patients with NORMAL LUNGS — PEEP may raise ICP by IMPEDING CEREBRAL VENOUS DRAINAGE.
Matters most in TBI, stroke and neurosurgical patients.

cards.q: Give the four hemodynamic changes PEEP causes.
cards.a:
Give the four hemodynamic changes PEEP causes.
↑ PAP (expanded alveoli compress pulmonary capillaries → ↑PVR) · ↑ CVP (blood backs up in the systemic veins — high CVP does NOT always mean good preload) · ↓ aortic pressure · ↓ cardiac output.

cards.q: Give the organ downstream effects of PEEP.
cards.a:
Give the organ downstream effects of PEEP.
↓ renal perfusion → ↓ URINE OUTPUT, Na⁺ and water retention.
Hepatic perfusion falls ONLY when PEEP is added to PPV — the liver tolerates plain PPV; the kidneys are MORE SENSITIVE than the liver.
↓ GI perfusion; overdistended alveoli create alveolar DEAD SPACE.

cards.q: Does 'physiologic PEEP' appear in your sources?
cards.a:
Does 'physiologic PEEP' appear in your sources?
⚠ NO — 'physiologic PEEP' (and physiological/normal PEEP) appears in NONE of the 62 deck files, and returns ZERO matches in Hess's 4,441 pages.
The vault discusses applied/therapeutic PEEP and auto-PEEP, but never defines a baseline physiologic PEEP value, and never connects glottic closure to an intrinsic end-expiratory pressure.

cards.q: Define auto-PEEP and explain why it increases work of breathing.
cards.a:
Define auto-PEEP and explain why it increases work of breathing.
UNINTENTIONAL PEEP — air trapped in the lungs at end-expiration because the patient never FINISHED EXHALING before the next breath started.
It RAISES the baseline pressure, so the patient must drag airway pressure BELOW that raised baseline to reach the sensitivity threshold — triggering becomes much harder.

cards.q: ⚠ How high can distal airway pressure be while the ventilator reads zero?
cards.a:
⚠ How high can distal airway pressure be while the ventilator reads zero?
As high as 15 cmH₂O, while the ventilator's PROXIMAL manometer still reads zero (or just the set PEEP).

cards.q: Name the causes of auto-PEEP.
cards.a:
Name the causes of auto-PEEP.
Air trapping / significant airway obstruction (COPD, asthma, secretions) · high frequency (> 20/min), including excessive PS driving the rate up · insufficient inspiratory flow → long I-time · insufficient expiratory time — I:E roughly 1:1 or inverse · breath stacking in IMV · excessive V_T or rate · tracheal gas insufflation with continuous flow.

cards.q: How do you DETECT and MEASURE auto-PEEP?
cards.a:
How do you DETECT and MEASURE auto-PEEP?
Detect: the HIGH PEEP ALARM, rising PIP, and HYPOTENSION.
Measure: OCCLUDE THE EXPIRATORY PORT just before the next inspiration — for accuracy the patient should be SEDATED OR PARALYZED.

cards.q: Give the five fixes for auto-PEEP.
cards.a:
Give the five fixes for auto-PEEP.
↑ FLOW RATE (shortens I-time, lengthens E-time) · ↓ V_T (shortens I-time) · ↓ FREQUENCY (lengthens E-time) · keep PS frequency < 20/min · ↓ air trapping with BRONCHODILATORS in reversible obstruction.

cards.q: ⚠ When do you apply THERAPEUTIC PEEP to offset auto-PEEP?
cards.a:
⚠ When do you apply THERAPEUTIC PEEP to offset auto-PEEP?
AFTER you've made the ventilator adjustments — NOT instead of them.
It offsets auto-PEEP from small-airway air trapping when setting changes can't correct it.

cards.q: Work the vignette: COPD patient, RR 20, V_T 700, flow 40 L/min, with rising PIP, auto-PEEP and hypotension. What do you do?
cards.a:
Work the vignette: COPD patient, RR 20, V_T 700, flow 40 L/min, with rising PIP, auto-PEEP and hypotension. What do you do?
LOWER V_T · LOWER RR · INCREASE FLOW · INCREASE EXPIRATORY TIME.

cards.q: Name the three groups of ventilator alarms.
cards.a:
Name the three groups of ventilator alarms.
INPUT POWER alarms (loss of electricity/battery, loss of air or O₂ pneumatic source < 50 psig) · CONTROL CIRCUIT alarms (settings out of range, failed Short Self Test → ventilator inoperative) · OUTPUT alarms (pressure, volume, flow, time, inspired gas, exhaled gas).

cards.q: What is the rule about silencing an alarm?
cards.a:
What is the rule about silencing an alarm?
NEVER silence an alarm without finding the cause.
Alarm → look at the PATIENT → look at the VENTILATOR → determine cause → fix it.

cards.q: Name the causes of a HIGH pressure alarm.
cards.a:
Name the causes of a HIGH pressure alarm.
Secretions / mucus plug / blood clot in the ETT · kinked ET tube · patient BITING the ETT · bronchospasm · PNEUMOTHORAX · water in the tubing, obstructed filter or partially closed HME · decreased compliance (ARDS, pulmonary edema, atelectasis, pneumonia, fibrosis) · coughing/fighting the ventilator · breath stacking and air trapping · herniated ETT cuff.

cards.q: Name the causes of a LOW pressure alarm.
cards.a:
Name the causes of a LOW pressure alarm.
Circuit DISCONNECTION · leaks in the circuit · ET tube CUFF LEAK · loose/disconnected sensor lines.
Paired with the LOW EXPIRED VOLUME alarm — same causes.

cards.q: Name the causes of a HIGH PEEP alarm and a LOW PEEP alarm.
cards.a:
Name the causes of a HIGH PEEP alarm and a LOW PEEP alarm.
HIGH PEEP: auto-PEEP · air trapping · insufficient inspiratory flow (long I-time) · insufficient expiratory time · extreme high compliance.
LOW PEEP: circuit leak or ET tube cuff leak — the circuit can't hold the set PEEP.

cards.q: Name the causes of a HIGH FREQUENCY alarm — and the rule about its limit.
cards.a:
Name the causes of a HIGH FREQUENCY alarm — and the rule about its limit.
The patient's NEED to increase minute ventilation (rapid shallow breathing) · incorrect settings (insufficient flow or PS) · excessive sensitivity → AUTO-TRIGGERING.
⚠ The high-frequency alarm limit must NOT be raised without clear justification.

cards.q: Name the causes of an APNEA / low frequency alarm.
cards.a:
Name the causes of an APNEA / low frequency alarm.
Circuit disconnection · OVERSEDATION · prolonged neuromuscular block · respiratory center dysfunction · respiratory muscle fatigue.

cards.q: What does PIP contain that Pplat does not?
cards.a:
What does PIP contain that Pplat does not?
PIP contains BOTH the pressure to overcome AIRWAY RESISTANCE and the pressure to overcome COMPLIANCE.
Pplat is measured with FLOW STOPPED, so it reflects LUNG + CHEST WALL COMPLIANCE ONLY — it does NOT include airway resistance.

cards.q: Give the formula for transairway pressure and airway resistance.
cards.a:
Give the formula for transairway pressure and airway resistance.
ΔP (PIP − Pplat) = the TRANSAIRWAY PRESSURE (P_TA).
Raw = ΔP ÷ flow.

cards.q: ↑ PIP with UNCHANGED Pplat — what problem, and what causes it?
cards.a:
↑ PIP with UNCHANGED Pplat — what problem, and what causes it?
A RESISTANCE problem — the airway got narrower; the lungs themselves did not change, so Pplat stays put.
Bronchospasm · secretions · mucus plug · kinked or bitten ETT · water in the circuit · obstructed HME/filter.

cards.q: ↑ PIP AND ↑ Pplat rising proportionally — what problem, and what causes it?
cards.a:
↑ PIP AND ↑ Pplat rising proportionally — what problem, and what causes it?
A COMPLIANCE problem — the lungs got stiffer.
ARDS · pulmonary edema · pneumothorax · atelectasis · pneumonia · fibrosis.

cards.q: Give the one-line rule for PIP and Pplat.
cards.a:
Give the one-line rule for PIP and Pplat.
'When PIP and Plateau move TOGETHER, think LUNGS. When only PIP moves, think AIRWAYS.'

cards.q: On a P/V loop, what does a shift toward the pressure axis mean?
cards.a:
On a P/V loop, what does a shift toward the pressure axis mean?
A shift toward the PRESSURE axis (RIGHT) = DECREASED compliance.
A shift toward the VOLUME axis (LEFT) = INCREASED compliance (emphysema).

cards.q: Give normal airway resistance and its two abnormal thresholds.
cards.a:
Give normal airway resistance and its two abnormal thresholds.
Normal Raw = 0.6–2.4 cmH₂O/L/sec (≈1–3).
Raw > 5 → think AIRWAY OBSTRUCTION.
Raw > 10 → think SEVERE BRONCHOSPASM / mucus plugging / kinked ETT.

cards.q: Give normal adult inspiratory flow and normal static compliance.
cards.a:
Give normal adult inspiratory flow and normal static compliance.
Inspiratory flow 40–60 L/min.
Static compliance 60–100 mL/cmH₂O (≈80).

cards.q: ⚠ Give the plateau pressure ceiling — and why do the decks disagree?
cards.a:
⚠ Give the plateau pressure ceiling — and why do the decks disagree?
< 30 cm H₂O is the MODERN / ARDSNet lung-protective target, endorsed by the newer decks and ALL the speaker notes.
< 35 cm H₂O is the OLDER Chang 'safe airway pressure' threshold on the printed slides.
⚠ Both appear on the SAME SLIDE in the Wk 5 deck, so either could be keyed — but < 30 is the one the deck says to remember: 'If you remember one ventilator pressure in ARDS, remember this one.'

cards.q: Give the full Chang lung-protection pressure threshold set.
cards.a:
Give the full Chang lung-protection pressure threshold set.
PIP < 50 cm H₂O
PPlat < 35 cm H₂O (ARDSNet: < 30)
mPaw < 30 cm H₂O
PEEP < 10 cm H₂O — flagged as OUTDATED: PEEP should be individualized; many ARDS patients need 10–15 or higher
Driving pressure (ΔP = PPlat − PEEP) ideally < 15 cm H₂O

cards.q: ⚠ Why does Pplat matter more than PIP?
cards.a:
⚠ Why does Pplat matter more than PIP?
Because PPlat reflects ALVEOLAR pressure and is therefore a MUCH BETTER INDICATOR OF VILI RISK than PIP.
PIP limits are HISTORICAL.

cards.q: Give the lung-protective tidal volumes.
cards.a:
Give the lung-protective tidal volumes.
Lung-protective V_T 4–6 mL/kg · permissive hypercapnia 4–7 mL/kg · versus a normal ~10 mL/kg.

cards.q: Do the decks give a NORMAL PIP or Pplat?
cards.a:
Do the decks give a NORMAL PIP or Pplat?
⚠ NO — no deck in the vault states a 'normal' PIP or PPlat reference range. All values given are SAFETY CEILINGS, not normals.
The only quasi-normal anchor is an illustrative baseline of V_T 500 mL at PIP 20 cmH₂O in healthy lungs.
Look up normal PIP/Pplat ranges in Egan's.

cards.q: What is the Otis equation, and where is it in your sources?
cards.a:
What is the Otis equation, and where is it in your sources?
⚠ GENUINELY ABSENT — 'Otis' returns ZERO matches across all 62 decks AND in Hess's 4,441 pages.
It determines the OPTIMAL RESPIRATORY FREQUENCY — the rate at which total work of breathing is MINIMUM for a given minute ventilation.
That is why obstructive patients breathe SLOWLY AND DEEPLY and restrictive patients breathe RAPIDLY AND SHALLOWLY. Source it from Egan's.

cards.q: What does the equation of motion describe — and must you memorize it?
cards.a:
What does the equation of motion describe — and must you memorize it?
The relationship between the FORCES that generate airflow and the MECHANICAL PROPERTIES of the respiratory system (compliance and resistance).
The decks state plainly: 'You do NOT need to memorize this equation, just understand what it MEANS.'

cards.q: Give the equation of motion and name its two loads.
cards.a:
Give the equation of motion and name its two loads.
P_vent(t) = (E × V) + (R × V̇)
E × V = the ELASTIC load · R × V̇ = the RESISTIVE load.
E = elastance (inverse of compliance), V = volume, R = resistance, V̇ = flow.

cards.q: In the equation of motion, which quantities are variables and which are constants?
cards.a:
In the equation of motion, which quantities are variables and which are constants?
PRESSURE, VOLUME and FLOW are VARIABLES (functions of time).
RESISTANCE and COMPLIANCE are CONSTANTS.
The respiratory system is modeled as ONE flow-conducting tube connected to ONE elastic compartment.

cards.q: Apply the equation of motion to an asthma patient and to an ARDS patient.
cards.a:
Apply the equation of motion to an asthma patient and to an ARDS patient.
ASTHMA: airway resistance ↑ → the R × V̇ term ↑ → PRESSURE ↑. High resistance, normal compliance — extra pressure to push gas through narrowed airways.
ARDS: compliance ↓ → the ELASTIC term ↑ → PRESSURE ↑. Low compliance, normal resistance — extra pressure to inflate stiff lungs.
Both raise peak pressure, but for DIFFERENT reasons — which is exactly the PIP-vs-Pplat distinction.

cards.q: Give the two constants derived from the equation of motion.
cards.a:
Give the two constants derived from the equation of motion.
Raw = ΔP ÷ V̇ (ΔP = PIP − Pplat). Raw and ΔP are DIRECTLY related; Raw and flow are INVERSELY related.
C = ΔV ÷ ΔP — use PIP for DYNAMIC, Pplat for STATIC compliance. C and volume are DIRECTLY related; C and ΔP/WOB are INVERSELY related.

cards.q: ⚠ What do NIPPV, NPPV, NIV and BiPAP have in common?
cards.a:
⚠ What do NIPPV, NPPV, NIV and BiPAP have in common?
They are FOUR NAMES FOR THE SAME THERAPY. The three decks each title it differently.
This is a NAMING trap, not a physiology trap — when a stem swaps one for another, nothing about the machine, the mask, or the settings has changed.

cards.q: ⚠ What is the ONE real distinction inside the NIV family?
cards.a:
⚠ What is the ONE real distinction inside the NIV family?
CPAP (ONE pressure) vs BiPAP (TWO pressures).
CPAP is a TYPE of NIV — but it is NOT BiPAP.

cards.q: Define noninvasive ventilation, and what does it require?
cards.a:
Define noninvasive ventilation, and what does it require?
Ventilatory support applied WITHOUT the insertion of an artificial airway — no ET tube, no trach.
It requires an INTERFACE — a mask creating a tight seal over the nose or mouth — which lets the machine force oxygen-rich air into the lungs using positive pressure.

cards.q: ⚠ What is the absolute prerequisite for a BiPAP candidate?
cards.a:
⚠ What is the absolute prerequisite for a BiPAP candidate?
The patient MUST BE SPONTANEOUSLY BREATHING.

cards.q: ⚠ What will NIV NOT do?
cards.a:
⚠ What will NIV NOT do?
NIV will NOT CURE the patient's underlying disease — it provides SUPPORT until the condition is treated by other means.

cards.q: Define CPAP, and what does it improve?
cards.a:
Define CPAP, and what does it improve?
A continuous pressure greater than atmospheric maintained throughout the ENTIRE breathing cycle — the SAME one pressure on inhalation and exhalation.
There are NO mandatory breaths, so the patient must be breathing spontaneously.
CPAP only improves OXYGENATION. Most often used for sleep apnea, because it keeps the airway open.

cards.q: Why does BiPAP improve BOTH ventilation and oxygenation?
cards.a:
Why does BiPAP improve BOTH ventilation and oxygenation?
Because it delivers TWO pressures — IPAP and EPAP — which can be adjusted INDEPENDENTLY.
Often used for COPD or heart failure patients.

cards.q: Give the first-line therapy for acute pulmonary edema.
cards.a:
Give the first-line therapy for acute pulmonary edema.
CPAP at 8–12 cmH₂O with 100% oxygen.

cards.q: Define IPAP and say what it controls.
cards.a:
Define IPAP and say what it controls.
Inspiratory Positive Airway Pressure — a pressure above 0 cmH₂O applied ONLY during INSPIRATION.
Think VENTILATION. It works like the peak airway pressure in conventional ventilation, so increasing IPAP INCREASES the delivered V_T. The deck says IPAP 'improves Ventilation & Hypoxemia.'

cards.q: Give the memory hook for which pressure the patient spends more time at.
cards.a:
Give the memory hook for which pressure the patient spends more time at.
INSPIRATORY pressure — the patient spends LESS time at it.
EXPIRATORY pressure — the patient spends MORE time at it.

cards.q: Define EPAP and say what it controls.
cards.a:
Define EPAP and say what it controls.
Expiratory Positive Airway Pressure — a pressure above 0 cmH₂O applied CONTINUOUSLY during BOTH inspiration and exhalation. It is the BASELINE pressure, similar to CPAP or PEEP.
Think OXYGENATION (SpO₂). Increasing EPAP improves oxygenation by improving FRC and reducing SHUNTING.

cards.q: Define FRC.
cards.a:
Define FRC.
The gas remaining after a NORMAL exhalation, with the diaphragm at rest.
The notes flag this as 'MOST IMPORTANT.'

cards.q: Give the pressure support formula, and work the example.
cards.a:
Give the pressure support formula, and work the example.
PS = IPAP − EPAP.
Worked: IPAP 15, EPAP 5 → PS of 10.

cards.q: ⚠ What is the minimum allowable pressure support?
cards.a:
⚠ What is the minimum allowable pressure support?
PS must NEVER be less than 4 cmH₂O — 'there must be a difference of at least 4 cmH₂O.'

cards.q: ⚠ State the rule about raising EPAP.
cards.a:
⚠ State the rule about raising EPAP.
You can ALWAYS increase IPAP without increasing EPAP — but you can NEVER increase EPAP without increasing IPAP BY THE SAME AMOUNT.

cards.q: Why can't you raise EPAP alone? Work it with IPAP 15 / EPAP 5.
cards.a:
Why can't you raise EPAP alone? Work it with IPAP 15 / EPAP 5.
Because it COLLAPSES the pressure support.
Raise EPAP from 5 to 7 and leave IPAP at 15 → PS falls from 10 to 8. Keep going and you fall below the 4 cmH₂O minimum and LOSE the patient's tidal volume.
Raising BOTH by the same amount preserves the PS while raising the baseline.

cards.q: Summarize what raising IPAP does versus raising EPAP.
cards.a:
Summarize what raising IPAP does versus raising EPAP.
Increased IPAP (without changing EPAP) = increased V_T (increased PS).
Increased EPAP = increased OXYGENATION.

cards.q: Give the typical BiPAP starting settings.
cards.a:
Give the typical BiPAP starting settings.
IPAP 8–12 cmH₂O · EPAP 4–6 cmH₂O · PS = IPAP − EPAP (minimum 4) · BUR (Backup Rate) 10–12, plus FiO₂ and Rise.
Both IPAP and EPAP are adjusted in increments of 2.

cards.q: What does a complete BiPAP order look like?
cards.a:
What does a complete BiPAP order look like?
IPAP 15, EPAP 5, RR 12, FiO₂ 40%, I-Time, Rise.

cards.q: Give the IBW formulas and the target V_T multiplier.
cards.a:
Give the IBW formulas and the target V_T multiplier.
Female IBW = 45 + 2.3 × (inches over 5 ft)
Male IBW = 50 + 2.3 × (inches over 5 ft)
Then × 8 mL/kg.

cards.q: Work it: target V_T for a 5'6" female and a 6' male.
cards.a:
Work it: target V_T for a 5'6" female and a 6' male.
5'6" female: IBW = 45 + (2.3 × 6) = 59 kg → 59 × 8 = 472 mL, round to ~500 mL.
6' male: IBW = 50 + (2.3 × 12) = 78 kg → 78 × 8 = 624 mL, round to ~600 mL.

cards.q: What does S/T mode do?
cards.a:
What does S/T mode do?
Spontaneous/Timed. If the patient FAILS TO TRIGGER a breath within the interval determined by the Rate, the machine triggers a MANDATORY breath at the set I-Time.

cards.q: ⚠ Is the Rate in S/T mode a set rate?
cards.a:
⚠ Is the Rate in S/T mode a set rate?
NO — it is a BACKUP rate (BUR).
The machine is there to CATCH DROPPED BREATHS, not to run the patient.

cards.q: How do you set the backup rate — and work an example?
cards.a:
How do you set the backup rate — and work an example?
Set it TWO TO FIVE BREATHS BELOW the patient's spontaneous respiratory rate.
Worked: patient spontaneously breathing at 16 → set the backup around 11–14.

cards.q: Name the goals of NIV therapy.
cards.a:
Name the goals of NIV therapy.
Improve oxygenation · improve ventilation · reverse hypoxemia · reverse acute respiratory failure · provide relief for respiratory distress · reverse respiratory muscle fatigue · improve pulmonary mechanics · prevent or reverse atelectasis · improve lung compliance.

cards.q: What is the PRIMARY goal of BiPAP?
cards.a:
What is the PRIMARY goal of BiPAP?
To REVERSE ACUTE RESPIRATORY FAILURE WITHOUT the insertion of an artificial airway.

cards.q: Give the four advantages of NPPV over intubation.
cards.a:
Give the four advantages of NPPV over intubation.
(1) Greater FLEXIBILITY in starting and stopping support — the mask comes off and goes back on.
(2) Preserves AIRWAY DEFENSE, SPEECH and SWALLOWING — the patient can eat, drink and talk.
(3) Avoids the TRAUMA of intubation and the complications of artificial airways and VAP.
(4) May REDUCE THE NEED FOR MONITORING.

cards.q: Give the three headline BiPAP indications from the RCP 202 deck.
cards.a:
Give the three headline BiPAP indications from the RCP 202 deck.
(1) Help PREVENT INTUBATION for end-stage COPD patients
(2) Support patients with CHRONIC VENTILATORY FAILURE
(3) Patients with RESTRICTIVE diseases, NEUROMUSCULAR diseases, and NOCTURNAL HYPOVENTILATION

cards.q: Give the fuller list of common NIV indications.
cards.a:
Give the fuller list of common NIV indications.
Acute respiratory failure · severe hypoxemia · severe asthma · COPD exacerbation · acute heart failure · post-extubation support · moderate acidemia · moderate hypercarbia · nocturnal hypoventilation · obesity hypoventilation syndrome · sleep apnea.

cards.q: Give the three inclusion criteria layered on top of every NIV indication.
cards.a:
Give the three inclusion criteria layered on top of every NIV indication.
The patient must be SPONTANEOUSLY BREATHING, COOPERATIVE, and ABLE TO FIT AND TOLERATE A MASK.

cards.q: Name the contraindications to NIV.
cards.a:
Name the contraindications to NIV.
Lack of cooperation · cardiac arrest · respiratory arrest · excessive secretions · inability to fit a mask · inability to protect the airway · severe facial burns or trauma.
