cards.q: What is the PATTERN behind every NIV contraindication?
cards.a:
What is the PATTERN behind every NIV contraindication?
Every one is either 'the patient CAN'T PARTICIPATE' (uncooperative, arrested, can't protect the airway) or 'the MASK CAN'T WORK' (won't fit, face is burned/traumatized, secretions will be aspirated).

cards.q: Name the hazards and complications of NIV.
cards.a:
Name the hazards and complications of NIV.
AEROPHAGIA (swallowing air into the stomach) · airway dryness · aspiration · claustrophobia · decreased cardiac output · dry mouth · secretion build-up inside the mask · eye irritation from an air leak · pressure sores from the mask, tubing and straps.

cards.q: How do you correct a HIGH CO₂ on BiPAP — and why does it work?
cards.a:
How do you correct a HIGH CO₂ on BiPAP — and why does it work?
INCREASE IPAP or PS.
This increases V_T → which increases MINUTE VENTILATION → which BLOWS OFF CO₂.

cards.q: How do you correct a LOW CO₂ on BiPAP?
cards.a:
How do you correct a LOW CO₂ on BiPAP?
DECREASE PS or IPAP.

cards.q: How do you correct oxygenation on BiPAP?
cards.a:
How do you correct oxygenation on BiPAP?
Change the FiO₂ or the EPAP — raising EPAP raises FRC.

cards.q: A patient on a nasal mask complains of nasal congestion. What do you do?
cards.a:
A patient on a nasal mask complains of nasal congestion. What do you do?
Add HUMIDIFICATION.

cards.q: Define RISE, and how do you set it?
cards.a:
Define RISE, and how do you set it?
The SPEED at which the inspiratory pressure rises from EPAP to the set target pressure (IPAP).
Set it to MATCH the patient's WORK OF BREATHING.
A LOWER Rise number = FASTER pressurization.

cards.q: ⚠ What is I-Time set according to?
cards.a:
⚠ What is I-Time set according to?
The RATE (the Backup Rate) ONLY — NOT according to what the patient is actually doing.

cards.q: Define RAMP, and give its time range.
cards.a:
Define RAMP, and give its time range.
It helps the patient adapt by GRADUALLY/LINEARLY INCREASING both IPAP and EPAP from SUBTHERAPEUTIC levels up to the user-set pressures over a user-set interval.
It reduces patient ANXIETY.
Set to Off, or between 5 and 45 minutes.

cards.q: Give the normal Total Leak range and the number it must never exceed.
cards.a:
Give the normal Total Leak range and the number it must never exceed.
Normal Total Leak is 7–25.
⚠ It should NEVER exceed 60 — above 60 the patient is NOT VENTILATING.

cards.q: ⚠ What does a Total Leak reading of '---' or '0' mean?
cards.a:
⚠ What does a Total Leak reading of '---' or '0' mean?
The mask is TOO TIGHT. You should NEVER see '---' or '0' on the screen.

cards.q: When do you use TOTAL Leak versus PATIENT Leak?
cards.a:
When do you use TOTAL Leak versus PATIENT Leak?
TOTAL Leak — when the CIRCUIT TEST HAS been completed and leak compensation accomplished with after-market equipment (Vyaire, Fisher & Paykel).
PATIENT Leak — when NO Circuit Test was done with an after-market product (in which case you must complete the Circuit Test), or when using Respironics circuit and mask, which are PRE-COMPENSATED from the factory.

cards.q: Give the practical V60 rule for which leak to watch.
cards.a:
Give the practical V60 rule for which leak to watch.
'Respironics mask' selected → focus on PATIENT Leak.
'Other' mask selected WITH a Leak Test performed → focus on TOTAL Leak and its TREND relative to the Leak Test value.
The deck's blunt note: 'Patient Leak = No Good.'

cards.q: ⚠ How do you set the Lo Rate alarm — and what happens if you get it wrong?
cards.a:
⚠ How do you set the Lo Rate alarm — and what happens if you get it wrong?
Set it ONE HIGHER than the set RR (BUR) — if the set RR is 12, set Lo Rate to 13.
⚠ Otherwise the V60 states 'Alarm disabled…' — a low rate alarm AT OR BELOW the set rate is DISABLED = BAD.

cards.q: How do you set the HIP and LIP alarms?
cards.a:
How do you set the HIP and LIP alarms?
HIP (High Inspiratory Pressure): 5 to 10 ABOVE IPAP.
LIP (Low Inspiratory Pressure): 2 to 3 BELOW IPAP.
LIP T: similar to apnea time.

cards.q: How are the Hi/Lo V_T, Hi RR and Lo V_E alarms set?
cards.a:
How are the Hi/Lo V_T, Hi RR and Lo V_E alarms set?
Hi V_T, Lo V_T and Hi RR: based on the ACTUAL PATIENT MEASUREMENTS.
Lo V_E: normally 4 or 5 L/min.
RCP 105 adds: high and low pressure alarms at ±5 in S/T mode; Low Minute Ventilation start at 4, adjust to 10–20% lower than baseline; V_T alarms 150 mL above and below the observed or desired V_T.

cards.q: What defines SUCCESSFUL application of NIV?
cards.a:
What defines SUCCESSFUL application of NIV?
Overall IMPROVEMENT OF THE PATIENT'S ABG.
Specifically: the PaO₂ should INCREASE and the PaCO₂ should DECREASE.

cards.q: Besides the ABG, what do you monitor on BiPAP?
cards.a:
Besides the ABG, what do you monitor on BiPAP?
The Total Leak TREND (7–25, never over 60, never '---' or 0) · the actual measured V_T and RR against your alarm limits · SpO₂ · the patient's WORK OF BREATHING (which drives your Rise setting).

cards.q: ⚠ Give the time-bound failure criterion for NIV.
cards.a:
⚠ Give the time-bound failure criterion for NIV.
For a patient in respiratory failure who CONTINUES TO DETERIORATE 30 MINUTES after initiation of NIV, the best option is to INTUBATE and initiate mechanical ventilation.

cards.q: Describe the NASAL mask and its advantages.
cards.a:
Describe the NASAL mask and its advantages.
Covers only the nose, sits at the top of the nasal bone and rests above the upper lip. The most common mask worn with CPAP by sleep apnea patients, generally well tolerated.
Advantages: less risk of ASPIRATION · enhanced SECRETION CLEARANCE · less CLAUSTROPHOBIA · easier SPEECH · less DEAD SPACE.

cards.q: What is the nasal mask's biggest complication — and how do you fit one?
cards.a:
What is the nasal mask's biggest complication — and how do you fit one?
LEAKAGE in MOUTH-BREATHERS, plus nasal dryness and drainage.
Fit it by choosing the SMALLEST mask that does NOT OBSTRUCT the nostrils.

cards.q: Give the trade-off of the ORONASAL mask.
cards.a:
Give the trade-off of the ORONASAL mask.
BETTER SEAL, leakage less of a concern.
⚠ But risks ASPIRATION, REGURGITATION, and ASPHYXIATION if the machine/electricity/gas fails — though most now have built-in SAFETY VALVES.

cards.q: ⚠ Describe nasal pillows — and the one thing they are NOT recommended for.
cards.a:
⚠ Describe nasal pillows — and the one thing they are NOT recommended for.
Prongs that fit into the nose — the SMALLEST and MOST COMFORTABLE interface.
Complications: nasal congestion, dry mouth, nose bleeds, mouth leak.
⚠ Commonly used for CPAP but NOT recommended for BiPAP.

cards.q: When is a FULL-FACE mask indicated?
cards.a:
When is a FULL-FACE mask indicated?
When there is SIGNIFICANT MOUTH-BREATHING — such as during an acute COPD exacerbation.
It is the LARGEST and MOST UNCOMFORTABLE interface.

cards.q: What do vented masks require?
cards.a:
What do vented masks require?
A VENT for exhalation, and they use only ONE corrugated tube to connect to the ventilator.

cards.q: What is AVAPS, and what does it combine?
cards.a:
What is AVAPS, and what does it combine?
Average Volume-Assured Pressure Support — the pressure support is AUTOMATICALLY ADJUSTED to maintain a user-defined TARGET V_T.
It combines the attributes of PRESSURE CONTROL and VOLUME-TARGETED ventilation — the comfort of a pressure mode with a guaranteed volume.

cards.q: What is C-Flex for, and how does it work?
cards.a:
What is C-Flex for, and how does it work?
For patients who are UNCOMFORTABLE EXHALING against CPAP.
C-Flex REDUCES THE PRESSURE AT THE START OF EXHALATION, and the set CPAP pressure RETURNS TO THE SET LEVEL BEFORE THE END of exhalation.

cards.q: Where can you find the BiPAP Circuit Test steps?
cards.a:
Where can you find the BiPAP Circuit Test steps?
⚠ NOT covered in the available decks — the two 'BiPAP Circuit Test' slides contain only unlabeled step numbers; the actual steps were IMAGES.
Look up the Respironics V60 Circuit/Leak Test procedure in the operator's manual, or ask the instructor — the Circuit Test is what lets you trust Total Leak over Patient Leak.

cards.q: Give the normal ARTERIAL blood gas values.
cards.a:
Give the normal ARTERIAL blood gas values.
pH 7.35–7.45 · PaCO₂ 35–45 mm Hg · HCO₃⁻ 22–28 mEq/L (NBRC uses 22–26) · PaO₂ 80–100 mm Hg · BE −2 to +2 mEq/L.

cards.q: Give the normal VENOUS blood gas values.
cards.a:
Give the normal VENOUS blood gas values.
pH 7.30–7.40 · PCO₂ 42–48 mm Hg · HCO₃⁻ 24–30 mEq/L · PO₂ 35–45 mm Hg · BE −2 to +2 mEq/L.

cards.q: Explain WHY each venous value differs from the arterial value.
cards.a:
Explain WHY each venous value differs from the arterial value.
pH is LOWER because of acid production in the tissues.
CO₂ is HIGHER because that blood is carrying CO₂ back from the tissues to the lungs.
Bicarbonate is slightly HIGHER from ongoing buffering and metabolic activity.
Oxygen is MUCH LOWER because oxygen has already been delivered to the tissues.

cards.q: Give the 'perfect gas' the deck uses for every calculation.
cards.a:
Give the 'perfect gas' the deck uses for every calculation.
pH 7.40 / PaCO₂ 40 mm Hg / HCO₃⁻ 24 mEq/L.

cards.q: ⚠ Does the deck give a normal SaO₂ — and what does Hess say?
cards.a:
⚠ Does the deck give a normal SaO₂ — and what does Hess say?
⚠ NO — the deck's Normal Blood Gas Values table lists only pH, PaCO₂, HCO₃⁻, PaO₂ and BE. SaO₂ appears only inside case studies and in the note that it is CALCULATED.
HESS Table 4-9 gives it: SaO₂ 95%–98% breathing room air at sea level — slightly tighter than the 95–100% commonly quoted.

cards.q: Which ABG value do you check FIRST, and what does it tell you?
cards.a:
Which ABG value do you check FIRST, and what does it tell you?
the pH. pH is the REFEREE — it tells you the DIRECTION of the disturbance, and then PaCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ tell you WHICH SYSTEM caused it.
Below 7.35 = acidosis (acidemia) · above 7.45 = alkalosis (alkalemia).

cards.q: ⚠ What is normal for a NEWBORN ABG?
cards.a:
⚠ What is normal for a NEWBORN ABG?
Slightly ACIDOTIC is NORMAL.

cards.q: Which system controls PaCO₂, and which direction does it move the pH?
cards.a:
Which system controls PaCO₂, and which direction does it move the pH?
The LUNGS, which regulate it MOMENT-TO-MOMENT.
It moves the pH in the OPPOSITE direction.

cards.q: Trace hypoventilation through to the acid-base result.
cards.a:
Trace hypoventilation through to the acid-base result.
Hypoventilation → CO₂ builds up → combines with water → forms CARBONIC ACID → lowers pH.
↑ PaCO₂ → ↓ pH → RESPIRATORY ACIDOSIS.

cards.q: Trace hyperventilation through to the acid-base result.
cards.a:
Trace hyperventilation through to the acid-base result.
Hyperventilation → excess CO₂ blown off → carbonic acid falls → pH rises.
↓ PaCO₂ → ↑ pH → RESPIRATORY ALKALOSIS.

cards.q: ⚠ In an ACUTE PaCO₂ shift, why is the HCO₃⁻ still near normal?
cards.a:
⚠ In an ACUTE PaCO₂ shift, why is the HCO₃⁻ still near normal?
Because respiratory changes happen QUICKLY — the acute shift arrives BEFORE the kidneys have had any time to compensate.

cards.q: Which system controls HCO₃⁻, and which direction does it move the pH?
cards.a:
Which system controls HCO₃⁻, and which direction does it move the pH?
The KIDNEYS, which provide LONG-TERM compensation.
It moves the pH in the SAME direction: ↑HCO₃⁻ → ↑pH (metabolic alkalosis); ↓HCO₃⁻ → ↓pH (metabolic acidosis).

cards.q: Why does bicarbonate FALL in metabolic acidosis?
cards.a:
Why does bicarbonate FALL in metabolic acidosis?
Because it is the body's main BUFFER: when fixed acids release H⁺, bicarbonate combines with those H⁺ to form carbonic acid, which breaks down into water and CO₂ — and in the process HCO₃⁻ GETS USED UP.

cards.q: ⚠ What should a significantly ELEVATED HCO₃⁻ always make you suspect?
cards.a:
⚠ What should a significantly ELEVATED HCO₃⁻ always make you suspect?
It is the hallmark of CHRONIC compensation — always suspect a LONG-STANDING RESPIRATORY DISORDER.
Renal compensation is slow — 3 to 5 days minimum.

cards.q: What does PaO₂ tell you — and why must you still read it with the pH?
cards.a:
What does PaO₂ tell you — and why must you still read it with the pH?
It reflects OXYGEN TENSION in arterial blood and tells you about OXYGENATION, not acid-base.
⚠ But SEVERE HYPOXEMIA can create a MIXED disorder.

cards.q: What happens at a PaO₂ of about 60 mm Hg?
cards.a:
What happens at a PaO₂ of about 60 mm Hg?
The PERIPHERAL CHEMORECEPTORS are stimulated and signal the brain to INCREASE VENTILATION.
That is why hypoxemia is the MOST COMMON cause of acute alveolar hyperventilation.

cards.q: What happens to acid-base when the PaO₂ is severely low?
cards.a:
What happens to acid-base when the PaO₂ is severely low?
Tissues switch to ANAEROBIC METABOLISM and produce LACTIC ACID — adding a METABOLIC ACIDOSIS on top, making BOTH the pH and the HCO₃⁻ LOWER than expected for that PaCO₂.

cards.q: Define Base Excess and give its normal range.
cards.a:
Define Base Excess and give its normal range.
−2 to +2 mEq/L in BOTH arterial and venous blood.
It is the QUICK WAY TO IDENTIFY METABOLIC DISTURBANCES.

cards.q: What does a NEGATIVE vs POSITIVE base excess mean?
cards.a:
What does a NEGATIVE vs POSITIVE base excess mean?
NEGATIVE = a base DEFICIT → METABOLIC ACIDOSIS.
POSITIVE = EXCESS base → METABOLIC ALKALOSIS.
BE earns its own line because it helps when the CO₂ and bicarbonate don't clearly show the full metabolic picture.

cards.q: What is the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation USED FOR?
cards.a:
What is the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation USED FOR?
To CALCULATE the bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) — and other derived values such as base excess — from the directly measured pH and PCO₂.
It mathematically links pH, the RESPIRATORY component (PCO₂/carbonic acid), and the METABOLIC component (HCO₃⁻).

cards.q: Is the Henderson-Hasselbalch formula itself written out in the deck?
cards.a:
Is the Henderson-Hasselbalch formula itself written out in the deck?
⚠ NO — only its PURPOSE is stated. The equation is pH = pKa + log[HCO₃⁻ ÷ (0.03 × PaCO₂)].
Get the written formula from your textbook or RCP 101 notes if the instructor wants you to reproduce it.

cards.q: ⚠ Which THREE values does a blood gas analyzer directly MEASURE?
cards.a:
⚠ Which THREE values does a blood gas analyzer directly MEASURE?
pH · PCO₂ · PO₂. ONLY those three.

cards.q: ⚠ Which ABG values are CALCULATED — and what's the consequence?
cards.a:
⚠ Which ABG values are CALCULATED — and what's the consequence?
HCO₃⁻ · base excess · SaO₂.
⚠ If ONE of the three electrodes is off, EVERY calculated value on the report is also wrong — which is why calibration and QC matter so much.

cards.q: How is a blood gas analyzer calibrated?
cards.a:
How is a blood gas analyzer calibrated?
By inserting solutions or gases with KNOWN values — ONE HIGH and ONE LOW — and adjusting the machine's readings to match.
Low calibration gas or insufficient buffer solution will cause AUTO-CALIBRATION TO FAIL.

cards.q: Describe blood gas quality control — levels, volume and tolerance.
cards.a:
Describe blood gas quality control — levels, volume and tolerance.
Control solutions at THREE levels — ACIDOTIC, ALKALOTIC and NORMAL — in ampules of 2–3 mL.
Results must fall within ±2 STANDARD DEVIATIONS; anything outside that range is an error.

cards.q: Give the Westgard rules as the deck states them.
cards.a:
Give the Westgard rules as the deck states them.
Plotted on a LEVEY-JENNINGS chart.
ONE control outside the SD = a WARNING.
TWO OR MORE consecutive controls outside the SD = an OUT-OF-CONTROL situation, requiring the electrode to be RECALIBRATED OR REPLACED.

cards.q: Which electrode measures PCO₂, and how does it work?
cards.a:
Which electrode measures PCO₂, and how does it work?
SEVERINGHAUS.
It detects the CHANGES IN pH caused by CO₂ diffusion — CO₂ diffuses across a membrane into a solution, changes that solution's pH, and the pH change is read as a CO₂ value.

cards.q: Which electrode measures PO₂, and how does it work?
cards.a:
Which electrode measures PO₂, and how does it work?
CLARK.
A POLAROGRAPHIC method in which oxygen is REDUCED AT A CATHODE, producing a CURRENT PROPORTIONAL to the amount of oxygen present.

cards.q: Which electrode measures pH, and how does it work?
cards.a:
Which electrode measures pH, and how does it work?
SANZ. A GLASS electrode sensitive to HYDROGEN IONS (H⁺).

cards.q: Define fixed (nonvolatile) acids and name them.
cards.a:
Define fixed (nonvolatile) acids and name them.
Acids the LUNGS CANNOT REMOVE — they must be BUFFERED by bicarbonate and EXCRETED by the kidneys.
Lactic acid · keto acids (from fat breakdown, as in DKA) · acids from salicylate/aspirin intoxication · phosphoric and sulfuric acids from the catabolism of proteins, fats and carbohydrates.

cards.q: What happens to the bicarbonate and the anion gap when fixed acids accumulate?
cards.a:
What happens to the bicarbonate and the anion gap when fixed acids accumulate?
They release H⁺, which CONSUMES HCO₃⁻ — LOWERING the bicarbonate and RAISING the anion gap.

cards.q: ⚠ What is the volatile acid — and is the term used in your deck?
cards.a:
⚠ What is the volatile acid — and is the term used in your deck?
CARBONIC ACID (H₂CO₃) — the one the LUNGS can blow off as CO₂.
⚠ The exact term 'volatile acid' does NOT appear anywhere in this deck — only the mechanism. Confirm the wording your instructor wants.

cards.q: What is the relationship between H⁺ and pH?
cards.a:
What is the relationship between H⁺ and pH?
INVERSE.
MORE free H⁺ = LOWER pH = more ACIDIC.
FEWER H⁺ = HIGHER pH = more ALKALOTIC.

cards.q: Give the buffering chain from acid buildup to a rising anion gap.
cards.a:
Give the buffering chain from acid buildup to a rising anion gap.
Acids build up → release H⁺ → H⁺ combines with HCO₃⁻ to form CARBONIC ACID → carbonic acid breaks down into WATER and CO₂ → bicarbonate DROPS (used up) and the ANION GAP RISES.
The deck's analogy: bicarbonate is FIREFIGHTERS — the bigger the fire (extra acid), the more firefighters get used up.

cards.q: Name the four ways LOSING H⁺ causes metabolic alkalosis.
cards.a:
Name the four ways LOSING H⁺ causes metabolic alkalosis.
Vomiting · gastric suctioning · H⁺ shifting INTO cells in hypokalemia · renal H⁺ excretion from steroids or aldosterone.

cards.q: Give Hess's pH equation and the blood's H⁺ concentration.
cards.a:
Give Hess's pH equation and the blood's H⁺ concentration.
pH = −log[H⁺].
A solution with [H⁺] of 10⁻⁷ mol/L (100 nmol/L) has pH 7.
'The normal pH of the blood is slightly alkaline (pH of 7.4), which corresponds to [H⁺] of 40 nmol/L.'

cards.q: Give the five systematic ABG interpretation steps.
cards.a:
Give the five systematic ABG interpretation steps.
(1) Check the pH FIRST.
(2) Check PaCO₂, then HCO₃⁻, to identify the disorder.
(3) Assess COMPENSATION.
(4) Assess OXYGENATION.
(5) CORRELATE with the patient and the baseline.

cards.q: In step 2, how do you name the disorder?
cards.a:
In step 2, how do you name the disorder?
PaCO₂ abnormal = RESPIRATORY.
HCO₃⁻ abnormal = METABOLIC.
BOTH abnormal = MIXED.

cards.q: Distinguish PARTIAL from FULL compensation.
cards.a:
Distinguish PARTIAL from FULL compensation.
PARTIAL = the pH is STILL ABNORMAL while the opposite system is adjusting.
FULL/COMPLETE = the pH is BACK IN THE NORMAL RANGE but the other value is still off.

cards.q: ⚠ Why is step 5 — correlating with the patient — non-negotiable?
cards.a:
⚠ Why is step 5 — correlating with the patient — non-negotiable?
Because in a CHRONIC patient the 'abnormal' numbers ARE their normal.
Always compare to the patient's OWN PREVIOUS ABGs.

cards.q: An ABG shows acute respiratory acidosis but the patient is alert, in no distress, saturating 98%. What do you do?
cards.a:
An ABG shows acute respiratory acidosis but the patient is alert, in no distress, saturating 98%. What do you do?
QUESTION THE RESULT. Suspect SAMPLING ERROR, PROCESSING DELAY, or WRONG PATIENT.
Ask: was the sample drawn correctly, processed promptly, and reported accurately?

cards.q: Give the pattern and example for ACUTE ALVEOLAR HYPERVENTILATION with hypoxemia.
cards.a:
Give the pattern and example for ACUTE ALVEOLAR HYPERVENTILATION with hypoxemia.
pH ↑ > 7.45 · PaCO₂ ↓ < 35 · HCO₃⁻ decreased but still normal · PaO₂ decreased.
Example: pH 7.52 / PaCO₂ 28 / HCO₃⁻ 22 / PaO₂ 61.

cards.q: Give the pattern and example for ACUTE VENTILATORY FAILURE with hypoxemia.
cards.a:
Give the pattern and example for ACUTE VENTILATORY FAILURE with hypoxemia.
pH ↓ < 7.35 · PaCO₂ ↑ > 45 · HCO₃⁻ increased but still normal · PaO₂ decreased.
Example: pH 7.16 / PaCO₂ 79 / HCO₃⁻ 26 / PaO₂ 57.

cards.q: Give the pattern and example for CHRONIC VENTILATORY FAILURE with hypoxemia.
cards.a:
Give the pattern and example for CHRONIC VENTILATORY FAILURE with hypoxemia.
pH NORMAL · PaCO₂ increased · HCO₃⁻ increased SIGNIFICANTLY · PaO₂ decreased. = COMPENSATED respiratory acidosis.
Example: pH 7.36 / PaCO₂ 79 / HCO₃⁻ 43 / PaO₂ 61.

cards.q: Give the pattern and example for ACUTE HYPERVENTILATION ON CHRONIC ventilatory failure.
cards.a:
Give the pattern and example for ACUTE HYPERVENTILATION ON CHRONIC ventilatory failure.
pH ↑ (alkalosis) · PaCO₂ ↓ FROM THE CHRONIC BASELINE · HCO₃⁻ ↑ (chronic compensation) · PaO₂ decreased.
Example: pH 7.52 / PaCO₂ 51 / HCO₃⁻ 40 / PaO₂ 46.

cards.q: Give the pattern and example for ACUTE VENTILATORY FAILURE ON CHRONIC.
cards.a:
Give the pattern and example for ACUTE VENTILATORY FAILURE ON CHRONIC.
pH ↓ (acidosis) · PaCO₂ ↑↑ FROM THE CHRONIC BASELINE · HCO₃⁻ ↑ (chronic compensation) · PaO₂ decreased.
Example: pH 7.28 / PaCO₂ 99 / HCO₃⁻ 45 / PaO₂ 34.

cards.q: Give the patterns and examples for METABOLIC alkalosis and acidosis.
cards.a:
Give the patterns and examples for METABOLIC alkalosis and acidosis.
METABOLIC ALKALOSIS: pH increased · PaCO₂ normal · HCO₃⁻ increased · PaO₂ normal. Example: pH 7.56 / PaCO₂ 44 / HCO₃⁻ 27 / PaO₂ 94.
METABOLIC ACIDOSIS: pH decreased · PaCO₂ normal · HCO₃⁻ decreased · PaO₂ normal. Example: pH 7.26 / PaCO₂ 37 / HCO₃⁻ 18 / PaO₂ 94.

cards.q: Give the pattern and example for LACTIC ACIDOSIS.
cards.a:
Give the pattern and example for LACTIC ACIDOSIS.
pH decreased · PaCO₂ normal or decreased · HCO₃⁻ decreased · PaO₂ DECREASED.
Example: pH 7.21 / PaCO₂ 35 / HCO₃⁻ 14 / PaO₂ 34.
The DECREASED PaO₂ is what separates it from plain metabolic acidosis.

cards.q: Work the side-by-side: from a chronic baseline of 7.36/77/43/61, what do acute failure and acute hyperventilation each produce?
cards.a:
Work the side-by-side: from a chronic baseline of 7.36/77/43/61, what do acute failure and acute hyperventilation each produce?
Acute ventilatory failure ON TOP → 7.28 / 99 / 44 / 39.
Acute hyperventilation ON TOP → 7.51 / 52 / 40 / 49.

cards.q: What does UNCOMPENSATED mean, and which patterns show it?
cards.a:
What does UNCOMPENSATED mean, and which patterns show it?
The opposite system has NOT HAD TIME to respond yet.
Every ACUTE pattern — e.g. in acute ventilatory failure the HCO₃⁻ is 'increased but remains WITHIN THE NORMAL RANGE because there has been little to no renal compensation yet.'

cards.q: Give the DKA example of PARTIAL compensation, and explain why it can't normalize.
cards.a:
Give the DKA example of PARTIAL compensation, and explain why it can't normalize.
pH 6.98 with PaCO₂ driven down to 24 mm Hg by KUSSMAUL respirations.
The compensation HELPS but CANNOT NORMALIZE the pH because the metabolic derangement is EXTREME.

cards.q: Give the metabolic alkalosis example of partial compensation.
cards.a:
Give the metabolic alkalosis example of partial compensation.
pH 7.66, PaCO₂ 57 (HYPOVENTILATING to retain CO₂), HCO₃⁻ 61 = severe metabolic alkalosis with PARTIAL respiratory compensation.

cards.q: ⚠ What is the timing 'tell' that distinguishes lung from kidney compensation?
cards.a:
⚠ What is the timing 'tell' that distinguishes lung from kidney compensation?
The LUNGS compensate FAST (moment-to-moment). The KIDNEYS take 3 TO 5 DAYS.

cards.q: ⚠ What must you NOT do to a fully compensated chronic patient?
cards.a:
⚠ What must you NOT do to a fully compensated chronic patient?
Do NOT aggressively 'correct' their PaCO₂ down toward 40 — that REMOVES their metabolic compensation and produces ALKALOSIS and CLINICAL DETERIORATION.

cards.q: Give the ACUTE rule for a 10 mm Hg rise in PaCO₂.
cards.a:
Give the ACUTE rule for a 10 mm Hg rise in PaCO₂.
pH FALLS ~0.06 units and HCO₃⁻ RISES ~1 mEq/L (from buffering, before any renal compensation).
For 20 mm Hg: pH falls ~0.12 and HCO₃⁻ rises ~2.

cards.q: Work it: PaCO₂ rises acutely from 40 to 60. Predict the pH and HCO₃⁻.
cards.a:
Work it: PaCO₂ rises acutely from 40 to 60. Predict the pH and HCO₃⁻.
20 ÷ 10 = 2 increments.
pH: 2 × 0.06 = 0.12 → 7.40 − 0.12 = 7.28.
HCO₃⁻: 24 + (2 × 1) = 26 mEq/L.

cards.q: ⚠ The measured pH and HCO₃⁻ are BOTH lower than the acute rules predict. What do you suspect?
cards.a:
⚠ The measured pH and HCO₃⁻ are BOTH lower than the acute rules predict. What do you suspect?
LACTIC ACID from severe hypoxemia adding a METABOLIC ACIDOSIS on top.

cards.q: Give the CHRONIC rules for a 10 mm Hg PaCO₂ change.
cards.a:
Give the CHRONIC rules for a 10 mm Hg PaCO₂ change.
For every 10 mm Hg INCREASE, HCO₃⁻ rises ~3.5–4 mEq/L.
For every 10 mm Hg DECREASE, HCO₃⁻ falls ~4–5 mEq/L.
Chronic changes occur when the ventilatory problem persists several days.

cards.q: ⚠ How does the size of the bicarbonate move tell you acute from chronic?
cards.a:
⚠ How does the size of the bicarbonate move tell you acute from chronic?
Acute ≈ 1 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg. Chronic ≈ 3.5–5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg.
A BIG bicarbonate move means CHRONIC; a SMALL one means ACUTE.

cards.q: Give the METABOLIC ALKALOSIS compensation rule and work the example.
cards.a:
Give the METABOLIC ALKALOSIS compensation rule and work the example.
For every 1 mEq/L INCREASE in HCO₃⁻, PaCO₂ should INCREASE by 0.7 mm Hg.
Worked: HCO₃⁻ 24 → 29 (a rise of 5) → expected PaCO₂ rise = 0.7 × 5 = 3.5 mm Hg.
Verified when the HCO₃⁻ AND the pH are BOTH HIGHER than expected for the PaCO₂.

cards.q: Give the METABOLIC ACIDOSIS compensation rule and its timing.
cards.a:
Give the METABOLIC ACIDOSIS compensation rule and its timing.
For every 1 mEq/L DECREASE in HCO₃⁻, PaCO₂ should DECREASE by 1.2 mm Hg.
This respiratory compensation BEGINS WITHIN THE FIRST HOUR and is COMPLETE BY 12 TO 24 HOURS — versus 3–5 days for renal.
That fast respiratory response is exactly what KUSSMAUL respirations are in DKA.

cards.q: ⚠ When do you use the anion gap, and what question does it answer?
cards.a:
⚠ When do you use the anion gap, and what question does it answer?
ONLY when a patient HAS METABOLIC ACIDOSIS — to determine WHY the bicarbonate is low: is ACID BEING ADDED, or is BICARBONATE BEING LOST?

cards.q: Give the anion gap formula, work it with normal values, and give the normal range.
cards.a:
Give the anion gap formula, work it with normal values, and give the normal range.
Anion gap = [Na⁺] − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻)
= 140 − (105 + 24) = 140 − 129 = 11 mEq/L
Normal range 9 to 14 mEq/L.
It rests on the law of ELECTRONEUTRALITY — total cations must equal total anions.

cards.q: What does a HIGH anion gap mean?
cards.a:
What does a HIGH anion gap mean?
Metabolic acidosis from the ACCUMULATION OF FIXED ACIDS — lactic acids, keto acids, salicylate intoxication — because those acids release H⁺ that CONSUMES HCO₃⁻ while ADDING UNMEASURED ANIONS.
Above 14 mEq/L.

cards.q: What does a NORMAL anion gap with metabolic acidosis mean?
cards.a:
What does a NORMAL anion gap with metabolic acidosis mean?
LOSS of HCO₃⁻ (renal disease, severe diarrhea).
As bicarbonate falls, Cl⁻ RISES to replace it to preserve electroneutrality — so the gap STAYS NORMAL. This is HYPERCHLOREMIC metabolic acidosis.

cards.q: Give the quick anion gap takeaway.
cards.a:
Give the quick anion gap takeaway.
HIGH gap = TOO MUCH ACID. NORMAL gap = BICARBONATE LOSS.

cards.q: ⚠ Give Hess's anion gap normal — and how does Hess contradict itself?
cards.a:
⚠ Give Hess's anion gap normal — and how does Hess contradict itself?
Hess Ch 4: Anion gap = [Na⁺] − ([Cl⁻] + [HCO₃⁻]), normal 12 ± 4 mmol/L (roughly 8–16).
⚠ Hess Ch 5 gives a DIFFERENT formula: ([Na⁺] + [K⁺]) − ([CO₂] + [Cl⁻]), with the rule 'if the gap exceeds 12 mmol/L, excessive unmeasured anions are likely.'
What reconciles them: [K⁺] is often OMITTED because its concentration is normally low.
The potassium term is OPTIONAL; 'about 12' is the anchor. If a question supplies a formula, USE THE ONE GIVEN.

cards.q: Name the unmeasured anions worth recognising.
cards.a:
Name the unmeasured anions worth recognising.
Lactate (liver disease, tissue hypoxia) · ketones (diabetic and alcoholic ketoacidosis) · salicylates · uraemic acidosis · glycolate and oxalate · ethylene glycol · free fatty acids · methyl malonate.

cards.q: ⚠ How can the anion gap MISLEAD in the ICU?
cards.a:
⚠ How can the anion gap MISLEAD in the ICU?
In HYPOALBUMINAEMIA — since ALBUMIN is itself an unmeasured anion, a high-gap LACTIC ACIDOSIS can look DECEPTIVELY NORMAL in a hypoalbuminaemic patient.

cards.q: Name the causes of METABOLIC ALKALOSIS.
cards.a:
Name the causes of METABOLIC ALKALOSIS.
HYPOKALEMIA (low K⁺ drives H⁺ into cells and the kidney excretes H⁺ to retain K⁺) · HYPOCHLOREMIA (Cl⁻ loss forces HCO₃⁻ retention) · gastric suctioning and VOMITING (direct loss of HCl — both H⁺ and Cl⁻) · excessive CORTICOSTEROIDS · excessive SODIUM BICARBONATE · DIURETIC therapy · HYPOVOLEMIA (volume contraction stimulates RAAS).

cards.q: Name the causes of METABOLIC ACIDOSIS.
cards.a:
Name the causes of METABOLIC ACIDOSIS.
LACTIC ACIDOSIS (most common) · KETOACIDOSIS (most commonly diabetes mellitus) · SALICYLATE INTOXICATION · RENAL FAILURE · CHRONIC DIARRHEA.

cards.q: Name the FOUR ways salicylate causes acidosis.
cards.a:
Name the FOUR ways salicylate causes acidosis.
(1) Increasing LACTIC ACID
(2) Producing KETONES from fat metabolism
(3) Accumulating SALICYLIC ACID itself
(4) Impairing RENAL ACID EXCRETION

cards.q: What is the MOST COMMON cause of acute alveolar hyperventilation, and what is the mechanism?
cards.a:
What is the MOST COMMON cause of acute alveolar hyperventilation, and what is the mechanism?
HYPOXEMIA.
PaO₂ drops to ~60 mm Hg → PERIPHERAL CHEMORECEPTORS sense it → signal the brain to increase ventilatory rate → more CO₂ exhaled → RESPIRATORY ALKALOSIS (↑pH, ↓PaCO₂).

cards.q: Where does the low PaO₂ driving hyperventilation come from?
cards.a:
Where does the low PaO₂ driving hyperventilation come from?
A DECREASED V/Q ratio (e.g. asthma) · CAPILLARY SHUNTING (e.g. atelectasis — blood flowing past non-ventilated alveoli) · VENOUS ADMIXTURE.

cards.q: Name the six mechanisms that reduce PaCO₂.
cards.a:
Name the six mechanisms that reduce PaCO₂.
Decreased lung COMPLIANCE (stiff lungs → faster breathing) · stimulation of the CENTRAL CHEMORECEPTORS · activation of the DEFLATION reflex · activation of the IRRITANT reflex · stimulation of the J RECEPTORS (juxtapulmonary-capillary receptors responding to pulmonary congestion or edema) · PAIN AND ANXIETY.

cards.q: ⚠ Why does a chronic patient CHOOSE to retain CO₂?
cards.a:
⚠ Why does a chronic patient CHOOSE to retain CO₂?
As the disease worsens, the WORK OF BREATHING increases until the patient EXPENDS MORE OXYGEN TRYING TO BREATHE THAN THEY GAIN through effective ventilation.
To conserve energy they adopt a pattern that prioritizes WORK efficiency rather than VENTILATORY efficiency — slower and more controlled, which reduces WOB even though it causes CO₂ retention.

cards.q: Trace chronic ventilatory failure from the breathing change to the compensated gas.
cards.a:
Trace chronic ventilatory failure from the breathing change to the compensated gas.
Alveolar ventilation slowly falls → PaO₂ decreases, PaCO₂ increases → pH begins to fall → BECAUSE IT IS SLOW the kidneys have time to RETAIN BICARBONATE → pH pulled back toward normal.
Result: chronic ventilatory failure with hypoxemia = COMPENSATED RESPIRATORY ACIDOSIS.

cards.q: Name the diseases associated with chronic ventilatory failure.
cards.a:
Name the diseases associated with chronic ventilatory failure.
OBSTRUCTIVE: chronic bronchitis, emphysema, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis.
RESTRICTIVE: tuberculosis, fungal diseases, kyphoscoliosis, chronic interstitial lung diseases, bronchopulmonary dysplasia.

cards.q: ⚠ An ABG looks like partially compensated metabolic alkalosis but the patient is markedly hypoxemic. What is it really?
cards.a:
⚠ An ABG looks like partially compensated metabolic alkalosis but the patient is markedly hypoxemic. What is it really?
ACUTE ALVEOLAR HYPERVENTILATION SUPERIMPOSED ON CHRONIC VENTILATORY FAILURE.
The marked HYPOXEMIA is the clue — a low oxygen level is NOT typically seen in pure metabolic alkalosis.

cards.q: Give the mechanism for acute hyperventilation on chronic ventilatory failure.
cards.a:
Give the mechanism for acute hyperventilation on chronic ventilatory failure.
A chronic COPD patient acquires an ACUTE SHUNT-PRODUCING DISEASE (pneumonia) → gets MORE HYPOXEMIC → HYPERVENTILATES → drives the PaCO₂ DOWN FROM THEIR HIGH BASELINE.

cards.q: Work the deck's fatal case: emphysema + RLL pneumonia at 7.55/49/45/44, prior gas 7.39/77/46/72. What happened?
cards.a:
Work the deck's fatal case: emphysema + RLL pneumonia at 7.55/49/45/44, prior gas 7.39/77/46/72. What happened?
He was in IMPENDING VENTILATORY FAILURE.
He FATIGUED, his RR fell, PaCO₂ climbed ABOVE baseline, and he DIED 17 HOURS LATER.
ALWAYS COMPARE TO BASELINE.

cards.q: Why is an arterial puncture performed?
cards.a:
Why is an arterial puncture performed?
To determine the adequacy of VENTILATION (PaCO₂), OXYGENATION (PaO₂), and ACID-BASE status (pH) · to assess the need for interventions · to monitor severity and progression of disease.

cards.q: Give the ABG site order, and what infants get.
cards.a:
Give the ABG site order, and what infants get.
RADIAL is FIRST choice — easy access plus collateral circulation.
Then BRACHIAL.
FEMORAL is LAST choice — used when blood pressure is low (e.g. 60/40).
Infants get CAPILLARY samples / HEEL STICKS.

cards.q: Describe the modified Allen's test result you need.
cards.a:
Describe the modified Allen's test result you need.
The hand should PINK UP within 1–2 SECONDS after releasing the ulnar artery.
If it does NOT, use another site.

cards.q: ⚠ On which arm must you NEVER draw an ABG?
cards.a:
⚠ On which arm must you NEVER draw an ABG?
An arm with a DIALYSIS SHUNT — use the other arm.

cards.q: How is the ABG syringe prepared, and how long do you hold pressure?
cards.a:
How is the ABG syringe prepared, and how long do you hold pressure?
Needle secure, BEVEL UP, plunger drawn back.
Hold pressure AT LEAST 5 MINUTES or until bleeding stops — longer on anticoagulants.

cards.q: ⚠ AIR BUBBLES in the sample — what happens to each value?
cards.a:
⚠ AIR BUBBLES in the sample — what happens to each value?
PaCO₂ FALSELY LOW — CO₂ diffuses out into the bubble.
PaO₂ moves toward ROOM-AIR partial pressure (150 torr).
pH INCREASES because CO₂ was lost — the sample looks more ALKALOTIC than it really is.

cards.q: ⚠ TOO MUCH HEPARIN — what happens to each value?
cards.a:
⚠ TOO MUCH HEPARIN — what happens to each value?
PaCO₂ decreases toward 0.
PaO₂ moves toward room air (150 torr).
pH DECREASES toward 7.0 because HEPARIN IS ACIDIC. A dilution error.

cards.q: ⚠ IMPROPER COOLING (sample not iced) — what happens to each value?
cards.a:
⚠ IMPROPER COOLING (sample not iced) — what happens to each value?
Metabolism continues: PaCO₂ INCREASES · PaO₂ DECREASES · pH DECREASES.

cards.q: Name the four ABG error categories.
cards.a:
Name the four ABG error categories.
PREANALYTIC — air bubbles, wrong anticoagulant, venous contamination, delays.
ANALYTIC — malfunctioning electrodes, poor QC.
POSTANALYTIC — wrong patient info, transcription mistakes, failing to record FiO₂, sampling less than 20 minutes after an FiO₂ change.
INTERPRETATION — misclassifying the result.

cards.q: Name the puncture-site hazards.
cards.a:
Name the puncture-site hazards.
HEMATOMA (disrupts blood flow) · BLEEDING · CLOTTING and VESSEL SPASM · TISSUE TRAUMA to muscles, bones and nerves.

cards.q: What are the two purposes of an indwelling arterial line?
cards.a:
What are the two purposes of an indwelling arterial line?
(1) CONTINUOUS monitoring of systemic BLOOD PRESSURE.
(2) Easy access for ABG SAMPLING without repeated sticks.
Placed in the radial, brachial or femoral artery; newborns get an UMBILICAL arterial line.

cards.q: ⚠ Where must the arterial line transducer be leveled — and what happens if it isn't?
cards.a:
⚠ Where must the arterial line transducer be leveled — and what happens if it isn't?
LEVEL WITH THE CATHETER.
ABOVE the site → readings too LOW. BELOW the site → readings too HIGH.
The zero reference is the PHLEBOSTATIC AXIS: the 4th intercostal space at the MID-AXILLARY line — the level of the right atrium.

cards.q: Give the steps for sampling from an arterial line.
cards.a:
Give the steps for sampling from an arterial line.
Withdraw ~3–5 mL to clear the DEAD SPACE → attach the ABG syringe to the sampling port and collect → RETURN the 3–5 mL to the patient (closed systems — this prevents hospital-acquired anemia; open systems require DISCARDING it) → flush the catheter.

cards.q: The waveform fails to return after flushing an A-line. What's wrong?
cards.a:
The waveform fails to return after flushing an A-line. What's wrong?
The STOPCOCK IS IN THE WRONG POSITION, and the line needs to be ZEROED.

cards.q: ⚠ In CO poisoning, which two ABG-related values lie?
cards.a:
⚠ In CO poisoning, which two ABG-related values lie?
The SpO₂ reads NORMAL because CO BINDS HEMOGLOBIN, and the PaO₂ may ALSO look normal since DISSOLVED oxygen is unaffected.
Draw an ABG, check PaO₂ and SaO₂, and confirm with a CO-OXIMETER.

cards.q: ⚠ Why can an anemic patient be hypoxic with a normal PaO₂?
cards.a:
⚠ Why can an anemic patient be hypoxic with a normal PaO₂?
Because the CaO₂ (oxygen CONTENT) is reduced when hemoglobin is low — and ABGs do NOT measure CARRYING CAPACITY.

cards.q: What ABG pattern do you expect in pulmonary embolism?
cards.a:
What ABG pattern do you expect in pulmonary embolism?
V/Q MISMATCH — PaO₂ often DECREASES and PaCO₂ may be LOW OR NORMAL from hyperventilation.
⚠ The patient's condition may NOT MATCH the ABG — confirm with IMAGING.

cards.q: Give the deck's bottom line about ABGs that don't fit.
cards.a:
Give the deck's bottom line about ABGs that don't fit.
'If the ABG results don't fit the patient's presentation, QUESTION THEM.'

cards.q: Define asthma with its four descriptors.
cards.a:
Define asthma with its four descriptors.
A CHRONIC, INFLAMMATORY, OBSTRUCTIVE, NON-CONTAGIOUS airway disease with varying levels of severity.

cards.q: Why is asthma called OBSTRUCTIVE — and what is its 'fingerprint'?
cards.a:
Why is asthma called OBSTRUCTIVE — and what is its 'fingerprint'?
Airflow is limited mostly on EXHALATION, from the combination of bronchoconstriction, inflammation and mucus.
The fingerprint is VARIABILITY — symptoms and airflow limitation vary over TIME and in INTENSITY.

cards.q: Name the classic asthma symptoms — and what is an 'attack' properly called?
cards.a:
Name the classic asthma symptoms — and what is an 'attack' properly called?
Shortness of breath · wheezing · chest tightness · coughing · waking at night with any of those (a sign of poor control).
An 'attack' is properly called an EXACERBATION.

cards.q: Name the four classic asthma triggers.
cards.a:
Name the four classic asthma triggers.
Exercise · allergen or irritant exposure · change in weather · viral respiratory infection.

cards.q: ⚠ Can a symptom-free asthma patient still have a life-threatening episode?
cards.a:
⚠ Can a symptom-free asthma patient still have a life-threatening episode?
YES — a patient can go WEEKS TO MONTHS symptom-free and still have a sudden, severe, or even LIFE-THREATENING episode.
The reason: airway HYPERRESPONSIVENESS sitting on top of CHRONIC UNDERLYING INFLAMMATION.

cards.q: Give the pharmacology deck's 4-step trigger cascade.
cards.a:
Give the pharmacology deck's 4-step trigger cascade.
Trigger → IgE / MAST CELL activation → release of HISTAMINE and LEUKOTRIENES → narrowed airways, increased resistance, wheezing and SOB.

cards.q: Give the U.S. asthma prevalence numbers.
cards.a:
Give the U.S. asthma prevalence numbers.
About 25 MILLION people — 18.4 million adults (7.6%) and 6.2 million children (8.4%).
6.5% of all physician office visits · ~1.9 million ED visits/year · 3,651 deaths/year.

cards.q: How does asthma prevalence differ by sex across the lifespan?
cards.a:
How does asthma prevalence differ by sex across the lifespan?
More common in BOYS than girls in CHILDHOOD — but the pattern FLIPS after puberty, so it is more common in WOMEN than men in adults.

cards.q: Give the worldwide asthma figures.
cards.a:
Give the worldwide asthma figures.
About 235 MILLION people.
More than 80% of asthma deaths occur in LOW- AND MIDDLE-INCOME countries.
Asthma is the MOST COMMON CHRONIC DISEASE among children worldwide.

cards.q: Name the three headline pathologic changes in asthma.
cards.a:
Name the three headline pathologic changes in asthma.
REVERSIBLE BRONCHOCONSTRICTION · AIRWAY INFLAMMATION · INCREASED AIRWAY HYPERRESPONSIVENESS.

cards.q: Describe the structural airway changes in asthma.
cards.a:
Describe the structural airway changes in asthma.
Bronchial smooth muscle CONSTRICTS and with repeated stimulation HYPERTROPHIES UP TO 3× NORMAL THICKNESS.
Mucosa infiltrated with EOSINOPHILS → inflammation and edema.
CHARCOT-LEYDEN CRYSTALS from eosinophil breakdown in allergic asthma.
GOBLET CELL HYPERPLASIA plus enlarged mucous glands → thick tenacious mucus → MUCUS PLUGS and ATELECTASIS.

cards.q: What do the asthma airway changes create functionally?
cards.a:
What do the asthma airway changes create functionally?
AIR TRAPPING and ALVEOLAR HYPERINFLATION.
Between episodes, many changes may be ABSENT in mild-to-moderate asthma. In severe/chronic disease, bronchial wall inflammation leads to FIBROSIS from remodeling.

cards.q: Describe the SENSITIZATION phase of extrinsic asthma.
cards.a:
Describe the SENSITIZATION phase of extrinsic asthma.
FIRST allergen exposure stimulates IgE PRODUCTION, and those IgE antibodies ATTACH TO MAST CELLS in the bronchial walls.

cards.q: What happens on RE-EXPOSURE in extrinsic asthma?
cards.a:
What happens on RE-EXPOSURE in extrinsic asthma?
Allergen BINDS the IgE → the mast cell DEGRANULATES → dumps HISTAMINE, LEUKOTRIENES, PROSTAGLANDINS, ECF-A, NCF and PAF.
Those mediators cause BRONCHOCONSTRICTION, MUCUS HYPERSECRETION, and INCREASED VASCULAR PERMEABILITY → airway EDEMA.

cards.q: Distinguish the EARLY from the LATE phase asthma response.
cards.a:
Distinguish the EARLY from the LATE phase asthma response.
EARLY: starts within MINUTES, usually resolves within about 1 HOUR.
LATE: starts HOURS later as EOSINOPHILS, BASOPHILS, NEUTROPHILS and T-CELLS migrate in — and lasts LONGER.
Having both is a BIPHASIC response.

cards.q: Which cells and interleukins sustain asthma inflammation?
cards.a:
Which cells and interleukins sustain asthma inflammation?
Th2 LYMPHOCYTES release IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13.

cards.q: Define airway hyperresponsiveness, and what drives it?
cards.a:
Define airway hyperresponsiveness, and what drives it?
An EXAGGERATED BRONCHOCONSTRICTOR RESPONSE to stimuli — not just allergens, but exercise, cold air, irritants and infections.
Driven by increased SENSITIVITY to mediators (histamine, leukotrienes) and by OVERACTIVE airway smooth muscle with increased contractility and growth.
AHR is WHY symptoms vary day to day, and it is measured with bronchoprovocation testing.

cards.q: Name the features of airway REMODELING.
cards.a:
Name the features of airway REMODELING.
THICKENED airway walls (increased collagen and myofibroblasts) · increased SMOOTH MUSCLE MASS · epithelial injury and repair producing MORE MUCUS-PRODUCING CELLS · eosinophil-driven FIBROSIS · a THICKENED BASEMENT MEMBRANE · DAMAGED CILIA.

cards.q: ⚠ What happens if airway remodeling progresses?
cards.a:
⚠ What happens if airway remodeling progresses?
Obstruction becomes PARTIALLY IRREVERSIBLE — FIXED AIRFLOW LIMITATION.

cards.q: Name the three HOST risk factors for asthma.
cards.a:
Name the three HOST risk factors for asthma.
GENETIC predisposition / family history · SEX differences (more in boys in childhood, higher in women after puberty) · OBESITY, associated with worse control and REDUCED RESPONSE TO THERAPY.

cards.q: Name the ENVIRONMENTAL asthma triggers.
cards.a:
Name the ENVIRONMENTAL asthma triggers.
Air pollution and TOBACCO SMOKE · occupational exposures and irritant gases · viral respiratory infections (RSV, rhinovirus) · diet (cow's milk, soy, processed foods) and early environmental exposures.
Take-home: asthma usually develops from a COMBINATION of genetic susceptibility and environmental exposure.

cards.q: ⚠ Why do beta-blockers worsen asthma?
cards.a:
⚠ Why do beta-blockers worsen asthma?
Because they BLOCK the β₂ RECEPTORS responsible for BRONCHODILATION.

cards.q: Which food additives can provoke an asthma attack?
cards.a:
Which food additives can provoke an asthma attack?
SULFITES (dried fruits, shrimp, beer, wine) and the dye TARTRAZINE.

cards.q: Why is exercise-induced bronchoconstriction worse in cold air?
cards.a:
Why is exercise-induced bronchoconstriction worse in cold air?
It is thought to come from COOLING AND DRYING of the airways.

cards.q: Name the other asthma provokers besides drugs and additives.
cards.a:
Name the other asthma provokers besides drugs and additives.
GERD (bronchospasm and chronic cough) · NOCTURNAL asthma (symptoms worsen at night) · PERIMENSTRUAL asthma (hormonal fluctuation) · emotional STRESS · ALLERGIC BRONCHOPULMONARY ASPERGILLOSIS (ABPA), a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus.

cards.q: Name the five asthma phenotypes.
cards.a:
Name the five asthma phenotypes.
Allergic (Atopic) · Nonallergic · Late-onset · Asthma with fixed airflow limitation · Asthma with obesity.

cards.q: Describe the ALLERGIC and NONALLERGIC phenotypes.
cards.a:
Describe the ALLERGIC and NONALLERGIC phenotypes.
ALLERGIC (Atopic): CHILDHOOD onset · family history of atopy common · EOSINOPHILIC inflammation · RESPONDS WELL to ICS.
NONALLERGIC: often ADULT onset · may be NEUTROPHILIC or eosinophilic · POOR response to ICS.

cards.q: Describe the LATE-ONSET and OBESITY phenotypes.
cards.a:
Describe the LATE-ONSET and OBESITY phenotypes.
LATE-ONSET: adulthood, often WOMEN · usually nonallergic · needs HIGHER ICS doses; CORTICOSTEROID-RESISTANT.
ASTHMA WITH OBESITY: any onset · prominent symptoms, MINIMAL EOSINOPHILIA · BMI > 30 · HARDER to control.

cards.q: Describe EXTRINSIC asthma.
cards.a:
Describe EXTRINSIC asthma.
Allergic / atopic. Triggered by specific allergens — dust mites, pollen, pet dander, mold.
Associated with ATOPY and ELEVATED IgE, works through mast cell activation, more common in children and younger adults, and often travels with eczema, allergic rhinitis and hay fever.

cards.q: Describe INTRINSIC asthma.
cards.a:
Describe INTRINSIC asthma.
Nonallergic / nonatopic. NOT linked to allergen exposure, has NORMAL IgE levels, usually develops LATER IN ADULTHOOD.
Set off by nonspecific stimuli: respiratory infections, exercise, cold air, stress, GERD, certain medications.
There is significant OVERLAP between the two in real patients.

cards.q: Which two bodies publish the asthma guidelines?
cards.a:
Which two bodies publish the asthma guidelines?
NAEPP (U.S., under NHLBI/NIH) and GINA (international, updated annually).

cards.q: Give the SPIROMETRY thresholds that diagnose asthma.
cards.a:
Give the SPIROMETRY thresholds that diagnose asthma.
↓ FEV₁ and ↓ FEV₁/FVC.
Adults < 0.75–0.80 · children < 0.90.

cards.q: Give the bronchodilator REVERSIBILITY threshold for adults and children.
cards.a:
Give the bronchodilator REVERSIBILITY threshold for adults and children.
Adults: ↑ FEV₁ ≥ 12% AND/OR ≥ 200 mL.
Children: ↑ FEV₁ ≥ 12% OF PREDICTED.

cards.q: Give the PEFR variability thresholds that support an asthma diagnosis.
cards.a:
Give the PEFR variability thresholds that support an asthma diagnosis.
Daily variability > 10% in ADULTS, > 13% in CHILDREN.

cards.q: What response after 4 weeks of anti-inflammatory therapy supports asthma?
cards.a:
What response after 4 weeks of anti-inflammatory therapy supports asthma?
↑ FEV₁ ≥ 12% OR PEFR ↑ ≥ 20%.

cards.q: What makes a methacholine challenge POSITIVE?
cards.a:
What makes a methacholine challenge POSITIVE?
A ≥ 20% DECREASE in FEV₁ = airway hyperresponsiveness.

cards.q: Give the physical exam findings in asthma.
cards.a:
Give the physical exam findings in asthma.
SOB with PURSED-LIP breathing · increased A-P diameter (BARREL CHEST) · accessory muscle use and RETRACTIONS (more in kids) · HYPERRESONANT/tympanic percussion · DIFFUSE BILATERAL WHEEZING with PROLONGED EXPIRATION · diaphoresis/cyanosis/anxiety · thick white sputum · tachycardia and tachypnea.

cards.q: ⚠ Define pulsus paradoxus in asthma and give its mechanism.
cards.a:
⚠ Define pulsus paradoxus in asthma and give its mechanism.
An exaggerated drop in systolic BP of > 10 mmHg during INSPIRATION, from SEVERE AIR TRAPPING IMPEDING VENOUS RETURN.
In severe episodes it is a RED FLAG.

cards.q: Give the asthma CXR findings.
cards.a:
Give the asthma CXR findings.
Increased A-P diameter · HYPERLUCENT lung fields · FLATTENED DIAPHRAGMS.
May be NORMAL between exacerbations.

cards.q: ⚠ Give the ABG trajectory in an asthma exacerbation.
cards.a:
⚠ Give the ABG trajectory in an asthma exacerbation.
EARLY: acute RESPIRATORY ALKALOSIS + HYPOXEMIA.
SEVERE/LATE: acute RESPIRATORY ACIDOSIS (ventilatory failure).

cards.q: Name the asthma lab findings.
cards.a:
Name the asthma lab findings.
Sputum EOSINOPHILIA · CHARCOT-LEYDEN CRYSTALS · CURSCHMANN SPIRALS · elevated IgE in extrinsic asthma.
FeNO marks EOSINOPHILIC airway inflammation.

cards.q: Give the PEFR and SaO₂ cutoffs for MILD, MODERATE and SEVERE exacerbation.
cards.a:
Give the PEFR and SaO₂ cutoffs for MILD, MODERATE and SEVERE exacerbation.
MILD: PEFR ≥ 80% predicted or personal best · SaO₂ > 95%.
MODERATE: PEFR 50–80% · SaO₂ 92–95%.
SEVERE: PEFR < 50% · SaO₂ < 92%.

cards.q: Describe speech and wheeze across the exacerbation severities.
cards.a:
Describe speech and wheeze across the exacerbation severities.
MILD: breathless with WALKING; EXPIRATORY wheeze only.
MODERATE: breathless while TALKING, speaks in PHRASES; wheeze throughout expiration ± inspiratory.
SEVERE: speaks in SINGLE WORDS, breathless AT REST, sits upright, cannot lie down; BIPHASIC wheeze.

cards.q: ⚠ Give the RESPIRATORY ARREST IMMINENT findings.
cards.a:
⚠ Give the RESPIRATORY ARREST IMMINENT findings.
DROWSY, CONFUSED · SILENT CHEST (minimal/no wheeze) · PARADOXICAL thoracoabdominal movement · LOSS of pulsus paradoxus (muscle fatigue) · BRADYCARDIA · rising PaCO₂ · respiratory acidosis.

cards.q: ⚠ What does a SILENT CHEST mean in asthma?
cards.a:
⚠ What does a SILENT CHEST mean in asthma?
A silent chest is NEVER IMPROVEMENT — it is a LATE, CRITICAL WARNING that airflow has nearly STOPPED.

cards.q: Give the SEVERE exacerbation respiratory rate and pulsus paradoxus.
cards.a:
Give the SEVERE exacerbation respiratory rate and pulsus paradoxus.
RR often > 30/min with marked retractions.
Pulsus paradoxus > 25 mmHg.

cards.q: ⚠ Do your decks cover the NAEPP chronic severity categories and Steps 1–6?
cards.a:
⚠ Do your decks cover the NAEPP chronic severity categories and Steps 1–6?
NO — the four named decks NEVER lay out Intermittent/Mild/Moderate/Severe Persistent or a numbered Step 1–6 ladder.
Look them up in the NAEPP EPR-3 classification table and the Hess Ch 32 p806 Fig 32-8 stepwise therapy figure.

cards.q: What DO the decks say about the stepwise approach?
cards.a:
What DO the decks say about the stepwise approach?
Management uses a STEPWISE approach — STEP UP (short-term or sustained) for poor control, STEP DOWN after ≥ 3 MONTHS of stable control.
Step 2 = MILD PERSISTENT asthma; Cromolyn and antileukotrienes are alternatives to ICS for Step 2 care.
Cromolyn is PREFERRED in infants and young children needing Step 2 care because of ICS safety profiles.

cards.q: ⚠ Give the single most important distinction between relievers and controllers.
cards.a:
⚠ Give the single most important distinction between relievers and controllers.
RELIEVERS (rescue) open the airway NOW and do NOTHING for inflammation.
CONTROLLERS are taken DAILY to suppress inflammation and do NOTHING for an acute attack.

cards.q: ⚠ State the LABA safety rule.
cards.a:
⚠ State the LABA safety rule.
LABAs are NEVER used ALONE in asthma — they must ALWAYS be paired with an INHALED CORTICOSTEROID.
Never in patients already controlled on low- or medium-dose ICS, and children must use a LABA in conjunction with a corticosteroid.

cards.q: Give the SABA onset, peak, duration and the two generics.
cards.a:
Give the SABA onset, peak, duration and the two generics.
Onset 15 min · peak 30–60 min · duration 4–6 hr.
ALBUTEROL (Proventil HFA, Ventolin HFA, ProAir HFA, AccuNeb) and LEVALBUTEROL (Xopenex, ~5–8 hr).

cards.q: Give racemic epinephrine's onset, duration and actual indication.
cards.a:
Give racemic epinephrine's onset, duration and actual indication.
Onset 3–5 min, duration < 3 hr (~2 hr).
Mainly UPPER-AIRWAY mucosal vasoconstriction/edema — CROUP, POST-EXTUBATION STRIDOR, EPIGLOTTITIS — NOT routine asthma.
SVN 2.25%, 0.25–0.5 mL.

cards.q: Give the LABA onset and duration, and name the generics.
cards.a:
Give the LABA onset and duration, and name the generics.
Onset 20 min · duration 12–24 hr.
Salmeterol · Formoterol · Arformoterol · Indacaterol · Olodaterol · Vilanterol; plus extended-release albuterol.

cards.q: Name the inhaled corticosteroids and their role.
cards.a:
Name the inhaled corticosteroids and their role.
Beclomethasone · Budesonide · Fluticasone · Ciclesonide · Mometasone.
(QVAR, Pulmicort, Flovent/Arnuity Ellipta, Alvesco.)
The FOUNDATION of long-term control — ↓ airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness.

cards.q: Name the four ICS + LABA combination products.
cards.a:
Name the four ICS + LABA combination products.
Fluticasone/Salmeterol = ADVAIR · Budesonide/Formoterol = SYMBICORT · Mometasone/Formoterol = DULERA · Fluticasone furoate/Vilanterol = BREO (Ellipta).

cards.q: Name the three leukotriene modifiers and their brands.
cards.a:
Name the three leukotriene modifiers and their brands.
MONTELUKAST (Singulair) · ZAFIRLUKAST (Accolate) · ZILEUTON (Zyflo / Zyflo CR).
Oral anti-inflammatories — good for allergic and exercise-induced asthma.

cards.q: Name the four asthma biologics and what each blocks.
cards.a:
Name the four asthma biologics and what each blocks.
OMALIZUMAB (Xolair) — blocks IgE.
BENRALIZUMAB (Fasenra), MEPOLIZUMAB (Nucala), RESLIZUMAB (Cinqair) — block IL-5/eosinophils.
Injectable add-ons for SEVERE asthma.

cards.q: Give the typical nebulized albuterol dose, and what chemical class is it?
cards.a:
Give the typical nebulized albuterol dose, and what chemical class is it?
2.5 mg in 3 mL normal saline, or by MDI.
It is a SALIGENIN agent — catechol nucleus modified at the carbon-3 site for β₂ selectivity.

cards.q: What makes levalbuterol different from albuterol?
cards.a:
What makes levalbuterol different from albuterol?
It is the PURE (R)-ISOMER.
The R-isomer does the bronchodilating; the S-isomer is roughly 100× LESS POTENT and MAY WORSEN airway responsiveness.
Comes as 0.31, 0.63 and 1.25 mg/3 mL plus a 1.25 mg/0.5 mL concentrate.

cards.q: Name the SABA side effects.
cards.a:
Name the SABA side effects.
TREMOR · TACHYCARDIA · palpitations · hypertension or hypotension · headache · nausea/vomiting · HYPOKALEMIA · HYPERGLYCEMIA · a FALL IN PaO₂ from worsened V/Q matching · tolerance/loss of bronchoprotection · PARADOXICAL BRONCHOSPASM.

cards.q: ⚠ Give the stop-and-notify heart rate threshold during a bronchodilator treatment.
cards.a:
⚠ Give the stop-and-notify heart rate threshold during a bronchodilator treatment.
A 20 bpm OR 20% INCREASE over baseline.

cards.q: Why are catecholamines useless orally?
cards.a:
Why are catecholamines useless orally?
They are inactivated by COMT (duration only 1.5–3 hr) and by HEAT, LIGHT and AIR.

cards.q: Give salmeterol's route, onset, peak and duration.
cards.a:
Give salmeterol's route, onset, peak and duration.
DPI ONLY · onset 20 min (SLOWER than albuterol) · peak at 3–5 hours · duration 12 hours.

cards.q: Give formoterol's onset, duration, routes and approval.
cards.a:
Give formoterol's onset, duration, routes and approval.
β₂-selective with a FAST 3-MINUTE onset and up to 12 hours duration.
Available as SVN and DPI.
Approved for asthma maintenance and prevention of exercise-induced bronchospasm in adults and children ≥ 5 years.

cards.q: Which LABAs are COPD-maintenance drugs, and which is combo-only?
cards.a:
Which LABAs are COPD-maintenance drugs, and which is combo-only?
Arformoterol (Brovana) — a single isomer of formoterol, nebulizer solution, 12 hours.
Indacaterol (Arcapta) and Olodaterol (Striverdi Respimat) — ultra-long-acting at up to 24 hours.
VILANTEROL is NOT available as monotherapy — only in Breo, Anoro and Trelegy Ellipta.

cards.q: What is the mechanistic difference between LABAs and SABAs?
cards.a:
What is the mechanistic difference between LABAs and SABAs?
LABAs are LIPOPHILIC; SABAs are HYDROPHILIC.
That lets LABAs approach the β-receptor LATERALLY.

cards.q: What side effect does long-term ICS cause, and how is it prevented?
cards.a:
What side effect does long-term ICS cause, and how is it prevented?
ORAL THRUSH — patients must RINSE THE MOUTH after use.

cards.q: ⚠ Give the three rules for cromolyn.
cards.a:
⚠ Give the three rules for cromolyn.
PROPHYLACTIC USE ONLY — NEVER during acute bronchospasm.
It can take 2–4 WEEKS to show improvement.
⚠ GINA does NOT include cromolyn as an asthma treatment agent.

cards.q: Distinguish the two types of antileukotriene, with doses.
cards.a:
Distinguish the two types of antileukotriene, with doses.
RECEPTOR BLOCKERS: Montelukast (Singulair) — oral 4 mg, 10 mg, 5 mg chewable; Zafirlukast (Accolate) — 10 mg bid ages 5–11, 20 mg bid ages 12+.
SYNTHESIS INHIBITOR: Zileuton (Zyflo) — 600 mg QID, inhibits the 5-LIPOXYGENASE (5-LO) enzyme.

cards.q: ⚠ What monitoring does zileuton require?
cards.a:
⚠ What monitoring does zileuton require?
LIVER FUNCTION MONITORING, and caution with THEOPHYLLINE and WARFARIN.

cards.q: ⚠ How effective are antileukotrienes?
cards.a:
⚠ How effective are antileukotrienes?
They work in only about 50–70% of patients and are NOT OPTIMAL AS MONOTHERAPY.

cards.q: What are biologics chemically, how are they given, and what is the worst risk?
cards.a:
What are biologics chemically, how are they given, and what is the worst risk?
DNA-derived HUMANIZED IgG ANTIBODIES given PARENTERALLY.
⚠ The most severe risk is ANAPHYLAXIS.

cards.q: Give the GREEN zone peak flow range and action.
cards.a:
Give the GREEN zone peak flow range and action.
80–100% of personal best.
Well controlled — no symptoms, usual activities possible.
Action: CONTINUE daily controller medications as prescribed.

cards.q: Give the YELLOW zone peak flow range and action.
cards.a:
Give the YELLOW zone peak flow range and action.
50–80% of personal best.
Worsening control — increased symptoms, increased SABA use, nighttime awakening.
Action: INCREASE rescue medication per plan, CONTINUE controller, contact provider if no improvement, aim to return to GREEN.

cards.q: Give the RED zone peak flow range and action.
cards.a:
Give the RED zone peak flow range and action.
< 50% of personal best.
Severe / poor control — severe SOB, symptoms > 24 hours, limited activity.
Action: use rescue medication IMMEDIATELY, add systemic therapy if prescribed, contact provider URGENTLY.

cards.q: ⚠ What are the EMERGENCY signs on an asthma action plan?
cards.a:
⚠ What are the EMERGENCY signs on an asthma action plan?
Difficulty WALKING OR TALKING from dyspnea · CYANOSIS of lips or nails · severe distress.
Action: CALL 911 / go to the hospital IMMEDIATELY.

cards.q: ⚠ What are the ventilator indications for the asthmatic?
cards.a:
⚠ What are the ventilator indications for the asthmatic?
Acute ventilatory failure — specifically STATUS ASTHMATICUS with FATIGUE, a RISING PaCO₂, a DECREASING pH, and a DECREASING PaO₂.

cards.q: ⚠ What ABG shift is the red flag for impending respiratory failure in asthma?
cards.a:
⚠ What ABG shift is the red flag for impending respiratory failure in asthma?
A patient who moves from RESPIRATORY ALKALOSIS into a NORMAL OR RISING PaCO₂ IS TIRING OUT.

cards.q: What do you escalate through BEFORE intubating an asthmatic?
cards.a:
What do you escalate through BEFORE intubating an asthmatic?
Oxygen therapy up to CPAP/BiPAP · CONTINUOUS NEBULIZED ALBUTEROL (generally 10–15 mg/hour in an adult), specifically used to try to avoid respiratory failure, intubation and mechanical ventilation · and adjuncts: HELIOX, MAGNESIUM SULFATE and SUBCUTANEOUS EPINEPHRINE.

cards.q: Name the three adjunct therapies for refractory asthma.
cards.a:
Name the three adjunct therapies for refractory asthma.
HELIOX · MAGNESIUM SULFATE · SUBCUTANEOUS EPINEPHRINE.

cards.q: How do you treat a severe or life-threatening asthma exacerbation immediately?
cards.a:
How do you treat a severe or life-threatening asthma exacerbation immediately?
Short-acting bronchodilators + SYSTEMIC CORTICOSTEROIDS + supplemental OXYGEN.
Give IM EPINEPHRINE if features of ANAPHYLAXIS are present.

cards.q: Name the asthma lifestyle and environmental interventions.
cards.a:
Name the asthma lifestyle and environmental interventions.
Lifestyle: SMOKING CESSATION · physical activity · healthy diet · weight reduction in obese patients · breathing exercises · stress management.
Environmental: avoid occupational exposures, indoor allergens (mold, dust mites, pets), and indoor/outdoor air pollution.

cards.q: What is bronchial thermoplasty?
cards.a:
What is bronchial thermoplasty?
CONTROLLED HEAT applied to the airway wall to REDUCE SMOOTH MUSCLE in SEVERE asthma.

cards.q: When do you refer an asthma patient for expert care?
cards.a:
When do you refer an asthma patient for expert care?
When the DIAGNOSIS IS UNCERTAIN, OCCUPATIONAL asthma is suspected, control stays POOR, the patient is AT RISK FOR ASTHMA-RELATED DEATH, or side effects are a problem.
Once control is achieved, maintain it at the LOWEST EFFECTIVE STEP AND DOSE.

cards.q: ⚠ Give the order of administration when multiple inhaled therapies are ordered.
cards.a:
⚠ Give the order of administration when multiple inhaled therapies are ordered.
(1) BRONCHODILATOR ± anticholinergic (albuterol, or albuterol + ipratropium/DuoNeb) — to OPEN the airways so everything downstream deposits DEEPER.
(2) INHALED CORTICOSTEROID (budesonide/Pulmicort, fluticasone/Flovent).
(3) ANTIBIOTICS (e.g. tobramycin for pneumonia).

cards.q: ⚠ What must you give before or with a mucolytic, and why?
cards.a:
⚠ What must you give before or with a mucolytic, and why?
A BRONCHODILATOR — to REDUCE THE RISK OF BRONCHOSPASM.

cards.q: Define COPD with its four descriptors.
cards.a:
Define COPD with its four descriptors.
PREVENTABLE, TREATABLE, PROGRESSIVE, IRREVERSIBLE airflow limitation caused by an ABNORMAL INFLAMMATORY RESPONSE to harmful particles or gases — most commonly CIGARETTE SMOKE.
Once the process starts the airflow limitation is IRREVERSIBLE and gets WORSE over time.

cards.q: What does COPD mean PATHOLOGICALLY?
cards.a:
What does COPD mean PATHOLOGICALLY?
AIRSPACE ENLARGEMENT DISTAL TO THE TERMINAL BRONCHIOLES · GOBLET CELL HYPERTROPHY · MUCUS GLAND HYPERPLASIA.

cards.q: Name the five key COPD terms to own.
cards.a:
Name the five key COPD terms to own.
Chronic ventilatory failure · chronic hypercapnia · INCREASED lung compliance · DECREASED elastic recoil · chronic CO₂ retention.

cards.q: Name the four classic COPD symptoms.
cards.a:
Name the four classic COPD symptoms.
DYSPNEA (especially on exertion) · CHRONIC COUGH · MUCUS/SPUTUM production · WHEEZING.
⚠ These raise suspicion — they are NOT diagnostic by themselves.

cards.q: What is GOLD?
cards.a:
What is GOLD?
The Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease — an international expert committee that publishes the worldwide standard of care.

cards.q: When should you CONSIDER COPD?
cards.a:
When should you CONSIDER COPD?
Patients OVER 40 with DYSPNEA, CHRONIC COUGH or SPUTUM production, a history of SMOKING or risk-factor exposure, or a FAMILY HISTORY of COPD.

cards.q: ⚠ Give the one criterion that CONFIRMS COPD.
cards.a:
⚠ Give the one criterion that CONFIRMS COPD.
A POST-BRONCHODILATOR FEV₁/FVC < 0.70.
⚠ The word POST-BRONCHODILATOR is the whole point — COPD is confirmed when the obstruction DOES NOT GO AWAY after a bronchodilator.

cards.q: Why does the FEV₁/FVC ratio fall in COPD?
cards.a:
Why does the FEV₁/FVC ratio fall in COPD?
The FEV₁ falls MORE than the FVC, because OBSTRUCTION SLOWS EXPIRATION — which is what drags the ratio down.
A normal person exhales about 80–85% of the FVC in the first second, versus roughly 66% in the example COPD spirogram.

cards.q: Give the four GOLD stages by FEV₁ % predicted.
cards.a:
Give the four GOLD stages by FEV₁ % predicted.
GOLD 1 — MILD: ≥ 80% predicted
GOLD 2 — MODERATE: 50–79%
GOLD 3 — SEVERE: 30–49%
GOLD 4 — VERY SEVERE: ≤ 30%

cards.q: ⚠ What do the GOLD stages NOT do?
cards.a:
⚠ What do the GOLD stages NOT do?
They do NOT diagnose COPD (they are applied AFTER obstruction is confirmed by FEV₁/FVC < 0.70) and they do NOT capture SYMPTOM BURDEN or EXACERBATION RISK.

cards.q: Name the four areas GOLD wants assessed before treating.
cards.a:
Name the four areas GOLD wants assessed before treating.
AIRFLOW LIMITATION (spirometry) · SYMPTOMS (mMRC, CAT) · EXACERBATION RISK (history) · COMORBIDITIES.

cards.q: Describe the mMRC scale and its cutoff.
cards.a:
Describe the mMRC scale and its cutoff.
Modified Medical Research Council dyspnea scale — runs 0 to 4 and measures BREATHLESSNESS ONLY.
Score < 1 = LOW risk · score ≥ 2 = HIGH risk. It PREDICTS MORTALITY.

cards.q: Describe the CAT and its cutoff.
cards.a:
Describe the CAT and its cutoff.
COPD Assessment Test — an 8-ITEM questionnaire, each item scored 0 to 5, total 0 to 40.
Covers cough, mucus, chest tightness, breathlessness with activity, confidence leaving home, sleep and energy.
Score < 10 = LOW risk · score ≥ 10 = HIGH risk.

cards.q: Define GOLD Groups A and B and give the initial therapy for each.
cards.a:
Define GOLD Groups A and B and give the initial therapy for each.
GROUP A — fewer symptoms, low risk: CAT < 10, ≤ 1 exacerbation, no hospitalizations → A BRONCHODILATOR — SABA or LABA; SABA as needed for rescue.
GROUP B — more symptoms, low risk: CAT ≥ 10, ≤ 1 exacerbation → LABA or LAMA (e.g. Spiriva); SABA for rescue.

cards.q: Define GOLD Groups C and D and give the initial therapy for each.
cards.a:
Define GOLD Groups C and D and give the initial therapy for each.
GROUP C — fewer symptoms, high risk: CAT < 10, ≥ 2 exacerbations, ≥ 1 hospitalization → LAMA (BEST at reducing exacerbations); often dual LAMA + LABA or LABA + ICS.
GROUP D — more symptoms, high risk: CAT ≥ 10, ≥ 2 exacerbations, ≥ 1 hospitalization → COMBINATION FROM THE START — LAMA + LABA or LABA + ICS; may add roflumilast or azithromycin.

cards.q: ⚠ What is roflumilast (Daliresp) — and what is it NOT?
cards.a:
⚠ What is roflumilast (Daliresp) — and what is it NOT?
It is NOT a steroid.
It is a PHOSPHODIESTERASE-4 (PDE-4) INHIBITOR that reduces inflammation and exacerbations in SEVERE COPD.

cards.q: Why is azithromycin sometimes used long-term in COPD?
cards.a:
Why is azithromycin sometimes used long-term in COPD?
For its ANTI-INFLAMMATORY and ANTIBACTERIAL effects.

cards.q: Give the general COPD treatment escalation.
cards.a:
Give the general COPD treatment escalation.
Short-acting bronchodilators → long-acting bronchodilators → combination therapy → individualized management.

cards.q: How many Americans have COPD, and why is it underdiagnosed?
cards.a:
How many Americans have COPD, and why is it underdiagnosed?
Between 10 and 15 MILLION have chronic bronchitis, emphysema, or both.
Patients BLAME early dyspnea and cough ON AGING and don't seek care until the disease has progressed.

cards.q: How has the sex distribution of COPD changed?
cards.a:
How has the sex distribution of COPD changed?
Historically more common in MEN because of smoking rates — it now affects both genders ABOUT EQUALLY.
In some regions WOMEN have HIGHER hospitalization and mortality rates, because their lungs may be more susceptible to smoke and environmental exposure.

cards.q: Describe the AIRWAY changes in COPD pathophysiology.
cards.a:
Describe the AIRWAY changes in COPD pathophysiology.
Inflammation THICKENS the walls · submucosal glands ENLARGE and goblet cells INCREASE · mucus production goes UP · CILIARY FUNCTION DROPS · MUCUS PLUGGING obstructs airflow.

cards.q: Describe the PARENCHYMAL changes in COPD pathophysiology.
cards.a:
Describe the PARENCHYMAL changes in COPD pathophysiology.
ALVEOLAR WALLS ARE DESTROYED, so surface area for gas exchange FALLS · lung compliance INCREASES · ELASTIC RECOIL IS LOST.

cards.q: Trace loss of elastic recoil to barrel chest.
cards.a:
Trace loss of elastic recoil to barrel chest.
Losing recoil and the structural support of the small airways → the DISTAL AIRWAYS COLLAPSE during expiration → AIR TRAPPING and HYPERINFLATION → BARREL CHEST.

cards.q: Why does chronic CO₂ retention develop in advanced COPD?
cards.a:
Why does chronic CO₂ retention develop in advanced COPD?
Work of breathing rises so much that the patient SPENDS MORE OXYGEN BREATHING THAN THEY GAIN, so the body shifts to a MECHANICALLY EASIER but LESS EFFECTIVE pattern.

cards.q: What partly compensates for lost gas exchange in emphysema?
cards.a:
What partly compensates for lost gas exchange in emphysema?
COLLATERAL VENTILATION through the PORES OF KOHN and CANALS OF LAMBERT.

cards.q: Give the CLINICAL definition of chronic bronchitis.
cards.a:
Give the CLINICAL definition of chronic bronchitis.
A chronic PRODUCTIVE COUGH for ≥ 3 MONTHS in each of 2 CONSECUTIVE YEARS, after EXCLUDING other causes.

cards.q: Where does the name 'Blue Bloater' come from?
cards.a:
Where does the name 'Blue Bloater' come from?
CYANOSIS ('blue') from hypoxemia, PLUS FLUID RETENTION from RIGHT HEART FAILURE secondary to PULMONARY HYPERTENSION.

cards.q: Give the PATHOLOGIC definition of emphysema.
cards.a:
Give the PATHOLOGIC definition of emphysema.
PERMANENT ENLARGEMENT and DESTRUCTION of the air spaces DISTAL TO THE TERMINAL BRONCHIOLES, with alveolar wall destruction and NO OBVIOUS FIBROSIS.

cards.q: Where does the name 'Pink Puffer' come from?
cards.a:
Where does the name 'Pink Puffer' come from?
'PINK' = relatively PRESERVED OXYGENATION early on.
'PUFFER' = PURSED-LIP BREATHING that creates BACK-PRESSURE to keep the airways open during exhalation.

cards.q: ⚠ Does GOLD use the terms chronic bronchitis and emphysema?
cards.a:
⚠ Does GOLD use the terms chronic bronchitis and emphysema?
NO — GOLD does NOT use them in its formal definition of COPD.
But both remain clinically and epidemiologically useful, and the two conditions OFTEN COEXIST.

cards.q: Contrast body habitus, color and cough in Pink Puffer vs Blue Bloater.
cards.a:
Contrast body habitus, color and cough in Pink Puffer vs Blue Bloater.
PINK PUFFER: thin, CACHECTIC · reddish/'pink' · MINIMAL cough, little or no sputum.
BLUE BLOATER: stocky/overweight · CYANOSIS · chronic PRODUCTIVE cough, copious PURULENT sputum.

cards.q: Contrast breath sounds and percussion in Pink Puffer vs Blue Bloater.
cards.a:
Contrast breath sounds and percussion in Pink Puffer vs Blue Bloater.
PINK PUFFER: DECREASED / QUIET CHEST · HYPERRESONANT percussion.
BLUE BLOATER: WHEEZES AND CRACKLES · NORMAL percussion.

cards.q: ⚠ Contrast the DLCO in emphysema vs chronic bronchitis — and why.
cards.a:
⚠ Contrast the DLCO in emphysema vs chronic bronchitis — and why.
EMPHYSEMA: DECREASED — the ALVEOLAR-CAPILLARY MEMBRANE IS DESTROYED.
CHRONIC BRONCHITIS: typically NORMAL — the ALVEOLI ARE INTACT, the AIRWAYS are obstructed.

cards.q: Contrast the radiology of emphysema vs chronic bronchitis.
cards.a:
Contrast the radiology of emphysema vs chronic bronchitis.
EMPHYSEMA: HYPERINFLATION, FLAT DIAPHRAGM, BLEBS/BULLAE.
CHRONIC BRONCHITIS: INCREASED BRONCHOVASCULAR MARKINGS, CARDIOMEGALY.

cards.q: Contrast pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale and Hct in the two phenotypes.
cards.a:
Contrast pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale and Hct in the two phenotypes.
EMPHYSEMA: cor pulmonale UNCOMMON; Hct/Hgb normal in mild–moderate, may ↑ late.
CHRONIC BRONCHITIS: cor pulmonale COMMON; POLYCYTHEMIA common (chronic hypoxemia → ↑ erythropoietin).

cards.q: ⚠ Explain WHY the electrolytes shift in chronic CO₂ retention.
cards.a:
⚠ Explain WHY the electrolytes shift in chronic CO₂ retention.
Chronic CO₂ retention makes the kidneys RETAIN BICARBONATE to buffer acidity — and as HCO₃⁻ RISES, Cl⁻ FALLS to keep electrical neutrality (HYPOCHLOREMIA).
HYPERNATREMIA follows because chronic CO₂ retention and hypoxia STIMULATE ALDOSTERONE AND ADH, driving sodium and water retention.

cards.q: Which organisms grow in chronic bronchitis sputum?
cards.a:
Which organisms grow in chronic bronchitis sputum?
Streptococcus pneumoniae · Haemophilus influenzae · Moraxella catarrhalis.
(Emphysema sputum is usually normal — minimal sputum.)

cards.q: Describe PANACINAR emphysema.
cards.a:
Describe PANACINAR emphysema.
Enlarges and destroys ALL air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles — the ENTIRE ACINUS.
Typically the LOWER lung zones · strongly associated with ALPHA-1 ANTITRYPSIN DEFICIENCY · the MORE SEVERE form because of the major loss of gas-exchange surface area.

cards.q: Describe CENTRIACINAR emphysema.
cards.a:
Describe CENTRIACINAR emphysema.
Damages mainly the RESPIRATORY BRONCHIOLES — the CENTRAL portion of the acinus — while the PERIPHERAL ALVEOLI are relatively SPARED.
The MOST COMMON type · strongly associated with CIGARETTE SMOKING and CHRONIC BRONCHITIS · usually more prominent in the UPPER LOBES.

cards.q: Define cachexia, and why does it happen in COPD?
cards.a:
Define cachexia, and why does it happen in COPD?
A patient SEVERELY UNDERWEIGHT and PHYSICALLY WASTED due to CHRONIC ILLNESS ('kuh-KEK-tik').
These patients spend so much energy on the WORK OF BREATHING that the significant energy expenditure produces WEIGHT LOSS and a thin, cachectic appearance with VISIBLE MUSCLE WASTING.
It is NOT simply being thin — it is DISEASE-DRIVEN WASTING.

cards.q: Name the nonpulmonary consequences of COPD.
cards.a:
Name the nonpulmonary consequences of COPD.
CACHEXIA / weight loss and muscle wasting · COR PULMONALE (right-sided heart failure from pulmonary hypertension) producing peripheral edema, JVD/distended neck veins, cardiomegaly · POLYCYTHEMIA · ELECTROLYTE DISTURBANCE (↓Cl⁻, ↑Na⁺) · DIGITAL CLUBBING · CYANOSIS.

cards.q: Which comorbidities commonly coexist with COPD?
cards.a:
Which comorbidities commonly coexist with COPD?
CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE · ANXIETY · GERD · METABOLIC DISORDERS — all of which complicate management.

cards.q: What does HAVING COPD put the patient at risk FOR?
cards.a:
What does HAVING COPD put the patient at risk FOR?
Increased risk of HEART DISEASE · a higher likelihood of LUNG CANCER · plus cor pulmonale and right heart failure · acute on chronic ventilatory failure · recurrent exacerbations.

cards.q: ⚠ What is the BEST predictor of a future COPD exacerbation?
cards.a:
⚠ What is the BEST predictor of a future COPD exacerbation?
A PRIOR ONE — especially ≥ 2 exacerbations in the past year, or ANY exacerbation requiring HOSPITALIZATION.
Risk rises significantly in GOLD 3 and GOLD 4 patients because their baseline lung function is already severely reduced.

cards.q: Name the risk factors FOR DEVELOPING COPD.
cards.a:
Name the risk factors FOR DEVELOPING COPD.
GENETIC predisposition (AAT deficiency) · AGE and GENDER · IMPAIRED LUNG GROWTH during gestation and childhood · EXPOSURE TO PARTICLES (tobacco smoke the biggest contributor, biomass smoke, occupational dust/fumes, air pollution) · SOCIOECONOMIC STATUS (poverty, low nutrition, pollution) · ASTHMA/bronchial hyperreactivity · CHRONIC BRONCHITIS · RESPIRATORY INFECTIONS · TUBERCULOSIS.

cards.q: What does alpha-1 antitrypsin do, and what happens without it?
cards.a:
What does alpha-1 antitrypsin do, and what happens without it?
Produced in the LIVER to protect the lungs from NEUTROPHIL ELASTASE, an enzyme that breaks down connective tissue.
When AAT is low, elastase RUNS UNOPPOSED and DESTROYS THE ELASTIC TISSUE of the lung — a risk factor for EARLY or SEVERE emphysema (classically PANACINAR, LOWER LOBES).

cards.q: Give the three AAT phenotypes.
cards.a:
Give the three AAT phenotypes.
MM = NORMAL levels.
ZZ = LOW levels, HIGH RISK for COPD, often at a YOUNGER age.
MZ = variable/intermediate risk, but CAN PASS THE GENE to children.

cards.q: When do you screen for AAT deficiency, and what level is suggestive?
cards.a:
When do you screen for AAT deficiency, and what level is suggestive?
Screen when a patient YOUNGER THAN 45 presents with a history and clinical indicators of COPD.
A serum level BELOW 15% TO 20% of normal is highly suggestive of emphysema caused by AATD.

cards.q: Give the COPD chest x-ray findings.
cards.a:
Give the COPD chest x-ray findings.
HYPERLUCENCY · HYPERINFLATION · increased A-P DIAMETER · FLATTENED/DEPRESSED DIAPHRAGMS — all reflecting air trapping and lost elastic recoil.

cards.q: ⚠ Give the typical chronic COPD ABG — and what happens in an exacerbation?
cards.a:
⚠ Give the typical chronic COPD ABG — and what happens in an exacerbation?
CHRONIC: COMPENSATED (partial or full) RESPIRATORY ACIDOSIS WITH HYPOXEMIA — CO₂ elevated but the kidneys have retained bicarbonate to defend the pH.
EXACERBATION: ACUTE ON CHRONIC respiratory acidosis.
⚠ This matters because the pH can DROP FAST even with a HIGH bicarbonate.

cards.q: Give the COPD PFT findings.
cards.a:
Give the COPD PFT findings.
DECREASED FLOWS — FEV₁, FEV₁/FVC and FEF₂₅₋₇₅ are ALL reduced, from increased airway resistance and loss of elastic recoil.

cards.q: Give GOLD's definition of a COPD exacerbation.
cards.a:
Give GOLD's definition of a COPD exacerbation.
An ACUTE EVENT characterized by a WORSENING of respiratory symptoms BEYOND NORMAL DAY-TO-DAY VARIATIONS that LEADS TO A CHANGE IN MEDICATION.

cards.q: Give the three COPD exacerbation severities by treatment required.
cards.a:
Give the three COPD exacerbation severities by treatment required.
MILD: requires initial use of inhaled SABAs, ± a short-acting antimuscarinic.
MODERATE: requires SABAs PLUS an ANTIBIOTIC and/or ORAL CORTICOSTEROIDS.
SEVERE: requires an ER VISIT, HOSPITALIZATION or ICU ADMISSION — associated with ACUTE VENTILATORY FAILURE.

cards.q: Give the qualifying threshold for continuous LTOT in COPD.
cards.a:
Give the qualifying threshold for continuous LTOT in COPD.
SaO₂ ≤ 88% OR PaO₂ ≤ 55 torr on ROOM AIR — meeting EITHER qualifies the patient for home O₂.

cards.q: Give the Medicare criteria for nocturnal oxygen therapy.
cards.a:
Give the Medicare criteria for nocturnal oxygen therapy.
Nocturnal oximetry demonstrating a > 5% DROP in SpO₂, OR an SpO₂ LESS THAN 88% — PLUS signs or symptoms of hypoxemia (e.g. impaired cognitive process, insomnia).
Basically the same as the continuous LTOT criteria.

cards.q: Define a desaturation event and the ODI threshold for SAHS.
cards.a:
Define a desaturation event and the ODI threshold for SAHS.
