A desaturation event is an SpO₂ drop of 4% OR MORE.
The Oxygen Desaturation Index (ODI) is the average number of desaturation events per HOUR OF SLEEP.
An ODI of 15 OR MORE indicates Sleep Apnea–Hypopnea Syndrome.

cards.q: ⚠ Give the COPD oxygen target and the reasoning.
cards.a:
⚠ Give the COPD oxygen target and the reasoning.
SpO₂ of about 88–92%.
Correct hypoxemia WITHOUT giving more oxygen than the patient needs — since EXCESSIVE FiO₂ CAN WORSEN HYPERCAPNIA in some COPD patients.
Delivery: LOW-FLOW, or a precise-FiO₂ device at higher flow — VENTURI MASK or HIGH-FLOW NASAL CANNULA.

cards.q: Name the four therapist-driven protocols in COPD.
cards.a:
Name the four therapist-driven protocols in COPD.
(1) OXYGEN protocol — target SpO₂ 88–92%.
(2) AEROSOLIZED BRONCHODILATOR protocol — for bronchospasm, airway inflammation, retained secretions.
(3) AIRWAY CLEARANCE / bronchial hygiene — CPT, PEP, IPV, deep breathing with cough.
(4) MECHANICAL VENTILATION protocol — for hypoxemic or hypercapnic respiratory failure and acute-on-chronic exacerbations.

cards.q: Give the CBABE mnemonic and what it lists.
cards.a:
Give the CBABE mnemonic and what it lists.
The reversible-obstruction indications for β-agonists:
Cystic fibrosis · Bronchiectasis · Asthma · Bronchitis · Emphysema.

cards.q: ⚠ What ventilatory support comes FIRST in a COPD exacerbation?
cards.a:
⚠ What ventilatory support comes FIRST in a COPD exacerbation?
Start with NIV/NIPPV EARLY to reduce work of breathing and AVOID INTUBATION when possible — escalating to full support if the patient decompensates.

cards.q: ⚠ What is the single most important long-term COPD intervention?
cards.a:
⚠ What is the single most important long-term COPD intervention?
Referral to a SMOKING CESSATION program, including NICOTINE REPLACEMENT THERAPY.

cards.q: Name the other long-term COPD treatments beyond inhalers.
cards.a:
Name the other long-term COPD treatments beyond inhalers.
ICS in SELECTED patients (frequent exacerbations or asthma-overlap) · VACCINATIONS — flu, pneumococcal, Tdap · ANTIBIOTICS when indicated by SPUTUM CULTURE (not routinely) · PULMONARY REHABILITATION · proper NUTRITION with monitored fluid intake · NIPPV for acute exacerbations BEFORE intubation · patient and family EDUCATION · END-OF-LIFE and PALLIATIVE CARE discussions.

cards.q: Interpret the worked case ABG on 2 L/min NC: pH 7.24, PaCO₂ 110, HCO₃⁻ 46, PaO₂ 47, SaO₂ 77%.
cards.a:
Interpret the worked case ABG on 2 L/min NC: pH 7.24, PaCO₂ 110, HCO₃⁻ 46, PaO₂ 47, SaO₂ 77%.
ACUTE ON CHRONIC VENTILATORY FAILURE with MODERATE–SEVERE HYPOXEMIA.
The markedly elevated HCO₃⁻ of 46 shows the CHRONIC retention; the pH of 7.24 shows the ACUTE decompensation on top.

cards.q: Worked case: FEV₁ 35% predicted, mMRC 3, 2 exacerbations/year. What is the classification and plan?
cards.a:
Worked case: FEV₁ 35% predicted, mMRC 3, 2 exacerbations/year. What is the classification and plan?
Classification: GOLD 3, Group D.
Plan: notify physician STAT · start NIV and oxygen per protocol · airway clearance (CPT QID, suction PRN) · SABA + antimuscarinic aerosols · escalate to mechanical ventilation if he keeps decompensating. Antibiotics + steroids likely needed given PURULENT sputum.

cards.q: What does the worked case demonstrate about phenotypes?
cards.a:
What does the worked case demonstrate about phenotypes?
The MIXED phenotype — chronic bronchitis features (productive cough, wheezes, crackles, edema) alongside emphysema features (↓ DLCO, hyperresonance, pursed-lip breathing).

cards.q: How are ETTs sized, and what is the full stocked range?
cards.a:
How are ETTs sized, and what is the full stocked range?
By INTERNAL DIAMETER in millimeters. The full range runs size 2 to 10 mm ID.

cards.q: Give the adult ETT sizes for women and men.
cards.a:
Give the adult ETT sizes for women and men.
Women: 7 to 7.5 mm ID.
Men: 8 to 8.5 mm ID.

cards.q: Give the laryngoscope blade sizes and the two blade types.
cards.a:
Give the laryngoscope blade sizes and the two blade types.
Sizes 00 to 4.
MACINTOSH (CURVED) sits in the VALLECULA and lifts the epiglottis INDIRECTLY.
MILLER (STRAIGHT) lifts the epiglottis DIRECTLY.

cards.q: ⚠ Where is the narrowest point of the airway in adults versus children?
cards.a:
⚠ Where is the narrowest point of the airway in adults versus children?
ADULTS: the GLOTTIS (vocal cords), and the trachea below is CYLINDRICAL.
CHILDREN: the CRICOID RING, and the airway is FUNNEL-SHAPED.

cards.q: Why is 1 mm of edema catastrophic in an infant but tolerated in an adult?
cards.a:
Why is 1 mm of edema catastrophic in an infant but tolerated in an adult?
Because the child starts with a much smaller airway — 1 mm of circumferential edema can cut an INFANT'S airway diameter by MORE THAN 50%.

cards.q: ⚠ What does newer imaging suggest about the pediatric glottis — and what do you answer on the NBRC?
cards.a:
⚠ What does newer imaging suggest about the pediatric glottis — and what do you answer on the NBRC?
Newer MRI/CT imaging suggests the pediatric GLOTTIS may be as narrow as the CRICOID — one reason cuffed ETTs are now routinely used in pediatrics.
⚠ But for the NBRC answer: ADULTS = GLOTTIS, CHILDREN = CRICOID RING.

cards.q: Give Hess's pediatric ETT size formula and the practical habits around it.
cards.a:
Give Hess's pediatric ETT size formula and the practical habits around it.
For children 1 to 10 years: ETT size (mm ID) = (Age in years ÷ 4) + 4.
Have one half-size LARGER and one SMALLER available; length-based tapes are useful for children weighing 35 kg or less.

cards.q: ⚠ What cuff pressure does Hess want in a CHILD — and how does it differ from adults?
cards.a:
⚠ What cuff pressure does Hess want in a CHILD — and how does it differ from adults?
Below 20 cm H₂O in a child — LOWER than the adult 20–30 cm H₂O target.
Cuffed ETTs are as safe as uncuffed for infants and children in hospital, with a use case when lung compliance is low and high airway pressures are needed.

cards.q: Give Hess's infant ETT depth rule.
cards.a:
Give Hess's infant ETT depth rule.
Add 6 cm to the infant's weight in kilograms to estimate the insertion distance measured from the LIPS.

cards.q: Why were uncuffed tubes traditional in neonates?
cards.a:
Why were uncuffed tubes traditional in neonates?
The CRICOID CARTILAGE provides a FUNCTIONAL CUFF, so adequate ventilation is achievable despite some leak — and an uncuffed tube prevents cuff-related tracheal injury.

cards.q: ⚠ Give the cuff pressure range to memorize.
cards.a:
⚠ Give the cuff pressure range to memorize.
20 to 30 cm H₂O.
The single most testable number in the airway deck — stated twice.

cards.q: Why is 30 cm H₂O the CEILING for cuff pressure?
cards.a:
Why is 30 cm H₂O the CEILING for cuff pressure?
Tracheal capillary perfusion pressure is normally 25 to 35 mm Hg, and because the pressure transmitted from the cuff to the tracheal wall is usually LESS than the pressure inside the cuff, 30 cm H₂O is the maximum acceptable intracuff pressure.
Above that you risk MUCOSAL ISCHEMIA, TRACHEAL WALL NECROSIS and STENOSIS.

cards.q: Why is 20 cm H₂O the FLOOR for cuff pressure?
cards.a:
Why is 20 cm H₂O the FLOOR for cuff pressure?
Below 20 cm H₂O, MICROASPIRATION past the cuff becomes likely — which is the PRIMARY ROUTE TO VAP.

cards.q: Convert the cuff pressure range to mm Hg, and give the conversion factor.
cards.a:
Convert the cuff pressure range to mm Hg, and give the conversion factor.
1 mmHg = 1.36 cmH₂O (or 1 cmH₂O ≈ 0.735 mmHg).
20–30 cm H₂O ≈ 14.7 to 22.05 mm Hg.
The deck adds cuff pressure should stay < 25 mm Hg — and LOWER than 25 if the patient is HYPOTENSIVE.

cards.q: Name the two causes of a HIGH cuff pressure.
cards.a:
Name the two causes of a HIGH cuff pressure.
A tube that is TOO SMALL, and INCORRECT ETT POSITIONING.

cards.q: Name the two cuff types — and which is used today, and why?
cards.a:
Name the two cuff types — and which is used today, and why?
HIGH-VOLUME, LOW-PRESSURE and LOW-VOLUME, HIGH-PRESSURE.
Most cuffs used today are HIGH-VOLUME, LOW-PRESSURE — because HIGH TRACHEAL WALL PRESSURES INJURE MUCOSA.

cards.q: Describe Minimal Occlusion Volume, and why end-inspiration?
cards.a:
Describe Minimal Occlusion Volume, and why end-inspiration?
Place the stethoscope diaphragm on the TRACHEA and inflate SLOWLY until NO AIR LEAK is heard at END-INSPIRATION.
End-inspiration is when the trachea is at MAXIMUM DIAMETER.

cards.q: Describe the Minimal Leak Technique.
cards.a:
Describe the Minimal Leak Technique.
Inflate until leaks STOP, then SLOWLY REMOVE a small amount of air until a SLIGHT LEAK is heard at END-INSPIRATION.

cards.q: ⚠ Is the minimal leak technique obsolete? Answer for a 202 exam.
cards.a:
⚠ Is the minimal leak technique obsolete? Answer for a 202 exam.
NOT according to Hess — Hess presents both neutrally: 'the cuff can be inflated with a minimum occlusion pressure technique OR a minimum leak technique.'
⚠ 'MLT is no longer recommended' is the HEUER / VAP-bundle position from your 203 book, NOT Hess's.
On a 202 exam, treat MOV and MLT as two named options with MOV generally preferred.

cards.q: Describe the Bivona foam cuff and its pressure.
cards.a:
Describe the Bivona foam cuff and its pressure.
A large-diameter, HIGH-RESIDUAL-VOLUME POLYURETHANE FOAM cuff in a SILICONE SHEATH.
Air is EVACUATED before insertion, then the pilot port is LEFT OPEN TO ATMOSPHERE so intracuff pressure sits at ambient level.
Lateral tracheal wall pressure rarely exceeds 20 mm Hg (27 cm H₂O).

cards.q: What does the Mallampati classification assess, and how is it performed?
cards.a:
What does the Mallampati classification assess, and how is it performed?
How EASY OR DIFFICULT an airway will be to manage, based on HOW MUCH OF THE OROPHARYNX IS VISIBLE when the patient opens the mouth widely and extends the tongue.
Part of the MOUTH portion of the three-part assessment (nose → mouth → neck) — and the mouth and neck portions are the most clinically important.

cards.q: Give the structures visible in Mallampati Class I and II.
cards.a:
Give the structures visible in Mallampati Class I and II.
CLASS I: soft palate, UVULA, FAUCES and TONSILLAR PILLARS — easiest, easy airway.
CLASS II: soft palate and PART of the uvula — generally an easy airway.

cards.q: Give the structures visible in Mallampati Class III and IV.
cards.a:
Give the structures visible in Mallampati Class III and IV.
CLASS III: ONLY the soft palate; the uvula is mostly HIDDEN — potentially difficult airway.
CLASS IV: ONLY the HARD PALATE — most difficult, high-risk airway.

cards.q: How is the Mallampati score also used in sleep medicine?
cards.a:
How is the Mallampati score also used in sleep medicine?
As an OSA SCREENING tool — a score of 3 or 4 suggests anatomical narrowing (enlarged tongue, tonsillar hypertrophy, limited airway space) and predicts increased risk of obstructive sleep apnea.
Class IV is specifically associated with DIFFICULT INTUBATION AND increased incidence of SLEEP APNEA.

cards.q: Which two other airway-assessment findings carry the same warning as a high Mallampati?
cards.a:
Which two other airway-assessment findings carry the same warning as a high Mallampati?
MACROGLOSSIA → potentially difficult intubation.
POOR NECK MOBILITY / SHORT THICK NECK → potentially difficult airway management.

cards.q: Give the neck circumference thresholds that predict a difficult airway.
cards.a:
Give the neck circumference thresholds that predict a difficult airway.
> 43 cm (17 in) in MEN and > 37 cm (15 in) in WOMEN.
Poor neck range of motion predicts difficult BAG-VALVE-MASK ventilation — not just difficult intubation.

cards.q: What is the MACOCHA score?
cards.a:
What is the MACOCHA score?
A SEVEN-ITEM difficult-intubation prediction tool, developed from 1,000 consecutive intubations and validated in 400 more.
The risk of difficult intubation and serious complications rises PROPORTIONALLY WITH THE SCORE.

cards.q: ⚠ What is the deck's warning about difficult-airway prediction tools?
cards.a:
⚠ What is the deck's warning about difficult-airway prediction tools?
Given a roughly 10% INCIDENCE of difficult airways in hospital intubations, the value of these tools is their POSITIVE PREDICTIVE VALUE — and a REASSURING SCORE NEVER EXCUSES SKIPPING A BACKUP AIRWAY PLAN.

cards.q: Name the bedside signs of a difficult airway.
cards.a:
Name the bedside signs of a difficult airway.
Large tongue · neck mass · ANTERIOR LARYNX position · decreased mandibular space · reduced mouth opening · limited neck extension · dental overbite.

cards.q: When is Rapid Sequence Intubation used, and what are its three phases?
cards.a:
When is Rapid Sequence Intubation used, and what are its three phases?
In patients who have a GAG REFLEX and would otherwise be difficult to intubate.
PRETREATMENT → INDUCTION → PARALYSIS.

cards.q: What does PRETREATMENT do, and how far in advance is it given?
cards.a:
What does PRETREATMENT do, and how far in advance is it given?
BLUNTS the anticipated ADVERSE EFFECTS of the drugs and the procedure.
Given about 3 to 5 MINUTES before the rest.
Sedatives/anxiolytics, analgesics, plus adjuncts.

cards.q: Name the three RSI pretreatment adjuncts and what each is for.
cards.a:
Name the three RSI pretreatment adjuncts and what each is for.
LIDOCAINE — historically to blunt RISING ICP; now controversial.
FENTANYL — blunts the SYMPATHETIC RESPONSE, especially in head injury or cardiovascular disease.
ATROPINE — in PEDIATRICS, to prevent BRADYCARDIA.

cards.q: What is the purpose of the INDUCTION phase?
cards.a:
What is the purpose of the INDUCTION phase?
To produce UNCONSCIOUSNESS and AMNESIA so the patient is UNAWARE of the intubation.
Purpose: SEDATION, UPPER AIRWAY RELAXATION, and an AMNESTIC RESPONSE.
Induction agents are given within SECONDS of the paralytic.

cards.q: Which paralytic is most commonly used in RSI, and what is the alternative?
cards.a:
Which paralytic is most commonly used in RSI, and what is the alternative?
SUCCINYLCHOLINE (depolarizing, FAST onset, VERY SHORT duration) is most common.
ROCURONIUM (non-depolarizing, similar onset but MUCH LONGER duration) is the alternative when succinylcholine is unsafe.
Vecuronium and pancuronium are longer-acting and used LESS OFTEN in RSI.

cards.q: How long after the paralytic do you intubate?
cards.a:
How long after the paralytic do you intubate?
30 to 60 SECONDS.

cards.q: ⚠ How do you CHOOSE among the four induction agents?
cards.a:
⚠ How do you CHOOSE among the four induction agents?
ETOMIDATE when you CANNOT AFFORD A BLOOD PRESSURE DROP.
KETAMINE when the patient is already HYPOTENSIVE or BRONCHOSPASTIC.
PROPOFOL when you want FAST ON/FAST OFF and the pressure can take a hit.
MIDAZOLAM when a SLOWER benzodiazepine onset is acceptable.

cards.q: Give etomidate's and ketamine's hemodynamic profile.
cards.a:
Give etomidate's and ketamine's hemodynamic profile.
ETOMIDATE: HEMODYNAMICALLY STABLE — the stable choice. Won't drop the pressure; use in the UNSTABLE patient.
KETAMINE: TOLERATED IN HYPOTENSION. Good in hypotension OR bronchospasm.

cards.q: Give propofol's and midazolam's profile and cautions.
cards.a:
Give propofol's and midazolam's profile and cautions.
PROPOFOL: RAPID onset, SHORT duration; CAN CAUSE HYPOTENSION. Used in conjunction with a paralytic to optimize intubating conditions.
MIDAZOLAM: a BENZODIAZEPINE providing sedation/amnesia; SLOWER onset — not ideal when seconds matter.

cards.q: ⚠ What is ketamine's emergence phenomenon — and how much does it actually matter?
cards.a:
⚠ What is ketamine's emergence phenomenon — and how much does it actually matter?
EMERGENCE PHENOMENON (also emergence reaction or delirium) — vivid, disturbing DREAMS as the patient emerges from dissociative anesthesia. ⚠ It is NOT 're-emergence' — a distractor built on the wrong prefix is easy to fall for.
Hess weighs it lightly: 'uncommon after a SINGLE INDUCTION DOSE.' It is a caution for repeated or prolonged use — NOT a reason to avoid ketamine for intubation, where its haemodynamic stability is the point.

cards.q: ⚠ Which induction-agent details are NOT in your deck?
cards.a:
⚠ Which induction-agent details are NOT in your deck?
DOSES · exact ONSET/DURATION times · ETOMIDATE'S ADRENAL SUPPRESSION · KETAMINE'S dissociative class / catecholamine release / raised ICP-IOP caution · PROPOFOL INFUSION SYNDROME.
The deck gives only the one-line clinical positioning for each agent — look the rest up in your pharmacology chapter.

cards.q: Name the two mechanisms of VAP that ETT design tries to attack.
cards.a:
Name the two mechanisms of VAP that ETT design tries to attack.
(1) DRAINAGE OF SUBGLOTTIC SECRETIONS PAST THE CUFF.
(2) BIOFILM developing INSIDE THE TUBE LUMEN that then drains or is pushed into the lung.

cards.q: Describe a subglottic secretion drainage tube, and name three.
cards.a:
Describe a subglottic secretion drainage tube, and name three.
A separate DORSAL LUMEN with a port opening ABOVE THE CUFF, connected to continuous or intermittent NEGATIVE PRESSURE, so pooled secretions are removed before they leak past the cuff.
Hi-Lo Evac · SealGuard · TaperGuard. The tracheostomy equivalent is the BLOM tube with a subglottic suction cannula replacing the standard inner cannula.

cards.q: ⚠ What is the honest controversy about SSD tubes?
cards.a:
⚠ What is the honest controversy about SSD tubes?
A meta-analysis reported a significant VAP reduction — BUT the reduction has NOT translated into DECREASED MORTALITY, these devices have a HIGH MECHANICAL FAILURE RATE, and the benefit may actually come from the ULTRATHIN POLYURETHANE CUFFS some of these tubes carry rather than the suction lumen.

cards.q: Name the other VAP-relevant hardware items in the airway deck.
cards.a:
Name the other VAP-relevant hardware items in the airway deck.
Cuff pressure 20–30 cm H₂O · the CLOSED SUCTION SYSTEM (catheter becomes part of the circuit, minimizing circuit breaks and preserving end-expiratory lung volume) · the endOclear ETT-cleaning device · JUDICIOUS saline instillation rather than with every pass · AVOIDING routine NASAL intubation, whose sinusitis increases the risk of a ventilator-associated event.
ETTs coated with ANTIBIOTICS and SILVER have shown reduced VAP in trials.

cards.q: Define VAP and give its epidemiology.
cards.a:
Define VAP and give its epidemiology.
Pneumonia developing 48 HOURS OR MORE after endotracheal intubation and initiation of mechanical ventilation.
Affects 10 to 25% of ventilated patients · ~25% of all ICU-acquired infections · mortality 33 to 50% · incidence in the first 5 days is 3%.
The single greatest risk factor is PROLONGED MECHANICAL VENTILATION.

cards.q: ⚠ Why is VAP prevention delivered as a BUNDLE?
cards.a:
⚠ Why is VAP prevention delivered as a BUNDLE?
Because NO SINGLE INTERVENTION PREVENTS VAP — they work ONLY WHEN USED TOGETHER.

cards.q: Give the four core VAP bundle elements as printed in Chang.
cards.a:
Give the four core VAP bundle elements as printed in Chang.
(1) Maintain proper CUFF PRESSURE (20–30 cm H₂O) — the most important RT responsibility.
(2) Change ventilator circuits every 7 days.
(3) Change inline suction devices and HME every 24 hours.
(4) Use ET tubes with a separate DORSAL LUMEN for subglottic secretion removal.

cards.q: ⚠ Which two printed VAP bundle items does the deck itself flag as OUTDATED?
cards.a:
⚠ Which two printed VAP bundle items does the deck itself flag as OUTDATED?
#2 (circuits every 7 days) and #3 (inline suction/HME every 24 hours).
Current guidance: do NOT change circuits on a routine schedule — change only when VISIBLY SOILED or MALFUNCTIONING, because unnecessary changes INCREASE CONTAMINATION.

cards.q: What does the deck call 'by far the simplest and most cost-effective way' to reduce VAP?
cards.a:
What does the deck call 'by far the simplest and most cost-effective way' to reduce VAP?
GOOD HAND HYGIENE or GLOVES.

cards.q: Give the head-of-bed angle for VAP prevention — and its two contraindications.
cards.a:
Give the head-of-bed angle for VAP prevention — and its two contraindications.
Elevate 30–45 degrees AT ALL TIMES.
⚠ Contraindicated AFTER NEUROSURGERY or with SEVERE HYPOTENSION.

cards.q: Name the other deck-listed VAP prevention methods.
cards.a:
Name the other deck-listed VAP prevention methods.
Use NONINVASIVE ventilation to avoid an artificial airway altogether · schedule a SEDATIVE VACATION 6 to 8 hours daily · EARLY WEANING · decontamination of the oropharynx / ORAL CHLORHEXIDINE · use an ORAL (not nasal) FEEDING TUBE · aspiration precautions · ETTs with ULTRATHIN, TAPERED cuff membranes or SILVER/antimicrobial coating.

cards.q: Give the current-practice VAP bundle as taught in the notes.
cards.a:
Give the current-practice VAP bundle as taught in the notes.
Head of bed 30–45° · daily SPONTANEOUS AWAKENING TRIAL (SAT) · daily SPONTANEOUS BREATHING TRIAL (SBT) · ORAL CARE with antiseptic solution · appropriate CUFF PRESSURE · SUBGLOTTIC SECRETION DRAINAGE · EARLY MOBILITY.

cards.q: ⚠ If you remember only four things about VAP prevention, what are they?
cards.a:
⚠ If you remember only four things about VAP prevention, what are they?
(1) Cuff pressure 20–30 cm H₂O
(2) Head of bed 30–45°
(3) Excellent hand hygiene
(4) Get the patient OFF the ventilator as soon as it is safe
The deck's summary: 'The single best way to prevent VAP is EARLY LIBERATION from mechanical ventilation whenever it is safe to do so.'

cards.q: How is VAP diagnosed, and what are the test statistics?
cards.a:
How is VAP diagnosed, and what are the test statistics?
Suspect with FEVER + LEUKOCYTOSIS OR LEUKOPENIA + PURULENT SECRETIONS + a NEW OR PROGRESSIVE INFILTRATE on CXR.
Infiltrates plus TWO of the three clinical criteria: sensitivity 69%, specificity 75%.
A modified CPIS > 6 SUPPORTS the diagnosis but is only a SCREENING tool — confirm the organism with BAL or PROTECTED SPECIMEN BRUSH.

cards.q: Contrast EARLY and LATE VAP organisms.
cards.a:
Contrast EARLY and LATE VAP organisms.
EARLY (first 48 hours): UPPER-AIRWAY FLORA — H. influenzae and S. pneumoniae.
LATE (> 7 days): RESISTANT HOSPITAL ORGANISMS including MRSA and GRAM-NEGATIVE BACILLI.

cards.q: Describe the OPA — material, path, and what it does NOT enter.
cards.a:
Describe the OPA — material, path, and what it does NOT enter.
A RIGID, HARD-PLASTIC device inserted BETWEEN THE LIPS AND TEETH, extending from the lips back to the pharynx along the natural curvature of the tongue — WITHOUT entering the larynx or esophagus.
Types: BERMAN and GUEDEL.

cards.q: ⚠ Give the single most important OPA-vs-NPA distinction.
cards.a:
⚠ Give the single most important OPA-vs-NPA distinction.
An OPA requires the ABSENCE of a gag reflex and must NOT be used in SEMI-COMATOSE or ALERT patients.
The NPA is the airway for the patient WHO DOES NOT AROUSE BUT STILL COUGHS.

cards.q: What goes wrong if an OPA is too large, or too small?
cards.a:
What goes wrong if an OPA is too large, or too small?
TOO LARGE: the tip presses the EPIGLOTTIS against the POSTERIOR PHARYNGEAL WALL or LARYNX, obstructing both device and airway.
TOO SMALL or improperly inserted: pushes the TONGUE against the posterior pharynx — also obstructing.

cards.q: Describe OPA insertion.
cards.a:
Describe OPA insertion.
Stand at the head, HYPEREXTEND head/neck, use the CROSS-FINGER technique to open the mouth, then either a 180° (ANTI-ANATOMIC) rotation or a lateral/90° rotation — PREFERRED in pediatric or small patients.

cards.q: Name the OPA's other uses and its complications.
cards.a:
Name the OPA's other uses and its complications.
Uses: doubles as a BITE BLOCK; may make BMV ventilation more effective.
Complications: REGURGITATION and ASPIRATION are the major risks; TEETH BROKEN OR TORN OUT if the patient bites down.

cards.q: Describe the NPA — material, path, and where the tip rests.
cards.a:
Describe the NPA — material, path, and where the tip rests.
PLASTIC OR RUBBER, inserted into the naris and directed along the FLOOR of the nose PARALLEL to the HARD PALATE, so its tip rests BEHIND THE TONGUE just ABOVE THE EPIGLOTTIS.
Lubricate with WATER-SOLUBLE GEL.

cards.q: Name the NPA's uses and its complications.
cards.a:
Name the NPA's uses and its complications.
Uses: BYPASS upper airway obstruction · AID BRONCHOSCOPE passage · REDUCE TRAUMA from repeated NT suctioning.
Complications: LARYNGOSPASM, COUGHING, NOSEBLEEDS; prolonged use → SINUS INFECTIONS.

cards.q: ⚠ Give Hess's headline NPA contraindication.
cards.a:
⚠ Give Hess's headline NPA contraindication.
'In patients with SEVERE FACIAL OR HEAD TRAUMA, insertion of a nasopharyngeal airway may result, in rare cases, in CRANIAL VAULT INTUBATION — this risk is greatest in patients with BASILAR SKULL FRACTURES.'
The tube can be driven THROUGH THE FRACTURE INTO THE CRANIUM.

cards.q: Give Hess's other NPA cautions.
cards.a:
Give Hess's other NPA cautions.
Improper insertion can LACERATE the superior aspect of the SOFT PALATE or damage the TURBINATES · use with caution in patients with LOW PLATELET COUNTS or on ANTICOAGULATION (excessive bleeding) · inserting an NPA into a patient draining BLOOD OR CSF may cause INFECTION · prolonged use may cause sinus infection.

cards.q: ⚠ What are the OPA and NPA measuring landmarks — and where do you find them?
cards.a:
⚠ What are the OPA and NPA measuring landmarks — and where do you find them?
OPA = corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw/earlobe.
NPA = tip of the nose to the earlobe.
⚠ NOT in the deck — standard exam content; get them from Egan's airway chapter.

cards.q: Define endotracheal intubation, and give the downsides of the ORAL route.
cards.a:
Define endotracheal intubation, and give the downsides of the ORAL route.
Placement of a tube through the mouth or nose, through the GLOTTIS, and into the TRACHEA.
Oral is the DEFAULT and FASTER route — but it is UNCOMFORTABLE, causes GAGGING, and produces EXCESSIVE SECRETIONS.

cards.q: When is NASOtracheal intubation the choice?
cards.a:
When is NASOtracheal intubation the choice?
When ACCESS TO THE MOUTH IS UNAVAILABLE, as in trauma surgery — and specifically for TRISMUS (lockjaw), ORAL TRAUMA or deformities, MANDIBLE FRACTURE, and a SHORT NECK.

cards.q: Give the advantages and disadvantages of nasal intubation.
cards.a:
Give the advantages and disadvantages of nasal intubation.
ADVANTAGES: BETTER TOLERATED than orotracheal, with potential for LESS TRACHEAL INJURY.
DISADVANTAGES: HARDER to insert · requires a SMALLER ETT → HIGHER AIRFLOW RESISTANCE · a real incidence of SINUSITIS → increased risk of a VENTILATOR-ASSOCIATED EVENT.

cards.q: ⚠ How does the EQUIPMENT differ between oral and nasal intubation?
cards.a:
⚠ How does the EQUIPMENT differ between oral and nasal intubation?
STYLET: OPTIONAL for oral — NOT USED in nasal.
MAGILL FORCEPS: optional for oral — REQUIRED for nasal.
A BITE BLOCK is placed between the teeth for oral so the patient cannot bite the tube.

cards.q: Name the signs of CORRECT endotracheal placement.
cards.a:
Name the signs of CORRECT endotracheal placement.
BILATERAL BREATH SOUNDS (auscultate along the MIDAXILLARY LINE, because esophageal air sounds transmit to the anterior thorax) · NO VOCAL SOUNDS · no airflow through the vocal cords after cuff inflation · air movement at the ETT opening if breathing spontaneously · immediate improvement in SpO₂ · a POSITIVE EXHALED CO₂ INDICATOR.

cards.q: Name the signs of ESOPHAGEAL intubation.
cards.a:
Name the signs of ESOPHAGEAL intubation.
ABSENT BREATH SOUNDS · rapidly DETERIORATING vital signs and SpO₂ · GASTRIC SOUNDS AND DISTENTION with bag-mask ventilation · ASPIRATION.

cards.q: ⚠ Give the GOLD STANDARD for confirming tube placement.
cards.a:
⚠ Give the GOLD STANDARD for confirming tube placement.
DIRECT VISUALIZATION of the tube passing through the VOCAL CORDS, PLUS continuous END-TIDAL CO₂, PLUS bilateral breath sounds and chest rise.
⚠ Feeling air at the tube is SUPPORTIVE, NOT CONFIRMATORY.

cards.q: How does the esophageal detection device work, and what replaced it?
cards.a:
How does the esophageal detection device work, and what replaced it?
It works because the TRACHEA IS RIGID and stays open while the ESOPHAGUS IS COLLAPSIBLE.
RAPID syringe filling / bulb reinflation = TRACHEA. DELAYED filling = ESOPHAGUS.
Should NOT be used if EXCESSIVE AIR is present in the stomach — and continuous WAVEFORM CAPNOGRAPHY has largely replaced it.

cards.q: Give the whole ventilation-vs-oxygenation distinction in one line.
cards.a:
Give the whole ventilation-vs-oxygenation distinction in one line.
VENTILATION = CO₂ = PaCO₂.
OXYGENATION = O₂ = PaO₂.

cards.q: Define ventilatory failure by the numbers.
cards.a:
Define ventilatory failure by the numbers.
PaCO₂ > 45 mm Hg WITH pH < 7.35.
Ventilation is about moving air in and out to CLEAR CO₂; when it fails you get hypoventilation → ↑PaCO₂ → respiratory acidosis.

cards.q: Define oxygenation failure by the numbers.
cards.a:
Define oxygenation failure by the numbers.
SEVERE HYPOXEMIA (PaO₂ < 40 mm Hg) IN SPITE OF a HIGH FiO₂ (50% to 100%).

cards.q: ⚠ Can ventilation and oxygenation fail independently?
cards.a:
⚠ Can ventilation and oxygenation fail independently?
YES — that is the whole point.
A patient can have a perfectly NORMAL PaCO₂ and a TERRIBLE PaO₂ (ARDS, shunt), or a NORMAL PaO₂ and a LETHAL PaCO₂ (opioid overdose).

cards.q: Opioid overdose with PaCO₂ 105, pH 7.14, PaO₂ 36 — is this a ventilation or an oxygenation problem?
cards.a:
Opioid overdose with PaCO₂ 105, pH 7.14, PaO₂ 36 — is this a ventilation or an oxygenation problem?
A VENTILATION problem FIRST.

cards.q: ⚠ Distinguish HYPOXEMIA from HYPOXIA.
cards.a:
⚠ Distinguish HYPOXEMIA from HYPOXIA.
HYPOXEMIA = low oxygen in the BLOOD — a blood-oxygen problem measured by PaO₂ and SaO₂.
HYPOXIA = inadequate oxygen delivery to the TISSUES — an organ problem; the tissues are starving.

cards.q: Give an example of hypoxemia WITHOUT hypoxia, and hypoxia WITHOUT hypoxemia.
cards.a:
Give an example of hypoxemia WITHOUT hypoxia, and hypoxia WITHOUT hypoxemia.
HYPOXEMIA WITHOUT HYPOXIA: a PaO₂ of 60 with NORMAL hemoglobin and NORMAL cardiac output — mild hypoxemia, hiking at altitude.
HYPOXIA WITHOUT HYPOXEMIA: a PaO₂ of 100 with a HEMOGLOBIN OF 4 — CO poisoning, severe anemia, shock.
The first patient is delivering FAR MORE oxygen to the tissues.

cards.q: Give the normal hemoglobin ranges.
cards.a:
Give the normal hemoglobin ranges.
Adult men 13.5 to 17.5 g/dL · adult women 12.0 to 15.5 g/dL.

cards.q: ⚠ Why is oxygenation monitored with CaO₂ rather than PaO₂ alone, and what is the formula?
cards.a:
⚠ Why is oxygenation monitored with CaO₂ rather than PaO₂ alone, and what is the formula?
Because CaO₂ captures BOTH the oxygen BOUND TO HEMOGLOBIN and the oxygen DISSOLVED IN PLASMA.
CaO₂ = (SaO₂ × Hb × 1.34) + 0.003(PaO₂)

cards.q: At what PaO₂ do the peripheral chemoreceptors fire — and what PaO₂ is acceptable in COPD?
cards.a:
At what PaO₂ do the peripheral chemoreceptors fire — and what PaO₂ is acceptable in COPD?
They fire when PaO₂ falls to about 60 mm Hg, triggering HYPERVENTILATION.
In COPD a PaO₂ around 55–60 mm Hg can be acceptable.

cards.q: Name the four causes of respiratory failure.
cards.a:
Name the four causes of respiratory failure.
(1) HYPOVENTILATION
(2) V/Q MISMATCH
(3) INTRAPULMONARY SHUNT
(4) DIFFUSION DEFECT
⚠ The deck's own caveat: THREE of these four are really OXYGENATION (hypoxemic) failure — not true VENTILATORY failure.

cards.q: Describe HYPOVENTILATION as a cause of failure — including the A-a gradient.
cards.a:
Describe HYPOVENTILATION as a cause of failure — including the A-a gradient.
Not enough fresh air reaches the alveoli: ↑PaCO₂ → ↓PAO₂ → ↓PaO₂, with a NORMAL A-a GRADIENT.
Causes: drug overdose, neuromuscular disease, CNS depression, chest wall disorders, severe obesity hypoventilation.

cards.q: Describe V/Q MISMATCH — its causes and its response to oxygen.
cards.a:
Describe V/Q MISMATCH — its causes and its response to oxygen.
Ventilation and perfusion both present but NOT MATCHED.
Causes: COPD, asthma, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, PE.
It is the MOST COMMON cause of hypoxemia, and it USUALLY IMPROVES WITH OXYGEN.

cards.q: Describe INTRAPULMONARY SHUNT — its causes and what it needs.
cards.a:
Describe INTRAPULMONARY SHUNT — its causes and what it needs.
PERFUSION WITHOUT VENTILATION — 'wasted pulmonary perfusion.'
Causes: atelectasis, pneumonia, ARDS, pulmonary edema.
It produces REFRACTORY hypoxemia that responds POORLY to oxygen and needs RECRUITMENT (PEEP/CPAP) instead.

cards.q: Describe a DIFFUSION DEFECT — and why does it worsen with exercise?
cards.a:
Describe a DIFFUSION DEFECT — and why does it worsen with exercise?
O₂ CANNOT CROSS the alveolar-capillary membrane. Causes: pulmonary fibrosis, interstitial lung disease, thickened membrane.
It WORSENS WITH EXERCISE because CAPILLARY TRANSIT TIME SHORTENS.

cards.q: Give the normal capillary transit time and oxygen equilibration time.
cards.a:
Give the normal capillary transit time and oxygen equilibration time.
Transit ≈ 0.75 SECONDS; oxygen usually equilibrates in 0.25 SECONDS — plenty of reserve until the membrane thickens.

cards.q: ⚠ What weight is tidal volume ALWAYS set from — and why?
cards.a:
⚠ What weight is tidal volume ALWAYS set from — and why?
IDEAL/PREDICTED body weight (IBW/PBW) — NEVER actual body weight.
HEIGHT, not weight, determines LUNG SIZE.

cards.q: Give the IBW formulas as taught in these decks.
cards.a:
Give the IBW formulas as taught in these decks.
Female: IBW (kg) = 45 + 2.3 × (inches over 5 feet)
Male: IBW (kg) = 50 + 2.3 × (inches over 5 feet)

cards.q: ⚠ Which female PBW constant do you use — 45 or 45.5?
cards.a:
⚠ Which female PBW constant do you use — 45 or 45.5?
Use 45 on a 202 exam — it is what your deck teaches and what its six worked examples grade against.
⚠ But 45.5 is the published ARDSNet constant and what Heuer prints, so BOTH circulate.
The gap is under a kilogram and moves a tidal volume by about 10 mL — the exam risk is NOT KNOWING TWO CONSTANTS EXIST.

cards.q: Work the IBW and V_T at 8 mL/kg for a 5'6" female and a 6'0" male.
cards.a:
Work the IBW and V_T at 8 mL/kg for a 5'6" female and a 6'0" male.
5'6" FEMALE: 45 + 2.3(6) = 59 kg → 472 mL → set ~500 mL.
6'0" MALE: 50 + 2.3(12) = 78 kg → 624 mL → set ~600 mL.

cards.q: Work the IBW and V_T at 8 mL/kg for a 5'0" female and a 5'0" male.
cards.a:
Work the IBW and V_T at 8 mL/kg for a 5'0" female and a 5'0" male.
5'0" FEMALE: 45 + 2.3 = 47.3 kg → 378 mL → set ~400 mL.
5'0" MALE: 50 + 2.3 = 52.3 kg → 418 mL → set ~400 mL.

cards.q: Give the typical adult STARTING tidal volumes and the initial V_T range.
cards.a:
Give the typical adult STARTING tidal volumes and the initial V_T range.
Initial V_T on initiation: 5–10 mL/kg IBW (historically 8–10; modern practice 6–8 mL/kg is far more common).
Typical adult starting volumes: FEMALE ≈ 350–450 mL · MALE ≈ 400–500 mL.

cards.q: ⚠ Give the ONE tidal volume number to remember for ARDS.
cards.a:
⚠ Give the ONE tidal volume number to remember for ARDS.
≈ 6 mL/kg PREDICTED BODY WEIGHT.
'If you remember one number for ARDS, remember 6 mL/kg predicted body weight. That's what you'll see in every ICU.'
ARDSNet strategy: V_T 4–6 mL/kg IBW with PPlat < 30 cmH₂O.

cards.q: Give the permissive hypercapnia tidal volume and the PaCO₂ it allows.
cards.a:
Give the permissive hypercapnia tidal volume and the PaCO₂ it allows.
4–7 mL/kg, allowing PaCO₂ to rise > 50 mm Hg.

cards.q: ⚠ NBRC pearl: PIP ↑, plateau ↑, and the patient has ARDS. What is the safest initial adjustment?
cards.a:
⚠ NBRC pearl: PIP ↑, plateau ↑, and the patient has ARDS. What is the safest initial adjustment?
DECREASE the V_T — NOT increase it.

cards.q: ⚠ Why is the SaO₂ on a standard ABG a CALCULATED value?
cards.a:
⚠ Why is the SaO₂ on a standard ABG a CALCULATED value?
Because the analyzer uses the OXYHEMOGLOBIN DISSOCIATION CURVE to calculate SaO₂ from a MEASURED PaO₂.
That means it ASSUMES NORMAL HEMOGLOBIN FUNCTION and CANNOT distinguish normal hemoglobin from COHb or MetHb.
HEMOXIMETRY (co-oximetry) is required for a TRUE, DIRECTLY MEASURED SaO₂.

cards.q: Define P50 and give its normal value.
cards.a:
Define P50 and give its normal value.
The PO₂ at 50% SATURATION — normally about 27 mm Hg.

cards.q: What causes a RIGHT shift, and what does it do?
cards.a:
What causes a RIGHT shift, and what does it do?
HYPERTHERMIA / increased temperature — from infection, tissue necrosis, leukemia, or any ↑ in metabolic rate and O₂ utilization.
Hemoglobin RELEASES oxygen MORE READILY to the tissues.

cards.q: ⚠ What is the clinical trap of a RIGHT shift?
cards.a:
⚠ What is the clinical trap of a RIGHT shift?
It produces a LOWER oxygen saturation at ANY GIVEN PaO₂ — the SpO₂/SaO₂ LOOKS DESATURATED even though the PaO₂ has NOT fallen.
⚠ Do NOT mistake this for a new gas-exchange problem.

cards.q: Give the memory trick for a LEFT shift and its consequence.
cards.a:
Give the memory trick for a LEFT shift and its consequence.
'LEFT = LOVE' — hemoglobin LOVES oxygen and WON'T LET IT GO.
Tissues do not receive oxygen efficiently, especially BRAIN tissue → cerebral tissue hypoxia → neurologic injury.

cards.q: Which acid-base state causes a LEFT shift, and what is the clinical rule?
cards.a:
Which acid-base state causes a LEFT shift, and what is the clinical rule?
PROLONGED RESPIRATORY ALKALOSIS — hyperventilation > 24 hours, sustained low PaCO₂.
This is the reason to AVOID a prolonged PaCO₂ < 30 mmHg unless directed by neurosurgery/neurocritical care.

cards.q: ⚠ How does CO poisoning harm you TWICE?
cards.a:
⚠ How does CO poisoning harm you TWICE?
CO BOTH REDUCES O₂-CARRYING CAPACITY AND IMPAIRS UNLOADING — it shifts the curve LEFT so the remaining O₂ is held MORE TIGHTLY and released LESS readily.

cards.q: What is methemoglobinemia, and which therapy causes it?
cards.a:
What is methemoglobinemia, and which therapy causes it?
IRON OXIDIZED to the FERRIC (Fe³⁺) state instead of normal FERROUS (Fe²⁺).
A known complication of INHALED NITRIC OXIDE therapy.
MetHb CANNOT BIND oxygen (functional anemia), and even the remaining normal hemoglobin binds oxygen MORE TIGHTLY.

cards.q: ⚠ Give the pulse-ox signature of methemoglobinemia and its treatment.
cards.a:
⚠ Give the pulse-ox signature of methemoglobinemia and its treatment.
The oximeter reads ~82–86% EVEN WHEN PaO₂ IS VERY HIGH, and the saturation DOES NOT IMPROVE WITH OXYGEN — 'REFRACTORY HYPOXEMIA.'
Look for CHOCOLATE-BROWN BLOOD that does NOT turn red on exposure to O₂; confirm by CO-OXIMETRY; treat with METHYLENE BLUE.

cards.q: Which way is fetal hemoglobin shifted, and why does that help?
cards.a:
Which way is fetal hemoglobin shifted, and why does that help?
LEFT compared with adult hemoglobin — HIGHER O₂ AFFINITY, which FAVORS LOADING AT THE PLACENTA.

cards.q: Define anatomic dead space and give the rule to memorize.
cards.a:
Define anatomic dead space and give the rule to memorize.
The CONDUCTING AIRWAYS — nose, mouth, trachea, bronchi.
1 mL PER POUND of body weight — so a 150 lb person has about 150 mL.

cards.q: Define alveolar dead space and explain the mechanism.
cards.a:
Define alveolar dead space and explain the mechanism.
Lung volume that cannot take part in gas exchange because of REDUCED OR ABSENT PULMONARY PERFUSION.
The alveolus IS VENTILATED but NO BLOOD ARRIVES — so O₂ enters but no blood picks it up, and CO₂ never gets delivered.

cards.q: Name the causes of alveolar dead space.
cards.a:
Name the causes of alveolar dead space.
PULMONARY EMBOLISM (the most common board answer) · severe HYPOTENSION · CARDIOGENIC SHOCK · CARDIAC ARREST · OVERDISTENDED ALVEOLI from excessive PEEP.

cards.q: Define physiologic dead space, and explain why V_D/V_T rises when V_T falls.
cards.a:
Define physiologic dead space, and explain why V_D/V_T rises when V_T falls.
Physiologic V_D = ANATOMIC V_D + ALVEOLAR V_D.
V_D/V_T rises when V_T falls because V_D STAYS CONSTANT while the breath gets SMALLER.
Worked: 150 ÷ 500 = 30%, but 150 ÷ 300 = 50%.

cards.q: What does a high physiologic V_D/V_T do to the patient?
cards.a:
What does a high physiologic V_D/V_T do to the patient?
It causes a PERSISTENT INCREASE IN THE WORK OF BREATHING — and when the patient can no longer sustain that WOB, VENTILATORY AND OXYGENATION FAILURE FOLLOW.

cards.q: ⚠ Give the normal V_D/V_T — and which number do you use on a 202 exam?
cards.a:
⚠ Give the normal V_D/V_T — and which number do you use on a 202 exam?
⚠ The DECK supplies NO normal V_D/V_T — only the 30% from its own 500 mL worked example.
On a 202 exam use HESS's 0.3–0.4 — Hess is this course's textbook and prints it in its Normal Values table.
Heuer's 0.25–0.35 is the 203 figure. Either way, > 0.6–0.7 predicts WEANING FAILURE.

cards.q: ⚠ Give the one-line discriminator between dead space and shunt.
cards.a:
⚠ Give the one-line discriminator between dead space and shunt.
DEAD SPACE is wasted AIR. SHUNT is wasted BLOOD.
Dead space = ventilation WITHOUT perfusion (PE, shock).
Shunt = perfusion WITHOUT ventilation (atelectasis, pneumonia, ARDS, pulmonary edema).

cards.q: Which mechanism is LEAST responsive to oxygen therapy, and why?
cards.a:
Which mechanism is LEAST responsive to oxygen therapy, and why?
SHUNT — you CANNOT push oxygen into an alveolus that is COLLAPSED or FLUID-FILLED.
That is why shunt produces REFRACTORY hypoxemia and requires RECRUITMENT — PEEP, CPAP, reopening alveoli — rather than more FiO₂.
Normally LESS THAN 5% of blood misses gas exchange.

cards.q: Define the A-a gradient and say what a large one means.
cards.a:
Define the A-a gradient and say what a large one means.
P(A−a)O₂ = PAO₂ − PaO₂ — how much oxygen was AVAILABLE IN THE ALVEOLUS versus how much ACTUALLY MADE IT INTO THE BLOOD.
A SMALL gradient = good gas exchange. A LARGE gradient = impaired oxygen transfer from V/Q mismatch, diffusion defect, or shunt.

cards.q: Give the alveolar gas equation and its constants.
cards.a:
Give the alveolar gas equation and its constants.
PAO₂ = FiO₂ × (Pb − PH₂O) − (PaCO₂ ÷ RQ)
Pb ≈ 760 mm Hg at sea level · PH₂O ≈ 47 mm Hg at body temperature · RQ ≈ 0.8 · FiO₂ = 0.21 on room air, 1.0 on 100% O₂.

cards.q: ⚠ Give the A-a shortcut equation and its restriction.
cards.a:
⚠ Give the A-a shortcut equation and its restriction.
P(A−a)O₂ = (1000 − PaCO₂/0.8) − PaO₂
⚠ This is ONLY an APPROXIMATION, valid when the patient is on 100% OXYGEN.

cards.q: Give the normal A-a gradient values, including the age adjustment.
cards.a:
Give the normal A-a gradient values, including the age adjustment.
5–15 mm Hg in a young adult on ROOM AIR, increasing with age by the rough estimate [Age ÷ 4] + 4.
Up to 100–200 mm Hg is acceptable on 100% O₂.

cards.q: ⚠ How do you INTERPRET the A-a gradient — the payoff?
cards.a:
⚠ How do you INTERPRET the A-a gradient — the payoff?
A NORMAL A-a gradient WITH a HIGH PaCO₂ → HYPOVENTILATION (or high altitude) — a pure VENTILATION problem.
An INCREASED A-a gradient → LUNG DISEASE (V/Q mismatch, diffusion defect, shunt) — an OXYGENATION problem.

cards.q: Give the ACUTE PaCO₂-to-pH arithmetic.
cards.a:
Give the ACUTE PaCO₂-to-pH arithmetic.
From baseline pH 7.40 / PaCO₂ 40 / HCO₃⁻ 24:
For every 10 mm Hg RISE in PaCO₂: pH falls ~0.06, HCO₃⁻ rises ~1 mEq/L.
For every 20 mm Hg rise: pH falls 0.12, HCO₃⁻ rises 2 mEq/L.
Worked: PaCO₂ 40 → 60 gives pH ≈ 7.28 and HCO₃⁻ ≈ 26.

cards.q: Give the CHRONIC PaCO₂-to-bicarbonate arithmetic and the timing.
cards.a:
Give the CHRONIC PaCO₂-to-bicarbonate arithmetic and the timing.
Renal compensation takes 3 to 5 DAYS.
For every 10 mm Hg RISE in PaCO₂: HCO₃⁻ rises ~3.5–4 mEq/L.
For every 10 mm Hg FALL: HCO₃⁻ drops ~4–5 mEq/L.

cards.q: ⚠ Name the two traps the deck flags about PaCO₂ arithmetic.
cards.a:
⚠ Name the two traps the deck flags about PaCO₂ arithmetic.
(1) If the pH AND HCO₃⁻ are BOTH LOWER than predicted for the PaCO₂, suspect ADDED LACTIC ACIDOSIS from severe hypoxemia — oxygenation failure feeding back into acid-base.
(2) A markedly elevated HCO₃⁻ is the hallmark of CHRONIC compensation — do NOT rapidly drive a chronic retainer's PaCO₂ toward 40, because removing the CO₂ UNMASKS the retained bicarbonate and produces ALKALOSIS and clinical deterioration.

cards.q: ⚠ Why is CO poisoning the headline example of hypoxia WITHOUT hypoxemia?
cards.a:
⚠ Why is CO poisoning the headline example of hypoxia WITHOUT hypoxemia?
The PaO₂ is NORMAL and the SpO₂ LOOKS NORMAL — yet the tissues are SUFFOCATING.
CO binds hemoglobin, so the hemoglobin is OCCUPIED and cannot carry oxygen — while PaO₂ stays normal because DISSOLVED oxygen in the plasma is UNAFFECTED, and PaO₂ is what the ABG MEASURES.

cards.q: What is the deck's blunt instruction in suspected CO poisoning?
cards.a:
What is the deck's blunt instruction in suspected CO poisoning?
DO NOT TRUST THE SpO₂. A standard pulse oximeter reads FALSELY NORMAL.
Draw an ABG, check PaO₂ and SaO₂, and confirm with a CO-OXIMETER.

cards.q: Give Hess's treatment rationale for CO poisoning.
cards.a:
Give Hess's treatment rationale for CO poisoning.
'Supplemental O₂ is useful because it DISPLACES CO FROM Hb and DECREASES THE HALF-LIFE of carboxyhaemoglobin and CO in the tissues.'
This effect is GREATLY FACILITATED by HYPERBARIC O₂ therapy.

cards.q: ⚠ Why do the decks print different numbers for the same parameter?
cards.a:
⚠ Why do the decks print different numbers for the same parameter?
They are NOT errors in the study guide — they are REAL DISAGREEMENTS between the PRINTED CHANG TEXTBOOK SLIDES and the NEWER SPEAKER NOTES and HESS DECKS.
Know both numbers, and know which one YOUR INSTRUCTOR uses.

cards.q: ⚠ What are the TWO plateau pressure ceilings in your decks, and which do you use?
cards.a:
⚠ What are the TWO plateau pressure ceilings in your decks, and which do you use?
PPlat < 35 cm H₂O on the printed Chang textbook slides.
PPlat < 30 cm H₂O — the ARDSNet recommendation, cited on that SAME slide and endorsed in ALL the speaker notes: 'Today, the accepted goal is a Plateau Pressure below 30 whenever possible.'
LEARN BOTH. < 30 is the modern lung-protective target; < 35 is the older Chang 'safe airway pressure' threshold.

cards.q: ⚠ What PEEP ceiling do the printed Chang slides give, and why do the notes call it outdated?
cards.a:
⚠ What PEEP ceiling do the printed Chang slides give, and why do the notes call it outdated?
PEEP < 10 cm H₂O on the printed Chang threshold table.
INDIVIDUALIZED — many ARDS patients need 10–15 cm H₂O or higher — the speaker notes on that same slide explicitly label the printed < 10 figure OUTDATED.
Quote < 10 if asked for Chang's printed threshold; know that current practice INDIVIDUALIZES PEEP.

cards.q: Which PEEP danger thresholds do the decks KEEP?
cards.a:
Which PEEP danger thresholds do the decks KEEP?
PEEP > 10 cm H₂O (or P̄aw > 30, or PIP > 50) raises BAROTRAUMA risk.
PEEP > 15 with intra-abdominal pressure > 20 harms the CARDIOVASCULAR, RENAL and PULMONARY systems.

cards.q: ⚠ Six different tidal volume ranges appear across the vault. How do you resolve them?
cards.a:
⚠ Six different tidal volume ranges appear across the vault. How do you resolve them?
LARGER/OLDER: 8–10 mL/kg IBW (printed PSV titration) · 5–10 mL/kg initial setting · the textbook's '< 10 mL/kg.'
SMALLER/LUNG-PROTECTIVE: ≈ 6 mL/kg PBW (modern standard) · 4–6 mL/kg ARDSNet · 4–7 mL/kg permissive hypercapnia · 6–8 mL/kg per the speaker notes.
MATCH THE NUMBER TO THE CLINICAL CONTEXT THE QUESTION DESCRIBES.

cards.q: ⚠ What do the printed VAP bundle and its speaker notes each say about circuit and HME change intervals?
cards.a:
⚠ What do the printed VAP bundle and its speaker notes each say about circuit and HME change intervals?
PRINTED Chang bundle: change circuits every 7 DAYS and inline suction/HME every 24 HOURS.
SPEAKER NOTES on that same slide: do NOT change on a routine schedule — only when VISIBLY SOILED or MALFUNCTIONING, because unnecessary changes INCREASE CONTAMINATION.
Report BOTH: recite the printed four-element bundle if asked to list Chang's elements, then add that current guidance is change-when-soiled.
Same caveat for silver-coated ETTs — not routinely used today.

cards.q: ⚠ Why is the ECMO 54% figure different in kind from the other deck conflicts?
cards.a:
⚠ Why is the ECMO 54% figure different in kind from the other deck conflicts?
This is NOT a difference of opinion — it is a COMPRESSION THAT REVERSES THE MEANING.
The DECK says 'Severe ARDS survival, when managed with ECMO, > 54%.'
HESS says 'Adult patients with severe ARDS managed IN AN ICU have a survival rate of approximately 54%' — the CONVENTIONAL-CARE COMPARATOR.
DO NOT report 54% as an ECMO survival rate. Cumulative respiratory-ECMO survival is 61%; the two trial arms were 56% (CESAR) and 60% (EOLIA).

cards.q: Give the three exam-strategy rules.
cards.a:
Give the three exam-strategy rules.
'Know what you know; and know you know it!!'
'NBRC WORLD ONLY — forget about everything else!!'
'TRUST YOUR FIRST INSTINCT WHEN YOU CHOOSE AN ANSWER!!'

cards.q: Word play: what does BRONCHOPROVOCATION TEST mean?
cards.a:
Word play: what does BRONCHOPROVOCATION TEST mean?
Methacholine Challenge.

cards.q: Word play: what do CARDIO-RESPIRATORY ARREST and CHRONIC HYPERCARBIA mean?
cards.a:
Word play: what do CARDIO-RESPIRATORY ARREST and CHRONIC HYPERCARBIA mean?
Cardio-Respiratory arrest = FULL ARREST.
Chronic Hypercarbia = CO₂ RETAINER.

cards.q: Word play: what does CONTROLLED O₂ CONCENTRATION mean?
cards.a:
Word play: what does CONTROLLED O₂ CONCENTRATION mean?
Specific FiO₂.

cards.q: ⚠ Word play: what does HEART FAILURE equate to — and what is the catch?
cards.a:
⚠ Word play: what does HEART FAILURE equate to — and what is the catch?
Heart Failure = Cardiac Arrest = Cardiac Failure.
⚠ O₂ does NOT help.

cards.q: ⚠ Word play: what does HFNC mean — and what does it NOT mean?
cards.a:
⚠ Word play: what does HFNC mean — and what does it NOT mean?
VapoTherm or Optiflow.
⚠ NOT 'HFNC' up to 15 L — that is not high-flow.

cards.q: ⚠ Word play: does DEVELOPING COPD mean an exacerbation?
cards.a:
⚠ Word play: does DEVELOPING COPD mean an exacerbation?
NO — Developing COPD does NOT equal Exacerbation.

cards.q: Word play: what is an EXPIRATORY BALLOON VALVE?
cards.a:
Word play: what is an EXPIRATORY BALLOON VALVE?
A ONE-WAY VALVE.

cards.q: ⚠ Word play: what does HOSPITAL FOR OBSERVATION mean?
cards.a:
⚠ Word play: what does HOSPITAL FOR OBSERVATION mean?
FLOOR CARE — NOT ICU.

cards.q: Word play: what do INDUCTION AGENTS and IMBALANCE mean?
cards.a:
Word play: what do INDUCTION AGENTS and IMBALANCE mean?
Induction Agents = ANESTHETIC MEDS.
Imbalance = MISMATCH.

cards.q: Word play: what do INCLUSION CRITERIA and EXCLUSION CRITERIA mean?
cards.a:
Word play: what do INCLUSION CRITERIA and EXCLUSION CRITERIA mean?
Inclusion Criteria = INDICATION.
Exclusion Criteria = CONTRAINDICATION.

cards.q: Word play: what do LIBERATION PARAMETERS and LONG-STANDING mean?
cards.a:
Word play: what do LIBERATION PARAMETERS and LONG-STANDING mean?
Liberation Parameters = WEANING.
Long-standing = CHRONIC.

cards.q: Word play: what does MAINSTAY mean?
cards.a:
Word play: what does MAINSTAY mean?
Best suited for / THERAPY OF CHOICE.

cards.q: Word play: what do NIPPV, NPPV, NIV and BiPAP have in common?
cards.a:
Word play: what do NIPPV, NPPV, NIV and BiPAP have in common?
They ALL mean the same thing.

cards.q: Word play: what do NO PURPOSEFUL MOVEMENT TO COMMAND and OXYGEN-INDUCED HYPOVENTILATION mean?
cards.a:
Word play: what do NO PURPOSEFUL MOVEMENT TO COMMAND and OXYGEN-INDUCED HYPOVENTILATION mean?
No purposeful movement to command = UNCONSCIOUS.
Oxygen-induced Hypoventilation = KNOCKED OUT THE HYPOXIC DRIVE.

cards.q: Word play: what do PBW, RADIOLUCENCY, RRT and SIMV mean?
cards.a:
Word play: what do PBW, RADIOLUCENCY, RRT and SIMV mean?
PBW = IBW.
Radiolucency = DARK AREAS (clear lungs).
Rapid Response Team (RRT) = Medical Emergency Team (MET).
SIMV = IMV.

cards.q: ⚠ Name the special precaution words that signal a trick.
cards.a:
⚠ Name the special precaution words that signal a trick.
Adequate · At least · Blunted · Except · First · Most commonly used · Most likely · Next · Nonpulmonary · Not · Observation · Precedence (importance) · Recommend at this time · Routinely · Severe · Significance.

cards.q: ⚠ Define the three precaution words that carry a specific meaning.
cards.a:
⚠ Define the three precaution words that carry a specific meaning.
HASTEN = quick to do something.
OBLITERATED = blocked out / can't see.
WARRANTS = justification for.

cards.q: ⚠ Name the four trick-word traps spelled out in the deck.
cards.a:
⚠ Name the four trick-word traps spelled out in the deck.
'Aggressive pain control' does NOT mean too much meds.
'Changes to treatment plan' and ACTUAL ORDERS are NOT the same.
'Eliminate' does NOT mean 'Filter' — LUNGS vs KIDNEYS.
'Mechanical Ventilation' = VENT OR BiPAP, not vents only.

cards.q: ⚠ Which two words are NOT the same?
cards.a:
⚠ Which two words are NOT the same?
SEVERE and SIGNIFICANT are NOT THE SAME.

cards.q: What does PISS stand for?
cards.a:
What does PISS stand for?
Pin Index Safety System.

cards.q: ⚠ Explain the doctrine of DOUBLE EFFECT.
cards.a:
⚠ Explain the doctrine of DOUBLE EFFECT.
THE 'INTENTION' IS THE DIFFERENCE.
A doctor who INTENDS TO HASTEN DEATH by injecting a large dose of morphine acts IMPERMISSIBLY — because he intends to bring about the patient's death.
A doctor who INTENDED TO RELIEVE PAIN with that SAME DOSE and merely FORESAW the hastening of death acts PERMISSIBLY.
